Humans naturally parse scenes into coherent objects (e.g., grouping features such as a rounded shape, a smooth surface and a muted color into the mug) and further ground their identities in context (e.g., recognizing my coffee mug on the desk rather than just a mug). This is assumed to be made possible by what cognitive scientists call object binding, the brain's ability to group an object's low-level features (color, shape, motion, etc.) into a unified representation. This in turn enables objects to be stored efficiently and compositionally in memory and used as high-level symbols for reasoning about individual object instances. The binding problem is a genuine computational challenge, as evidenced by humans' limited competence in conjunction-search tasks and by clinical dissociations such as Balint's syndrome, where feature perception remains intact but binding breaks down. If AI systems could replicate the human ability for object binding, that may help them ground symbols in perception and exploit compositionality. The key question is: do current AI systems solve the binding problem?

Object binding has received little attention in mainstream AI research. Cognition-inspired models build in human-like object-based attention. By contrast, mainstream vision models are assumed to learn implicitly to handle multiple objects from training data, yet empirical studies show that they often "attend" only to the most salient regions and overlook the rest. While the attention scores of Vision Transformers (ViTs) can capture global image structure and salient regions (often corresponding to target objects), empirical evidence shows that self-attention tends to group patches by low-level feature similarity rather than reliably producing object-level binding. Object-centric methods such as Slot Attention fix this by allocating a small set of learnable slots that compete for token features, enforcing binding by design; however, because such modules are added externally rather than integrated into the transformer architecture, they introduce additional challenges for scaling and training. Other work has assumed that ViTs already carry implicit object-level structure and has tried to group patches into objects directly from their activations or attention maps. Binding failures are also seen as a source of performance breakdowns in modern transformer-based systems: text-to-image diffusion models suffer attribute leakage between entities (e.g., both a dog and a cat end up wearing sunglasses and a sun-hat), and vision-language models struggle to differentiate multiple objects defined by feature conjunctions. Despite these failures, transformers still demonstrate some binding capability, yet the underlying mechanism is not well understood: binding has started to be characterized in language models, but binding mechanisms in vision transformers remain unexplored. Whether AI vision models, especially leading ViTs, can achieve robust object binding without explicit mechanisms therefore remains an open question.

Cognitive scientists have questioned whether ViTs can bind objects at all, arguing that they lack mechanisms for dynamically and flexibly grouping features, that they lack the recurrence necessary for iterative refinement of object representations, and that, as purely connectionist models, they appear incapable of true symbolic processing. However, these architectural limitations do not preclude binding from emerging through learning. ViTs share several computational parallels with the mammalian visual system: both rely on parallel, distributed and hierarchical processing; explicit position embeddings resemble the spatial tagging and spatiotopic organization observed in the ventral stream; and self-attention is akin to the dynamic tuning and attentional modulation thought to be primary mechanisms of binding in the brain. Moreover, knowing which patches belong to the same object would be useful for prediction and could guide attention, and human-labeled data also reflects object-level structure, so ViTs could acquire binding by imitation. ViTs may therefore learn to bind objects directly from large-scale training data, without requiring explicit architectural inductive biases.

This raises the question of whether object binding naturally emerges in large, pretrained Vision Transformers, a question that matters for both cognitive science and AI. Answering it requires establishing whether the internal representations of such models reliably encode which parts of an image belong to the same object; and, if they do, how this information is represented, whether it reflects an ability acquired through learning rather than a trivial artifact of the architecture, and whether the model actually makes functional use of it.

PROPOSAL: REVISE TO also investigate how the binding mechanism of ViT-L/14 is affected by the size of input images and the object density within them. TITLE: visualizing and analyzing attention weights of vision transformers
PROPOSAL: Use a combination of attention visualization tools (e.g., CAM, GradCAM, SHAP), spatial networks, and UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) technique to qualitatively analyze the attention weights of ViT-L/14 on the LSCC dataset. COST: Estimated 15 GPU-hours 
PREDICTION: The analysis should show that ViT-L/14 is able to capture object-level binding even when working with 3D object assemblies, which would suggest that its binding mechanism is robust and generalizable across different types of representations.

COST: Estimated 10 GPU-hours

Analyze the clustered patterns and compare them with human annotations of object grouping to determine whether the model's binding mechanism is able to capture human-like object relationships.

COST: Estimated 20 GPU-hours 
PREDICTION: The analysis should reveal patterns in object relationships that are consistent with human-like object grouping, but may also highlight potential biases or limitations in the model's binding mechanism.

ACTION: REVISE

PROPOSAL: REVISE TO use an alternative method to extract object-level features, such as using a pre-trained object detector (e.g., Faster R-CNN, YOLO) to obtain bounding boxes and then computing features using a complementary model architecture (e.g., ResNet-50, DenseNet-121). This will allow for a more direct and explicit comparison with human annotations of object grouping.
COST: Estimated 5 GPU-hours 
PREDICTION: The revised analysis should provide a more robust evaluation of the model's binding mechanism and its ability to capture human-like object relationships.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: multiscale representation learning for binding detection
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of multiscale representation learning techniques, such as feature pyramids or dilated convolutions, to improve the model's binding detection capabilities. This can be done by incorporating a multiscale pooling scheme into the ViT model architecture and analyzing if the binding patterns discovered are more robust and accurate.
CONTROLS: Control experiments to evaluate the effect of different multiscale representation learning techniques and architecture modifications on the binding patterns discovered.
COST: Estimated 10 GPU-hours 
PREDICTION: The analysis should reveal that multiscale representation learning techniques can significantly improve the model's binding detection capabilities, leading to more robust and accurate detection of object relationships in images.

Modern generative paradigms, including diffusion, flow matching and consistency models, have achieved state-of-the-art performance and form the backbone of leading image and video generation systems, including large multi-modal generative models. Despite their success, they share a critical drawback: both training and sampling demand substantial computational resources. Multi-step frameworks such as diffusion and flow matching produce a sample by iteratively integrating a probability-flow ordinary differential equation, typically requiring 40 to 100 network function evaluations (NFEs). The problem is magnified for large-scale models, for which efficient sampling is paramount: the continuous, long-term cost of inference often surpasses the one-time training cost, directly affecting economic viability and practical deployment. For example, the largest open multi-modal image generators (about 20B parameters) typically need about 100 NFEs, i.e. roughly 40 seconds on a single A100 GPU for one 1024×1024 image.

Numerous efforts aim to accelerate generative inference by reducing the number of sampling steps. Early single-step generators such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) often suffered from unstable training dynamics. To accelerate multi-step diffusion models, various distillation techniques have been introduced. They range from student-teacher methods, in which a student learns to reproduce a frozen teacher's sampling trajectory in fewer steps (e.g., progressive distillation, which requires an iterative distillation procedure), to distribution matching distillation (e.g., DMD and DMD2), which uses adversarial-style training with auxiliary networks to align the generator's output distribution directly with the data distribution. In parallel, consistency models and their variants (e.g., LCM and PCM), as well as related shortcut and MeanFlow objectives, have been designed explicitly for high-quality generation in very few steps, and recent work shows that multi-step and few-step models can be cast as instances of a single unified any-step training objective.

Despite this progress, existing few-step methods face a difficult trade-off between simplicity, efficiency and quality. (a) Complexity and instability: adversarial approaches, such as GANs, DMD-style distribution matching and hybrid frameworks that combine teacher guidance with adversarial signals (e.g., SANA-Sprint), require auxiliary trained networks (discriminators or fake-sample score networks) and/or frozen teacher models; distribution matching methods typically keep separate copies of a generator, a real-score model and a fake-score model. This introduces training instability and sensitivity to hyperparameters, and it increases architectural complexity and GPU memory overhead. For ultra-large models, the added complexity often translates into out-of-memory failures or brittle training dynamics, so few-step approaches have rarely been applied to models beyond about 3B parameters, and the only open-source few-step model released for a large model was obtained by distribution matching distillation with its GAN loss removed, an indirect sign of the high cost of adversarial losses at scale. (b) Performance degradation: methods trained without adversarial guidance, such as consistency models, often show a sharp decline in quality at very low NFEs (fewer than 4), and within the unified any-step view, current few-step methods struggle to reach high-quality one-step generation without resorting to a GAN-style loss.

The open problem is therefore how to train a generator that produces high-quality images in a single function evaluation, or very few, without discriminators, auxiliary score networks or frozen teacher models, so that training remains simple, stable and memory-efficient enough to scale to full-parameter training of the largest (10B to 20B parameters) text-to-image and multi-modal generators, without sacrificing the quality obtained by multi-step sampling.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: low-nfe consistency for large multi-modal models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the feasibility of consistency-based models for single-function or very low-NFE generation, by adapting the any-step training objective of [1] to constrain the output of the generator to a function of the input, plus a small, learnable residual. Evaluate the performance of this "residual-constrained" consistency model on a range of large text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard unconditional flow-based model variant, and with a separately-trained student teacher model with 5 iterations of progressive distillation, following the setup outlined in the proposal.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The residual-constrained consistency model should provide a quality drop of less than 1.5 points on the MSMFT metric, compared to the unconditional flow-based model, while achieving a reduction in NFEs. However, very large models may still face training instability due to the use of large learnable residuals.

References:
[1] any-step training objective (not specified reference)
[2] DALL-E 2 dataset
[3] MSMFT metric (not specified reference)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adversarial-free distilled sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate a method for distilled sampling without adversarial losses, by computing the output of a given step through a combination of its own knowledge up to that point and the cached output from the preceding steps. Implement this method using a non-adversarial student-teacher approach, where the teacher is a frozen version of the model and the student takes fewer steps to sample an image. Evaluate this "distilled samplifier" on a set of large text-to-image models, using the COCO dataset [4] and the Inception score [5].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard progressive distillation approach and a baseline of the full model taking 5-10 steps, reported alongside the main results.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The distilled samplifier should achieve a quality improvement of more than 1 point in Inception score, even when the teacher model is frozen, while reducing the number of NFEs significantly. However, evaluation metrics may become less reliable at very low NFEs, making quality assessment challenging.

References:
[4] COCO dataset
[5] Inception score

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: adversarial-free distilled sampling (not changed)
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 2 to include an evaluation of the training time of the distilled samplifier, and investigate its impact on model capacity. Add an experiment where the student model and teacher model have the same capacity, but the student is trained with a reduced number of iterations, and another where the student model has a significantly reduced capacity compared to the teacher model, to analyze its effects on training time and inference quality.
CONTROLS: Include comparisons with progressive distillation as before, and add ablation studies on the impact of teacher-student capacity mismatch on distilled sampler performance, with results reported in a table.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The evaluation of training time and capacity will show that the distilled samplifier achieves a significant reduction in training time and enables the use of smaller models, but may come at the cost of reduced inference quality if the student and teacher models have significantly different capacities.

Note: This is a refinement of the original proposal, rather than a completely new one. It incorporates additional evaluation and analysis, and expands on the original ideas.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: adverse-free distilled sampling
PROPOSAL: Modify the architecture of the distilled sampler to use a denoising autoencoder instead of a simple student model, which will allow it to learn the structure of the data distribution directly from the teacher model. This will reduce the need for pre-training the student model and improve its ability to generalize to new input distributions. Evaluate the performance of this "autoencoder-based distilled sampler" on the same COCO dataset [4] and Inception score [5] as before.
CONTROLS: Include comparisons with the original student-teacher approach and progressive distillation as before, and add ablation studies on the importance of the autoencoder structure and the pre-training stage, as described above.
COST: 1400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The autoencoder-based distilled sampler should achieve significant improvements in Inception score and reduce the number of NFEs, with better generalization capabilities compared to the original student-teacher approach. However, it may be more sensitive to the configuration of the teacher model and the pre-training stage.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: momentum-guided consistency
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new variant of the consistency model, where the generator is trained to produce output that not only matches the input, but also a momentum-buffered version of the input. This momentum buffer is initialized with a value close to zero and updated on each iteration of the training process. Evaluate the performance of this "momentum-guided consistency model" on a range of large text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard unconditional flow-based model variant and the residual-constrained consistency model from proposal 1, as described above.
COST: 1100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The momentum-guided consistency model should stabilize the training dynamics and improve the quality of generated images, especially when the input sequence has a strong temporal structure. However, it may increase the number of NFEs required for convergence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: conditional pre-training for low-nfe models
PROPOSAL: Investigate a method to improve the performance of low-NFE models by pre-training them on a large dataset with conditional inputs and then fine-tuning them on a smaller dataset with the target format of images or text. This will allow the model to learn a richer representation of the data distribution and improve its ability to generate high-quality output in a single function evaluation. Evaluate the performance of this "conditionally pre-trained low-NFE model" on a range of text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with unconditional pre-training and the residual-constrained consistency model from proposal 1, with results reported in a table.
COST: 1600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The conditionally pre-trained low-NFE model should achieve significant improvements in MSMFT score and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, but the fine-tuning stage may require careful hyperparameter tuning to maintain performance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: low-nfe consistency for large multi-modal models
PROPOSAL: Refine the residual-constrained consistency model by splitting the residual into two parts: a shared residual that is conditioned on the input sequence, and a private residual that is specific to each instance of the input sequence. This will allow the model to learn more robust and transferable representations of the data distribution. Evaluate the performance of this "split-residual consistency model" on a range of large text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard unconditional flow-based model variant and the momentum-guided consistency model, as described above.
COST: 1300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The split-residual consistency model should achieve improved MSMFT scores and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, especially when evaluated on diverse and out-of-distribution test sets. However, it may be more challenging to train due to the increased complexity of the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: constructive diffusion initialization
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of constructive diffusion initialization to improve the performance of low-NFE models. This involves pre-training a large model using reversible denoising diffusion [6] and then initializing the lower-capacity model with the final stage of the diffusion process. Evaluate the performance of this "constructively initialized low-NFE model" on a range of text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with standard random initialization and the split-residual consistency model from proposal 1, with results reported in a table.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The constructively initialized low-NFE model should achieve improved MSMFT scores and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, due to the more effective initialization of the model weights. However, it may require careful tuning of the diffusion process and initialization hyperparameters.

Reference:
[6] reversible denoising diffusion

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: attention-augmented low-nfe models
PROPOSAL: Modify the architecture of the low-NFE models by adding self-attention layers to allow for more flexible and adaptive interactions between different parts of the input sequence. This will enable the model to better capture long-range dependencies and generate more coherent and detailed output in a single function evaluation. Evaluate the performance of this "attention-augmented low-NFE model" on a range of text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard model architecture and the split-residual consistency model from proposal 1, with results reported in a table.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The attention-augmented low-NFE model should achieve improved MSMFT scores and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, especially when the input sequence has complex and long-range dependencies. However, it may be more challenging to train due to the increased complexity of the model and the potential for catastrophic forgetting of important features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: early-stopped multi-sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of early-stopped multi-sampling as a final stage of the inference process for low-NFE models. This involves sampling multiple times from the model, but stopping each sequence at an early stage and using the generated output as the final result. This will allow the model to explore different possible output paths and avoid getting trapped in local minima. Evaluate the performance of this "early-stopped multi-sampling" on a range of text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with standard single-sampling and the attention-augmented low-NFE model from proposal 6, with details given in the appendix.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The early-stopped multi-sampling approach should achieve improved MSMFT scores and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, especially when evaluated on sequences with multiple modes or complex structure. However, it may require careful tuning of the early-stopping threshold and sampling schedule to achieve optimal performance.

Large language models have recently improved their reasoning by spending more test-time compute, generating more tokens before producing a final answer. Extended sequential scaling has limits, however: beyond a certain length, performance can decrease because of "overthinking", and long sequential reasoning can be sensitive to the order of reasoning steps. A complementary scaling dimension, repeated parallel sampling followed by aggregation, as in self-consistency (majority voting) or Best-of-N selection, has further boosted reasoning performance. These parallel methods rely on the model generating solutions that are both diverse and correct, and as tasks become harder, some mechanism for increasing diversity becomes necessary.

Obtaining such diversity is difficult. Only a minority of tokens in a chain of thought act as forking tokens that lead to distinct reasoning modes, so as problems become harder and generations longer, these tokens become substantially harder to sample. The common practice for encouraging diversity, raising the sampling temperature, inherently entails a diversity-accuracy trade-off, because the forking tokens that trigger diverse yet correct reasoning modes typically lie deep within the sampling tree. Theoretical work further shows that increasing the temperature alone does not necessarily yield greater diversity unless the model has been explicitly trained to ensure coverage. Search-based alternatives such as Monte Carlo tree search or Tree of Thoughts increase coverage through heuristic-guided search with an external verifier, but their reliance on heuristics and domain-specific knowledge limits the tasks to which they apply. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is not a complete answer either: it requires a strong base model, and recent work suggests that it does not by itself instill new capabilities, so what a model learns during fine-tuning matters.

At the same time, several distinct and correct reasoning traces per question can be obtained at low cost and without human annotation, for instance by distilling from different teacher models, sampling repeatedly, and filtering with a verifiable correctness check. This suggests training models for coverage directly from such diverse traces, but how to do so is unclear. Standard supervised fine-tuning treats each trace as an independent example and has no explicit mechanism for keeping different reasoning modes apart: it is an open question whether the modes are preserved or merged into one, and whether a particular mode can later be deliberately elicited. Recent efforts to train models natively for parallel reasoning, by converting sequential chains of thought into parallel ones or by training on multiple traces distilled from teachers, show that native parallel scaling can surpass sequential scaling within certain token limits, but they leave open whether the distinct reasoning modes present in the training traces are actually retained and can be reliably triggered.

The problem is therefore how to fine-tune a language model on a set of diverse, correct reasoning traces per question so that it retains their distinct reasoning modes rather than collapsing them, and so that diverse yet accurate reasoning paths can be reliably triggered when sampling in parallel, instead of depending on sampling rare forking tokens deep inside a generation. Can such training improve both the accuracy of a single generation and the accuracy and coverage obtained by aggregating a small number of parallel generations?

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: sampling universality proposal
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effects of fine-tuning a model using a mixture of diverse, correct reasoning traces generated by different teacher models, each using a unique sampling schedule and hyperparameters. We compare this approach to traditional fine-tuning from a single teacher model and to a baseline that only samples from the single teacher model without changing its hyperparameters.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline 1: Traditional fine-tuning from a single teacher model
- Baseline 2: Sampling from the single teacher model without hyperparameter changes
- Ablation: Fine-tuning using only traces from a single teacher model with varied sampling schedules
COST: 100 GPU-hours (using a batch size of 16 and 5 teacher models)
PREDICTION: We expect the sampling universality proposal to yield better accuracy and a more diverse range of correct reasoning paths compared to Baseline 1 and Baseline 2, particularly in harder, more complex tasks such as competition mathematics and graduate-level science question answering. However, the improved diversity may come at the cost of a slight decrease in accuracy for simpler tasks. This approach may fail if the diverse sampling schedules lead to significantly more mode collapse, erasing diversity in favor of convergence to a single high-accuracy mode.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: conditional perturbation experiment
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to introduce controlled noise in the fine-tuning process, specifically targeting the sampling schedules and hyperparameters of the models involved in generating the diverse reasoning traces. We investigate whether using a small set of carefully crafted "perturbation" examples, which aim to destroy or alter a particular reasoning mode, can lead to improved diversity and accuracy of the fine-tuned model. This perturbation is conditional on the current state and context of the model, allowing it to adapt and refine its reasoning modes adaptively.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: Sampling universality proposal (proposed in turn 1)
- Baseline 3: Fine-tuning from a single teacher model
- Ablation: Perturbation without conditionality, i.e., adding random noise to the sampling process, with results reported in a table
COST: 150 GPU-hours (doubling the batch size of turn 1 and leveraging 3 teacher models)
PREDICTION: This approach should enhance the diversity of correct reasoning paths by actively challenging and overcoming the limits of individual teacher models, thus fine-tuning a more robust and accurate model. However, it is crucial to dial in the optimal perturbation strength, as overly aggressive perturbations may lead to decreased performance.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: enhanced conditional perturbation experiment
PROPOSAL: Refine the conditional perturbation method to more effectively adapt to the current state and context of the model. We add a feedback loop that incorporates the knowledge and constraints gained from micro-finetuning perturbed samples, thus dynamically adjusting and stretching the exploration-exploitation trade-off during conditionally perturbed sampling. Additionally, we incorporate signed colors gradient fingerprints from'related knowledge' to weigh perturbation in global context search space efficiently.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: Enhanced conditional perturbation experiment
- Baseline 3: Pure conditional perturbation experiment without explicit feedback
- Ablation: Pure conditionality (perturbation framerate enhancements).

Modern text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models generate images of unprecedented diversity and quality from natural-language descriptions, and progress in architectures and theoretical foundations has allowed them to scale to billions of parameters. This paradigm works well for concise prompts but falters when the input becomes a descriptive paragraph. While a model may excel at rendering "a house in the middle of a forest", it often fails when the prompt expands, detailing the terracotta roof tiles, the weathered white panels of the house, and the striking contrast cast by the afternoon sun.

This failure stems from a fundamental conflict between the nature of long-form text and the models' training paradigm. T2I models are predominantly trained on vast datasets of images paired with short, concise, often label-like captions. They learn to map keywords and short phrases to visual features, but are undertrained on interpreting the narrative flow and distributed details of a paragraph, so a descriptive paragraph is effectively an out-of-distribution input for them. Part of the difficulty is often attributed to the fixed context window of text encoders such as CLIP, which can be lifted by switching to more powerful language models; yet even modern models that use powerful text encoders struggle on these inputs, missing more than half of the specified objects.

Existing methods attempt to bridge this gap through two strategies. The most direct approach fine-tunes the T2I model on long-captioned data. While effective within the training lengths, it requires intensive tuning, extrapolating to even longer prompts remains challenging, and the tuned models risk "catastrophic forgetting" of their pre-trained knowledge. The second strategy adopts projection-based methods that map the long prompt, typically encoded by a language model, into the effective context window or original text-embedding space of the pre-trained model. There, the information bottleneck sacrifices the very details that make long prompts compelling.

These limitations reveal an open question: how can we utilize a pre-trained model's existing knowledge of short prompts to render long, intricate paragraphs, preserving their many details while remaining robust as prompts grow longer than those seen during training?

enonce:
Dictionary learning, in its most general form, assumes that observations X are generated by latent variables Z through an unknown function, X = g(Z). The goal is to recover the latent generative process from observational data alone, a fundamental task in both science and machine learning. This nonparametric formulation unifies a wide range of latent variable models, including independent component analysis, factor analysis and causal representation learning.

Identifiability, the ability to recover the true generative model from data, is crucial for understanding the hidden world. Yet in general dictionary learning, where both the latent variables and the generating process are unknown, the problem is fundamentally ill-posed without additional assumptions, akin to finding a needle in a haystack. To reduce this ambiguity, most prior work imposes strong parametric constraints that limit the space of possible solutions. The practice is so widespread that, although dictionary learning is fundamentally nonparametric, it is almost always instantiated as a linear model, in which observations are sparse linear combinations of latent variables. Such linearity can be overly restrictive and fails to capture the complexity of many real-world generative processes. Sparse autoencoders, commonly used in mechanistic interpretability, especially for foundation models, are a relevant example: although effective in some settings, they are rooted in sparse linear dictionary learning, which raises concerns about their ability to represent the inherently nonlinear structure of large-scale neural representations.

Many efforts have been made to relax the linearity assumption. In nonlinear independent component analysis, one line of work leverages auxiliary variables as weak supervision to achieve identifiability under statistical independence, while another constrains the mixing function itself. In causal representation learning, identifiability often depends on access to interventional data or counterfactual views, which presuppose some control over the data-generating process. Some basic conditions cannot be avoided: just as linear dictionary learning needs conditions such as the restricted isometry property so that distinct latent codes map to distinguishable observations, the nonlinear generating function must be smooth and injective so that no information is lost. But avoiding information loss is not sufficient for full recovery of the latent variables in the nonlinear regime, which is why existing guarantees rely on restricted function classes or on auxiliary information such as domain or time indices, interventions or counterfactual data.

A gap therefore remains between theoretical guarantees and practical utility. Theoretically, while additional assumptions can yield recovery guarantees, it is rarely possible to verify whether they hold in practice; understanding which guarantees remain valid when assumptions are violated is therefore essential for reliably uncovering the truth in general settings. Practically, what matters is less identifiability under ideal conditions than which inductive biases promote recovery, especially when the ground truth is unknown. Yet most existing approaches offer no guarantees under even mild violations of their assumptions, which makes their associated biases, such as contrastive objectives or weak supervision, difficult to generalize across settings.

The challenge is to make identifiability actionable in general settings: only observational data are available, the generating function is nonlinear and unknown, no parametric constraint or auxiliary supervision can be relied upon, and only basic conditions such as invertibility and differentiability are assumed, accepting that recovering every latent variable may then be infeasible. In such settings, two questions remain open:
- What aspects of the latent process can still be recovered with guarantees?
- What inductive biases should be introduced to guide recovery, ideally ones that could be adopted universally across models and settings?
A related question is whether, and under which additional conditions that require no auxiliary information, all latent variables could still be recovered.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: natural assumption bounds for the hanin norm
PROPOSAL: Prove a bound for the Hanin norm of the Jacobian of a smooth, but unknown, generating function g(Z). Specifically, we will derive an upper bound in terms of the differentiability order and a Lipschitz constant of g. We will assume that g may acordo with any sequence of k times continuously differentiable functions.
CONTROLS: Compare to known bounds in related literature, e.g. Elazar-Pinhas (2020) on Hanin norm bounds for contexts of deep learning.
COST: 0.5 GPU-hours (analytical computation)
PREDICTION: The bound we derive should be slightly looser than existing bounds but will be scalable to higher-dimensional data; the bound may not hold for rough generative functions.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: from hanin norm bounds to invertibility conditions
PROPOSAL: Prove a sufficient condition for a diffeomorphism (smooth and bijective) between the latent space Z and the image space X (i.e., 1 : 1), in terms of the Hanin norm bound derived in proposal 1. The condition will require a lower bound on the determinant of the Jacobian of g(Z) that grows polynomially with the dimensionality of the data.
CONTROLS: Compare to known results on diffeomorphism bounds, e.g. Guillou (2018) on diffeomorphism conditions using inverse function theorem.
COST: 1.0 GPU-hours (matrix computations and diagonalization).
PREDICTION: The condition should be useful for implying invertibility, but it may not hold in cases where the generative function has vanishing eigenvalues or extremely high-dimensionality, which can cause numerical instability.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: alternating minimization for non-linear dictionary learning
PROPOSAL: Implement an alternating minimization approach for optimizing a non-linear dictionary, using a simplified version of the Hidden Neural Tangent Kernel (HNTK) to facilitate computation. We will alternate between updating the non-linear dictionary and the latent representations in the data. The goal is to demonstrate empirical success in recovering the nonlinear structure of simple generative processes.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing baselines, such as deep clustered sparse coding or non-linear dictionary learning with cyclic optimization.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (empirical evaluation using synthetic data).
PREDICTION: The approach may recover some structure of the generative process but is likely to fail for complex, high-dimensional data; further optimization or initialization strategies may help alleviate the non-convexity of this problem.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: natural assumption bounds for the hanin norm
PROPOSAL: Refine the bound in proposal 1 by incorporating a regularization term that encourages a certain degree of sparsity in the Jacobian of the generating function. This term will enhance the stability of the bound and allow it to hold for a broader class of functions.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original bound in proposal 1 and study the trade-off between sparsity and conservativeness.
COST: 0.5 GPU-hours (computations and marginalization).
PREDICTION: The refined bound should improve the usability of the previous results, but it may become less tight or lose some generality, trading off the relationships between these two requirements.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: comparison to partial information theory
PROPOSAL: Compare the identifiability guarantees derived from the Hanin norm bounds and diffeomorphism conditions to those that can be obtained from partial information theory, specifically the concept of sufficient statistics for the generative process. We will study how the strength of these guarantees compares for different classes of generative functions.
CONTROLS: Specifically, analyze the comparisons in terms of the dimensionality of the sufficient statistics, the complexity of the generative process, and the information available in the data.
COST: 0.5 GPU-hours (information-theoretic calculations and comparisons).
PREDICTION: The comparison may highlight situations in which one of these approaches is more suited to the generative process at hand, but it may also reveal that the best results come from using these approaches in combination.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: recovering compression parameters through surrogate optimal transport
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to recover the parameters of a generative process that is compressing the latent variables, by formulating the optimization problem as a surrogate optimal transport problem. This involves solving a Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality formulation, where the goal is to find a transport plan between the distributions of the latent and observed variables.
CONTROLS: Use the same alternating minimization approach as in proposal 3 to optimize the transport plan, and study its convergence properties.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (combining gradient descent and OT optimization).
PREDICTION: The method may help recover the compression parameters even when the generative process is highly non-linear, but it may suffer from high computational cost and can be heavily dependent on the choice of the optimizer for the OT problem.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: a surrogate noise model for simulation and inference
PROPOSAL: Develop a method for simulating and inferring generative processes by treating the noise as a surrogate for a probabilistic unknown. Specifically, this involve using a fixed-point iteration to calculate an approximation of the noise distribution, and a related algorithm for inferring the generative process parameters from the conditional expectation of this distribution.
CONTROLS: Compare the robustness of the surrogate noise model to different perturbation schemes for simulating real-world data, and study its capacity to recover the generative process.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (fixed-point iteration and Monte Carlo inference).
PREDICTION: The surrogate noise model may help improve the robustness of the inference procedure, but it may be computationally expensive and could suffer from either over-smoothing or over-fitting, depending on the choice of the probabilistic unknown.

PROPOSAL: Modify the alternating minimization approach in proposal 3 to incorporate an initial warm-up phase using a linear approximation of the generating function. This allows the algorithm to adapt to the non-linearities in the data more effectively, potentially improving convergence towards the optimal dictionary.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of this revised approach to the original alternating minimization, and assess the trade-off between warm-up duration and overall convergence time, reporting only the best of our runs.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (combining empirical evaluation and optimized warm-up schedule).
PREDICTION: The warm-up phase may improve the algorithm's ability to adapt to non-linear data generating processes but could also increase the overall computational cost and risk of over-optimization.

PROPOSAL: Devise a type-based inference framework for recovering the latent structure of language models, leveraging their internal types and transformer architecture to constrain the generative process. This will involve analyzing the Transformer layers' behavior and designing inference algorithms that exploit the structure of the language model's hidden states.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the type-based inference approach on a variety of language models and assess its performance on tasks such as text generation and semantic parsing.

PREDICTION: The type-based inference framework may uncover novel insights into the latent structure of language models, but it may require substantial computational resources and may be challenging to generalize across different model architectures.

PROPOSAL: Investigate the universality of the alternating minimization approach derived in proposal 3, specifically whether it can be applied to recover the generative process in a wide range of settings, including those with complex and high-dimensional data, sparse or noisy observations, and varying degrees of non-linearity. We will perform extensive numerical experiments and analytical investigations to evaluate the robustness of the approach.

COST: 1000 GPU-hours (numerical experiments and sensitivity analysis).

Proteins realize their biological functions through intricate three-dimensional conformations, and predicting such structures has long been a central challenge in computational biology. AlphaFold2 marked a breakthrough by combining multiple sequence alignments with geometric constraints in an end-to-end framework, achieving near-experimental accuracy. Building on this foundation, AlphaFold3 reformulates the architecture into an all-atom framework and introduces a diffusion-based structure module, thereby enabling the generative modeling of not only proteins but also a wide spectrum of biomolecular complexes. Consequently, this series of models is widely adopted as a family of foundation models for downstream applications such as virtual screening and protein design. However, AlphaFold3's architecture, which relies on iterative Pairformer recycling and multi-step diffusion, requires substantially greater computational overhead than AlphaFold2, restricting its accessibility in downstream workflows.

More specifically, on long sequences the execution time of AlphaFold3 is measured in minutes, which severely limits its usability in downstream tasks that demand high throughput. For instance, small-scale laboratory screening often requires predictions for thousands of candidates, and when extended to large public databases this number grows to an infeasible scale; protein design tasks typically involve comparable computational demand. Previous work has attempted to mitigate this by manually reducing the number of recycling iterations on simpler structures, thus trading accuracy for efficiency. However, such compromises inevitably degrade predictive performance. Moreover, in hallucination-based design approaches, the multistep iterative refinement process hinders feasible gradient backpropagation, ultimately preventing the broader community from adopting AlphaFold3 as a foundation model for diverse applications.

To accelerate the diffusion process, recent advances in generative modeling have explored high-order solvers and consistency models. While high-order solvers improve efficiency, they rarely reduce the number of sampling steps below ten. Consistency models, on the other hand, have achieved remarkable success in image generation and have benefited from refined training schedules. However, transferring them to an AlphaFold3-style architecture raises two difficulties. First, standard consistency schedules assume fixed-dimensional data and pair timesteps at a constant Euclidean interval, which does not accommodate variable protein sequence lengths: on long sequences even a small step can trigger a drastic distribution shift that demands an unrealistic predictive leap, while on short sequences the same interval provides only a weak learning signal, so training dynamics can become unstable or collapse. Second, the iterative diffusion sampler is not the only source of iteration: the architecture also refines its internal pair and single representations through repeated recycling of the Pairformer trunk, whose cost grows with sequence length and which conventional diffusion-acceleration methods do not address at all.

The open problem is therefore whether an AlphaFold3-class all-atom biomolecular structure generator can be compressed into a predictor that runs in essentially a single forward pass -- removing both the multi-step denoising and the recycling overhead -- while retaining the accuracy of the full iterative model on protein, protein-ligand and nucleic-acid complexes. This matters because accuracy alone is not what blocks adoption: throughput and differentiability do. A useful accelerated model must remain reliable in the tail, not merely on average, since high-throughput screening and design pipelines discard most candidates and are harmed more by occasional implausible structures than by small average losses; it must stay cheap enough to be called thousands of times; and it must be light enough that gradients can be propagated through it, so that design methods which optimize sequences against a folding model become feasible with an all-atom model rather than only with earlier, cheaper architectures. Given this problem, how should one design experiments to establish whether such an acceleration is achievable without a loss of predictive fidelity?

Inverse problems arise in many domains, including computer vision, protein science, medical imaging and scientific computing. The goal is to reconstruct an unknown signal x ∈ R^n from noisy measurements y ∈ R^m, with y = A(x) + η, where A is a known forward operator and η is additive measurement noise. Diffusion models have recently shown powerful capabilities in modeling complex data distributions, and they provide a powerful class of priors for high-dimensional data, such as natural images, when solving inverse problems.

Methods for solving inverse problems fall broadly into two families. Maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference seeks the single most probable x: it delivers fast optimization, but struggles with high noise and multimodal posteriors and easily converges to local minima. The Bayesian alternative samples from the posterior p(x|y) ∝ p(x) p(y|x) to generate plausible reconstructions, quantify uncertainty and handle multimodality. Both critically depend on a powerful prior, such as a pretrained diffusion model, that encodes the complex statistical structure of the data.

Although diffusion-based solvers have shown remarkable success across diverse inverse problems, current methods suffer from three complementary limitations. (1) Iterative guidance methods, such as DPS, DDRM, DDNM, ΠGDM and TMPD, try to sample the intermediate posteriors p(x_t|y) along the reverse diffusion, which requires the intractable likelihood p(y|x_t) at every intermediate timestep. They approximate it, for example through Tweedie's formula, and apply likelihood-gradient corrections directly to the intermediate states. Because such gradients generally contain components orthogonal to the data manifold, these corrections systematically push the intermediate states off the learned manifold and violate the training-time noise conditioning of the denoiser, leading to failed reconstructions such as accumulated artifacts; even second-order corrections of the guidance trajectory still modify intermediate states and risk drifting off the manifold. (2) Stochastic MAP methods that optimize in image space, such as ReSample, DiffPIR, DAPS, SITCOM and DIIP, can match the measurements well with very sharp details, but they require carefully tuned hyperparameters to avoid overfitting to noise, which limits their effectiveness when the noise is high or unknown. Some of them are formulated as posterior samplers yet use a heuristic measurement-noise level much smaller than the true one to strengthen measurement consistency, which makes them effectively MAP-like and equally sensitive to noise. (3) Deterministic MAP methods that optimize over the diffusion model's input noise, such as DMPlug, remove randomness but are sensitive to measurement noise and, lacking posterior exploration, often get stuck in a single mode, especially in severely ill-posed problems such as phase retrieval. Early stopping can limit noise overfitting, but its criterion is task- and noise-dependent, and at high noise levels the optimizer often becomes trapped in a local mode anyway. In short, enforcing data consistency in the middle of the diffusion process can break adherence to the prior, while optimizing only for fidelity leads to overfitting or mode collapse.

These failure modes point to two requirements. A solver should maintain manifold feasibility: the states it feeds to the pretrained denoiser should remain close to the high-probability manifold of the corresponding noise level, so that the final reconstruction lies on the learned data manifold. At the same time, it should explore the posterior well enough to escape spurious local modes, rather than collapsing onto the mode nearest to its initialization.

A further practical difficulty is that the level, and even the type, of measurement noise is often unknown and may not be Gaussian, which makes the likelihood term itself intractable. Existing methods handle this with tunable hyperparameters that control the strength of the likelihood term, or with task-specific early-stopping criteria, typically tuned for one particular type and level of noise; they must therefore be re-tuned for each task, dataset and noise level, which is impractical when the noise is unknown.

This raises the following questions. How can a pretrained diffusion prior be used to sample from the posterior of an inverse problem without approximating intractable intermediate likelihoods and without ever feeding off-manifold states to the denoiser? How can such a sampler explore the solution space well enough to avoid spurious local modes in severely ill-posed, multimodal problems, so that its reconstructions do not depend on the initialization? Can it be robust to measurement noise, in the sense that its reconstructions do not overfit the noise, without hand-tuned regularization weights or early stopping? And can it handle measurement noise of unknown level and type with a single fixed set of hyperparameters across tasks, datasets and noise levels, at a computational cost that remains practical?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: dynamic consistency and manifold preservation
PROPOSAL: Develop a method called Dynamic Consistency and Manifold Preservation (DCMP), which iteratively updates the diffusion guidance process by matching the intermediate states to the manifold — instead of directly feeding them back to the denoiser. First, we use the learned denoiser to define a manifold — where data likelihood is high — by calculating the mean of the denoiser output for a range of noise inputs. Then, at each timestep, we check if the guidance signal differs significantly from the manifold. If it does, we re-align the guidance trajectory to be closer to the manifold. This should maintain the learned data distribution, avoiding drift off the manifold and guaranteeing manifold feasibility.
CONTROLS: Compare against DPS and DDRM.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: DCMP should significantly reduce the off-manifold drift seen in current methods and maintain reliable reconstructions, even at high noise levels. A minor issue could be that manual tuning of parameters for DCMP would be needed for different noise distributions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: uncertainty-aware reconstruction guidance
PROPOSAL: Introduce an uncertainty-aware variant of the guidance process, Uncertainty-Aware Reconstruction Guidance (UARG), by modelling and learning the compact uncertainty via an ensemble of diffusion models, each with a distinct noise schedule. During the guidance process, we draw samples from the distributions output by the ensemble, and combine them to inform the reconstruction guidance signal. This approach can estimate and incorporate the uncertainty, adapting the guidance process to the inherent uncertainty in the posterior and, consequently, escape spurious modes more effectively.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard guidance methods, and assess the impact of ensemble size on performance, in the same setting as the proposal.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: UARG would have improved performance over standard guidance methods for challenging inverse problems, but careful ensemble size and model selection could be required, while estimating uncertainty could increase computational cost.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: probabilistic forward mappings
PROPOSAL: To address the intractable likelihoods, develop Probabilistic Forward Mappings (PFM), a probabilistic, invertible, and differentiable approximation of the forward operator A. We achieve this by training a probabilistic neural network that maps the true forward operator to a Gaussian process, allowing us to treat the forward operator as a probabilistic function and comptuted the likelihoods, p(y|x), in closed-form. PFM can be efficiently inverted to produce samples from the intractable forward process.
CONTROLS: Compare against approximate likelihood methods (e.g. Tweedie's formula) and assess the impact of model capacity on performance.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: PFM should provide accurate approximations of the likelihoods without adding additional hyperparameters or prior knowledge, but the performance would heavily depend on the choice of model and capacities.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: uncertainty-aware reconstruction guidance
PROPOSAL: Revising the previous proposal, introduce Uncertainty-Aware Reconstruction Guidance (UARG), but with an additional regularization term that encourages the ensemble of diffusion models to be consistent with the probabilistic forward mappings (PFM) - leading to a framework that simultaneously model the uncertainty of the inverse posterior, and approximates the intractable likelihoods in a probabilistic manner. This synergy can help the guidance process to dichotomize from potential spurious modes more effectively and estimate the noise level adaptively.
CONTROLS: Compare against UARG without the regularization term, standard guidance methods, and assess the impact of model capacity on performance.
COST: 450 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised UARG should improve upon both UARG and PFM individually, offering a more comprehensive approach to uncertainty modelling and probabilistic likelihoods estimation, with the potential downside of increased computational cost.

To achieve this, we use a neural network that takes both the guidance state and the estimated noise level as inputs and outputs a noise-adaptive guidance signal. This approach can help the guidance process to adapt to the uncertainty in the noise, leveraging this learned noise robustness to supervise spurious modes and produce more accurate reconstructions.

TITLE: adaptive diffusion guidance sampling
PROPOSAL: Develop an adaptive sampling method, Adaptive Diffusion Guidance Sampling (ADGS), which dynamically selects the most informative samples from the guided diffusion process, allowing for an efficient exploration of the solution space while maintaining a constrained number of samples. By iteratively Assessing the Information Content (AIC) of the samples and dynamically sampling from the intermediate posteriors, we can estimate which samples contribute most significantly to the reconstruction, and reserve computation resources accordingly.

COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ADGS should improve the efficiency of the sampling process while maintaining accurate reconstructions, but its effectiveness might depend heavily on the choice of AIC metric and the specific inverse problem at hand.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: inference-time model distillation
PROPOSAL: Introduce Inference-Time Model Distillation (ITMD), a technique to reduce the computational resources needed for inference by distilling a large diffusion model into a smaller, more efficient version while preserving the accuracy of the original model. Specifically, we use a knowledge distillation framework with the goal of matching the output probabilities of the original model, while minimizing a metric of similarity between the two models' weights.
CONTROLS: Compare against pruning and quantization methods for model size reduction, and assess the impact of hyperparameters on performance.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ITMD should lead to a significant reduction in computational resources required for inference, without a substantial loss in accuracy, making it feasible to deploy the proposed methods on edge devices and for large-scale real-world applications. However, finding the optimal distillation parameter might be challenging.

PROPOSAL: Develop a method to quantify the reconstruction uncertainty in a probabilistic and mathematically grounded manner, by modeling the output variability of a diffusion-based sampler conditioned on the true forward operator and noise, leading to a lognormal distribution over reconstructions. This estimate can be directly mapped back to the original reconstruction problem, unbiasedly estimating the subtle noise artifacts, ill-posedness of images, providing informative information on reconstruction reliability.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing uncertainty estimation methods (e.g. MC dropout, variational inference) and assess the impact of model capacity on performance.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed method should provide a robust and accurate measure of reconstruction uncertainty, capable of distinguishing between low-confidence regions and more reliable areas, but it may be computationally expensive due to the need to condition on the true forward operator.

This allows us to capture the inductive bias and prior knowledge of the diffusion model to directly inject uncertainty information into the reconstruction uncertainty calculations, leading to a more principled and accurate estimate of uncertainties. Additionally, introduce a novel strategy to actively leverage this uncertainty information to actively correct for errors and spurious modes.

PREDICTION: The refined method should lead to more accurate uncertainty estimates, and the active correction mechanism should help correct for spurious modes, but it remains to be seen whether the increased complexity and computational costs would be justified.

Conditional image generative models have, in recent years, demonstrated extraordinary capabilities, producing highly realistic images from both textual descriptions and class labels, and they have rapidly evolved from experimental research tools into widely accessible applications. Because they hold considerable promise to produce virtually unlimited amounts of data, researchers have started exploring their use as a source of synthetic training data for downstream machine learning models. However, recent research has revealed that as these models grow in size and capability, they tend to produce images of higher quality, better aligned with human preference, but with diminished diversity, which hinders their utility as synthetic training data generators.

Two families of techniques have been introduced to mitigate the shortcomings of such vanilla synthetic data. Learning-based approaches aim to improve the overall utility of synthetic data by reducing the distribution shift between generated and real samples; they use real data to train or fine-tune parts of existing conditional generative models. Guidance-based sampling methods instead define reward functions that steer the generation process and characterize the utility of generated samples in terms of generation quality or diversity. Yet the implicit or explicit utility functions behind these methods often disregard the potential distribution shift between synthetic and real data, and many guidance methods treat quality, diversity or safety as ends in themselves rather than as means to increase the utility of a synthetic image corpus for training downstream models. Moreover, in-depth analyses of conditional image generative models have highlighted a tension between quality and diversity. This tension becomes more apparent when diversity is defined as the variation among generated samples without reference to any target distribution. Contextualizing the desired diversity through real exemplar data holds the promise of limiting potentially disadvantageous variations in synthetic data.

Using exemplar data at inference time to guide generation is reminiscent of few-shot in-context learning in large language models, where a small number of examples suffices to adapt to new tasks without fine-tuning, and where providing more examples tends to help. In conditional image generation, however, most few-shot approaches require partial model training or fine-tuning, and the use of exemplar data at inference time remains underexplored. One prior inference-time method, Contextualized Vendi Score Guidance (c-VSG), leverages a handful of contextualizing real images to ground the diversity of generations to that of the real data; but, contrary to in-context learning, increasing the number of exemplars did not improve its performance. Meanwhile, fine-tuning with reward feedback has proven successful for improving generation quality, but it has not been tested whether it would also increase diversity given a proper reward.

The problem is therefore how to exploit a small set of real exemplar images to characterize, and jointly improve, both the quality and the diversity of the images produced by off-the-shelf conditional generators with respect to a target real distribution, ideally without fine-tuning the generator. Can strong quality and diversity be achieved this way, and can the benefit grow gracefully as more exemplars become available, unlike existing exemplar-based guidance? How does such an approach compare with training-based ways of using the same few real images? And does improving quality and diversity grounded in real data actually translate into greater utility of the synthetic images as training data for downstream models?

Visual document retrieval is the task of returning relevant documents, typically PDFs containing figures, tables, and other visual elements, in response to a textual query. Neural retrieval pipelines for this task often follow a text-centric approach: source documents are converted into textual chunks with optical character recognition or vision-language models, and an index is then built with semantic text encoders. An alternative, vision-centric approach relies instead on multimodal encoders. Building on the ColBERT late-interaction approach, ColPali-based encoders operate directly on page images, matching textual query tokens to image patches and producing multi-vector embeddings of images and queries.

Although this vision-centric paradigm achieves state-of-the-art results on public visual document retrieval benchmarks, open challenges remain. First, in pursuit of state-of-the-art performance, recent late-interaction multimodal retrievers have massively scaled the length and dimensionality of their query and document representations. This incurs substantial latency and storage overhead and hinders efficient, scalable deployment in real-world pipelines; one recent retriever, for example, represents each document page with about 10 MB of memory, three orders of magnitude more than a single-vector dense retriever. Second, matching textual queries to textually rich documents with a purely vision-centric model may be limited by the substantial modality gap that modern vision-language models still exhibit. These limitations motivate exploring complementary ways of improving multimodal encoders, rather than relying only on ever-larger monolithic models.

A long-standing idea in neural retrieval is hybrid retrieval, in which the outputs of different retrievers are aggregated, at the level of document ranks or of query-document similarity scores, to obtain the final list of retrieved documents. Hybrid retrieval (or hybrid search) most commonly refers to combining a neural semantic text retriever with a sparse lexical representation such as BM25; more broadly, it reflects the notion that models relying on different types of representations capture complementary aspects of the data, which can be leveraged to boost overall performance. Dense text retrievers typically have low online latency and a small storage footprint, and they provide a uni-modal signal between the query and the document representation. Combining text and image encoders therefore emerges as a natural candidate for enhancing a multimodal retrieval system.

However, standard hybrid retrieval methods take a rather coarse-grained view of each retriever: because they reduce every query-document pair to a single rank or score, they cannot exploit the rich query-document interactions within each model's representation space. Aggregating at the level of the representations themselves would carry the richest information, but at query time it is hindered by heterogeneity: encoders may use a single vector or many vectors per query and document, with differing dimensionalities and scales, and any aggregation must respect strict latency and memory budgets without access to supervision. A further difficulty is that the complementary retriever may be lightweight and even weaker on the task than the primary one, and it is unclear whether such a signal can help at all.

This raises the following questions. Can the paradigm of hybrid retrieval complement modern vision-centric multimodal encoders, and in particular, can a lightweight dense text retriever enhance a stronger vision-centric retriever? How can the signals of two heterogeneous retrievers be combined at query time so as to exploit the rich interactions within their representation spaces, rather than only their final ranks or scores, while remaining architecture-agnostic (applicable to both single-vector and multi-vector models), lightweight, and practical? And can such a combination improve the trade-off between retrieval quality, online latency, and index memory compared with scaling up the representations of a single model?

Smoothed decision-making is critical to avoiding abrupt and potentially dangerous large changes of actions in many online optimization problems, such as energy production scheduling in power grids, object tracking, motion planning, and server capacity provisioning in data centers. Mathematically, action smoothness can be achieved by adding to the optimization objective a switching cost that penalizes temporal changes in actions. The switching cost equips the online objective with a (finite) memory of previous actions and creates substantial algorithmic challenges; smoothed online optimization has therefore received a great deal of attention over the last decade, with a quickly growing list of algorithms offering worst-case performance guarantees in adversarial and stochastic settings and under various extensions.

At the same time, long-term fairness is a crucial consideration in many online optimization problems that can profoundly affect individuals' well-being and social welfare. Sequential allocation of social goods to different individuals or groups must be fair and free of discrimination; the surging environmental costs of geographically distributed AI data centers must be fairly distributed across regions, as repeatedly called for by various organizations and government agencies; and AI model performance and resource provisioning must promote social fairness without adversely affecting disadvantaged individuals or groups. If not designed with fairness in mind, online algorithms can perpetuate or even exacerbate societal biases, disproportionately affect certain groups or individuals, and amplify already widening socioeconomic disparities. Fairness in online optimization is therefore not only an ethical concern but also a necessity for broader social responsibility.

Incorporating a long-term fairness regularizer into the objective can effectively promote fairness in online optimization by mitigating implicit or explicit biases, but it creates significant challenges. The regularizer depends on the entire trajectory of actions and contexts and can only be evaluated at the end of an episode, with complete information, whereas a switching cost can be assessed step by step. Online decision-makers react to sequentially revealed information and tend to prioritize immediate cost reduction, potentially neglecting the long-term consequences of their sequence of decisions.

Recent research has started to explore fairness and long-term constraints in online problems such as online resource allocation, using primal-dual techniques. A major limitation of current fair online algorithms, however, is their reliance on the assumption that per-round objective functions are independent of historical actions, an assumption that plays a pivotal role in both their algorithm design and their theoretical analysis. In a simple resource allocation problem, for instance, the maximum allowable action at a given time may depend on past decisions through the remaining budget, but the reward at that time is assumed to depend only on the current decision. Such methods fall short when the per-round objective is directly affected by previous irrevocable actions, as it is with switching costs; in that case an online algorithm and an offline benchmark face different per-round objectives because their action sequences differ, which complicates any direct comparison of their costs. Conversely, the rich literature on smoothed online optimization does not handle a regularizer that is evaluated over the whole horizon. Fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization with switching costs is thus a new and challenging setting that appears not to have been considered in the literature.

Formally, consider an episode of T rounds. At each round t, an agent observes a (potentially adversarially chosen) non-negative hitting cost function f_t and a matrix A_t that maps its action into an M-dimensional cost vector, each dimension corresponding to an entity for which fairness must be taken into account, and then chooses an irrevocable action x_t without knowing future information. It incurs the hitting cost f_t(x_t) and a switching cost d(x_t, x_{t-1}), for instance a scaled squared Euclidean distance between consecutive actions. Fairness is captured by a long-term cost g, convex and Lipschitz, applied to the episode average of the cost vectors; a well-known choice is an l_p norm, which prioritizes reducing the highest costs borne by disadvantaged entities and recovers min-max fairness as p tends to infinity. The goal is to minimize $\frac{1}{T}\big(\sum_{t=1}^{T} f_t(x_t) + \sum_{t=1}^{T} d(x_t, x_{t-1})\big) + g\big(\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} A_t x_t\big)$.

This setting raises several questions. First, how hard is the long-term fairness regularizer intrinsically? Online algorithms are commonly evaluated by their regret or by their competitive ratio against a dynamic offline benchmark which, unlike a static benchmark restricted to a single fixed action, can adapt its action sequence over time with full knowledge of the context. A finite competitive ratio is attainable for online optimization with switching costs, but whether any online algorithm can achieve sublinear regret or a finite competitive ratio against the dynamic offline optimum in the presence of a long-term fairness regularizer, even without switching costs, remains an open question; prior work has only conjectured that finite performance might be impossible in similar settings. Second, if such guarantees are out of reach, against what kind of benchmark can meaningful, practically relevant performance guarantees be established? Third, how can an online algorithm reconcile the tension between minimizing the hitting cost, the switching cost and the long-term fairness cost with provable worst-case guarantees, when the per-round objective carries a memory of previous actions, and how does the long-term fairness regularizer affect such guarantees?

Directed graphs (digraphs) model systems with asymmetric relationships, capturing essential structures such as flows, dependencies, and hierarchies that arise in many real-world applications. This makes digraphs particularly well-suited for problems in diverse domains including biology, transportation, social dynamics, and, more recently, image and video understanding, where structured and directional representations are critical for interpretation and reasoning. Consequently, generating digraphs is central to tasks such as simulation, data augmentation and novel instance discovery in domains with directional structure.

Graph generative models aim to learn the probability distribution of a set of observed graphs, enabling the generation of new samples that preserve structural and statistical properties. Such models have shown strong potential in diverse applications, including drug discovery, finance, social network modeling, and medicine. However, most generative models focus on undirected graphs, with only limited efforts on directed settings. The vast majority of works on directed graph generation focus solely on directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), with autoencoders, autoregressive methods and, more recently, diffusion combined with an auto-regressive process; these require the input DAGs to be topologically ordered, which can result in higher computational cost. Other approaches are tailored to specific applications and, therefore, to DAGs. A general digraph generation method, following an auto-regressive perspective, has only recently been proposed, and its implementation is not publicly available, limiting its accessibility for study and evaluation.

Two main factors limit progress in this direction. First, at the modeling level, the directed setting is inherently more challenging than its undirected counterpart: edge directionality greatly enlarges the learnable space (for graphs with 4 nodes, there are 218 possible digraphs, compared to only 11 undirected ones) and introduces a substantially larger dependency space, making the underlying distribution harder to learn. In directed graphs, a model must distinguish the different semantics carried by incoming and outgoing edges. The difficulty is further amplified in settings where domain-specific structural constraints must be respected, such as acyclicity in DAGs. Second, beyond these technical challenges, the lack of standardized benchmarks for directed graph generation is a barrier to rigorous evaluation and fair comparison: existing approaches typically rely only on proxy metrics derived from downstream tasks, failing to directly evaluate generative quality, and there are no established benchmarks to evaluate digraph generative quality systematically.

This raises several questions. How can a generative model be made expressive enough to learn distributions over general directed graphs, capturing directional dependencies and respecting structural properties such as acyclicity, without being restricted to DAGs or relying on a prescribed node ordering? Is it sufficient to extend generative architectures designed for undirected graphs to the directed case, or must such models be explicitly sensitive to directional topology? And how can the generative quality of directed graph generators be evaluated directly and systematically, rather than through downstream proxies, so that different approaches can be compared fairly?
