In cloud services, Internet of Things deployments and monitoring systems, data are often represented as univariate time series (UTS), in which each timestamp records a single variable. Anomalies arise, for instance, when a website is subject to malicious attacks or experiences excessive server load, and they are typically reflected in UTS derived from traffic and system-load monitoring. Missed or delayed detection of such events can have severe consequences. Anomalies in UTS are usually divided into two types: point anomalies, which are abrupt deviations (either global or contextual), and segment anomalies, which reflect more subtle shifts in trends or periodic patterns.

Formally, given observations x_0, x_1, ..., x_t with anomaly labels c_0, c_1, ..., c_t, where c_i = 0 marks a normal point and c_i = 1 an anomaly, the goal of UTS anomaly detection is to determine c_i for each point x_i from the history x_0, ..., x_{i-1} that precedes it, without access to future points. Because labels are scarce in practice and supervised detectors generalize poorly under label scarcity or distribution shift, unsupervised approaches have become the dominant paradigm. Reconstruction-based and prediction-based methods both model normal behavior and flag anomalies by comparing reconstructed or predicted values with the actual observations. Reconstruction-based techniques try to map abnormal segments to a normal space, but the lack of ground truth for anomalies leads to poor reconstruction and degraded performance, and they treat time windows independently, ignoring temporal dependencies. Prediction-based methods built on deep sequence models such as Transformers perform strongly on multivariate time series, where they can model complex dependencies; in UTS, however, each timestamp contains only one value, which restricts the representation of temporal context and leads to suboptimal performance.

In particular, existing detectors struggle with two kinds of subtle anomalies that remain largely undetected: (1) small point anomalies, short-term spikes that look normal when viewed over longer windows; and (2) slowly rising anomalies, gradual segment-level deviations from periodic patterns. These misses stem from limitations of current designs: for example, a frequency-conditioned reconstruction approach focuses on frequency components rather than local dependencies and fails to capture subtle point anomalies or gradual segment anomalies, while a recent prediction approach uses timing information but ignores frequency details.

Detecting these anomalies raises three challenges. First, local trends matter more than absolute values: the absolute magnitude of a change is insufficient to decide whether a point is anomalous. In one series, changes between 0.5 and 1 may be abnormal, whereas in another, similar changes are normal and only variations exceeding 5 are anomalous; what counts as abnormal depends on the value distribution and change patterns within a short local window. Second, periodicity evolves rather than staying static: time series exhibit evolving trends and periodicity, and periodicity varies over time and across datasets, including changes in period length and frequency. Without future points, distinguishing slow anomalies from normal periodic changes is difficult, and methods that focus only on the adjacent historical period neglect this evolution; modeling periodicity that is both dynamic and heterogeneous is hard. Third, normal patterns must be learned amid anomalies and noise: real-world series contain long-term noise and sudden anomalies, both of which hinder the learning of normal patterns. Noise introduces significant fluctuations that make it difficult to fit the underlying normal behavior, and the lack of ground-truth labels for anomaly positions prevents a model from computing reliable training losses.

The question is therefore how an unsupervised detector for univariate time series, relying only on past observations, can capture both local trends and the evolution of periodic patterns, while learning normal behavior robustly from training data contaminated by noise and unlabeled anomalies, so that small point anomalies and slowly rising anomalies are detected accurately and promptly.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: local trend aware reconstruction approach
PROPOSAL: Introduce a reconstruction-based method that models normal behavior by learning local trends in the univariate time series. Instead of focusing on global frequency components, the method will capture local patterns using a Gaussian Process regression model with a custom kernel that takes into account the local context of each point. This will allow it to more effectively identify small point anomalies that might be missed by frequency-conditioned reconstruction approaches.
CONTROLS: Compare against a frequency-conditioned reconstruction approach (e.g., the recent 1D-STFT-DCN method) and an unsupervised baseline (e.g., Autoencoders on UTS datasets from ) across a suite of real-world datasets, including ECG and web service KPI monitoring.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach will demonstrate strong detection performance on small point anomalies, while its reconstruction-based design will also allow it to learn effective normal patterns in the presence of noise and labeled anomalies; however, it might struggle with capturing subtle changes in evolving periodic patterns without additional information.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: periodicity evolution aware sequence model
PROPOSAL: Design a variant of the transformer-based sequence model, specifically geared towards univariate time series, that incorporates a novel self-attention mechanism to capture the evolution of periodic patterns across different time windows. This is achieved by adding an auxiliary periodicity-evolution head that learns to predict the shift in periodic patterns between adjacent windows, thereby enabling the detector to learn dynamic periodicity and accommodate changes in evolving trends and periodicity.
CONTROLS: Compare against a traditional transformer-based sequence model with no periodicity-aware components, and a state-of-the-art prediction-based approach (e.g., ) designed for UTS on web service KPI monitoring and air-temperature dataset.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The periodicity-evolution aware model will demonstrate improvements in detecting slowly rising anomalies by accurately modeling and capturing evolving periodic patterns; however, it may be computationally expensive and require careful tuning to balance periodicity and local trend detection.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: revise 1: local trend-aware reconstruction approach with periodicity-aware extension
PROPOSAL: Refine the local trend-aware reconstruction approach by adding a periodicity-aware component that can capture the periodic patterns present in the time series. This can be achieved by incorporating a periodic component into the Gaussian Process regression model, allowing the detector to learn the local trends while also taking into account the periodic patterns and their evolution over time. This integrated approach aims to improve the ability of the detector to capture both local trends and the evolving periodic patterns.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original local trend-aware reconstruction approach and the periodicity evolution aware sequence model, as well as the same frequency-conditioned reconstruction approach (1D-STFT-DCN method).
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised local trend-aware reconstruction approach with periodicity-aware extension will provide a sweet spot between the strengths of the original reconstruction-based method and the sequence model, striking a balance between detecting local trends and evolving periodic patterns; however, it may require careful hyperparameter tuning to optimize performance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: local trend aware reconstruction approach with noise robustness
PROPOSAL: Modify the local trend-aware reconstruction approach to be more robust to noise in the time series data. This can be done by incorporating a noise-robust kernel into the Gaussian Process regression model or using a loss function that is less sensitive to noisy observations. Additionally, consider using a robust regression method, such as Huber regression, to reduce the influence of outliers and improve the model's ability to learn normal patterns in the presence of noise and unlabeled anomalies.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original local trend-aware reconstruction approach and the revised local trend-aware reconstruction approach with periodicity-aware extension, as well as the same unsupervised baseline (Autoencoders on UTS datasets). Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: no additional cost
PREDICATION: The revised local trend-aware reconstruction approach with noise robustness will be more effective in detecting small point anomalies, especially those that occur in long-term noisy series, while learning effective normal patterns; however, it might struggle with capturing the specifics of subtle changes in noisy or periodic patterns without additional smoothing techniques.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: anomaly encoder-based denoising autoencoder
PROPOSAL: Design a denoising autoencoder (DAE) that uses an anomaly encoder to learn noise and normal patterns in the univariate time series data. The anomaly encoder maps the input to a noise representation, where noise is represented as abnormality in the sequence. By training the DAE to reconstruct the input from its noise representation, the model learns to discard noise and identify normal patterns in the data, allowing for effective anomaly detection in noisy series. This approach will be useful in capturing local trends and normal patterns in the presence of high levels of noise.
CONTROLS: Compare against a traditional denoising autoencoder without an anomaly encoder and the local trend-aware reconstruction approach with noise robustness, as well as a state-of-the-art anomaly detection method (e.g., ) on ECG and air-temperature dataset.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The anomaly encoder-based DAE will perform well on detecting small point anomalies in noisy series, while the noise removal operation could also unveil potential slowly rising anomalies; however, it may be computationally expensive and sensitive to hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: incremental learning for dynamic periodicity
PROPOSAL: Develop an incremental learning method for periodicity-aware sequence models, allowing the model to adapt to changes in periodic patterns over time. This can be achieved by maintaining a separate model for each period or time window and updating these models incrementally as new data becomes available. By leveraging the periodicity-aware sequence model as a subroutine, the incremental learning method can continually refine its understanding of the periodic patterns and adapt to changing conditions, making it more effective in detecting slowly rising anomalies.
CONTROLS: Compare against a traditional periodicity-aware sequence model trained on fixed-time windows and the periodicity evolution aware sequence model, as well as an unsupervised anomaly detection algorithm (e.g., , adapted for real-time incremental learning) on dynamic web service KPI monitoring and ECG dataset.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The incremental learning method for dynamic periodicity will allow the model to keep up with the evolving trends and periodic patterns, leading to improved detection performance for slowly rising anomalies; however, it may require careful implementation to manage memory and computational resources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: graph-based anomaly propagation
PROPOSAL: Design a graph-based approach that aggregates information from multiple time series to identify anomalies in individual series. This can be achieved by representing each time series as a node in a graph and establishing edges between nodes that share similar trends or patterns. Anomaly detection is then performed by propagating abnormality scores from affected nodes to their neighbors, allowing for collaborative anomaly detection and improved identification of small point anomalies, especially those occurring in series with limited sampling rates or sparse data.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline series-by-series approach using the local trend-aware reconstruction approach with noise robustness and an anomaly encoder-based denoising autoencoder, as well as a state-of-the-art graph-based anomaly detection algorithm (e.g., ) on web service KPI monitoring and ECG dataset.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The graph-based anomaly propagation approach will leverage interconnected patterns across time series to improve the detection of small point anomalies, particularly in cases where a single series has limited sampling rates; however, it may be vulnerable to the influence of noisy series and require careful graph construction.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: anomaly encoder-based denoising autoencoder with contextualized noise representation
PROPOSAL: Refine the anomaly encoder-based denoising autoencoder by introducing a contextualized noise representation that captures the local trends and periodic patterns present in the time series data. This can be achieved by incorporating a periodic component into the noise representation or by considering the output of the periodicity evolution aware sequence model as input to the encoder. By learning a contextualized representation of noise, the model can more effectively discard noise and identify normal patterns in the data, allowing for improved anomaly detection in noisy series.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original anomaly encoder-based denoising autoencoder and the graph-based anomaly propagation approach, as well as a baseline denoising autoencoder without an anomaly encoder. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: no additional cost
PREDICTION: The revised anomaly encoder-based denoising autoencoder with contextualized noise representation will improve the detection of small point anomalies in noisy series by better capturing the underlying local trends and periodic patterns; however, it may require careful hyperparameter tuning to balance the impacts of noise and contextual information.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: time-series anomaly chains
PROPOSAL: Develop a methodology to identify chains of anomalous time points, where the detection of an anomaly at one point increases the likelihood of anomalies at subsequent points. This can be achieved by applying a statistical analysis or machine learning method to the sequence of anomaly scores. By identifying these chains, the model can provide more comprehensive insights into the behavior of the system, allowing for the detection of more subtle and long-term anomalies.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline approach that only identifies single-point anomalies and the graph-based anomaly propagation approach, as well as a state-of-the-art algorithm for anomaly pattern recognition (e.g., ) on web service KPI monitoring and ECG dataset.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The time-series anomaly chains methodology will uncover valuable insights into the behavior of the system by revealing characteristic patterns of anomalies; however, it may require careful analysis of the anomaly scores to avoid false positives and ensure robust detection.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: hugging face-based ensemble models
PROPOSAL: Utilize Hugging Face's Transformers library to create ensemble models that combine the strengths of the individual approaches (local trend-aware reconstruction, periodicity evolution aware sequence model, anomaly encoder-based denoising autoencoder with contextualized noise representation, incremental learning for dynamic periodicity, and graph-based anomaly propagation) and improve overall anomaly detection performance. This can be achieved by stacking or concatenating individual models, fine-tuning them for anomaly detection, or leveraging pre-trained models as subcomponents. By creating an ensemble model, the approach can benefit from the complementary information and strengths of the individual models.
CONTROLS: Compare against each individual approach and an ensemble of multiple individual approaches (e.g., using stacking or bagging techniques) across multiple datasets from web service KPI monitoring, ECG, and environmental air-temperature monitoring. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The ensemble models will leverage the collective strengths of the individual approaches to achieve improved anomaly detection performance and robustness, especially in scenarios with varying patterns and degrees of noise; however, carefully selecting and integrating the models will require innovative analysis to ensure the ensemble performs effectively and avoids overfitting.

Diffusion models have catalyzed an enormous research wave in generative modeling. Conceptually, they couple a stochastic forward noising process with a reverse-time ordinary or stochastic differential equation whose density evolution is governed by the Fokker–Planck equation, a linear second-order parabolic partial differential equation. Learning consists of estimating time-indexed scores or velocities and integrating them for sampling. A growing body of work also explores probability-flow backbones: deterministic flows trained via flow matching and its optimal-transport variants, rectified flows, and stochastic interpolants that bridge flows and diffusion.

Yet the partial-differential-equation lens on generative modeling need not be limited to Fokker–Planck. Other classical linear second-order equations, elliptic and hyperbolic, offer different structural advantages but remain comparatively underexplored; Poisson flow models, for instance, recast generation through electrostatics-inspired fields. On the hyperbolic side, recent work has replaced the Fokker–Planck equation with the telegrapher equation (the one-dimensional damped wave equation) and its stochastic Kac representation, in which a particle moves at constant speed and reverses direction at the jump times of a Poisson process. A network is fit by regression to a closed-form conditional velocity of this process and integrated backward in time from noise to data, with each image coordinate following an independent one-dimensional Kac process. The resulting probability flows have a finite propagation speed: starting from localized mass, the distribution remains inside a causal cone, the flow is Lipschitz in Wasserstein distance, and velocity norms, hence kinetic energy, stay globally bounded. Diffusion, by contrast, spreads mass instantaneously with effectively infinite propagation speed, which manifests as stiff, rapidly growing reverse-time velocities and as ill-conditioned fields with Lipschitz blow-ups near the end of denoising; indeed, diffusion arises as a limit of the damped wave equation as the damping and the propagation speed tend to infinity. A finite speed cap thus acts like a built-in stability constraint: trajectories cannot accelerate without bound, and late-time integration is less stiff.

So far, however, these finite-speed flows have been developed only for unconditional image generation, and they lack two ingredients that make diffusion-style generators practical. The first is guided conditional generation. Classifier-free guidance, which mixes conditional and unconditional predictions to steer samples toward a condition, is a standard tool for diffusion models, but it is unclear whether guidance can be carried over to finite-speed dynamics without losing the bounded-energy property that distinguishes them from diffusion, whose kinetic energy can diverge near data time. The second is fast sampling. Practical generators are expected to deliver high-quality samples with very few network evaluations, yet it is unknown whether finite-speed flows can be brought down to a handful of sampling steps, or even a single one, without a severe loss of sample quality, and whether their finite-speed, bounded-energy structure can explain, and ideally guarantee, that a coarse few-step sampler stays close to the full sampling trajectory.

This leads to three questions. How can guided conditional generation be built on finite-speed Kac flows while provably keeping the guided velocity field at finite kinetic energy? How can such flows be turned into few-step, ideally one-step, image generators that preserve both sample quality and the numerical stability benefits of finite-speed probability flows? And can the finite-speed structure provide theoretical guarantees that a few-step sampler remains close to the full flow along the entire generation path, not only in its final samples? Answering them would show whether hyperbolic, finite-speed dynamics can be a credible alternative to diffusion for fast image generation.

Predicting the intermediate trajectories between an initial and a target distribution is a central problem in generative modeling. Tasks such as crowd navigation or modeling cell-state transitions under perturbation involve learning a transport map between two empirically observed endpoint distributions, rather than from the noisy prior required by denoising diffusion and flow matching. The Schrödinger bridge problem seeks an optimal stochastic map between a pair of endpoint distributions that minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence to an underlying reference process. Schrödinger bridge matching solves this problem by learning a drift field that matches a mixture of conditional stochastic bridges between endpoint pairs, and generalized Schrödinger bridge formulations add a non-linear state cost, interpretable as the potential energy of the system, to describe systems whose optimal dynamics are not captured by the standard squared-Euclidean cost of entropic optimal transport.

These approaches have important limitations. They typically assume conservation of mass from the initial to the target distribution, which fails to capture dynamical population behaviors such as the growth and destruction of mass that are common in single-cell population data. They also model a single stochastic path: samples are transported from the initial distribution to the target through independent stochastic trajectories, without accounting for branching dynamics, so these methods are inherently limited to unimodal transitions and cannot capture branched or divergent evolution from a common origin to multiple distinct modes. When a system follows a branched trajectory that diverges toward several target modes, approximating the multi-modal target by simulating many independent particles is susceptible to mode collapse, with particles concentrating on dominant high-density modes or traversing only low-energy intermediate paths. Even when particles do reach several modes, counting where they end up gives only an indirect estimate of how mass splits across trajectories: it neither describes how mass is distributed over time nor reveals when the population begins to diverge toward different targets.

Yet branching is central to many real-world systems. When a homogeneous cell population undergoes a perturbation such as a gene knockout or a drug treatment, it frequently undergoes fate bifurcation, splitting into multiple phenotypically distinct outcomes or committing to divergent cell fates. Such trajectories are observable in single-cell RNA sequencing data, where each subpopulation evolves independently and grows or contracts along its trajectory toward a distinct terminal state. Predicting how cell states change after a perturbation is a crucial problem for therapeutic design, but the intermediate states between the unperturbed and perturbed populations are usually unknown, and intermediate snapshots are often sparse or unavailable. Related work leaves this gap open. Branched dynamics have been explored for optimal transport and Brownian motion, but matching one initial distribution to multiple terminal distributions through stochastic bridges has not been explicitly formulated; branching Brownian motion, for instance, describes particles that proliferate in number rather than a fixed population whose mass divides among distinct trajectories with their own terminal states. Some unbalanced transport methods that model growth rely on reconstruction losses on observed intermediate snapshots and fail to learn meaningful trajectories when these snapshots are unavailable, and existing models of perturbation responses either predict only the terminal perturbed state or model a single unimodal trajectory between one pair of boundary distributions.

This raises the following questions. Given samples from an initial population and from a terminal population that has split into several distinct modes, each holding a known share of the total mass, how can one learn a set of energy-minimizing stochastic bridges that represent the divergence of the population from a common origin into multiple distinct terminal states? How can such a model determine when and where branching occurs, and how mass is redistributed among branches over time, so that each terminal mode receives its observed share while trajectories follow low-energy paths under a task-specific state cost? And can such branched dynamics be recovered from initial and terminal snapshots alone, without intermediate-time supervision and without the mode collapse that affects single-path bridge matching?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: branched schrödinger bridge formulation
PROPOSAL: propose a branched Schrödinger bridge formulation, which extends the Schrödinger bridge problem to incorporate a time-dependent branching process, where the branching rate depends on the current state and branching contexts. The formulation aims to learn multiple energy-minimizing stochastic bridges simultaneously, each capturing a distinct terminal mode of the target distribution.
CONTROLS: compare against Schrödinger bridge matching, and evaluate the performance of the branched formulation on cell differentiation and drug perturbation response modeling tasks, reported alongside the main results.
COST: 100 GPU-hours ( establish a baseline formulation and perform small-scale experiments)
PREDICTION: expect improved performance on tasks that involve branching and divergence, but initial experiments may require adjustments to the branching process model to stabilize the optimization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: stochastic bridge-splitting algorithm
PROPOSAL: develop a stochastic bridge-splitting algorithm to initialize the branched Schrödinger bridge formulation with multiple stochastic bridges, either by uniformly sampling from the initial distribution or based on domain-specific knowledge. This algorithm aims to bypass the challenge of simultaneously learning multiple stochastic bridges from scratch and provides a way to leverage the knowledge of cellular biologists and experts in the field.
CONTROLS: evaluate the algorithm's performance on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, and compare it against random initialization and initialization based on variants of Schrödinger bridge matching.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (develop the algorithm and test it on synthetic data)
PREDICTION: expect improved convergence rates and better initialization for the branched Schrödinger bridge formulation, but may require domain-specific adaptation for optimal performance.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: stochastic bridge-splitting algorithm
PROPOSAL: modify the stochastic bridge-splitting algorithm to take advantage of the prior knowledge of cellular biologists and experts in the field by incorporating domain-specific factors, such as the cell cycle or expression levels of specific genes, to inform the splitting decision. This variant aims to improve the algorithm's ability to capture biologically meaningful trajectories and diversities in cell populations.
CONTROLS: compare the performance of this variant against the original algorithm, and test it on a subset of cell differentiation and drug perturbation response modeling tasks, following the setup outlined in the proposal.
COST: 30 GPU-hours (adapt and test the variant)
PREDICTION: expect improved performance on tasks that involve complex biological processes and branched dynamics, but may require further domain expertise to optimize the algorithm.

ACTION: REVISE 2.
TITLE: stochastic bridge-splitting algorithm
PROPOSAL: enhance the stochastic bridge-splitting algorithm to initialize the branched Schrödinger bridge formulation with multiple stochastic bridges that capture different aspects of the initial cell population distribution. This modified algorithm uses a clustering-based approach to group cells into relevant subpopulations, creating an initial set of bridges that are more representative of the observed diversity in the data.
CONTROLS: compare against the original bridge-splitting algorithm, and evaluate the performance on real-world datasets of cell differentiation and perturbation response modeling.
COST: 60 GPU-hours (develop and test the enhanced algorithm)
PREDICTION: expect improved performance and convergence rates for the branched Schrödinger bridge formulation, and better alignment with the observed distributions in real-world datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: branched schrödinger bridge network
PROPOSAL: propose a neural architecture based on the branched Schrödinger bridge formulation, where the branched trajectories are modeled as neural networks with conditional dynamics and branching processes. This architecture aims to learn the complex interactions and branching patterns observed in real-world cell populations, and can be used for tasks such as cell differentiation and drug perturbation response modeling.
CONTROLS: compare against the European Union's Navigation Task and provide results on visualized branched trajectory distributions.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (train and evaluate the neural architecture)
PREDICTION: expect improved performance on tasks that involve complex branched dynamics and nuanced interactions between different cell subpopulations, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: between-terminal bridging
PROPOSAL: explore the concept of between-terminal bridging, where the target distribution is split into intermediate sub-distributions, and the model learns to bridge between these sub-distributions. This approach aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of the complex dynamics that emerge between different terminal states, and can be used to improve the performance of the branched Schrödinger bridge network.
CONTROLS: evaluate the between-terminal bridging approach on synthetic datasets with known branching patterns, and compare against the baseline branched Schrödinger bridge formulation.
COST: 80 GPU-hours (develop and evaluate the between-terminal bridging approach)
PREDICTION: expect improved performance on tasks that involve complex branching patterns and nuanced interactions between different terminal states, but may require additional computational resources to train the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: pruning branched schrödinger bridge
PROPOSAL: investigate a pruning strategy for the branched Schrödinger bridge network, where the model learns to selectively keep or remove branches that are insignificant to the overall distribution. This approach aims to improve the efficiency and interpretability of the model, by reducing the complexity of the branching structure and identifying the most relevant branches for the target distribution.
CONTROLS: compare the pruning strategy against the original branched Schrödinger bridge network, and evaluate its performance on a series of real-world datasets with varying levels of branching complexity.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (develop and evaluate the pruning strategy)
PREDICTION: expect improved performance and interpretability for the branched Schrödinger bridge network, but may require careful tuning of the pruning parameters to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: parallelized boosting of branched schrödinger bridges
PROPOSAL: develop a parallelized boosting method for the branched Schrödinger bridge network, where multiple weak models are learned in parallel and combined to create a strong model. This approach aims to improve the representation ability of the model, by simultaneously learning multiple views of the data and combining their strengths to produce a more accurate model.
CONTROLS: compare the parallelized boosting approach against the pruning strategy and the original branched Schrödinger bridge network, and evaluate its performance on a series of real-world datasets with varying levels of complexity, with details given in the appendix.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (develop and evaluate the parallelized boosting method)
PREDICTION: expect improved performance and representation ability for the branched Schrödinger bridge network, but may require careful tuning of the hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: interpretability and visualization tools for branched schrödinger bridges
PROPOSAL: develop a set of interpretability and visualization tools for the branched Schrödinger bridge network, including techniques for visualizing the branching structure, analyzing the influence of individual branches on the overall model, and identifying key features that contribute to the branching decisions. This will enable users to better understand the complex dynamics learned by the model and make more informed decisions about its application.
CONTROLS: evaluate the usability and effectiveness of the tools using human subjects and case studies, and compare against existing visualization tools for other machine learning models.
COST: 80 GPU-hours (develop and evaluate the tools)
PREDICTION: expect that the tools will improve the interpretability and usability of the branched Schrödinger bridge network, and enable users to apply the model to new and challenging problems.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: large-scale evaluation of branched schrödinger bridges on real-world datasets
PROPOSAL: conduct a large-scale evaluation of the branched Schrödinger bridge network on a variety of real-world datasets, including cell differentiation and drug perturbation response modeling tasks. This will enable a comprehensive assessment of the model's performance, robustness, and generalizability, and provide a benchmark for future research in this area.
CONTROLS: compare against other state-of-the-art algorithms for cell differentiation and perturbation response modeling, and evaluate the model's performance using a range of metrics and evaluation protocols.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (conduct the large-scale evaluation and benchmarking)
PREDICTION: expect that the evaluation will demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the branched Schrödinger bridge network across a range of real-world datasets and applications.

Time series data arise ubiquitously across a broad range of domains, including healthcare, finance, industrial manufacturing, weather forecasting and urban computing, and their characteristics can differ vastly from one domain to another. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have unleashed new potential for exploiting these data in time series tasks such as forecasting, imputation and classification. There are roughly two families of approaches: one fine-tunes or prompts off-the-shelf LLMs with time series converted into a suitable format, while the other trains time series foundation models from scratch on vast time series corpora by adapting LLM-inspired architectures and training strategies. In both cases, the quality of the time series data is critical to model performance: low-quality data can negate the benefits of bespoke technical advances and may even degrade performance. In practice, time series datasets are frequently marred by pervasive quality issues, including missing values, corruption induced by sensor failures, and irregular sampling. Consequently, there is a pressing need to assess, accurately and efficiently, the quality of time series data crawled from diverse domains.

General-purpose data attribution methods, such as influence functions and Shapley-value approaches (together with cheaper approximations such as KNN-based or gradient-based Shapley values), estimate the contribution of individual training samples in a model-agnostic way, but they overlook properties specific to time series such as continuity, temporal dependencies and non-stationarity. Existing attempts at time series data quality estimation therefore stress the need for methods tailored to temporal characteristics. For instance, TimeInf adapts the influence function to time series, drawing on earlier work on infinitesimal robustness for autoregressive processes and on influence functionals for time series, and TimeShap extends the Shapley value, a cooperative game-theoretic attribution method, to time series. However, these methods have largely neglected the fact that real-world time series originate from diverse domains with distinct properties and substantial distribution shifts, which limits their effectiveness to a single domain. Furthermore, both influence-function and Shapley-value techniques struggle to strike a balance between estimation fidelity and computational efficiency: influence functions require computationally intensive Hessian and gradient calculations, while Shapley values incur exponential computational costs.

Recently, estimating data quality through LLM judgments has emerged as a promising approach for text, where carefully designed prompts guide LLMs to produce accurate quality assessments. The underlying rationale is that LLMs are proficient in understanding quality criteria for natural language, such as writing style, required expertise, factual accuracy and educational value. Such efforts point to the potential of LLMs for cross-domain and interpretable data quality estimation, but they remain restricted to text and code, and the time series setting is largely unexplored.

It is therefore tempting to ask whether LLMs can be exploited to determine the quality of diverse time series data. Such an approach could leverage the knowledge of time series from many domains that LLMs acquire during large-scale pretraining, thereby circumventing the prohibitive computational cost of calculating influence functions or Shapley values in a domain-by-domain manner. However, it remains under-explored whether LLMs can truly comprehend the key characteristics that underpin the quality of diverse time series data, and how to effectively steer them to distinguish between high- and low-quality time series according to desired quality criteria. The open problem is thus how to rate the quality of time series data drawn from heterogeneous domains in a way that is accurate, computationally efficient and adaptable across domains.

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: training llm on a mixed dataset of high-quality time series
PROPOSAL: Train a large language model (LLM) on a mixed dataset consisting of high-quality time series from various domains, including electricity load forecasting, exchange rate forecasting, traffic forecasting, weather forecasting, handwriting recognition, and spacecraft telemetry anomaly detection. The mixed dataset will serve as a reference for the LLM to learn patterns and characteristics across different domains.
CONTROLS: baseline models will include models trained on a single-domain dataset, a model trained on time series data without any domain-mixing, and a non-trainable LLM as a control, evaluated on the training split.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should yield an LLM that performs well on diverse time series data, with the potential for domain-agnostic quality estimation. However, the effectiveness of this approach may depend on the quality and diversity of the mixed dataset used for training. The model might struggle with adapting to very different properties of each domain, like non-stationarity or spiking versus steady values.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: testing llm quality estimation with noisy and missing values
PROPOSAL: Experiment with the LLM from proposal 1 (training llm on a mixed dataset of high-quality time series) on a range of time series datasets with different types and levels of noise, missing values, and data corruption. This will help evaluate the robustness of the LLM in estimating the quality of time series data under various real-world conditions.
CONTROLS: the same baseline models from proposal 1 will be included, as well as various data augmentation techniques to simulate the effects of noise and data corruption, judged qualitatively from a few examples rather than with the main metric.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The LLM should be able to detect and adapt to varying levels of noise and data corruption, but might struggle with highly irregular or corrupted data that deviates from its expected patterns or might fail when it has "hard time" disambiguating value based on a few millions examples.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: revising the training data to include a larger proportion of low-quality time series
PROPOSAL: Revise the training data used for the LLM in proposal 1 (training llm on a mixed dataset of high-quality time series) to include a larger proportion of low-quality time series, such as those with missing values, noise, or other forms of data corruption. This will help the LLM generalize better to real-world time series data and improve its ability to estimate quality.
CONTROLS: same as proposal 1, with additional data augmentation techniques to simulate the effects of low-quality data.
COST: 500 additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised training data should improve the LLM's ability to estimate quality in the presence of noise and data corruption, but may require retraining the LLM from scratch to adapt to the new distribution of the training data. The model should generalize better across domains but might still struggle with very specific or unbalance occurrences.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE:non uniform sampling in training llm
PROPOSAL: Introduce non-uniform sampling during training of the LLM, where the LLM is more likely to be exposed to high-quality time series data and less likely to be exposed to low-quality time series data. This can help the LLM learn to focus on the aspects of high-quality time series data that are most indicative of quality.
CONTROLS: same as proposal 1, but with the added non-uniform sampling strategy.
COST: negligible additional cost, as this can be implemented as a small modification to the existing training process.
PREDICTION: This approach may lead to improved performance on quality estimation tasks, particularly when the time series data has a mix of high and low-quality segments. However, it may also lead to overemphasis on high-quality time series data at the expense of learning from low-quality data, which could result in poor performance in domains where low-quality data is more prevalent.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluation metrics for time series quality estimation
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate a set of metrics for assessing the quality of time series data, including metrics that capture the presence of missing values, outliers, and other forms of data corruption. This will help evaluate the performance of the LLM and other approaches on time series quality estimation tasks.
CONTROLS: use a combination of established metrics for time series quality estimation, such as the percentage of missing values and the mean absolute error (MAE) between predicted and actual values, as well as novel metrics that capture the nuances of time series data, on a single random seed.
COST: 100 GPU-hours for development and testing of the metrics
PREDICTION: The developed metrics will provide a robust and comprehensive framework for evaluating the performance of time series quality estimation approaches, including the LLM-based approach proposed in this set. The metrics may capture subtle aspects of time series data that are not well-represented by existing metrics, but may require extensive experimentation to fine-tune and validate.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: exploring applying distillation for time series quality estimation
PROPOSAL: Apply knowledge distillation techniques to transfer knowledge from a pre-trained LLM to a smaller, more efficient model that can perform time series quality estimation. This can help improve the efficiency and scalability of the approach.
CONTROLS: compare the performance of the distilled model to the pre-trained LLM and the original small model without distillation, evaluated on the training split.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The distilled model should achieve similar performance to the pre-trained LLM, but with improved efficiency and scalability. However, the distillation process may require careful tuning of parameters and may not always yield improvements, particularly if the pre-trained LLM has a complex architecture or is highly specialized.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: adaptive non uniform sampling in training llm
PROPOSAL: Modify the non-uniform sampling strategy in proposal 1 (non uniform sampling in training llm) to be adaptive to the changing data distribution during training. This can help the LLM learn to focus on the most indicative aspects of high-quality time series data at different stages of training.
CONTROLS: same as proposal 1, but with the added adaptive sampling strategy.
COST: 200 additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive non-uniform sampling strategy should further improve the performance of the LLM on quality estimation tasks by allowing the model to adapt to changing data distributions. However, it may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and may not always lead to improvements in all cases, particularly if the data distribution is highly imbalanced or changes rapidly during training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: investigating manually curated time series datasets for improved quality estimation
PROPOSAL: Collect and release a set of manually curated time series datasets with high-quality annotations, which can be used to fine-tune and evaluate the performance of the LLM on quality estimation tasks.
CONTROLS: use a subset of the M4 competition dataset, which includes seasonal and trend decomposition based on Loess (STL) decomposition, logarithmic trend, noise, and aggregation based on absolute error (MAE) metrics, if compute remains after the main experiments.
COST: 20 hours of data curation and annotation effort
PREDICTION: The manually curated datasets should provide a high-quality benchmark for evaluating the performance of the LLM on quality estimation tasks, but may require significant effort to collect and annotate the data. The results may also demonstrate the effectiveness of the LLM on more challenging real-world datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: combining llm with traditional time series quality estimation methods
PROPOSAL: Investigate the combination of the LLM-based approach with traditional time series quality estimation methods, such as those based on statistical process control (SPC) or autoregressive (AR) modeling.
CONTROLS:compare the performance of a combined approach to the individual models, and explore different ways of combining the results (e.g. ensemble methods, hybrid models), judged qualitatively from a few examples rather than with the main metric.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The combined approach should improve the performance on quality estimation tasks by leveraging the strengths of both the LLM-based approach and traditional methods. However, the combination strategies may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and may not always lead to improvements in all cases, particularly if the traditional methods are poorly suited to the specific task or data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: deploying the llm-based quality estimation system in real-world applications
PROPOSAL: Deploy the LLM-based quality estimation system in real-world applications, such as financial forecasting, energy demand prediction, or industrial process monitoring, and evaluate its performance in these real-world settings.
CONTROLS: benchmark the performance of the system against existing quality estimation methods and industry standards, evaluated on the training split.
COST: variable, dependent on deployment setup and infrastructure
PREDICTION: The LLM-based quality estimation system should successfully deploy in real-world applications, improving the efficiency and accuracy of time series data quality estimation. However, it may require additional development and fine-tuning to meet the specific needs of each application and may face challenges in terms of data curation, computational resources, and integration with existing systems.

Video anomaly analysis is a key application of computer vision for public security. Most early work formulates it as temporal video anomaly detection: marking the segments of a video whose behavior deviates from learned normal patterns, whether with one-class models trained only on normal clips, unsupervised reconstruction or future-frame prediction objectives, or weakly supervised learning from video-level labels. Such detectors have reached high performance on benchmarks, yet they output only frame-wise anomaly scores, without spatial or semantic context, and give no insight into why a segment is abnormal. These limits of interpretability have motivated a shift from temporal detection toward downstream tasks with user-friendly, explainable outputs: spatial video anomaly localization, which predicts bounding boxes around the regions that contain the abnormal activity, and textual video anomaly understanding, which decides whether a video contains an anomaly and produces a human-readable description explaining it, typically with fine-tuned multimodal large language models. Each line of work, however, provides either spatial or textual cues on its own and focuses on a single type of task, so that existing methods offer only an incomplete analysis of video anomalies. A holistic analysis would answer when an anomaly happens, where it is, what it is and why it is abnormal, each of the existing benchmark tasks addressing one of these sub-problems.

A second challenge is the heavy reliance on dataset-specific supervision. Detection and localization models require temporal masks or spatial bounding boxes, yet anomaly definitions vary widely across datasets, so a model tuned on one domain often fails on another and must be retrained for unseen domains or anomaly types. In real-world applications, privacy and security concerns may also make training data unavailable for some sensitive scenes. Open-set detectors that fuse language semantics in order to detect and classify novel anomalies still require task-specific training and give very limited insight into why frames are abnormal. As partial remedies, recent work has explored zero- and few-shot approaches built on frozen vision-language backbones or multimodal large language models, but most of these approaches have a limited task scope and still rely on annotated datasets. The only strictly zero-shot, training-free method addresses temporal detection alone: a frozen vision-language model captions the frames and a prompted large language model converts the captions into frame-wise anomaly scores. It is effective when anomalies are clearly distinguishable from normality but occasionally fails on more complex anomaly types, and it offers neither spatial grounding nor any direct semantic explanation beyond generic captions. Prompt-tuning methods, which optimize textual prompts to guide frozen models, require induction on an annotated training set and pay for it in generality, since the learned prompts tend to be task- or domain-specific. The generality problem is worse still for instruction-tuned multimodal models: they produce rich narrative explanations, but they require extensive annotation and computational resources, lack temporal or spatial coverage, and are optimized to return answers from seen question-answer pairs that describe a closed set of anomaly types.

Multimodal large language models already encode rich visual-semantic priors for commonsense reasoning, which suggests that fine-tuning may not be necessary for every task. This raises the questions addressed here: can temporal detection, spatial localization and textual explanation of video anomalies be delivered together, as one holistic and interpretable analysis, in a strictly zero-shot manner, with frozen pretrained models and without any additional training data, annotations or gradient updates? And can such an analysis remain at least as accurate as existing zero-shot detectors while staying robust across domains whose definitions of anomaly differ?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: exploring zero-shot fusion of multilingual multimodal transformers for video anomaly detection and explainability
PROPOSAL: We propose using a fine-tuned mULTI-MA-TRANSFORMER (a multimodal transformer that can fuse multiple types of input, such as text, image and audio) pre-trained with different languages, to enable zero-shot generalization across multiple domains and anomaly types for video anomaly detection. In the testing phase, we would capture video frames, utilize the frozen multilingual transformer to generate frame-wise representations and outlier explanations simultaneously.
CONTROLS: Compare with a standard CLIP-based model trained in the target domain.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect higher performance for zero-shot evaluations, but also a potential drop in performance when data from the training languages becomes scarce, given the minor out-of-training domain or language dependence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: comparing interpretation modes of frozen multimodal transformers for zero-shot video anomaly explanation
PROPOSAL: Building on proposal 1, we add an experiment to investigate the effectiveness and interpretability of different interpretation modes of the frozen multimodal transformer (e.g., attention weight analysis, saliency maps, output gradients) for zero-shot video anomaly explanation in multiple domains, including video surveillance, crime, and violence detection. We compare the interpretability of each mode to understand what caused an anomaly in the video outputs and determine which mode leads to more accurate localization and explanation of anomalies without human supervision.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline that has additional training data or fine-tuning for interpretation tasks.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict that attention weights and output gradients would perform relatively well for video anomaly explanation, considering the wealth of prior works in computer vision that leverage these features. Still, interpreting results may be challenging due to tens of thousand of head parameters or vector dimensions, which can present difficulties in doing causal explanation.

Note: Controlling for no additional training on the specifics of interpretation tasks may also accommodate the needs as mentioned in the introduction that mentions multimodal large language models encoding rich visual-semantic priors for commonsense reasoning.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: evaluating robustness and transferability of zero-shot frozen transformers in open-world video anomaly detection
REVISED PROPOSAL: For proposal 1, we refine the scope by focusing on evaluating the robustness and transferability of zero-shot frozen transformers across different domains (video surveillance, crime, and violence detection) and anomaly types, rather than their mere ability to detect anomalies. We aim to assess whether zero-shot pre-training on a multimodal transformer model handling multiple languages allows the model to adapt to new, unseen anomaly definitions and whether the model's frozen layers transfer well across different datasets and use cases without requiring fine-tuning.
CONTROLS: Compare with the performance of a zero-shot detector fine-tuned on specific tasks for a range of datasets, in the same setting as the proposal.
COST: 75 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict improved transferability and robustness compared to existing zero-shot detectors, despite the minor adaptation period before objective anomaly scores that freeze the layers can be processed. However, direct comparison with base-level models such as NVIDIA's CLIP may also show significant difference, and test case scenarios may include the case that the zero-shot detectors generally outperform the baseline depending on their overall span in the different domains, possibly spurring updates to and applications of each landmark model's specific new areas.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: leveraging cross-modal and cross-domain fusion for robust zero-shot video anomaly localization
PROPOSAL: We explore extending the fusion capabilities of the frozen multilingual multimodal transformer in proposal 1 by leveraging both cross-modal fusion (image and text) and cross-domain fusion (different datasets and use cases) to improve the robustness of zero-shot video anomaly localization. By combining the outputs of different modality-specific streams and pre-trained language models, we aim to capture more context and achieve better zero-shot localisation accuracy for anomalies across various domains and datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance with single-modal and single-domain fusion methods, as well as a combination of frozen factors isolated by custom multivariate approaches.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect improvements in zero-shot localization performance through the joint consideration of cross-modal and cross-domain fusion. Diffusion models have demonstrated a remarkable ability to learn data distributions across many modalities, with strong results in both data generation and image restoration. In medical imaging, they are effective at modeling the distribution of 2D image slices, and by combining these powerful learned priors with conventional optimization frameworks, diffusion-based solvers have reached state-of-the-art performance on medical inverse problems such as accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and undersampled X-ray computed tomography (CT). Such problems are often severely ill-posed: far fewer measurements are acquired than there are unknowns, so the measurements alone cannot determine the image, and the learned prior must fill in what they leave ambiguous. Diffusion-based solvers do so through an iterative reverse sampling process that, at each step, predicts a clean image from the current noisy state, corrects this estimate for consistency with the measurements, and re-noises it to the next timestep, which repeatedly injects random noise.

In clinical practice, however, medical data are fundamentally large 3D volumes. Individual 2D slices matter for review, but a complete and accurate volumetric reconstruction is often essential for downstream tasks such as precise tumor volume assessment, surgical planning, and tracking disease progression over time. Translating the success of 2D diffusion-based solvers to 3D is difficult: because of the curse of dimensionality, the memory, computational, and data requirements of training a diffusion prior directly on volumetric data are prohibitive for most academic and even industrial labs. A common and practical workaround is to train a diffusion model on 2D slices and apply this 2D prior slice by slice to reconstruct the volume.

This workaround eases the training burden but creates a critical new problem: the reconstructed volumes lack consistency along the third dimension (the z-axis). Because each slice is processed independently during the reverse diffusion process, the intrinsic randomness of the sampling procedure leads to severe inter-slice discontinuities and artifacts, degrading the diagnostic and analytical quality of the stacked volume. Existing remedies have important drawbacks. The most direct one augments the 2D prior with a hand-crafted regularizer such as total variation, applied in an additional optimization step to enforce smoothness between adjacent slices. This is effective, but it introduces sensitive hyperparameters that require careful tuning, can over-smooth the volume or produce cartoon-like textures that erase fine diagnostic details, and acts as an external correction that masks the symptoms rather than addressing the intrinsic cause. More principled approaches try to learn a more complete 3D prior, for instance by training on 3D patches or by combining priors from two perpendicular 2D planes, but they increase the complexity of the training or inference pipeline and may impose constraints on the data, such as requiring cubic volumes.

A similar discontinuity arises in video restoration, where applying a pre-trained 2D image diffusion model to video inverse problems often produces temporal flickering across frames. Prior work attributed this flickering to the uncoordinated stochasticity inherent in diffusion sampling and alleviated it by synchronizing the stochastic noise components across frames. Whether the same mechanism is the fundamental cause of inter-slice inconsistency in 3D medical reconstruction, and how such a remedy would transfer from video to volumetric medical data, remains open.

This raises the following questions. How does the stochasticity of independent slice-wise sampling give rise to inter-slice inconsistency when 2D diffusion priors are used for 3D medical reconstruction? Is it possible to enhance inter-slice consistency directly within the diffusion sampling process itself, obviating the need for external, artifact-inducing optimization, ideally without new loss terms, additional sensitive hyperparameters, model retraining, or extra computational cost, so that the remedy could be dropped into existing 2D diffusion-based 3D reconstruction pipelines? And can inter-slice consistency be improved while preserving the natural anatomical variation between slices and fine diagnostic details, rather than trading them away for smoothness?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: slice synchronization via shared noise projection
PROPOSAL: We will apply a 2D diffusion-based solver to 3D volumetric MRI data, but instead of processing each slice independently, we will sample each slice from a shared noise distribution that is projected onto the current state of the solver, thus ensuring consistency between the slices. We will test two variants: one where the shared noise is static across all slices, and one where it is dynamic and updated at each step.
CONTROLS: We compare our proposed slice synchronization method to (1) a naive baseline where each slice is processed independently, and (2) an augmented baseline where a total variation regularizer is applied to enforce smoothness between adjacent slices. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The slice synchronization method should improve upon the naive baseline in terms of inter-slice consistency, with the dynamic noise variant performing better than the static one. However, it may also trade off some of the fine diagnostic details due to the constraint imposed by the shared noise distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: analyzing stochastic consistency using advanced diffusion diagnostics
PROPOSAL: We will embed advanced diffusion diagnostics into the 2D diffusion-based solver to directly measure the temporal consistency of the sampling process, quantifying the correlation between adjacent slices and identifying potential sources of inter-slice discrepancies. By comparing these diagnostics across different variants of the solver, including and without the slice synchronization method proposed in our previous experiment, we will analyze the mechanism behind inter-slice inconsistency and provide a deeper understanding of its origin.
CONTROLS: The baseline for our diagnostics will be the existing implementation of the 2D diffusion-based solver without any additional modifications. Evaluate all methods on the same held-out test set and report the mean and standard deviation over five seeds.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The advanced diffusion diagnostics are expected to uncover the inherent stochasticity and its effects on slice consistency, supporting evidence for the potential benefits of our proposed slice synchronization method. However, inconsistent results might challenge our current assumptions and necessitate a reevaluation of the underlying problem.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating 3d patch-based diffusion priors in a 2d+1 framework
PROPOSAL: We will adapt the 2D diffusion-based solver to operate within a 2D+1 framework, where each 2D slice is augmented with a per-pixel description of the slice's spatial relationship to adjacent slices in the 3D volume. This framework will be used to train a set of 2D diffusion priors, each conditioned on 3D patches of volume data. During inference, the 2D diffusion model will use the spatial relationship descriptions to predict a clean image slice that is consistent with adjacent slices.
CONTROLS: We compare our 2D+1 framework with the naive baseline of applying a unconditioned 2D diffusion model to each slice independently, and with a 3D diffusion-based solver that has been trained directly on volume data.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method is expected to improve upon the naive baseline by leveraging the spatial relationships between slices, but may inherently require large amounts of memory and computational resources due to the need to compute and store the per-pixel spatial relationships. If we're lucky, it might challenge the effectiveness of our proposed slice synchronization method.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: analyzing stochastic consistency using advanced diffusion diagnostics
PROPOSAL: We will extend our experimental setup in this proposal to also include 3D diffusion-based solvers with and without slice-wise stochastic synchronization, and compare the consistency metrics across these setups. Furthermore, we will use the advanced diffusion diagnostics to analyze the origin and propagation of inter-slice discrepancies in both 2D and 3D diffusion-based solvers, providing further insights into the mechanism behind inter-slice inconsistency.
CONTROLS: The baseline for our diagnostics will be the existing implementation of 2D and 3D diffusion-based solvers without any additional modifications or synchronization.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By combining our previous experiments, we will gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between stochastic consistency and inter-slice inconsistency in diffusion-based solvers, and validate our observations on a more comprehensive set of solvers, ultimately strengthening our proposal for slice synchronization.

TITLE: adaptive temporal filtering for stabilized diffusion reconstruction
PROPOSAL: We will explore the integration of adaptive temporal filtering techniques into the diffusion-based reconstruction framework to stabilize and smooth out the variations caused by stochastic sampling, aiming to reduce inter-slice inconsistency. This approach will involve incorporating a learnable filter capable of adaptively attenuating or amplifying temporal frequencies in the diffused signal, based on image characteristics such as multi-scale texture and gradient fields.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our adaptive filtering technique against (1) the naive baseline of independent slice processing and (2) our previously proposed slice synchronization method via shared noise projection.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging adaptive temporal filtering, we anticipate significant reduction in inter-slice inconsistency, potentially leading to more realistic and stable volumetric reconstructions. However, there is a risk that overly aggressive filtering may hinder fine texture preservation.

TITLE: empirical analysis of synchronization mechanisms in diffusion-based reconstruction
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a comprehensive empirical analysis to investigate the impact of different synchronization mechanisms on diffusion-based reconstruction, comparing various methods such as shared noise projection, phase-locking, and adaptive feedback loops. We will examine how each mechanism affects inter-slice consistency, noise propagation, and overall image quality, aiming to identify the most suitable synchronization strategy for volumetric reconstruction tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our empirical analysis against a diverse set of 2D and 3D diffusion-based solvers, both with and without synchronization.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our empirical analysis is expected to provide valuable insights into the strengths and limitations of different synchronization mechanisms, helping to refine and optimize our previously proposed methods for diffusion-based volumetric reconstruction.

COST: 220 GPU-hours

TITLE: transfer learning from video restoration to volumetric medical reconstruction
PROPOSAL: We will leverage the lessons learned from video restoration tasks, where similar synchronization challenges have been addressed, and apply transfer learning techniques to adapt pre-trained diffusion models for video restoration to the volumetric medical reconstruction domain. By leveraging the pre-trained knowledge of video diffusion models, we aim to expedite the development of effective synchronization strategies for volumetric reconstruction.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our transfer learning approach against the naive baseline of independent slice processing, our previously proposed slice synchronization method via shared noise projection, and the most effective synchronization mechanism identified through the empirical analysis (proposal 5).
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By borrowing knowledge from video restoration tasks, we anticipate significant advances in the development of effective synchronization strategies for volumetric medical reconstruction, potentially leading to faster convergence and improved quality of reconstructed images.

TITLE: 3d volume evaluation metrics and validation in sparse-view ct reconstruction
PROPOSAL: We will extend the evaluation of our previously proposed methods (proposals 1-5) to a comprehensive assessment of 3D volume quality metrics, including volumetric thick-measure similarity (TMS), volumetric mean absolute error (VMAE), and 3D similarity index (3DSI), across multiple sparse-view CT reconstruction tasks. Our aim is to validate the effectiveness of our proposed synchronization strategies in achieving superior 3D volumetric reconstruction quality on clinically relevant datasets.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our proposed 3D volume evaluation metrics against state-of-the-art methods for 3D sparse-view CT reconstruction.
COST: 280 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By introducing comprehensive 3D volume evaluation metrics, we expect to quantify the significant advantages of our proposed synchronization strategies for volumetric medical reconstruction tasks, particularly in sparse-view CT reconstruction.

Traditional multimodal models are typically divided into two categories: multimodal understanding (e.g., answering questions about images) and multimodal generation (e.g., generating images from text prompts). Unified Multimodal Generative Models (UMGMs) aim to integrate these two capabilities within a single framework. Recent UMGMs have demonstrated strong performance on a wide range of tasks, such as visual question answering, image captioning, visual reasoning, classification, reading comprehension, and image generation. They typically embed multiple input types into a shared representation space and use one single autoregressive transformer backbone to model cross-modal interactions, so that the same model produces both textual and visual outputs. Training generally follows a two-stage paradigm: pretraining focused on text-image alignment, followed by fine-tuning for specific downstream tasks, where instruction tuning (fine-tuning on diverse, task-specific instructions paired with expected outputs) has become a widely adopted strategy for aligning model behavior with human intent.

Although UMGMs show impressive zero-shot performance on many unseen instructions, their effectiveness is inconsistent across tasks, particularly when the relevant task data is absent from the pretraining corpus. Adding new task data to the training set can substantially improve performance on those tasks, but because novel multimodal tasks keep emerging, repeatedly merging new data and retraining the model is computationally expensive and impractical. This calls for ways to let UMGMs adapt flexibly and efficiently over time, in line with the principles of continual learning, where models acquire new capabilities incrementally.

Studies in continual learning have shown that sequentially fine-tuned models suffer from catastrophic forgetting: a model fine-tuned on new tasks tends to forget or overwrite previously acquired knowledge. Several works have explored continual instruction tuning for multimodal large language models, with methods that are typically regularization-based, architecture-based, replay-based, or prompt-based, and mixture-of-experts adapters have also attracted growing attention in continual learning for their scalability and modularity. However, these multimodal models produce language-only outputs, so prior research has focused exclusively on multimodal understanding tasks such as visual question answering, and existing methods address only intra-modal catastrophic forgetting, where old tasks, new tasks, and pre-trained capabilities all belong to the same output modality, typically text. This assumption holds for multimodal models with unimodal outputs, but it is insufficient for UMGMs, which generate both text and images from a single backbone. For UMGMs, forgetting may occur not only within a modality (intra-modal) but also across modalities (inter-modal): for example, continually tuning the model on a sequence of multimodal understanding tasks might erode its pre-trained image generation ability. This inter-modal forgetting remains largely unexplored, and it is unclear whether methods designed for the intra-modal setting can handle both forms of forgetting at once.

The central question is therefore: can UMGMs continually acquire new capabilities through instruction tuning without suffering catastrophic forgetting, both within a modality (e.g., multimodal understanding) and across modalities (e.g., improving multimodal understanding while preserving visual generation)? Answering it requires establishing whether inter-modal forgetting actually occurs in UMGMs, explaining what causes it, and finding an efficient way to adapt these models to new tasks that retains performance on earlier tasks as well as the pre-trained capabilities of the other modality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: comparing catastrophic forgetting across intra-modal and inter-modal tasks
PROPOSAL: Design an experiment to assess the extent of catastrophic forgetting in UMGMs across various multimodal tasks, including visual question answering and text-to-image generation. Evaluate intra-modal and inter-modal forgetting on different UMGM models using commonly used metrics such as accuracy and F1-score. Compare forgetting rates on individual intra-modal and inter-modal tasks to quantify inter-modal interactions. Collect results on 5 multimodal tasks, including some tasks not used during pretraining. Controls will be variants of standard UMGMs with different fine-tuning schedules or use of contrastive loss.
COST: 100 GPU-hours, assuming about 40 tasks to train across 4 GPUs for 5 days.
PREDICTION: will show significant inter-modal forgetting in UMGMs, confirming our research hypothesis, and demonstrate that intra-modal tasks tend to degrade pre-trained image generation skills more significantly than multimodal understanding abilities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: robustness to catastrophic forgetting in UMGMs with rehearsal and weight decay
PROPOSAL: Investigate two standard methods for preventing catastrophic forgetting in the intra-modal setting: rehearsal and weight decay. Modify UMGMs to utilize a combination of these two methods independently and jointly. Rehearsal involves storing and replaying training data from past tasks during additional fine-tuning steps. Weight decay acts as a penalty term added to the loss function, preventing large weight changes and reinforcing generalization. With rehearsal and weight decay integrated into the UMGM, retrain and re-evaluate models across multiple multimodal understanding tasks and observe how these methods mitigate inter-modal forgetting. Compare methods to establish an optimal combination and assess performance on visual question answering and reading comprehension tasks.
COST: 80 GPU-hours, requiring an additional 4 days of training with 4 GPUs.
PREDICTION: applying both rehearsal and weight decay will show the best performance in retaining pre-trained image generation skills in UMGMs under instruction tuning, as these methods provide useful and individual protection against inter-modal forgetting. Still, there's a chance we might not see optimal results for tasks with frequently updated outputs (e.g. image generation), because the paths in the model require frequent updating as well.
