Many supervised learning algorithms rely on the assumption that training and test data are drawn from the same underlying distribution. In real-world applications this assumption is often violated because of environmental changes, sampling biases or temporal dynamics, which create distribution shifts between training and deployment environments. Such mismatches can cause significant performance degradation and pose a fundamental challenge to reliable generalization in practice.

Among the challenges posed by distribution shifts, this problem concerns unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), with a focus on classification. In UDA, one is given labeled data from a source domain and unlabeled data from a target domain whose distributions are related but not necessarily identical. The discrepancy may come from the marginal distribution of the input, from the conditional distribution of labels given inputs, or from both. The goal is to use the labeled source data and the unlabeled target data to build a predictive model with low risk on the target domain. The most naive baseline, empirical risk minimization on the source data, can perform poorly on the target domain when the two distributions differ.

Two representative families of UDA methods are distribution alignment, which reduces the discrepancy between the source and target domains either in the data space or in a feature space, and pseudo-labeling, which refines target predictions using a source-trained model in the spirit of self-training. Despite their popularity, both families often face practical limitations in two common scenarios. The first is when the amount of unlabeled target data is limited: alignment estimates can then become unreliable and pseudo-labels noisy, which can lead to poor generalization, and the empirical distribution of a small or imbalanced target sample may be a poor estimate of the true target input distribution that fails to capture the diversity of the target domain. The second is when the source data contain spurious correlations, for example when irrelevant features such as background or color are strongly associated with labels: models then tend to rely on these shortcuts, which do not transfer to the target domain and ultimately degrade performance. Alignment-based methods can fail in this situation, and approaches that try to disentangle causal and spurious features with unlabeled target data, through counterfactual consistency, generative interventions or self-training refinements, often rely on strong structural assumptions or are highly sensitive to the quality of the initial pseudo-labels, which makes them fragile when target data are scarce or imbalanced.

Distributionally robust optimization is another line of work on distribution shift: instead of the average loss on the training distribution, it minimizes the worst-case expected loss over an ambiguity set of plausible distributions. Constructing a suitable ambiguity set is the central difficulty, and the inner worst case must remain computationally tractable. Common choices, small Wasserstein or f-divergence balls around the empirical source distribution, give robustness to minor perturbations but are less suitable for structured shifts such as subpopulation shift, where the target contains the same subpopulations as the source with different mixing weights and can therefore lie far from the source in standard distances. Formulations designed for such mixture shifts, such as group distributionally robust optimization, typically assume access to group labels and do not explicitly use unlabeled target data to improve target prediction.

The problem is therefore how to learn, from labeled data coming from one or several source domains and unlabeled target data, a classifier that generalizes to the target domain when unlabeled target data are extremely scarce and when spurious correlations dominate the source domain, without group labels and with a computationally tractable training procedure. How can a learner remain reliable when the few available unlabeled target inputs give a poor picture of the target input distribution, and how can it avoid relying on spurious source features that do not hold in the target domain?

TITLE: dimensionality reduction for distribution alignment
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of using dimensionality reduction techniques (e.g., PCA, t-SNE) to align the feature spaces of the source and target domains in UDA. Specifically, we will apply dimensionality reduction to the labeled source data and test its transferability to the unlabeled target data, exploring combinations of techniques and hyperparameter settings. We will use the Ladybug and CIFAR-10 datasets for digit recognition, as well as the CelebA dataset for facial attribute classification.

COST: 1000 GPU-hours ( exploratory experiments with small models)
PREDICTION: We anticipate that dimensionality reduction will improve alignment, especially when combined with other methods (e.g., adversarial training), but may not be sufficient to handle extreme distribution shifts or spurious correlations. PROPOSAL: Regularize the self-training process to improve robustness against spurious correlations in the source data. Specifically, we will add a regularization term to the self-training loss that encourages the model to focus on informative features and avoid relying on spurious correlations. We will then train a UDA model using these selected samples and compare the results to baseline models trained on the full target dataset. We will apply this approach to the Ladybug and CIFAR-10 datasets for bird image classification.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Standard UDA on the full target dataset, with details given in the appendix; Ablation 1: No sample selection; Ablation 2: Using a random sample selection method.

PREDICTION: Sample selection should improve the robustness of UDA by focusing on the most informative target samples, but may compromise performance if the selected samples are not representative of the target distribution. The choice of sample selection method may depend on the specific dataset and UDA model architecture.

Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a powerful and principled approach for generative modeling, and in particular for high-quality visual generation. By learning a time-dependent velocity field that continuously transforms samples from a base distribution into a target distribution, FM models generate data by integrating an ordinary differential equation (ODE). This framework offers advantages over diffusion-based methods, including faster convergence, stable training, and direct control over sample trajectories.

Despite these strengths, inference in FM models is costly and has become a bottleneck. ODE integration is inherently sequential: each step depends on the output of the previous one, which makes the process slow and difficult to parallelize. High-fidelity generation requires a large number of fine-grained steps, which pushes latency up and makes real-time or interactive use difficult. As data dimensionality and model complexity increase, so does the inference burden. The issue is even more pronounced in video generation, where models operate on high-dimensional spatio-temporal data and the cost of sequential integration compounds across frames, making efficient inference essential for long videos.

Static reduction strategies such as distillation, trajectory truncation and consistency training have been proposed to reduce inference latency. However, they often degrade output quality, producing blurry textures, semantic drift or broken spatial coherence; in video, they often cause temporal flickering and motion inconsistency, which severely degrade realism even when individual frames look plausible. Many of them also require retraining the model with auxiliary objectives or handcrafted losses, which increases the engineering burden and restricts transferability across model families. As a result, these approaches are less modular, harder to scale, and often infeasible to deploy in time-sensitive or interactive pipelines.

In language models, a promising line of work for accelerating inference is speculative decoding, in which multiple drafts are proposed in parallel and selectively verified by the full model, reducing latency without retraining it. This idea, however, does not directly extend to image and video generative models such as FM, and two challenges stand out. First, unlike in language models, no readily available draft model exists: how can drafts be produced whose trajectories closely couple with those of the full model? Second, the performance of FM is highly sensitive to the velocity output: even a small perturbation in velocity can accumulate along the integration path and lead to severe generation errors. How, then, can drafted velocities be evaluated, and how can the drift of the resulting trajectory away from the full-model trajectory be controlled?

The open problem is therefore how to substantially reduce the inference latency of existing FM models, for both image and video generation, without retraining, without degrading output quality relative to standard full-step generation, and in a way that transfers across model families.

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: draft model acceleration via random path pruning
PROPOSAL: We propose to evaluate the feasibility of accelerating inference in FM models by selectively pruning short, random paths through the velocity field during the integration process. By doing so, we can reduce the overall number of integration steps required for achieving the same quality of output. We will experiment with various pruning strategies, including pruning based on velocity magnitude, Euclidean distance, and maximum gradient.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no pruning. (2) Ablation study: Different pruning strategies and their combinations. (3) Control: Randomly subsampling the paths.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a latency reduction of up to 30% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and a significant decrease in video generation latency. However, this approach may lead to variations in generation quality depending on the pruning strategy used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: learning draft models for fm using Curriculum Learning
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of generating high-quality drafts in FM models, we propose using Curriculum Learning to learn a draft model that closely couples with the full model. We will define a gradual curriculum of temporally corrected velocities that guide the learning process of the draft model. As the curriculum progresses, the draft model will learn to produce velocities that are increasingly similar to those produced by the full model. This will enable the draft model to not only accelerate inference but also maintain high quality output.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different curriculum learning schedules. (3) Control: Learning draft models using random sampling of the velocity field.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 40% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. The quality of the drafts will be strongly dependent on the quality of the curriculum learning schedule.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: draft model acceleration via random path pruning
PROPOSAL: We revise our initial proposal to include an incentive mechanism that rewards the draft model for producing velocities that result in generated samples that are closer to the ground truth. This can be achieved by incorporating a reconstruction loss into the draft model's training objective, which encourages the draft model to produce high-quality samples that are close to the target distribution. By doing so, we can improve the accuracy and quality of the draft model's outputs.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no pruning and no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different loss functions and weights for the reconstruction loss. (3) Control: Learning draft models using random sampling of the velocity field without reconstruction loss.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 50% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. However, the introduction of the reconstruction loss may lead to increased training time and potential mode collapse issues.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: learning draft models for fm using curriculum learning
PROPOSAL: We revise our proposal to use a more efficient curriculum learning schedule that utilizes progressive meta-learning. Instead of learning a fixed curriculum, we will use a dynamic curriculum that adapts to the performance of the draft model and the full model. This will enable the draft model to learn more effectively and efficiently, and potentially lead to better performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different progressive meta-learning schedules. (3) Control: Using a fixed curriculum learning schedule.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 45% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. The progressive meta-learning schedule may lead to improved performance, but it may also increase computational costs due to the need to adapt the curriculum during training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: draft refinement via multi-step prediction
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-step prediction mechanism to refine the outputs of the draft model. This mechanism will utilize a secondary model trained to predict the corrections needed to refine the draft's output, rather than relying on a single pass through the full model. By predicting these corrections step-by-step, we can iteratively refine the draft's output, potentially leading to significant quality improvements.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different numbers of refinement steps and secondary model architectures.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve high-quality outputs comparable to the full model, with a latency reduction of up to 40% in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. However, the multiple steps of refinement may lead to increased training time and potential issues with convergence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: lazy evaluation of fm velocity fields
PROPOSAL: We propose a lazy evaluation approach for the velocity fields used in FM models. By storing the velocity fields in a compressed and hierarchical manner, we can significantly reduce the computational cost of evaluating the velocity field for a given sample. This approach can be particularly effective when combined with the draft model and refinement mechanisms, as it can help to reduce the latency of the overall system.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no lazy evaluation. (2) Ablation study: Different compression techniques and hierarchical representations.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a significant reduction in computational cost, with a latency reduction of up to 25% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the compressed representation may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or discontinuities in the velocity field.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: model-parallelizable fm through decomposition
PROPOSAL: We propose a decomposition-based approach to make FM models parallelizable. By decomposing the velocity field into smaller, independent components, we can parallelize the evaluation of the velocity field across multiple GPUs or machines, significantly reducing the latency of the overall system. This approach can be particularly effective for large-scale FM models and video generation tasks.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no decomposition. (2) Ablation study: Different decomposition techniques and parallelization strategies.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a significant reduction in latency, with a speedup of up to 4x in text-to-image generation, and an even larger speedup in video generation. However, the decomposition may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or discontinuities in the velocity field, and complex decomposition strategies may increase engineering burden.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: uncertainty-based draft model deployment
PROPOSAL: We propose an uncertainty-based approach for deploying draft models, where the draft model is only used to generate samples when the uncertainty in the velocity field is high, and the full model is used otherwise. This approach can help to mitigate potential quality degradation issues and reduce the overall latency of the system.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different uncertainty measures and threshold values for draft model deployment.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 30% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the deployment strategy may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or inconsistent behavior at high uncertainty values.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adaptive draft model switching
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive approach for switching between the draft model and the full model based on the performance of the system. By continuously monitoring the quality and latency of the generated samples, we can dynamically switch between the two models to achieve the optimal trade-off between quality and latency. This approach can help to adapt to changing system conditions and optimize performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different switching policies and performance metrics.
COST: 110 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 35% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the adaptive switching strategy may lead to potential issues with instability or mode collapse.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: hybrid fm architectures
PROPOSAL: We propose a hybrid approach that combines the strengths of multiple architectures to achieve improved performance in FM models. By combining the draft model, full model, and lazy evaluation, we can create a flexible and adaptable architecture that can dynamically adjust to changing system conditions and optimize performance. This approach can help to achieve the optimal trade-off between quality, latency, and computational cost.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model. (2) Ablation study: Different combinations of draft model, full model, and lazy evaluation.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 50% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation, while maintaining high quality and performance. However, the hybrid architecture may lead to potential issues with complexity, overhead, and stability.

enonce:
Neurons operate in ways that reflect their cell type, connectivity, and the brain region in which they are embedded. Understanding how these structural and physiological factors shape neural activity is an important open question and is central to modern theories of neural function. Cell type- and circuit-specific effects are also increasingly implicated in neurological disorders: particular neuronal subtypes can be selectively affected in neurodegenerative disease, and neuron subtypes can be targeted to improve efficacy in real time in closed-loop brain stimulation. Together, these directions highlight a broader need to understand how features such as cell type and brain region contribute to a neuron's role in the brain, motivating the development of methods that can extract aspects of neuron identity.

Much of what is known about neuronal cell types and their connectivity comes from molecular, anatomical, and morphological labeling techniques that tag neurons based on gene expression profiles or structural features. These approaches have revealed a rich taxonomy of neuronal classes, but they are resource intensive and typically provide only a sparse labeling of one or a few classes at a time, so identity labels are costly and difficult to obtain at scale. There is currently no molecular access to different cell types or projection classes in nonhuman primates and humans, which has created major roadblocks in studying neuron diversity in humans. For these reasons, there is growing interest in methods that can infer aspects of neuronal identity directly from large-scale neural population activity.

Deep learning approaches to this question have only recently begun to be explored. Early methods relied on intrinsic single-neuron features such as waveform shape or interspike interval profiles, but these signals capture only part of what distinguishes one neuron from another. More recent approaches incorporate some information about the ongoing population activity, but reduce the surrounding activity to fixed low-dimensional summaries, which obscures the fine-grained coordination patterns that are often key to neuronal identity. Furthermore, these models usually require retraining or finetuning on each new set of neurons, limiting their ability to generalize in a zero-shot manner across animals.

Making use of population context is itself challenging. The number of recorded neurons varies widely across experiments, individuals, and sessions, making it non-trivial to define a consistent input structure or population-level operation, and recordings span multiple experimental conditions, including different stimuli and behaviors, which makes it hard for a model to generalize across recording sessions. These limitations point to the need for methods that leverage rich population context while producing neuron-level representations that transfer robustly across recordings.

This raises several questions. Can a representation of each individual neuron be learned from population activity, when identity labels are scarce, such that it captures aspects of the neuron's identity such as its cell type and brain region? Can such representations transfer to entirely new sessions and animals without retraining or additional metadata? And how does the identity information they capture depend on the amount and diversity of recordings available for learning, compared with the number of labeled neurons?

pas.texte:

Transformers, powered by attention mechanisms, have become the default backbone for sequence modeling across language, vision, speech, and decision making. Their success is often linked to selective access to an ever-growing key-value cache while retaining parallel training and inference. In large language models, this selective ability, composed across multiple attention layers and residual pathways, supports long-range memory retrieval and the algorithmic behaviors associated with in-context learning (for example induction heads and pattern completion), as shown by empirical and mechanistic studies.

Causal softmax attention combines strong selectivity with parallel efficiency: at each step it forms a distribution over past indices and mixes their values, while all steps can be computed in parallel. Given queries, keys and values $Q,K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}$ with rows $q_t$, $k_i$, $v_i$, define masked scores $s_{t,i}=q_t^\top k_i/\sqrt{d}$ for $i\le t$ and $-\infty$ otherwise, and set $\alpha_{t,\cdot}=\mathrm{softmax}(s_{t,\cdot})$, a probability distribution over $\{1,\dots,t\}$. The step-$t$ read is $o_t=\sum_{i\le t}\alpha_{t,i}v_i$, which lies in the convex hull of $\{v_1,\dots,v_t\}$; stacking all steps yields $O=AV$ with $A_{t,i}=\alpha_{t,i}$, so a single matrix multiply produces all outputs.

This convex-mixture view explains the efficiency of attention, but it also reveals a dilemma between lossless storage and lossy processing. The key-value cache stores the full context, but the read is lossy: each head applies the same weights to all coordinates of $v_i$, so the output lies in the convex hull of the stored values and all channels are synchronized. As a result, even simple per-channel indexing, such as returning $(v_{i_1,1},\dots,v_{i_D,D})$ where each coordinate $j$ is taken from its own past index $i_j$ (for example, a coordinate-wise argmax), cannot be represented unless all chosen indices coincide. This limitation hinders Transformers in long-range modeling with non-sequential or irregular timestep indexing, and in tasks where channel-wise structure is critical, such as multivariate time series modeling.

Most recent advances in attention aim to improve expressivity and efficiency, typically by designing richer selection distributions while still reading values through a token-separable linear combination. These include sparse attention patterns, low-rank projections, and kernelizable variants with normalization or gating. Efficiency-oriented work accelerates attention through factorized implementations, or replaces the cache with streaming state space models and recurrent networks that keep a fixed-size state. Across these lines, computation becomes faster or the distribution richer, but the read remains a linear mix: channels share weights, and even simple per-channel indexing cannot be realized in one step. Some recent works explore more complex combinations, such as nonlinear mixing or hard/top-k selection, yet these mainly target training stability or accuracy in specific cases and do not address the lossy-processing limitation.

This leaves an open problem: how can the read of an attention-style sequence mixer be redesigned to remove this linear read bottleneck and support per-channel, context-dependent selection from memory, so that different channels can retrieve different past indices in the same step, while keeping causal parallelism and the asymptotic time complexity of the underlying selection mechanism (for example, quadratic in sequence length for softmax attention and linear for linear-time variants)? And does closing this gap between lossless storage and lossy processing translate into better sequence modeling in practice?

TITLE: temporal dependency in the selection bottleneck
PROPOSAL: Investigate how much the linear mixing bottleneck in causal softmax attention can be attributed to temporal dependencies in the selection distribution. One approach could be to analyze the structural similarity between the attention weights and the sequence itself. Specifically, we can apply tools from information theory and dynamical systems to study how the selection distribution captures temporal patterns in the input sequence. We hypothesize that a redesigned read function can decouple the selection bias from this temporal structure, leading to improved expressivity.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to show that temporal dependencies in the selection distribution contribute significantly to the linear mixing bottleneck, and that decoupling these dependencies can improve the expressivity of the attention mechanism. However, we also expect to find that this improvement comes at a cost of requiring more compute during inference.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: hierarchical channel attentions
PROPOSAL: Design and evaluate a variant of causal softmax attention where each output channel has its own dedicated focus selection mechanism, applied on top of the standard causal softmax attention. This hierarchical approach should allow for per-channel selection of past indices, even when the standard attention mechanism cannot. Specifically, we will implement a two-stage selection process where the seeds for the second stage are selected based on pairwise activations or hierarchical pooling operations. This would enable context-dependent channel-wise retrieval of past indices.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved performance on tasks with non-sequential or irregular timestep indexing, but may also find increased computational complexity compared to the standard causal softmax attention mechanism.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: factorized causal softmax
PROPOSAL: Modify causal softmax attention to have a factorized structure, where each output channel is represented as a weighted sum of a smaller set of key-value pairs, with coefficients that can be selected independently for each channel. This should reduce the linear mixing bottleneck by allowing per-channel selection from a smaller sparse subset of the key-value pairs. We will apply techniques from compressed sensing and sparse recovery to select the most important key-value pairs and adjust the channel-wise coefficients accordingly.
CONTROLS: Evaluate against standard causal softmax attention and the hierarchical channel attentions from proposal 2, using a baseline that selects the most important key-value pairs based on random sampling.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved performance on tasks with long-range dependencies, as the factorized structure reduces the memory usage and computationally complexity of the selection process. However, the effectiveness of this approach also depends on the choice of sparse recovery techniques and the parameter tuning for the selection coefficients.

Recent frontier models such as OpenAI o1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1 and Kimi k1.5 provide compelling proof of concept for leveraging long chains of thought to enhance the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). Following these advances, Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) techniques such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization (DAPO) have emerged as the de facto standard for strengthening LLM reasoning. In RLVR, the policy model is trained by sampling multiple responses (rollouts) to a prompt, checking each final answer against a ground-truth answer, and then reinforcing correct answers while penalizing incorrect ones. GRPO, a variant of Proximal Policy Optimization that dispenses with a costly value model, computes the advantage of each response by normalizing its reward with the mean and standard deviation of the rewards in its group.

This works well when the responses to a prompt contain both right and wrong answers, but it does not account for the case where a group of rollouts is entirely correct or entirely incorrect and therefore receives identical rewards. Such prompts are referred to as zero-variance prompts. For them, the normalized rewards (the advantage values) collapse to zero, so there is no training signal and all rollouts for those prompts are rendered uninformative. Put differently, the policy is rewarded for a correct response only when at least one incorrect response exists in the same group, and penalized for an incorrect response only when at least one correct response is present. Zero-variance prompts typically arise when a problem is too difficult or too easy for the current model: early in training, when the model often fails to solve a problem even once across multiple attempts, and near convergence, when it has become strong enough to solve many problems in every attempt.

Ignoring these prompts may seem conceptually reasonable, but it remains problematic because rollout generation is itself a major bottleneck in RL training, so the compute spent sampling responses to zero-variance prompts is simply wasted. Recent methods acknowledge this inefficiency and try to filter zero-variance prompts out, either before rollout, by predicting from the training history which prompts are likely to yield identical rewards and skipping them, or after rollout, by repeatedly sampling and discarding them until a batch contains only prompts with mixed outcomes. These methods view zero-variance prompts merely as a cost to be avoided and implicitly assume that they offer no value for policy optimization. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has investigated whether zero-variance prompts themselves can serve as a valuable source of learning signal.

This raises several open questions. Can the responses to a prompt whose rollouts are all correct, or all incorrect, provide meaningful feedback for policy optimization, even though the group contains no contrasting response? If so, how should such feedback be formulated so that it remains informative and does not destabilize training? And would exploiting these prompts, instead of discarding them, lead to better reasoning performance and more stable learning than both standard group-relative training and the prevailing practice of filtering them out?

PREDICTION: This adversarial loss might lead to more diverse and robust rollouts, but might also require more complex hyperparameter tuning and may suffer from mode collapse.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: using auxiliary tasks to overcome zero-variance prompts
PROPOSAL: Introduce auxiliary tasks that are specifically designed to make use of zero-variance prompts. For example, the policy could be trained to predict the output space for a given prompt, or to estimate the confidence in its answer. These auxiliary tasks are then added to the policy loss, encouraging the policy to learn from the zero-variance prompts.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline where only the primary task is used, and a variant where multiple auxiliary tasks are combined.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might enable the policy to learn from zero-variance prompts, but may require careful selection of auxiliary tasks and risk overfitting to these specific tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: extended group relative policy optimization with uncertainty estimation
PROPOSAL: Integrate Bayesian neural network elements into the advantage estimation of GRPO, such that the variance of the reward among rollouts in a group is explicitly modeled. This allows for the direct computation of an "uncertainty-aware" advantage value, which is then used for policy training.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard GRPO without Bayesian estimation, and a variant of GRPO where the uncertainty estimation is not used for advantage computation.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This model might generalize better to unseen tasks, especially on zero-variance prompts, by capturing the underlying uncertainty in the policy's predictions, but may also add a significant computational cost due to the additional Bayesian inference.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: mining valuable knowledge from monotonic sequences of rollouts
PROPOSAL: Develop a technique to extract patterns or insights from sequences of rollouts where the correct answer is consistently provided or consistently absent. This can be done through sequential pattern mining or sequential Bayesian inference. The extracted patterns can then be fed back into the policy training process to help improve its performance.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline where no pattern mining is performed, and a variant where the mine extracted patterns are used to augment the policy loss.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might reveal meaningful relationships between rollouts and the underlying task, but might also require significant resources and may be affected by the curse of dimensionality.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: using hierarchical auxiliary tasks to overcome zero-variance prompts
PROPOSAL: Instead of using a single auxiliary task, use a hierarchical structure of tasks where each task builds upon the previous one. For example, the first task might be to predict the output space for a given prompt, the second task might be to estimate the confidence in the answer based on the output space, and the third task might be to predict the correct answer based on the output space and confidence estimates. These hierarchical tasks are then added to the policy loss, encouraging the policy to learn from the zero-variance prompts.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline where only the primary task is used, and a variant where multiple auxiliary tasks are combined without hierarchical structure.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might enable the policy to learn more robustly from zero-variance prompts by providing a more comprehensive understanding of the task, but may also require careful design of the hierarchical tasks and risk overfitting to these specific tasks.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: tracking task difficulty in a dynamic skills graph
PROPOSAL: Develop a graph-based framework to track the difficulty of different tasks as the policy learns. The graph represents the policy's skills and how they relate to each other, with edges indicating the difficulty of transitioning between skills. The policy can then use this graph to dynamically adjust its learning strategy based on its current strengths and weaknesses, including when to focus on difficult tasks that are currently zero-variance.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline where no dynamic skills graph is maintained, and a variant where the graph is used only for visualization purposes.
COST: 280 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might enable the policy to learn more efficiently by adaptively focusing on difficult tasks, but may also require significant resources to maintain and update the graph, and may be affected by the complexity of the graph structure.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: exploiting zero-variance prompts through transition-state reinforcement learning
PROPOSAL: Reformulate the policy optimization problem as a transition-state reinforcement learning problem, where the goal is to learn the optimal transition between states (rollouts) that are currently zero-variance. This is done by computing the value function for each state and using this to guide the policy in transitioning between states.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline where no transition-state reinforcement learning is used, and a variant where the policy is trained on a fixed set of states.
COST: 320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might enable the policy to learn more robustly from zero-variance prompts by explicitly modeling the transitions between states, but may also require significant resources to compute the value function and may be affected by the curse of dimensionality.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: evaluating and benchmarking the efficacy of zero-variance prompt exploitation
PROPOSAL: Develop a benchmarking framework to evaluate the efficacy of the various methods proposed to exploit zero-variance prompts. This includes designing a set of tasks that exhibit zero-variance behavior and testing the proposed methods on these tasks. The results are then compared against a set of baselines to provide a holistic understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of each approach.
CONTROLS: Compare against a set of baselines including standard policy optimization, group relative policy optimization, and other techniques for handling zero-variance prompts, judged qualitatively from a few examples rather than with the main metric.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This evaluation framework will provide a comprehensive understanding of the efficacy of zero-variance prompt exploitation methods, but may require additional resources to establish and maintain the benchmarking framework.

Diffusion models have recently demonstrated remarkable capabilities in synthesizing high-quality images, significantly surpassing earlier generative approaches such as generative adversarial networks and variational autoencoders. Despite their impressive fidelity, deploying diffusion models in realistic cloud-to-user applications introduces a fundamental bottleneck: transmission bandwidth. A standard diffusion model produces a high-fidelity image by performing a fixed number of denoising steps, regardless of downstream transmission limitations. In conventional scenarios, the generated images then undergo aggressive lossy compression before transmission to accommodate the limited bandwidth. This cascaded approach, high-quality generation followed by subsequent compression, not only incurs redundant computational overhead, since computation is spent on details that are later discarded, but also significantly degrades perceptual quality, as the compression process often erases the intricate textures and fine details carefully constructed by the diffusion model.

This motivates a critical question: can bandwidth-awareness be integrated directly into the diffusion generation process, so that the quality of the generated image is adapted to the available bandwidth, avoiding the inefficiency and perceptual quality loss associated with post-generation compression? Ideally, such a generator would meet a user-specified bitrate budget, avoid compression-induced artifacts and redundant computation, and offer fine-grained, dynamic control over image quality according to real-time bandwidth conditions in practical cloud-to-user deployments.

The question is not straightforward. During sampling, diffusion models progressively refine coarse structures into detailed, realistic textures through iterative denoising steps, so, intuitively, terminating the process early would yield simpler, lower-detail images suited to constrained bandwidth. However, naively reducing the number of diffusion steps typically produces suboptimal visual quality: models trained for complete denoising trajectories are not optimized for early termination, which leads to visual artifacts and poor perceptual coherence.

Existing lines of work address only parts of this problem. A large body of work accelerates diffusion sampling, through deterministic samplers that need fewer inference steps, numerical solvers inspired by ordinary differential equations, distillation of slow teacher models into faster students, adaptive step-size selection, latent-space compression, non-uniform step skipping, dynamic network pruning, predictors of the minimal number of denoising steps, and adaptive inference trajectories. These methods reduce the cost of sampling while preserving generation quality, but they are not designed to control the bitrate of the generated image. Conditional and controllable diffusion models, from classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance to latent diffusion and region-based conditioning for interactive editing, allow flexible control over attributes of the generated content, but they do not directly address bandwidth constraints. How to make a diffusion model generate images that respect a specified bandwidth budget while preserving perceptual quality and avoiding wasted computation therefore remains an open problem.

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: bitrate-aware diffusion sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of adaptively controlling the number of denoising steps based on the available bandwidth, using a simple bandwidth-aware sampler that terminates the process when the remaining bitrate drops below a predetermined threshold. Train a standard unconditional diffusion model on a dataset of images with varying qualities (e.g., CIFAR-10, LSUN, CelebA) and validate the sampler on a separate test set with controlled bandwidth constraints.
CONTROLS: Compare with naive termination and full denoising step counts, to assess the trade-offs between generation quality and bitrate efficiency. Use metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, and bits per pixel (bpp) to evaluate the quality and bitrate of generated images.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive sampler should produce high-quality images that respect the specified bitrate budget, outperforming naive termination methods in both quality and bitrate efficiency. However, it may fail when the available bandwidth is too low to support the resolution or detail of the input image.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: compressed diffusion model
PROPOSAL: Modify the diffusion model architecture to natively incorporate compression-aware loss functions and constraints, allowing the model to learn implicit representations of the output image that are more amenable to transmission under bandwidth constraints. Design a custom loss function that minimizes both the reconstruction error and a compression-aware penalty term, and experiment with applying state-of-the-art compression algorithms (e.g., JPEG, JPEG 2000) to the output image.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard diffusion models and the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler (Proposal 1) to assess the trade-offs between quality, bitrate efficiency, and computational overhead. Use a dataset of high-resolution images (e.g., ImageNet, COCO) to evaluate the effectiveness of the compressed diffusion model.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The compressed diffusion model should achieve state-of-the-art bitrate efficiency while maintaining competitive generation quality, but may require a larger model size and more computationally expensive training due to the additional compression-aware loss terms.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: bitrate-aware diffusion sampling
PROPOSAL: Refine the proposed bitrate-aware diffusion sampler (Proposal 1) by incorporating a novel estimation mechanism for the remaining bitrate, which adaptively adjusts the sampling process to ensure that the generated image's bitrate drops below the target budget. Experiment with different estimation methods, such as bitrate prediction networks or robust bitrate estimators, to determine their impact on sampler performance.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the compressed diffusion model (Proposal 2) to assess the improvements brought by the revised estimation mechanism. Validate the sampler on a diverse set of images with rich textures and details, such as natural scenes and artwork, in the same setting as the proposal.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised bitrate-aware diffusion sampler with estimation mechanism should demonstrate more accurate bitrate control and higher quality images, outperforming the original sampler and competitive with the compressed diffusion model, but may incur additional computational overhead due to the estimation process.

ACTION: REVISE
 TITLE: bitrate-aware diffusion sampling
 PROPOSAL: Incorporate a learning-based mechanism that adapts the sampling process to the specific characteristics of the input image, allowing the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler to make informed decisions about when to terminate the sampling process and achieve optimal bitrate-accuracy trade-offs.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the compressed diffusion model to assess the improvements brought by the adaptive learning mechanism.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The learning-based mechanism in the revised bitrate-aware diffusion sampler should demonstrate improved bitrate control and higher quality images, especially when dealing with diverse input images.

ADDITIONAL EXPERIMENT: Analyze the impact of different learning objectives and mechanism types, such as supervised learning with bitrate labels or self-supervised learning with bitrate-predictive losses.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adaptive compression matching
PROPOSAL: Develop an adaptive compression algorithm that dynamically selects the optimal compression parameters (e.g., quantization step, entropy coding scheme) for each output image, based on the estimated bitrate-accuracy trade-offs learned by the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler. This approach allows for real-time bitrate adaptation, ensuring that the generated image respects the available bandwidth while maintaining optimal quality.
CONTROLS: Compare with the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the compressed diffusion model to evaluate the benefits of adaptive compression matching. Use a dataset of high-resolution images with varying complexities.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive compression matching algorithm should demonstrate improved bitrate efficiency and quality, outperforming both the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the compressed diffusion model, especially under time-varying bandwidth constraints.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: joint bitrate-aware diffusion training
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel training framework that jointly optimizes the diffusion model, the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler, and the adaptive compression matching algorithm to achieve a balanced solution that respects the bitrate budget while preserving high image quality. Use a hierarchical optimization approach, where the model is trained to minimize a combination of image quality metrics and the estimated bitrate.
CONTROLS: Compare with separate training and adaptation of the diffusion model, bitrate-aware diffusion sampler, and adaptive compression matching algorithm to evaluate the benefits of joint training. Validate the approach using a real-world image transmission application.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Joint bitrate-aware diffusion training should produce a model that achieves superior bitrate-accuracy trade-offs, outperforming the separate training approach, but may require a larger model size and more computationally expensive training due to the additional optimizer.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: adaptive compression matching
PROPOSAL: Modify the adaptive compression matching algorithm (Proposal 3) to incorporate a bitrate-effective distortion metric, such as structural similarity (SSIM) or perceptual quality (PQ), which balances the trade-off between visual quality and bitrate. This modification enables the adaptive compression matching algorithm to more effectively optimize the compression process and reduce the required bitrate while maintaining high image quality.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original adaptive compression matching algorithm (Proposal 3) and the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler to evaluate the benefits of incorporating a bitrate-effective distortion metric.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised adaptive compression matching algorithm should achieve better bitrate efficiency and higher quality images, surpassing the original adaptation approach and competitive with the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler, while maintaining efficient bitrate control under a wide range of bandwidth conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: partial image rendering
PROPOSAL: Develop a partial image rendering technique that selectively renders regions of an image with varying resolutions, based on the available bandwidth and the importance of each region. Use the adaptive compression matching algorithm (Proposal 3) to compress the rendered regions and adaptively adjust their resolutions based on the estimated bitrate and visual quality.
CONTROLS: Compare with the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the joint bitrate-aware diffusion training approach to evaluate the benefits of partial image rendering. Use a dataset of complex images with varying scene compositions.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The partial image rendering technique should achieve significant bitrate efficiency improvements and preserve high image quality, outperforming both the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the joint bitrate-aware diffusion training approach, especially for large and dynamic images.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: dynamic bitrate scheduling
PROPOSAL: Design a dynamic bitrate scheduling framework that adjusts the bitrate of an image transmission based on real-time network conditions, user preferences, and content demands. Use the partial image rendering technique (Proposal 5) to render the image in multiple resolutions and allocate bandwidth dynamically based on the estimated bitrate and visual quality of each region.
CONTROLS: Compare with static bitrate scheduling approaches, such as fixed bitrate allocation or adaptive bitrate allocation using image features, to evaluate the benefits of dynamic bitrate scheduling. Validate the approach using a real-world network simulation.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The dynamic bitrate scheduling framework should achieve optimal bitrate-accuracy trade-offs and efficiently allocate bandwidth under varying network conditions, outperforming static scheduling approaches, but may require a more complex system architecture and communication protocol.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: dynamic bitrate scheduling
PROPOSAL: Extend the dynamic bitrate scheduling framework (Proposal 6) to incorporate machine learning-based prediction of network conditions and user preferences, allowing for proactive bitrate planning and real-time adjustments. Use the joint bitrate-aware diffusion training approach (Proposal 4) to train a model that learns to predict optimal bitrate allocation and rendering decisions based on these factors.

PREDICTION: The revised dynamic bitrate scheduling framework with machine learning-based prediction and proactive planning should outperform other approaches in terms of optimizing bitrate-accuracy trade-offs, reducing transmission latency, and improving overall user experience, but may require larger training datasets and higher computational resources.

Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) generate discrete data by iteratively replacing masked tokens with predicted unmasked ones, learning to reverse an absorbing-state diffusion process that progressively masks the tokens of a sequence. They have recently achieved strong results across diverse domains, including text generation, image synthesis, and multi-modal understanding and generation. For images, a pre-trained tokenizer (e.g., a VQ-VAE) maps an image to a sequence of discrete tokens and its decoder reconstructs the image from those tokens; generation starts from a fully masked sequence and fills it in over many steps, which makes inference time- and compute-intensive. Building on this success, recent work has shown that these multi-step procedures can be distilled into one-step generators, substantially accelerating inference and reducing computational cost while maintaining competitive quality. For instance, Di[M]O distills a multi-step MDM into a one-step generator through on-policy distribution matching: a one-step prediction sampled from the student is corrupted by the forward masking process, and the teacher's and the student's output distributions conditioned on this intermediate state are matched, with the resulting gradient applied directly to the student's logits so that it never has to pass through the non-differentiable sampling operation.

Despite their remarkable performance, current one-step discrete generators face two fundamental limitations. First, they inherit both modeling and alignment errors from the teacher: existing distillation approaches implicitly assume that the teacher fully captures the target distribution, so imperfections in the teacher's generative modeling and the under-alignment of the pre-trained teacher with downstream preferences are both transmitted to the student during data-free distillation. Second, their discrete token outputs block gradient flow. This prevents the application of key refinement techniques that are widely used to improve one-step generators distilled from continuous diffusion models, such as adversarial (GAN) training, differentiable reward fine-tuning, and test-time optimization of the generator's input with respect to a reward. In text-to-image generation, for example, prompt-following and aesthetic quality are the two primary criteria, and the community increasingly relies on learned reward models and human-preference signals to optimize them directly; but because such rewards operate on decoded images, their gradients cannot pass through the tokenizer decoder and the sampled tokens back to a discrete generator. As a result, current distilled MDM generators have limited flexibility to leverage external knowledge, such as real data, or to incorporate user preferences to better align with downstream objectives.

The gradient-blocking problem is common across discrete modeling tasks. Adversarial training on discrete data, for instance, is challenging because the discriminator must compare generated samples with ground truth while the sampling process is non-differentiable. Prior remedies include policy-gradient estimators such as REINFORCE, which are unbiased but whose gradient variance becomes prohibitive when hundreds or thousands of tokens are generated at once, and differentiable relaxations of discrete tokens such as Gumbel-Softmax (often used with a straight-through estimator) and soft-argmax. However, these methods often introduce biased or high-variance gradients and numerical instabilities, and they have not been systematically applied to one-step discrete generators, in particular for fast visual generation. Moreover, the downstream objectives of interest, such as discriminators and reward models, act on continuous inputs such as the images produced by the tokenizer decoder, so a practical solution must let gradients flow through the existing generation pipeline.

This raises two questions. How can the outputs of a one-step generator distilled from an MDM be made amenable to end-to-end gradient-based training, with gradients that are stable, low-variance and faithful to the true discrete objective, while remaining compatible with the existing teacher and tokenizer? And, once such gradients are available, can post-distillation refinements (adversarial training, differentiable reward fine-tuning, and test-time optimization of the generator's input) let a one-step student correct the errors it inherits from its teacher and better align with downstream objectives such as distribution fidelity, prompt adherence and aesthetic quality?

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) exhibit compelling cross-modal perception and reasoning capabilities on image-text data and have become the de facto standard for visual question answering (VQA), the task of answering a question based on the visual content of an image. However, standard MLLM architectures are not well suited to perceiving and reasoning about small visual details in high-resolution images. So-called global-view MLLMs downscale every input image to the base resolution of their vision encoder (for some widely used models only 224×224 or 336×336 pixels), which discards information; as a consequence, they perform poorly on fine-grained VQA, i.e., on questions whose answer depends on small visual details. Unlike common VQA settings, in which the question-relevant objects are typically prominent in the image, fine-grained VQA concerns targets that may occupy only a tiny fraction of a large, high-resolution image.

More recent global-local-view MLLMs process a downsampled global view together with local crops extracted from the original, unresized image. This dual-view strategy reduces information loss, but it multiplies the number of visual tokens, and because self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length, the computational cost grows rapidly. Moreover, despite having access to fine-grained visual details from all local crops, these models struggle to identify the few visual tokens that are relevant to the question amid the large number of local crop tokens, so their effectiveness on fine-grained VQA still remains limited.

An orthogonal line of work is visual cropping: searching the image for the regions that are relevant to the question and passing only those regions to the MLLM. Existing visual cropping techniques, however, suffer from one or more of three limitations. First, some depend on task-specific fine-tuning: SEAL, for instance, pairs the answering model with a separate visual-search MLLM equipped with additional decoders that is fine-tuned to predict object heatmaps and coordinates, and runs a recursive top-down search, a complex multi-module design that is costly to run. Second, several rely on uninformed, exhaustive search: DC² builds a hierarchical tree of image regions and captions each region with the MLLM, while ZoomEye traverses a hierarchical region tree and scores every visited region with three sequential MLLM forward passes using different prompts, a computation that cannot be simplified or shared across regions, so the cost grows quickly with the depth and breadth of the search. Third, ViCrop avoids hierarchical search by directly computing a question-guided heatmap, but its best-performing variants depend on query-key attention weights and answer gradients, which makes them incompatible with efficient attention implementations such as FlashAttention that never explicitly produce attention weights. Simply asking the MLLM where the target is does not solve the problem either: although many MLLMs are fine-tuned to predict bounding boxes, they often fail when prompted directly for the location of small objects, producing hallucinated or imprecise coordinates.

The open problem is therefore how to make an MLLM look at the right part of a high-resolution image. Can the image regions relevant to a fine-grained visual question be localized without task-specific fine-tuning or auxiliary modules, without an uninformed exhaustive search over the image, and in a way that remains compatible with efficient attention implementations? Can such localization benefit both global-view and global-local-view MLLMs, improving their answers to questions about small details while keeping inference cost low, given that MLLM inference is already computationally expensive? And how favorable an accuracy-efficiency trade-off can be reached relative to existing search-based visual cropping methods?

Transporting mass between probability distributions is a ubiquitous problem in machine learning and beyond. Optimal transport (OT) provides a principled approach to such problems by seeking to minimise the total cost of transportation under a chosen cost function, and computational OT, from Sinkhorn's algorithm to more recent neural approaches, has been applied successfully in domains such as biology and extensively within machine learning. More recently, ideas from the flow-based approaches that have revolutionised generative modelling have been leveraged to solve the entropy-regularised dynamic OT problem known as the Schrödinger bridge (SB): finding the most likely evolution of a population between two prescribed distributions, relative to a reference stochastic process. With a Brownian reference process, the static form of this problem is exactly entropy-regularised OT for the quadratic cost. Flow-based SB solvers offer significant scalability advantages, enabling the approximation of OT maps between high-dimensional continuous datasets such as images. Early flow-based solvers were built on the classical Iterative Proportional Fitting (IPF) scheme, which preserves both marginals only at convergence, requires expensive caching of simulated trajectories and tends to 'forget' the reference measure; such methods have since been superseded by solvers based on the Iterative Markovian Fitting (IMF) scheme, which avoids these issues.

Beyond the standard two-marginal problem, multi-marginal OT seeks a joint coupling over several marginals that minimises a total cost. Tree-structured costs are often considered, as they frequently arise in applications while allowing improved scalability by exploiting the tree structure. In the corresponding tree-structured SB problem, stochastic processes run along the edges of a tree and marginals are prescribed only at a subset of the vertices; with Brownian motion along each edge as the reference, it is an entropy-regularised multi-marginal OT problem with a tree-structured quadratic cost. Star-shaped trees, with marginals fixed on the leaves and an unknown centre, are of particular significance because they correspond to an entropy-regularised form of the Wasserstein barycentre problem. The Wasserstein barycentre provides a natural notion of 'average' for probability distributions and is widely studied because of its importance in applications such as Bayesian learning, clustering and representation learning. Computing barycentres is notoriously challenging. Many successful approaches approximate the solution with a finite set of points, but such in-sample methods struggle to scale as dimensionality increases and cannot generate new samples; alternative methods provide continuous approximations through neural parameterisations, but often require multi-level or adversarial optimisation procedures. To date, the only neural ODE/SDE approach to barycentre computation extends the IPF-based diffusion Schrödinger bridge to the tree-structured SB setting, and therefore inherits the drawbacks of IPF; it has been reported to suffer training instability at low entropic regularisation, struggling to match the prescribed marginals at the vertices.

In parallel, one of the most successful approaches to Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation is the iterative fixed-point method, which repeatedly updates a candidate barycentre by solving for the OT map from it to each marginal and pushing it forward through the weighted average of these maps. It performs strongly and has been observed to converge in only a few iterations, but every iteration requires solving a complete OT problem to each marginal, which is expensive because solving even a single OT problem can be challenging.

This raises several questions. Can a scalable, flow-based solver be built for the tree-structured SB problem, and hence for entropic Wasserstein barycentres, that avoids the shortcomings of IPF-based schemes while being guaranteed to converge to the tree-structured SB solution? In the barycentre case, can the fast convergence of fixed-point schemes be retained without paying for a complete OT solve to every marginal at every iteration? And can flow-based barycentre solvers of this kind offer a viable alternative to existing algorithms for continuous Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation?

Graphs are powerful abstractions for representing complex relationships between entities, from social networks to molecular structures, and learning effective graph representations is crucial for node classification, graph classification and link prediction. Over the past decade, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become the dominant paradigm for graph representation learning, building representations through a message-passing mechanism that iteratively aggregates local neighborhood information. Despite its success, message passing faces several key limitations, such as limited expressiveness and difficulty in capturing long-range dependencies. Numerous efforts address different aspects of these limitations: graph transformer architectures incorporate long-range interactions across broader graph contexts, positional encodings inject structural priors to improve global topological awareness, and graph rewiring techniques modify the topology to mitigate structural bottlenecks and enhance information diffusion.

However, these advances remain constrained by a cognitive discrepancy. Humans perceive global structure intuitively, following visual Gestalt principles: they understand the whole before analyzing the individual parts. GNNs and their variants, by contrast, operate through bottom-up processing. People instantly recognize ring structures, symmetric structures and critical bridges in a drawing of a graph, yet even advanced architectures struggle with such basic topological understanding: standard message-passing networks provably cannot identify bridges, and graphs that people tell apart at a glance can fool message passing unless sophisticated topological computations are added. Although architectural innovations have made significant theoretical and practical progress, their essence is still to identify and repair different aspects of the inherent defects of message passing. Approaches that perceive graphs visually remain largely unexplored for graph learning, despite their natural alignment with how humans perceive network structures, and despite a flourishing computer vision ecosystem whose models excel at holistic pattern recognition and global structure understanding. Recent work has begun to bring graph drawings into existing architectures, for instance into vision-language models for graph reasoning or into GNNs to enhance expressivity, but it treats graph layouts and vision models as black boxes, without examining how visual and message-passing models fundamentally differ in the way they understand graphs.

A second obstacle is measurement. Established benchmarks built from molecules, citation networks or protein interaction graphs tightly couple domain-specific node features with topology, which makes their separate contributions hard to quantify and can let models succeed through feature-based shortcuts rather than genuine structural understanding. Models that replace the true molecular topology with fixed-structure expander graphs have been shown to match or exceed performance on several molecular benchmarks, suggesting that node features often dominate structural information in standard datasets, potentially masking differences in how models perceive graph topology. The theoretical evaluation of GNNs has centered on the Weisfeiler-Lehman test, which measures the ability to distinguish pairs of non-isomorphic graphs of the same size; valuable for theory, it is limited to binary discrimination between fixed-size graph pairs. Recent graph benchmarks oriented toward large language models focus on structural analysis tasks such as node counting, cycle detection and path finding, and typically rely on a limited set of random graph generators (such as Erdős–Rényi or Watts–Strogatz) that inadequately capture topological diversity. What remains missing is a way to assess human-like graph cognition: the intuitive ability to perceive, abstract and reason about fundamental global graph properties, and to recognize the same connectivity patterns across varying scales and contexts.

This leads to the questions addressed here. Could models designed for visual perception, which carry no graph-specific inductive bias, offer a viable pathway to graph structural understanding, and do they process graph information in the same way as message-passing GNNs or through fundamentally different strategies? How can a model's ability to perceive and abstract global graph properties be evaluated rigorously, in isolation from domain-specific features, including whether it recognizes the same structural pattern regardless of graph size? And what does it take for a graph learning model to acquire the holistic, scale-robust understanding of topology that humans display effortlessly?

Large language models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress across a wide range of natural language understanding and generation tasks, but their massive parameter counts demand prohibitively large computational and memory resources for both training and deployment. Even in settings with a reasonable amount of compute, training or fine-tuning such models remains challenging.

One promising way to reduce the computational burden of fine-tuning is low-precision floating-point (FP) arithmetic such as FP8. Modern accelerators (e.g., NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, AMD CDNA 3, Google TPUs) increasingly support low-precision FP arithmetic natively, and FP8 can theoretically double the throughput of FP16 matrix multiplication. Because FP8 formats (such as E4M3 or E5M2) have a narrow representable range, a higher-precision tensor must first be scaled by a per-tensor factor obtained from a max-reduction over its absolute values, and then scaled element-wise and rounded, before the low-precision multiplication can run. This quantization overhead is memory-bound and grows quadratically with matrix size, whereas the cost of matrix multiplication grows cubically. As a consequence, FP8 is known to accelerate mainly large-dimensional matrix multiplications (empirically, when each matrix dimension exceeds roughly 4K elements), while small-dimensional computations can even suffer an unexpected slowdown.

These overheads are especially critical for low-rank adaptation (LoRA), a widely used approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning. LoRA keeps the pretrained weights frozen and inserts small trainable low-rank matrices (adapters) that capture task-specific knowledge, greatly reducing memory cost by training few parameters. For such small-dimensional matrices, the overhead of FP8 quantization can outweigh the gains of FP8 multiplication, and the separate forward and backward paths of the adapters add further quantization operations at every iteration. Yet fast LoRA fine-tuning matters in practice: many applications require training numerous adapters, for example one adapter per user for personalized recommendation or personalized alignment from human feedback, task-specific adapters for multi-task learning and mixtures of LoRA experts, adapters for different domains, multilingual summarization, and rapid updates in dynamic, user-specific environments. Efficiently accelerating LoRA fine-tuning is therefore essential for timely, scalable and cost-effective adaptation of LLMs under practical computational constraints.

Existing lines of work leave this gap open. Quantized LoRA methods (such as QLoRA with 4-bit NormalFloat weights, QA-LoRA with group-wise INT4 weights, and follow-ups that refine the quantization with integer linear programming, SVD-based adapter initialization, dynamic rank allocation or information recovery) compress the frozen backbone through weight-only quantization. They focus on memory efficiency rather than fine-tuning speed: the added quantization and dequantization often make them slower than standard LoRA, and weight-only quantization cannot exploit hardware acceleration of low-precision matrix multiplication. Conversely, FP8 training methods (hybrid E4M3/E5M2 formats, mixed-precision FP8 training with high-precision master weights, studies of large-scale FP8 stability and outliers, unit scaling) are designed for the large-dimensional matrices of full LLM training, not for the small matrices that characterize LoRA.

This raises the following questions. How large is the quantization overhead when FP8 arithmetic is applied to LoRA fine-tuning, which parts of the computation does it come from, and does it persist across typical adapter ranks? Can LoRA fine-tuning be organized so that it genuinely benefits from native FP8 arithmetic, delivering real end-to-end speedups over existing quantized LoRA methods, while retaining the memory savings that make LoRA attractive and reaching accuracy comparable to existing quantized LoRA fine-tuning?

Modern problem-solving increasingly relies on neural networks, which encode vast amounts of information in their trainable parameters during learning, with applications ranging from computer vision and natural language processing to the natural sciences. While these parameters capture rich knowledge, accessing and interpreting it remains a challenge.

Metanetworks were introduced to analyze and process other neural networks by treating their weights, gradients and sparsity patterns as structured inputs. Early work focused on evaluating the generalization of trained networks and revealing properties of their behavior, commonly by flattening the parameters or extracting statistics from them before feeding them into multi-layer perceptrons. Metanetworks have since been applied to extracting structure from implicit neural representations, learning optimizers, editing models, evaluating policies and enabling Bayesian inference. Designing them nevertheless remains challenging because of the complexity and high dimensionality of the structures they operate on.

A major difficulty is functional equivalence: many distinct parameter configurations realize the same input-output function. Swapping two hidden units of a multi-layer perceptron leaves its input-output mapping unchanged, provided their outgoing connections are permuted accordingly, and for networks with tanh activations the input-output mapping is known to determine the architecture and the weights up to permutations and sign flips. Such identifiability results have been extended to broader classes of multi-layer perceptrons and to convolutional networks, and recent work has characterized the symmetry groups of multihead attention and mixture-of-experts layers, establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for functional equivalence. The parameter space is thus only a proxy for the underlying function class, and the map from parameters to functions is not injective. A metanetwork that relies solely on raw parameters therefore risks overlooking the symmetries of the architecture it processes, and may produce incompatible outputs for two networks that compute exactly the same function.

Building on the permutation symmetry of hidden neurons, permutation-equivariant metanetworks have been developed that account for neuron reordering within hidden layers, and more recent architectures extend beyond permutations by incorporating additional symmetries such as scaling and sign changes. Equivariance (for metanetworks that output weights) or invariance (for metanetworks that output predictions) with respect to a symmetry group of the processed architecture guarantees that different parameterizations of the same function are treated consistently. However, these approaches enforce strict equivariance at the level of individual weights, which imposes rigid constraints on the layers and often leads to sparse, less expressive models. Yet the true goal is not to preserve the weights themselves but the functions they implement, that is, to respect the functional equivalence classes of the parameters. Strict equivariance is a sufficient way to achieve this, but it is not clear that it is necessary.

Relaxed or approximate equivariance has emerged elsewhere in deep learning to handle imperfect symmetries in real-world data, for instance through relaxed convolution weights, soft constraints added to the training objective or relaxed group convolutions, and its bias-variance trade-offs have been analyzed theoretically. These relaxations were, however, developed for symmetries that only approximately hold, and often treat equivariance as something to be approximated. In weight space, by contrast, the symmetries are exact and are precisely what defines functional equivalence, so it is unclear how weight-level equivariance could be loosened without breaking the guarantee that functionally equivalent inputs are processed consistently.

This raises several questions. Is strict equivariance necessary for metanetworks? What is the right requirement for a map acting on weights to preserve functional identity, so that functionally equivalent inputs always yield functionally equivalent outputs, and can a requirement weaker than strict equivariance meet it? Can metanetwork layers satisfying such a requirement be built in a principled, practical and trainable way for the architectures whose weights metanetworks commonly process, such as feedforward, convolutional and multihead attention networks? And would moving beyond strict equivariance in this way give metanetworks a better trade-off between symmetry preservation and representational expressivity in practice?
