ACTION: ADD
TITLE: manipulating symmetry constraints for metanetworks
PROPOSAL: Explore the theoretical implications of modifying the symmetry constraints imposed on weights in metanetworks to relax strict equivariance. Specifically, we will derive a formal framework for relaxing permuto-equivariance by introducing a penalty term that measures the deviation from pointwise equivariance in the space of weight permutations. The goal is to provide a principled approach for balancing symmetry preservation and representational expressivity.
CONTROLS: Compare the derived relaxed framework with the existing strict permuto-equivariant architectures and assess their performance in various settings (multiple architectures, loss functions, dataset sizes).
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed framework will provide a better trade-off between accuracy and efficiency, while maintaining the capability to process and learn from multiple symmetries; However, tuning the penalty term may lead to brittle behavior in certain scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: characterizing the space of functionally equivalent weights
PROPOSAL: Investigate the topological properties of the space of weights in a deep neural network, focusing on the quotient space obtained by taking into account the symmetries that leave the input-output function invariant. Through a combination of algebraic topology and deep learning techniques, we will characterize the connectivity and holes in this space, providing insights into the number of distinct, functionally equivalent weight configurations. This understanding will inform the design of more efficient and robust metanetworks.
CONTROLS: Compare the results from different classes of neural networks (e.g., fully-connected, convolutional, recurrent) and loss functions to understand their impact on the topology of the weight space.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The study will reveal that the weight space exhibits a complex topological structure, with multiple holes and connected components; however, the specific characteristics may vary significantly depending on the network architecture and loss function used.

Generative models significantly enhance the efficiency of chemical space exploration in drug discovery by directly sampling molecules with desired properties. However, a key bottleneck in their practical deployment is low synthetic accessibility: generated molecules are often difficult or impossible to produce in the laboratory. To address this limitation, recent work has turned to template-based methods that emulate the chemical synthesis process by constructing synthesis trees that link molecular building blocks through known reaction templates. These representations, while useful for downstream experimental validation, do not describe the underlying 3D geometry and thus cannot capitalize on the conformational information that is often crucial for diverse chemical and biological properties.

Parallel advances in generative molecular design have explored spatial modeling at the atomic level. Inspired by advances in protein structure prediction and by generative frameworks such as diffusion and flow matching, recent work has focused on directly sampling 3D atomic coordinates of small molecules, learning to generate spatially meaningful, property-aligned conformations along with molecular graphs. The ability to model atomic coordinates directly increases the expressivity of these approaches, enabling applications such as pocket-conditioned generation, scaffold hopping, analog discovery, and molecular optimization. However, without considering practical synthesis routes, integrating synthesizability constraints into these models remains a major challenge, and most existing 3D generative approaches do not ensure that proposed molecules can be made in practice. While recent work has addressed synthesizability for 2D molecular graphs, extending such constraints to 3D, and to geometry-based conditional generation, remains largely unexplored.

Several obstacles stand in the way. Directly optimizing synthesizability scores is often unreliable, so the predominant route to synthetic accessibility has been to assemble molecules from commercially available building blocks joined by known reaction templates; yet such generators typically emit only molecular graphs and no atomic coordinates. The representations commonly available for 3D work are also ill-suited to synthesis awareness: synthon-based representations do not guarantee that a valid synthesis route exists, do not provide one even when it does, and lack the flexibility to constrain the reaction space, which matters when one wants to prioritize high-yield, high-reliability reactions or to remain within the limits of automated synthesis platforms. Relying instead on external, black-box reaction simulators to couple building blocks offers no fine-grained control when a reagent has several reaction centers, and such steps do not define atom mappings between reactants and products, making it impossible to trace product atoms back to their parent building blocks. A further difficulty is that most 3D molecule generation methods require the number of atoms to be specified in advance, which is awkward when the identity of the constituent building blocks is itself still being decided. Finally, the few approaches that do couple synthesis pathways with 3D structure optimize an external reward and typically require a full training run for each target pocket, which is costly and exposes the generator to reward hacking.

This raises the central questions. Can a single generative model sample small molecules so that each sample comes with both a physically realistic 3D conformation and an explicit, traceable route by which it could actually be made, instead of treating geometry and synthesizability as separate concerns handled in sequence or by post hoc filtering? What kind of data and molecular representation would such a model require, given that existing conformer datasets carry no synthesis information and existing synthesis-aware representations carry no geometry? How should synthesizability and geometric quality be measured so that claims of practical makeability are credible rather than an artifact of the scoring tool used? And can one amortized model, once trained, serve the geometry-conditioned design problems that drug discovery actually poses, such as completing or connecting parts of a known three-dimensional ligand, or designing novel molecules that reproduce a desired spatial arrangement of interaction features for a target, without external scoring functions and without retraining for each new target?

Understanding how a scene has changed and forecasting how it will look next from Satellite Image Time Series (SITS) is fundamental to many critical applications, yet it poses a profound challenge: predicting the future requires a deep understanding of past change. Two tasks are central. In temporal change description, given a sequence of temporally ordered satellite images of the same area, the goal is to generate a natural-language description that accurately summarizes the key dynamic changes that occurred over the observation period, such as urban expansion or agricultural cycles; this requires comprehending the temporal evolution and, ideally, the underlying causal narrative of the changes. In future satellite image forecasting, given the same historical sequence, the goal is to generate a plausible image for the next time point. A critical and often overlooked requirement is that the forecast be temporally consistent: the generated changes should be a logical continuation of the trends and dynamics observed in the historical data, not merely a plausible standalone picture.

Although foundation models such as Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and diffusion-based image generators have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their application to this domain remains fragmented and fundamentally limited. On the understanding side, static image captioning ignores temporal context, while existing temporal change description methods lack the semantic depth of MLLMs: they fuse information across images through simple interactions, their long-range temporal reasoning is limited, and they struggle to capture why changes occur. General-purpose MLLMs, even video-capable ones, are not optimized for this setting either: video-centric models are typically tuned for densely sampled frames with fixed, short intervals, whereas consecutive satellite acquisitions are sparse and irregular, with gaps that can span several years. On the generation side, single-image synthesis cannot model evolution, and temporal forecasting approaches struggle with long-term consistency because they do not grasp the semantic drivers of change: their conditioning is typically low-level (e.g., edge maps), based on simple metadata, or limited to text guidance, and it lacks fine-grained temporal semantic interaction, so they can generate what a scene looks like but cannot reason about why it should look that way given its history. As a result, change understanding and future forecasting have been treated as disjointed tasks, even though both are limited by a common bottleneck: modeling long-range temporal dynamics.

This raises several questions. How can a model reason about why changes occurred across a long, irregularly sampled sequence of satellite images, and describe them accurately? How can such an understanding of past change be used to generate what will happen next, so that the forecast is a temporally consistent continuation of the observed trajectory rather than only a realistic-looking image? Can enhancing long-range temporal understanding improve performance on both tasks simultaneously, with the understanding of past change directly informing the forecast? Finally, how can the temporal consistency of a forecast be rigorously evaluated, given that standard image-quality metrics cannot penalize a prediction that is perceptually realistic but inconsistent with historical trends?

Geometry reconstruction is a fundamental problem that enables a wide range of applications in fields such as virtual reality and robotics. In recent years, neural reconstruction methods have gained significant attention; a key advantage of these methods is their ability to represent the geometry of a scene continuously, which can help in many downstream tasks. However, vision-based sensors often struggle in adverse weather conditions, or even become completely unusable when objects are obscured by occlusions.

Radio frequency (RF) sensing, specifically wireless millimeter-wave (mmWave) sensing, can see through occlusions, remains robust under challenging visibility conditions and, unlike X-rays, is not dangerous to humans, making it a compelling alternative for 3D reconstruction. This could open up many applications, for example checking whether the items inside a box are the correct items, are damaged, or pose a threat, without ever opening the box. On the other hand, mmWave resolution is extremely low compared to vision: a single radar image provides far less visual context than a camera image, which makes it hard to extract a 3D reconstruction from one radar image alone. Some prior RF systems have performed 3D point cloud reconstruction or human body tracking by leveraging movement or by emulating larger antenna apertures, but the recovered point clouds are still too sparse and noisy to reliably recover detailed geometry; through-wall human sensing relies on human motion to combat specularity, and deep learning on mmWave radar data has mostly targeted self-driving scenarios, where image resolution matters little. Other works have proposed neural implicit representations for RF sensing, aiming to concentrate scene information out of heavy noise through neural optimization, but these systems are designed for large-scale environments such as streets or satellite imagery and are far from achieving millimeter-level precision. When objects are close to the radar, the propagation characteristics of RF signals change dramatically: incoming waves can no longer be approximated as planar, so processing methods designed for large-scale scenes, such as beamforming, introduce a considerable amount of distortion and noise, often exceeding the noise acceptable for gradient descent and leading to unstable optimization. Existing neural RF reconstruction work is thus either limited to far-range scenes or, for individual objects, evaluated only on simulated data, which for wireless signals cannot come close to representing the complexity of real-world measurements. Meanwhile, the multi-view reconstruction and inverse rendering methods of computer vision (multi-view stereo, neural radiance fields, Gaussian splatting, neural implicit surfaces, physically based inverse rendering) are all derived from RGB images and are not easily transferable to mmWave data: even lensless RGB images can be mapped back to a lens-based imaging model without altering the underlying ray physics, whereas for RF signals such a transformation is fundamentally invalid.

The open problem is therefore to overcome the fundamental dilemma between massive RF noise in the input and the reconstruction of complete, high-resolution, millimeter-level 3D surface geometry of near-range objects, including objects hidden behind occlusions. This is not straightforward, because inferring surface geometry from RF signals differs fundamentally from image-based reconstruction in three main ways. First, wireless systems lack a lens-based imaging model: whereas lenses filter and focus the relevant light rays, radar antenna arrays perform lensless imaging and capture all incoming RF signals without directional filtering, which leads to low signal-to-noise ratios because irrelevant signals cannot be excluded. Second, RF signals and visible light propagate differently: visible light is predominantly scattered diffusely by surfaces, whereas RF signals, whose wavelengths are on the order of millimeters, are dominated by specular reflections, so volumetric rendering techniques designed for scattering-based vision sensors are unsuitable for RF imaging. Third, physically modeling lensless RF measurements is computationally expensive: whereas lens-based rendering samples along 1D rays, modeling what each antenna receives requires accounting for contributions from the full 3D space, leading to cubic complexity that makes naive implementations intractable at millimeter resolution.

How can accurate, millimeter-level 3D geometry of near-range objects be reconstructed from noisy real-world RF measurements, in line of sight and through occlusions, despite lensless imaging, specular reflections and the cost of modeling signal contributions from the full 3D space?

Visual localization of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) is essential for applications such as digital-twin modeling, mapping, surveillance, large-area and infrastructure inspection, and search-and-rescue operations, yet it faces challenges that ground-level localization systems do not address. Ground-level approaches benefit from similar viewpoints between query and reference images, whereas aerial applications encounter dramatic perspective differences and must scale to large areas. In many scenarios, these systems require high-precision localization while operating with limited resources, for example without an internet connection or without GNSS/GPS support, which makes large image databases or heavy 3D models impractical.

Current UAV localization algorithms either retrieve the closest match from a database of posed images, which is inaccurate, or rely on 3D models of the scene, which are expensive in memory and computation; in resource-limited settings, such as connectivity-limited environments, this can degrade accuracy. Image retrieval methods based on global descriptors struggle with the large viewpoint and illumination changes of UAV imagery, and even with view synthesis or self-supervised learning their performance drops under extreme perspective shifts, so retrieval alone remains insufficient for accurate 6-DoF localization. Structure-based methods build a 3D model with structure-from-motion, establish 2D-3D correspondences against meshes or dense depth maps, and estimate the pose with PnP solvers inside RANSAC, but such complete 3D models require extensive manual effort to create for each operational area. Most UAV-specific positioning methods estimate only 2-DoF or 3-DoF poses rather than the full 6-DoF pose required by advanced applications. Recent approaches based on level-of-detail (LoD) city models improve storage efficiency, but they still assume unchanged environments, perform poorly in building-sparse areas such as highways, and depend on positioning sensors for initialization.

A compelling alternative is geodata, such as orthographic aerial views (digital orthophotos) and elevation maps (digital surface models). Such data are lightweight, scalable and better suited to low-resource settings, and they are increasingly accessible through free releases from government geoportals, for instance in the European Union; where public access is limited, they can be synthesized with photogrammetric tools. For example, covering an area of approximately 0.265 km² can require a 3D model of around 8 GB, whereas geodata require about 30 times less memory. Surprisingly, no existing UAV localization approach seems to fully leverage these data sources: previous work has not used the combination of orthophotos and elevation models for UAV pose estimation, so no existing method is directly applicable to this scenario. Modern feature matchers (dense, semi-dense, sparse, and geometry-aware) perform robustly in many scenarios, but their effectiveness with orthographic geodata remains unexplored. A major reason for this gap is the absence of aligned cross-domain datasets and of full-pose, paired, large-scale benchmarks designed for localization with these types of geodata. Existing UAV localization datasets provide only partial pose information (2-DoF or 3-DoF), feature predominantly nadir views with limited viewpoint diversity, rely on entirely synthetic environments or synthetically rendered views that introduce domain gaps, or lack integrated geodata; the one concurrent collection that includes orthographic geodata focuses its pose evaluation on 3-DoF and suffers from a misalignment between its low-resolution satellite imagery and its aerial photogrammetry data. Furthermore, visual localization methods often need to solve image retrieval before estimating the pose; because these two steps are coupled, it is difficult to disentangle the contribution of each component to the final error.

The problem is therefore the following: given an orthophoto raster, an elevation raster, and a query UAV image taken from an arbitrary viewpoint, determine the georeferenced 6-DoF pose of the camera (localization) and, optionally, its intrinsic parameters (calibration). The key challenge is bridging two fundamentally different projection models: perspective projection for UAV imagery and orthographic projection for geodata. This difference creates a domain gap that is particularly pronounced in oblique views, where perspective distortion is significant. A second domain gap arises from visual and structural discrepancies between query and reference data caused by differences in acquisition time: reference geodata may have been collected months or years before a flight, so orthophotos differ in appearance (color shifts, illumination variations, seasonal differences) and elevation models differ in geometry (construction changes, vegetation growth, infrastructure evolution). These changes vary unpredictably across locations and seasons, cannot easily be addressed through simple data augmentation or domain adaptation, and cannot be faithfully replicated by synthetic alternatives.

This raises several open questions. Can lightweight 2.5D orthographic geodata serve as the only reference for accurate full 6-DoF UAV pose estimation and camera calibration? Can state-of-the-art feature matchers, designed largely for perspective imagery, bridge the perspective-orthographic gap, especially for oblique viewpoints, and how can the perspective disparity between query and reference be reduced? How difficult is it to recover camera intrinsics from aerial imagery in this setting? And how do characteristics of the reference data, namely temporal visual and structural domain shifts, data resolution, and the covisibility between the query image and the reference area (which depends on imperfect upstream retrieval), affect localization accuracy?

Knowledge distillation is a fundamental technique in machine learning, widely used for model compression, transfer learning, and improving generalization. Its core idea is to transfer knowledge from a "teacher" model to a (typically smaller) "student" model by training the student to match the teacher's output probabilities rather than categorical one-hot labels. This softened supervision has been shown to improve performance across a range of tasks. Consequently, a substantial body of research has focused on designing distillation mechanisms, such as dynamic temperature scaling, feature-based distillation, and task-aware teacher-student matching, typically assuming a large teacher that is optimized to maximize its own performance.

Despite its widespread adoption, the theoretical foundations of knowledge distillation remain only partially understood. In particular, the impact of the teacher's output probabilities on the student's optimization trajectory and generalization has not been fully characterized. Existing explanations attribute the usefulness of distillation to the regularizing effect of the teacher's soft estimates, to trade-offs such as precision versus recall or knowledge inheritance versus exploration, or to factors such as data geometry and optimization bias. Insights into how distillation affects the optimization itself have been developed only for special cases, such as self-distillation or a student that is a compressed version of the teacher, and rely on dedicated gradient approximations. A principled understanding of how distillation affects common learning algorithms, such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants, for arbitrary teachers, is still lacking.

Recent works have begun to view distillation through a Bayesian lens, interpreting the teacher's outputs as (possibly noisy) estimates of the true class posterior probabilities of the data-generating distribution. From this statistical viewpoint, learning from accurate class posteriors has been argued to reduce the variance of the student's objective, and excess-risk and generalization bounds have been derived in terms of the distance between the teacher's predictions and the true posteriors. These analyses, however, characterize the statistical properties of the risk rather than the behavior of the learning algorithm that actually trains the student. The probabilistic perspective thus opens relatively unexplored questions about the dynamics of SGD-based learning under probabilistic supervision, and about how the statistical calibration of the teacher influences the student. Teacher calibration has been recognized as a key driver of distillation, but it remains unclear how the quality of the teacher's probability estimates should guide the way teachers are built.

This raises several questions. How does supervising a student with the exact class posterior probabilities, instead of one-hot labels, change the convergence behavior and stability of SGD-based learning and the generalization of the resulting student? In the realistic case where the teacher provides only imperfect, noisy estimates of these posteriors, how does the level of estimation error affect the student's convergence, generalization and accuracy, and under what conditions does probabilistic supervision remain preferable to one-hot labels? Finally, what practical guidelines follow for designing or choosing teacher models, beyond maximizing the teacher's own accuracy, so that their outputs provide better supervision for students trained with SGD-based optimizers?

Use a partly correctly labeled dataset (e.g., corrupted versions of CIFAR-10 or ImageNet) and analyze the student's learning dynamics as a function of the noise level and its distribution. Compare the convergence behavior of the student when trained with different types of noise (e.g., Gaussian, uniform, batching noise).
CONTROLS: Baseline: training the student with perfectly labeled data; Ablations: varying the type and level of noise. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to observe an optimal level of noise above which the student's convergence degrades, and that the type of noise can significantly impact the student's learning behavior.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: investigating the dynamics of sgd under probabilistic supervision
PROPOSAL: Study the optimization dynamics of SGD when used to train a student model under probabilistic supervision from a teacher model. Analyze how the teacher's estimation errors and the student's learning behavior are impacted by the choice of learning rate, batch size, and regularization. Explore the interplay between the student's convergence behavior and the teacher's calibration.
CONTROLS: Baseline: SGD with one-hot labels; Ablations: varying the learning rate, batch size, and regularization. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to gain insights into how SGD adapts under probabilistic supervision, and how the optimization dynamics depend on the learning parameters and the teacher's estimation accuracy.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: exploring the teacher's calibration in knowledge distillation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the relationship between the teacher's calibration and the student's performance under probabilistic supervision. Consider a teacher model that outputs noisy estimates of the true class posterior probabilities and analyze how the quality of these estimates affects the student's convergence, generalization, and accuracy. Use a dataset with ground-truth posterior probabilities (e.g., from a pre-trained teacher model) to evaluate the teacher's calibration and its impact on the student.
CONTROLS: Baseline: training the student with one-hot labels; Ablations: varying the teacher's temperature and estimation accuracy. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to identify a correlation between the teacher's calibration and the student's performance, and that improved teacher calibration leads to better student generalization and accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: analyzing teacher calibration for robust knowledge distillation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the relationship between teacher calibration and robustness in knowledge distillation. Design adversarial attacks on the student model that are induced by the teacher's noisy estimates of posterior probabilities, and analyze how teacher calibration affects the student's robustness to these attacks. Evaluate the robustness of the student model using metrics such as fooling rates and robust accuracy.
CONTROLS: Baseline: training the student with one-hot labels; Ablations: varying the teacher's temperature and estimation accuracy. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to demonstrate that teacher calibration has a significant impact on the student's robustness to adversarial attacks, and that improved teacher calibration leads to more robust student models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: comparing knowledge distillation with multiple teacher models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of using multiple teacher models with different calibrations on the student's performance and robustness. Train multiple teacher models with varying temperatures and estimation accuracies, and use the output of each teacher as soft labels for the student. Compare the performance of the student models trained with single and multiple teachers, and evaluate the trade-offs between performance, robustness, and complexity.
CONTROLS: Baseline: training the student with one-hot labels; Ablations: varying the number of teachers and their calibrations. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to show that using multiple teacher models can improve the student's performance and robustness compared to single teacher models, but that the optimal combination of teachers depends on the problem and dataset.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: investigating knowledge distillation for transfer learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of knowledge distillation for transfer learning, where the teacher model is pre-trained on a different dataset and the student model is trained on a new, related dataset. Analyze the transfer of knowledge from the teacher to the student, and evaluate the impact of the teacher's calibration on the student's performance. Consider using domain adaptation techniques to align the teacher and student datasets.
CONTROLS: Baseline: training the student from scratch; Ablations: varying the pre-training dataset and transfer method. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to show that knowledge distillation can facilitate effective transfer learning, but that the choice of teacher model, calibration, and transfer method are critical to achieving good performance on the target dataset.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: practically guiding teacher design for knowledge distillation
PROPOSAL: Develop practical guidelines for designing teacher models that produce better-provided supervision for students under knowledge distillation. Consider factors such as teacher model complexity, calibration quality, and dataset size, and analyze their impact on the student's performance and robustness. Develop a framework for selecting and tuning teacher models based on the specific requirements of the task and dataset.
CONTROLS: Baseline: training the teacher on a standard benchmark dataset; Ablations: varying the teacher model architecture, calibration, and dataset size. Evaluate all methods on the same held-out test set and report the mean and standard deviation over five seeds.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to provide a set of practical guidelines for designing teacher models that produce effective supervision for students, and to demonstrate the impact of these guidelines on the student's performance and robustness across various tasks and datasets.

Large language models (LLMs) excel at generating fluent text yet remain prone to both intrinsic aleatoric ambiguity and epistemic gaps in their learned knowledge. The latter can lead to hallucinations—confident outputs that are factually incorrect. Quantifying these uncertainties is critical for building safe AI systems deployable in high-stakes applications. In free-form natural language generation tasks such as question answering, this is especially challenging, as lexically distinct responses can still be semantically equivalent: uncertainty has to be measured over meanings rather than over token sequences.

A standard way to do so defines a distribution over semantic clusters of responses, obtained by marginalizing over output sequences and approximated by Monte Carlo sampling. The total predictive uncertainty over these clusters decomposes into an aleatoric part, the entropy over clusters (semantic entropy), which captures the irreducible ambiguity among valid answers, and an epistemic part, which reflects the model's lack of knowledge or data coverage. For a question such as "Name a way to measure the Hubble constant", several distinct but correct answers (for instance, the distance ladder or gravitational lensing time delays) reflect aleatoric uncertainty, whereas answers that contradict scientific facts or admit ignorance reveal gaps in the model's knowledge and signal that it should abstain.

Estimating these quantities often relies on drawing large IID sample sets, which often contain semantically redundant outputs and waste compute. Semantic entropy quantifies aleatoric uncertainty by clustering generated outputs into semantic equivalence classes, and mutual information computed via iterative prompting has been used to lower-bound certain forms of epistemic uncertainty; despite their conceptual appeal, both require extensive sampling to produce stable estimates, limiting their use in low-resource settings. Diversity-oriented heuristics such as temperature scaling or nucleus sampling, on the other hand, do not account for semantics. A more recent method steers generation toward semantic diversity, but it relies on token substitutions and remains restricted to autoregressive models (ARMs). Moreover, diversity heuristics are commonly applied during sampling without correcting for the bias they introduce, even though the uncertainties of interest are defined under the model's own distribution.

Meanwhile, uncertainty estimation methods have focused on ARMs, whereas masked diffusion models (MDMs), which extend masked language modeling by learning iterative denoising schedules that progressively resolve masked spans, have recently emerged as strong alternatives. Despite achieving text quality on par with state-of-the-art ARMs, MDMs remain largely overlooked in the context of uncertainty quantification.

This leaves several questions open. How can stable estimates of semantic aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty be obtained for free-form answers from a small, fixed budget of generations, so that the samples cover distinct meanings instead of repeating the same ones? How can this be done while keeping the estimates faithful to the model's own predictive distribution? And can a single approach serve both autoregressive and masked diffusion language models?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: uncertainty quantification for masked diffusion models
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the feasibility of using a modified version of the recent method for steering generation toward semantic diversity to MDMs, and adapt it for use with a small, fixed budget of generations. This involves replacing the token substitutions with masked diffusion-based sampling methods and investigating the effect on semantic aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty estimates.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original token substitution approach in the context of ARMs, to see if the MDM adaptation maintains performance; ablate the effect of varying the number of mask schedules used during sampling.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The modified approach may achieve comparable or even better results for MDMs compared to the original token substitution method, especially with a small budget of generations. However, it might struggle with estimating epistemic uncertainty due to the complexity of the masked diffusion process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating aleatoric uncertainty estimates with i.i.d. sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of varying the batch size and sampling method (e.g., uniform, top-k, temperature scaling) on the stability and accuracy of semantic aleatoric uncertainty estimates using a fixed number of IID samples, focusing on maintaining semantic diversity while minimizing wasteful redundancy.
CONTROLS: Compare with the baseline I.I.D. sampling using a standard batch size and sampling method (e.g., greedy or argmax), to see the effects of batch size and sampling strategy on uncertainty estimates; explore the effect of using nested or stratified sampling to better capture semantic diversity.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that large batch sizes hinder semantic diversity, while better sampling strategies can largely mitigate this issue. However, the approach may still be computationally expensive, limiting its scalability to various applications.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 2
TITLE: exploiting semantic clusters for aleatoric uncertainty estimation
revise: Replace the proposal with a new approach that explicitly incorporates semantic clustering into the I.I.D. sampling process, leveraging a pre-trained clustering model to identify and prioritize distinct semantic clusters from a given prompt. This would enable the generation of a smaller, more diverse set of samples that better capture semantic aleatoric uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline I.I.D. sampling approach without explicit clustering, to see the effect of incorporating clustering on the accuracy and stability of aleatoric uncertainty estimates; ablate the impact of using different clustering models or thresholding strategies to select relevant clusters.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show significant improvements in the quality and accuracy of aleatoric uncertainty estimates, particularly when the sentence-level clustering model is fine-tuned on the specific question-answering task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: leveraging mutual information for epistemic uncertainty estimation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of mutual information as a lower bound for epistemic uncertainty, specifically leveraging the iterative prompting approach from previous work to estimate the mutual information between the input prompt and the generated responses, while controlling for the introduction of bias through diversity heuristics.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline approach that uses a simple variances-based estimator; ablate the effect of using different model architectures, batch sizes, and sampling methods on the resulting epistemic uncertainty estimates; compare with a known lower bound estimator using embeddings for a validation of the estimates.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that mutual information can provide a strong lower bound for epistemic uncertainty, outperforming the variance-based estimator, but the complexity and sensitivity of the method might limit its applicability in certain contexts.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 3
TITLE: better lower bounds for conditional epistemic uncertainty estimation
REVISION: Introduce a corrected and improved version of mutual information estimation that specifically targets conditional epistemic uncertainty, accounting for the input prompt and the generated responses. This involves refining the iterative prompting approach and leveraging a learned embedding space to better capture the conditional structure of the uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original proposal and validate the estimates by comparing with known and established results from other works that operate under similar contexts, with details given in the appendix.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The improved approach may significantly enhance the quality of the epistemic uncertainty estimates, closing the gap with the gold standard methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: constrained sampling for aleatoric uncertainty estimation
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel sampling approach that incorporates constraints on the generated responses, specifically designed to promote semantic diversity while controlling for ambiguity. This will be achieved through a combination of pre-trained semantic embeddings and a customized sampling algorithm, which iteratively refines the response space to better capture aleatoric uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline I.I.D. sampling approach and the clustering-based approach from proposal 2; ablate the impact of using different embedding spaces or constraint functions on the resulting uncertainty estimates, following the setup outlined in the proposal.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that the proposed constrained sampling approach can effectively balance the trade-off between semantic diversity and ambiguity, resulting in highly accurate and stable aleatoric uncertainty estimates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: analyzing the effect of sampling temperature on uncertainty estimation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of sampling temperature on semantic diversity and accuracy of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty estimates for both autoregressive and masked diffusion language models. This will be achieved through a comprehensive analysis of generated responses under various temperature settings, and the resulting uncertainty estimates compared against baseline approaches.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original sampling temperature settings used in the baseline approaches; ablate the effect of using different initial temperatures or other sampling strategies.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that a specific temperature range is optimal for both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty estimation, with deviating from this range negatively impacting the quality of the estimates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: estimating epistemic uncertainty via proxy tasks
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of proxy tasks and side objectives to estimate epistemic uncertainty in language models. This involves training a meta-model that learns to predict epistemic uncertainty by ranking the confidence of different models on proxy tasks, and evaluating its performance on real-world uncertainty estimation tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare with the mutual information-based approach from proposal 3; ablate the impact of using different proxy tasks or side objectives on the resulting uncertainty estimates.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that proxy tasks and side objectives can provide a novel and effective way to estimate epistemic uncertainty, potentially outperforming the mutual information-based approach in certain contexts, but the method's effectiveness may depend on the choice of proxy task and quality of the meta-model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: comparison across language model architectures
PROPOSAL: Compare and contrast the performance of the uncertainty estimation methods developed in this work across different language model architectures, including autoregressive and masked diffusion models. This will involve adapting the proposed approaches to each model type and evaluating their effectiveness on a range of uncertainty estimation tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare with oracles, or established methods for uncertainty esimation on each model type; ablate the impact of using different model architectures or training procedures on the resulting uncertainty estimates, following the setup outlined in the proposal.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that different types of language models have distinct strengths and weaknesses in terms of uncertainty estimation, and that the proposed approaches can effectively adapt to these differences, leading to improved overall performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: guidelines for uncertainty-aware model selection
PROPOSAL: Derive practical guidelines for selecting language models based on their uncertainty estimation capabilities, by investigating the relationships between uncertainty estimation performance, model architecture, and task requirements.
CONTROLS: Compare with established methods for model selection and calibration; evaluate the impact of incorporating uncertainty-aware selection on downstream task performance.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that incorporating uncertainty-aware model selection can significantly improve the robustness and reliability of language models in various applications, leading to better decision-making in real-world scenarios.

Large language models can be knowledge edited, that is, updated to incorporate new or corrected facts without retraining from scratch. This capability is crucial for keeping models up to date with evolving information and for correcting errors on the fly. Large vision-language models (LVLMs), which combine textual and visual understanding, make knowledge editing even more challenging: they encode factual knowledge in both their textual and their visual pathways, and they require mechanisms that update the knowledge of both modalities consistently. Efficiently editing LVLMs is crucial for real-world applications, such as swiftly correcting critical visual recognition errors (e.g., a model misidentifying Donald Trump as Boris Johnson). However, research on multimodal knowledge editing remains scarce compared with the extensive studies on text-only language models.

Existing benchmarks for LVLM knowledge editing are limited in scope. They typically focus only on visual knowledge updates, such as changing the identity that an image is recognized as, and overlook scenarios in which textual facts about an entity (e.g., its attributes, roles or affiliations) must also be updated. Furthermore, they do not evaluate continual editing, in which multiple knowledge updates are performed sequentially, nor do they test a model's ability to reason compositionally over edited facts. This is a critical gap, because real-world knowledge updates often arrive incrementally and involve intertwined visual and textual information: once a model has been corrected about who appears in a photo and, separately, updated with a new fact about that person, a question about the person in the photo can only be answered correctly by combining both edits.

Existing editing approaches face fundamental difficulties in this setting. External-memory editors store edited knowledge outside the model and retrieve relevant information at inference time without modifying model parameters, which makes them suitable for long-term retention. However, they typically transplant text-based retrieval strategies from language models directly, ignoring visual cues that are necessary for matching multimodal queries to the right edits, which can reduce retrieval accuracy. They also face an internalization issue: the model may over-rely on its stale internal knowledge, especially when the retrieved information conflicts with what it has learned, leading to incorrect answers. Conversely, internal-memory editors embed edits directly into model parameters via fine-tuning or low-rank adaptation, viewing the feed-forward network as a key-value memory that stores in-model knowledge. Although beneficial for internalizing edits, these methods typically store visual and textual edits within a unified representation space, risking cross-modal interference and representation collapse; moreover, sequential internal edits suffer from catastrophic forgetting, degrading previously stored knowledge with successive updates.

This raises several questions. How can an LVLM accommodate a continual sequence of interleaved visual and textual edits so that each new edit takes effect while earlier edits are retained, without interference between modalities? How can separately edited visual and textual facts be integrated to answer compositional queries that require both, even when externally retrieved evidence and the model's internal knowledge disagree? And how can editors be evaluated in this continual and compositional setting, which existing benchmarks do not cover?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: unified multimodal editing via policy updating
PROPOSAL: We will design a mechanism that updates the knowledge network of an LVLM by integrating visual and textual edits. Specifically, we will utilize a policy-based approach, where the model learns to update its knowledge by consuming policy embeddings that encode the edits. This allows the model to learn a consensual representation of the edits and integrate them seamlessly into its existing knowledge network. We will employ a transformer-based encoder-decoder framework, fine-tune on a set of multimodal datasets, and evaluate on a range of tasks including knowledge-based visual question answering and text-image retrieval.
CONTROLS: baseline comparison with traditional external-memory editing strategies, ablation study on the importance of policy embeddings, fine-tuning without policy embeddings. Evaluate all methods on the same held-out test set and report the mean and standard deviation over five seeds.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this approach should outperform traditional external-memory editors in multimodal knowledge editing tasks, and potentially provide more robust and flexible updates. However, it may struggle with catastrophic forgetting if not properly regularized.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: testing catastrophic forgetting resistance in multimodal editing
PROPOSAL: Given the concerns about catastrophic forgetting in internal-memory editors, we will introduce a regularized training objective that encourages the model to retain previously updated knowledge while incorporating new edits. Specifically, we will propose a knowledge distillation objective that emphasizes the retention of salient information from the model's initial knowledge state, which we will then blend with the information from the latest edit. We hypothesize that this approach will improve the model's ability to retain previously updated knowledge.
CONTROLS: quantitative evaluation of catastrophic forgetting, comparison with other regularization schemes (e.g., L1/L2 penalty, gradient regularization), ablation study on the importance of the knowledge distillation objective. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this approach should significantly reduce catastrophic forgetting in multimodal editing tasks, but may come at the expense of slower convergence rates or decreased model accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: multi-step evaluation methodology for multimodal knowledge editors
PROPOSAL: To better assess the performance of multimodal knowledge editors, we will propose a multi-step evaluation methodology that measures their performance over a series of incremental update steps. Specifically, we will evaluate the model's accuracy on a range of tasks (e.g., visual question answering, text-image retrieval) across multiple update steps, using metrics that capture both short-term and long-term recall. This will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the model's ability to retain previously updated knowledge over time.
CONTROLS: comparisons with existing evaluation methodologies (e.g., one-shot update, batch update), ablation study on the importance of evaluating model performance over multiple update steps. Evaluate all methods on the same held-out test set and report the mean and standard deviation over five seeds.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this evaluation methodology should provide a more nuanced understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of moment-to-moment performance of multimodal editors but may require an additional increase in data annotation and new evaluation frameworks.

ACTION: REVISE
number: 3
TITLE: refined multi-step evaluation methodology for multimodal knowledge editors
PROPOSAL: To further refine our multi-step evaluation methodology, we will introduce a difficulty metric that measures the average difficulty of the tasks presented to the model over multiple update steps. This metric will be used to normalize the model's performance across different difficulty levels, allowing for a more fair comparison between models. Additionally, we will also track the model's performance on a set of compositional questions that require integrating previously updated knowledge with new information.
CONTROLS: comparison with the original multi-step evaluation methodology, ablation study on the importance of the difficulty metric and compositional questions. Evaluate all methods on the same held-out test set and report the mean and standard deviation over five seeds.
COST: no additional compute, modification of existing proposal
PREDICTION: the refined methodology should provide a more robust and nuanced understanding of the model's performance, but may require careful tuning of the difficulty metric to ensure it accurately captures the model's abilities.

ACTION: REVISE
number: 3
TITLE: refined multi-step evaluation methodology for multimodal knowledge editors
PROPOSAL: To further refine our multi-step evaluation methodology, we will introduce a difficulty metric that measures the average difficulty of the tasks presented to the model over multiple update steps. This metric will be used to normalize the model's performance across different difficulty levels, allowing for a more fair comparison between models. Additionally, we will also track the model's performance on a set of compositional questions that require integrating previously updated knowledge with new information. Furthermore, we will evaluate how the model's performance changes as the number of update steps increases.
CONTROLS: comparison with the original multi-step evaluation methodology, ablation study on the importance of the difficulty metric and compositional questions. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 40 GPU-hours for additional data collection and analysis
PREDICTION: the refined methodology should provide a more robust and nuanced understanding of the model's performance, but may require careful tuning of the difficulty metric to ensure it accurately captures the model's abilities.

ACTION: REVISE
number: 1
TITLE: unified multimodal editing via policy updating for realistic image editing
PROPOSAL: We will extend our policy-based editing approach to handle more realistic image editing tasks, such as object removal, object insertion, and image inpainting. We will use synthetic datasets with variable image complexity, pose, and occlusions to simulate real-world scenarios. Our goal is to demonstrate that our policy-based editing framework can successfully update LVLMs to handle such complex image editing tasks.
CONTROLS: comparison with state-of-the-art image editing methodologies (e.g., DeepFill v2), evaluation of the model's ability to generalize to new, unseen scenarios. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this extension should enable our policy-based editing framework to handle more complex and realistic image editing tasks, but may require careful tuning of the model's architecture and the policy updates to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adversarial evaluation of multimodal knowledge editors
PROPOSAL: To provide a more comprehensive assessment of multimodal knowledge editors, we will introduce an adversarial evaluation framework that tests the model's resilience tocrafted attacks designed to compromise its performance. Specifically, we will use strong and strategic attacks (e.g., semantic adversarial examples, multi-step attacks) to probe the model's vulnerabilities and evaluate its robustness.
CONTROLS: comparisons with state-of-the-art attack and defense methods (e.g., adversarial training), ablation study on the impact of different attack strategies. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this evaluation framework should help identify potential vulnerabilities in multimodal knowledge editors and provide valuable insights into the limitations of these models, but may require significant computational resources and careful tuning of the attack strategies.

ACTION: REVISIE
number: 2
TITLE: testing catastrophic forgetting resistance in multimodal editing with mixed update scenarios
PROPOSAL: We will modify our previous approach to testing catastrophic forgetting resistance in multimodal editing by introducing mixed update scenarios that combine visual and textual updates in a single step. Specifically, we will design a set of experiments that update the model's knowledge with both visual and textual information simultaneously, and evaluate its ability to retain previously learned knowledge.
CONTROLS: comparison with single-modality update scenarios (i.e., only visual or only textual updates), ablation study on the impact of mixed update scenarios. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this modification should provide a more comprehensive understanding of the model's ability to handle mixed update scenarios, but may require careful tuning of the model's architecture to avoid catastrophic forgetting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: hybrid multimodal editing with knowledge graph episodic memory
PROPOSAL: We will develop a hybrid approach that combines the strengths of policy-based editing and knowledge graph episodic memory. Specifically, we will design a model that uses a knowledge graph to store and retrieve multimodal information, and leverages policy updates to incorporate new knowledge into the model. This approach should enable the model to adapt to new information and retain previously learned knowledge over time.
CONTROLS: comparison with policy-based editing and knowledge graph episodic memory, ablation study on the impact of the hybrid approach. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this hybrid approach should provide a robust and adaptive way to update multimodal knowledge, but may require careful tuning of the model's architecture and the knowledge graph to avoid information overload and catastrophic forgetting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluation of multimodal knowledge editors on real-world applications
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the performance of our multimodal knowledge editors on real-world applications such as fact-checking, image classification, and question answering. Specifically, we will use datasets such as the Wikipedia dataset for fact-checking and the ImageNet dataset for image classification, and evaluate the model's performance using metrics such as accuracy, F1 score, and mean average precision.
CONTROLS: comparison with state-of-the-art models and baselines, ablation study on the impact of different evaluation metrics. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this evaluation will provide a real-world assessment of the performance of our multimodal knowledge editors and shed light on their strengths and limitations, but may require significant resources and expertise to design and collect the necessary datasets.

Recent advances in computer graphics and vision have highlighted image relighting, that is, changing the illumination of an existing image, as a critical task for film production, augmented reality and digital content creation. Full-image relighting, in which both the objects and the surrounding scene must be relit, remains a challenging problem.

Existing works can be grouped into object-centric approaches, which often ignore or replace the background, and scene-level methods, which attempt full-image relighting but remain largely data-driven: they struggle to generalize beyond the training distribution without extensive and diverse data, and cannot maintain the lighting of self-luminous objects. Even state-of-the-art foreground relighting methods still suffer from albedo inconsistency and imprecise lighting control: relighting can, for instance, alter the colors of a carpet, or make light intended to come from the left appear to come from the left rear although the scene contains no internal light source. Other lines of work have their own restrictions. Many methods address only portraits or isolated objects. Scribble-based control of scene lighting lacks precision and has been limited to indoor scenes. Outdoor full-image relighting methods either require surface normals as input or rely on directional lighting models that generalize poorly to indoor scenes. A recent generative approach that simulates both inverse rendering (recovering intrinsic properties such as albedo, surface normals, roughness and metallicity from an image) and forward rendering conditions the forward step on irradiance, which makes precise lighting control challenging, and is limited to indoor scenes. Intrinsic decomposition methods are themselves hampered by the difficulty of acquiring large-scale training data and are mostly designed for specific scenarios, such as indoor scenes or single objects. These limitations point to the lack of a physically interpretable representation of the scene in current relighting methods and to the inherent limitations of data-driven priors, both of which stand in the way of controllable and physically plausible full-image relighting.

Three major challenges follow. First, data with diverse and complex scene illumination are hard to acquire: obtaining high-quality images of full scenes under diverse and controlled lighting conditions is resource-intensive and technically challenging, and it is infeasible to capture real-world datasets that show the same scene under multiple lighting conditions. Existing datasets that provide intrinsic components focus mainly on indoor scenes and do not render images under varying lighting conditions. Second, ensuring physical plausibility is difficult, as purely data-driven approaches often generate results that violate basic light transport principles. Third, limited data-driven priors restrict generalizability, leading to poor robustness to unseen materials, lighting conditions and realistic scene compositions, and existing attempts to bridge the gap between synthetic training data and real images for full-scene relighting remain suboptimal. Full scenes add a further difficulty: self-luminous objects and built-in light sources, such as light coming through windows, interfere with controlling the direction and intensity of the new lighting while keeping the background consistent.

This raises the following questions. How can an entire image, objects and scene together, indoor or outdoor, be relit under a user-specified lighting condition with precise control of light direction and intensity, while preserving the albedo and material appearance of its surfaces, the content and consistency of the background, and the lighting of self-luminous elements? How can a relighting model be made to respect basic light transport, so that shading, highlights and shadows follow the new lighting across a wide variety of materials? And how can such a model generalize to real-world images with unseen materials, lighting conditions and scene compositions when paired data under controlled lighting are scarce and real captures of the same scene under multiple lightings are infeasible?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: view-dependent radiance decomposition
PROPOSAL: Investigate the potential of view-dependent radiance decomposition for physically plausible full-image relighting. We'll apply a novel decomposition method, focusing on recovering the high-frequency components of radiance with respect to view angles, and assess its performance on synthetic datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare with current state-of-the-art full-image relighting methods and our own simplified radiance decomposition approach without view-dependent components.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This decomposition method can improve full-image relighting accuracy, especially in scenes with complex environments and non-diffuse materials. However, it may struggle with cases where objects have strong view-independent light transport properties.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: intrinsic image decomposition with boundary handling
PROPOSAL: Design an intrinsic image decomposition method that explicitly handles scene boundaries to allow for accurate training and realistic rendering. We'll apply a boundary-aware physics-based model, including Fresnel terms for surface normals and conductance models for lighting, to retrieve intrinsic components with sharper edges and reduced artifacts.
CONTROLS: Compare with current intrinsic image decomposition methods that neglect or approximate boundary conditions, as well as our own simplified boundary- handling approach using standard convolutional filters.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This boundary- handling model should improve decomposition accuracy, especially at scene boundaries, but may require additional computational resources to handle the increased model complexity.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: multi-scale neural rendering for lighting control
PROPOSAL: Train a multi-scale neural rendering model to generate photorealistic images with user-specified lighting conditions, focusing on precise control of light direction, intensity, and shading while maintaining physical plausibility. We'll test our model on a synthetic dataset with varying lighting conditions and scene complexities.
CONTROLS: Compare with current state-of-the-art full-image relighting methods and ablate the contributions of different model components (e.g., multi-scale architecture, physics-based rendering) to lighting control.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This model should demonstrate robust lighting control and achieve state-of-the-art relighting accuracy, but may require large-scale synthetic training data to capture the desired physical plausibility.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: hybrid radiance decomposition with view-dependent components
PROPOSAL: Revise the initial view-dependent radiance decomposition approach to combine low-frequency radiance with view-dependent high-frequency components, using a multi-resolution network to separate and refine rough and detailed radiance information. This hybrid approach should leverage the strengths of both techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original view-dependent radiance decomposition and additively decompose the improvements from combining the two approaches.
COST: 10 additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This hybrid approach should achieve a better trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency, but requires careful tuning of the multi-resolution network architecture to prevent overfitting or underfitting.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: scene-aware lighting transfer
PROPOSAL: Develop a scene-aware lighting transfer method that analyzes the scene geometry and intrinsic properties to reason about the optimal lighting direction, intensity, and type. We'll train a scene-understanding network to predict these parameters from the intrinsic components and apply them to the scene for context-aware relighting.
CONTROLS: Evaluate our method on both synthetic and real-world scenes, comparing with standard lighting transfer techniques and assessing its ability to preserve scene content and color consistency, with details given in the appendix.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This scene-aware lighting transfer approach should significantly improve the realism and consistency of relighting results, but may struggle with complex or noisy scenes where it's difficult to establish a clear understanding of the scene's intrinsic properties.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation
PROPOSAL: Investigate discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation techniques that can more accurately model the lighting behavior at object boundaries, taking into account the object's albedo, shape, and surrounding environment. We'll apply a Fréchet variant of the Poisson equation to recover a piecewise-continuous lighting solution for each object in the scene.
CONTROLS: Compare with the relighting results from our existing methods, specifically testing the improvement in shading, highlights, and shadows caused by accounting for discontinuities in lighting, as described above.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should lead to improved lighting realism at object boundaries, especially for scenes with closely-spaced or complexly-shaped objects. However, the estimation complexity may increase significantly for scenes with many objects or intricate geometry.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: partial-diffuse-specular separation from multi-scale detail
PROPOSAL: Propose a multi-scale separation approach to extract partial, diffuse, and specular components from an image, using a detail refinement and coarsening scheme to improve partial-diffuse-specular separation performance. This is crucial for accurate radiance decomposition and relighting, allowing for more precise modeling of surface reflectance and directional scatter.
CONTROLS: Compare this multi-scale method with standard separation approaches in terms of graininess, adaptivity, and relighting results on various synthetic and real-world datasets.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This separation method should enhance the physical plausibility of relighting results by restoring accurate partial-diffuse-specular structure, but may struggle with scenes having complex and multi-scale surface roughness.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: interactively-controllable neural relighting
PROPOSAL: Develop a neural network-based relighting framework that enables real-time, user-interaction-driven control over lighting direction, intensity, and color. We'll introduce a neural representation of relighting parameters that can be modulated by user inputs, facilitating end-user relighting control without requiring extensive domain knowledge or graphics expertise.
CONTROLS: Compare user-interaction accuracy and relighting result quality with those from black-box full-image relighting approaches and investigate the synergies between user interactions and scholar-crafted physics-based relighting.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This interactive method should significantly enhance user experience by providing fine-grained control over relighting but may encounter limitations in extrapolating efficiently beyond the demonstration range, especially with materials that embrace a comprehensive physical representation of dynamic relighting behaviors.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: leveraging real-world relighting validation and synergy 
PROPOSAL: Investigate the potential for real-world relighting and data acquisition synergies in our existing methods, validating their performance in real-world scenes and datasets while also augmenting synthesis-based approaches for real-world-driven full-image relighting models. This real-world focus is essential to providing the physically-grounded formulation needed for accurate data-driven full-image relighting models, known as real-world-driven validation.
CONTROLS: Assess the relighting quality improvement when training models on synthetic scenes that have been validated against real-world data, then testing these improved synth+real-scene methods on unseen real-world scenes (not used in training or during synthesis) and various internal priors, following the setup outlined in the proposal.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Incorporating real-world validation should further improve relighting quality and robustness but may require larger-scale datasets and optimizing computational efficiency to outperform faster synthesis-based methods.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: hybrid discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation
PROPOSAL: Revise the discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation approach by integrating the hybrid radiance decomposition with view-dependent components to leverage the strengths of both in modelling light transport discontinuities, achieving a finer-grain representation and improving accuracy in scenes with complex lighting settings, thus achieving another remarkable trade-off between the complexity of these discontinuity-controlled scenes and the minimal added runtime cost for updates and finer-control analyzers.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the hybrid estimation approach's convergence and accuracy for a wider range of images, dataset sources, and resolutions, with comparison against other highest-rated scene-bound and label-driven estimation-centric synthesis-based approaches to see if improved autonomous controlled synthesis, together with improving measurement-based renderings and meta-anals, aligns to general relighting tasks.
COST: 5 additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This hybrid lighting estimation approach should achieve even greater accuracy and physics-based realism in scene lighting modeling, while still benefiting from improvements and interchange handling, improving practical workflows and tools efficiency in digitally-rendered content or view-based sensory ensemble simulations.

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a wide range of natural language tasks, driven in part by advances in transformer-based architectures. While much effort has been devoted to understanding attention mechanisms and token-wise interactions, the role of feed-forward networks (FFNs), and particularly of their nonlinear components, remains underexplored, even though FFNs dominate both the parameter budget and the computational footprint of transformer-based models.

Despite their apparent simplicity, FFNs perform high-dimensional nonlinear transformations that regulate information flow by reorganizing, compressing, and propagating the information extracted by attention modules across layers. Understanding how these transformations behave, how they evolve across depth and over the course of training, and how they interact with architectural design choices (for example normalization or the choice of activation function) and with the choice of optimizer remains a fundamental open question; in practice, such design choices are still largely made by trial and error.

One challenge in interpreting FFNs is the absence of systematic and efficient tools for characterizing how latent representations are structured and transformed by nonlinear activations. FFN transformations unfold in a high-dimensional latent space that is far less accessible to direct visualization and probing than multi-head attention. Prior work has used attention maps to study the input-contextualization effect of FFNs, and has characterized FFN geometry through piecewise-affine spline partitions. Neither lens shows what the nonlinearity does to the overall geometry of the latent representation, for instance how much of the available high-dimensional latent space is actually used before and after the activation, or how this changes from layer to layer and during training.

This raises several questions. What does the FFN nonlinearity do to the structure of the latent representation it receives, and how does this vary across layers and over training? How do architectural and optimizer choices shape this behavior? Can these properties be measured efficiently enough to be tracked continuously while training large models, in a way that remains comparable across layers and model configurations? Do the resulting measurements relate to a model's generalization ability, so that they could serve as diagnostics to guide architectural and optimizer choices beyond trial and error? Finally, are these behaviors specific to attention-based transformers, or are they a more general property of deep feed-forward layers?

Grounding procedural steps in videos is crucial for enabling machines to follow along and assist humans in complex tasks such as cooking a recipe, assembling furniture, or performing maintenance work. This ability is particularly valuable for real-time procedural guidance in augmented and extended reality applications, where recognizing task progress allows users wearing headsets or smart glasses to receive timely, step-specific instructions. The task of Video Step Grounding (VSG) takes as input a list of procedural steps extracted from an instructional article (e.g., a recipe or a how-to guide) and a video of the same task, and aims to identify which of the steps are performed in the video, that is, which step, if any, each part of the video depicts (a segment may also show an action outside the listed steps).

Existing VSG approaches align procedural step descriptions with their corresponding video frames. Earlier works relied on weakly-supervised learning from instructional narrations, while more recent methods increasingly leverage language models and large-scale pretraining, for instance using language models to turn noisy narrations or speech transcripts into steps and pseudo-labels for training. These strategies face two key limitations. First, they need a training set, entailing the cost of collecting (and potentially annotating) it; moreover, a training set can bias models toward the specific videos and procedural tasks it depicts, limiting their generalization capability. Second, they assume offline processing, where the entire video is available ahead of time, which makes them unsuitable for real-world applications that process a live video stream and must make decisions as it unfolds.

This calls for addressing VSG online and without training: video segments arrive one after the other, and whether the current segment depicts a given step must be decided using only that segment and the segments preceding it, with no task-specific training data. This setting is challenging. Predictions must be made from partial evidence, and without the task-specific representations that would typically be learned from a dedicated training set. The task also requires fine-grained video understanding, since key steps of instructional tasks often involve similar objects or scenes: "inserting a screw" or "aligning parts" may look alike in tasks such as "Assemble a chair" and "Fix a table", making them hard to distinguish without nuanced semantic understanding. Large pretrained multimodal models have demonstrated impressive zero-shot performance on a wide variety of tasks without further tuning, and work on video-language alignment has moved away from frame-caption embedding similarity, which struggles to capture temporal dynamics, toward such models; yet whether off-the-shelf models can ground procedural steps when they only see the current short segment remains an open question. Moreover, a prediction made from the current segment alone has no memory of what has already happened in the video, so uncertain observations cannot benefit from past evidence, while storing and reprocessing the whole history is impractical on a live stream.

The research questions are therefore: can video step grounding be performed online, on a streaming video and without any training, at a level competitive with training-based offline methods? And how can knowledge from past segments be injected into the prediction for the current segment, without storing the whole history and while preserving a zero-shot, training-free approach?
