ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating baseline models for online video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate a set of strong multimodal model baselines for video step grounding, adapted to process only one video segment at a time. Specifically, we will investigate large-scale multimodal transformer models like CLIP, and recent multimodal variants like OSIM and VisIoL, with a focus on evaluating their zero-shot performance when processing a live video stream one segment at a time. We will measure performance using metrics like accuracy, F1-score, and Hamming loss on real-world video step grounding benchmarks from instructional cooking recipe videos and egocentric procedural activity videos.
CONTROLS: We will compare our zero-shot baseline models to models that have been pre-trained on VSG tasks and fine-tuned on a specific dataset, providing an offline benchmark for comparison. We will also evaluate various ablations of our zero-shot models, including the effect of using different types of multimodal input (e.g., frame, audio, or both) and different window sizes for segmenting video frames, in the same setting as the proposal
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that competing zero-shot models struggle due to the lack of task-specific information in the model, however strong multimodal models that are not specifically designed for this task can still achieve good performance due to their general-purpose multimodal capabilities, and ablation studies will point towards multimodal input as a key factor for zero-shot performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adding contextualized embeddings for video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will investigate using contextualized embeddings to improve the performance of online video step grounding. Specifically, we will experiment with using pre-trained BERT-like models to generate text embeddings for the step descriptions, and multimodal transformer models to generate visual embeddings for the video frames. We will then use a common encodings space for the step descriptions and video frames to compute similarity scores. This approach aims to capture the nuances of language and visual context that are crucial for accurately grounding video steps.
CONTROLS: We will control for the quality of the step descriptions by evaluating the RAKE (Rapid Automatic Keyword Extraction) score of the text, and we will compare our contextualized embeddings approach to a baseline model that uses keyword matching between step descriptions and video frames, with results reported in a table. We will also evaluate the effect of using different quality and quantities of step descriptions on model performance.
COST: 8000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that using contextualized embeddings improves the performance of video step grounding, especially in scenarios where step descriptions have high RAKE scores, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: revising evaluating baseline models for online video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate a set of strong multimodal model baselines for video step grounding, adapted to process only one video segment at a time, focusing on the use of cross-modal learning. Specifically, we will investigate how different cross-modal fusion methods (e.g., concatenation, attention, and late fusion) can improve the zero-shot performance of large-scale multimodal transformer models like CLIP, and recent multimodal variants like OSIM and VisIoL. We will measure performance using metrics like accuracy, F1-score, and Hamming loss on real-world video step grounding benchmarks from instructional cooking recipe videos and egocentric procedural activity videos.
CONTROLS: We will compare our zero-shot baseline models to models that have been pre-trained on VSG tasks and fine-tuned on a specific dataset, providing an offline benchmark for comparison, as described above. We will also evaluate various ablations of our zero-shot models, including the effect of using different types of multimodal input (e.g., frame, audio, or both) and different window sizes for segmenting video frames. Additionally, we will control for the impact of cross-modal learning on model performance by adapting the original two-step fine-tuning approach for cross-modal training in online videos.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that cross-modal learning is a key factor for achieving strong zero-shot performance in video step grounding, and that different cross-modal fusion methods perform differently on various VSG tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: improving adding contextualized embeddings for video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will improve our approach to using contextualized embeddings for video step grounding by incorporating attention mechanisms to dynamically weigh the importance of different tokens in both the step descriptions and video frames. Specifically, we will experiment with using multi-head attention to compute attention weights that align the text and visual embeddings, and use these attention weights to fuse the embeddings. We will explore different options for initialising the attention weights, such as using dominant keywords from the step description or learned weights from the model.
CONTROLS: We will compare our improved contextualized embeddings approach to our previous baseline method, and evaluate its performance with different options for initialising the attention weights. We will also control for the impact of attention mechanisms on model performance by comparing our results with a baseline model that uses a pre-defined fusion scheme, as described above.
COST: 7000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that our improved contextualized embeddings approach with attention mechanisms outperforms our previous baseline method, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: leveraging semantic graph reasoning for video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will investigate using semantic graph reasoning to reason about the relationship between video segments and step descriptions in video step grounding. Specifically, we will construct a knowledge graph that represents the semantic relationships between entities and actions in the step descriptions, and then use a graph neural network to reason about the relevance of the video segments to the step descriptions. We will evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks and compare it to our contextualized embeddings approach.
CONTROLS: We will control for the quality of the knowledge graph by evaluating the accuracy of the entity and action recognition methods used to construct the graph, and we will compare our graph reasoning approach to a baseline model that uses a simple matching scheme between the step descriptions and video segments, with results reported in a table.
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that semantic graph reasoning can improve the performance of video step grounding by capturing complex relationships between video segments and step descriptions, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: injecting temporal context with transformer encoder layers
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate the impact of injecting temporal context to our baseline models for video step grounding using transformer encoder layers. Specifically, we will modify our multimodal transformer model to include an additional encoder layer that takes into account the temporal relationships between consecutive video frames, and evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks. We will compare our results to our baseline model without temporal context and other state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of the additional encoder layer on model performance by comparing it to a baseline model with a reduced number of layers, and we will evaluate the effect of different window sizes for segmenting video frames on the performance of our model, following the setup outlined in the proposal.
COST: 6500
PREDICTION: We expect to find that injecting temporal context improves the performance of our baseline model by capturing the nuances of the video sequence, and that this approach performs well even when the video sequence has a complex structure.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: enhancing leveraging semantic graph reasoning for video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will enhance our approach to using semantic graph reasoning for video step grounding by incorporating a procedure for iteratively refining the knowledge graph and re-reasoning about the relationship between video segments and step descriptions. Specifically, we will experiment with an iterative process that involves re-scoring the relevance of video segments to step descriptions based on the refined knowledge graph, and re-ranking the step descriptions based on their relevance to the video segments. We will evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks and compare it to our previous graph reasoning approach.
CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of the iterative refinement process on model performance by comparing it to a baseline model that uses a simple matching scheme between the step descriptions and video segments, and we will evaluate the effect of different refinement thresholds on the performance of our model, as described above.
COST: 8500
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the iterative refinement process improves the performance of our graph reasoning approach by capturing more nuanced relationships between video segments and step descriptions, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

TITLE: fusing visual and language features with adaptive fusion mechanism
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate the impact of using an adaptive fusion mechanism to fuse the visual and language features extracted from the video frames and step descriptions in video step grounding. Specifically, we will design a mechanism that dynamically adjusts the weighting of the visual and language features based on the contextual information present in the step descriptions and video frames, and evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks.
CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of the adaptive fusion mechanism on model performance by comparing it to a baseline model that uses a fixed weighting scheme for the visual and language features, and we will evaluate the effect of different fusion mechanisms on the performance of our model, in the same setting as the proposal.
COST: 7200
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the adaptive fusion mechanism improves the performance of our baseline model by capturing the complex relationships between the visual and language features, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

Real-world reinforcement learning (RL) systems often struggle with reward specification: it is notoriously difficult to craft a reward function that captures the intended goals in all scenarios, so designers rely on proxy rewards that only approximate the true objective. Agents that optimize such imperfect proxies can discover unintended, exploitative behaviors that achieve high proxy return while yielding poor true outcomes, a phenomenon known as reward hacking. Reward hacking is not merely hypothetical: it has led to undesirable or even catastrophic consequences in safety-critical settings and is common in real-world deployments. At the same time, interpretability and transparency of RL policies are increasingly recognized as requirements for real-world acceptance: policymakers and practitioners in safety-critical domains need systems that are not only robust but also understandable, so that they can identify which decision-making criteria lead to undesirable outcomes, mitigate risks, and ensure compliance with safety regulations. RL algorithms for high-stakes applications therefore face two fundamental challenges: robustness to uncertain or poorly specified rewards, and interpretability that facilitates oversight by human stakeholders.

Recent work has begun to formalize reward hacking and to develop principled mitigations. In one such framework, the agent is given a proxy reward and a reference policy, while the true reward is hidden. The proxy is called r-correlated with the true reward if the two maintain a correlation coefficient r > 0 on the state-action pairs encountered by the reference policy, that is, under the reference policy's state-action occupancy measure. This definition permits the proxy and the true reward to diverge arbitrarily in parts of the state-action space that the reference policy does not visit, which are precisely the regions an RL agent may exploit under intensive optimization. Reward hacking is then said to occur when optimizing an r-correlated proxy yields a policy with lower true reward than the reference policy. The mitigation proposed within that framework, Occupancy-Regularized Policy Optimization (ORPO), augments the standard RL objective with a regularization term that penalizes the chi-squared divergence between the learned policy's state-action occupancy measure and that of the reference policy, with a strength that depends on the correlation level, and it guarantees a lower bound on the improvement in true reward.

Despite this progress, existing solutions to reward hacking have several limitations. First, their effectiveness relies heavily on the specific proxy reward. Designing good proxies is hard: in real-world scenarios, proxies are often derived heuristically or empirically from noisy or limited data, which leaves uncertainty about their exact relationship to the true reward, and the correlation level itself is typically known only approximately. Robustness to variations in the proxy is therefore crucial for dependable deployment, yet a method that regularizes against one fixed proxy offers only a weak guarantee on worst-case performance when the proxy could be any reward consistent with the assumed correlation, including an adversarially chosen one. Second, current methods treat the reward function as a black box and learn complex policies with no easily interpretable structure, making it hard to understand why a policy avoids reward hacking or to trust its behavior in novel situations; moreover, they cannot easily incorporate prior knowledge about the true reward when such knowledge is available.

This raises several research questions. Given only a proxy reward, a reference policy and an assumed correlation level, how can one learn a policy whose true performance is guaranteed against the entire class of rewards consistent with the correlation constraint, rather than against a single trusted proxy? Can such a guarantee be turned into an objective that is tractable to optimize with standard policy-optimization tools? How should state-action pairs that the reference policy rarely or never visits, where the correlation constraint says nothing about the true reward, be handled? When prior knowledge about the structure of the true reward is available, how can it be exploited to avoid excessive conservatism and to expose, in an interpretable way, which aspects of the reward a learned policy is most vulnerable to? Finally, how can one obtain policies whose performance remains robust and stable when the true correlation between proxy and true reward is uncertain or misspecified?

Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly expanded in capability and are now widely used in domains such as conversational agents, healthcare and finance, where they often process sensitive personal information. Early privacy concerns focused mainly on memorization and leakage of training data, but recent studies show that LLMs can also infer private attributes of an author, such as location, identity or demographics, from subtle semantic cues in seemingly innocuous text. With sufficiently capable models, such inferences can be surprisingly accurate and often go undetected by users, who continue to share content unaware of the risk. Moreover, text sent to external services may be intercepted in transit or retained by providers, for example for model training, increasing the risk of misuse or data breaches.

Traditional anonymization methods rely on rule-based de-identification, such as named entity recognition or pattern matching, to remove surface-level identifiers like names, social security numbers or explicit locations. They frequently overlook the context-dependent semantics that LLMs can exploit, so private information that is embedded in context rather than stated explicitly remains inferable. This gap calls for anonymization techniques that account for semantic context and defend against inference-based privacy threats, while preserving the meaning and readability of the text, that is, techniques that achieve a good privacy-utility trade-off.

A growing body of work pursues LLM-based anonymization to protect semantic-level private information from model inference. In feedback-guided adversarial anonymization, an LLM anonymizer rewrites the input text while a second LLM, acting as an adversary, attempts to infer private attributes from the rewritten output; based on this adversarial feedback, the anonymizer iteratively refines its output to prevent the inferences that remain possible. With GPT-4 as both anonymizer and adversary, this approach achieves a substantially better privacy-utility trade-off than traditional industry-grade anonymizers. However, reliance on large proprietary models is costly and requires sending the very text that should be protected to potentially untrusted external systems. Attempts to transfer these anonymization capabilities into smaller models have been explored only to a limited extent, and existing approaches still depend on a proprietary model to provide the adversarial feedback, incurring similar costs and privacy concerns.

The open problem is therefore whether, and how, small language models that can run locally under modest compute budgets can become effective anonymizers that protect semantic-level private information against inference by strong LLM adversaries, without relying on any external model at inference time. Can such models reach a privacy-utility trade-off comparable to, or better than, that of anonymizers built on frontier proprietary LLMs, including on texts where personal information is conveyed by the overall context rather than by explicit mentions, while remaining cheap enough to deploy in settings with strict data-confidentiality requirements?

Reinforcement learning has been highly effective in many domains, ranging from robotics to gaming and recommender systems. Value-based algorithms such as Deep Q-Networks are a cornerstone of off-policy reinforcement learning and are widely used in discrete action spaces because of their simplicity, training stability, and sample-efficiency. However, they rely on estimating Q-values for individual state-action pairs and require a maximization over the action space, both to derive the greedy policy and to evaluate the best next-state value in the Bellman target. This maximization is straightforward when the actions can be enumerated, but in continuous action spaces evaluating the Q-value over the entire action space becomes computationally infeasible, which has traditionally restricted value-based methods to discrete actions.

In continuous control, actor-critic methods such as DDPG, TD3, and SAC are typically used instead: a critic is trained on off-policy data to estimate Q-values, and an actor (policy) is trained to output actions that maximize the critic. While powerful, these methods often suffer from instability caused by the coupled training of actor and critic, from sensitivity to hyperparameters, and from the difficulty of predicting in high-dimensional action spaces. The additional actor network brings its own hyperparameters, which makes reproducibility a challenge, and adds computational and memory overhead. Moreover, an actor trained by gradient ascent on the Q-function landscape can only find locally optimal actions, which becomes a serious limitation when the Q-function is complex or non-convex, for instance when the action space is constrained so that actions must remain within specific safety bounds. Training several actors to explore different modes of the Q-function alleviates this, but adds computational overhead and inference-time latency, and the actor's parameterization may still be too limited to capture complex optimal actions.

Actor-free, value-based alternatives must instead carry out the maximization over continuous actions themselves, and finding the maximizing action has been their primary bottleneck. Methods that perform this maximization numerically, through mixed-integer programming, the cross-entropy method and other sampling-based or evolutionary search, or gradient ascent on the action, tend either to return suboptimal local maxima or to be computationally impractical, and sampling becomes progressively less efficient as the action dimension grows. Discretizing the action space is effective in low dimensions but does not scale to high-dimensional tasks. Another line of work restricts the functional form of the Q-function so that its maximizer can be obtained directly, for example by assuming that the advantage is quadratic in the action or that the Q-function is convex in the action; such assumptions limit expressivity and practical applicability. Representing the Q-function with a radial basis function output layer makes the best action easier to identify, but introduces an implicit trade-off between how expressive the Q-function can be in modeling multiple local optima and how accurately its maximizing action is recovered.

This raises the question of whether an actor-free, value-based algorithm can efficiently and accurately select optimal actions in continuous action spaces without imposing restrictive assumptions on the shape of the Q-function, while remaining stable to train, robust across diverse tasks, and scalable to high-dimensional action spaces. Such an algorithm would retain the simplicity of Q-learning and avoid the cost and instability of learning a separate actor; it could also avoid the local optima that trap gradient-based actors when the Q-function is highly non-convex, as in constrained action spaces. Can such an approach be made competitive with established actor-critic methods for continuous control, and can it outperform them where gradient-based action maximization struggles?

Recording dynamic scenes from multiple viewpoints has become increasingly common in everyday life. From concerts and sports events to lectures and birthday parties, people often capture the same moment using different handheld devices. These multi-view recordings present a rich opportunity to reconstruct scenes in 4D, enable bullet-time effects, or enhance the capabilities of existing vision models. However, these videos are typically captured independently, without synchronization or known camera poses, making it difficult to align and fuse them coherently.

The task is the following: given a set of asynchronous videos that capture the same dynamic scene from different viewpoints, estimate a time offset for each video, to be applied to its original out-of-sync clock, so that after correction frames sharing the same clock time correspond to the exact same moment across all videos.

Existing synchronization methods rely on controlled environments, manual annotations, specific patterns such as human pose, audio signals such as flashes or claps, or expensive hardware setups such as time-coded devices, none of which are available in casually captured videos. Human-centric approaches, which use body pose as the synchronization signal, are limited by the accuracy of pose estimation and by the number of people present, and they struggle in scenes without prominent human activity. Audio-based approaches only work in quiet environments and do not carry over to in-the-wild settings where audio is noisy or unavailable. Methods that jointly optimize camera poses and temporal offsets within a learned scene representation are often constrained to specific environments or object types. Geometry-based methods estimate temporal offsets from multi-view geometric constraints, but typically assume static scenes or a fixed viewpoint. Meanwhile, structure-from-motion and learned camera-pose estimators recover camera geometry accurately, yet they rely predominantly on static visual cues and therefore fall short of synchronizing dynamic scenes.

Building a practical and robust synchronization system that works on videos in the wild is challenging. Camera poses are unknown and cameras may move, so the geometric relationship between each pair of cameras must itself be estimated reliably. The moving objects that carry the timing information are not known in advance and are generally small and blurry. Associating points across cameras with significantly different viewpoints is difficult. The offsets to be recovered are continuous, while observations arrive only at discrete frame times. Finally, not all views overlap, so some pairs of cameras may share little spatial or temporal overlap.

This raises several questions. How can a set of casually captured, unposed and unsynchronized videos of the same dynamic scene be aligned in time with high precision, without specialized capture, audio, manual correction, or assumptions about the scene content such as the presence of people? Which visual evidence can reliably reveal the temporal offset between two cameras whose poses are unknown and possibly changing over time? And how can a single, globally consistent offset be recovered for every video when the evidence relating some pairs of views is weak, ambiguous or missing? Answering these questions would open the door to scalable, unconstrained multi-view 4D scene understanding and to downstream tasks, such as 4D reconstruction of dynamic scenes, that depend on synchronized input.

Facial rigging aims to make a static neutral facial mesh animatable by defining a set of controllable deformations, typically represented either as blendshape rigs driven by activated action units in systems based on the Facial Action Coding System (FACS), or as skeletal rigs driven by joint positions. Whereas full-body auto-rigging usually follows a two-step pipeline of skeleton construction and skinning, facial rigs are often anatomically inspired and implemented with FACS blendshapes. In a linear FACS blendshape rig, each blendshape is a vertex offset from the neutral mesh corresponding to one action unit, i.e. a specific muscle movement such as "Right Eye Close", and a complex expression is obtained by adding the weighted offsets of the activated blendshapes to the neutral mesh. Rigging is an essential step for creative AI, bringing digital avatars to life by enabling expressive and realistic facial movements across a wide range of applications. However, creating a facial rig is laborious and expensive, often requiring skilled artists tens of hours to complete a single asset. Methods that transfer expressions from 2D images or videos to 3D avatars do not remove this bottleneck, since they assume that the avatar already has a rig.

Existing facial auto-rigging methods typically transfer a complete set of blendshapes from a predefined template mesh to a neutral target mesh, which often requires dense correspondences or a mesh topology shared by the template and the target. More recent approaches build transferable latent spaces between faces or use triangulation-agnostic networks to bypass these limitations, but they still require a template blendshape rig, which can compromise accuracy when the template and target shapes differ substantially. Only one prior approach, NFR, can directly rig facial meshes from explicitly controllable FACS parameters without relying on a template, and it has so far been demonstrated primarily on humanoid heads. Furthermore, existing approaches, NFR included, have yet to accommodate meshes with multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs or teeth, which limits their ability to animate highly expressive avatars: an "eye look-down" pose, for example, is difficult to reproduce if the mesh lacks eyeballs.

Learning such a rigging model also raises a data problem. Accurate 3D supervision requires neutral meshes paired with complete rigs made by artists, and because manual rigging is so costly such rigged examples are scarce; a model trained solely on them is likely to generalize poorly to the wide variety of facial shapes, styles and topologies met in practice.

The problem is therefore to automatically turn a single static neutral facial mesh into an expressive rig controllable by FACS parameters (i) without relying on predefined template blendshapes, so that target meshes need not closely resemble a template; (ii) for in-the-wild meshes with varying topologies and shapes, including both humanoid and non-humanoid heads; and (iii) for meshes made of multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs and teeth, which must move coherently with the rest of the face. How can such a rigging system be built, and how can it be trained to generalize across this diversity when only a limited number of rigged meshes is available as 3D ground truth?

Deep learning models have achieved impressive success across a wide range of tasks, yet they can behave unpredictably when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) data that differ significantly from the training distribution, making high-confidence but incorrect predictions. OOD detection seeks to identify such inputs and is critical for reliable deployment in open-world scenarios, including safety-critical applications and scientific discovery tasks. The challenge becomes even more pronounced for graph-structured data, because of their non-Euclidean nature and complex topological structures.

Recent advances in graph-level OOD detection fall broadly into two categories. End-to-end methods train OOD-specific graph neural networks (GNNs) from scratch using only unlabeled in-distribution (ID) data; they typically rely on unsupervised objectives such as graph contrastive learning to extract discriminative representations that can separate ID and OOD samples during inference. Post-hoc methods instead start from well-trained GNNs and fine-tune OOD detectors that refine the predictions or representations at inference time. Among them, a recent test-time method, GOODAT, directly optimizes a learnable graph masker on the test samples without altering the pre-trained model. This test-time setting with data-centric modification is more practical, because it removes the dependency on labeled training data and on model retraining.

The test-time problem can be stated as follows. A GNN has been pre-trained on graphs from an unlabeled ID dataset. At test time it faces unlabeled graphs that mix held-out ID graphs, disjoint from the pre-training graphs, with graphs drawn from a different, OOD distribution. The goal is a detector that assigns each test graph a score, a higher score meaning a greater probability that the graph comes from the OOD distribution, using only the pre-trained model and the test graphs: the parameters of the pre-trained model are not modified, and neither the training data nor any ground-truth label is used.

Despite the progress of this data-centric paradigm, a less-explored challenge persists. A pre-trained model can effectively extract information from ID data, but when it infers on both ID and OOD test graphs it lacks ground-truth information indicative of the underlying distribution, information that is often embedded within the graph structure. Test graphs typically comprise distinctive components, whose capture could intuitively differentiate OOD samples from ID graphs, together with irrelevant structural elements. The pervasive presence of similar irrelevant structural elements in ID and OOD graphs, a structural redundancy that induces semantic shifts, hinders current methods from accurately capturing and distinguishing the essential structures of ID and OOD data. The existing test-time method tries to address this concern by using graph maskers to identify subgraphs in the test data that are similar to those in the ID training graphs, but it fundamentally relies on learnable graph augmentations, which can inadvertently alter the semantic information of substructures or lead to information loss, thereby compromising the reliability of OOD detection.

This raises the following questions. How can a well-trained GNN, left unchanged, be endowed at test time with the ability to capture the essential, distinctive structural information of test graphs while discarding irrelevant structural redundancy, without altering the semantics of their substructures? How can what is essential for telling ID from OOD graphs be separated from what is redundant in a principled and tractable way, when neither ground-truth labels nor OOD examples are available? And can such a test-time detector yield more reliable OOD scores than existing end-to-end and post-hoc approaches while remaining practical in computational cost?

Semantic segmentation has improved significantly with recent advances in deep neural networks, but it requires a large volume of fine-grained pixel-level labels, which are time-consuming and labor-intensive to obtain. Because images themselves are readily available, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) and semi-supervised learning (SSL) have been introduced to handle label-scarce scenarios: UDA learns from labeled synthetic data and transfers knowledge to real, unlabeled target domains, while SSL uses a tiny portion of annotated data to generalize to unseen data. Both are gaining attention as promising ways to reduce the reliance on extensive annotation in semantic segmentation.

In both settings, models are trained on annotated and unlabeled data simultaneously. Mainstream methods follow two paradigms. Self-training methods use a temporally smoothed exponential moving average (EMA) model as a teacher to generate stable pseudo-labels for unlabeled data, while consistency regularization methods encourage the model to produce consistent predictions for the same sample under different perturbation views; recent state-of-the-art methods combine the two. Both can be summarized as pseudo-label learning, in which the network's own predictions serve as supervision for unlabeled data. In the widely adopted form of this paradigm, the teacher's prediction is converted into a hard pseudo-label through an argmax and encoded one-hot, a confidence-based quality estimate (threshold filtering or a weighting function) controls how much each pseudo-label contributes, and training uses a cross-entropy loss.

Despite promising results, pseudo-labels inevitably contain errors that mislead training, and these errors are further amplified during training because of the one-hot encoding. Typical remedies use filter-out mechanisms that train only on high-confidence pseudo-labels, but this makes the model focus on easy samples while neglecting difficult ones, resulting in sub-optimal performance. Another alternative assigns weights according to pseudo-label confidence, but such weighting functions require careful design and selection of hyperparameters, which compromises their applicability. Other work designs new optimization criteria, for example inspired by negative learning. Existing work thus concentrates on selection strategies for pseudo-labels and rarely considers the impact of the encoding form assigned to classes.

This omission matters most for confusing classes. For instance, pixels of the class sheep may be confused by the classifier with horse or cow, and the resulting erroneous pseudo-label is encoded one-hot through the argmax, committing the supervision entirely to a wrong class. Similar classes plausibly share common visual attributes (sheep and cows, for example, both have horns and hooves), which leads to confusing pseudo-labels that further misguide training, yet a one-hot target cannot express what the confused classes have in common. How to utilize the shared attributes among confusing classes to design a suitable encoding form for pseudo-label learning remains rarely explored.

This raises several questions. Can the class encoding used by the segmentation model and its pseudo-labels be redesigned so that supervision stays informative even when the class decision for a pixel is wrong? Under such an encoding, how should pseudo-labels be generated from the teacher's predictions so that they introduce less noise than hard one-hot labels, and what training objective is appropriate? Can an alternative encoding be shown, both theoretically and empirically, to match one-hot encoding in the fully supervised setting while being more robust to label noise in pseudo-label learning? Finally, since the encoding form is orthogonal to pseudo-label selection strategies, can such a change be integrated into existing self-training and consistency-regularization frameworks for both UDA and SSL, across different segmentation architectures?

Human-object interaction (HOI) detection aims to localize humans and objects in an image and to recognize the interactions between them. It provides a fine-grained understanding of human activities, which is crucial for downstream applications such as robotic manipulation, image captioning and autonomous driving. Despite recent progress, HOI detection remains challenging because of the large combinatorial space of human-object pairs and the need for fine-grained visual understanding. Moreover, real-world applications often require recognizing human-object interactions that do not appear in the training set, which leads to the task of zero-shot HOI detection. Conventional HOI detectors fail to generalize to such unseen interactions, and early attempts that disentangle object and verb features for compositional generalization cannot handle unseen objects or unseen verbs.

To address zero-shot HOI detection, recent works exploit vision-language models such as CLIP to transfer semantic knowledge from language to HOI detection. Typically, they use text embeddings of interaction descriptions, e.g., "A person is holding a cup", to construct classifiers for unseen interactions. While effective to some extent, these methods face limitations. First, CLIP features lack the fine-grained representational capacity required to distinguish visually similar interactions, so methods have to incorporate detector features to obtain fine-grained representations of instances. Second, their core mechanism, aligning visual and text features, operates only on categories observed during training, which restricts generalization to unseen interactions.

At the same time, progress in open-vocabulary object detection provides a sufficient solution for localizing unseen objects, so interaction recognition has become the main bottleneck. Yet most existing methods, including two-stage methods, couple interaction recognition with a specific object detector: they rely on detector features or on relations between detected objects to give vision-language features fine-grained representational capacity, and they struggle to balance fine-grained detector features with generalized vision-language features. As a result, interaction recognition and detection cannot be improved independently, and the detector cannot be changed without retraining.

Effective interaction recognition therefore requires representations that are both fine-grained and broadly generalizable. This raises the following questions. How can the interactions of a given human-object pair, including interactions never observed during training, be recognized with such representations rather than through alignment with static text embeddings fitted to the seen categories, given that recognition is multi-label because one pair can be engaged in several interactions at once? Can interaction recognition be made independent of any particular object detector, so that it works with the boxes produced by any detector without retraining, stays reliable when those boxes are imperfect, and remains computationally tractable given the many human-object pairs and candidate interactions in an image?

Multimodal learning has become a cornerstone of many real-world applications, such as autonomous perception, medical diagnosis, and human-computer interaction. By integrating information from multiple sources, such as vision, audio, and text, multimodal systems aim to improve performance and generalization. However, multimodal data often exhibit a significant imbalance between modalities due to noise, lack of information, or sensor heterogeneity, so that a dominant modality may overshadow the others and hinder the learning of weak modalities. Unimodal prediction accuracy is widely used to detect modality imbalance; it is a simple and effective metric, but it is inherently sensitive to noise and perturbations. This vulnerability often leads to fragile performance in practice and limits the reliability of accuracy-based definitions of strong and weak modalities in real-world deployments.

Modality imbalance arises in early, intermediate, and late fusion alike. Late fusion, also known as decision-level fusion, combines the outputs (logits) of modality-specific models, either with equal weights (static late fusion) or with weights that vary across samples (dynamic late fusion). It remains one of the most widely adopted paradigms because of its modular design, interpretability, and strong compatibility with unimodal pre-trained models. Yet, lacking feature-level compensation or cross-modal interaction, late fusion tends to amplify the influence of strong modalities while weakening the role of lower-quality ones, so that predictions from disadvantaged modalities often carry little weight or even introduce noise into the final decision. A large body of work has attempted to alleviate this imbalance by enhancing the predictive performance of weak modalities, for example by aggregating independently trained modality-specific classifiers, confidence-based weighting, modality dropout or gating, adaptive ensembling, or knowledge distillation from dominant modalities.

While effective in certain scenarios, these methods often implicitly aim to align weak modalities with dominant ones in terms of prediction accuracy, attempting to bring them closer to their stronger counterparts. Such over-alignment raises several concerns: (1) it may suppress the distinct and complementary information encoded in weak modalities, causing modality-specific information loss; (2) it risks error propagation, as the dominant modality's errors are amplified when weak modalities follow them blindly; and (3) through excessive conformity, weak modalities may lose the predictive advantages they originally held on some samples.

Robustness makes the issue more pressing. Multimodal cooperation is inherently sensitive to perturbations such as data noise, label noise, and incomplete modalities, because modalities are heterogeneous and vary in reliability in real-world conditions. Prior studies have highlighted that the robustness of a multimodal system can be bottlenecked by a single weak modality, revealing a strong link between modality imbalance and overall system reliability. Existing work addresses robustness by incorporating uncertainty modeling, designing robustness-aware fusion strategies, quantifying multimodal robustness with dedicated evaluation metrics, or connecting it with generalization error bounds. However, most of these approaches emphasize prediction-consistency modeling and pay little attention to the instability of the decision space, that is, a model's high sensitivity to input perturbations near the decision boundary, where even minor changes can cause large shifts in prediction; they also tend to require more complex architectures with limited generalizability across tasks with different class granularity.

This raises several questions. How can a dominant modality help a weak modality within a decision-level fusion system without forcing it to conform, so that the weak modality keeps its unique, complementary information and does not inherit the dominant modality's errors? Given that judging modality strength by unimodal accuracy or confidence is itself fragile under noise, how can one reliably determine which modality is dominant and which is weak? How do the predictions of the individual modalities determine the robustness of the fused decision to input perturbations, and can a remedy for modality imbalance come with a theoretical guarantee on that robustness? Finally, can such a remedy both narrow the performance gap between modalities and make the fused prediction more reliable under noisy and imbalanced conditions?

Deep neural networks trained with first-order optimization methods have achieved remarkable empirical success across diverse domains. Despite their widespread adoption, a rigorous theoretical understanding of their optimization dynamics and generalization behavior remains incomplete, particularly for networks with ReLU activations. The difficulty stems from the non-smoothness and non-convexity of the loss landscape induced by ReLU activations and network architectures, which complicate classical analyses. Intriguingly, over-parameterized models often reach zero training error and still generalize well in the absence of explicit regularization, a phenomenon that has spurred substantial theoretical research into its underlying mechanisms.

A prominent line of research analyzes neural network training through the neural tangent kernel (NTK). In the infinite-width limit, the dynamics of gradient descent (GD) can be characterized by functions in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of the NTK, and convergence guarantees have been established for both shallow and deep networks: provided the width is sufficiently large, GD converges to a global minimum within a neighborhood of its initialization. In this regime, generalization errors of order $L\sqrt{\mathbf{y}^\top(\mathbf{H}^\infty)^{-1}\mathbf{y}/n}$ have been obtained for networks of depth $L$ trained on $n$ examples, where $\mathbf{H}^\infty$ denotes the NTK Gram matrix over the training data, but only for widths polynomial in $n$, $L$ and $1/\lambda_0$, with $\lambda_0$ the smallest eigenvalue of $\mathbf{H}^\infty$. Requiring $\lambda_0>0$ is a strong assumption, because this eigenvalue tends to zero as the size of the training set grows. A weaker assumption is that the data are separable by the NTK features at initialization with a margin $\gamma$. Under this assumption, a logarithmic width suffices for two-layer ReLU networks, with a risk bound of order $1/(\gamma^2\sqrt{n})$ derived from Rademacher complexity; this width result relies on the 1-homogeneity of two-layer ReLU networks, a property that does not hold for deep networks. Extensions to deep ReLU networks yield bounds that still decay only as $1/\sqrt{n}$ and contain either factors exponential in depth, such as $4^L$, or additional width-dependent terms. A rate of order $1/(\gamma^2 n)$ has so far been derived only for two-layer ReLU networks. More generally, uniform-convergence analyses based on Rademacher complexity or covering numbers can lead to vacuous bounds, typically depend exponentially on the depth, and usually yield rates of order $1/\sqrt{n}$.

A complementary line of research relies on algorithmic stability. Building on the observation that the spectral norm of the Hessian of wide networks scales with the width $m$ as $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{m})$, stability analyses have obtained bounds of order $\widetilde{O}(1/(n\gamma^2))$ for shallow networks, which is almost optimal in view of known lower bounds, and have been extended to deep networks with bounds of order $\widetilde{O}(e^{O(L)}/(n\gamma^2))$. These analyses, however, assume smooth activation functions and cannot be applied to non-smooth ReLU networks; for deep networks, they also incur an exponential dependence on depth, both in the bound and in the required width.

In summary, existing results either exhibit the suboptimal $1/\sqrt{n}$ dependence on the sample size, are restricted to shallow networks, require smooth activations, or depend exponentially on the depth $L$. A natural and fundamental question is therefore whether GD on deep ReLU networks can achieve generalization rates comparable to the minimax optimal rates established in the kernel setting, namely the SVM-type rate of order $1/(n\gamma^2)$. Specifically, for fully connected deep ReLU networks trained by gradient descent with the logistic loss on binary classification data that are NTK-separable with margin $\gamma$: Can risk bounds of the optimal order $1/(\gamma^2 n)$ be established? Can the exponential dependence on the depth $L$ be replaced by a polynomial dependence $\mathrm{poly}(L)$? And how much over-parameterization (network width) do such guarantees require?

Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a pivotal technique for advancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models on complex tasks. In reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR), the language model is treated as a policy whose chain of thought is modeled as a sequence of actions, and it is optimized with rewards from an automatic verifier that compares the final answer extracted from each sampled solution with a reference answer. Most RLVR algorithms are on-policy; a widely used example is Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which estimates the advantage of each trajectory by normalizing its reward against a group of trajectories sampled for the same question. On-policy optimization is stable but computationally expensive, because the experience generated during the costly rollout phase is typically discarded after a single gradient update. This not only squanders substantial compute but also forfeits the opportunity for the model to learn from its own earlier successful explorations, which makes training inefficient, can make it unstable, and imposes a bottleneck on scaling RL for reasoning.

Experience replay is a classical RL technique to address this issue: previously collected interactions are stored and reused, which improves sample efficiency, helps stabilize training and accelerates convergence, and prioritized variants emphasize the most informative transitions. It has been argued that AI is entering a period in which experience will become the dominant medium of improvement. A non-trivial challenge, however, lies in how to exploit past experiences according to their differing value and how to manage the replay process over the course of learning, and efficient experience replay mechanisms remain largely underexplored in RLVR for large reasoning models. Recent off-policy approaches incorporate historical or external data, for example by mixing expert demonstrations with on-policy updates or by deriving direct off-policy update rules, and recent replay methods for reasoning models reuse successful trajectories collected early in training or produced by a well-trained policy. However, the impact of the quality of the data within the replay buffer remains underexplored, and several replay methods do not correct for the distribution mismatch between the past policy that generated a stored trajectory and the current policy.

Several features make the problem challenging. An experience in RLVR consists of a question together with the trajectories sampled for it, and it is unclear whether all questions are equally useful for training, or whether all successful trajectories for a question are equally worth reusing. Because the verifiable reward only checks the final answer, a successful trajectory may still rest on invalid reasoning. The usefulness of a stored experience may also change as the model's capabilities evolve during training. Finally, reusing past successes pushes the policy toward exploitation, while prior work shows that aggressively minimizing policy entropy can cause collapse, so the reuse of experience has to be balanced against continued exploration.

This raises the following research questions. What makes a reasoning experience valuable for RLVR optimization, and which measurable properties of a question and of its trajectories, available during training, indicate that value? Given the vast quantity of experience collected during rollouts, how can a reasoning model effectively exploit its own stream of experience, deciding which past experiences to keep, prioritize and replay, how to combine them with fresh on-policy exploration, and how to account for the policy mismatch of replayed trajectories, so as to maximize learning toward scaling RL compute for large reasoning models and to improve reasoning performance, sample efficiency and training stability relative to standard on-policy RLVR?

Score learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for modeling complex probability distributions, driving progress in generative modeling, Bayesian inverse problems and sampling. Given a data measure $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, one considers its Gaussian-smoothed version $\mu_\sigma$, defined as the law of $X + \sigma Z$ (variance-exploding smoothing) or of $\sqrt{1-\sigma^2} X + \sigma Z$ (variance-preserving smoothing), where $X \sim \mu_{\mathrm{data}}$ and $Z$ is a standard Gaussian vector, with density $p_\sigma$. A key step in this framework is to approximate the score function $\nabla \log p_\sigma$, typically by score matching, and to use it to sample from $\mu_\sigma$, possibly across a range of noise levels: through the reverse process of a diffusion model, through Langevin dynamics driven by the learned score, or through predictor-corrector schemes that combine the two.

A central challenge is the low-temperature limit, that is, learning the score of $\mu_\sigma$ as $\sigma \to 0$, which encodes the most detailed information about the data. This regime is also the most valuable in practice: low-noise scores underpin many probabilistic learning frameworks, including diffusion models, whose noise schedules are designed to emphasize low noise levels and often require substantial post-training engineering to stabilize the learned scores. Yet accurately estimating the score in the small-$\sigma$ regime remains notoriously difficult. This raises a basic question: if the learned score is unavoidably inaccurate at small noise levels, what do score-based methods actually recover, and why do they nevertheless produce realistic samples?

A natural setting for this question is the widely adopted manifold hypothesis, which posits that $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$ is supported on a compact, low-dimensional manifold embedded in a high-dimensional ambient space. The data then carry two kinds of information: the geometry of their support, and the particular density of the data on that support. Existing convergence theory for diffusion and score-based samplers shows that the generated law approaches the target when the learned score is accurate, with error bounds that scale directly with the score mismatch, and related work studies other factors such as the dependence on dimension. These results, however, treat geometry and density together in the score error and do not say whether score errors affect the recovery of the support and the recovery of the on-manifold density differently. A growing body of work suggests that diffusion models often capture the data support while missing fine-grained distributional structure, but this evidence comes from restricted settings: estimating the intrinsic dimension of the manifold, linear manifolds (linear subspaces) only, or primarily empirical observations. Sufficient regularity conditions are known under which highly accurate scores concentrate mass near the manifold, but not how approximation errors may scale with $\sigma$. Likewise, it is established that under the manifold hypothesis the score develops a singularity in the small-noise regime, becoming orthogonal to the manifold and acting as a geometric projection onto it; yet these analyses fold the distributional information into a generic bounded remainder term and do not isolate the terms that involve the data density.

A first set of questions is therefore the following. In the small-$\sigma$ regime, at which orders in $\sigma$ do information about the manifold geometry and information about the data density enter the log-density and the score of $\mu_\sigma$? What accuracy, expressed as a rate in $\sigma$, must a learned score achieve for the distribution produced by a sampler to concentrate on the data manifold, and what accuracy is needed for it to recover $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$ itself? Do these two requirements differ and, when a score is accurate enough for the first but not for the second, what can be said about the distribution that is produced on the manifold?

A second set of questions concerns which target is worth learning. For tasks that depend only on the geometry of the data, such as approximating the Laplace-Beltrami operator and heat kernels or computing geodesic and diffusion distances, it is well known that samples drawn uniformly with respect to the manifold's intrinsic (Riemannian) volume measure are the most useful; uniform samples also support principled exploration of the manifold, yielding diverse samples while mitigating biases present in $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$. Classical graph-based normalizations achieve uniform sampling on a manifold by cancelling the sampling density, but they are designed to approximate geometric operators from neighborhood graphs and do not scale readily to high-dimensional, large-scale generative modeling; a recent alternative fine-tunes diffusion models so that they produce uniform samples, at the cost of additional training. Can the uniform distribution on the data manifold be obtained from a score model trained on samples of a non-uniform $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$, and how much score error can such a procedure tolerate compared with exact recovery of $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$? Any answer must cope with the fact that a score produced by a parameterized model is generally not a gradient field, so that the Langevin dynamics it drives is non-reversible and its stationary distribution has no closed form. Asymptotic analyses of such stationary distributions, based on WKB-type expansions of the stationary Fokker-Planck equation, typically focus on low-dimensional special examples or on drifts with a single stable point, whereas data supported on a manifold give rise to a whole manifold of stable points.

Finally, the same issues arise in Bayesian inverse problems, where a latent signal $x$ is observed through a measurement map with noise, $y = A(x) + \xi$, and inference amounts to sampling the posterior $p(x \mid y) \propto p(y \mid x) p_{\mathrm{prior}}(x)$. Plug-and-play methods run posterior Langevin dynamics that combine the gradient of the log-likelihood with a (possibly learned) prior score, and a common choice of prior is the smoothed data density $p_\sigma$ with small $\sigma$. Existing guarantees that such updates sample the correct posterior require the learned prior score to have vanishing error, or even to be exact, which is difficult to achieve at small $\sigma$. How does the choice of prior affect the score accuracy needed for correct posterior sampling? Answering these questions would clarify what score-based methods can reliably learn from imperfect scores in the low-noise regime, which learning objectives are realistic there, and whether these distinctions matter in practice for score-based generative models.

The ability to model complex, real-world phenomena is one of the central challenges in machine learning. Domains such as geospatial modeling, where terrain varies drastically across regions, or speech analysis, where signals exhibit bursts of volatility, are often characterized by pronounced non-stationarity: their statistical properties change across the input space, so that sharp, localized events can coexist with smooth, slowly varying regions. Gaussian processes (GPs) offer a principled framework for such problems, providing robust uncertainty estimates and flexible, non-parametric modeling. Despite these advantages, exact GPs suffer from two major limitations: their expressivity is constrained by the choice of kernel, and exact inference costs O(N^3) time and O(N^2) memory in the number N of training points, rendering it impractical for modern large-scale applications.

Most current approaches force a trade-off between expressivity and efficiency. On one hand, random Fourier features achieve impressive scalability: the kernel is approximated by an explicit, finite-dimensional feature map obtained by Monte Carlo sampling from its spectral density, so that the GP reduces to a Bayesian linear regression whose cost is linear in the number of data points, and the approximation error is backed by theoretical guarantees. Yet this construction depends on Bochner's theorem, which fundamentally restricts it to stationary kernels that assume uniform behavior across the entire domain; its globally supported sinusoidal features are inherently spatially invariant. Applying such models to non-stationary data leads to systematic mis-specification, resulting in compromised predictive accuracy and uncalibrated uncertainty estimates. Sparse variational GPs reduce the cost of exact inference through a set of inducing points, but they rely on iterative optimization whose cost grows cubically with the number of inducing points. On the other hand, expressive models such as deep GPs, spectral mixture kernels, and input-dependent kernels can capture non-stationarity, but they often reintroduce prohibitive computational costs, complex inference schemes, and challenges in optimization and hyperparameter tuning, and they typically retain a high complexity in the number of training points. Hybrid approaches that combine scalable approximations with expressive models, such as kernel interpolation, deep kernel learning, deep random features, and adaptive or compositional Fourier-feature representations, still tend to trade off scalability, expressivity, and interpretability.

The gap between scalable stationary models and complex non-stationary ones therefore remains. This raises the central question of whether the random-feature paradigm can be generalized beyond Bochner's theorem to the non-stationary setting: can one construct an explicit, randomly sampled feature map whose induced kernel adapts to local, input-dependent structure, while preserving the linear-in-data training and prediction cost that makes random features attractive? Such a construction should also be principled, with guarantees, comparable to those available for random Fourier features, that the induced kernel is valid and that the random approximation converges to it as the number of features grows. Finally, it remains open whether such an approach can offer a better trade-off between predictive accuracy, uncertainty quality, and computational cost than both stationary random features and more complex non-stationary GP models.

The multi-objective multi-armed bandit problem generalizes the classical, single-objective multi-armed bandit to settings with multiple, potentially conflicting objectives. Pulling an arm yields a vector of objective-specific rewards, so a single "best" arm is often ill-defined and optimality must account for trade-offs across objectives. The setting of interest here is the multi-objective linear contextual bandit: at each round, every arm of a finite set is described by a d-dimensional context vector, which may be chosen adversarially; each of the L objectives has its own fixed but unknown parameter vector; and the agent, after choosing an arm, observes an L-dimensional reward vector whose entry for each objective is the inner product of the arm's context with that objective's parameter, plus zero-mean sub-Gaussian noise.

One simple way to handle trade-offs is scalarization, which maps reward vectors to a scalar via, for example, weighted sums, minimax, or other nonlinear transforms, thereby reducing the problem to a single-objective bandit. However, selecting a suitable scalarization is itself nontrivial, and an arm that is optimal under one scalarization can be markedly suboptimal under another. An alternative is to reason directly in the vector space via Pareto optimality: the Pareto front comprises the arms whose mean reward vectors are not dominated component-wise by that of any other arm. Because it compares reward vectors objective-wise, Pareto optimality is more general than committing to a fixed scalarization. Performance is then usually measured by the Pareto regret, which sums over rounds the smallest uniform increase that would make the mean reward vector of the chosen arm non-dominated.

Prior work on Pareto regret in multi-objective bandits proposes and studies upper-confidence-bound (UCB) algorithms, which typically compute an empirical Pareto front at every round and are therefore complex. Approaches that identify the Pareto front by eliminating arms do not carry over to the contextual setting, where the Pareto front changes with the contexts and an arm discarded early may later be Pareto optimal. By contrast, the Pareto regret of Thompson Sampling has not been studied for multi-objective bandits: the only Thompson Sampling algorithm proposed for this problem comes without theoretical analysis, and the analyses of randomized scalarization in multi-objective Bayesian optimization concern the Bayesian regret under a known Gaussian prior, with bounds that increase with the number of objectives. This gap is noteworthy: in many single-objective contextual and non-contextual bandits, Thompson Sampling and its variants are empirically competitive with or superior to UCB methods, yet their worst-case (frequentist) analyses are typically more delicate. Extending Thompson Sampling to several objectives introduces additional challenges, including coordinating randomized samples across multiple objectives, ensuring optimism of the randomized estimates across all objectives simultaneously, and handling the possibility of multiple Pareto-optimal arms.

A second issue concerns the performance measure itself. The standard Pareto regret compares per-round mean reward vectors; consequently, a policy that plays only Pareto-optimal arms incurs zero Pareto regret, even when an alternative selection of arms over the same number of rounds would yield strictly larger cumulative rewards in every objective. Pareto regret therefore does not distinguish between policies that obtain different cumulative rewards while selecting only Pareto-optimal arms, and the resulting shortfall can grow with the number of rounds.

This raises two questions. First, can a computationally efficient, Thompson Sampling-type randomized algorithm for the multi-objective linear contextual bandit be designed with worst-case Pareto regret guarantees, how close can these guarantees come to those known for randomized algorithms in the single-objective linear setting, and how must they depend on the number of objectives? Second, how should optimality and regret be defined in this setting so that they also account for cumulative rewards under repeated selections, penalizing policies that are Pareto optimal round by round but inefficient in aggregate?

Diffusion models, and text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models in particular, have made astonishing progress in the quality of generated images. At the same time, emerging work on generative depth estimation has revealed that advanced T2I models hold a latent potential for depth estimation: the rich visual priors stored in a pre-trained T2I model can be leveraged to obtain strong zero-shot monocular depth estimation. Exploring a framework that bridges image generation and depth estimation is an essential step toward building unified models for both generation and visual perception.

Existing routes toward such unification each carry a substantial cost. The pioneering generative depth estimation paradigm repurposes a pre-trained T2I diffusion model by fine-tuning its denoising network with full parameters on depth data. It achieves powerful zero-shot depth estimation, but the parameter updates made during training irreversibly and catastrophically degrade the model's original image generation capability; later generative depth estimators that refine this recipe (for example with flow matching, geometry switchers or detail-preserving tuning strategies) inherit the same full-parameter fine-tuning and therefore the same loss. A second route unifies generation and depth estimation with a parallel dual-model architecture, in which two diffusion models run side by side and interact through feature-exchange operations; this requires running two diffusion models in parallel, and the interaction registers new knowledge into the pre-trained generator, which can affect its original image generation behaviour. A third, data-driven route trains a unified generation-and-perception model from scratch on massive multitask data (on the order of a hundred million samples). Despite remarkable progress, these solutions may be considered inefficient or resource-intensive, and potentially suboptimal.

Since a rich visual prior is already stored in advanced T2I models, a natural question arises: can a T2I model effortlessly acquire depth estimation capability without degrading its image generation capability? More concretely, starting from a fixed pre-trained T2I model, with a focus on modern transformer-based diffusion models, how can its latent depth estimation ability be unleashed so that a single model serves both image generation and depth estimation, keeping the original generation ability fully intact, adding only a small fraction of extra learnable parameters, and without resorting to massive multitask training data, while still reaching depth accuracy competitive with full-parameter fine-tuning and with existing unified models?

The problem is challenging. Among the effectively infinite pixel-level combinations that a T2I model learns to generate, there may exist underlying information highly correlated with scene depth; however, because text prompts provide only weak guidance and depth information is sparsely represented within the overall data distribution, extracting depth-relevant features from a fixed pre-trained T2I model is difficult. Any additional capacity must also make efficient use of the visual knowledge already present in the pre-trained model, so that depth estimation is obtained at a small parameter and data cost rather than by building and training a second large model.

PREDICTION: With the 2-layer MLP, we expect to see improved performance on the depth estimation task, especially on the Make3D and KITTI datasets where the model will benefit from the increased capacity to capture subtle depth variations.

Large language models can be knowledge edited, that is, updated to incorporate new or corrected facts without retraining from scratch. This capability is crucial for keeping models up to date with evolving information and for correcting errors on the fly. Large vision-language models (LVLMs), which combine textual and visual understanding, make knowledge editing even more challenging: they encode factual knowledge in both their textual and their visual pathways, and they require mechanisms that update the knowledge of both modalities consistently. Efficiently editing LVLMs is crucial for real-world applications, such as swiftly correcting critical visual recognition errors (e.g., a model misidentifying Donald Trump as Boris Johnson). However, research on multimodal knowledge editing remains scarce compared with the extensive studies on text-only language models.

Existing benchmarks for LVLM knowledge editing are limited in scope. They typically focus only on visual knowledge updates, such as changing the identity that an image is recognized as, and overlook scenarios in which textual facts about an entity (e.g., its attributes, roles or affiliations) must also be updated. Furthermore, they do not evaluate continual editing, in which multiple knowledge updates are performed sequentially, nor do they test a model's ability to reason compositionally over edited facts. This is a critical gap, because real-world knowledge updates often arrive incrementally and involve intertwined visual and textual information: once a model has been corrected about who appears in a photo and, separately, updated with a new fact about that person, a question about the person in the photo can only be answered correctly by combining both edits.

Existing editing approaches face fundamental difficulties in this setting. External-memory editors store edited knowledge outside the model and retrieve relevant information at inference time without modifying model parameters, which makes them suitable for long-term retention. However, they typically transplant text-based retrieval strategies from language models directly, ignoring visual cues that are necessary for matching multimodal queries to the right edits, which can reduce retrieval accuracy. They also face an internalization issue: the model may over-rely on its stale internal knowledge, especially when the retrieved information conflicts with what it has learned, leading to incorrect answers. Conversely, internal-memory editors embed edits directly into model parameters via fine-tuning or low-rank adaptation, viewing the feed-forward network as a key-value memory that stores in-model knowledge. Although beneficial for internalizing edits, these methods typically store visual and textual edits within a unified representation space, risking cross-modal interference and representation collapse; moreover, sequential internal edits suffer from catastrophic forgetting, degrading previously stored knowledge with successive updates.

This raises several questions. How can an LVLM accommodate a continual sequence of interleaved visual and textual edits so that each new edit takes effect while earlier edits are retained, without interference between modalities? How can separately edited visual and textual facts be integrated to answer compositional queries that require both, even when externally retrieved evidence and the model's internal knowledge disagree? And how can editors be evaluated in this continual and compositional setting, which existing benchmarks do not cover?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: unified multimodal editing via policy updating
PROPOSAL: We will design a mechanism that updates the knowledge network of an LVLM by integrating visual and textual edits. Specifically, we will utilize a policy-based approach, where the model learns to update its knowledge by consuming policy embeddings that encode the edits. This allows the model to learn a consensual representation of the edits and integrate them seamlessly into its existing knowledge network. We will employ a transformer-based encoder-decoder framework, fine-tune on a set of multimodal datasets, and evaluate on a range of tasks including knowledge-based visual question answering and text-image retrieval.
CONTROLS: baseline comparison with traditional external-memory editing strategies, ablation study on the importance of policy embeddings, fine-tuning without policy embeddings. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this approach should outperform traditional external-memory editors in multimodal knowledge editing tasks, and potentially provide more robust and flexible updates. However, it may struggle with catastrophic forgetting if not properly regularized.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: testing catastrophic forgetting resistance in multimodal editing
PROPOSAL: Given the concerns about catastrophic forgetting in internal-memory editors, we will introduce a regularized training objective that encourages the model to retain previously updated knowledge while incorporating new edits. Specifically, we will propose a knowledge distillation objective that emphasizes the retention of salient information from the model's initial knowledge state, which we will then blend with the information from the latest edit. We hypothesize that this approach will improve the model's ability to retain previously updated knowledge.
CONTROLS: quantitative evaluation of catastrophic forgetting, comparison with other regularization schemes (e.g., L1/L2 penalty, gradient regularization), ablation study on the importance of the knowledge distillation objective
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this approach should significantly reduce catastrophic forgetting in multimodal editing tasks, but may come at the expense of slower convergence rates or decreased model accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: multi-step evaluation methodology for multimodal knowledge editors
PROPOSAL: To better assess the performance of multimodal knowledge editors, we will propose a multi-step evaluation methodology that measures their performance over a series of incremental update steps. Specifically, we will evaluate the model's accuracy on a range of tasks (e.g., visual question answering, text-image retrieval) across multiple update steps, using metrics that capture both short-term and long-term recall. This will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the model's ability to retain previously updated knowledge over time.
CONTROLS: comparisons with existing evaluation methodologies (e.g., one-shot update, batch update), ablation study on the importance of evaluating model performance over multiple update steps
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this evaluation methodology should provide a more nuanced understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of moment-to-moment performance of multimodal editors but may require an additional increase in data annotation and new evaluation frameworks.

ACTION: REVISE
number: 3
TITLE: refined multi-step evaluation methodology for multimodal knowledge editors
PROPOSAL: To further refine our multi-step evaluation methodology, we will introduce a difficulty metric that measures the average difficulty of the tasks presented to the model over multiple update steps. This metric will be used to normalize the model's performance across different difficulty levels, allowing for a more fair comparison between models. Additionally, we will also track the model's performance on a set of compositional questions that require integrating previously updated knowledge with new information.

PROPOSAL: We will extend our policy-based editing approach to handle more realistic image editing tasks, such as object removal, object insertion, and image inpainting. Our goal is to demonstrate that our policy-based editing framework can successfully update LVLMs to handle such complex image editing tasks.
