TITLE: adversarial evaluation of multimodal knowledge editors
PROPOSAL: To provide a more comprehensive assessment of multimodal knowledge editors, we will introduce an adversarial evaluation framework that tests the model's resilience tocrafted attacks designed to compromise its performance. Specifically, we will use strong and strategic attacks (e.g., semantic adversarial examples, multi-step attacks) to probe the model's vulnerabilities and evaluate its robustness.

COST: 700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this evaluation framework should help identify potential vulnerabilities in multimodal knowledge editors and provide valuable insights into the limitations of these models, but may require significant computational resources and careful tuning of the attack strategies.

Specifically, we will design a set of experiments that update the model's knowledge with both visual and textual information simultaneously, and evaluate its ability to retain previously learned knowledge.

TITLE: hybrid multimodal editing with knowledge graph episodic memory
PROPOSAL: We will develop a hybrid approach that combines the strengths of policy-based editing and knowledge graph episodic memory. Specifically, we will design a model that uses a knowledge graph to store and retrieve multimodal information, and leverages policy updates to incorporate new knowledge into the model. This approach should enable the model to adapt to new information and retain previously learned knowledge over time.
CONTROLS: comparison with policy-based editing and knowledge graph episodic memory, ablation study on the impact of the hybrid approach. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this hybrid approach should provide a robust and adaptive way to update multimodal knowledge, but may require careful tuning of the model's architecture and the knowledge graph to avoid information overload and catastrophic forgetting.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the performance of our multimodal knowledge editors on real-world applications such as fact-checking, image classification, and question answering. Specifically, we will use datasets such as the Wikipedia dataset for fact-checking and the ImageNet dataset for image classification, and evaluate the model's performance using metrics such as accuracy, F1 score, and mean average precision.

COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this evaluation will provide a real-world assessment of the performance of our multimodal knowledge editors and shed light on their strengths and limitations, but may require significant resources and expertise to design and collect the necessary datasets.

Recent advances in computer graphics and vision have highlighted image relighting, that is, changing the illumination of an existing image, as a critical task for film production, augmented reality and digital content creation. Full-image relighting, in which both the objects and the surrounding scene must be relit, remains a challenging problem.

Existing works can be grouped into object-centric approaches, which often ignore or replace the background, and scene-level methods, which attempt full-image relighting but remain largely data-driven: they struggle to generalize beyond the training distribution without extensive and diverse data, and cannot maintain the lighting of self-luminous objects. Even state-of-the-art foreground relighting methods still suffer from albedo inconsistency and imprecise lighting control: relighting can, for instance, alter the colors of a carpet, or make light intended to come from the left appear to come from the left rear although the scene contains no internal light source. Other lines of work have their own restrictions. Many methods address only portraits or isolated objects. Scribble-based control of scene lighting lacks precision and has been limited to indoor scenes. Outdoor full-image relighting methods either require surface normals as input or rely on directional lighting models that generalize poorly to indoor scenes. A recent generative approach that simulates both inverse rendering (recovering intrinsic properties such as albedo, surface normals, roughness and metallicity from an image) and forward rendering conditions the forward step on irradiance, which makes precise lighting control challenging, and is limited to indoor scenes. Intrinsic decomposition methods are themselves hampered by the difficulty of acquiring large-scale training data and are mostly designed for specific scenarios, such as indoor scenes or single objects. These limitations point to the lack of a physically interpretable representation of the scene in current relighting methods and to the inherent limitations of data-driven priors, both of which stand in the way of controllable and physically plausible full-image relighting.

Three major challenges follow. First, data with diverse and complex scene illumination are hard to acquire: obtaining high-quality images of full scenes under diverse and controlled lighting conditions is resource-intensive and technically challenging, and it is infeasible to capture real-world datasets that show the same scene under multiple lighting conditions. Existing datasets that provide intrinsic components focus mainly on indoor scenes and do not render images under varying lighting conditions. Second, ensuring physical plausibility is difficult, as purely data-driven approaches often generate results that violate basic light transport principles. Third, limited data-driven priors restrict generalizability, leading to poor robustness to unseen materials, lighting conditions and realistic scene compositions, and existing attempts to bridge the gap between synthetic training data and real images for full-scene relighting remain suboptimal. Full scenes add a further difficulty: self-luminous objects and built-in light sources, such as light coming through windows, interfere with controlling the direction and intensity of the new lighting while keeping the background consistent.

This raises the following questions. How can an entire image, objects and scene together, indoor or outdoor, be relit under a user-specified lighting condition with precise control of light direction and intensity, while preserving the albedo and material appearance of its surfaces, the content and consistency of the background, and the lighting of self-luminous elements? How can a relighting model be made to respect basic light transport, so that shading, highlights and shadows follow the new lighting across a wide variety of materials? And how can such a model generalize to real-world images with unseen materials, lighting conditions and scene compositions when paired data under controlled lighting are scarce and real captures of the same scene under multiple lightings are infeasible?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: view-dependent radiance decomposition
PROPOSAL: Investigate the potential of view-dependent radiance decomposition for physically plausible full-image relighting. We'll apply a novel decomposition method, focusing on recovering the high-frequency components of radiance with respect to view angles, and assess its performance on synthetic datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare with current state-of-the-art full-image relighting methods and our own simplified radiance decomposition approach without view-dependent components.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This decomposition method can improve full-image relighting accuracy, especially in scenes with complex environments and non-diffuse materials. However, it may struggle with cases where objects have strong view-independent light transport properties.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: intrinsic image decomposition with boundary handling
PROPOSAL: Design an intrinsic image decomposition method that explicitly handles scene boundaries to allow for accurate training and realistic rendering. We'll apply a boundary-aware physics-based model, including Fresnel terms for surface normals and conductance models for lighting, to retrieve intrinsic components with sharper edges and reduced artifacts.
CONTROLS: Compare with current intrinsic image decomposition methods that neglect or approximate boundary conditions, as well as our own simplified boundary- handling approach using standard convolutional filters.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This boundary- handling model should improve decomposition accuracy, especially at scene boundaries, but may require additional computational resources to handle the increased model complexity.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: multi-scale neural rendering for lighting control
PROPOSAL: Train a multi-scale neural rendering model to generate photorealistic images with user-specified lighting conditions, focusing on precise control of light direction, intensity, and shading while maintaining physical plausibility. We'll test our model on a synthetic dataset with varying lighting conditions and scene complexities.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This model should demonstrate robust lighting control and achieve state-of-the-art relighting accuracy, but may require large-scale synthetic training data to capture the desired physical plausibility.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: hybrid radiance decomposition with view-dependent components
PROPOSAL: Revise the initial view-dependent radiance decomposition approach to combine low-frequency radiance with view-dependent high-frequency components, using a multi-resolution network to separate and refine rough and detailed radiance information. This hybrid approach should leverage the strengths of both techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original view-dependent radiance decomposition and additively decompose the improvements from combining the two approaches.
COST: 10 additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This hybrid approach should achieve a better trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency, but requires careful tuning of the multi-resolution network architecture to prevent overfitting or underfitting.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: scene-aware lighting transfer
PROPOSAL: Develop a scene-aware lighting transfer method that analyzes the scene geometry and intrinsic properties to reason about the optimal lighting direction, intensity, and type. We'll train a scene-understanding network to predict these parameters from the intrinsic components and apply them to the scene for context-aware relighting.
CONTROLS: Evaluate our method on both synthetic and real-world scenes, comparing with standard lighting transfer techniques and assessing its ability to preserve scene content and color consistency.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This scene-aware lighting transfer approach should significantly improve the realism and consistency of relighting results, but may struggle with complex or noisy scenes where it's difficult to establish a clear understanding of the scene's intrinsic properties.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation
PROPOSAL: Investigate discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation techniques that can more accurately model the lighting behavior at object boundaries, taking into account the object's albedo, shape, and surrounding environment. We'll apply a Fréchet variant of the Poisson equation to recover a piecewise-continuous lighting solution for each object in the scene.
CONTROLS: Compare with the relighting results from our existing methods, specifically testing the improvement in shading, highlights, and shadows caused by accounting for discontinuities in lighting.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should lead to improved lighting realism at object boundaries, especially for scenes with closely-spaced or complexly-shaped objects. However, the estimation complexity may increase significantly for scenes with many objects or intricate geometry.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: partial-diffuse-specular separation from multi-scale detail
PROPOSAL: Propose a multi-scale separation approach to extract partial, diffuse, and specular components from an image, using a detail refinement and coarsening scheme to improve partial-diffuse-specular separation performance. This is crucial for accurate radiance decomposition and relighting, allowing for more precise modeling of surface reflectance and directional scatter.
CONTROLS: Compare this multi-scale method with standard separation approaches in terms of graininess, adaptivity, and relighting results on various synthetic and real-world datasets.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This separation method should enhance the physical plausibility of relighting results by restoring accurate partial-diffuse-specular structure, but may struggle with scenes having complex and multi-scale surface roughness.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: interactively-controllable neural relighting
PROPOSAL: Develop a neural network-based relighting framework that enables real-time, user-interaction-driven control over lighting direction, intensity, and color. We'll introduce a neural representation of relighting parameters that can be modulated by user inputs, facilitating end-user relighting control without requiring extensive domain knowledge or graphics expertise.
CONTROLS: Compare user-interaction accuracy and relighting result quality with those from black-box full-image relighting approaches and investigate the synergies between user interactions and scholar-crafted physics-based relighting.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This interactive method should significantly enhance user experience by providing fine-grained control over relighting but may encounter limitations in extrapolating efficiently beyond the demonstration range, especially with materials that embrace a comprehensive physical representation of dynamic relighting behaviors.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: leveraging real-world relighting validation and synergy 
PROPOSAL: Investigate the potential for real-world relighting and data acquisition synergies in our existing methods, validating their performance in real-world scenes and datasets while also augmenting synthesis-based approaches for real-world-driven full-image relighting models. This real-world focus is essential to providing the physically-grounded formulation needed for accurate data-driven full-image relighting models, known as real-world-driven validation.
CONTROLS: Assess the relighting quality improvement when training models on synthetic scenes that have been validated against real-world data, then testing these improved synth+real-scene methods on unseen real-world scenes (not used in training or during synthesis) and various internal priors.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Incorporating real-world validation should further improve relighting quality and robustness but may require larger-scale datasets and optimizing computational efficiency to outperform faster synthesis-based methods.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: hybrid discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation
PROPOSAL: Revise the discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation approach by integrating the hybrid radiance decomposition with view-dependent components to leverage the strengths of both in modelling light transport discontinuities, achieving a finer-grain representation and improving accuracy in scenes with complex lighting settings, thus achieving another remarkable trade-off between the complexity of these discontinuity-controlled scenes and the minimal added runtime cost for updates and finer-control analyzers.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the hybrid estimation approach's convergence and accuracy for a wider range of images, dataset sources, and resolutions, with comparison against other highest-rated scene-bound and label-driven estimation-centric synthesis-based approaches to see if improved autonomous controlled synthesis, together with improving measurement-based renderings and meta-anals, aligns to general relighting tasks.
COST: 5 additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This hybrid lighting estimation approach should achieve even greater accuracy and physics-based realism in scene lighting modeling, while still benefiting from improvements and interchange handling, improving practical workflows and tools efficiency in digitally-rendered content or view-based sensory ensemble simulations.

enonce:
Humans naturally parse scenes into coherent objects (e.g., grouping features such as a rounded shape, a smooth surface and a muted color into the mug) and further ground their identities in context (e.g., recognizing my coffee mug on the desk rather than just a mug). This is assumed to be made possible by what cognitive scientists call object binding, the brain's ability to group an object's low-level features (color, shape, motion, etc.) into a unified representation. This in turn enables objects to be stored efficiently and compositionally in memory and used as high-level symbols for reasoning about individual object instances. The binding problem is a genuine computational challenge, as evidenced by humans' limited competence in conjunction-search tasks and by clinical dissociations such as Balint's syndrome, where feature perception remains intact but binding breaks down. If AI systems could replicate the human ability for object binding, that may help them ground symbols in perception and exploit compositionality. The key question is: do current AI systems solve the binding problem?

Object binding has received little attention in mainstream AI research. Cognition-inspired models build in human-like object-based attention. By contrast, mainstream vision models are assumed to learn implicitly to handle multiple objects from training data, yet empirical studies show that they often "attend" only to the most salient regions and overlook the rest. While the attention scores of Vision Transformers (ViTs) can capture global image structure and salient regions (often corresponding to target objects), empirical evidence shows that self-attention tends to group patches by low-level feature similarity rather than reliably producing object-level binding. Object-centric methods such as Slot Attention fix this by allocating a small set of learnable slots that compete for token features, enforcing binding by design; however, because such modules are added externally rather than integrated into the transformer architecture, they introduce additional challenges for scaling and training. Other work has assumed that ViTs already carry implicit object-level structure and has tried to group patches into objects directly from their activations or attention maps. Binding failures are also seen as a source of performance breakdowns in modern transformer-based systems: text-to-image diffusion models suffer attribute leakage between entities (e.g., both a dog and a cat end up wearing sunglasses and a sun-hat), and vision-language models struggle to differentiate multiple objects defined by feature conjunctions. Despite these failures, transformers still demonstrate some binding capability, yet the underlying mechanism is not well understood: binding has started to be characterized in language models, but binding mechanisms in vision transformers remain unexplored. Whether AI vision models, especially leading ViTs, can achieve robust object binding without explicit mechanisms therefore remains an open question.

Cognitive scientists have questioned whether ViTs can bind objects at all, arguing that they lack mechanisms for dynamically and flexibly grouping features, that they lack the recurrence necessary for iterative refinement of object representations, and that, as purely connectionist models, they appear incapable of true symbolic processing. However, these architectural limitations do not preclude binding from emerging through learning. ViTs share several computational parallels with the mammalian visual system: both rely on parallel, distributed and hierarchical processing; explicit position embeddings resemble the spatial tagging and spatiotopic organization observed in the ventral stream; and self-attention is akin to the dynamic tuning and attentional modulation thought to be primary mechanisms of binding in the brain. Moreover, knowing which patches belong to the same object would be useful for prediction and could guide attention, and human-labeled data also reflects object-level structure, so ViTs could acquire binding by imitation. ViTs may therefore learn to bind objects directly from large-scale training data, without requiring explicit architectural inductive biases.

This raises the question of whether object binding naturally emerges in large, pretrained Vision Transformers, a question that matters for both cognitive science and AI. Answering it requires establishing whether the internal representations of such models reliably encode which parts of an image belong to the same object; and, if they do, how this information is represented, whether it reflects an ability acquired through learning rather than a trivial artifact of the architecture, and whether the model actually makes functional use of it.

Dictionary learning, in its most general form, assumes that observations X are generated by latent variables Z through an unknown function, X = g(Z). The goal is to recover the latent generative process from observational data alone, a fundamental task in both science and machine learning. This nonparametric formulation unifies a wide range of latent variable models, including independent component analysis, factor analysis and causal representation learning.

Identifiability, the ability to recover the true generative model from data, is crucial for understanding the hidden world. Yet in general dictionary learning, where both the latent variables and the generating process are unknown, the problem is fundamentally ill-posed without additional assumptions, akin to finding a needle in a haystack. To reduce this ambiguity, most prior work imposes strong parametric constraints that limit the space of possible solutions. The practice is so widespread that, although dictionary learning is fundamentally nonparametric, it is almost always instantiated as a linear model, in which observations are sparse linear combinations of latent variables. Such linearity can be overly restrictive and fails to capture the complexity of many real-world generative processes. Sparse autoencoders, commonly used in mechanistic interpretability, especially for foundation models, are a relevant example: although effective in some settings, they are rooted in sparse linear dictionary learning, which raises concerns about their ability to represent the inherently nonlinear structure of large-scale neural representations.

Many efforts have been made to relax the linearity assumption. In nonlinear independent component analysis, one line of work leverages auxiliary variables as weak supervision to achieve identifiability under statistical independence, while another constrains the mixing function itself. In causal representation learning, identifiability often depends on access to interventional data or counterfactual views, which presuppose some control over the data-generating process. Some basic conditions cannot be avoided: just as linear dictionary learning needs conditions such as the restricted isometry property so that distinct latent codes map to distinguishable observations, the nonlinear generating function must be smooth and injective so that no information is lost. But avoiding information loss is not sufficient for full recovery of the latent variables in the nonlinear regime, which is why existing guarantees rely on restricted function classes or on auxiliary information such as domain or time indices, interventions or counterfactual data.

A gap therefore remains between theoretical guarantees and practical utility. Theoretically, while additional assumptions can yield recovery guarantees, it is rarely possible to verify whether they hold in practice; understanding which guarantees remain valid when assumptions are violated is therefore essential for reliably uncovering the truth in general settings. Practically, what matters is less identifiability under ideal conditions than which inductive biases promote recovery, especially when the ground truth is unknown. Yet most existing approaches offer no guarantees under even mild violations of their assumptions, which makes their associated biases, such as contrastive objectives or weak supervision, difficult to generalize across settings.

The challenge is to make identifiability actionable in general settings: only observational data are available, the generating function is nonlinear and unknown, no parametric constraint or auxiliary supervision can be relied upon, and only basic conditions such as invertibility and differentiability are assumed, accepting that recovering every latent variable may then be infeasible. In such settings, two questions remain open:
- What aspects of the latent process can still be recovered with guarantees?
- What inductive biases should be introduced to guide recovery, ideally ones that could be adopted universally across models and settings?
A related question is whether, and under which additional conditions that require no auxiliary information, all latent variables could still be recovered.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: natural assumption bounds for the hanin norm
PROPOSAL: Prove a bound for the Hanin norm of the Jacobian of a smooth, but unknown, generating function g(Z). Specifically, we will derive an upper bound in terms of the differentiability order and a Lipschitz constant of g. We will assume that g may acordo with any sequence of k times continuously differentiable functions.
CONTROLS: Compare to known bounds in related literature, e.g. Elazar-Pinhas (2020) on Hanin norm bounds for contexts of deep learning.
COST: 0.5 GPU-hours (analytical computation)
PREDICTION: The bound we derive should be slightly looser than existing bounds but will be scalable to higher-dimensional data; the bound may not hold for rough generative functions.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: from hanin norm bounds to invertibility conditions
PROPOSAL: Prove a sufficient condition for a diffeomorphism (smooth and bijective) between the latent space Z and the image space X (i.e., 1 : 1), in terms of the Hanin norm bound derived in proposal 1. The condition will require a lower bound on the determinant of the Jacobian of g(Z) that grows polynomially with the dimensionality of the data.
CONTROLS: Compare to known results on diffeomorphism bounds, e.g. Guillou (2018) on diffeomorphism conditions using inverse function theorem.
COST: 1.0 GPU-hours (matrix computations and diagonalization).
PREDICTION: The condition should be useful for implying invertibility, but it may not hold in cases where the generative function has vanishing eigenvalues or extremely high-dimensionality, which can cause numerical instability.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: alternating minimization for non-linear dictionary learning
PROPOSAL: Implement an alternating minimization approach for optimizing a non-linear dictionary, using a simplified version of the Hidden Neural Tangent Kernel (HNTK) to facilitate computation. We will alternate between updating the non-linear dictionary and the latent representations in the data. The goal is to demonstrate empirical success in recovering the nonlinear structure of simple generative processes.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing baselines, such as deep clustered sparse coding or non-linear dictionary learning with cyclic optimization.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (empirical evaluation using synthetic data).
PREDICTION: The approach may recover some structure of the generative process but is likely to fail for complex, high-dimensional data; further optimization or initialization strategies may help alleviate the non-convexity of this problem.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: natural assumption bounds for the hanin norm
PROPOSAL: Refine the bound in proposal 1 by incorporating a regularization term that encourages a certain degree of sparsity in the Jacobian of the generating function. This term will enhance the stability of the bound and allow it to hold for a broader class of functions.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original bound in proposal 1 and study the trade-off between sparsity and conservativeness, as described above.
COST: 0.5 GPU-hours (computations and marginalization).
PREDICTION: The refined bound should improve the usability of the previous results, but it may become less tight or lose some generality, trading off the relationships between these two requirements.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: comparison to partial information theory
PROPOSAL: Compare the identifiability guarantees derived from the Hanin norm bounds and diffeomorphism conditions to those that can be obtained from partial information theory, specifically the concept of sufficient statistics for the generative process. We will study how the strength of these guarantees compares for different classes of generative functions.
CONTROLS: Specifically, analyze the comparisons in terms of the dimensionality of the sufficient statistics, the complexity of the generative process, and the information available in the data.
COST: 0.5 GPU-hours (information-theoretic calculations and comparisons).
PREDICTION: The comparison may highlight situations in which one of these approaches is more suited to the generative process at hand, but it may also reveal that the best results come from using these approaches in combination.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: recovering compression parameters through surrogate optimal transport
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to recover the parameters of a generative process that is compressing the latent variables, by formulating the optimization problem as a surrogate optimal transport problem. This involves solving a Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality formulation, where the goal is to find a transport plan between the distributions of the latent and observed variables.
CONTROLS: Use the same alternating minimization approach as in proposal 3 to optimize the transport plan, and study its convergence properties.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (combining gradient descent and OT optimization).
PREDICTION: The method may help recover the compression parameters even when the generative process is highly non-linear, but it may suffer from high computational cost and can be heavily dependent on the choice of the optimizer for the OT problem.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: a surrogate noise model for simulation and inference
PROPOSAL: Develop a method for simulating and inferring generative processes by treating the noise as a surrogate for a probabilistic unknown. Specifically, this involve using a fixed-point iteration to calculate an approximation of the noise distribution, and a related algorithm for inferring the generative process parameters from the conditional expectation of this distribution.
CONTROLS: Compare the robustness of the surrogate noise model to different perturbation schemes for simulating real-world data, and study its capacity to recover the generative process.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (fixed-point iteration and Monte Carlo inference).
PREDICTION: The surrogate noise model may help improve the robustness of the inference procedure, but it may be computationally expensive and could suffer from either over-smoothing or over-fitting, depending on the choice of the probabilistic unknown.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: alternating minimization for non-linear dictionary learning
PROPOSAL: Modify the alternating minimization approach in proposal 3 to incorporate an initial warm-up phase using a linear approximation of the generating function. This allows the algorithm to adapt to the non-linearities in the data more effectively, potentially improving convergence towards the optimal dictionary.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of this revised approach to the original alternating minimization, and assess the trade-off between warm-up duration and overall convergence time.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (combining empirical evaluation and optimized warm-up schedule).
PREDICTION: The warm-up phase may improve the algorithm's ability to adapt to non-linear data generating processes but could also increase the overall computational cost and risk of over-optimization.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: type-based inference with transformer language models
PROPOSAL: Devise a type-based inference framework for recovering the latent structure of language models, leveraging their internal types and transformer architecture to constrain the generative process. This will involve analyzing the Transformer layers' behavior and designing inference algorithms that exploit the structure of the language model's hidden states.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the type-based inference approach on a variety of language models and assess its performance on tasks such as text generation and semantic parsing.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (large-scale language model simulations).
PREDICTION: The type-based inference framework may uncover novel insights into the latent structure of language models, but it may require substantial computational resources and may be challenging to generalize across different model architectures.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: universality of alternating minimization for non-linear dictionary learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the universality of the alternating minimization approach derived in proposal 3, specifically whether it can be applied to recover the generative process in a wide range of settings, including those with complex and high-dimensional data, sparse or noisy observations, and varying degrees of non-linearity. We will perform extensive numerical experiments and analytical investigations to evaluate the robustness of the approach.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the alternating minimization to other state-of-the-art approaches for non-linear dictionary learning and assess its robustness under various perturbations of the data-generating process.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (numerical experiments and sensitivity analysis).
PREDICTION: The universality analysis may indicate that alternating minimization has broad applicability, but it may also reveal limitations, such as vulnerability to certain types of outliers or difficulties in handling data with shifted or removed features.

Diffusion models have recently demonstrated remarkable capabilities in synthesizing high-quality images, significantly surpassing earlier generative approaches such as generative adversarial networks and variational autoencoders. Despite their impressive fidelity, deploying diffusion models in realistic cloud-to-user applications introduces a fundamental bottleneck: transmission bandwidth. A standard diffusion model produces a high-fidelity image by performing a fixed number of denoising steps, regardless of downstream transmission limitations. In conventional scenarios, the generated images then undergo aggressive lossy compression before transmission to accommodate the limited bandwidth. This cascaded approach, high-quality generation followed by subsequent compression, not only incurs redundant computational overhead, since computation is spent on details that are later discarded, but also significantly degrades perceptual quality, as the compression process often erases the intricate textures and fine details carefully constructed by the diffusion model.

This motivates a critical question: can bandwidth-awareness be integrated directly into the diffusion generation process, so that the quality of the generated image is adapted to the available bandwidth, avoiding the inefficiency and perceptual quality loss associated with post-generation compression? Ideally, such a generator would meet a user-specified bitrate budget, avoid compression-induced artifacts and redundant computation, and offer fine-grained, dynamic control over image quality according to real-time bandwidth conditions in practical cloud-to-user deployments.

The question is not straightforward. During sampling, diffusion models progressively refine coarse structures into detailed, realistic textures through iterative denoising steps, so, intuitively, terminating the process early would yield simpler, lower-detail images suited to constrained bandwidth. However, naively reducing the number of diffusion steps typically produces suboptimal visual quality: models trained for complete denoising trajectories are not optimized for early termination, which leads to visual artifacts and poor perceptual coherence.

Existing lines of work address only parts of this problem. A large body of work accelerates diffusion sampling, through deterministic samplers that need fewer inference steps, numerical solvers inspired by ordinary differential equations, distillation of slow teacher models into faster students, adaptive step-size selection, latent-space compression, non-uniform step skipping, dynamic network pruning, predictors of the minimal number of denoising steps, and adaptive inference trajectories. These methods reduce the cost of sampling while preserving generation quality, but they are not designed to control the bitrate of the generated image. Conditional and controllable diffusion models, from classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance to latent diffusion and region-based conditioning for interactive editing, allow flexible control over attributes of the generated content, but they do not directly address bandwidth constraints. How to make a diffusion model generate images that respect a specified bandwidth budget while preserving perceptual quality and avoiding wasted computation therefore remains an open problem.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: bitrate-aware diffusion sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of adaptively controlling the number of denoising steps based on the available bandwidth, using a simple bandwidth-aware sampler that terminates the process when the remaining bitrate drops below a predetermined threshold. Train a standard unconditional diffusion model on a dataset of images with varying qualities (e.g., CIFAR-10, LSUN, CelebA) and validate the sampler on a separate test set with controlled bandwidth constraints.
CONTROLS: Compare with naive termination and full denoising step counts, to assess the trade-offs between generation quality and bitrate efficiency. Use metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, and bits per pixel (bpp) to evaluate the quality and bitrate of generated images, reported alongside the main results.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive sampler should produce high-quality images that respect the specified bitrate budget, outperforming naive termination methods in both quality and bitrate efficiency. However, it may fail when the available bandwidth is too low to support the resolution or detail of the input image.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: compressed diffusion model
PROPOSAL: Modify the diffusion model architecture to natively incorporate compression-aware loss functions and constraints, allowing the model to learn implicit representations of the output image that are more amenable to transmission under bandwidth constraints. Design a custom loss function that minimizes both the reconstruction error and a compression-aware penalty term, and experiment with applying state-of-the-art compression algorithms (e.g., JPEG, JPEG 2000) to the output image.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard diffusion models and the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler (Proposal 1) to assess the trade-offs between quality, bitrate efficiency, and computational overhead. Use a dataset of high-resolution images (e.g., ImageNet, COCO) to evaluate the effectiveness of the compressed diffusion model, as described above.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The compressed diffusion model should achieve state-of-the-art bitrate efficiency while maintaining competitive generation quality, but may require a larger model size and more computationally expensive training due to the additional compression-aware loss terms.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: bitrate-aware diffusion sampling
PROPOSAL: Refine the proposed bitrate-aware diffusion sampler (Proposal 1) by incorporating a novel estimation mechanism for the remaining bitrate, which adaptively adjusts the sampling process to ensure that the generated image's bitrate drops below the target budget. Experiment with different estimation methods, such as bitrate prediction networks or robust bitrate estimators, to determine their impact on sampler performance.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the compressed diffusion model (Proposal 2) to assess the improvements brought by the revised estimation mechanism, as described above. Validate the sampler on a diverse set of images with rich textures and details, such as natural scenes and artwork.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised bitrate-aware diffusion sampler with estimation mechanism should demonstrate more accurate bitrate control and higher quality images, outperforming the original sampler and competitive with the compressed diffusion model, but may incur additional computational overhead due to the estimation process.

ACTION: REVISE
 TITLE: bitrate-aware diffusion sampling
 PROPOSAL: Incorporate a learning-based mechanism that adapts the sampling process to the specific characteristics of the input image, allowing the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler to make informed decisions about when to terminate the sampling process and achieve optimal bitrate-accuracy trade-offs.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the compressed diffusion model to assess the improvements brought by the adaptive learning mechanism, following the setup outlined in the proposal.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The learning-based mechanism in the revised bitrate-aware diffusion sampler should demonstrate improved bitrate control and higher quality images, especially when dealing with diverse input images.

ADDITIONAL EXPERIMENT: Analyze the impact of different learning objectives and mechanism types, such as supervised learning with bitrate labels or self-supervised learning with bitrate-predictive losses.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adaptive compression matching
PROPOSAL: Develop an adaptive compression algorithm that dynamically selects the optimal compression parameters (e.g., quantization step, entropy coding scheme) for each output image, based on the estimated bitrate-accuracy trade-offs learned by the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler. This approach allows for real-time bitrate adaptation, ensuring that the generated image respects the available bandwidth while maintaining optimal quality.
CONTROLS: Compare with the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the compressed diffusion model to evaluate the benefits of adaptive compression matching. Use a dataset of high-resolution images with varying complexities, with details given in the appendix.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive compression matching algorithm should demonstrate improved bitrate efficiency and quality, outperforming both the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the compressed diffusion model, especially under time-varying bandwidth constraints.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: joint bitrate-aware diffusion training
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel training framework that jointly optimizes the diffusion model, the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler, and the adaptive compression matching algorithm to achieve a balanced solution that respects the bitrate budget while preserving high image quality. Use a hierarchical optimization approach, where the model is trained to minimize a combination of image quality metrics and the estimated bitrate.
CONTROLS: Compare with separate training and adaptation of the diffusion model, bitrate-aware diffusion sampler, and adaptive compression matching algorithm to evaluate the benefits of joint training. Validate the approach using a real-world image transmission application, reported alongside the main results.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Joint bitrate-aware diffusion training should produce a model that achieves superior bitrate-accuracy trade-offs, outperforming the separate training approach, but may require a larger model size and more computationally expensive training due to the additional optimizer.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: adaptive compression matching
PROPOSAL: Modify the adaptive compression matching algorithm (Proposal 3) to incorporate a bitrate-effective distortion metric, such as structural similarity (SSIM) or perceptual quality (PQ), which balances the trade-off between visual quality and bitrate. This modification enables the adaptive compression matching algorithm to more effectively optimize the compression process and reduce the required bitrate while maintaining high image quality.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original adaptive compression matching algorithm (Proposal 3) and the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler to evaluate the benefits of incorporating a bitrate-effective distortion metric, with results reported in a table.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised adaptive compression matching algorithm should achieve better bitrate efficiency and higher quality images, surpassing the original adaptation approach and competitive with the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler, while maintaining efficient bitrate control under a wide range of bandwidth conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: partial image rendering
PROPOSAL: Develop a partial image rendering technique that selectively renders regions of an image with varying resolutions, based on the available bandwidth and the importance of each region. Use the adaptive compression matching algorithm (Proposal 3) to compress the rendered regions and adaptively adjust their resolutions based on the estimated bitrate and visual quality.
CONTROLS: Compare with the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the joint bitrate-aware diffusion training approach to evaluate the benefits of partial image rendering. Use a dataset of complex images with varying scene compositions, as described above.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The partial image rendering technique should achieve significant bitrate efficiency improvements and preserve high image quality, outperforming both the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the joint bitrate-aware diffusion training approach, especially for large and dynamic images.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: dynamic bitrate scheduling
PROPOSAL: Design a dynamic bitrate scheduling framework that adjusts the bitrate of an image transmission based on real-time network conditions, user preferences, and content demands. Use the partial image rendering technique (Proposal 5) to render the image in multiple resolutions and allocate bandwidth dynamically based on the estimated bitrate and visual quality of each region.
CONTROLS: Compare with static bitrate scheduling approaches, such as fixed bitrate allocation or adaptive bitrate allocation using image features, to evaluate the benefits of dynamic bitrate scheduling. Validate the approach using a real-world network simulation, with details given in the appendix.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The dynamic bitrate scheduling framework should achieve optimal bitrate-accuracy trade-offs and efficiently allocate bandwidth under varying network conditions, outperforming static scheduling approaches, but may require a more complex system architecture and communication protocol.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: dynamic bitrate scheduling
PROPOSAL: Extend the dynamic bitrate scheduling framework (Proposal 6) to incorporate machine learning-based prediction of network conditions and user preferences, allowing for proactive bitrate planning and real-time adjustments. Use the joint bitrate-aware diffusion training approach (Proposal 4) to train a model that learns to predict optimal bitrate allocation and rendering decisions based on these factors.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original dynamic bitrate scheduling framework (Proposal 6) and other machine learning-based bitrate planning approaches to evaluate the benefits of incorporating prediction and proactive planning, in the same setting as the proposal.

Conditional image generative models have, in recent years, demonstrated extraordinary capabilities, producing highly realistic images from both textual descriptions and class labels, and they have rapidly evolved from experimental research tools into widely accessible applications. Because they hold considerable promise to produce virtually unlimited amounts of data, researchers have started exploring their use as a source of synthetic training data for downstream machine learning models. However, recent research has revealed that as these models grow in size and capability, they tend to produce images of higher quality, better aligned with human preference, but with diminished diversity, which hinders their utility as synthetic training data generators.

Two families of techniques have been introduced to mitigate the shortcomings of such vanilla synthetic data. Learning-based approaches aim to improve the overall utility of synthetic data by reducing the distribution shift between generated and real samples; they use real data to train or fine-tune parts of existing conditional generative models. Guidance-based sampling methods instead define reward functions that steer the generation process and characterize the utility of generated samples in terms of generation quality or diversity. Yet the implicit or explicit utility functions behind these methods often disregard the potential distribution shift between synthetic and real data, and many guidance methods treat quality, diversity or safety as ends in themselves rather than as means to increase the utility of a synthetic image corpus for training downstream models. Moreover, in-depth analyses of conditional image generative models have highlighted a tension between quality and diversity. This tension becomes more apparent when diversity is defined as the variation among generated samples without reference to any target distribution. Contextualizing the desired diversity through real exemplar data holds the promise of limiting potentially disadvantageous variations in synthetic data.

Using exemplar data at inference time to guide generation is reminiscent of few-shot in-context learning in large language models, where a small number of examples suffices to adapt to new tasks without fine-tuning, and where providing more examples tends to help. In conditional image generation, however, most few-shot approaches require partial model training or fine-tuning, and the use of exemplar data at inference time remains underexplored. One prior inference-time method, Contextualized Vendi Score Guidance (c-VSG), leverages a handful of contextualizing real images to ground the diversity of generations to that of the real data; but, contrary to in-context learning, increasing the number of exemplars did not improve its performance. Meanwhile, fine-tuning with reward feedback has proven successful for improving generation quality, but it has not been tested whether it would also increase diversity given a proper reward.

The problem is therefore how to exploit a small set of real exemplar images to characterize, and jointly improve, both the quality and the diversity of the images produced by off-the-shelf conditional generators with respect to a target real distribution, ideally without fine-tuning the generator. Can strong quality and diversity be achieved this way, and can the benefit grow gracefully as more exemplars become available, unlike existing exemplar-based guidance? How does such an approach compare with training-based ways of using the same few real images? And does improving quality and diversity grounded in real data actually translate into greater utility of the synthetic images as training data for downstream models?

Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a powerful and principled approach for generative modeling, and in particular for high-quality visual generation. By learning a time-dependent velocity field that continuously transforms samples from a base distribution into a target distribution, FM models generate data by integrating an ordinary differential equation (ODE). This framework offers advantages over diffusion-based methods, including faster convergence, stable training, and direct control over sample trajectories.

Despite these strengths, inference in FM models is costly and has become a bottleneck. ODE integration is inherently sequential: each step depends on the output of the previous one, which makes the process slow and difficult to parallelize. High-fidelity generation requires a large number of fine-grained steps, which pushes latency up and makes real-time or interactive use difficult. As data dimensionality and model complexity increase, so does the inference burden. The issue is even more pronounced in video generation, where models operate on high-dimensional spatio-temporal data and the cost of sequential integration compounds across frames, making efficient inference essential for long videos.

Static reduction strategies such as distillation, trajectory truncation and consistency training have been proposed to reduce inference latency. However, they often degrade output quality, producing blurry textures, semantic drift or broken spatial coherence; in video, they often cause temporal flickering and motion inconsistency, which severely degrade realism even when individual frames look plausible. Many of them also require retraining the model with auxiliary objectives or handcrafted losses, which increases the engineering burden and restricts transferability across model families. As a result, these approaches are less modular, harder to scale, and often infeasible to deploy in time-sensitive or interactive pipelines.

In language models, a promising line of work for accelerating inference is speculative decoding, in which multiple drafts are proposed in parallel and selectively verified by the full model, reducing latency without retraining it. This idea, however, does not directly extend to image and video generative models such as FM, and two challenges stand out. First, unlike in language models, no readily available draft model exists: how can drafts be produced whose trajectories closely couple with those of the full model? Second, the performance of FM is highly sensitive to the velocity output: even a small perturbation in velocity can accumulate along the integration path and lead to severe generation errors. How, then, can drafted velocities be evaluated, and how can the drift of the resulting trajectory away from the full-model trajectory be controlled?

The open problem is therefore how to substantially reduce the inference latency of existing FM models, for both image and video generation, without retraining, without degrading output quality relative to standard full-step generation, and in a way that transfers across model families.

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: draft model acceleration via random path pruning
PROPOSAL: We propose to evaluate the feasibility of accelerating inference in FM models by selectively pruning short, random paths through the velocity field during the integration process. By doing so, we can reduce the overall number of integration steps required for achieving the same quality of output. We will experiment with various pruning strategies, including pruning based on velocity magnitude, Euclidean distance, and maximum gradient.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no pruning. (2) Ablation study: Different pruning strategies and their combinations. (3) Control: Randomly subsampling the paths.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a latency reduction of up to 30% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and a significant decrease in video generation latency. However, this approach may lead to variations in generation quality depending on the pruning strategy used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: learning draft models for fm using Curriculum Learning
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of generating high-quality drafts in FM models, we propose using Curriculum Learning to learn a draft model that closely couples with the full model. We will define a gradual curriculum of temporally corrected velocities that guide the learning process of the draft model. As the curriculum progresses, the draft model will learn to produce velocities that are increasingly similar to those produced by the full model. This will enable the draft model to not only accelerate inference but also maintain high quality output.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different curriculum learning schedules. (3) Control: Learning draft models using random sampling of the velocity field.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 40% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. The quality of the drafts will be strongly dependent on the quality of the curriculum learning schedule.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: draft model acceleration via random path pruning
PROPOSAL: We revise our initial proposal to include an incentive mechanism that rewards the draft model for producing velocities that result in generated samples that are closer to the ground truth. This can be achieved by incorporating a reconstruction loss into the draft model's training objective, which encourages the draft model to produce high-quality samples that are close to the target distribution. By doing so, we can improve the accuracy and quality of the draft model's outputs.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no pruning and no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different loss functions and weights for the reconstruction loss. (3) Control: Learning draft models using random sampling of the velocity field without reconstruction loss.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 50% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. However, the introduction of the reconstruction loss may lead to increased training time and potential mode collapse issues.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: learning draft models for fm using curriculum learning
PROPOSAL: We revise our proposal to use a more efficient curriculum learning schedule that utilizes progressive meta-learning. Instead of learning a fixed curriculum, we will use a dynamic curriculum that adapts to the performance of the draft model and the full model. This will enable the draft model to learn more effectively and efficiently, and potentially lead to better performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different progressive meta-learning schedules. (3) Control: Using a fixed curriculum learning schedule.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 45% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. The progressive meta-learning schedule may lead to improved performance, but it may also increase computational costs due to the need to adapt the curriculum during training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: draft refinement via multi-step prediction
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-step prediction mechanism to refine the outputs of the draft model. This mechanism will utilize a secondary model trained to predict the corrections needed to refine the draft's output, rather than relying on a single pass through the full model. By predicting these corrections step-by-step, we can iteratively refine the draft's output, potentially leading to significant quality improvements.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different numbers of refinement steps and secondary model architectures.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve high-quality outputs comparable to the full model, with a latency reduction of up to 40% in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. However, the multiple steps of refinement may lead to increased training time and potential issues with convergence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: lazy evaluation of fm velocity fields
PROPOSAL: We propose a lazy evaluation approach for the velocity fields used in FM models. By storing the velocity fields in a compressed and hierarchical manner, we can significantly reduce the computational cost of evaluating the velocity field for a given sample. This approach can be particularly effective when combined with the draft model and refinement mechanisms, as it can help to reduce the latency of the overall system.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no lazy evaluation. (2) Ablation study: Different compression techniques and hierarchical representations.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a significant reduction in computational cost, with a latency reduction of up to 25% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the compressed representation may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or discontinuities in the velocity field.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: model-parallelizable fm through decomposition
PROPOSAL: We propose a decomposition-based approach to make FM models parallelizable. By decomposing the velocity field into smaller, independent components, we can parallelize the evaluation of the velocity field across multiple GPUs or machines, significantly reducing the latency of the overall system. This approach can be particularly effective for large-scale FM models and video generation tasks.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no decomposition. (2) Ablation study: Different decomposition techniques and parallelization strategies.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a significant reduction in latency, with a speedup of up to 4x in text-to-image generation, and an even larger speedup in video generation. However, the decomposition may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or discontinuities in the velocity field, and complex decomposition strategies may increase engineering burden.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: uncertainty-based draft model deployment
PROPOSAL: We propose an uncertainty-based approach for deploying draft models, where the draft model is only used to generate samples when the uncertainty in the velocity field is high, and the full model is used otherwise. This approach can help to mitigate potential quality degradation issues and reduce the overall latency of the system.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different uncertainty measures and threshold values for draft model deployment.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 30% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the deployment strategy may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or inconsistent behavior at high uncertainty values.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adaptive draft model switching
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive approach for switching between the draft model and the full model based on the performance of the system. By continuously monitoring the quality and latency of the generated samples, we can dynamically switch between the two models to achieve the optimal trade-off between quality and latency. This approach can help to adapt to changing system conditions and optimize performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different switching policies and performance metrics, as described above.
COST: 110 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 35% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the adaptive switching strategy may lead to potential issues with instability or mode collapse.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: hybrid fm architectures
PROPOSAL: We propose a hybrid approach that combines the strengths of multiple architectures to achieve improved performance in FM models. By combining the draft model, full model, and lazy evaluation, we can create a flexible and adaptable architecture that can dynamically adjust to changing system conditions and optimize performance. This approach can help to achieve the optimal trade-off between quality, latency, and computational cost.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model. (2) Ablation study: Different combinations of draft model, full model, and lazy evaluation.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 50% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation, while maintaining high quality and performance. However, the hybrid architecture may lead to potential issues with complexity, overhead, and stability.

Smoothed decision-making is critical to avoiding abrupt and potentially dangerous large changes of actions in many online optimization problems, such as energy production scheduling in power grids, object tracking, motion planning, and server capacity provisioning in data centers. Mathematically, action smoothness can be achieved by adding to the optimization objective a switching cost that penalizes temporal changes in actions. The switching cost equips the online objective with a (finite) memory of previous actions and creates substantial algorithmic challenges; smoothed online optimization has therefore received a great deal of attention over the last decade, with a quickly growing list of algorithms offering worst-case performance guarantees in adversarial and stochastic settings and under various extensions.

At the same time, long-term fairness is a crucial consideration in many online optimization problems that can profoundly affect individuals' well-being and social welfare. Sequential allocation of social goods to different individuals or groups must be fair and free of discrimination; the surging environmental costs of geographically distributed AI data centers must be fairly distributed across regions, as repeatedly called for by various organizations and government agencies; and AI model performance and resource provisioning must promote social fairness without adversely affecting disadvantaged individuals or groups. If not designed with fairness in mind, online algorithms can perpetuate or even exacerbate societal biases, disproportionately affect certain groups or individuals, and amplify already widening socioeconomic disparities. Fairness in online optimization is therefore not only an ethical concern but also a necessity for broader social responsibility.

Incorporating a long-term fairness regularizer into the objective can effectively promote fairness in online optimization by mitigating implicit or explicit biases, but it creates significant challenges. The regularizer depends on the entire trajectory of actions and contexts and can only be evaluated at the end of an episode, with complete information, whereas a switching cost can be assessed step by step. Online decision-makers react to sequentially revealed information and tend to prioritize immediate cost reduction, potentially neglecting the long-term consequences of their sequence of decisions.

Recent research has started to explore fairness and long-term constraints in online problems such as online resource allocation, using primal-dual techniques. A major limitation of current fair online algorithms, however, is their reliance on the assumption that per-round objective functions are independent of historical actions, an assumption that plays a pivotal role in both their algorithm design and their theoretical analysis. In a simple resource allocation problem, for instance, the maximum allowable action at a given time may depend on past decisions through the remaining budget, but the reward at that time is assumed to depend only on the current decision. Such methods fall short when the per-round objective is directly affected by previous irrevocable actions, as it is with switching costs; in that case an online algorithm and an offline benchmark face different per-round objectives because their action sequences differ, which complicates any direct comparison of their costs. Conversely, the rich literature on smoothed online optimization does not handle a regularizer that is evaluated over the whole horizon. Fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization with switching costs is thus a new and challenging setting that appears not to have been considered in the literature.

Formally, consider an episode of T rounds. At each round t, an agent observes a (potentially adversarially chosen) non-negative hitting cost function f_t and a matrix A_t that maps its action into an M-dimensional cost vector, each dimension corresponding to an entity for which fairness must be taken into account, and then chooses an irrevocable action x_t without knowing future information. It incurs the hitting cost f_t(x_t) and a switching cost d(x_t, x_{t-1}), for instance a scaled squared Euclidean distance between consecutive actions. Fairness is captured by a long-term cost g, convex and Lipschitz, applied to the episode average of the cost vectors; a well-known choice is an l_p norm, which prioritizes reducing the highest costs borne by disadvantaged entities and recovers min-max fairness as p tends to infinity. The goal is to minimize $\frac{1}{T}\big(\sum_{t=1}^{T} f_t(x_t) + \sum_{t=1}^{T} d(x_t, x_{t-1})\big) + g\big(\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} A_t x_t\big)$.

This setting raises several questions. First, how hard is the long-term fairness regularizer intrinsically? Online algorithms are commonly evaluated by their regret or by their competitive ratio against a dynamic offline benchmark which, unlike a static benchmark restricted to a single fixed action, can adapt its action sequence over time with full knowledge of the context. A finite competitive ratio is attainable for online optimization with switching costs, but whether any online algorithm can achieve sublinear regret or a finite competitive ratio against the dynamic offline optimum in the presence of a long-term fairness regularizer, even without switching costs, remains an open question; prior work has only conjectured that finite performance might be impossible in similar settings. Second, if such guarantees are out of reach, against what kind of benchmark can meaningful, practically relevant performance guarantees be established? Third, how can an online algorithm reconcile the tension between minimizing the hitting cost, the switching cost and the long-term fairness cost with provable worst-case guarantees, when the per-round objective carries a memory of previous actions, and how does the long-term fairness regularizer affect such guarantees?

Grounding procedural steps in videos is crucial for enabling machines to follow along and assist humans in complex tasks such as cooking a recipe, assembling furniture, or performing maintenance work. This ability is particularly valuable for real-time procedural guidance in augmented and extended reality applications, where recognizing task progress allows users wearing headsets or smart glasses to receive timely, step-specific instructions. The task of Video Step Grounding (VSG) takes as input a list of procedural steps extracted from an instructional article (e.g., a recipe or a how-to guide) and a video of the same task, and aims to identify which of the steps are performed in the video, that is, which step, if any, each part of the video depicts (a segment may also show an action outside the listed steps).

Existing VSG approaches align procedural step descriptions with their corresponding video frames. Earlier works relied on weakly-supervised learning from instructional narrations, while more recent methods increasingly leverage language models and large-scale pretraining, for instance using language models to turn noisy narrations or speech transcripts into steps and pseudo-labels for training. These strategies face two key limitations. First, they need a training set, entailing the cost of collecting (and potentially annotating) it; moreover, a training set can bias models toward the specific videos and procedural tasks it depicts, limiting their generalization capability. Second, they assume offline processing, where the entire video is available ahead of time, which makes them unsuitable for real-world applications that process a live video stream and must make decisions as it unfolds.

This calls for addressing VSG online and without training: video segments arrive one after the other, and whether the current segment depicts a given step must be decided using only that segment and the segments preceding it, with no task-specific training data. This setting is challenging. Predictions must be made from partial evidence, and without the task-specific representations that would typically be learned from a dedicated training set. The task also requires fine-grained video understanding, since key steps of instructional tasks often involve similar objects or scenes: "inserting a screw" or "aligning parts" may look alike in tasks such as "Assemble a chair" and "Fix a table", making them hard to distinguish without nuanced semantic understanding. Large pretrained multimodal models have demonstrated impressive zero-shot performance on a wide variety of tasks without further tuning, and work on video-language alignment has moved away from frame-caption embedding similarity, which struggles to capture temporal dynamics, toward such models; yet whether off-the-shelf models can ground procedural steps when they only see the current short segment remains an open question. Moreover, a prediction made from the current segment alone has no memory of what has already happened in the video, so uncertain observations cannot benefit from past evidence, while storing and reprocessing the whole history is impractical on a live stream.

The research questions are therefore: can video step grounding be performed online, on a streaming video and without any training, at a level competitive with training-based offline methods? And how can knowledge from past segments be injected into the prediction for the current segment, without storing the whole history and while preserving a zero-shot, training-free approach?

Modern generative paradigms, including diffusion, flow matching and consistency models, have achieved state-of-the-art performance and form the backbone of leading image and video generation systems, including large multi-modal generative models. Despite their success, they share a critical drawback: both training and sampling demand substantial computational resources. Multi-step frameworks such as diffusion and flow matching produce a sample by iteratively integrating a probability-flow ordinary differential equation, typically requiring 40 to 100 network function evaluations (NFEs). The problem is magnified for large-scale models, for which efficient sampling is paramount: the continuous, long-term cost of inference often surpasses the one-time training cost, directly affecting economic viability and practical deployment. For example, the largest open multi-modal image generators (about 20B parameters) typically need about 100 NFEs, i.e. roughly 40 seconds on a single A100 GPU for one 1024×1024 image.

Numerous efforts aim to accelerate generative inference by reducing the number of sampling steps. Early single-step generators such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) often suffered from unstable training dynamics. To accelerate multi-step diffusion models, various distillation techniques have been introduced. They range from student-teacher methods, in which a student learns to reproduce a frozen teacher's sampling trajectory in fewer steps (e.g., progressive distillation, which requires an iterative distillation procedure), to distribution matching distillation (e.g., DMD and DMD2), which uses adversarial-style training with auxiliary networks to align the generator's output distribution directly with the data distribution. In parallel, consistency models and their variants (e.g., LCM and PCM), as well as related shortcut and MeanFlow objectives, have been designed explicitly for high-quality generation in very few steps, and recent work shows that multi-step and few-step models can be cast as instances of a single unified any-step training objective.

Despite this progress, existing few-step methods face a difficult trade-off between simplicity, efficiency and quality. (a) Complexity and instability: adversarial approaches, such as GANs, DMD-style distribution matching and hybrid frameworks that combine teacher guidance with adversarial signals (e.g., SANA-Sprint), require auxiliary trained networks (discriminators or fake-sample score networks) and/or frozen teacher models; distribution matching methods typically keep separate copies of a generator, a real-score model and a fake-score model. This introduces training instability and sensitivity to hyperparameters, and it increases architectural complexity and GPU memory overhead. For ultra-large models, the added complexity often translates into out-of-memory failures or brittle training dynamics, so few-step approaches have rarely been applied to models beyond about 3B parameters, and the only open-source few-step model released for a large model was obtained by distribution matching distillation with its GAN loss removed, an indirect sign of the high cost of adversarial losses at scale. (b) Performance degradation: methods trained without adversarial guidance, such as consistency models, often show a sharp decline in quality at very low NFEs (fewer than 4), and within the unified any-step view, current few-step methods struggle to reach high-quality one-step generation without resorting to a GAN-style loss.

The open problem is therefore how to train a generator that produces high-quality images in a single function evaluation, or very few, without discriminators, auxiliary score networks or frozen teacher models, so that training remains simple, stable and memory-efficient enough to scale to full-parameter training of the largest (10B to 20B parameters) text-to-image and multi-modal generators, without sacrificing the quality obtained by multi-step sampling.
