Neurons operate in ways that reflect their cell type, connectivity, and the brain region in which they are embedded. Understanding how these structural and physiological factors shape neural activity is an important open question and is central to modern theories of neural function. Cell type- and circuit-specific effects are also increasingly implicated in neurological disorders: particular neuronal subtypes can be selectively affected in neurodegenerative disease, and neuron subtypes can be targeted to improve efficacy in real time in closed-loop brain stimulation. Together, these directions highlight a broader need to understand how features such as cell type and brain region contribute to a neuron's role in the brain, motivating the development of methods that can extract aspects of neuron identity.

Much of what is known about neuronal cell types and their connectivity comes from molecular, anatomical, and morphological labeling techniques that tag neurons based on gene expression profiles or structural features. These approaches have revealed a rich taxonomy of neuronal classes, but they are resource intensive and typically provide only a sparse labeling of one or a few classes at a time, so identity labels are costly and difficult to obtain at scale. There is currently no molecular access to different cell types or projection classes in nonhuman primates and humans, which has created major roadblocks in studying neuron diversity in humans. For these reasons, there is growing interest in methods that can infer aspects of neuronal identity directly from large-scale neural population activity.

Deep learning approaches to this question have only recently begun to be explored. Early methods relied on intrinsic single-neuron features such as waveform shape or interspike interval profiles, but these signals capture only part of what distinguishes one neuron from another. More recent approaches incorporate some information about the ongoing population activity, but reduce the surrounding activity to fixed low-dimensional summaries, which obscures the fine-grained coordination patterns that are often key to neuronal identity. Furthermore, these models usually require retraining or finetuning on each new set of neurons, limiting their ability to generalize in a zero-shot manner across animals.

Making use of population context is itself challenging. The number of recorded neurons varies widely across experiments, individuals, and sessions, making it non-trivial to define a consistent input structure or population-level operation, and recordings span multiple experimental conditions, including different stimuli and behaviors, which makes it hard for a model to generalize across recording sessions. These limitations point to the need for methods that leverage rich population context while producing neuron-level representations that transfer robustly across recordings.

This raises several questions. Can a representation of each individual neuron be learned from population activity, when identity labels are scarce, such that it captures aspects of the neuron's identity such as its cell type and brain region? Can such representations transfer to entirely new sessions and animals without retraining or additional metadata? And how does the identity information they capture depend on the amount and diversity of recordings available for learning, compared with the number of labeled neurons?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: neural representation learning from neuropixels data
PROPOSAL: Train a neural generative model, like a variational autoencoder (VAE) or normalizing flow, on Neuropixels electrophysiology recordings to learn rich representations of neural activity. Evaluate learned representations using a permutation invariant testing framework to assess their ability to distinguish between cell types.
CONTROLS: Compare against a hand-crafted feature-based approach and a random baseline. Also include an ablation study where the model is trained without access to population context (i.e., per-neuron activity instead of population activity).
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The learned representations should be more effective at distinguishing between cell types than the baseline, and the ablation study should show a performance degradation when removing population context.

This proposal aims to learn rich representations of neural activity from Neuropixels recordings and evaluate their effectiveness in distinguishing between cell types. By using a permutation invariant testing framework, we can assess the quality of the learned representations without worrying about the specific ordering of the data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating learned representations with calcium imaging data
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the representations learned from Neuropixels data on a separate task using calcium imaging recordings, which provide spatial information about brain activity. Specifically, use a topic modeling approach to see if the learned representations can recover the brain region information encoded in the calcium imaging data.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The representations learned from Neuropixels data should be more informative and transferable to calcium imaging data than the other baselines, indicating their ability to capture spatial information about brain activity.

This proposal aims to evaluate the transferability of the learned representations across different types of neural activity recordings and brain imaging modalities. By comparing against different baselines, we can assess the effectiveness of the learned representations in a downstream task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: zero-shot generalization of learned representations
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the zero-shot generalization of the learned representations across mice, by training the model on one mouse and testing its ability to classify cell types in a different mouse without any additional training or metadata. Compare against a fine-tuning approach.
CONTROLS: Compare against a fine-tuned model and a model trained on a large dataset and then transferred to the target mouse.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The learned representations should generalize well to new mice without fine-tuning, and the fine-tuning approach should improve performance but require a significant amount of additional metadata and processing time.

This proposal aims to evaluate the ability of the learned representations to generalize across subjects (mice) without the need for additional metadata or fine-tuning, which is a critical aspect of achieving true transferability.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: zero-shot generalization of learned representations
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the zero-shot generalization of the learned representations across different recording sessions, by training the model on one session and testing its ability to classify cell types in a different session without any additional training or metadata. this includes sessions with different stimuli, different behaving tasks, or different tetrode locations. Compare against a fine-tuning approach and evaluate whether session-specific contextual information is required for optimal performance.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The learned representations should generalize well to new sessions without fine-tuning, but the performance might degrade in sessions with different stimuli or behaving tasks. Adding session-specific contextual information in the model architecture or during training might improve performance.

This revised proposal focuses on evaluating the ability of the learned representations to generalize across different recording sessions with varying conditions, which is essential for deploying the model in real-world applications where new sessions are continuously being recorded.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: impact of population size on representation quality
PROPOSAL: Investigate how the number of neurons in the population affects the quality of the learned representations, by training the model on populations of varying sizes and evaluating its performance on a standard classification task. Compare against a model trained on a large dataset with a fixed population size.
CONTROLS: Compare against a small population size (e.g., 10 neurons) and a large population size (e.g., 100 neurons).

PREDICTION: Increasing the population size should improve the quality of the learned representations, but the rate of improvement will depend on the specific neural activity patterns and the model architecture.

This proposal aims to understand the impact of population size on the quality of the learned representations, which is an essential aspect of deploying these models in real-world applications where the number of recorded neurons can vary significantly.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: inductive bias of learned representations
PROPOSAL: Investigate the inductive bias of the learned representations by training the model on different types of neural activity patterns (e.g., with or without placebo stimuli, or with different stimulus features) and evaluating its performance on a standard classification task. Compare against a model trained on a large dataset with a fixed set of inductive biases.
CONTROLS: Compare against a model trained on a dataset with a completely different type of inductive bias (e.g., spike phase versus stimulus features).
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The learned representations should adapt to the inductive bias of the training data and generalize well to similar types of neural activity patterns, but there might be a trade-off between generalization and robustness to changes in the inductive bias.

This proposal aims to understand the limitations and adaptability of the learned representations, which is essential for deploying these models in real-world applications where the neural activity patterns can vary significantly.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: model interpretability and neuron feature attribution
PROPOSAL: Investigate the interpretability of the learned representations by using techniques such as saliency maps, feature attribution, and importance scores to identify the most important neural features that contribute to the classification decisions. Compare against a model using random features or surrogate models.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The learned representations should be associated with a set of interpretable and important neural features, and the feature attribution scores should correlate with the actual neural activity patterns.

This proposal aims to understand the underlying mechanisms of the learned representations and identify the key neural features that contribute to the classification decisions. By analyzing the feature attribution scores, we can gain insights into the neural code and improve the model's interpretability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: out-of-distribution generalization and robustness
PROPOSAL: Investigate the out-of-distribution generalization and robustness of the learned representations by testing their performance on novel neural activity patterns, such as those from different saline conditions, age groups, or strains. Compare against a model trained on a large dataset with a fixed set of inductive biases.
CONTROLS: Compare against a model trained on a dataset with a completely different type of neural activity pattern.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The learned representations should be robust to some degree of novelty and out-of-distribution generalization, but the performance will degrade for more extreme or novel cases.

This proposal aims to evaluate the robustness and out-of-distribution generalization of the learned representations, which is essential for deploying these models in real-world applications where novel neural activity patterns may occur.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: ensemble methods for improving overall performance
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of ensemble methods, such as bagging, boosting, or stacking, to combine the predictions of multiple instances of the neural representation learning model, with the goal of improving overall performance and robustness. Compare against the single-model baseline.
CONTROLS: Compare against different ensemble methods and against a meta-learning approach that learns how to combine predictions from multiple models.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The ensemble methods should improve the overall performance of the neural representation learning model, particularly on tasks where robustness is critical, such as out-of-distribution generalization.

This proposal aims to improve the overall performance and robustness of the neural representation learning model by combining the predictions of multiple instances of the model using ensemble methods.

Many supervised learning algorithms rely on the assumption that training and test data are drawn from the same underlying distribution. In real-world applications this assumption is often violated because of environmental changes, sampling biases or temporal dynamics, which create distribution shifts between training and deployment environments. Such mismatches can cause significant performance degradation and pose a fundamental challenge to reliable generalization in practice.

Among the challenges posed by distribution shifts, this problem concerns unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), with a focus on classification. In UDA, one is given labeled data from a source domain and unlabeled data from a target domain whose distributions are related but not necessarily identical. The discrepancy may come from the marginal distribution of the input, from the conditional distribution of labels given inputs, or from both. The goal is to use the labeled source data and the unlabeled target data to build a predictive model with low risk on the target domain. The most naive baseline, empirical risk minimization on the source data, can perform poorly on the target domain when the two distributions differ.

Two representative families of UDA methods are distribution alignment, which reduces the discrepancy between the source and target domains either in the data space or in a feature space, and pseudo-labeling, which refines target predictions using a source-trained model in the spirit of self-training. Despite their popularity, both families often face practical limitations in two common scenarios. The first is when the amount of unlabeled target data is limited: alignment estimates can then become unreliable and pseudo-labels noisy, which can lead to poor generalization, and the empirical distribution of a small or imbalanced target sample may be a poor estimate of the true target input distribution that fails to capture the diversity of the target domain. The second is when the source data contain spurious correlations, for example when irrelevant features such as background or color are strongly associated with labels: models then tend to rely on these shortcuts, which do not transfer to the target domain and ultimately degrade performance. Alignment-based methods can fail in this situation, and approaches that try to disentangle causal and spurious features with unlabeled target data, through counterfactual consistency, generative interventions or self-training refinements, often rely on strong structural assumptions or are highly sensitive to the quality of the initial pseudo-labels, which makes them fragile when target data are scarce or imbalanced.

Distributionally robust optimization is another line of work on distribution shift: instead of the average loss on the training distribution, it minimizes the worst-case expected loss over an ambiguity set of plausible distributions. Constructing a suitable ambiguity set is the central difficulty, and the inner worst case must remain computationally tractable. Common choices, small Wasserstein or f-divergence balls around the empirical source distribution, give robustness to minor perturbations but are less suitable for structured shifts such as subpopulation shift, where the target contains the same subpopulations as the source with different mixing weights and can therefore lie far from the source in standard distances. Formulations designed for such mixture shifts, such as group distributionally robust optimization, typically assume access to group labels and do not explicitly use unlabeled target data to improve target prediction.

The problem is therefore how to learn, from labeled data coming from one or several source domains and unlabeled target data, a classifier that generalizes to the target domain when unlabeled target data are extremely scarce and when spurious correlations dominate the source domain, without group labels and with a computationally tractable training procedure. How can a learner remain reliable when the few available unlabeled target inputs give a poor picture of the target input distribution, and how can it avoid relying on spurious source features that do not hold in the target domain?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: dimensionality reduction for distribution alignment
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of using dimensionality reduction techniques (e.g., PCA, t-SNE) to align the feature spaces of the source and target domains in UDA. Specifically, we will apply dimensionality reduction to the labeled source data and test its transferability to the unlabeled target data, exploring combinations of techniques and hyperparameter settings. We will use the Ladybug and CIFAR-10 datasets for digit recognition, as well as the CelebA dataset for facial attribute classification.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours ( exploratory experiments with small models)
PREDICTION: We anticipate that dimensionality reduction will improve alignment, especially when combined with other methods (e.g., adversarial training), but may not be sufficient to handle extreme distribution shifts or spurious correlations. The combination of techniques and hyperparameter tuning is likely crucial for best performance.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: self-training with robust source classifiers
PROPOSAL: Modify the self-training paradigm to improve robustness against spurious correlations in the source data. Specifically, we will use robust source classifiers trained with input and label perturbations, such as adversarial training and data augmentation. We will also use these robust source models to generate pseudo-labels for the target data. The goal is to build a more reliable self-training pipeline that focuses on the most informative features and reduces the impact of spurious correlations.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours (more complex source models and training)
PREDICTION: The modified self-training pipeline should yield better performance and robustness, especially when the source data have strong spurious correlations. However, the improvements may come at the cost of increased model complexity, which could limit the applicability in resource-constrained scenarios.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: counterfactual reasoning with limited target data
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of counterfactual reasoning to improve UDA performance when target data is scarce. Specifically, we will adapt the counterfactual decision network framework to use limited target samples to infer latent counterfactual variables. We will then train a UDA model to predict on these counterfactuals, aiming to improve generalizability and reduce reliance on spurious correlations. As a starting point, we will use the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for digit recognition.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours (moderate-scale experiments with deeper models)
PREDICTION: Counterfactual reasoning holds promise for leveraging limited target data, but its effectiveness may be sensitive to the choice of target samples and the strength of spurious correlations in the source data. The method might struggle with very scarce data or extremely different input distributions.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: dimensionality reduction for distribution alignment
PROPOSAL: Expand the dimensionality reduction approach (1) by combining it with other methods for aligning the source and target domains. Specifically, we will explore the use of adversarial training and pseudo-labeling to further improve alignment, using dimensionality reduction as a preprocessing step to reduce the impact of spurious correlations. We will apply this combined approach to the Ladybug and CIFAR-10 datasets for digit recognition, as well as the CelebA dataset for facial attribute classification.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours (combining with other methods, but maintaining moderate complexity)
PREDICTION: The combination of dimensionality reduction and other methods should improve alignment and reduce the reliance on spurious correlations, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to optimize performance. The method may struggle with extremely different input distributions or very scarce target data.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: robustness regularization for self-training
PROPOSAL: Regularize the self-training process to improve robustness against spurious correlations in the source data. Specifically, we will add a regularization term to the self-training loss that encourages the model to focus on informative features and avoid relying on spurious correlations. We will implement this regularization using techniques such as dropout, weight decay, or early stopping. As a starting point, we will use the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for digit recognition.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours (moderate-scale experiments with regularized models)
PREDICTION: Regularization should improve the robustness of self-training by reducing overfitting to spurious correlations, but may compromise performance on data-rich scenarios or scenarios where the model can handle spurious correlations without regularization. The optimal regularization technique and strength may depend on the specific dataset and model architecture.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: sample selection for robust UDA
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of sample selection methods to improve robustness of UDA in scenarios where target data is scarce or imbalanced. Specifically, we will adapt sample selection methods (e.g., coherence-based sampling, density-based sampling) to select the most informative target samples for UDA. We will then train a UDA model using these selected samples and compare the results to baseline models trained on the full target dataset. We will apply this approach to the Ladybug and CIFAR-10 datasets for bird image classification.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours (large-scale experiments with selected samples)
PREDICTION: Sample selection should improve the robustness of UDA by focusing on the most informative target samples, but may compromise performance if the selected samples are not representative of the target distribution. The choice of sample selection method may depend on the specific dataset and UDA model architecture.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: self-training with robust source classifiers
PROPOSAL: Expand the self-training approach (2) to incorporate multiple levels of robustness and regularization. Specifically, we will combine the robust source classifier with robustness regularization (4) and sample selection (5) to improve the robustness of self-training. We will also explore the use of robust multi-instance learning to handle diverse and noisy target samples. We will apply this combined approach to the CelebA dataset for facial attribute classification and other datasets.
COST: 2200 GPU-hours (moderate-scale experiments with robust models)
PREDICTION: The combined approach should significantly improve the robustness of self-training by reducing overfitting to spurious correlations and handling noisy and diverse target samples, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to optimize performance. The method may be sensitive to the choice of robustness regularization technique and sample selection method.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: uncertainty-based pseudo-labeling for uda
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of uncertainty-based pseudo-labeling to improve UDA in scenarios where target data is scarce or imbalanced. Specifically, we will adapt Bayesian neural networks or Monte Carlo dropout to estimate the uncertainty of target predictions, and then use these uncertainty estimates to select high-confidence pseudo-labels for fine-tuning. We will compare the results to baseline models trained with standard pseudo-labeling and evaluate the impact of uncertainty-based pseudo-labeling on robustness and generalization. We will apply this approach to the CIFAR-10 and Ladybug datasets for image classification.
COST: 2800 GPU-hours (large-scale experiments with Bayesian neural networks or Monte Carlo dropout)

TITLE: transferable features selection for uda
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of transferable features selection to improve UDA in scenarios where the source and target domains have different feature distributions. Specifically, we will use feature selection techniques (e.g., mutual information, L1 regularization) to identify transferable features that are robust across domains. We will then train a UDA model using only these transferable features and evaluate its performance on the target domain. As a starting point, we will use the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for image classification.

Specifically, we will use a hierarchical neural architecture to adapt to multiple sub-populations or sub-tasks in a single model, rather than requiring separate models for each one. We will then evaluate the performance of this hierarchical approach on a range of UDA benchmarks, including the CIFAR-10 and Ladybug datasets.
COST: 4000 GPU-hours (large-scale experiments with hierarchical models)
PREDICTION: Hierarchical adaptability should improve the robustness and generalization of UDA by adapting to multiple sub-populations or sub-tasks in a single model, but may compromise performance if the hierarchical architecture is too complex or if the data is too sparse. The choice of hierarchical architecture may depend on the specific dataset and UDA model requirements.

Large language models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress across a wide range of natural language understanding and generation tasks, but their massive parameter counts demand prohibitively large computational and memory resources for both training and deployment. Even in settings with a reasonable amount of compute, training or fine-tuning such models remains challenging.

One promising way to reduce the computational burden of fine-tuning is low-precision floating-point (FP) arithmetic such as FP8. Modern accelerators (e.g., NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, AMD CDNA 3, Google TPUs) increasingly support low-precision FP arithmetic natively, and FP8 can theoretically double the throughput of FP16 matrix multiplication. Because FP8 formats (such as E4M3 or E5M2) have a narrow representable range, a higher-precision tensor must first be scaled by a per-tensor factor obtained from a max-reduction over its absolute values, and then scaled element-wise and rounded, before the low-precision multiplication can run. This quantization overhead is memory-bound and grows quadratically with matrix size, whereas the cost of matrix multiplication grows cubically. As a consequence, FP8 is known to accelerate mainly large-dimensional matrix multiplications (empirically, when each matrix dimension exceeds roughly 4K elements), while small-dimensional computations can even suffer an unexpected slowdown.

These overheads are especially critical for low-rank adaptation (LoRA), a widely used approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning. LoRA keeps the pretrained weights frozen and inserts small trainable low-rank matrices (adapters) that capture task-specific knowledge, greatly reducing memory cost by training few parameters. For such small-dimensional matrices, the overhead of FP8 quantization can outweigh the gains of FP8 multiplication, and the separate forward and backward paths of the adapters add further quantization operations at every iteration. Yet fast LoRA fine-tuning matters in practice: many applications require training numerous adapters, for example one adapter per user for personalized recommendation or personalized alignment from human feedback, task-specific adapters for multi-task learning and mixtures of LoRA experts, adapters for different domains, multilingual summarization, and rapid updates in dynamic, user-specific environments. Efficiently accelerating LoRA fine-tuning is therefore essential for timely, scalable and cost-effective adaptation of LLMs under practical computational constraints.

Existing lines of work leave this gap open. Quantized LoRA methods (such as QLoRA with 4-bit NormalFloat weights, QA-LoRA with group-wise INT4 weights, and follow-ups that refine the quantization with integer linear programming, SVD-based adapter initialization, dynamic rank allocation or information recovery) compress the frozen backbone through weight-only quantization. They focus on memory efficiency rather than fine-tuning speed: the added quantization and dequantization often make them slower than standard LoRA, and weight-only quantization cannot exploit hardware acceleration of low-precision matrix multiplication. Conversely, FP8 training methods (hybrid E4M3/E5M2 formats, mixed-precision FP8 training with high-precision master weights, studies of large-scale FP8 stability and outliers, unit scaling) are designed for the large-dimensional matrices of full LLM training, not for the small matrices that characterize LoRA.

This raises the following questions. How large is the quantization overhead when FP8 arithmetic is applied to LoRA fine-tuning, which parts of the computation does it come from, and does it persist across typical adapter ranks? Can LoRA fine-tuning be organized so that it genuinely benefits from native FP8 arithmetic, delivering real end-to-end speedups over existing quantized LoRA methods, while retaining the memory savings that make LoRA attractive and reaching accuracy comparable to existing quantized LoRA fine-tuning?

PROPOSAL: Investigate the quantization overhead when applying FP8 arithmetic to LoRA fine-tuning, using a combination of tuning existing Llama Large and DistilTrillion parameters. The overhead will be analyzed across a varying number of adapter ranks and sampled adapter dimensions (32, 64, 128). Find the shortest adapter dimension at which the overhead outweighs the benefits of FP8 arithmetic for a theoretical model of LoRA.

Large language models have recently improved their reasoning by spending more test-time compute, generating more tokens before producing a final answer. Extended sequential scaling has limits, however: beyond a certain length, performance can decrease because of "overthinking", and long sequential reasoning can be sensitive to the order of reasoning steps. A complementary scaling dimension, repeated parallel sampling followed by aggregation, as in self-consistency (majority voting) or Best-of-N selection, has further boosted reasoning performance. These parallel methods rely on the model generating solutions that are both diverse and correct, and as tasks become harder, some mechanism for increasing diversity becomes necessary.

Obtaining such diversity is difficult. Only a minority of tokens in a chain of thought act as forking tokens that lead to distinct reasoning modes, so as problems become harder and generations longer, these tokens become substantially harder to sample. The common practice for encouraging diversity, raising the sampling temperature, inherently entails a diversity-accuracy trade-off, because the forking tokens that trigger diverse yet correct reasoning modes typically lie deep within the sampling tree. Theoretical work further shows that increasing the temperature alone does not necessarily yield greater diversity unless the model has been explicitly trained to ensure coverage. Search-based alternatives such as Monte Carlo tree search or Tree of Thoughts increase coverage through heuristic-guided search with an external verifier, but their reliance on heuristics and domain-specific knowledge limits the tasks to which they apply. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is not a complete answer either: it requires a strong base model, and recent work suggests that it does not by itself instill new capabilities, so what a model learns during fine-tuning matters.

At the same time, several distinct and correct reasoning traces per question can be obtained at low cost and without human annotation, for instance by distilling from different teacher models, sampling repeatedly, and filtering with a verifiable correctness check. This suggests training models for coverage directly from such diverse traces, but how to do so is unclear. Standard supervised fine-tuning treats each trace as an independent example and has no explicit mechanism for keeping different reasoning modes apart: it is an open question whether the modes are preserved or merged into one, and whether a particular mode can later be deliberately elicited. Recent efforts to train models natively for parallel reasoning, by converting sequential chains of thought into parallel ones or by training on multiple traces distilled from teachers, show that native parallel scaling can surpass sequential scaling within certain token limits, but they leave open whether the distinct reasoning modes present in the training traces are actually retained and can be reliably triggered.

The problem is therefore how to fine-tune a language model on a set of diverse, correct reasoning traces per question so that it retains their distinct reasoning modes rather than collapsing them, and so that diverse yet accurate reasoning paths can be reliably triggered when sampling in parallel, instead of depending on sampling rare forking tokens deep inside a generation. Can such training improve both the accuracy of a single generation and the accuracy and coverage obtained by aggregating a small number of parallel generations?

Facial rigging aims to make a static neutral facial mesh animatable by defining a set of controllable deformations, typically represented either as blendshape rigs driven by activated action units in systems based on the Facial Action Coding System (FACS), or as skeletal rigs driven by joint positions. Whereas full-body auto-rigging usually follows a two-step pipeline of skeleton construction and skinning, facial rigs are often anatomically inspired and implemented with FACS blendshapes. In a linear FACS blendshape rig, each blendshape is a vertex offset from the neutral mesh corresponding to one action unit, i.e. a specific muscle movement such as "Right Eye Close", and a complex expression is obtained by adding the weighted offsets of the activated blendshapes to the neutral mesh. Rigging is an essential step for creative AI, bringing digital avatars to life by enabling expressive and realistic facial movements across a wide range of applications. However, creating a facial rig is laborious and expensive, often requiring skilled artists tens of hours to complete a single asset. Methods that transfer expressions from 2D images or videos to 3D avatars do not remove this bottleneck, since they assume that the avatar already has a rig.

Existing facial auto-rigging methods typically transfer a complete set of blendshapes from a predefined template mesh to a neutral target mesh, which often requires dense correspondences or a mesh topology shared by the template and the target. More recent approaches build transferable latent spaces between faces or use triangulation-agnostic networks to bypass these limitations, but they still require a template blendshape rig, which can compromise accuracy when the template and target shapes differ substantially. Only one prior approach, NFR, can directly rig facial meshes from explicitly controllable FACS parameters without relying on a template, and it has so far been demonstrated primarily on humanoid heads. Furthermore, existing approaches, NFR included, have yet to accommodate meshes with multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs or teeth, which limits their ability to animate highly expressive avatars: an "eye look-down" pose, for example, is difficult to reproduce if the mesh lacks eyeballs.

Learning such a rigging model also raises a data problem. Accurate 3D supervision requires neutral meshes paired with complete rigs made by artists, and because manual rigging is so costly such rigged examples are scarce; a model trained solely on them is likely to generalize poorly to the wide variety of facial shapes, styles and topologies met in practice.

The problem is therefore to automatically turn a single static neutral facial mesh into an expressive rig controllable by FACS parameters (i) without relying on predefined template blendshapes, so that target meshes need not closely resemble a template; (ii) for in-the-wild meshes with varying topologies and shapes, including both humanoid and non-humanoid heads; and (iii) for meshes made of multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs and teeth, which must move coherently with the rest of the face. How can such a rigging system be built, and how can it be trained to generalize across this diversity when only a limited number of rigged meshes is available as 3D ground truth?

In cloud services, Internet of Things deployments and monitoring systems, data are often represented as univariate time series (UTS), in which each timestamp records a single variable. Anomalies arise, for instance, when a website is subject to malicious attacks or experiences excessive server load, and they are typically reflected in UTS derived from traffic and system-load monitoring. Missed or delayed detection of such events can have severe consequences. Anomalies in UTS are usually divided into two types: point anomalies, which are abrupt deviations (either global or contextual), and segment anomalies, which reflect more subtle shifts in trends or periodic patterns.

Formally, given observations x_0, x_1, ..., x_t with anomaly labels c_0, c_1, ..., c_t, where c_i = 0 marks a normal point and c_i = 1 an anomaly, the goal of UTS anomaly detection is to determine c_i for each point x_i from the history x_0, ..., x_{i-1} that precedes it, without access to future points. Because labels are scarce in practice and supervised detectors generalize poorly under label scarcity or distribution shift, unsupervised approaches have become the dominant paradigm. Reconstruction-based and prediction-based methods both model normal behavior and flag anomalies by comparing reconstructed or predicted values with the actual observations. Reconstruction-based techniques try to map abnormal segments to a normal space, but the lack of ground truth for anomalies leads to poor reconstruction and degraded performance, and they treat time windows independently, ignoring temporal dependencies. Prediction-based methods built on deep sequence models such as Transformers perform strongly on multivariate time series, where they can model complex dependencies; in UTS, however, each timestamp contains only one value, which restricts the representation of temporal context and leads to suboptimal performance.

In particular, existing detectors struggle with two kinds of subtle anomalies that remain largely undetected: (1) small point anomalies, short-term spikes that look normal when viewed over longer windows; and (2) slowly rising anomalies, gradual segment-level deviations from periodic patterns. These misses stem from limitations of current designs: for example, a frequency-conditioned reconstruction approach focuses on frequency components rather than local dependencies and fails to capture subtle point anomalies or gradual segment anomalies, while a recent prediction approach uses timing information but ignores frequency details.

Detecting these anomalies raises three challenges. First, local trends matter more than absolute values: the absolute magnitude of a change is insufficient to decide whether a point is anomalous. In one series, changes between 0.5 and 1 may be abnormal, whereas in another, similar changes are normal and only variations exceeding 5 are anomalous; what counts as abnormal depends on the value distribution and change patterns within a short local window. Second, periodicity evolves rather than staying static: time series exhibit evolving trends and periodicity, and periodicity varies over time and across datasets, including changes in period length and frequency. Without future points, distinguishing slow anomalies from normal periodic changes is difficult, and methods that focus only on the adjacent historical period neglect this evolution; modeling periodicity that is both dynamic and heterogeneous is hard. Third, normal patterns must be learned amid anomalies and noise: real-world series contain long-term noise and sudden anomalies, both of which hinder the learning of normal patterns. Noise introduces significant fluctuations that make it difficult to fit the underlying normal behavior, and the lack of ground-truth labels for anomaly positions prevents a model from computing reliable training losses.

The question is therefore how an unsupervised detector for univariate time series, relying only on past observations, can capture both local trends and the evolution of periodic patterns, while learning normal behavior robustly from training data contaminated by noise and unlabeled anomalies, so that small point anomalies and slowly rising anomalies are detected accurately and promptly.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: local trend aware reconstruction approach
PROPOSAL: Introduce a reconstruction-based method that models normal behavior by learning local trends in the univariate time series. Instead of focusing on global frequency components, the method will capture local patterns using a Gaussian Process regression model with a custom kernel that takes into account the local context of each point. This will allow it to more effectively identify small point anomalies that might be missed by frequency-conditioned reconstruction approaches.
CONTROLS: Compare against a frequency-conditioned reconstruction approach (e.g., the recent 1D-STFT-DCN method) and an unsupervised baseline (e.g., Autoencoders on UTS datasets from ) across a suite of real-world datasets, including ECG and web service KPI monitoring.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach will demonstrate strong detection performance on small point anomalies, while its reconstruction-based design will also allow it to learn effective normal patterns in the presence of noise and labeled anomalies; however, it might struggle with capturing subtle changes in evolving periodic patterns without additional information.

TITLE: periodicity evolution aware sequence model
PROPOSAL: Design a variant of the transformer-based sequence model, specifically geared towards univariate time series, that incorporates a novel self-attention mechanism to capture the evolution of periodic patterns across different time windows. This is achieved by adding an auxiliary periodicity-evolution head that learns to predict the shift in periodic patterns between adjacent windows, thereby enabling the detector to learn dynamic periodicity and accommodate changes in evolving trends and periodicity.

PROPOSAL: Design a denoising autoencoder (DAE) that uses an anomaly encoder to learn noise and normal patterns in the univariate time series data. By training the DAE to reconstruct the input from its noise representation, the model learns to discard noise and identify normal patterns in the data, allowing for effective anomaly detection in noisy series. Proteins realize their biological functions through intricate three-dimensional conformations, and predicting such structures has long been a central challenge in computational biology. AlphaFold2 marked a breakthrough by combining multiple sequence alignments with geometric constraints in an end-to-end framework, achieving near-experimental accuracy. Building on this foundation, AlphaFold3 reformulates the architecture into an all-atom framework and introduces a diffusion-based structure module, thereby enabling the generative modeling of not only proteins but also a wide spectrum of biomolecular complexes. Consequently, this series of models is widely adopted as a family of foundation models for downstream applications such as virtual screening and protein design. However, AlphaFold3's architecture, which relies on iterative Pairformer recycling and multi-step diffusion, requires substantially greater computational overhead than AlphaFold2, restricting its accessibility in downstream workflows.

More specifically, on long sequences the execution time of AlphaFold3 is measured in minutes, which severely limits its usability in downstream tasks that demand high throughput. For instance, small-scale laboratory screening often requires predictions for thousands of candidates, and when extended to large public databases this number grows to an infeasible scale; protein design tasks typically involve comparable computational demand. Previous work has attempted to mitigate this by manually reducing the number of recycling iterations on simpler structures, thus trading accuracy for efficiency. However, such compromises inevitably degrade predictive performance. Moreover, in hallucination-based design approaches, the multistep iterative refinement process hinders feasible gradient backpropagation, ultimately preventing the broader community from adopting AlphaFold3 as a foundation model for diverse applications.

To accelerate the diffusion process, recent advances in generative modeling have explored high-order solvers and consistency models. While high-order solvers improve efficiency, they rarely reduce the number of sampling steps below ten. Consistency models, on the other hand, have achieved remarkable success in image generation and have benefited from refined training schedules. However, transferring them to an AlphaFold3-style architecture raises two difficulties. First, standard consistency schedules assume fixed-dimensional data and pair timesteps at a constant Euclidean interval, which does not accommodate variable protein sequence lengths: on long sequences even a small step can trigger a drastic distribution shift that demands an unrealistic predictive leap, while on short sequences the same interval provides only a weak learning signal, so training dynamics can become unstable or collapse. Second, the iterative diffusion sampler is not the only source of iteration: the architecture also refines its internal pair and single representations through repeated recycling of the Pairformer trunk, whose cost grows with sequence length and which conventional diffusion-acceleration methods do not address at all.

The open problem is therefore whether an AlphaFold3-class all-atom biomolecular structure generator can be compressed into a predictor that runs in essentially a single forward pass -- removing both the multi-step denoising and the recycling overhead -- while retaining the accuracy of the full iterative model on protein, protein-ligand and nucleic-acid complexes. This matters because accuracy alone is not what blocks adoption: throughput and differentiability do. A useful accelerated model must remain reliable in the tail, not merely on average, since high-throughput screening and design pipelines discard most candidates and are harmed more by occasional implausible structures than by small average losses; it must stay cheap enough to be called thousands of times; and it must be light enough that gradients can be propagated through it, so that design methods which optimize sequences against a folding model become feasible with an all-atom model rather than only with earlier, cheaper architectures. Given this problem, how should one design experiments to establish whether such an acceleration is achievable without a loss of predictive fidelity?

Geometry reconstruction is a fundamental problem that enables a wide range of applications in fields such as virtual reality and robotics. In recent years, neural reconstruction methods have gained significant attention; a key advantage of these methods is their ability to represent the geometry of a scene continuously, which can help in many downstream tasks. However, vision-based sensors often struggle in adverse weather conditions, or even become completely unusable when objects are obscured by occlusions.

Radio frequency (RF) sensing, specifically wireless millimeter-wave (mmWave) sensing, can see through occlusions, remains robust under challenging visibility conditions and, unlike X-rays, is not dangerous to humans, making it a compelling alternative for 3D reconstruction. This could open up many applications, for example checking whether the items inside a box are the correct items, are damaged, or pose a threat, without ever opening the box. On the other hand, mmWave resolution is extremely low compared to vision: a single radar image provides far less visual context than a camera image, which makes it hard to extract a 3D reconstruction from one radar image alone. Some prior RF systems have performed 3D point cloud reconstruction or human body tracking by leveraging movement or by emulating larger antenna apertures, but the recovered point clouds are still too sparse and noisy to reliably recover detailed geometry; through-wall human sensing relies on human motion to combat specularity, and deep learning on mmWave radar data has mostly targeted self-driving scenarios, where image resolution matters little. Other works have proposed neural implicit representations for RF sensing, aiming to concentrate scene information out of heavy noise through neural optimization, but these systems are designed for large-scale environments such as streets or satellite imagery and are far from achieving millimeter-level precision. When objects are close to the radar, the propagation characteristics of RF signals change dramatically: incoming waves can no longer be approximated as planar, so processing methods designed for large-scale scenes, such as beamforming, introduce a considerable amount of distortion and noise, often exceeding the noise acceptable for gradient descent and leading to unstable optimization. Existing neural RF reconstruction work is thus either limited to far-range scenes or, for individual objects, evaluated only on simulated data, which for wireless signals cannot come close to representing the complexity of real-world measurements. Meanwhile, the multi-view reconstruction and inverse rendering methods of computer vision (multi-view stereo, neural radiance fields, Gaussian splatting, neural implicit surfaces, physically based inverse rendering) are all derived from RGB images and are not easily transferable to mmWave data: even lensless RGB images can be mapped back to a lens-based imaging model without altering the underlying ray physics, whereas for RF signals such a transformation is fundamentally invalid.

The open problem is therefore to overcome the fundamental dilemma between massive RF noise in the input and the reconstruction of complete, high-resolution, millimeter-level 3D surface geometry of near-range objects, including objects hidden behind occlusions. This is not straightforward, because inferring surface geometry from RF signals differs fundamentally from image-based reconstruction in three main ways. First, wireless systems lack a lens-based imaging model: whereas lenses filter and focus the relevant light rays, radar antenna arrays perform lensless imaging and capture all incoming RF signals without directional filtering, which leads to low signal-to-noise ratios because irrelevant signals cannot be excluded. Second, RF signals and visible light propagate differently: visible light is predominantly scattered diffusely by surfaces, whereas RF signals, whose wavelengths are on the order of millimeters, are dominated by specular reflections, so volumetric rendering techniques designed for scattering-based vision sensors are unsuitable for RF imaging. Third, physically modeling lensless RF measurements is computationally expensive: whereas lens-based rendering samples along 1D rays, modeling what each antenna receives requires accounting for contributions from the full 3D space, leading to cubic complexity that makes naive implementations intractable at millimeter resolution.

How can accurate, millimeter-level 3D geometry of near-range objects be reconstructed from noisy real-world RF measurements, in line of sight and through occlusions, despite lensless imaging, specular reflections and the cost of modeling signal contributions from the full 3D space?

Recent frontier models such as OpenAI o1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1 and Kimi k1.5 provide compelling proof of concept for leveraging long chains of thought to enhance the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). Following these advances, Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) techniques such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization (DAPO) have emerged as the de facto standard for strengthening LLM reasoning. In RLVR, the policy model is trained by sampling multiple responses (rollouts) to a prompt, checking each final answer against a ground-truth answer, and then reinforcing correct answers while penalizing incorrect ones. GRPO, a variant of Proximal Policy Optimization that dispenses with a costly value model, computes the advantage of each response by normalizing its reward with the mean and standard deviation of the rewards in its group.

This works well when the responses to a prompt contain both right and wrong answers, but it does not account for the case where a group of rollouts is entirely correct or entirely incorrect and therefore receives identical rewards. Such prompts are referred to as zero-variance prompts. For them, the normalized rewards (the advantage values) collapse to zero, so there is no training signal and all rollouts for those prompts are rendered uninformative. Put differently, the policy is rewarded for a correct response only when at least one incorrect response exists in the same group, and penalized for an incorrect response only when at least one correct response is present. Zero-variance prompts typically arise when a problem is too difficult or too easy for the current model: early in training, when the model often fails to solve a problem even once across multiple attempts, and near convergence, when it has become strong enough to solve many problems in every attempt.

Ignoring these prompts may seem conceptually reasonable, but it remains problematic because rollout generation is itself a major bottleneck in RL training, so the compute spent sampling responses to zero-variance prompts is simply wasted. Recent methods acknowledge this inefficiency and try to filter zero-variance prompts out, either before rollout, by predicting from the training history which prompts are likely to yield identical rewards and skipping them, or after rollout, by repeatedly sampling and discarding them until a batch contains only prompts with mixed outcomes. These methods view zero-variance prompts merely as a cost to be avoided and implicitly assume that they offer no value for policy optimization. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has investigated whether zero-variance prompts themselves can serve as a valuable source of learning signal.

This raises several open questions. Can the responses to a prompt whose rollouts are all correct, or all incorrect, provide meaningful feedback for policy optimization, even though the group contains no contrasting response? If so, how should such feedback be formulated so that it remains informative and does not destabilize training? And would exploiting these prompts, instead of discarding them, lead to better reasoning performance and more stable learning than both standard group-relative training and the prevailing practice of filtering them out?

TITLE: extending group relative policy optimization to handle zero-variance prompts
PROPOSAL: This proposes a new variant of GRPO that uses a Bayesian estimation of the reward variance among rollouts in a group, even when all rollouts have the same reward. If the estimated variance is greater than a small epsilon, the reward normalization computes a non-zero advantage value, which is then used for training.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard GRPO, vanilla Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and a GRPO implementation that filters out zero-variance prompts before rollout.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This extension might confer a minor advantage over standard GRPO on zero-variance prompts, but may overfit to unrepresentative variance noise on other prompts.

The results are then compared against a set of baselines to provide a holistic understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of each approach.

Reinforcement learning has been highly effective in many domains, ranging from robotics to gaming and recommender systems. Value-based algorithms such as Deep Q-Networks are a cornerstone of off-policy reinforcement learning and are widely used in discrete action spaces because of their simplicity, training stability, and sample-efficiency. However, they rely on estimating Q-values for individual state-action pairs and require a maximization over the action space, both to derive the greedy policy and to evaluate the best next-state value in the Bellman target. This maximization is straightforward when the actions can be enumerated, but in continuous action spaces evaluating the Q-value over the entire action space becomes computationally infeasible, which has traditionally restricted value-based methods to discrete actions.

In continuous control, actor-critic methods such as DDPG, TD3, and SAC are typically used instead: a critic is trained on off-policy data to estimate Q-values, and an actor (policy) is trained to output actions that maximize the critic. While powerful, these methods often suffer from instability caused by the coupled training of actor and critic, from sensitivity to hyperparameters, and from the difficulty of predicting in high-dimensional action spaces. The additional actor network brings its own hyperparameters, which makes reproducibility a challenge, and adds computational and memory overhead. Moreover, an actor trained by gradient ascent on the Q-function landscape can only find locally optimal actions, which becomes a serious limitation when the Q-function is complex or non-convex, for instance when the action space is constrained so that actions must remain within specific safety bounds. Training several actors to explore different modes of the Q-function alleviates this, but adds computational overhead and inference-time latency, and the actor's parameterization may still be too limited to capture complex optimal actions.

Actor-free, value-based alternatives must instead carry out the maximization over continuous actions themselves, and finding the maximizing action has been their primary bottleneck. Methods that perform this maximization numerically, through mixed-integer programming, the cross-entropy method and other sampling-based or evolutionary search, or gradient ascent on the action, tend either to return suboptimal local maxima or to be computationally impractical, and sampling becomes progressively less efficient as the action dimension grows. Discretizing the action space is effective in low dimensions but does not scale to high-dimensional tasks. Another line of work restricts the functional form of the Q-function so that its maximizer can be obtained directly, for example by assuming that the advantage is quadratic in the action or that the Q-function is convex in the action; such assumptions limit expressivity and practical applicability. Representing the Q-function with a radial basis function output layer makes the best action easier to identify, but introduces an implicit trade-off between how expressive the Q-function can be in modeling multiple local optima and how accurately its maximizing action is recovered.

This raises the question of whether an actor-free, value-based algorithm can efficiently and accurately select optimal actions in continuous action spaces without imposing restrictive assumptions on the shape of the Q-function, while remaining stable to train, robust across diverse tasks, and scalable to high-dimensional action spaces. Such an algorithm would retain the simplicity of Q-learning and avoid the cost and instability of learning a separate actor; it could also avoid the local optima that trap gradient-based actors when the Q-function is highly non-convex, as in constrained action spaces. Can such an approach be made competitive with established actor-critic methods for continuous control, and can it outperform them where gradient-based action maximization struggles?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: maximization-free q-learning with importance sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate an actor-free, value-based algorithm where the Q-function is represented by a neural network, and the maximization over the action space is approximated using importance sampling. For a given state, sample multiple actions from a learned proposal distribution, compute the Q-values for each sampled action, and then use importance weights to correct for the probability of sampling. The proposal distribution is learned using the Q-function's gradients and can be reused across states.

Diffusion models have demonstrated a remarkable ability to learn data distributions across many modalities, with strong results in both data generation and image restoration. In medical imaging, they are effective at modeling the distribution of 2D image slices, and by combining these powerful learned priors with conventional optimization frameworks, diffusion-based solvers have reached state-of-the-art performance on medical inverse problems such as accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and undersampled X-ray computed tomography (CT). Such problems are often severely ill-posed: far fewer measurements are acquired than there are unknowns, so the measurements alone cannot determine the image, and the learned prior must fill in what they leave ambiguous. Diffusion-based solvers do so through an iterative reverse sampling process that, at each step, predicts a clean image from the current noisy state, corrects this estimate for consistency with the measurements, and re-noises it to the next timestep, which repeatedly injects random noise.

In clinical practice, however, medical data are fundamentally large 3D volumes. Individual 2D slices matter for review, but a complete and accurate volumetric reconstruction is often essential for downstream tasks such as precise tumor volume assessment, surgical planning, and tracking disease progression over time. Translating the success of 2D diffusion-based solvers to 3D is difficult: because of the curse of dimensionality, the memory, computational, and data requirements of training a diffusion prior directly on volumetric data are prohibitive for most academic and even industrial labs. A common and practical workaround is to train a diffusion model on 2D slices and apply this 2D prior slice by slice to reconstruct the volume.

This workaround eases the training burden but creates a critical new problem: the reconstructed volumes lack consistency along the third dimension (the z-axis). Because each slice is processed independently during the reverse diffusion process, the intrinsic randomness of the sampling procedure leads to severe inter-slice discontinuities and artifacts, degrading the diagnostic and analytical quality of the stacked volume. Existing remedies have important drawbacks. The most direct one augments the 2D prior with a hand-crafted regularizer such as total variation, applied in an additional optimization step to enforce smoothness between adjacent slices. This is effective, but it introduces sensitive hyperparameters that require careful tuning, can over-smooth the volume or produce cartoon-like textures that erase fine diagnostic details, and acts as an external correction that masks the symptoms rather than addressing the intrinsic cause. More principled approaches try to learn a more complete 3D prior, for instance by training on 3D patches or by combining priors from two perpendicular 2D planes, but they increase the complexity of the training or inference pipeline and may impose constraints on the data, such as requiring cubic volumes.

A similar discontinuity arises in video restoration, where applying a pre-trained 2D image diffusion model to video inverse problems often produces temporal flickering across frames. Prior work attributed this flickering to the uncoordinated stochasticity inherent in diffusion sampling and alleviated it by synchronizing the stochastic noise components across frames. Whether the same mechanism is the fundamental cause of inter-slice inconsistency in 3D medical reconstruction, and how such a remedy would transfer from video to volumetric medical data, remains open.

This raises the following questions. How does the stochasticity of independent slice-wise sampling give rise to inter-slice inconsistency when 2D diffusion priors are used for 3D medical reconstruction? Is it possible to enhance inter-slice consistency directly within the diffusion sampling process itself, obviating the need for external, artifact-inducing optimization, ideally without new loss terms, additional sensitive hyperparameters, model retraining, or extra computational cost, so that the remedy could be dropped into existing 2D diffusion-based 3D reconstruction pipelines? And can inter-slice consistency be improved while preserving the natural anatomical variation between slices and fine diagnostic details, rather than trading them away for smoothness?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: slice synchronization via shared noise projection
PROPOSAL: We will apply a 2D diffusion-based solver to 3D volumetric MRI data, but instead of processing each slice independently, we will sample each slice from a shared noise distribution that is projected onto the current state of the solver, thus ensuring consistency between the slices. We will test two variants: one where the shared noise is static across all slices, and one where it is dynamic and updated at each step.
CONTROLS: We compare our proposed slice synchronization method to (1) a naive baseline where each slice is processed independently, and (2) an augmented baseline where a total variation regularizer is applied to enforce smoothness between adjacent slices.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The slice synchronization method should improve upon the naive baseline in terms of inter-slice consistency, with the dynamic noise variant performing better than the static one. However, it may also trade off some of the fine diagnostic details due to the constraint imposed by the shared noise distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: analyzing stochastic consistency using advanced diffusion diagnostics
PROPOSAL: We will embed advanced diffusion diagnostics into the 2D diffusion-based solver to directly measure the temporal consistency of the sampling process, quantifying the correlation between adjacent slices and identifying potential sources of inter-slice discrepancies. By comparing these diagnostics across different variants of the solver, including and without the slice synchronization method proposed in our previous experiment, we will analyze the mechanism behind inter-slice inconsistency and provide a deeper understanding of its origin.
CONTROLS: The baseline for our diagnostics will be the existing implementation of the 2D diffusion-based solver without any additional modifications.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The advanced diffusion diagnostics are expected to uncover the inherent stochasticity and its effects on slice consistency, supporting evidence for the potential benefits of our proposed slice synchronization method. However, inconsistent results might challenge our current assumptions and necessitate a reevaluation of the underlying problem.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating 3d patch-based diffusion priors in a 2d+1 framework
PROPOSAL: We will adapt the 2D diffusion-based solver to operate within a 2D+1 framework, where each 2D slice is augmented with a per-pixel description of the slice's spatial relationship to adjacent slices in the 3D volume. This framework will be used to train a set of 2D diffusion priors, each conditioned on 3D patches of volume data. During inference, the 2D diffusion model will use the spatial relationship descriptions to predict a clean image slice that is consistent with adjacent slices.
CONTROLS: We compare our 2D+1 framework with the naive baseline of applying a unconditioned 2D diffusion model to each slice independently, and with a 3D diffusion-based solver that has been trained directly on volume data.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method is expected to improve upon the naive baseline by leveraging the spatial relationships between slices, but may inherently require large amounts of memory and computational resources due to the need to compute and store the per-pixel spatial relationships. If we're lucky, it might challenge the effectiveness of our proposed slice synchronization method.

PROPOSAL: We will explore the integration of adaptive temporal filtering techniques into the diffusion-based reconstruction framework to stabilize and smooth out the variations caused by stochastic sampling, aiming to reduce inter-slice inconsistency. Generative models significantly enhance the efficiency of chemical space exploration in drug discovery by directly sampling molecules with desired properties. However, a key bottleneck in their practical deployment is low synthetic accessibility: generated molecules are often difficult or impossible to produce in the laboratory. To address this limitation, recent work has turned to template-based methods that emulate the chemical synthesis process by constructing synthesis trees that link molecular building blocks through known reaction templates. These representations, while useful for downstream experimental validation, do not describe the underlying 3D geometry and thus cannot capitalize on the conformational information that is often crucial for diverse chemical and biological properties.

Parallel advances in generative molecular design have explored spatial modeling at the atomic level. Inspired by advances in protein structure prediction and by generative frameworks such as diffusion and flow matching, recent work has focused on directly sampling 3D atomic coordinates of small molecules, learning to generate spatially meaningful, property-aligned conformations along with molecular graphs. The ability to model atomic coordinates directly increases the expressivity of these approaches, enabling applications such as pocket-conditioned generation, scaffold hopping, analog discovery, and molecular optimization. However, without considering practical synthesis routes, integrating synthesizability constraints into these models remains a major challenge, and most existing 3D generative approaches do not ensure that proposed molecules can be made in practice. While recent work has addressed synthesizability for 2D molecular graphs, extending such constraints to 3D, and to geometry-based conditional generation, remains largely unexplored.

Several obstacles stand in the way. Directly optimizing synthesizability scores is often unreliable, so the predominant route to synthetic accessibility has been to assemble molecules from commercially available building blocks joined by known reaction templates; yet such generators typically emit only molecular graphs and no atomic coordinates. The representations commonly available for 3D work are also ill-suited to synthesis awareness: synthon-based representations do not guarantee that a valid synthesis route exists, do not provide one even when it does, and lack the flexibility to constrain the reaction space, which matters when one wants to prioritize high-yield, high-reliability reactions or to remain within the limits of automated synthesis platforms. Relying instead on external, black-box reaction simulators to couple building blocks offers no fine-grained control when a reagent has several reaction centers, and such steps do not define atom mappings between reactants and products, making it impossible to trace product atoms back to their parent building blocks. A further difficulty is that most 3D molecule generation methods require the number of atoms to be specified in advance, which is awkward when the identity of the constituent building blocks is itself still being decided. Finally, the few approaches that do couple synthesis pathways with 3D structure optimize an external reward and typically require a full training run for each target pocket, which is costly and exposes the generator to reward hacking.

This raises the central questions. Can a single generative model sample small molecules so that each sample comes with both a physically realistic 3D conformation and an explicit, traceable route by which it could actually be made, instead of treating geometry and synthesizability as separate concerns handled in sequence or by post hoc filtering? What kind of data and molecular representation would such a model require, given that existing conformer datasets carry no synthesis information and existing synthesis-aware representations carry no geometry? How should synthesizability and geometric quality be measured so that claims of practical makeability are credible rather than an artifact of the scoring tool used? And can one amortized model, once trained, serve the geometry-conditioned design problems that drug discovery actually poses, such as completing or connecting parts of a known three-dimensional ligand, or designing novel molecules that reproduce a desired spatial arrangement of interaction features for a target, without external scoring functions and without retraining for each new target?

Deep learning models have achieved impressive success across a wide range of tasks, yet they can behave unpredictably when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) data that differ significantly from the training distribution, making high-confidence but incorrect predictions. OOD detection seeks to identify such inputs and is critical for reliable deployment in open-world scenarios, including safety-critical applications and scientific discovery tasks. The challenge becomes even more pronounced for graph-structured data, because of their non-Euclidean nature and complex topological structures.

Recent advances in graph-level OOD detection fall broadly into two categories. End-to-end methods train OOD-specific graph neural networks (GNNs) from scratch using only unlabeled in-distribution (ID) data; they typically rely on unsupervised objectives such as graph contrastive learning to extract discriminative representations that can separate ID and OOD samples during inference. Post-hoc methods instead start from well-trained GNNs and fine-tune OOD detectors that refine the predictions or representations at inference time. Among them, a recent test-time method, GOODAT, directly optimizes a learnable graph masker on the test samples without altering the pre-trained model. This test-time setting with data-centric modification is more practical, because it removes the dependency on labeled training data and on model retraining.

The test-time problem can be stated as follows. A GNN has been pre-trained on graphs from an unlabeled ID dataset. At test time it faces unlabeled graphs that mix held-out ID graphs, disjoint from the pre-training graphs, with graphs drawn from a different, OOD distribution. The goal is a detector that assigns each test graph a score, a higher score meaning a greater probability that the graph comes from the OOD distribution, using only the pre-trained model and the test graphs: the parameters of the pre-trained model are not modified, and neither the training data nor any ground-truth label is used.

Despite the progress of this data-centric paradigm, a less-explored challenge persists. A pre-trained model can effectively extract information from ID data, but when it infers on both ID and OOD test graphs it lacks ground-truth information indicative of the underlying distribution, information that is often embedded within the graph structure. Test graphs typically comprise distinctive components, whose capture could intuitively differentiate OOD samples from ID graphs, together with irrelevant structural elements. The pervasive presence of similar irrelevant structural elements in ID and OOD graphs, a structural redundancy that induces semantic shifts, hinders current methods from accurately capturing and distinguishing the essential structures of ID and OOD data. The existing test-time method tries to address this concern by using graph maskers to identify subgraphs in the test data that are similar to those in the ID training graphs, but it fundamentally relies on learnable graph augmentations, which can inadvertently alter the semantic information of substructures or lead to information loss, thereby compromising the reliability of OOD detection.

This raises the following questions. How can a well-trained GNN, left unchanged, be endowed at test time with the ability to capture the essential, distinctive structural information of test graphs while discarding irrelevant structural redundancy, without altering the semantics of their substructures? How can what is essential for telling ID from OOD graphs be separated from what is redundant in a principled and tractable way, when neither ground-truth labels nor OOD examples are available? And can such a test-time detector yield more reliable OOD scores than existing end-to-end and post-hoc approaches while remaining practical in computational cost?
