Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a wide range of natural language tasks, driven in part by advances in transformer-based architectures. While much effort has been devoted to understanding attention mechanisms and token-wise interactions, the role of feed-forward networks (FFNs), and particularly of their nonlinear components, remains underexplored, even though FFNs dominate both the parameter budget and the computational footprint of transformer-based models.

Despite their apparent simplicity, FFNs perform high-dimensional nonlinear transformations that regulate information flow by reorganizing, compressing, and propagating the information extracted by attention modules across layers. Understanding how these transformations behave, how they evolve across depth and over the course of training, and how they interact with architectural design choices (for example normalization or the choice of activation function) and with the choice of optimizer remains a fundamental open question; in practice, such design choices are still largely made by trial and error.

One challenge in interpreting FFNs is the absence of systematic and efficient tools for characterizing how latent representations are structured and transformed by nonlinear activations. FFN transformations unfold in a high-dimensional latent space that is far less accessible to direct visualization and probing than multi-head attention. Prior work has used attention maps to study the input-contextualization effect of FFNs, and has characterized FFN geometry through piecewise-affine spline partitions. Neither lens shows what the nonlinearity does to the overall geometry of the latent representation, for instance how much of the available high-dimensional latent space is actually used before and after the activation, or how this changes from layer to layer and during training.

This raises several questions. What does the FFN nonlinearity do to the structure of the latent representation it receives, and how does this vary across layers and over training? How do architectural and optimizer choices shape this behavior? Can these properties be measured efficiently enough to be tracked continuously while training large models, in a way that remains comparable across layers and model configurations? Do the resulting measurements relate to a model's generalization ability, so that they could serve as diagnostics to guide architectural and optimizer choices beyond trial and error? Finally, are these behaviors specific to attention-based transformers, or are they a more general property of deep feed-forward layers?

Recording dynamic scenes from multiple viewpoints has become increasingly common in everyday life. From concerts and sports events to lectures and birthday parties, people often capture the same moment using different handheld devices. These multi-view recordings present a rich opportunity to reconstruct scenes in 4D, enable bullet-time effects, or enhance the capabilities of existing vision models. However, these videos are typically captured independently, without synchronization or known camera poses, making it difficult to align and fuse them coherently.

The task is the following: given a set of asynchronous videos that capture the same dynamic scene from different viewpoints, estimate a time offset for each video, to be applied to its original out-of-sync clock, so that after correction frames sharing the same clock time correspond to the exact same moment across all videos.

Existing synchronization methods rely on controlled environments, manual annotations, specific patterns such as human pose, audio signals such as flashes or claps, or expensive hardware setups such as time-coded devices, none of which are available in casually captured videos. Human-centric approaches, which use body pose as the synchronization signal, are limited by the accuracy of pose estimation and by the number of people present, and they struggle in scenes without prominent human activity. Audio-based approaches only work in quiet environments and do not carry over to in-the-wild settings where audio is noisy or unavailable. Methods that jointly optimize camera poses and temporal offsets within a learned scene representation are often constrained to specific environments or object types. Geometry-based methods estimate temporal offsets from multi-view geometric constraints, but typically assume static scenes or a fixed viewpoint. Meanwhile, structure-from-motion and learned camera-pose estimators recover camera geometry accurately, yet they rely predominantly on static visual cues and therefore fall short of synchronizing dynamic scenes.

Building a practical and robust synchronization system that works on videos in the wild is challenging. Camera poses are unknown and cameras may move, so the geometric relationship between each pair of cameras must itself be estimated reliably. The moving objects that carry the timing information are not known in advance and are generally small and blurry. Associating points across cameras with significantly different viewpoints is difficult. The offsets to be recovered are continuous, while observations arrive only at discrete frame times. Finally, not all views overlap, so some pairs of cameras may share little spatial or temporal overlap.

This raises several questions. How can a set of casually captured, unposed and unsynchronized videos of the same dynamic scene be aligned in time with high precision, without specialized capture, audio, manual correction, or assumptions about the scene content such as the presence of people? Which visual evidence can reliably reveal the temporal offset between two cameras whose poses are unknown and possibly changing over time? And how can a single, globally consistent offset be recovered for every video when the evidence relating some pairs of views is weak, ambiguous or missing? Answering these questions would open the door to scalable, unconstrained multi-view 4D scene understanding and to downstream tasks, such as 4D reconstruction of dynamic scenes, that depend on synchronized input.

Graphs are powerful abstractions for representing complex relationships between entities, from social networks to molecular structures, and learning effective graph representations is crucial for node classification, graph classification and link prediction. Over the past decade, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become the dominant paradigm for graph representation learning, building representations through a message-passing mechanism that iteratively aggregates local neighborhood information. Despite its success, message passing faces several key limitations, such as limited expressiveness and difficulty in capturing long-range dependencies. Numerous efforts address different aspects of these limitations: graph transformer architectures incorporate long-range interactions across broader graph contexts, positional encodings inject structural priors to improve global topological awareness, and graph rewiring techniques modify the topology to mitigate structural bottlenecks and enhance information diffusion.

However, these advances remain constrained by a cognitive discrepancy. Humans perceive global structure intuitively, following visual Gestalt principles: they understand the whole before analyzing the individual parts. GNNs and their variants, by contrast, operate through bottom-up processing. People instantly recognize ring structures, symmetric structures and critical bridges in a drawing of a graph, yet even advanced architectures struggle with such basic topological understanding: standard message-passing networks provably cannot identify bridges, and graphs that people tell apart at a glance can fool message passing unless sophisticated topological computations are added. Although architectural innovations have made significant theoretical and practical progress, their essence is still to identify and repair different aspects of the inherent defects of message passing. Approaches that perceive graphs visually remain largely unexplored for graph learning, despite their natural alignment with how humans perceive network structures, and despite a flourishing computer vision ecosystem whose models excel at holistic pattern recognition and global structure understanding. Recent work has begun to bring graph drawings into existing architectures, for instance into vision-language models for graph reasoning or into GNNs to enhance expressivity, but it treats graph layouts and vision models as black boxes, without examining how visual and message-passing models fundamentally differ in the way they understand graphs.

A second obstacle is measurement. Established benchmarks built from molecules, citation networks or protein interaction graphs tightly couple domain-specific node features with topology, which makes their separate contributions hard to quantify and can let models succeed through feature-based shortcuts rather than genuine structural understanding. Models that replace the true molecular topology with fixed-structure expander graphs have been shown to match or exceed performance on several molecular benchmarks, suggesting that node features often dominate structural information in standard datasets, potentially masking differences in how models perceive graph topology. The theoretical evaluation of GNNs has centered on the Weisfeiler-Lehman test, which measures the ability to distinguish pairs of non-isomorphic graphs of the same size; valuable for theory, it is limited to binary discrimination between fixed-size graph pairs. Recent graph benchmarks oriented toward large language models focus on structural analysis tasks such as node counting, cycle detection and path finding, and typically rely on a limited set of random graph generators (such as Erdős–Rényi or Watts–Strogatz) that inadequately capture topological diversity. What remains missing is a way to assess human-like graph cognition: the intuitive ability to perceive, abstract and reason about fundamental global graph properties, and to recognize the same connectivity patterns across varying scales and contexts.

This leads to the questions addressed here. Could models designed for visual perception, which carry no graph-specific inductive bias, offer a viable pathway to graph structural understanding, and do they process graph information in the same way as message-passing GNNs or through fundamentally different strategies? How can a model's ability to perceive and abstract global graph properties be evaluated rigorously, in isolation from domain-specific features, including whether it recognizes the same structural pattern regardless of graph size? And what does it take for a graph learning model to acquire the holistic, scale-robust understanding of topology that humans display effortlessly?

Understanding how a scene has changed and forecasting how it will look next from Satellite Image Time Series (SITS) is fundamental to many critical applications, yet it poses a profound challenge: predicting the future requires a deep understanding of past change. Two tasks are central. In temporal change description, given a sequence of temporally ordered satellite images of the same area, the goal is to generate a natural-language description that accurately summarizes the key dynamic changes that occurred over the observation period, such as urban expansion or agricultural cycles; this requires comprehending the temporal evolution and, ideally, the underlying causal narrative of the changes. In future satellite image forecasting, given the same historical sequence, the goal is to generate a plausible image for the next time point. A critical and often overlooked requirement is that the forecast be temporally consistent: the generated changes should be a logical continuation of the trends and dynamics observed in the historical data, not merely a plausible standalone picture.

Although foundation models such as Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and diffusion-based image generators have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their application to this domain remains fragmented and fundamentally limited. On the understanding side, static image captioning ignores temporal context, while existing temporal change description methods lack the semantic depth of MLLMs: they fuse information across images through simple interactions, their long-range temporal reasoning is limited, and they struggle to capture why changes occur. General-purpose MLLMs, even video-capable ones, are not optimized for this setting either: video-centric models are typically tuned for densely sampled frames with fixed, short intervals, whereas consecutive satellite acquisitions are sparse and irregular, with gaps that can span several years. On the generation side, single-image synthesis cannot model evolution, and temporal forecasting approaches struggle with long-term consistency because they do not grasp the semantic drivers of change: their conditioning is typically low-level (e.g., edge maps), based on simple metadata, or limited to text guidance, and it lacks fine-grained temporal semantic interaction, so they can generate what a scene looks like but cannot reason about why it should look that way given its history. As a result, change understanding and future forecasting have been treated as disjointed tasks, even though both are limited by a common bottleneck: modeling long-range temporal dynamics.

This raises several questions. How can a model reason about why changes occurred across a long, irregularly sampled sequence of satellite images, and describe them accurately? How can such an understanding of past change be used to generate what will happen next, so that the forecast is a temporally consistent continuation of the observed trajectory rather than only a realistic-looking image? Can enhancing long-range temporal understanding improve performance on both tasks simultaneously, with the understanding of past change directly informing the forecast? Finally, how can the temporal consistency of a forecast be rigorously evaluated, given that standard image-quality metrics cannot penalize a prediction that is perceptually realistic but inconsistent with historical trends?

Transformers, powered by attention mechanisms, have become the default backbone for sequence modeling across language, vision, speech, and decision making. Their success is often linked to selective access to an ever-growing key-value cache while retaining parallel training and inference. In large language models, this selective ability, composed across multiple attention layers and residual pathways, supports long-range memory retrieval and the algorithmic behaviors associated with in-context learning (for example induction heads and pattern completion), as shown by empirical and mechanistic studies.

Causal softmax attention combines strong selectivity with parallel efficiency: at each step it forms a distribution over past indices and mixes their values, while all steps can be computed in parallel. Given queries, keys and values $Q,K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}$ with rows $q_t$, $k_i$, $v_i$, define masked scores $s_{t,i}=q_t^\top k_i/\sqrt{d}$ for $i\le t$ and $-\infty$ otherwise, and set $\alpha_{t,\cdot}=\mathrm{softmax}(s_{t,\cdot})$, a probability distribution over $\{1,\dots,t\}$. The step-$t$ read is $o_t=\sum_{i\le t}\alpha_{t,i}v_i$, which lies in the convex hull of $\{v_1,\dots,v_t\}$; stacking all steps yields $O=AV$ with $A_{t,i}=\alpha_{t,i}$, so a single matrix multiply produces all outputs.

This convex-mixture view explains the efficiency of attention, but it also reveals a dilemma between lossless storage and lossy processing. The key-value cache stores the full context, but the read is lossy: each head applies the same weights to all coordinates of $v_i$, so the output lies in the convex hull of the stored values and all channels are synchronized. As a result, even simple per-channel indexing, such as returning $(v_{i_1,1},\dots,v_{i_D,D})$ where each coordinate $j$ is taken from its own past index $i_j$ (for example, a coordinate-wise argmax), cannot be represented unless all chosen indices coincide. This limitation hinders Transformers in long-range modeling with non-sequential or irregular timestep indexing, and in tasks where channel-wise structure is critical, such as multivariate time series modeling.

Most recent advances in attention aim to improve expressivity and efficiency, typically by designing richer selection distributions while still reading values through a token-separable linear combination. These include sparse attention patterns, low-rank projections, and kernelizable variants with normalization or gating. Efficiency-oriented work accelerates attention through factorized implementations, or replaces the cache with streaming state space models and recurrent networks that keep a fixed-size state. Across these lines, computation becomes faster or the distribution richer, but the read remains a linear mix: channels share weights, and even simple per-channel indexing cannot be realized in one step. Some recent works explore more complex combinations, such as nonlinear mixing or hard/top-k selection, yet these mainly target training stability or accuracy in specific cases and do not address the lossy-processing limitation.

This leaves an open problem: how can the read of an attention-style sequence mixer be redesigned to remove this linear read bottleneck and support per-channel, context-dependent selection from memory, so that different channels can retrieve different past indices in the same step, while keeping causal parallelism and the asymptotic time complexity of the underlying selection mechanism (for example, quadratic in sequence length for softmax attention and linear for linear-time variants)? And does closing this gap between lossless storage and lossy processing translate into better sequence modeling in practice?

Diffusion models have catalyzed an enormous research wave in generative modeling. Conceptually, they couple a stochastic forward noising process with a reverse-time ordinary or stochastic differential equation whose density evolution is governed by the Fokker–Planck equation, a linear second-order parabolic partial differential equation. Learning consists of estimating time-indexed scores or velocities and integrating them for sampling. A growing body of work also explores probability-flow backbones: deterministic flows trained via flow matching and its optimal-transport variants, rectified flows, and stochastic interpolants that bridge flows and diffusion.

Yet the partial-differential-equation lens on generative modeling need not be limited to Fokker–Planck. Other classical linear second-order equations, elliptic and hyperbolic, offer different structural advantages but remain comparatively underexplored; Poisson flow models, for instance, recast generation through electrostatics-inspired fields. On the hyperbolic side, recent work has replaced the Fokker–Planck equation with the telegrapher equation (the one-dimensional damped wave equation) and its stochastic Kac representation, in which a particle moves at constant speed and reverses direction at the jump times of a Poisson process. A network is fit by regression to a closed-form conditional velocity of this process and integrated backward in time from noise to data, with each image coordinate following an independent one-dimensional Kac process. The resulting probability flows have a finite propagation speed: starting from localized mass, the distribution remains inside a causal cone, the flow is Lipschitz in Wasserstein distance, and velocity norms, hence kinetic energy, stay globally bounded. Diffusion, by contrast, spreads mass instantaneously with effectively infinite propagation speed, which manifests as stiff, rapidly growing reverse-time velocities and as ill-conditioned fields with Lipschitz blow-ups near the end of denoising; indeed, diffusion arises as a limit of the damped wave equation as the damping and the propagation speed tend to infinity. A finite speed cap thus acts like a built-in stability constraint: trajectories cannot accelerate without bound, and late-time integration is less stiff.

So far, however, these finite-speed flows have been developed only for unconditional image generation, and they lack two ingredients that make diffusion-style generators practical. The first is guided conditional generation. Classifier-free guidance, which mixes conditional and unconditional predictions to steer samples toward a condition, is a standard tool for diffusion models, but it is unclear whether guidance can be carried over to finite-speed dynamics without losing the bounded-energy property that distinguishes them from diffusion, whose kinetic energy can diverge near data time. The second is fast sampling. Practical generators are expected to deliver high-quality samples with very few network evaluations, yet it is unknown whether finite-speed flows can be brought down to a handful of sampling steps, or even a single one, without a severe loss of sample quality, and whether their finite-speed, bounded-energy structure can explain, and ideally guarantee, that a coarse few-step sampler stays close to the full sampling trajectory.

This leads to three questions. How can guided conditional generation be built on finite-speed Kac flows while provably keeping the guided velocity field at finite kinetic energy? How can such flows be turned into few-step, ideally one-step, image generators that preserve both sample quality and the numerical stability benefits of finite-speed probability flows? And can the finite-speed structure provide theoretical guarantees that a few-step sampler remains close to the full flow along the entire generation path, not only in its final samples? Answering them would show whether hyperbolic, finite-speed dynamics can be a credible alternative to diffusion for fast image generation.

Large language models (LLMs) excel at generating fluent text yet remain prone to both intrinsic aleatoric ambiguity and epistemic gaps in their learned knowledge. The latter can lead to hallucinations—confident outputs that are factually incorrect. Quantifying these uncertainties is critical for building safe AI systems deployable in high-stakes applications. In free-form natural language generation tasks such as question answering, this is especially challenging, as lexically distinct responses can still be semantically equivalent: uncertainty has to be measured over meanings rather than over token sequences.

A standard way to do so defines a distribution over semantic clusters of responses, obtained by marginalizing over output sequences and approximated by Monte Carlo sampling. The total predictive uncertainty over these clusters decomposes into an aleatoric part, the entropy over clusters (semantic entropy), which captures the irreducible ambiguity among valid answers, and an epistemic part, which reflects the model's lack of knowledge or data coverage. For a question such as "Name a way to measure the Hubble constant", several distinct but correct answers (for instance, the distance ladder or gravitational lensing time delays) reflect aleatoric uncertainty, whereas answers that contradict scientific facts or admit ignorance reveal gaps in the model's knowledge and signal that it should abstain.

Estimating these quantities often relies on drawing large IID sample sets, which often contain semantically redundant outputs and waste compute. Semantic entropy quantifies aleatoric uncertainty by clustering generated outputs into semantic equivalence classes, and mutual information computed via iterative prompting has been used to lower-bound certain forms of epistemic uncertainty; despite their conceptual appeal, both require extensive sampling to produce stable estimates, limiting their use in low-resource settings. Diversity-oriented heuristics such as temperature scaling or nucleus sampling, on the other hand, do not account for semantics. A more recent method steers generation toward semantic diversity, but it relies on token substitutions and remains restricted to autoregressive models (ARMs). Moreover, diversity heuristics are commonly applied during sampling without correcting for the bias they introduce, even though the uncertainties of interest are defined under the model's own distribution.

Meanwhile, uncertainty estimation methods have focused on ARMs, whereas masked diffusion models (MDMs), which extend masked language modeling by learning iterative denoising schedules that progressively resolve masked spans, have recently emerged as strong alternatives. Despite achieving text quality on par with state-of-the-art ARMs, MDMs remain largely overlooked in the context of uncertainty quantification.

This leaves several questions open. How can stable estimates of semantic aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty be obtained for free-form answers from a small, fixed budget of generations, so that the samples cover distinct meanings instead of repeating the same ones? How can this be done while keeping the estimates faithful to the model's own predictive distribution? And can a single approach serve both autoregressive and masked diffusion language models?

Transporting mass between probability distributions is a ubiquitous problem in machine learning and beyond. Optimal transport (OT) provides a principled approach to such problems by seeking to minimise the total cost of transportation under a chosen cost function, and computational OT, from Sinkhorn's algorithm to more recent neural approaches, has been applied successfully in domains such as biology and extensively within machine learning. More recently, ideas from the flow-based approaches that have revolutionised generative modelling have been leveraged to solve the entropy-regularised dynamic OT problem known as the Schrödinger bridge (SB): finding the most likely evolution of a population between two prescribed distributions, relative to a reference stochastic process. With a Brownian reference process, the static form of this problem is exactly entropy-regularised OT for the quadratic cost. Flow-based SB solvers offer significant scalability advantages, enabling the approximation of OT maps between high-dimensional continuous datasets such as images. Early flow-based solvers were built on the classical Iterative Proportional Fitting (IPF) scheme, which preserves both marginals only at convergence, requires expensive caching of simulated trajectories and tends to 'forget' the reference measure; such methods have since been superseded by solvers based on the Iterative Markovian Fitting (IMF) scheme, which avoids these issues.

Beyond the standard two-marginal problem, multi-marginal OT seeks a joint coupling over several marginals that minimises a total cost. Tree-structured costs are often considered, as they frequently arise in applications while allowing improved scalability by exploiting the tree structure. In the corresponding tree-structured SB problem, stochastic processes run along the edges of a tree and marginals are prescribed only at a subset of the vertices; with Brownian motion along each edge as the reference, it is an entropy-regularised multi-marginal OT problem with a tree-structured quadratic cost. Star-shaped trees, with marginals fixed on the leaves and an unknown centre, are of particular significance because they correspond to an entropy-regularised form of the Wasserstein barycentre problem. The Wasserstein barycentre provides a natural notion of 'average' for probability distributions and is widely studied because of its importance in applications such as Bayesian learning, clustering and representation learning. Computing barycentres is notoriously challenging. Many successful approaches approximate the solution with a finite set of points, but such in-sample methods struggle to scale as dimensionality increases and cannot generate new samples; alternative methods provide continuous approximations through neural parameterisations, but often require multi-level or adversarial optimisation procedures. To date, the only neural ODE/SDE approach to barycentre computation extends the IPF-based diffusion Schrödinger bridge to the tree-structured SB setting, and therefore inherits the drawbacks of IPF; it has been reported to suffer training instability at low entropic regularisation, struggling to match the prescribed marginals at the vertices.

In parallel, one of the most successful approaches to Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation is the iterative fixed-point method, which repeatedly updates a candidate barycentre by solving for the OT map from it to each marginal and pushing it forward through the weighted average of these maps. It performs strongly and has been observed to converge in only a few iterations, but every iteration requires solving a complete OT problem to each marginal, which is expensive because solving even a single OT problem can be challenging.

This raises several questions. Can a scalable, flow-based solver be built for the tree-structured SB problem, and hence for entropic Wasserstein barycentres, that avoids the shortcomings of IPF-based schemes while being guaranteed to converge to the tree-structured SB solution? In the barycentre case, can the fast convergence of fixed-point schemes be retained without paying for a complete OT solve to every marginal at every iteration? And can flow-based barycentre solvers of this kind offer a viable alternative to existing algorithms for continuous Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation?

The ability to model complex, real-world phenomena is one of the central challenges in machine learning. Domains such as geospatial modeling, where terrain varies drastically across regions, or speech analysis, where signals exhibit bursts of volatility, are often characterized by pronounced non-stationarity: their statistical properties change across the input space, so that sharp, localized events can coexist with smooth, slowly varying regions. Gaussian processes (GPs) offer a principled framework for such problems, providing robust uncertainty estimates and flexible, non-parametric modeling. Despite these advantages, exact GPs suffer from two major limitations: their expressivity is constrained by the choice of kernel, and exact inference costs O(N^3) time and O(N^2) memory in the number N of training points, rendering it impractical for modern large-scale applications.

Most current approaches force a trade-off between expressivity and efficiency. On one hand, random Fourier features achieve impressive scalability: the kernel is approximated by an explicit, finite-dimensional feature map obtained by Monte Carlo sampling from its spectral density, so that the GP reduces to a Bayesian linear regression whose cost is linear in the number of data points, and the approximation error is backed by theoretical guarantees. Yet this construction depends on Bochner's theorem, which fundamentally restricts it to stationary kernels that assume uniform behavior across the entire domain; its globally supported sinusoidal features are inherently spatially invariant. Applying such models to non-stationary data leads to systematic mis-specification, resulting in compromised predictive accuracy and uncalibrated uncertainty estimates. Sparse variational GPs reduce the cost of exact inference through a set of inducing points, but they rely on iterative optimization whose cost grows cubically with the number of inducing points. On the other hand, expressive models such as deep GPs, spectral mixture kernels, and input-dependent kernels can capture non-stationarity, but they often reintroduce prohibitive computational costs, complex inference schemes, and challenges in optimization and hyperparameter tuning, and they typically retain a high complexity in the number of training points. Hybrid approaches that combine scalable approximations with expressive models, such as kernel interpolation, deep kernel learning, deep random features, and adaptive or compositional Fourier-feature representations, still tend to trade off scalability, expressivity, and interpretability.

The gap between scalable stationary models and complex non-stationary ones therefore remains. This raises the central question of whether the random-feature paradigm can be generalized beyond Bochner's theorem to the non-stationary setting: can one construct an explicit, randomly sampled feature map whose induced kernel adapts to local, input-dependent structure, while preserving the linear-in-data training and prediction cost that makes random features attractive? Such a construction should also be principled, with guarantees, comparable to those available for random Fourier features, that the induced kernel is valid and that the random approximation converges to it as the number of features grows. Finally, it remains open whether such an approach can offer a better trade-off between predictive accuracy, uncertainty quality, and computational cost than both stationary random features and more complex non-stationary GP models.

Time series data arise ubiquitously across a broad range of domains, including healthcare, finance, industrial manufacturing, weather forecasting and urban computing, and their characteristics can differ vastly from one domain to another. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have unleashed new potential for exploiting these data in time series tasks such as forecasting, imputation and classification. There are roughly two families of approaches: one fine-tunes or prompts off-the-shelf LLMs with time series converted into a suitable format, while the other trains time series foundation models from scratch on vast time series corpora by adapting LLM-inspired architectures and training strategies. In both cases, the quality of the time series data is critical to model performance: low-quality data can negate the benefits of bespoke technical advances and may even degrade performance. In practice, time series datasets are frequently marred by pervasive quality issues, including missing values, corruption induced by sensor failures, and irregular sampling. Consequently, there is a pressing need to assess, accurately and efficiently, the quality of time series data crawled from diverse domains.

General-purpose data attribution methods, such as influence functions and Shapley-value approaches (together with cheaper approximations such as KNN-based or gradient-based Shapley values), estimate the contribution of individual training samples in a model-agnostic way, but they overlook properties specific to time series such as continuity, temporal dependencies and non-stationarity. Existing attempts at time series data quality estimation therefore stress the need for methods tailored to temporal characteristics. For instance, TimeInf adapts the influence function to time series, drawing on earlier work on infinitesimal robustness for autoregressive processes and on influence functionals for time series, and TimeShap extends the Shapley value, a cooperative game-theoretic attribution method, to time series. However, these methods have largely neglected the fact that real-world time series originate from diverse domains with distinct properties and substantial distribution shifts, which limits their effectiveness to a single domain. Furthermore, both influence-function and Shapley-value techniques struggle to strike a balance between estimation fidelity and computational efficiency: influence functions require computationally intensive Hessian and gradient calculations, while Shapley values incur exponential computational costs.

Recently, estimating data quality through LLM judgments has emerged as a promising approach for text, where carefully designed prompts guide LLMs to produce accurate quality assessments. The underlying rationale is that LLMs are proficient in understanding quality criteria for natural language, such as writing style, required expertise, factual accuracy and educational value. Such efforts point to the potential of LLMs for cross-domain and interpretable data quality estimation, but they remain restricted to text and code, and the time series setting is largely unexplored.

It is therefore tempting to ask whether LLMs can be exploited to determine the quality of diverse time series data. Such an approach could leverage the knowledge of time series from many domains that LLMs acquire during large-scale pretraining, thereby circumventing the prohibitive computational cost of calculating influence functions or Shapley values in a domain-by-domain manner. However, it remains under-explored whether LLMs can truly comprehend the key characteristics that underpin the quality of diverse time series data, and how to effectively steer them to distinguish between high- and low-quality time series according to desired quality criteria. The open problem is thus how to rate the quality of time series data drawn from heterogeneous domains in a way that is accurate, computationally efficient and adaptable across domains.

enonce:
Knowledge distillation is a fundamental technique in machine learning, widely used for model compression, transfer learning, and improving generalization. Its core idea is to transfer knowledge from a "teacher" model to a (typically smaller) "student" model by training the student to match the teacher's output probabilities rather than categorical one-hot labels. This softened supervision has been shown to improve performance across a range of tasks. Consequently, a substantial body of research has focused on designing distillation mechanisms, such as dynamic temperature scaling, feature-based distillation, and task-aware teacher-student matching, typically assuming a large teacher that is optimized to maximize its own performance.

Despite its widespread adoption, the theoretical foundations of knowledge distillation remain only partially understood. In particular, the impact of the teacher's output probabilities on the student's optimization trajectory and generalization has not been fully characterized. Existing explanations attribute the usefulness of distillation to the regularizing effect of the teacher's soft estimates, to trade-offs such as precision versus recall or knowledge inheritance versus exploration, or to factors such as data geometry and optimization bias. Insights into how distillation affects the optimization itself have been developed only for special cases, such as self-distillation or a student that is a compressed version of the teacher, and rely on dedicated gradient approximations. A principled understanding of how distillation affects common learning algorithms, such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants, for arbitrary teachers, is still lacking.

Recent works have begun to view distillation through a Bayesian lens, interpreting the teacher's outputs as (possibly noisy) estimates of the true class posterior probabilities of the data-generating distribution. From this statistical viewpoint, learning from accurate class posteriors has been argued to reduce the variance of the student's objective, and excess-risk and generalization bounds have been derived in terms of the distance between the teacher's predictions and the true posteriors. These analyses, however, characterize the statistical properties of the risk rather than the behavior of the learning algorithm that actually trains the student. The probabilistic perspective thus opens relatively unexplored questions about the dynamics of SGD-based learning under probabilistic supervision, and about how the statistical calibration of the teacher influences the student. Teacher calibration has been recognized as a key driver of distillation, but it remains unclear how the quality of the teacher's probability estimates should guide the way teachers are built.

This raises several questions. How does supervising a student with the exact class posterior probabilities, instead of one-hot labels, change the convergence behavior and stability of SGD-based learning and the generalization of the resulting student? In the realistic case where the teacher provides only imperfect, noisy estimates of these posteriors, how does the level of estimation error affect the student's convergence, generalization and accuracy, and under what conditions does probabilistic supervision remain preferable to one-hot labels? Finally, what practical guidelines follow for designing or choosing teacher models, beyond maximizing the teacher's own accuracy, so that their outputs provide better supervision for students trained with SGD-based optimizers?

Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly expanded in capability and are now widely used in domains such as conversational agents, healthcare and finance, where they often process sensitive personal information. Early privacy concerns focused mainly on memorization and leakage of training data, but recent studies show that LLMs can also infer private attributes of an author, such as location, identity or demographics, from subtle semantic cues in seemingly innocuous text. With sufficiently capable models, such inferences can be surprisingly accurate and often go undetected by users, who continue to share content unaware of the risk. Moreover, text sent to external services may be intercepted in transit or retained by providers, for example for model training, increasing the risk of misuse or data breaches.

Traditional anonymization methods rely on rule-based de-identification, such as named entity recognition or pattern matching, to remove surface-level identifiers like names, social security numbers or explicit locations. They frequently overlook the context-dependent semantics that LLMs can exploit, so private information that is embedded in context rather than stated explicitly remains inferable. This gap calls for anonymization techniques that account for semantic context and defend against inference-based privacy threats, while preserving the meaning and readability of the text, that is, techniques that achieve a good privacy-utility trade-off.

A growing body of work pursues LLM-based anonymization to protect semantic-level private information from model inference. In feedback-guided adversarial anonymization, an LLM anonymizer rewrites the input text while a second LLM, acting as an adversary, attempts to infer private attributes from the rewritten output; based on this adversarial feedback, the anonymizer iteratively refines its output to prevent the inferences that remain possible. With GPT-4 as both anonymizer and adversary, this approach achieves a substantially better privacy-utility trade-off than traditional industry-grade anonymizers. However, reliance on large proprietary models is costly and requires sending the very text that should be protected to potentially untrusted external systems. Attempts to transfer these anonymization capabilities into smaller models have been explored only to a limited extent, and existing approaches still depend on a proprietary model to provide the adversarial feedback, incurring similar costs and privacy concerns.

The open problem is therefore whether, and how, small language models that can run locally under modest compute budgets can become effective anonymizers that protect semantic-level private information against inference by strong LLM adversaries, without relying on any external model at inference time. Can such models reach a privacy-utility trade-off comparable to, or better than, that of anonymizers built on frontier proprietary LLMs, including on texts where personal information is conveyed by the overall context rather than by explicit mentions, while remaining cheap enough to deploy in settings with strict data-confidentiality requirements?

The multi-objective multi-armed bandit problem generalizes the classical, single-objective multi-armed bandit to settings with multiple, potentially conflicting objectives. Pulling an arm yields a vector of objective-specific rewards, so a single "best" arm is often ill-defined and optimality must account for trade-offs across objectives. The setting of interest here is the multi-objective linear contextual bandit: at each round, every arm of a finite set is described by a d-dimensional context vector, which may be chosen adversarially; each of the L objectives has its own fixed but unknown parameter vector; and the agent, after choosing an arm, observes an L-dimensional reward vector whose entry for each objective is the inner product of the arm's context with that objective's parameter, plus zero-mean sub-Gaussian noise.

One simple way to handle trade-offs is scalarization, which maps reward vectors to a scalar via, for example, weighted sums, minimax, or other nonlinear transforms, thereby reducing the problem to a single-objective bandit. However, selecting a suitable scalarization is itself nontrivial, and an arm that is optimal under one scalarization can be markedly suboptimal under another. An alternative is to reason directly in the vector space via Pareto optimality: the Pareto front comprises the arms whose mean reward vectors are not dominated component-wise by that of any other arm. Because it compares reward vectors objective-wise, Pareto optimality is more general than committing to a fixed scalarization. Performance is then usually measured by the Pareto regret, which sums over rounds the smallest uniform increase that would make the mean reward vector of the chosen arm non-dominated.

Prior work on Pareto regret in multi-objective bandits proposes and studies upper-confidence-bound (UCB) algorithms, which typically compute an empirical Pareto front at every round and are therefore complex. Approaches that identify the Pareto front by eliminating arms do not carry over to the contextual setting, where the Pareto front changes with the contexts and an arm discarded early may later be Pareto optimal. By contrast, the Pareto regret of Thompson Sampling has not been studied for multi-objective bandits: the only Thompson Sampling algorithm proposed for this problem comes without theoretical analysis, and the analyses of randomized scalarization in multi-objective Bayesian optimization concern the Bayesian regret under a known Gaussian prior, with bounds that increase with the number of objectives. This gap is noteworthy: in many single-objective contextual and non-contextual bandits, Thompson Sampling and its variants are empirically competitive with or superior to UCB methods, yet their worst-case (frequentist) analyses are typically more delicate. Extending Thompson Sampling to several objectives introduces additional challenges, including coordinating randomized samples across multiple objectives, ensuring optimism of the randomized estimates across all objectives simultaneously, and handling the possibility of multiple Pareto-optimal arms.

A second issue concerns the performance measure itself. The standard Pareto regret compares per-round mean reward vectors; consequently, a policy that plays only Pareto-optimal arms incurs zero Pareto regret, even when an alternative selection of arms over the same number of rounds would yield strictly larger cumulative rewards in every objective. Pareto regret therefore does not distinguish between policies that obtain different cumulative rewards while selecting only Pareto-optimal arms, and the resulting shortfall can grow with the number of rounds.

This raises two questions. First, can a computationally efficient, Thompson Sampling-type randomized algorithm for the multi-objective linear contextual bandit be designed with worst-case Pareto regret guarantees, how close can these guarantees come to those known for randomized algorithms in the single-objective linear setting, and how must they depend on the number of objectives? Second, how should optimality and regret be defined in this setting so that they also account for cumulative rewards under repeated selections, penalizing policies that are Pareto optimal round by round but inefficient in aggregate?

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: maximum likelihood simulation
PROPOSAL: design a simulation-based framework to provide maximum likelihood estimates for the unknown objective parameter vectors in the multi-objective linear contextual bandit setting. we will generate synthetic contexts and rewards using a chosen distribution (e.g., standard normal) and the multiplier travel method to fit the reward functions to the data, for various setting parameters and numbers of objectives.
CONTROLS: ablation study of using different distributions and reward function estimation methods, comparison with the oracle knowledge scenario where the objective parameters are known.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this approach will provide a fast and efficient method to estimate objective parameters, but may struggle with small sample sizes or complex reward relationships.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: thompson sampling with pareto-conditional utility
PROPOSAL: investigate a Thompson Sampling algorithm that directly estimates the Pareto front using a utility function that conditions on the current Pareto set. at each round, the algorithm generates a set of candidate arms based on an empirical Pareto set, estimates the posterior distribution of the rewards for each arm using Thompson Sampling, and selects the arm with the highest estimated utility. the utility function compares the estimated rewards with the current Pareto front.
CONTROLS: comparison with UCB algorithms, ablation study of the utility function and the empirical Pareto set estimation.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this approach will be able to adapt to changing Pareto sets, but may require a large number of samples to accurately estimate the posterior distributions, and may struggle with large numbers of objectives or complex reward relationships.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: no update to prior proposal
REVISED TITLE: maximum likelihood simulation
PROPOSAL: extend the simulation-based framework to provide confidence intervals for the estimated objective parameter vectors, and analyze the convergence rate of the estimates as a function of the number of samples and the dimensionality of the context space. we will use bootstrapping to compute the standard errors of the estimates, and use the law of the iterated logarithm to establish a bound on the estimation error.
CONTROLS: comparison with the oracle knowledge scenario where the objective parameters are known, ablation study of different bootstrapping methods.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this updated proposal will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the simulation-based framework, but may require significant computational resources to analyze the convergence rate.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: pareto regret relaxation
PROPOSAL: propose a relaxation of the Pareto regret metric that accounts for cumulative rewards, by introducing a "discounted Pareto regret" metric that weights the regret at each round by the average cumulative reward obtained by the policy up to that round. we will analyze the optimality gap of a greedy algorithm that optimizes the discounted Pareto regret metric.
CONTROLS: comparison with the standard Pareto regret metric, analysis of the effect of the discount factor on the optimality gap.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this relaxation may provide a more nuanced understanding of the trade-offs between Pareto optimality and cumulative rewards, but may require careful tuning of the discount factor.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: pareto regret relaxation
PROPOSAL: refine the discounted Pareto regret metric by using a more sophisticated discounting strategy, such as a weighted average of the cumulative rewards obtained by the policy at different time horizons. we will analyze the effect of different weighting schemes on the optimality gap and the relative performance of different policies.
CONTROLS: comparison with the standard pareto regret metric, analysis of the effect of different weighting schemes on policy performance.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this refined metric may provide a more robust understanding of the trade-offs between Pareto optimality and cumulative rewards, but may require extensive computational resources to analyze the effect of different weighting schemes.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: bound on pareto regret
PROPOSAL: provide a high-probability bound on the Pareto regret of an arbitrary bandit algorithm, in terms of the number of samples, the dimensionality of the context space, and the number of objectives. we will use a combination of concentration inequalities and martingale techniques to derive a tight bound on the Pareto regret.
CONTROLS: comparison with existing bounds on single-objective bandits, analysis of the effect of the number of objectives on the bound.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this bound may provide a fundamental understanding of the Pareto regret metric, but may be challenging to derive and may not provide a good approximation for small sample sizes or complex reward relationships.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: thompson sampling with pareto-conditional utility
PROPOSAL: extend the Thompson Sampling algorithm with Pareto-conditional utility to handle multiple Pareto-optimal arms by introducing a hierarchical decision-making process. at each round, the algorithm will generate multiple candidate arms based on an empirical Pareto set, estimate the posterior distribution of the rewards for each arm using Thompson Sampling, and select the arm with the highest estimated utility. however, if multiple arms are tied for the highest utility, the algorithm will use a secondary selection criterion to break ties, such as the maximum estimated reward across all objectives.
CONTROLS: comparison with standard UCB algorithms, analysis of the effect of the hierarchical decision-making process on policy performance, in the same setting as the proposal.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this extended algorithm may be able to handle multiple Pareto-optimal arms more effectively than standard algorithms, but may require additional computational resources and may be more challenging to analyze theoretically.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: regularization of the empirical pareto set
PROPOSAL: introduce regularization techniques to stabilize the empirical Pareto set estimation in the multi-objective bandit setting. we will use L1 or L2 regularization to penalize the empirical Pareto set based on a chosen regularizer, and analyze the effect of regularization on the policy performance and regret.
CONTROLS: comparison with standard empirical Pareto set estimation, analysis of the effect of regularization on the robustness of the policy to outliers and noise.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this regularization approach may improve the stability and robustness of the policy, but may also increase the risk of over-smoothing the empirical Pareto set and sacrificing optimality.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: no update to prior proposal
PROPOSAL: extend the maximum likelihood simulation to estimate the cumulative rewards under repeated selections, by running multiple episodes of the simulation with different initial arm selections and averaging the cumulative rewards across episodes. we will use this approach to evaluate the performance of different policies on cumulative rewards, and analyze the effect of the number of episodes on the accuracy of the estimation.
CONTROLS: comparison with oracle knowledge scenario where the objective parameters are known, analysis of the effect of the number of episodes on the accuracy of the estimation.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this extension will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the simulation-based framework, but may require additional computational resources to estimate the cumulative rewards accurately.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: instrumental rewards for multi-objective bandits
PROPOSAL: develop an instrumental rewards approach to handle multi-objective bandits by learning an intermediate representation of the rewards that can be used to optimize a single objective function. we will use a combination of neural networks and reinforcement learning to learn the instrumental rewards, and analyze the effect of the instrumental rewards on the policy performance and regret.
CONTROLS: comparison with direct optimization of the multi-objective function, analysis of the effect of the number of objectives on the accuracy of the instrumental rewards.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this instrumental rewards approach may provide a more efficient and scalable solution to multi-objective bandits, but may also introduce additional challenges such as learning the instrumental rewards and handling the trade-offs between objectives.

Directed graphs (digraphs) model systems with asymmetric relationships, capturing essential structures such as flows, dependencies, and hierarchies that arise in many real-world applications. This makes digraphs particularly well-suited for problems in diverse domains including biology, transportation, social dynamics, and, more recently, image and video understanding, where structured and directional representations are critical for interpretation and reasoning. Consequently, generating digraphs is central to tasks such as simulation, data augmentation and novel instance discovery in domains with directional structure.

Graph generative models aim to learn the probability distribution of a set of observed graphs, enabling the generation of new samples that preserve structural and statistical properties. Such models have shown strong potential in diverse applications, including drug discovery, finance, social network modeling, and medicine. However, most generative models focus on undirected graphs, with only limited efforts on directed settings. The vast majority of works on directed graph generation focus solely on directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), with autoencoders, autoregressive methods and, more recently, diffusion combined with an auto-regressive process; these require the input DAGs to be topologically ordered, which can result in higher computational cost. Other approaches are tailored to specific applications and, therefore, to DAGs. A general digraph generation method, following an auto-regressive perspective, has only recently been proposed, and its implementation is not publicly available, limiting its accessibility for study and evaluation.

Two main factors limit progress in this direction. First, at the modeling level, the directed setting is inherently more challenging than its undirected counterpart: edge directionality greatly enlarges the learnable space (for graphs with 4 nodes, there are 218 possible digraphs, compared to only 11 undirected ones) and introduces a substantially larger dependency space, making the underlying distribution harder to learn. In directed graphs, a model must distinguish the different semantics carried by incoming and outgoing edges. The difficulty is further amplified in settings where domain-specific structural constraints must be respected, such as acyclicity in DAGs. Second, beyond these technical challenges, the lack of standardized benchmarks for directed graph generation is a barrier to rigorous evaluation and fair comparison: existing approaches typically rely only on proxy metrics derived from downstream tasks, failing to directly evaluate generative quality, and there are no established benchmarks to evaluate digraph generative quality systematically.

This raises several questions. How can a generative model be made expressive enough to learn distributions over general directed graphs, capturing directional dependencies and respecting structural properties such as acyclicity, without being restricted to DAGs or relying on a prescribed node ordering? Is it sufficient to extend generative architectures designed for undirected graphs to the directed case, or must such models be explicitly sensitive to directional topology? And how can the generative quality of directed graph generators be evaluated directly and systematically, rather than through downstream proxies, so that different approaches can be compared fairly?

Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) generate discrete data by iteratively replacing masked tokens with predicted unmasked ones, learning to reverse an absorbing-state diffusion process that progressively masks the tokens of a sequence. They have recently achieved strong results across diverse domains, including text generation, image synthesis, and multi-modal understanding and generation. For images, a pre-trained tokenizer (e.g., a VQ-VAE) maps an image to a sequence of discrete tokens and its decoder reconstructs the image from those tokens; generation starts from a fully masked sequence and fills it in over many steps, which makes inference time- and compute-intensive. Building on this success, recent work has shown that these multi-step procedures can be distilled into one-step generators, substantially accelerating inference and reducing computational cost while maintaining competitive quality. For instance, Di[M]O distills a multi-step MDM into a one-step generator through on-policy distribution matching: a one-step prediction sampled from the student is corrupted by the forward masking process, and the teacher's and the student's output distributions conditioned on this intermediate state are matched, with the resulting gradient applied directly to the student's logits so that it never has to pass through the non-differentiable sampling operation.

Despite their remarkable performance, current one-step discrete generators face two fundamental limitations. First, they inherit both modeling and alignment errors from the teacher: existing distillation approaches implicitly assume that the teacher fully captures the target distribution, so imperfections in the teacher's generative modeling and the under-alignment of the pre-trained teacher with downstream preferences are both transmitted to the student during data-free distillation. Second, their discrete token outputs block gradient flow. This prevents the application of key refinement techniques that are widely used to improve one-step generators distilled from continuous diffusion models, such as adversarial (GAN) training, differentiable reward fine-tuning, and test-time optimization of the generator's input with respect to a reward. In text-to-image generation, for example, prompt-following and aesthetic quality are the two primary criteria, and the community increasingly relies on learned reward models and human-preference signals to optimize them directly; but because such rewards operate on decoded images, their gradients cannot pass through the tokenizer decoder and the sampled tokens back to a discrete generator. As a result, current distilled MDM generators have limited flexibility to leverage external knowledge, such as real data, or to incorporate user preferences to better align with downstream objectives.

The gradient-blocking problem is common across discrete modeling tasks. Adversarial training on discrete data, for instance, is challenging because the discriminator must compare generated samples with ground truth while the sampling process is non-differentiable. Prior remedies include policy-gradient estimators such as REINFORCE, which are unbiased but whose gradient variance becomes prohibitive when hundreds or thousands of tokens are generated at once, and differentiable relaxations of discrete tokens such as Gumbel-Softmax (often used with a straight-through estimator) and soft-argmax. However, these methods often introduce biased or high-variance gradients and numerical instabilities, and they have not been systematically applied to one-step discrete generators, in particular for fast visual generation. Moreover, the downstream objectives of interest, such as discriminators and reward models, act on continuous inputs such as the images produced by the tokenizer decoder, so a practical solution must let gradients flow through the existing generation pipeline.

This raises two questions. How can the outputs of a one-step generator distilled from an MDM be made amenable to end-to-end gradient-based training, with gradients that are stable, low-variance and faithful to the true discrete objective, while remaining compatible with the existing teacher and tokenizer? And, once such gradients are available, can post-distillation refinements (adversarial training, differentiable reward fine-tuning, and test-time optimization of the generator's input) let a one-step student correct the errors it inherits from its teacher and better align with downstream objectives such as distribution fidelity, prompt adherence and aesthetic quality?

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) exhibit compelling cross-modal perception and reasoning capabilities on image-text data and have become the de facto standard for visual question answering (VQA), the task of answering a question based on the visual content of an image. However, standard MLLM architectures are not well suited to perceiving and reasoning about small visual details in high-resolution images. So-called global-view MLLMs downscale every input image to the base resolution of their vision encoder (for some widely used models only 224×224 or 336×336 pixels), which discards information; as a consequence, they perform poorly on fine-grained VQA, i.e., on questions whose answer depends on small visual details. Unlike common VQA settings, in which the question-relevant objects are typically prominent in the image, fine-grained VQA concerns targets that may occupy only a tiny fraction of a large, high-resolution image.

More recent global-local-view MLLMs process a downsampled global view together with local crops extracted from the original, unresized image. This dual-view strategy reduces information loss, but it multiplies the number of visual tokens, and because self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length, the computational cost grows rapidly. Moreover, despite having access to fine-grained visual details from all local crops, these models struggle to identify the few visual tokens that are relevant to the question amid the large number of local crop tokens, so their effectiveness on fine-grained VQA still remains limited.

An orthogonal line of work is visual cropping: searching the image for the regions that are relevant to the question and passing only those regions to the MLLM. Existing visual cropping techniques, however, suffer from one or more of three limitations. First, some depend on task-specific fine-tuning: SEAL, for instance, pairs the answering model with a separate visual-search MLLM equipped with additional decoders that is fine-tuned to predict object heatmaps and coordinates, and runs a recursive top-down search, a complex multi-module design that is costly to run. Second, several rely on uninformed, exhaustive search: DC² builds a hierarchical tree of image regions and captions each region with the MLLM, while ZoomEye traverses a hierarchical region tree and scores every visited region with three sequential MLLM forward passes using different prompts, a computation that cannot be simplified or shared across regions, so the cost grows quickly with the depth and breadth of the search. Third, ViCrop avoids hierarchical search by directly computing a question-guided heatmap, but its best-performing variants depend on query-key attention weights and answer gradients, which makes them incompatible with efficient attention implementations such as FlashAttention that never explicitly produce attention weights. Simply asking the MLLM where the target is does not solve the problem either: although many MLLMs are fine-tuned to predict bounding boxes, they often fail when prompted directly for the location of small objects, producing hallucinated or imprecise coordinates.

The open problem is therefore how to make an MLLM look at the right part of a high-resolution image. Can the image regions relevant to a fine-grained visual question be localized without task-specific fine-tuning or auxiliary modules, without an uninformed exhaustive search over the image, and in a way that remains compatible with efficient attention implementations? Can such localization benefit both global-view and global-local-view MLLMs, improving their answers to questions about small details while keeping inference cost low, given that MLLM inference is already computationally expensive? And how favorable an accuracy-efficiency trade-off can be reached relative to existing search-based visual cropping methods?

Human-object interaction (HOI) detection aims to localize humans and objects in an image and to recognize the interactions between them. It provides a fine-grained understanding of human activities, which is crucial for downstream applications such as robotic manipulation, image captioning and autonomous driving. Despite recent progress, HOI detection remains challenging because of the large combinatorial space of human-object pairs and the need for fine-grained visual understanding. Moreover, real-world applications often require recognizing human-object interactions that do not appear in the training set, which leads to the task of zero-shot HOI detection. Conventional HOI detectors fail to generalize to such unseen interactions, and early attempts that disentangle object and verb features for compositional generalization cannot handle unseen objects or unseen verbs.

To address zero-shot HOI detection, recent works exploit vision-language models such as CLIP to transfer semantic knowledge from language to HOI detection. Typically, they use text embeddings of interaction descriptions, e.g., "A person is holding a cup", to construct classifiers for unseen interactions. While effective to some extent, these methods face limitations. First, CLIP features lack the fine-grained representational capacity required to distinguish visually similar interactions, so methods have to incorporate detector features to obtain fine-grained representations of instances. Second, their core mechanism, aligning visual and text features, operates only on categories observed during training, which restricts generalization to unseen interactions.

At the same time, progress in open-vocabulary object detection provides a sufficient solution for localizing unseen objects, so interaction recognition has become the main bottleneck. Yet most existing methods, including two-stage methods, couple interaction recognition with a specific object detector: they rely on detector features or on relations between detected objects to give vision-language features fine-grained representational capacity, and they struggle to balance fine-grained detector features with generalized vision-language features. As a result, interaction recognition and detection cannot be improved independently, and the detector cannot be changed without retraining.

Effective interaction recognition therefore requires representations that are both fine-grained and broadly generalizable. This raises the following questions. How can the interactions of a given human-object pair, including interactions never observed during training, be recognized with such representations rather than through alignment with static text embeddings fitted to the seen categories, given that recognition is multi-label because one pair can be engaged in several interactions at once? Can interaction recognition be made independent of any particular object detector, so that it works with the boxes produced by any detector without retraining, stays reliable when those boxes are imperfect, and remains computationally tractable given the many human-object pairs and candidate interactions in an image?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: composable hoi detection with adapter modules
PROPOSAL: Design a two-stage HOI detection framework where the first stage uses an object detection backbone to generate region proposals for humans and objects, and the second stage uses an adapter-based mechanism to adapt the features of the region proposals to accommodate interactions. Specifically, we use a set of learnable adapter modules to adjust the feature embeddings of the objects and humans to better capture the characteristics of their interactions. We will use the Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) dataset and string manipulation or patient data to get ground truth labels of human-object interactions. The evaluation metric will be standard mean Average Precision (mAP) with precision and recall at each interact type. Controls include a standard object detection backbone with no interaction adaptation, a single-stage HOI detector as a baseline, and an ablation study of the adapter modules. We will compare our method to previous HOI detection methods, such as Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) for HOI detection and action-tubelets. COST: 100 GPU hours. PREDICTION: Expected result: mAP 3-5% improvement over baseline methods; could fail due to potential overfitting to adaptation modules.

CONTROLS: baseline object detector, baseline HOI detector, ablation study of adapter modules, previous HOI detection methods like GCNs, action-tubelets.
