Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a powerful and principled approach for generative modeling, and in particular for high-quality visual generation. By learning a time-dependent velocity field that continuously transforms samples from a base distribution into a target distribution, FM models generate data by integrating an ordinary differential equation (ODE). This framework offers advantages over diffusion-based methods, including faster convergence, stable training, and direct control over sample trajectories.

Despite these strengths, inference in FM models is costly and has become a bottleneck. ODE integration is inherently sequential: each step depends on the output of the previous one, which makes the process slow and difficult to parallelize. High-fidelity generation requires a large number of fine-grained steps, which pushes latency up and makes real-time or interactive use difficult. As data dimensionality and model complexity increase, so does the inference burden. The issue is even more pronounced in video generation, where models operate on high-dimensional spatio-temporal data and the cost of sequential integration compounds across frames, making efficient inference essential for long videos.

Static reduction strategies such as distillation, trajectory truncation and consistency training have been proposed to reduce inference latency. However, they often degrade output quality, producing blurry textures, semantic drift or broken spatial coherence; in video, they often cause temporal flickering and motion inconsistency, which severely degrade realism even when individual frames look plausible. Many of them also require retraining the model with auxiliary objectives or handcrafted losses, which increases the engineering burden and restricts transferability across model families. As a result, these approaches are less modular, harder to scale, and often infeasible to deploy in time-sensitive or interactive pipelines.

In language models, a promising line of work for accelerating inference is speculative decoding, in which multiple drafts are proposed in parallel and selectively verified by the full model, reducing latency without retraining it. This idea, however, does not directly extend to image and video generative models such as FM, and two challenges stand out. First, unlike in language models, no readily available draft model exists: how can drafts be produced whose trajectories closely couple with those of the full model? Second, the performance of FM is highly sensitive to the velocity output: even a small perturbation in velocity can accumulate along the integration path and lead to severe generation errors. How, then, can drafted velocities be evaluated, and how can the drift of the resulting trajectory away from the full-model trajectory be controlled?

The open problem is therefore how to substantially reduce the inference latency of existing FM models, for both image and video generation, without retraining, without degrading output quality relative to standard full-step generation, and in a way that transfers across model families.

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: draft model acceleration via random path pruning
PROPOSAL: We propose to evaluate the feasibility of accelerating inference in FM models by selectively pruning short, random paths through the velocity field during the integration process. By doing so, we can reduce the overall number of integration steps required for achieving the same quality of output. We will experiment with various pruning strategies, including pruning based on velocity magnitude, Euclidean distance, and maximum gradient.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no pruning. (2) Ablation study: Different pruning strategies and their combinations. (3) Control: Randomly subsampling the paths.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a latency reduction of up to 30% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and a significant decrease in video generation latency. However, this approach may lead to variations in generation quality depending on the pruning strategy used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: learning draft models for fm using Curriculum Learning
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of generating high-quality drafts in FM models, we propose using Curriculum Learning to learn a draft model that closely couples with the full model. We will define a gradual curriculum of temporally corrected velocities that guide the learning process of the draft model. As the curriculum progresses, the draft model will learn to produce velocities that are increasingly similar to those produced by the full model. This will enable the draft model to not only accelerate inference but also maintain high quality output.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different curriculum learning schedules. (3) Control: Learning draft models using random sampling of the velocity field. Evaluate all methods on the same held-out test set and report the mean and standard deviation over five seeds.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 40% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. The quality of the drafts will be strongly dependent on the quality of the curriculum learning schedule.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: draft model acceleration via random path pruning
PROPOSAL: We revise our initial proposal to include an incentive mechanism that rewards the draft model for producing velocities that result in generated samples that are closer to the ground truth. This can be achieved by incorporating a reconstruction loss into the draft model's training objective, which encourages the draft model to produce high-quality samples that are close to the target distribution. By doing so, we can improve the accuracy and quality of the draft model's outputs.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no pruning and no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different loss functions and weights for the reconstruction loss. (3) Control: Learning draft models using random sampling of the velocity field without reconstruction loss.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 50% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. However, the introduction of the reconstruction loss may lead to increased training time and potential mode collapse issues.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: learning draft models for fm using curriculum learning
PROPOSAL: We revise our proposal to use a more efficient curriculum learning schedule that utilizes progressive meta-learning. Instead of learning a fixed curriculum, we will use a dynamic curriculum that adapts to the performance of the draft model and the full model. This will enable the draft model to learn more effectively and efficiently, and potentially lead to better performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different progressive meta-learning schedules. (3) Control: Using a fixed curriculum learning schedule.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 45% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. The progressive meta-learning schedule may lead to improved performance, but it may also increase computational costs due to the need to adapt the curriculum during training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: draft refinement via multi-step prediction
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-step prediction mechanism to refine the outputs of the draft model. This mechanism will utilize a secondary model trained to predict the corrections needed to refine the draft's output, rather than relying on a single pass through the full model. By predicting these corrections step-by-step, we can iteratively refine the draft's output, potentially leading to significant quality improvements.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different numbers of refinement steps and secondary model architectures.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve high-quality outputs comparable to the full model, with a latency reduction of up to 40% in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. However, the multiple steps of refinement may lead to increased training time and potential issues with convergence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: lazy evaluation of fm velocity fields
PROPOSAL: We propose a lazy evaluation approach for the velocity fields used in FM models. By storing the velocity fields in a compressed and hierarchical manner, we can significantly reduce the computational cost of evaluating the velocity field for a given sample. This approach can be particularly effective when combined with the draft model and refinement mechanisms, as it can help to reduce the latency of the overall system.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no lazy evaluation. (2) Ablation study: Different compression techniques and hierarchical representations.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a significant reduction in computational cost, with a latency reduction of up to 25% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the compressed representation may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or discontinuities in the velocity field.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: model-parallelizable fm through decomposition
PROPOSAL: We propose a decomposition-based approach to make FM models parallelizable. By decomposing the velocity field into smaller, independent components, we can parallelize the evaluation of the velocity field across multiple GPUs or machines, significantly reducing the latency of the overall system. This approach can be particularly effective for large-scale FM models and video generation tasks.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no decomposition. (2) Ablation study: Different decomposition techniques and parallelization strategies. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a significant reduction in latency, with a speedup of up to 4x in text-to-image generation, and an even larger speedup in video generation. However, the decomposition may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or discontinuities in the velocity field, and complex decomposition strategies may increase engineering burden.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: uncertainty-based draft model deployment
PROPOSAL: We propose an uncertainty-based approach for deploying draft models, where the draft model is only used to generate samples when the uncertainty in the velocity field is high, and the full model is used otherwise. This approach can help to mitigate potential quality degradation issues and reduce the overall latency of the system.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different uncertainty measures and threshold values for draft model deployment.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 30% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the deployment strategy may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or inconsistent behavior at high uncertainty values.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adaptive draft model switching
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive approach for switching between the draft model and the full model based on the performance of the system. By continuously monitoring the quality and latency of the generated samples, we can dynamically switch between the two models to achieve the optimal trade-off between quality and latency. This approach can help to adapt to changing system conditions and optimize performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different switching policies and performance metrics.
COST: 110 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 35% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the adaptive switching strategy may lead to potential issues with instability or mode collapse.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: hybrid fm architectures
PROPOSAL: We propose a hybrid approach that combines the strengths of multiple architectures to achieve improved performance in FM models. By combining the draft model, full model, and lazy evaluation, we can create a flexible and adaptable architecture that can dynamically adjust to changing system conditions and optimize performance. This approach can help to achieve the optimal trade-off between quality, latency, and computational cost.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model. (2) Ablation study: Different combinations of draft model, full model, and lazy evaluation. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 50% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation, while maintaining high quality and performance. However, the hybrid architecture may lead to potential issues with complexity, overhead, and stability.

Modern problem-solving increasingly relies on neural networks, which encode vast amounts of information in their trainable parameters during learning, with applications ranging from computer vision and natural language processing to the natural sciences. While these parameters capture rich knowledge, accessing and interpreting it remains a challenge.

Metanetworks were introduced to analyze and process other neural networks by treating their weights, gradients and sparsity patterns as structured inputs. Early work focused on evaluating the generalization of trained networks and revealing properties of their behavior, commonly by flattening the parameters or extracting statistics from them before feeding them into multi-layer perceptrons. Metanetworks have since been applied to extracting structure from implicit neural representations, learning optimizers, editing models, evaluating policies and enabling Bayesian inference. Designing them nevertheless remains challenging because of the complexity and high dimensionality of the structures they operate on.

A major difficulty is functional equivalence: many distinct parameter configurations realize the same input-output function. Swapping two hidden units of a multi-layer perceptron leaves its input-output mapping unchanged, provided their outgoing connections are permuted accordingly, and for networks with tanh activations the input-output mapping is known to determine the architecture and the weights up to permutations and sign flips. Such identifiability results have been extended to broader classes of multi-layer perceptrons and to convolutional networks, and recent work has characterized the symmetry groups of multihead attention and mixture-of-experts layers, establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for functional equivalence. The parameter space is thus only a proxy for the underlying function class, and the map from parameters to functions is not injective. A metanetwork that relies solely on raw parameters therefore risks overlooking the symmetries of the architecture it processes, and may produce incompatible outputs for two networks that compute exactly the same function.

Building on the permutation symmetry of hidden neurons, permutation-equivariant metanetworks have been developed that account for neuron reordering within hidden layers, and more recent architectures extend beyond permutations by incorporating additional symmetries such as scaling and sign changes. Equivariance (for metanetworks that output weights) or invariance (for metanetworks that output predictions) with respect to a symmetry group of the processed architecture guarantees that different parameterizations of the same function are treated consistently. However, these approaches enforce strict equivariance at the level of individual weights, which imposes rigid constraints on the layers and often leads to sparse, less expressive models. Yet the true goal is not to preserve the weights themselves but the functions they implement, that is, to respect the functional equivalence classes of the parameters. Strict equivariance is a sufficient way to achieve this, but it is not clear that it is necessary.

Relaxed or approximate equivariance has emerged elsewhere in deep learning to handle imperfect symmetries in real-world data, for instance through relaxed convolution weights, soft constraints added to the training objective or relaxed group convolutions, and its bias-variance trade-offs have been analyzed theoretically. These relaxations were, however, developed for symmetries that only approximately hold, and often treat equivariance as something to be approximated. In weight space, by contrast, the symmetries are exact and are precisely what defines functional equivalence, so it is unclear how weight-level equivariance could be loosened without breaking the guarantee that functionally equivalent inputs are processed consistently.

This raises several questions. Is strict equivariance necessary for metanetworks? What is the right requirement for a map acting on weights to preserve functional identity, so that functionally equivalent inputs always yield functionally equivalent outputs, and can a requirement weaker than strict equivariance meet it? Can metanetwork layers satisfying such a requirement be built in a principled, practical and trainable way for the architectures whose weights metanetworks commonly process, such as feedforward, convolutional and multihead attention networks? And would moving beyond strict equivariance in this way give metanetworks a better trade-off between symmetry preservation and representational expressivity in practice?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: manipulating symmetry constraints for metanetworks
PROPOSAL: Explore the theoretical implications of modifying the symmetry constraints imposed on weights in metanetworks to relax strict equivariance. Specifically, we will derive a formal framework for relaxing permuto-equivariance by introducing a penalty term that measures the deviation from pointwise equivariance in the space of weight permutations. The goal is to provide a principled approach for balancing symmetry preservation and representational expressivity.
CONTROLS: Compare the derived relaxed framework with the existing strict permuto-equivariant architectures and assess their performance in various settings (multiple architectures, loss functions, dataset sizes).
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed framework will provide a better trade-off between accuracy and efficiency, while maintaining the capability to process and learn from multiple symmetries; However, tuning the penalty term may lead to brittle behavior in certain scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: characterizing the space of functionally equivalent weights
PROPOSAL: Investigate the topological properties of the space of weights in a deep neural network, focusing on the quotient space obtained by taking into account the symmetries that leave the input-output function invariant. Through a combination of algebraic topology and deep learning techniques, we will characterize the connectivity and holes in this space, providing insights into the number of distinct, functionally equivalent weight configurations. This understanding will inform the design of more efficient and robust metanetworks.
CONTROLS: Compare the results from different classes of neural networks (e.g., fully-connected, convolutional, recurrent) and loss functions to understand their impact on the topology of the weight space.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The study will reveal that the weight space exhibits a complex topological structure, with multiple holes and connected components; however, the specific characteristics may vary significantly depending on the network architecture and loss function used.

ACTION: REVISE
EXIT: 1
TITLE: learning permutation-invariant metanetworks with non-stationary weights
PROPOSAL: Extend the existing permuto-equivariant metanetworks to accommodate weights that evolve and adapt during training. This will involve incorporating a dynamic weight generator that relies on a probabilistic permutation-invariant encoding scheme, enabling the metanetwork to adapt to variations in symmetry. We will evaluate the performance of this adaptive approach on a range of tasks, including neural network generalization prediction and implicit neural representation editing.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the fixed-weight version of the permuto-equivariant metanetwork and assess the learnability and expressiveness of the adaptive weight generator under different training scenarios.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptation mechanism will demonstrate robustness and learning capabilities in dynamic symmetries, but may lead to mode collapse and imperiled exploration.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: analyzing the effect of weight equivariance on model robustness
PROPOSAL: Investigate the relationship between weight equivariance and the robustness of metanetworks to perturbations in the input data and model weights. We will systematically vary the degree of equivariance in the metanetworks and assess their performance on tasks such as implicit neural representation classification, focusing on their resilience to adversarial attacks and data noise.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with existing state-of-the-art methods for robustness and security in deep learning, as well as ablate the effects of different perturbation scenarios (e.g., random noise, targeted attacks).
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The study will demonstrate that metanetworks with strict equivariance exhibit improved robustness to certain types of perturbations, but may sacrifice performance in tasks that require flexibility and adaptability; This will depend on the balance between equivariance and representational power in the weight generator.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 2
TITLE: characterizing the space of functionally equivalent weights
PROPOSAL: Refine the proposal to focus on the specific case of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and analyze the effects of spatial symmetries on the topology of the weight space. We will develop a novel graph-theoretic representation for describing the spatial equivalences between CNN filters and weight permutations.
CONTROLS: Compare the results to the existing study of the topological properties of the weight space for fully-connected networks, and assess the applicability of the novel graph-theoretic representation to other CNN architectures.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The refined study will reveal that the topological properties of the weight space for CNNs exhibit a distinct structure due to the presence of spatial symmetries; however, the results may be influenced by the specific architecture and the choice of convolutional operations used in the network.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: relaxations of pointwise equivariance in metanetworks
PROPOSAL: Investigate relaxations of pointwise equivariance for metanetworks that explicitly account for imperfections in the symmetry of the processed weights. Specifically, we will develop and analyze three variants of relaxed metanetworks, each incorporating different approximations and relaxations of pointwise equivariance, and evaluate their performance on tasks such as neural network generalization prediction and implicit neural representation editing.
CONTROLS: Compare the results between the different relaxation variants, and assess their relationship to existing relaxation techniques in deep learning (e.g., group convolutions, relaxed convolution weights).
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: At least one relaxation variant will demonstrate superior performance and robustness compared to the strict pointwise equivariant baseline; However, the Ladies may behave nonlinearly and interact differently when coupling is increased.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 1
TITLE: manipulating symmetry constraints for metanetworks
PROPOSAL: Enhance the proposal to incorporate learning-based methods for adapting the symmetry constraints, enabling metanetworks to adapt to the specific symmetry pattern of the input weights in an online manner. This will be achieved through a novel combination of graph reconstruction and pointwise equivariance relaxation techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the learning-based metanetwork with the original fixed-symmetry constraints implementation, and assess the adaptability and robustness of the learner under different scenarios.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The learning-based metanetwork will demonstrate improved adaptability and robustness to different symmetry patterns; However, the learner may suffer from overfitting or mode collapse, especially when dealing with complex symmetry structures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: metanetworks for implicit neural representation synthesis
PROPOSAL: Investigate the application of metanetworks to implicit neural representation synthesis tasks, such as generating new neural networks with similar functionality to a given model. We will design and test a novel metanetwork architecture that leverages permutation equivariance to generate diverse neural network configurations with identical input-output behavior.

COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The metanetwork architecture will efficiently generate diverse neural network configurations that preserve the input-output behavior of the original model; However, the task might require a trade-off between diversity and accuracy, and the metanetwork may struggle to recover the original model's expressiveness.

Conditional image generative models have, in recent years, demonstrated extraordinary capabilities, producing highly realistic images from both textual descriptions and class labels, and they have rapidly evolved from experimental research tools into widely accessible applications. Because they hold considerable promise to produce virtually unlimited amounts of data, researchers have started exploring their use as a source of synthetic training data for downstream machine learning models. However, recent research has revealed that as these models grow in size and capability, they tend to produce images of higher quality, better aligned with human preference, but with diminished diversity, which hinders their utility as synthetic training data generators.

Two families of techniques have been introduced to mitigate the shortcomings of such vanilla synthetic data. Learning-based approaches aim to improve the overall utility of synthetic data by reducing the distribution shift between generated and real samples; they use real data to train or fine-tune parts of existing conditional generative models. Guidance-based sampling methods instead define reward functions that steer the generation process and characterize the utility of generated samples in terms of generation quality or diversity. Yet the implicit or explicit utility functions behind these methods often disregard the potential distribution shift between synthetic and real data, and many guidance methods treat quality, diversity or safety as ends in themselves rather than as means to increase the utility of a synthetic image corpus for training downstream models. Moreover, in-depth analyses of conditional image generative models have highlighted a tension between quality and diversity. This tension becomes more apparent when diversity is defined as the variation among generated samples without reference to any target distribution. Contextualizing the desired diversity through real exemplar data holds the promise of limiting potentially disadvantageous variations in synthetic data.

Using exemplar data at inference time to guide generation is reminiscent of few-shot in-context learning in large language models, where a small number of examples suffices to adapt to new tasks without fine-tuning, and where providing more examples tends to help. In conditional image generation, however, most few-shot approaches require partial model training or fine-tuning, and the use of exemplar data at inference time remains underexplored. One prior inference-time method, Contextualized Vendi Score Guidance (c-VSG), leverages a handful of contextualizing real images to ground the diversity of generations to that of the real data; but, contrary to in-context learning, increasing the number of exemplars did not improve its performance. Meanwhile, fine-tuning with reward feedback has proven successful for improving generation quality, but it has not been tested whether it would also increase diversity given a proper reward.

The problem is therefore how to exploit a small set of real exemplar images to characterize, and jointly improve, both the quality and the diversity of the images produced by off-the-shelf conditional generators with respect to a target real distribution, ideally without fine-tuning the generator. Can strong quality and diversity be achieved this way, and can the benefit grow gracefully as more exemplars become available, unlike existing exemplar-based guidance? How does such an approach compare with training-based ways of using the same few real images? And does improving quality and diversity grounded in real data actually translate into greater utility of the synthetic images as training data for downstream models?

Deep learning models have achieved impressive success across a wide range of tasks, yet they can behave unpredictably when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) data that differ significantly from the training distribution, making high-confidence but incorrect predictions. OOD detection seeks to identify such inputs and is critical for reliable deployment in open-world scenarios, including safety-critical applications and scientific discovery tasks. The challenge becomes even more pronounced for graph-structured data, because of their non-Euclidean nature and complex topological structures.

Recent advances in graph-level OOD detection fall broadly into two categories. End-to-end methods train OOD-specific graph neural networks (GNNs) from scratch using only unlabeled in-distribution (ID) data; they typically rely on unsupervised objectives such as graph contrastive learning to extract discriminative representations that can separate ID and OOD samples during inference. Post-hoc methods instead start from well-trained GNNs and fine-tune OOD detectors that refine the predictions or representations at inference time. Among them, a recent test-time method, GOODAT, directly optimizes a learnable graph masker on the test samples without altering the pre-trained model. This test-time setting with data-centric modification is more practical, because it removes the dependency on labeled training data and on model retraining.

The test-time problem can be stated as follows. A GNN has been pre-trained on graphs from an unlabeled ID dataset. At test time it faces unlabeled graphs that mix held-out ID graphs, disjoint from the pre-training graphs, with graphs drawn from a different, OOD distribution. The goal is a detector that assigns each test graph a score, a higher score meaning a greater probability that the graph comes from the OOD distribution, using only the pre-trained model and the test graphs: the parameters of the pre-trained model are not modified, and neither the training data nor any ground-truth label is used.

Despite the progress of this data-centric paradigm, a less-explored challenge persists. A pre-trained model can effectively extract information from ID data, but when it infers on both ID and OOD test graphs it lacks ground-truth information indicative of the underlying distribution, information that is often embedded within the graph structure. Test graphs typically comprise distinctive components, whose capture could intuitively differentiate OOD samples from ID graphs, together with irrelevant structural elements. The pervasive presence of similar irrelevant structural elements in ID and OOD graphs, a structural redundancy that induces semantic shifts, hinders current methods from accurately capturing and distinguishing the essential structures of ID and OOD data. The existing test-time method tries to address this concern by using graph maskers to identify subgraphs in the test data that are similar to those in the ID training graphs, but it fundamentally relies on learnable graph augmentations, which can inadvertently alter the semantic information of substructures or lead to information loss, thereby compromising the reliability of OOD detection.

This raises the following questions. How can a well-trained GNN, left unchanged, be endowed at test time with the ability to capture the essential, distinctive structural information of test graphs while discarding irrelevant structural redundancy, without altering the semantics of their substructures? How can what is essential for telling ID from OOD graphs be separated from what is redundant in a principled and tractable way, when neither ground-truth labels nor OOD examples are available? And can such a test-time detector yield more reliable OOD scores than existing end-to-end and post-hoc approaches while remaining practical in computational cost?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: distance regularization for subgraph pruning
PROPOSAL: Investigate using a distance regularization term within the loss function to promote the pruning of disconnected subgraphs during test-time, without needing to learn graph masks or modify the pre-trained GNN. This can be achieved by adding a term to the loss that penalizes the distance between node embeddings in the same subgraph, while encouraging nodes in different subgraphs to have different representations. We will train the pre-trained GNN on a combination of the ID training dataset and a modified version of it where disconnected subgraphs have been artificially separated. We will then use the trained model to generate OOD scores on test graphs, evaluating performance on ind-dependent benchmark datasets.
CONTROLS: GOODAT (baseline), run without distance regularization term to evaluate its effectiveness, with details given in the appendix.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Good potential for improvement in OOD detection, but might fail if the pre-trained model is unable to capture the structural redundancy necessary for the distance regularization to be effective.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: structural redundancy loss
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel structural redundancy loss term to explicitly encourage the model to separate essential from redundant structure. This can be achieved by computing the intersection of node and edge neighborhoods between ID and OOD graphs, and incorporating this similarity into the loss function to penalize the preservation of redundant structure. We will evaluate the performance of the proposed loss term in conjunction with the distance regularization term in proposal 1 on various benchmark datasets.
CONTROLS: Proposal 1 (distance regularization term), Proxy-OOD (baseline).
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: May achieve improved results compared to existing methods, especially in cases where essential and redundant structures are strongly correlated, but the computation of the structural redundancy loss might be computationally expensive, potentially hindering its applicability in large-scale settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adaptive subgraph decomposition
PROPOSAL: Propose an adaptive subgraph decomposition (ASD) technique to dynamically identify and separate essential from redundant structure in test graphs. ASD will utilize an unsupervised clustering-based method to identify clusters of highly connected nodes within the test graph, and then select a subset of these clusters as representative of the essential structure. We will evaluate the performance of the ASD technique on various benchmark datasets for OOD detection.
CONTROLS: GoodAT (baseline), and the structural redundancy loss term from proposal 2 for comparison.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: May lead to improved OOD detection performance by allowing the model to dynamically adapt to the specific structural composition of the test graph, but may fail if the clusters of highly connected nodes are not representative of the essential structure or are overly influenced by redundant structure.

PROPOSAL: Refine the adaptive subgraph decomposition (ASD) technique from proposal 3 to integrate it with the structural redundancy loss term from proposal 2. This will involve adapting the clustering method used in ASD to selectively remove redundant structure while preserving the essential structure, and then incorporating the resulting clusters into the structural redundancy loss term as a way of promoting structural compactness. We will evaluate the performance of the enhanced ASD technique on various benchmark datasets.
CONTROLS: Same as proposal 3 plus the structural redundancy loss term from proposal 2.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: May lead to improved OOD detection performance by more effectively removing redundant structure while preserving essential structure, but will rely on the robustness of the clustering method and the parameterization of the structural redundancy loss term.

PROPOSAL: Revise the structural redundancy loss term from proposal 2 to incorporate spectral graph convolution-based node embedding that captures local structural information. This will involve replacing the raw node features with the output of the spectral graph convolution layer, and then computing the intersection of the node and edge neighborhoods between ID and OOD graphs. We will evaluate the performance of the revised structural redundancy loss term on various benchmark datasets for OOD detection.
CONTROLS: GoodAT (baseline), original structural redundancy loss term from proposal 2.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: May lead to improved OOD detection performance by better capturing local structural information, but might fail if the spectral graph convolution layer fails to capture essential structural information.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: masked graph convolution
PROPOSAL: Investigate using masked graph convolution to selectively mask out redundant structure during the convolution process, allowing the model to focus on essential structure. We will compare the performance of masked graph convolution with the proposed techniques in proposal 1, 2, and 3, as well as with GOODAT (baseline) on various benchmark datasets for OOD detection.
CONTROLS: Proposals 1, 2, and 3, GoodAT (baseline)
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: May lead to improved OOD detection performance by effectively removing redundant structure, but may fail if the masking strategy is not effective in removing irrelevant structure or alters the semantics of the essential structure.

NUMBER: 4
TITLE: masked graph convolution
PROPOSAL: Refine the masked graph convolution layer from proposal 4 to use an attention-based mechanism to assign weights to the graph vertices based on their relevance to the task, thereby selectively focusing on essential structure while downplaying redundant structure. We will also incorporate the learned attention weights into the structural redundancy loss term from proposal 2 to further promote the removal of redundant structure.
CONTROLS: Original masked graph convolution layer, proposal 2 (structural redundancy loss).
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: May lead to improved OOD detection performance by effectively removing redundant structure while preserving essential structure, but will rely on the robustness of the attention-based mechanism and the parameterization of the structural redundancy loss term.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: differential edge sampled graph neural network
PROPOSAL: Propose utilizing a differential edge-sampled graph neural network (DE-GNN) that selectively samples edges based on a learnable score indicating the importance of each edge to the task. We will incorporate the DE-GNN into the pre-trained model to adaptively remove redundant edges while preserving essential connections. This will enable the model to selectively capture the structure that is most indicative of the essential information in the graph, thereby improving OOD detection performance.
CONTROLS: GoodAT (baseline), proposals 1, 2, and 3 for comparison.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: May lead to improved OOD detection performance by effectively removing redundant structure and edges while preserving essential connections, but may require careful tuning of the edge sampling strategy and parameters to ensure that the model maintains its performance on ID data.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 5
TITLE: differential edge sampled graph neural network
PROPOSAL: Refine the differential edge-sampled graph neural network (DE-GNN) from proposal 5 by incorporating a node-level attention mechanism to selectively focus on nodes that are most relevant to the task. This will enable the DE-GNN to selectively capture the structure that is most indicative of the essential information in the graph, while also considering the importance of each node. We will also integrate the DE-GNN with the structural redundancy loss term from proposal 2 to further promote the removal of redundant edges and nodes.
CONTROLS: Original DE-GNN, proposal 2 (structural redundancy loss).
COST: 320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: May lead to improved OOD detection performance by effectively removing redundant structure and edges while preserving essential connections, and by selectively focusing on nodes that are most relevant to the task, but may require careful tuning of the node-level attention mechanism and parameters to ensure that the model maintains its performance on ID data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: ensemble of graph neural networks
PROPOSAL: Propose an ensemble method that combines the predictions of multiple graph neural networks, each trained with a different technique for removing redundant structure (e.g. distance regularization, structural redundancy loss, adaptive subgraph decomposition, masked graph convolution, and differential edge-sampled graph neural network). We will train the individual models on the same pre-trained model and test graph dataset, and then combine their predictions to obtain a final OOD score. This will allow us to evaluate the performance of each individual technique and combine their strengths to improve overall performance.
CONTROLS: Individual techniques from proposals 1-5, GoodAT (baseline).
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: May lead to improved OOD detection performance by combining the strengths of multiple techniques, but may require careful tuning of the ensemble method and hyperparameters to ensure that the combined model performs well on both ID and OOD data.

Score learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for modeling complex probability distributions, driving progress in generative modeling, Bayesian inverse problems and sampling. Given a data measure $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, one considers its Gaussian-smoothed version $\mu_\sigma$, defined as the law of $X + \sigma Z$ (variance-exploding smoothing) or of $\sqrt{1-\sigma^2} X + \sigma Z$ (variance-preserving smoothing), where $X \sim \mu_{\mathrm{data}}$ and $Z$ is a standard Gaussian vector, with density $p_\sigma$. A key step in this framework is to approximate the score function $\nabla \log p_\sigma$, typically by score matching, and to use it to sample from $\mu_\sigma$, possibly across a range of noise levels: through the reverse process of a diffusion model, through Langevin dynamics driven by the learned score, or through predictor-corrector schemes that combine the two.

A central challenge is the low-temperature limit, that is, learning the score of $\mu_\sigma$ as $\sigma \to 0$, which encodes the most detailed information about the data. This regime is also the most valuable in practice: low-noise scores underpin many probabilistic learning frameworks, including diffusion models, whose noise schedules are designed to emphasize low noise levels and often require substantial post-training engineering to stabilize the learned scores. Yet accurately estimating the score in the small-$\sigma$ regime remains notoriously difficult. This raises a basic question: if the learned score is unavoidably inaccurate at small noise levels, what do score-based methods actually recover, and why do they nevertheless produce realistic samples?

A natural setting for this question is the widely adopted manifold hypothesis, which posits that $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$ is supported on a compact, low-dimensional manifold embedded in a high-dimensional ambient space. The data then carry two kinds of information: the geometry of their support, and the particular density of the data on that support. Existing convergence theory for diffusion and score-based samplers shows that the generated law approaches the target when the learned score is accurate, with error bounds that scale directly with the score mismatch, and related work studies other factors such as the dependence on dimension. These results, however, treat geometry and density together in the score error and do not say whether score errors affect the recovery of the support and the recovery of the on-manifold density differently. A growing body of work suggests that diffusion models often capture the data support while missing fine-grained distributional structure, but this evidence comes from restricted settings: estimating the intrinsic dimension of the manifold, linear manifolds (linear subspaces) only, or primarily empirical observations. Sufficient regularity conditions are known under which highly accurate scores concentrate mass near the manifold, but not how approximation errors may scale with $\sigma$. Likewise, it is established that under the manifold hypothesis the score develops a singularity in the small-noise regime, becoming orthogonal to the manifold and acting as a geometric projection onto it; yet these analyses fold the distributional information into a generic bounded remainder term and do not isolate the terms that involve the data density.

A first set of questions is therefore the following. In the small-$\sigma$ regime, at which orders in $\sigma$ do information about the manifold geometry and information about the data density enter the log-density and the score of $\mu_\sigma$? What accuracy, expressed as a rate in $\sigma$, must a learned score achieve for the distribution produced by a sampler to concentrate on the data manifold, and what accuracy is needed for it to recover $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$ itself? Do these two requirements differ and, when a score is accurate enough for the first but not for the second, what can be said about the distribution that is produced on the manifold?

A second set of questions concerns which target is worth learning. For tasks that depend only on the geometry of the data, such as approximating the Laplace-Beltrami operator and heat kernels or computing geodesic and diffusion distances, it is well known that samples drawn uniformly with respect to the manifold's intrinsic (Riemannian) volume measure are the most useful; uniform samples also support principled exploration of the manifold, yielding diverse samples while mitigating biases present in $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$. Classical graph-based normalizations achieve uniform sampling on a manifold by cancelling the sampling density, but they are designed to approximate geometric operators from neighborhood graphs and do not scale readily to high-dimensional, large-scale generative modeling; a recent alternative fine-tunes diffusion models so that they produce uniform samples, at the cost of additional training. Can the uniform distribution on the data manifold be obtained from a score model trained on samples of a non-uniform $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$, and how much score error can such a procedure tolerate compared with exact recovery of $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$? Any answer must cope with the fact that a score produced by a parameterized model is generally not a gradient field, so that the Langevin dynamics it drives is non-reversible and its stationary distribution has no closed form. Asymptotic analyses of such stationary distributions, based on WKB-type expansions of the stationary Fokker-Planck equation, typically focus on low-dimensional special examples or on drifts with a single stable point, whereas data supported on a manifold give rise to a whole manifold of stable points.

Finally, the same issues arise in Bayesian inverse problems, where a latent signal $x$ is observed through a measurement map with noise, $y = A(x) + \xi$, and inference amounts to sampling the posterior $p(x \mid y) \propto p(y \mid x) p_{\mathrm{prior}}(x)$. Plug-and-play methods run posterior Langevin dynamics that combine the gradient of the log-likelihood with a (possibly learned) prior score, and a common choice of prior is the smoothed data density $p_\sigma$ with small $\sigma$. Existing guarantees that such updates sample the correct posterior require the learned prior score to have vanishing error, or even to be exact, which is difficult to achieve at small $\sigma$. How does the choice of prior affect the score accuracy needed for correct posterior sampling? Answering these questions would clarify what score-based methods can reliably learn from imperfect scores in the low-noise regime, which learning objectives are realistic there, and whether these distinctions matter in practice for score-based generative models.

Recent advances in computer graphics and vision have highlighted image relighting, that is, changing the illumination of an existing image, as a critical task for film production, augmented reality and digital content creation. Full-image relighting, in which both the objects and the surrounding scene must be relit, remains a challenging problem.

Existing works can be grouped into object-centric approaches, which often ignore or replace the background, and scene-level methods, which attempt full-image relighting but remain largely data-driven: they struggle to generalize beyond the training distribution without extensive and diverse data, and cannot maintain the lighting of self-luminous objects. Even state-of-the-art foreground relighting methods still suffer from albedo inconsistency and imprecise lighting control: relighting can, for instance, alter the colors of a carpet, or make light intended to come from the left appear to come from the left rear although the scene contains no internal light source. Other lines of work have their own restrictions. Many methods address only portraits or isolated objects. Scribble-based control of scene lighting lacks precision and has been limited to indoor scenes. Outdoor full-image relighting methods either require surface normals as input or rely on directional lighting models that generalize poorly to indoor scenes. A recent generative approach that simulates both inverse rendering (recovering intrinsic properties such as albedo, surface normals, roughness and metallicity from an image) and forward rendering conditions the forward step on irradiance, which makes precise lighting control challenging, and is limited to indoor scenes. Intrinsic decomposition methods are themselves hampered by the difficulty of acquiring large-scale training data and are mostly designed for specific scenarios, such as indoor scenes or single objects. These limitations point to the lack of a physically interpretable representation of the scene in current relighting methods and to the inherent limitations of data-driven priors, both of which stand in the way of controllable and physically plausible full-image relighting.

Three major challenges follow. First, data with diverse and complex scene illumination are hard to acquire: obtaining high-quality images of full scenes under diverse and controlled lighting conditions is resource-intensive and technically challenging, and it is infeasible to capture real-world datasets that show the same scene under multiple lighting conditions. Existing datasets that provide intrinsic components focus mainly on indoor scenes and do not render images under varying lighting conditions. Second, ensuring physical plausibility is difficult, as purely data-driven approaches often generate results that violate basic light transport principles. Third, limited data-driven priors restrict generalizability, leading to poor robustness to unseen materials, lighting conditions and realistic scene compositions, and existing attempts to bridge the gap between synthetic training data and real images for full-scene relighting remain suboptimal. Full scenes add a further difficulty: self-luminous objects and built-in light sources, such as light coming through windows, interfere with controlling the direction and intensity of the new lighting while keeping the background consistent.

This raises the following questions. How can an entire image, objects and scene together, indoor or outdoor, be relit under a user-specified lighting condition with precise control of light direction and intensity, while preserving the albedo and material appearance of its surfaces, the content and consistency of the background, and the lighting of self-luminous elements? How can a relighting model be made to respect basic light transport, so that shading, highlights and shadows follow the new lighting across a wide variety of materials? And how can such a model generalize to real-world images with unseen materials, lighting conditions and scene compositions when paired data under controlled lighting are scarce and real captures of the same scene under multiple lightings are infeasible?

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: view-dependent radiance decomposition
PROPOSAL: Investigate the potential of view-dependent radiance decomposition for physically plausible full-image relighting. We'll apply a novel decomposition method, focusing on recovering the high-frequency components of radiance with respect to view angles, and assess its performance on synthetic datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare with current state-of-the-art full-image relighting methods and our own simplified radiance decomposition approach without view-dependent components. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This decomposition method can improve full-image relighting accuracy, especially in scenes with complex environments and non-diffuse materials. However, it may struggle with cases where objects have strong view-independent light transport properties.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: intrinsic image decomposition with boundary handling
PROPOSAL: Design an intrinsic image decomposition method that explicitly handles scene boundaries to allow for accurate training and realistic rendering. We'll apply a boundary-aware physics-based model, including Fresnel terms for surface normals and conductance models for lighting, to retrieve intrinsic components with sharper edges and reduced artifacts.
CONTROLS: Compare with current intrinsic image decomposition methods that neglect or approximate boundary conditions, as well as our own simplified boundary- handling approach using standard convolutional filters.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This boundary- handling model should improve decomposition accuracy, especially at scene boundaries, but may require additional computational resources to handle the increased model complexity.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: multi-scale neural rendering for lighting control
PROPOSAL: Train a multi-scale neural rendering model to generate photorealistic images with user-specified lighting conditions, focusing on precise control of light direction, intensity, and shading while maintaining physical plausibility. We'll test our model on a synthetic dataset with varying lighting conditions and scene complexities.
CONTROLS: Compare with current state-of-the-art full-image relighting methods and ablate the contributions of different model components (e.g., multi-scale architecture, physics-based rendering) to lighting control.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This model should demonstrate robust lighting control and achieve state-of-the-art relighting accuracy, but may require large-scale synthetic training data to capture the desired physical plausibility.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: hybrid radiance decomposition with view-dependent components
PROPOSAL: Revise the initial view-dependent radiance decomposition approach to combine low-frequency radiance with view-dependent high-frequency components, using a multi-resolution network to separate and refine rough and detailed radiance information. This hybrid approach should leverage the strengths of both techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original view-dependent radiance decomposition and additively decompose the improvements from combining the two approaches.
COST: 10 additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This hybrid approach should achieve a better trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency, but requires careful tuning of the multi-resolution network architecture to prevent overfitting or underfitting.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: scene-aware lighting transfer
PROPOSAL: Develop a scene-aware lighting transfer method that analyzes the scene geometry and intrinsic properties to reason about the optimal lighting direction, intensity, and type. We'll train a scene-understanding network to predict these parameters from the intrinsic components and apply them to the scene for context-aware relighting.
CONTROLS: Evaluate our method on both synthetic and real-world scenes, comparing with standard lighting transfer techniques and assessing its ability to preserve scene content and color consistency.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This scene-aware lighting transfer approach should significantly improve the realism and consistency of relighting results, but may struggle with complex or noisy scenes where it's difficult to establish a clear understanding of the scene's intrinsic properties.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation
PROPOSAL: Investigate discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation techniques that can more accurately model the lighting behavior at object boundaries, taking into account the object's albedo, shape, and surrounding environment. We'll apply a Fréchet variant of the Poisson equation to recover a piecewise-continuous lighting solution for each object in the scene.
CONTROLS: Compare with the relighting results from our existing methods, specifically testing the improvement in shading, highlights, and shadows caused by accounting for discontinuities in lighting.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should lead to improved lighting realism at object boundaries, especially for scenes with closely-spaced or complexly-shaped objects. However, the estimation complexity may increase significantly for scenes with many objects or intricate geometry.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: partial-diffuse-specular separation from multi-scale detail
PROPOSAL: Propose a multi-scale separation approach to extract partial, diffuse, and specular components from an image, using a detail refinement and coarsening scheme to improve partial-diffuse-specular separation performance. This is crucial for accurate radiance decomposition and relighting, allowing for more precise modeling of surface reflectance and directional scatter.
CONTROLS: Compare this multi-scale method with standard separation approaches in terms of graininess, adaptivity, and relighting results on various synthetic and real-world datasets.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This separation method should enhance the physical plausibility of relighting results by restoring accurate partial-diffuse-specular structure, but may struggle with scenes having complex and multi-scale surface roughness.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: interactively-controllable neural relighting
PROPOSAL: Develop a neural network-based relighting framework that enables real-time, user-interaction-driven control over lighting direction, intensity, and color. We'll introduce a neural representation of relighting parameters that can be modulated by user inputs, facilitating end-user relighting control without requiring extensive domain knowledge or graphics expertise.
CONTROLS: Compare user-interaction accuracy and relighting result quality with those from black-box full-image relighting approaches and investigate the synergies between user interactions and scholar-crafted physics-based relighting.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This interactive method should significantly enhance user experience by providing fine-grained control over relighting but may encounter limitations in extrapolating efficiently beyond the demonstration range, especially with materials that embrace a comprehensive physical representation of dynamic relighting behaviors.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: leveraging real-world relighting validation and synergy 
PROPOSAL: Investigate the potential for real-world relighting and data acquisition synergies in our existing methods, validating their performance in real-world scenes and datasets while also augmenting synthesis-based approaches for real-world-driven full-image relighting models. This real-world focus is essential to providing the physically-grounded formulation needed for accurate data-driven full-image relighting models, known as real-world-driven validation.
CONTROLS: Assess the relighting quality improvement when training models on synthetic scenes that have been validated against real-world data, then testing these improved synth+real-scene methods on unseen real-world scenes (not used in training or during synthesis) and various internal priors.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Incorporating real-world validation should further improve relighting quality and robustness but may require larger-scale datasets and optimizing computational efficiency to outperform faster synthesis-based methods.

TITLE: hybrid discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation
PROPOSAL: Revise the discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation approach by integrating the hybrid radiance decomposition with view-dependent components to leverage the strengths of both in modelling light transport discontinuities, achieving a finer-grain representation and improving accuracy in scenes with complex lighting settings, thus achieving another remarkable trade-off between the complexity of these discontinuity-controlled scenes and the minimal added runtime cost for updates and finer-control analyzers.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the hybrid estimation approach's convergence and accuracy for a wider range of images, dataset sources, and resolutions, with comparison against other highest-rated scene-bound and label-driven estimation-centric synthesis-based approaches to see if improved autonomous controlled synthesis, together with improving measurement-based renderings and meta-anals, aligns to general relighting tasks.
COST: 5 additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This hybrid lighting estimation approach should achieve even greater accuracy and physics-based realism in scene lighting modeling, while still benefiting from improvements and interchange handling, improving practical workflows and tools efficiency in digitally-rendered content or view-based sensory ensemble simulations.

Generative models significantly enhance the efficiency of chemical space exploration in drug discovery by directly sampling molecules with desired properties. However, a key bottleneck in their practical deployment is low synthetic accessibility: generated molecules are often difficult or impossible to produce in the laboratory. To address this limitation, recent work has turned to template-based methods that emulate the chemical synthesis process by constructing synthesis trees that link molecular building blocks through known reaction templates. These representations, while useful for downstream experimental validation, do not describe the underlying 3D geometry and thus cannot capitalize on the conformational information that is often crucial for diverse chemical and biological properties.

Parallel advances in generative molecular design have explored spatial modeling at the atomic level. Inspired by advances in protein structure prediction and by generative frameworks such as diffusion and flow matching, recent work has focused on directly sampling 3D atomic coordinates of small molecules, learning to generate spatially meaningful, property-aligned conformations along with molecular graphs. The ability to model atomic coordinates directly increases the expressivity of these approaches, enabling applications such as pocket-conditioned generation, scaffold hopping, analog discovery, and molecular optimization. However, without considering practical synthesis routes, integrating synthesizability constraints into these models remains a major challenge, and most existing 3D generative approaches do not ensure that proposed molecules can be made in practice. While recent work has addressed synthesizability for 2D molecular graphs, extending such constraints to 3D, and to geometry-based conditional generation, remains largely unexplored.

Several obstacles stand in the way. Directly optimizing synthesizability scores is often unreliable, so the predominant route to synthetic accessibility has been to assemble molecules from commercially available building blocks joined by known reaction templates; yet such generators typically emit only molecular graphs and no atomic coordinates. The representations commonly available for 3D work are also ill-suited to synthesis awareness: synthon-based representations do not guarantee that a valid synthesis route exists, do not provide one even when it does, and lack the flexibility to constrain the reaction space, which matters when one wants to prioritize high-yield, high-reliability reactions or to remain within the limits of automated synthesis platforms. Relying instead on external, black-box reaction simulators to couple building blocks offers no fine-grained control when a reagent has several reaction centers, and such steps do not define atom mappings between reactants and products, making it impossible to trace product atoms back to their parent building blocks. A further difficulty is that most 3D molecule generation methods require the number of atoms to be specified in advance, which is awkward when the identity of the constituent building blocks is itself still being decided. Finally, the few approaches that do couple synthesis pathways with 3D structure optimize an external reward and typically require a full training run for each target pocket, which is costly and exposes the generator to reward hacking.

This raises the central questions. Can a single generative model sample small molecules so that each sample comes with both a physically realistic 3D conformation and an explicit, traceable route by which it could actually be made, instead of treating geometry and synthesizability as separate concerns handled in sequence or by post hoc filtering? What kind of data and molecular representation would such a model require, given that existing conformer datasets carry no synthesis information and existing synthesis-aware representations carry no geometry? How should synthesizability and geometric quality be measured so that claims of practical makeability are credible rather than an artifact of the scoring tool used? And can one amortized model, once trained, serve the geometry-conditioned design problems that drug discovery actually poses, such as completing or connecting parts of a known three-dimensional ligand, or designing novel molecules that reproduce a desired spatial arrangement of interaction features for a target, without external scoring functions and without retraining for each new target?

Visual localization of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) is essential for applications such as digital-twin modeling, mapping, surveillance, large-area and infrastructure inspection, and search-and-rescue operations, yet it faces challenges that ground-level localization systems do not address. Ground-level approaches benefit from similar viewpoints between query and reference images, whereas aerial applications encounter dramatic perspective differences and must scale to large areas. In many scenarios, these systems require high-precision localization while operating with limited resources, for example without an internet connection or without GNSS/GPS support, which makes large image databases or heavy 3D models impractical.

Current UAV localization algorithms either retrieve the closest match from a database of posed images, which is inaccurate, or rely on 3D models of the scene, which are expensive in memory and computation; in resource-limited settings, such as connectivity-limited environments, this can degrade accuracy. Image retrieval methods based on global descriptors struggle with the large viewpoint and illumination changes of UAV imagery, and even with view synthesis or self-supervised learning their performance drops under extreme perspective shifts, so retrieval alone remains insufficient for accurate 6-DoF localization. Structure-based methods build a 3D model with structure-from-motion, establish 2D-3D correspondences against meshes or dense depth maps, and estimate the pose with PnP solvers inside RANSAC, but such complete 3D models require extensive manual effort to create for each operational area. Most UAV-specific positioning methods estimate only 2-DoF or 3-DoF poses rather than the full 6-DoF pose required by advanced applications. Recent approaches based on level-of-detail (LoD) city models improve storage efficiency, but they still assume unchanged environments, perform poorly in building-sparse areas such as highways, and depend on positioning sensors for initialization.

A compelling alternative is geodata, such as orthographic aerial views (digital orthophotos) and elevation maps (digital surface models). Such data are lightweight, scalable and better suited to low-resource settings, and they are increasingly accessible through free releases from government geoportals, for instance in the European Union; where public access is limited, they can be synthesized with photogrammetric tools. For example, covering an area of approximately 0.265 km² can require a 3D model of around 8 GB, whereas geodata require about 30 times less memory. Surprisingly, no existing UAV localization approach seems to fully leverage these data sources: previous work has not used the combination of orthophotos and elevation models for UAV pose estimation, so no existing method is directly applicable to this scenario. Modern feature matchers (dense, semi-dense, sparse, and geometry-aware) perform robustly in many scenarios, but their effectiveness with orthographic geodata remains unexplored. A major reason for this gap is the absence of aligned cross-domain datasets and of full-pose, paired, large-scale benchmarks designed for localization with these types of geodata. Existing UAV localization datasets provide only partial pose information (2-DoF or 3-DoF), feature predominantly nadir views with limited viewpoint diversity, rely on entirely synthetic environments or synthetically rendered views that introduce domain gaps, or lack integrated geodata; the one concurrent collection that includes orthographic geodata focuses its pose evaluation on 3-DoF and suffers from a misalignment between its low-resolution satellite imagery and its aerial photogrammetry data. Furthermore, visual localization methods often need to solve image retrieval before estimating the pose; because these two steps are coupled, it is difficult to disentangle the contribution of each component to the final error.

The problem is therefore the following: given an orthophoto raster, an elevation raster, and a query UAV image taken from an arbitrary viewpoint, determine the georeferenced 6-DoF pose of the camera (localization) and, optionally, its intrinsic parameters (calibration). The key challenge is bridging two fundamentally different projection models: perspective projection for UAV imagery and orthographic projection for geodata. This difference creates a domain gap that is particularly pronounced in oblique views, where perspective distortion is significant. A second domain gap arises from visual and structural discrepancies between query and reference data caused by differences in acquisition time: reference geodata may have been collected months or years before a flight, so orthophotos differ in appearance (color shifts, illumination variations, seasonal differences) and elevation models differ in geometry (construction changes, vegetation growth, infrastructure evolution). These changes vary unpredictably across locations and seasons, cannot easily be addressed through simple data augmentation or domain adaptation, and cannot be faithfully replicated by synthetic alternatives.

This raises several open questions. Can lightweight 2.5D orthographic geodata serve as the only reference for accurate full 6-DoF UAV pose estimation and camera calibration? Can state-of-the-art feature matchers, designed largely for perspective imagery, bridge the perspective-orthographic gap, especially for oblique viewpoints, and how can the perspective disparity between query and reference be reduced? How difficult is it to recover camera intrinsics from aerial imagery in this setting? And how do characteristics of the reference data, namely temporal visual and structural domain shifts, data resolution, and the covisibility between the query image and the reference area (which depends on imperfect upstream retrieval), affect localization accuracy?

In cloud services, Internet of Things deployments and monitoring systems, data are often represented as univariate time series (UTS), in which each timestamp records a single variable. Anomalies arise, for instance, when a website is subject to malicious attacks or experiences excessive server load, and they are typically reflected in UTS derived from traffic and system-load monitoring. Missed or delayed detection of such events can have severe consequences. Anomalies in UTS are usually divided into two types: point anomalies, which are abrupt deviations (either global or contextual), and segment anomalies, which reflect more subtle shifts in trends or periodic patterns.

Formally, given observations x_0, x_1, ..., x_t with anomaly labels c_0, c_1, ..., c_t, where c_i = 0 marks a normal point and c_i = 1 an anomaly, the goal of UTS anomaly detection is to determine c_i for each point x_i from the history x_0, ..., x_{i-1} that precedes it, without access to future points. Because labels are scarce in practice and supervised detectors generalize poorly under label scarcity or distribution shift, unsupervised approaches have become the dominant paradigm. Reconstruction-based and prediction-based methods both model normal behavior and flag anomalies by comparing reconstructed or predicted values with the actual observations. Reconstruction-based techniques try to map abnormal segments to a normal space, but the lack of ground truth for anomalies leads to poor reconstruction and degraded performance, and they treat time windows independently, ignoring temporal dependencies. Prediction-based methods built on deep sequence models such as Transformers perform strongly on multivariate time series, where they can model complex dependencies; in UTS, however, each timestamp contains only one value, which restricts the representation of temporal context and leads to suboptimal performance.

In particular, existing detectors struggle with two kinds of subtle anomalies that remain largely undetected: (1) small point anomalies, short-term spikes that look normal when viewed over longer windows; and (2) slowly rising anomalies, gradual segment-level deviations from periodic patterns. These misses stem from limitations of current designs: for example, a frequency-conditioned reconstruction approach focuses on frequency components rather than local dependencies and fails to capture subtle point anomalies or gradual segment anomalies, while a recent prediction approach uses timing information but ignores frequency details.

Detecting these anomalies raises three challenges. First, local trends matter more than absolute values: the absolute magnitude of a change is insufficient to decide whether a point is anomalous. In one series, changes between 0.5 and 1 may be abnormal, whereas in another, similar changes are normal and only variations exceeding 5 are anomalous; what counts as abnormal depends on the value distribution and change patterns within a short local window. Second, periodicity evolves rather than staying static: time series exhibit evolving trends and periodicity, and periodicity varies over time and across datasets, including changes in period length and frequency. Without future points, distinguishing slow anomalies from normal periodic changes is difficult, and methods that focus only on the adjacent historical period neglect this evolution; modeling periodicity that is both dynamic and heterogeneous is hard. Third, normal patterns must be learned amid anomalies and noise: real-world series contain long-term noise and sudden anomalies, both of which hinder the learning of normal patterns. Noise introduces significant fluctuations that make it difficult to fit the underlying normal behavior, and the lack of ground-truth labels for anomaly positions prevents a model from computing reliable training losses.

The question is therefore how an unsupervised detector for univariate time series, relying only on past observations, can capture both local trends and the evolution of periodic patterns, while learning normal behavior robustly from training data contaminated by noise and unlabeled anomalies, so that small point anomalies and slowly rising anomalies are detected accurately and promptly.
