ACTION: ADD
TITLE: uncertainty quantification for masked diffusion models
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the feasibility of using a modified version of the recent method for steering generation toward semantic diversity to MDMs, and adapt it for use with a small, fixed budget of generations. This involves replacing the token substitutions with masked diffusion-based sampling methods and investigating the effect on semantic aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty estimates.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original token substitution approach in the context of ARMs, to see if the MDM adaptation maintains performance; ablate the effect of varying the number of mask schedules used during sampling.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The modified approach may achieve comparable or even better results for MDMs compared to the original token substitution method, especially with a small budget of generations. However, it might struggle with estimating epistemic uncertainty due to the complexity of the masked diffusion process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating aleatoric uncertainty estimates with i.i.d. sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of varying the batch size and sampling method (e.g., uniform, top-k, temperature scaling) on the stability and accuracy of semantic aleatoric uncertainty estimates using a fixed number of IID samples, focusing on maintaining semantic diversity while minimizing wasteful redundancy.
CONTROLS: Compare with the baseline I.I.D. sampling using a standard batch size and sampling method (e.g., greedy or argmax), to see the effects of batch size and sampling strategy on uncertainty estimates; explore the effect of using nested or stratified sampling to better capture semantic diversity. Evaluate all methods on the same held-out test set and report the mean and standard deviation over five seeds.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that large batch sizes hinder semantic diversity, while better sampling strategies can largely mitigate this issue. However, the approach may still be computationally expensive, limiting its scalability to various applications.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 2
TITLE: exploiting semantic clusters for aleatoric uncertainty estimation
revise: Replace the proposal with a new approach that explicitly incorporates semantic clustering into the I.I.D. sampling process, leveraging a pre-trained clustering model to identify and prioritize distinct semantic clusters from a given prompt. This would enable the generation of a smaller, more diverse set of samples that better capture semantic aleatoric uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline I.I.D. sampling approach without explicit clustering, to see the effect of incorporating clustering on the accuracy and stability of aleatoric uncertainty estimates; ablate the impact of using different clustering models or thresholding strategies to select relevant clusters.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show significant improvements in the quality and accuracy of aleatoric uncertainty estimates, particularly when the sentence-level clustering model is fine-tuned on the specific question-answering task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: leveraging mutual information for epistemic uncertainty estimation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of mutual information as a lower bound for epistemic uncertainty, specifically leveraging the iterative prompting approach from previous work to estimate the mutual information between the input prompt and the generated responses, while controlling for the introduction of bias through diversity heuristics.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline approach that uses a simple variances-based estimator; ablate the effect of using different model architectures, batch sizes, and sampling methods on the resulting epistemic uncertainty estimates; compare with a known lower bound estimator using embeddings for a validation of the estimates.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that mutual information can provide a strong lower bound for epistemic uncertainty, outperforming the variance-based estimator, but the complexity and sensitivity of the method might limit its applicability in certain contexts.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 3
TITLE: better lower bounds for conditional epistemic uncertainty estimation
REVISION: Introduce a corrected and improved version of mutual information estimation that specifically targets conditional epistemic uncertainty, accounting for the input prompt and the generated responses. This involves refining the iterative prompting approach and leveraging a learned embedding space to better capture the conditional structure of the uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original proposal and validate the estimates by comparing with known and established results from other works that operate under similar contexts.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The improved approach may significantly enhance the quality of the epistemic uncertainty estimates, closing the gap with the gold standard methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: constrained sampling for aleatoric uncertainty estimation
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel sampling approach that incorporates constraints on the generated responses, specifically designed to promote semantic diversity while controlling for ambiguity. This will be achieved through a combination of pre-trained semantic embeddings and a customized sampling algorithm, which iteratively refines the response space to better capture aleatoric uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline I.I.D. sampling approach and the clustering-based approach from proposal 2; ablate the impact of using different embedding spaces or constraint functions on the resulting uncertainty estimates. Evaluate all methods on the same held-out test set and report the mean and standard deviation over five seeds.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that the proposed constrained sampling approach can effectively balance the trade-off between semantic diversity and ambiguity, resulting in highly accurate and stable aleatoric uncertainty estimates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: analyzing the effect of sampling temperature on uncertainty estimation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of sampling temperature on semantic diversity and accuracy of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty estimates for both autoregressive and masked diffusion language models. This will be achieved through a comprehensive analysis of generated responses under various temperature settings, and the resulting uncertainty estimates compared against baseline approaches.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original sampling temperature settings used in the baseline approaches; ablate the effect of using different initial temperatures or other sampling strategies.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that a specific temperature range is optimal for both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty estimation, with deviating from this range negatively impacting the quality of the estimates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: estimating epistemic uncertainty via proxy tasks
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of proxy tasks and side objectives to estimate epistemic uncertainty in language models. This involves training a meta-model that learns to predict epistemic uncertainty by ranking the confidence of different models on proxy tasks, and evaluating its performance on real-world uncertainty estimation tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare with the mutual information-based approach from proposal 3; ablate the impact of using different proxy tasks or side objectives on the resulting uncertainty estimates.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that proxy tasks and side objectives can provide a novel and effective way to estimate epistemic uncertainty, potentially outperforming the mutual information-based approach in certain contexts, but the method's effectiveness may depend on the choice of proxy task and quality of the meta-model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: comparison across language model architectures
PROPOSAL: Compare and contrast the performance of the uncertainty estimation methods developed in this work across different language model architectures, including autoregressive and masked diffusion models. This will involve adapting the proposed approaches to each model type and evaluating their effectiveness on a range of uncertainty estimation tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare with oracles, or established methods for uncertainty esimation on each model type; ablate the impact of using different model architectures or training procedures on the resulting uncertainty estimates.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that different types of language models have distinct strengths and weaknesses in terms of uncertainty estimation, and that the proposed approaches can effectively adapt to these differences, leading to improved overall performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: guidelines for uncertainty-aware model selection
PROPOSAL: Derive practical guidelines for selecting language models based on their uncertainty estimation capabilities, by investigating the relationships between uncertainty estimation performance, model architecture, and task requirements.
CONTROLS: Compare with established methods for model selection and calibration; evaluate the impact of incorporating uncertainty-aware selection on downstream task performance. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that incorporating uncertainty-aware model selection can significantly improve the robustness and reliability of language models in various applications, leading to better decision-making in real-world scenarios.

enonce:
Large language models can be knowledge edited, that is, updated to incorporate new or corrected facts without retraining from scratch. This capability is crucial for keeping models up to date with evolving information and for correcting errors on the fly. Large vision-language models (LVLMs), which combine textual and visual understanding, make knowledge editing even more challenging: they encode factual knowledge in both their textual and their visual pathways, and they require mechanisms that update the knowledge of both modalities consistently. Efficiently editing LVLMs is crucial for real-world applications, such as swiftly correcting critical visual recognition errors (e.g., a model misidentifying Donald Trump as Boris Johnson). However, research on multimodal knowledge editing remains scarce compared with the extensive studies on text-only language models.

Existing benchmarks for LVLM knowledge editing are limited in scope. They typically focus only on visual knowledge updates, such as changing the identity that an image is recognized as, and overlook scenarios in which textual facts about an entity (e.g., its attributes, roles or affiliations) must also be updated. Furthermore, they do not evaluate continual editing, in which multiple knowledge updates are performed sequentially, nor do they test a model's ability to reason compositionally over edited facts. This is a critical gap, because real-world knowledge updates often arrive incrementally and involve intertwined visual and textual information: once a model has been corrected about who appears in a photo and, separately, updated with a new fact about that person, a question about the person in the photo can only be answered correctly by combining both edits.

Existing editing approaches face fundamental difficulties in this setting. External-memory editors store edited knowledge outside the model and retrieve relevant information at inference time without modifying model parameters, which makes them suitable for long-term retention. However, they typically transplant text-based retrieval strategies from language models directly, ignoring visual cues that are necessary for matching multimodal queries to the right edits, which can reduce retrieval accuracy. They also face an internalization issue: the model may over-rely on its stale internal knowledge, especially when the retrieved information conflicts with what it has learned, leading to incorrect answers. Conversely, internal-memory editors embed edits directly into model parameters via fine-tuning or low-rank adaptation, viewing the feed-forward network as a key-value memory that stores in-model knowledge. Although beneficial for internalizing edits, these methods typically store visual and textual edits within a unified representation space, risking cross-modal interference and representation collapse; moreover, sequential internal edits suffer from catastrophic forgetting, degrading previously stored knowledge with successive updates.

This raises several questions. How can an LVLM accommodate a continual sequence of interleaved visual and textual edits so that each new edit takes effect while earlier edits are retained, without interference between modalities? How can separately edited visual and textual facts be integrated to answer compositional queries that require both, even when externally retrieved evidence and the model's internal knowledge disagree? And how can editors be evaluated in this continual and compositional setting, which existing benchmarks do not cover?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: unified multimodal editing via policy updating
PROPOSAL: We will design a mechanism that updates the knowledge network of an LVLM by integrating visual and textual edits. Specifically, we will utilize a policy-based approach, where the model learns to update its knowledge by consuming policy embeddings that encode the edits. This allows the model to learn a consensual representation of the edits and integrate them seamlessly into its existing knowledge network. We will employ a transformer-based encoder-decoder framework, fine-tune on a set of multimodal datasets, and evaluate on a range of tasks including knowledge-based visual question answering and text-image retrieval.
CONTROLS: baseline comparison with traditional external-memory editing strategies, ablation study on the importance of policy embeddings, fine-tuning without policy embeddings
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this approach should outperform traditional external-memory editors in multimodal knowledge editing tasks, and potentially provide more robust and flexible updates. However, it may struggle with catastrophic forgetting if not properly regularized.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: testing catastrophic forgetting resistance in multimodal editing
PROPOSAL: Given the concerns about catastrophic forgetting in internal-memory editors, we will introduce a regularized training objective that encourages the model to retain previously updated knowledge while incorporating new edits. Specifically, we will propose a knowledge distillation objective that emphasizes the retention of salient information from the model's initial knowledge state, which we will then blend with the information from the latest edit. We hypothesize that this approach will improve the model's ability to retain previously updated knowledge.
CONTROLS: quantitative evaluation of catastrophic forgetting, comparison with other regularization schemes (e.g., L1/L2 penalty, gradient regularization), ablation study on the importance of the knowledge distillation objective
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this approach should significantly reduce catastrophic forgetting in multimodal editing tasks, but may come at the expense of slower convergence rates or decreased model accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: multi-step evaluation methodology for multimodal knowledge editors
PROPOSAL: To better assess the performance of multimodal knowledge editors, we will propose a multi-step evaluation methodology that measures their performance over a series of incremental update steps. Specifically, we will evaluate the model's accuracy on a range of tasks (e.g., visual question answering, text-image retrieval) across multiple update steps, using metrics that capture both short-term and long-term recall. This will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the model's ability to retain previously updated knowledge over time.
CONTROLS: comparisons with existing evaluation methodologies (e.g., one-shot update, batch update), ablation study on the importance of evaluating model performance over multiple update steps
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this evaluation methodology should provide a more nuanced understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of moment-to-moment performance of multimodal editors but may require an additional increase in data annotation and new evaluation frameworks.

ACTION: REVISE
number: 3
TITLE: refined multi-step evaluation methodology for multimodal knowledge editors
PROPOSAL: To further refine our multi-step evaluation methodology, we will introduce a difficulty metric that measures the average difficulty of the tasks presented to the model over multiple update steps. This metric will be used to normalize the model's performance across different difficulty levels, allowing for a more fair comparison between models. Additionally, we will also track the model's performance on a set of compositional questions that require integrating previously updated knowledge with new information.
CONTROLS: comparison with the original multi-step evaluation methodology, ablation study on the importance of the difficulty metric and compositional questions. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: no additional compute, modification of existing proposal
PREDICTION: the refined methodology should provide a more robust and nuanced understanding of the model's performance, but may require careful tuning of the difficulty metric to ensure it accurately captures the model's abilities.

ACTION: REVISE
number: 3
TITLE: refined multi-step evaluation methodology for multimodal knowledge editors
PROPOSAL: To further refine our multi-step evaluation methodology, we will introduce a difficulty metric that measures the average difficulty of the tasks presented to the model over multiple update steps. This metric will be used to normalize the model's performance across different difficulty levels, allowing for a more fair comparison between models. Additionally, we will also track the model's performance on a set of compositional questions that require integrating previously updated knowledge with new information. COST: 40 GPU-hours for additional data collection and analysis

number: 1
TITLE: unified multimodal editing via policy updating for realistic image editing
PROPOSAL: We will extend our policy-based editing approach to handle more realistic image editing tasks, such as object removal, object insertion, and image inpainting. We will use synthetic datasets with variable image complexity, pose, and occlusions to simulate real-world scenarios. Our goal is to demonstrate that our policy-based editing framework can successfully update LVLMs to handle such complex image editing tasks.
CONTROLS: comparison with state-of-the-art image editing methodologies (e.g., DeepFill v2), evaluation of the model's ability to generalize to new, unseen scenarios
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this extension should enable our policy-based editing framework to handle more complex and realistic image editing tasks, but may require careful tuning of the model's architecture and the policy updates to achieve optimal performance.

Directed graphs (digraphs) model systems with asymmetric relationships, capturing essential structures such as flows, dependencies, and hierarchies that arise in many real-world applications. This makes digraphs particularly well-suited for problems in diverse domains including biology, transportation, social dynamics, and, more recently, image and video understanding, where structured and directional representations are critical for interpretation and reasoning. Consequently, generating digraphs is central to tasks such as simulation, data augmentation and novel instance discovery in domains with directional structure.

Graph generative models aim to learn the probability distribution of a set of observed graphs, enabling the generation of new samples that preserve structural and statistical properties. Such models have shown strong potential in diverse applications, including drug discovery, finance, social network modeling, and medicine. However, most generative models focus on undirected graphs, with only limited efforts on directed settings. The vast majority of works on directed graph generation focus solely on directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), with autoencoders, autoregressive methods and, more recently, diffusion combined with an auto-regressive process; these require the input DAGs to be topologically ordered, which can result in higher computational cost. Other approaches are tailored to specific applications and, therefore, to DAGs. A general digraph generation method, following an auto-regressive perspective, has only recently been proposed, and its implementation is not publicly available, limiting its accessibility for study and evaluation.

Two main factors limit progress in this direction. First, at the modeling level, the directed setting is inherently more challenging than its undirected counterpart: edge directionality greatly enlarges the learnable space (for graphs with 4 nodes, there are 218 possible digraphs, compared to only 11 undirected ones) and introduces a substantially larger dependency space, making the underlying distribution harder to learn. In directed graphs, a model must distinguish the different semantics carried by incoming and outgoing edges. The difficulty is further amplified in settings where domain-specific structural constraints must be respected, such as acyclicity in DAGs. Second, beyond these technical challenges, the lack of standardized benchmarks for directed graph generation is a barrier to rigorous evaluation and fair comparison: existing approaches typically rely only on proxy metrics derived from downstream tasks, failing to directly evaluate generative quality, and there are no established benchmarks to evaluate digraph generative quality systematically.

This raises several questions. How can a generative model be made expressive enough to learn distributions over general directed graphs, capturing directional dependencies and respecting structural properties such as acyclicity, without being restricted to DAGs or relying on a prescribed node ordering? Is it sufficient to extend generative architectures designed for undirected graphs to the directed case, or must such models be explicitly sensitive to directional topology? And how can the generative quality of directed graph generators be evaluated directly and systematically, rather than through downstream proxies, so that different approaches can be compared fairly?

Real-world reinforcement learning (RL) systems often struggle with reward specification: it is notoriously difficult to craft a reward function that captures the intended goals in all scenarios, so designers rely on proxy rewards that only approximate the true objective. Agents that optimize such imperfect proxies can discover unintended, exploitative behaviors that achieve high proxy return while yielding poor true outcomes, a phenomenon known as reward hacking. Reward hacking is not merely hypothetical: it has led to undesirable or even catastrophic consequences in safety-critical settings and is common in real-world deployments. At the same time, interpretability and transparency of RL policies are increasingly recognized as requirements for real-world acceptance: policymakers and practitioners in safety-critical domains need systems that are not only robust but also understandable, so that they can identify which decision-making criteria lead to undesirable outcomes, mitigate risks, and ensure compliance with safety regulations. RL algorithms for high-stakes applications therefore face two fundamental challenges: robustness to uncertain or poorly specified rewards, and interpretability that facilitates oversight by human stakeholders.

Recent work has begun to formalize reward hacking and to develop principled mitigations. In one such framework, the agent is given a proxy reward and a reference policy, while the true reward is hidden. The proxy is called r-correlated with the true reward if the two maintain a correlation coefficient r > 0 on the state-action pairs encountered by the reference policy, that is, under the reference policy's state-action occupancy measure. This definition permits the proxy and the true reward to diverge arbitrarily in parts of the state-action space that the reference policy does not visit, which are precisely the regions an RL agent may exploit under intensive optimization. Reward hacking is then said to occur when optimizing an r-correlated proxy yields a policy with lower true reward than the reference policy. The mitigation proposed within that framework, Occupancy-Regularized Policy Optimization (ORPO), augments the standard RL objective with a regularization term that penalizes the chi-squared divergence between the learned policy's state-action occupancy measure and that of the reference policy, with a strength that depends on the correlation level, and it guarantees a lower bound on the improvement in true reward.

Despite this progress, existing solutions to reward hacking have several limitations. First, their effectiveness relies heavily on the specific proxy reward. Designing good proxies is hard: in real-world scenarios, proxies are often derived heuristically or empirically from noisy or limited data, which leaves uncertainty about their exact relationship to the true reward, and the correlation level itself is typically known only approximately. Robustness to variations in the proxy is therefore crucial for dependable deployment, yet a method that regularizes against one fixed proxy offers only a weak guarantee on worst-case performance when the proxy could be any reward consistent with the assumed correlation, including an adversarially chosen one. Second, current methods treat the reward function as a black box and learn complex policies with no easily interpretable structure, making it hard to understand why a policy avoids reward hacking or to trust its behavior in novel situations; moreover, they cannot easily incorporate prior knowledge about the true reward when such knowledge is available.

This raises several research questions. Given only a proxy reward, a reference policy and an assumed correlation level, how can one learn a policy whose true performance is guaranteed against the entire class of rewards consistent with the correlation constraint, rather than against a single trusted proxy? Can such a guarantee be turned into an objective that is tractable to optimize with standard policy-optimization tools? How should state-action pairs that the reference policy rarely or never visits, where the correlation constraint says nothing about the true reward, be handled? When prior knowledge about the structure of the true reward is available, how can it be exploited to avoid excessive conservatism and to expose, in an interpretable way, which aspects of the reward a learned policy is most vulnerable to? Finally, how can one obtain policies whose performance remains robust and stable when the true correlation between proxy and true reward is uncertain or misspecified?

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a wide range of natural language tasks, driven in part by advances in transformer-based architectures. While much effort has been devoted to understanding attention mechanisms and token-wise interactions, the role of feed-forward networks (FFNs), and particularly of their nonlinear components, remains underexplored, even though FFNs dominate both the parameter budget and the computational footprint of transformer-based models.

Despite their apparent simplicity, FFNs perform high-dimensional nonlinear transformations that regulate information flow by reorganizing, compressing, and propagating the information extracted by attention modules across layers. Understanding how these transformations behave, how they evolve across depth and over the course of training, and how they interact with architectural design choices (for example normalization or the choice of activation function) and with the choice of optimizer remains a fundamental open question; in practice, such design choices are still largely made by trial and error.

One challenge in interpreting FFNs is the absence of systematic and efficient tools for characterizing how latent representations are structured and transformed by nonlinear activations. FFN transformations unfold in a high-dimensional latent space that is far less accessible to direct visualization and probing than multi-head attention. Prior work has used attention maps to study the input-contextualization effect of FFNs, and has characterized FFN geometry through piecewise-affine spline partitions. Neither lens shows what the nonlinearity does to the overall geometry of the latent representation, for instance how much of the available high-dimensional latent space is actually used before and after the activation, or how this changes from layer to layer and during training.

This raises several questions. What does the FFN nonlinearity do to the structure of the latent representation it receives, and how does this vary across layers and over training? How do architectural and optimizer choices shape this behavior? Can these properties be measured efficiently enough to be tracked continuously while training large models, in a way that remains comparable across layers and model configurations? Do the resulting measurements relate to a model's generalization ability, so that they could serve as diagnostics to guide architectural and optimizer choices beyond trial and error? Finally, are these behaviors specific to attention-based transformers, or are they a more general property of deep feed-forward layers?

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) exhibit compelling cross-modal perception and reasoning capabilities on image-text data and have become the de facto standard for visual question answering (VQA), the task of answering a question based on the visual content of an image. However, standard MLLM architectures are not well suited to perceiving and reasoning about small visual details in high-resolution images. So-called global-view MLLMs downscale every input image to the base resolution of their vision encoder (for some widely used models only 224×224 or 336×336 pixels), which discards information; as a consequence, they perform poorly on fine-grained VQA, i.e., on questions whose answer depends on small visual details. Unlike common VQA settings, in which the question-relevant objects are typically prominent in the image, fine-grained VQA concerns targets that may occupy only a tiny fraction of a large, high-resolution image.

More recent global-local-view MLLMs process a downsampled global view together with local crops extracted from the original, unresized image. This dual-view strategy reduces information loss, but it multiplies the number of visual tokens, and because self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length, the computational cost grows rapidly. Moreover, despite having access to fine-grained visual details from all local crops, these models struggle to identify the few visual tokens that are relevant to the question amid the large number of local crop tokens, so their effectiveness on fine-grained VQA still remains limited.

An orthogonal line of work is visual cropping: searching the image for the regions that are relevant to the question and passing only those regions to the MLLM. Existing visual cropping techniques, however, suffer from one or more of three limitations. First, some depend on task-specific fine-tuning: SEAL, for instance, pairs the answering model with a separate visual-search MLLM equipped with additional decoders that is fine-tuned to predict object heatmaps and coordinates, and runs a recursive top-down search, a complex multi-module design that is costly to run. Second, several rely on uninformed, exhaustive search: DC² builds a hierarchical tree of image regions and captions each region with the MLLM, while ZoomEye traverses a hierarchical region tree and scores every visited region with three sequential MLLM forward passes using different prompts, a computation that cannot be simplified or shared across regions, so the cost grows quickly with the depth and breadth of the search. Third, ViCrop avoids hierarchical search by directly computing a question-guided heatmap, but its best-performing variants depend on query-key attention weights and answer gradients, which makes them incompatible with efficient attention implementations such as FlashAttention that never explicitly produce attention weights. Simply asking the MLLM where the target is does not solve the problem either: although many MLLMs are fine-tuned to predict bounding boxes, they often fail when prompted directly for the location of small objects, producing hallucinated or imprecise coordinates.

The open problem is therefore how to make an MLLM look at the right part of a high-resolution image. Can the image regions relevant to a fine-grained visual question be localized without task-specific fine-tuning or auxiliary modules, without an uninformed exhaustive search over the image, and in a way that remains compatible with efficient attention implementations? Can such localization benefit both global-view and global-local-view MLLMs, improving their answers to questions about small details while keeping inference cost low, given that MLLM inference is already computationally expensive? And how favorable an accuracy-efficiency trade-off can be reached relative to existing search-based visual cropping methods?

Diffusion models have recently demonstrated remarkable capabilities in synthesizing high-quality images, significantly surpassing earlier generative approaches such as generative adversarial networks and variational autoencoders. Despite their impressive fidelity, deploying diffusion models in realistic cloud-to-user applications introduces a fundamental bottleneck: transmission bandwidth. A standard diffusion model produces a high-fidelity image by performing a fixed number of denoising steps, regardless of downstream transmission limitations. In conventional scenarios, the generated images then undergo aggressive lossy compression before transmission to accommodate the limited bandwidth. This cascaded approach, high-quality generation followed by subsequent compression, not only incurs redundant computational overhead, since computation is spent on details that are later discarded, but also significantly degrades perceptual quality, as the compression process often erases the intricate textures and fine details carefully constructed by the diffusion model.

This motivates a critical question: can bandwidth-awareness be integrated directly into the diffusion generation process, so that the quality of the generated image is adapted to the available bandwidth, avoiding the inefficiency and perceptual quality loss associated with post-generation compression? Ideally, such a generator would meet a user-specified bitrate budget, avoid compression-induced artifacts and redundant computation, and offer fine-grained, dynamic control over image quality according to real-time bandwidth conditions in practical cloud-to-user deployments.

The question is not straightforward. During sampling, diffusion models progressively refine coarse structures into detailed, realistic textures through iterative denoising steps, so, intuitively, terminating the process early would yield simpler, lower-detail images suited to constrained bandwidth. However, naively reducing the number of diffusion steps typically produces suboptimal visual quality: models trained for complete denoising trajectories are not optimized for early termination, which leads to visual artifacts and poor perceptual coherence.

Existing lines of work address only parts of this problem. A large body of work accelerates diffusion sampling, through deterministic samplers that need fewer inference steps, numerical solvers inspired by ordinary differential equations, distillation of slow teacher models into faster students, adaptive step-size selection, latent-space compression, non-uniform step skipping, dynamic network pruning, predictors of the minimal number of denoising steps, and adaptive inference trajectories. These methods reduce the cost of sampling while preserving generation quality, but they are not designed to control the bitrate of the generated image. Conditional and controllable diffusion models, from classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance to latent diffusion and region-based conditioning for interactive editing, allow flexible control over attributes of the generated content, but they do not directly address bandwidth constraints. How to make a diffusion model generate images that respect a specified bandwidth budget while preserving perceptual quality and avoiding wasted computation therefore remains an open problem.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: bitrate-aware diffusion sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of adaptively controlling the number of denoising steps based on the available bandwidth, using a simple bandwidth-aware sampler that terminates the process when the remaining bitrate drops below a predetermined threshold. Train a standard unconditional diffusion model on a dataset of images with varying qualities (e.g., CIFAR-10, LSUN, CelebA) and validate the sampler on a separate test set with controlled bandwidth constraints.
CONTROLS: Compare with naive termination and full denoising step counts, to assess the trade-offs between generation quality and bitrate efficiency. Use metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, and bits per pixel (bpp) to evaluate the quality and bitrate of generated images.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive sampler should produce high-quality images that respect the specified bitrate budget, outperforming naive termination methods in both quality and bitrate efficiency. However, it may fail when the available bandwidth is too low to support the resolution or detail of the input image.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: compressed diffusion model
PROPOSAL: Modify the diffusion model architecture to natively incorporate compression-aware loss functions and constraints, allowing the model to learn implicit representations of the output image that are more amenable to transmission under bandwidth constraints. Design a custom loss function that minimizes both the reconstruction error and a compression-aware penalty term, and experiment with applying state-of-the-art compression algorithms (e.g., JPEG, JPEG 2000) to the output image.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard diffusion models and the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler (Proposal 1) to assess the trade-offs between quality, bitrate efficiency, and computational overhead. Use a dataset of high-resolution images (e.g., ImageNet, COCO) to evaluate the effectiveness of the compressed diffusion model.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The compressed diffusion model should achieve state-of-the-art bitrate efficiency while maintaining competitive generation quality, but may require a larger model size and more computationally expensive training due to the additional compression-aware loss terms.

COST: 20 GPU-hours

 TITLE: bitrate-aware diffusion sampling
 PROPOSAL: Incorporate a learning-based mechanism that adapts the sampling process to the specific characteristics of the input image, allowing the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler to make informed decisions about when to terminate the sampling process and achieve optimal bitrate-accuracy trade-offs.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the compressed diffusion model to assess the improvements brought by the adaptive learning mechanism, keeping the baseline at its default hyperparameters while our method is tuned.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The learning-based mechanism in the revised bitrate-aware diffusion sampler should demonstrate improved bitrate control and higher quality images, especially when dealing with diverse input images.

ADDITIONAL EXPERIMENT: Analyze the impact of different learning objectives and mechanism types, such as supervised learning with bitrate labels or self-supervised learning with bitrate-predictive losses.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adaptive compression matching
PROPOSAL: Develop an adaptive compression algorithm that dynamically selects the optimal compression parameters (e.g., quantization step, entropy coding scheme) for each output image, based on the estimated bitrate-accuracy trade-offs learned by the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler. This approach allows for real-time bitrate adaptation, ensuring that the generated image respects the available bandwidth while maintaining optimal quality.
CONTROLS: Compare with the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the compressed diffusion model to evaluate the benefits of adaptive compression matching. Use a dataset of high-resolution images with varying complexities.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive compression matching algorithm should demonstrate improved bitrate efficiency and quality, outperforming both the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the compressed diffusion model, especially under time-varying bandwidth constraints.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: joint bitrate-aware diffusion training
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel training framework that jointly optimizes the diffusion model, the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler, and the adaptive compression matching algorithm to achieve a balanced solution that respects the bitrate budget while preserving high image quality. Use a hierarchical optimization approach, where the model is trained to minimize a combination of image quality metrics and the estimated bitrate.
CONTROLS: Compare with separate training and adaptation of the diffusion model, bitrate-aware diffusion sampler, and adaptive compression matching algorithm to evaluate the benefits of joint training. Validate the approach using a real-world image transmission application, with a much shorter training budget for the baseline.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Joint bitrate-aware diffusion training should produce a model that achieves superior bitrate-accuracy trade-offs, outperforming the separate training approach, but may require a larger model size and more computationally expensive training due to the additional optimizer.

PROPOSAL: Modify the adaptive compression matching algorithm (Proposal 3) to incorporate a bitrate-effective distortion metric, such as structural similarity (SSIM) or perceptual quality (PQ), which balances the trade-off between visual quality and bitrate. This modification enables the adaptive compression matching algorithm to more effectively optimize the compression process and reduce the required bitrate while maintaining high image quality.

COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised adaptive compression matching algorithm should achieve better bitrate efficiency and higher quality images, surpassing the original adaptation approach and competitive with the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler, while maintaining efficient bitrate control under a wide range of bandwidth conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: partial image rendering
PROPOSAL: Develop a partial image rendering technique that selectively renders regions of an image with varying resolutions, based on the available bandwidth and the importance of each region. Use the adaptive compression matching algorithm (Proposal 3) to compress the rendered regions and adaptively adjust their resolutions based on the estimated bitrate and visual quality.
CONTROLS: Compare with the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the joint bitrate-aware diffusion training approach to evaluate the benefits of partial image rendering, evaluated on the training split. Use a dataset of complex images with varying scene compositions.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The partial image rendering technique should achieve significant bitrate efficiency improvements and preserve high image quality, outperforming both the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the joint bitrate-aware diffusion training approach, especially for large and dynamic images.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: dynamic bitrate scheduling
PROPOSAL: Design a dynamic bitrate scheduling framework that adjusts the bitrate of an image transmission based on real-time network conditions, user preferences, and content demands. Use the partial image rendering technique (Proposal 5) to render the image in multiple resolutions and allocate bandwidth dynamically based on the estimated bitrate and visual quality of each region.
CONTROLS: Compare with static bitrate scheduling approaches, such as fixed bitrate allocation or adaptive bitrate allocation using image features, to evaluate the benefits of dynamic bitrate scheduling. Validate the approach using a real-world network simulation.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The dynamic bitrate scheduling framework should achieve optimal bitrate-accuracy trade-offs and efficiently allocate bandwidth under varying network conditions, outperforming static scheduling approaches, but may require a more complex system architecture and communication protocol.

TITLE: dynamic bitrate scheduling

Geometry reconstruction is a fundamental problem that enables a wide range of applications in fields such as virtual reality and robotics. In recent years, neural reconstruction methods have gained significant attention; a key advantage of these methods is their ability to represent the geometry of a scene continuously, which can help in many downstream tasks. However, vision-based sensors often struggle in adverse weather conditions, or even become completely unusable when objects are obscured by occlusions.

Radio frequency (RF) sensing, specifically wireless millimeter-wave (mmWave) sensing, can see through occlusions, remains robust under challenging visibility conditions and, unlike X-rays, is not dangerous to humans, making it a compelling alternative for 3D reconstruction. This could open up many applications, for example checking whether the items inside a box are the correct items, are damaged, or pose a threat, without ever opening the box. On the other hand, mmWave resolution is extremely low compared to vision: a single radar image provides far less visual context than a camera image, which makes it hard to extract a 3D reconstruction from one radar image alone. Some prior RF systems have performed 3D point cloud reconstruction or human body tracking by leveraging movement or by emulating larger antenna apertures, but the recovered point clouds are still too sparse and noisy to reliably recover detailed geometry; through-wall human sensing relies on human motion to combat specularity, and deep learning on mmWave radar data has mostly targeted self-driving scenarios, where image resolution matters little. Other works have proposed neural implicit representations for RF sensing, aiming to concentrate scene information out of heavy noise through neural optimization, but these systems are designed for large-scale environments such as streets or satellite imagery and are far from achieving millimeter-level precision. When objects are close to the radar, the propagation characteristics of RF signals change dramatically: incoming waves can no longer be approximated as planar, so processing methods designed for large-scale scenes, such as beamforming, introduce a considerable amount of distortion and noise, often exceeding the noise acceptable for gradient descent and leading to unstable optimization. Existing neural RF reconstruction work is thus either limited to far-range scenes or, for individual objects, evaluated only on simulated data, which for wireless signals cannot come close to representing the complexity of real-world measurements. Meanwhile, the multi-view reconstruction and inverse rendering methods of computer vision (multi-view stereo, neural radiance fields, Gaussian splatting, neural implicit surfaces, physically based inverse rendering) are all derived from RGB images and are not easily transferable to mmWave data: even lensless RGB images can be mapped back to a lens-based imaging model without altering the underlying ray physics, whereas for RF signals such a transformation is fundamentally invalid.

The open problem is therefore to overcome the fundamental dilemma between massive RF noise in the input and the reconstruction of complete, high-resolution, millimeter-level 3D surface geometry of near-range objects, including objects hidden behind occlusions. This is not straightforward, because inferring surface geometry from RF signals differs fundamentally from image-based reconstruction in three main ways. First, wireless systems lack a lens-based imaging model: whereas lenses filter and focus the relevant light rays, radar antenna arrays perform lensless imaging and capture all incoming RF signals without directional filtering, which leads to low signal-to-noise ratios because irrelevant signals cannot be excluded. Second, RF signals and visible light propagate differently: visible light is predominantly scattered diffusely by surfaces, whereas RF signals, whose wavelengths are on the order of millimeters, are dominated by specular reflections, so volumetric rendering techniques designed for scattering-based vision sensors are unsuitable for RF imaging. Third, physically modeling lensless RF measurements is computationally expensive: whereas lens-based rendering samples along 1D rays, modeling what each antenna receives requires accounting for contributions from the full 3D space, leading to cubic complexity that makes naive implementations intractable at millimeter resolution.

How can accurate, millimeter-level 3D geometry of near-range objects be reconstructed from noisy real-world RF measurements, in line of sight and through occlusions, despite lensless imaging, specular reflections and the cost of modeling signal contributions from the full 3D space?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: spectral clustering for rf feature extraction
PROPOSAL: This experiment uses spectral clustering to automatically extract salient RF features relevant for 3D reconstruction in the presence of occlusions. We will train a spectral clustering model on a dataset of mmWave radar images and evaluate its performance in extracting features that are useful for 3D reconstruction. We will compare the performance of spectral clustering to other approaches like PCA and t-SNE.
CONTROLS: We will use mmWave radar images from the existing DriveWave dataset as controls and compare the performance of the spectral clustering model to other approaches. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: Estimated to require 10 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the spectral clustering model.
PREDICTION: We expect spectral clustering to improve feature extraction in occluded scenes, but we worry that the model may struggle to generalize across different occlusion patterns and radar sensor settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: neural indoor/outdoor discriminators for robustness
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes adding a neural indoor/outdoor discriminator module to the RF 3D reconstruction network to improve robustness in indoor and outdoor domains with varying levels of occlusions. We will train a neural network to distinguish between indoor and outdoor environments and use this module to adapt the reconstruction network for improved performance.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the proposed model to the state-of-the-art RF 3D reconstruction model without the discriminator module, using the same mmWave radar image dataset. We will also evaluate the performance of the model in both indoor and outdoor scenarios.
COST: Estimated to require an additional 20 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the model with the discriminator module.
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the addition of the indoor/outdoor discriminator module will improve the robustness and accuracy of the RF 3D reconstruction network in both indoor and outdoor scenarios, but may require careful tuning of the discriminator network to achieve good performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: volumetric processing for through-occlusion imaging
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes adapting the volumetric processing approach used in computer vision for 3D shape reconstruction to the RF domain, using a combination of simulated RF data and real-world mmWave radar images to train and evaluate the performance of this approach in through-occlusion imaging.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of volumetric processing to state-of-the-art RF 3D reconstruction methods, using datasets of mmWave radar images with and without occlusions.
COST: Estimated to require 15 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the volumetric processing model.
PREDICTION: We expect that volumetric processing will help improve the accuracy and robustness of through-occlusion imaging, but may require careful tuning of the model architecture and training parameters to achieve good performance.

TITLE: volumetric processing for through-occlusion imaging

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: dictionary learning for radar feature extraction
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes using dictionary learning to extract and represent features from mmWave radar data in a more robust and efficient manner. We will train a dictionary learning model on a large dataset of mmWave radar images and evaluate its performance in extracting features that are useful for 3D reconstruction.

PREDICTION: We expect dictionary learning to improve the accuracy and efficiency of feature extraction, but may require careful tuning of the dictionary learning parameters and the choice of dictionary size to achieve good performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: hierarchical neural network for 3d reconstruction
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes using a hierarchical neural network architecture to improve the accuracy and robustness of 3D reconstruction from mmWave radar data. We will train a hierarchical neural network model on a large dataset of mmWave radar images and evaluate its performance in reconstructing detailed 3D surface geometry.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the hierarchical neural network to other 3D reconstruction methods, such as volumetric processing and dictionary learning, using the same mmWave radar image dataset. We will also evaluate the performance of the model in different occlusion patterns and box sizes.

PREDICTION: We expect the hierarchical neural network to improve the accuracy and robustness of 3D reconstruction, but may require careful tuning of the model architecture and training parameters to achieve good performance, particularly when dealing with complex occlusion patterns and small box sizes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: debiasing radar data for 3d reconstruction
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes using debiasing techniques to mitigate the effects of system-induced bias in mmWave radar data and improve the accuracy of 3D reconstruction. We will apply debiasing techniques to a large dataset of mmWave radar images and evaluate the impact on 3D reconstruction performance.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of debiasing techniques to other methods, such as dictionary learning and hierarchical neural networks, using the same mmWave radar image dataset.
COST: Estimated to require 30 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the debiasing techniques.
PREDICTION: We expect debiasing to improve the accuracy and robustness of 3D reconstruction, but may require careful tuning of the debiasing parameters and the choice of debiasing method to achieve good performance.

TITLE: physics-informed neural networks for rf modeling
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes using physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to model the underlying physics of mmWave radar data and improve the accuracy of 3D reconstruction. We will train a PINN model on a large dataset of mmWave radar images and evaluate its performance in reconstructing detailed 3D surface geometry.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of PINN to other methods, such as dictionary learning and hierarchical neural networks, using the same mmWave radar image dataset. We will also evaluate the performance of the model in different occlusion patterns and box sizes.
COST: Estimated to require 50 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the PINN model.
PREDICTION: We expect PINN to improve the accuracy and robustness of 3D reconstruction, but may require careful tuning of the PINN architecture and training parameters to achieve good performance, particularly when dealing with complex occlusion patterns and small box sizes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: multi-task learning for comprehensive 3d understanding
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes using multi-task learning to integrate multiple 3D reconstruction tasks, including obstacle detection, shape estimation, and labeling, into a single unified framework. We will train a multi-task learning model on a large dataset of mmWave radar images and evaluate its performance in achieving comprehensive 3D understanding.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of multi-task learning to other methods, such as dictionary learning and hierarchical neural networks, using the same mmWave radar image dataset. We will also evaluate the performance of the model in different occlusion patterns and box sizes.
COST: Estimated to require 60 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the multi-task learning model.
PREDICTION: We expect multi-task learning to significantly improve the accuracy and robustness of 3D reconstruction, especially in complex scenarios with multiple tasks and occlusions.

enonce:
Diffusion models have catalyzed an enormous research wave in generative modeling. Conceptually, they couple a stochastic forward noising process with a reverse-time ordinary or stochastic differential equation whose density evolution is governed by the Fokker–Planck equation, a linear second-order parabolic partial differential equation. Learning consists of estimating time-indexed scores or velocities and integrating them for sampling. A growing body of work also explores probability-flow backbones: deterministic flows trained via flow matching and its optimal-transport variants, rectified flows, and stochastic interpolants that bridge flows and diffusion.

Yet the partial-differential-equation lens on generative modeling need not be limited to Fokker–Planck. Other classical linear second-order equations, elliptic and hyperbolic, offer different structural advantages but remain comparatively underexplored; Poisson flow models, for instance, recast generation through electrostatics-inspired fields. On the hyperbolic side, recent work has replaced the Fokker–Planck equation with the telegrapher equation (the one-dimensional damped wave equation) and its stochastic Kac representation, in which a particle moves at constant speed and reverses direction at the jump times of a Poisson process. A network is fit by regression to a closed-form conditional velocity of this process and integrated backward in time from noise to data, with each image coordinate following an independent one-dimensional Kac process. The resulting probability flows have a finite propagation speed: starting from localized mass, the distribution remains inside a causal cone, the flow is Lipschitz in Wasserstein distance, and velocity norms, hence kinetic energy, stay globally bounded. Diffusion, by contrast, spreads mass instantaneously with effectively infinite propagation speed, which manifests as stiff, rapidly growing reverse-time velocities and as ill-conditioned fields with Lipschitz blow-ups near the end of denoising; indeed, diffusion arises as a limit of the damped wave equation as the damping and the propagation speed tend to infinity. A finite speed cap thus acts like a built-in stability constraint: trajectories cannot accelerate without bound, and late-time integration is less stiff.

So far, however, these finite-speed flows have been developed only for unconditional image generation, and they lack two ingredients that make diffusion-style generators practical. The first is guided conditional generation. Classifier-free guidance, which mixes conditional and unconditional predictions to steer samples toward a condition, is a standard tool for diffusion models, but it is unclear whether guidance can be carried over to finite-speed dynamics without losing the bounded-energy property that distinguishes them from diffusion, whose kinetic energy can diverge near data time. The second is fast sampling. Practical generators are expected to deliver high-quality samples with very few network evaluations, yet it is unknown whether finite-speed flows can be brought down to a handful of sampling steps, or even a single one, without a severe loss of sample quality, and whether their finite-speed, bounded-energy structure can explain, and ideally guarantee, that a coarse few-step sampler stays close to the full sampling trajectory.

This leads to three questions. How can guided conditional generation be built on finite-speed Kac flows while provably keeping the guided velocity field at finite kinetic energy? How can such flows be turned into few-step, ideally one-step, image generators that preserve both sample quality and the numerical stability benefits of finite-speed probability flows? And can the finite-speed structure provide theoretical guarantees that a few-step sampler remains close to the full flow along the entire generation path, not only in its final samples? Answering them would show whether hyperbolic, finite-speed dynamics can be a credible alternative to diffusion for fast image generation.

Diffusion models, and text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models in particular, have made astonishing progress in the quality of generated images. At the same time, emerging work on generative depth estimation has revealed that advanced T2I models hold a latent potential for depth estimation: the rich visual priors stored in a pre-trained T2I model can be leveraged to obtain strong zero-shot monocular depth estimation. Exploring a framework that bridges image generation and depth estimation is an essential step toward building unified models for both generation and visual perception.

Existing routes toward such unification each carry a substantial cost. The pioneering generative depth estimation paradigm repurposes a pre-trained T2I diffusion model by fine-tuning its denoising network with full parameters on depth data. It achieves powerful zero-shot depth estimation, but the parameter updates made during training irreversibly and catastrophically degrade the model's original image generation capability; later generative depth estimators that refine this recipe (for example with flow matching, geometry switchers or detail-preserving tuning strategies) inherit the same full-parameter fine-tuning and therefore the same loss. A second route unifies generation and depth estimation with a parallel dual-model architecture, in which two diffusion models run side by side and interact through feature-exchange operations; this requires running two diffusion models in parallel, and the interaction registers new knowledge into the pre-trained generator, which can affect its original image generation behaviour. A third, data-driven route trains a unified generation-and-perception model from scratch on massive multitask data (on the order of a hundred million samples). Despite remarkable progress, these solutions may be considered inefficient or resource-intensive, and potentially suboptimal.

Since a rich visual prior is already stored in advanced T2I models, a natural question arises: can a T2I model effortlessly acquire depth estimation capability without degrading its image generation capability? More concretely, starting from a fixed pre-trained T2I model, with a focus on modern transformer-based diffusion models, how can its latent depth estimation ability be unleashed so that a single model serves both image generation and depth estimation, keeping the original generation ability fully intact, adding only a small fraction of extra learnable parameters, and without resorting to massive multitask training data, while still reaching depth accuracy competitive with full-parameter fine-tuning and with existing unified models?

The problem is challenging. Among the effectively infinite pixel-level combinations that a T2I model learns to generate, there may exist underlying information highly correlated with scene depth; however, because text prompts provide only weak guidance and depth information is sparsely represented within the overall data distribution, extracting depth-relevant features from a fixed pre-trained T2I model is difficult. Any additional capacity must also make efficient use of the visual knowledge already present in the pre-trained model, so that depth estimation is obtained at a small parameter and data cost rather than by building and training a second large model.

TITLE: extracting depth from visual priors
PROPOSAL: Train a linear layer on top of the pre-trained T2I diffusion model's feature extractor, using a small subset of the model's parameters to predict depth values on the validation set of the Diadem dataset. We'll use the Adam optimizer and a learning rate of 1e-4 for 10 epochs.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: Directly fine-tuning the model on the depth data with full parameters as a baseline for comparison.
- Ablation: Train the model with random weights instead of the pre-trained weights.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that this linear layer will learn to extract depth-relevant features from the pre-trained model, leading to a reasonable amount of depth estimation accuracy. However, we anticipate that the model may fail when dealing with complex or cluttered scenes, resulting in large errors.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: extracting depth from visual priors
PROPOSAL: Revise to use a smaller learning rate of 1e-5 and an additional batch normalization layer after the linear layer to improve the performance and stability of the network. Also, run the model on the NYU-Depth-V2 dataset, as it has a larger number of samples and varying depth ranges. We'll train the model for 20 epochs to see if the additional depth diversity helps the model generalizing and improving its depth prediction accuracy.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: Directly fine-tuning the model on the depth data with full parameters.
- Ablation: Remove the batch normalization layer to check its contribution to the model's performance.
- Experiment: Use the model to estimate depth values on both the image and surface normal generation tasks, to verify if the learned depth priors are robust across different generative tasks.
COST: 75 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: With the batch normalization and lower learning rate, we expect the model to learn more effectively and have better generalization performance on the NYU-Depth-V2 dataset, resulting in higher accuracy and lower errors compared to the previous experiment.

ACTION: REVISE

PROPOSAL: Update to use a 2-layer MLP with 128 units and ReLU activation instead of a linear layer. Also, evaluate the model on the Make3D and KITTI datasets to gauge its performance on more diverse and challenging scenes.

COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: With the 2-layer MLP, we expect to see improved performance on the depth estimation task, especially on the Make3D and KITTI datasets where the model will benefit from the increased capacity to capture subtle depth variations.

ACTION: REVISE

PROPOSAL: Modify the existing model by adding a lightweight visual attention mechanism to focus on the most informative regions in the input image when predicting depth. We'll use a simple 2D attention layer to capture spatial dependencies between pixels.

PREDICTION: By incorporating the visual attention mechanism, we hope to see an improvement in the model's ability to capture subtle depth variations and more accurately predict depth values, leading to increased accuracy and lower errors.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating on surface normal estimation
PROPOSAL: Adapt the pre-trained T2I model to predict surface normals by training a 3D convolutional layer on top of the feature extractor, with an additional cosine similarity loss for surface normal regression. Evaluate the adapted model on the T-NeRF dataset, which contains 3D scenes with varying surface normals.
CONTROLS:

COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By adapting the pre-trained T2I model to predict surface normals, we expect to see improved performance on surface normal estimation, with a significant reduction in the normal error and perception error.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: sparse depth estimation with attention
PROPOSAL: Modify the existing depth estimation model to predict sparse depth maps using a novel sparse attention mechanism. This mechanism will focus on a subset of pixels that are most informative for depth estimation, reducing the number of model parameters and computations required for training and inference.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: Compare the performance of the proposed sparse depth estimation method with the baseline model from 'extracting depth from visual priors'.
- Ablation: Remove the sparse attention mechanism to investigate its contribution to the model's performance on sparse depth estimation.
- Experiment: Evaluate the model's performance on sparse depth estimation tasks, such as estimating depth from a set of sparse points or bounding boxes.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By using sparse attention, we expect to see improved performance on sparse depth estimation tasks, with a significant reduction in model parameters and computations required for training and inference, leading to increased efficiency and faster deployment.

ACTION: REVISE

COST: 120 GPU-hours

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: meta-learning for task-agnostic depth and surface normal estimation
PROPOSAL: Explore a meta-learning approach that allows the model to learn a task-agnostic representation that can be adapted to multiple tasks, including depth and surface normal estimation. We'll use a few-shot learning framework and require the model to learn only from a few samples of each task.

- Experiment: Evaluate the model's performance on tasks that require adaptation to new unseen scenarios, such as 3D reconstruction and object detection.

PREDICTION: By adopting a meta-learning approach, we expect to see improved performance on tasks that require adaptation to new unseen scenarios, with a better understanding of the model's ability to generalize across different tasks and scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: deploying to real-world scenarios
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the performance of the proposed methods on a real-world dataset, such as the ScanNet dataset, which contains 3D scans of real-world environments. - Ablation: Remove the real-world dataset and evaluate the models on synthetic datasets only.
- Experiment: Evaluate the performance of the models on real-world tasks, such as 3D mapping and object detection.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By deploying the models to real-world scenarios, we expect to see improved performance on tasks that require robustness and adaptability to real-world environments, with a better understanding of the models' ability to generalize to unseen scenarios.

Visual document retrieval is the task of returning relevant documents, typically PDFs containing figures, tables, and other visual elements, in response to a textual query. Neural retrieval pipelines for this task often follow a text-centric approach: source documents are converted into textual chunks with optical character recognition or vision-language models, and an index is then built with semantic text encoders. An alternative, vision-centric approach relies instead on multimodal encoders. Building on the ColBERT late-interaction approach, ColPali-based encoders operate directly on page images, matching textual query tokens to image patches and producing multi-vector embeddings of images and queries.

Although this vision-centric paradigm achieves state-of-the-art results on public visual document retrieval benchmarks, open challenges remain. First, in pursuit of state-of-the-art performance, recent late-interaction multimodal retrievers have massively scaled the length and dimensionality of their query and document representations. This incurs substantial latency and storage overhead and hinders efficient, scalable deployment in real-world pipelines; one recent retriever, for example, represents each document page with about 10 MB of memory, three orders of magnitude more than a single-vector dense retriever. Second, matching textual queries to textually rich documents with a purely vision-centric model may be limited by the substantial modality gap that modern vision-language models still exhibit. These limitations motivate exploring complementary ways of improving multimodal encoders, rather than relying only on ever-larger monolithic models.

A long-standing idea in neural retrieval is hybrid retrieval, in which the outputs of different retrievers are aggregated, at the level of document ranks or of query-document similarity scores, to obtain the final list of retrieved documents. Hybrid retrieval (or hybrid search) most commonly refers to combining a neural semantic text retriever with a sparse lexical representation such as BM25; more broadly, it reflects the notion that models relying on different types of representations capture complementary aspects of the data, which can be leveraged to boost overall performance. Dense text retrievers typically have low online latency and a small storage footprint, and they provide a uni-modal signal between the query and the document representation. Combining text and image encoders therefore emerges as a natural candidate for enhancing a multimodal retrieval system.

However, standard hybrid retrieval methods take a rather coarse-grained view of each retriever: because they reduce every query-document pair to a single rank or score, they cannot exploit the rich query-document interactions within each model's representation space. Aggregating at the level of the representations themselves would carry the richest information, but at query time it is hindered by heterogeneity: encoders may use a single vector or many vectors per query and document, with differing dimensionalities and scales, and any aggregation must respect strict latency and memory budgets without access to supervision. A further difficulty is that the complementary retriever may be lightweight and even weaker on the task than the primary one, and it is unclear whether such a signal can help at all.

This raises the following questions. Can the paradigm of hybrid retrieval complement modern vision-centric multimodal encoders, and in particular, can a lightweight dense text retriever enhance a stronger vision-centric retriever? How can the signals of two heterogeneous retrievers be combined at query time so as to exploit the rich interactions within their representation spaces, rather than only their final ranks or scores, while remaining architecture-agnostic (applicable to both single-vector and multi-vector models), lightweight, and practical? And can such a combination improve the trade-off between retrieval quality, online latency, and index memory compared with scaling up the representations of a single model?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: contrastive hybrid retriever
PROPOSAL: Investigate the Contrastive Hybrid Retriever (CHR) model, which combines a lightweight dense text retriever with a stronger vision-centric retriever using a contrastive loss function that minimizes the distance between matching pairs while maximizing the distance between non-matching pairs, effectively aligning the representation spaces of the two models.
CONTROLS: Compare against the baseline of using the vision-centric retriever alone, and ablate the CHR model by swapping out the dense text retriever with a BM25 indexer to understand the impact of the text retrieval component.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: CHR model outperforms the baseline vision-centric retriever while improving online latency and reducing storage requirements; however, performance may degrade if the lightweight dense text retriever is too weak compared to the vision-centric retriever.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: latent space alignment
PROPOSAL: Develop a method for latent space alignment between the representations of the two heterogeneous retrievers using a neural autoencoder, which maps the complex representation space of the vision-centric retriever to a lower-dimensional space that can be compared directly with the lower-dimensional representation space of the lightweight dense text retriever.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the proposal against a baseline that averages or concatenates the two representation spaces without alignment, and compare the proposed method to existing methods for alignment.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Latent space alignment improves the combination of the two models, reducing the modality gap and improving retrieval quality; however, the method may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: gradient-based aggregation
PROPOSAL: Introduce a gradient-based aggregation method that calculates the weighted sum of the outputs of the two retrievers based on the gradient of the loss function with respect to the aggregation weights, allowing for optimal alignment of the retina representation spaces at each query.
CONTROLS: Compare against the baseline of using a simple weighted average aggregation method, and evaluate the impact of using different aggregation weights and regularization techniques.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Gradient-based aggregation improves the combination of the two models, achieving state-of-the-art results on retrieval quality while reducing online latency and index memory requirements; however, the method may be computationally expensive and require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

TITLE: content-based fusion
PROPOSAL: Explore a content-based fusion approach to combine the retrievals from the vision-centric and dense text retrievers, by computing afteicher weighted sum of the two retrieval scores based on features extracted from the query and document representations, such as their similarity in terms of tokens, entities, or categories.
CONTROLS: Compare against the baseline of using a simple weighted average of the two retrieval scores, and evaluate the impact of different weighting strategies and feature extraction techniques.
