ACTION: ADD
TITLE: retriever ensemble embedding
PROPOSAL: Develop a retriever ensemble embedding (REE) approach, which generates an ensemble representation for each document by averaging or concatenating the representation vectors of multiple retrievers, and then scores the similarity between the query representation and the ensemble representations of documents.
CONTROLS: Compare against the baseline of using a single retriever representation, and evaluate the impact of different ensemble methods and hyperparameter settings.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: REE improves retrieval quality and reduces the modality gap between the two retrievers, but may increase online latency and index memory requirements due to the need to store and compute ensemble representations.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: content-based fusion
PROPOSAL: Modify the content-based fusion approach to use a weighted sum of the similarities between query-document pairs computed using different feature extraction techniques, such as token-level similarity, entity-level similarity, and category-level similarity, to improve the robustness of the fusion method.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the revised method against the original content-based fusion and compare against a baseline of no fusion using feature extraction techniques.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (note: this is a revision of proposal 4)
PREDICTION: The revised content-based fusion method improves retrieval quality and reduces the modality gap between the two retrievers by incorporating multiple feature extraction techniques, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adversarial attention
PROPOSAL: Introduce an adversarial attention mechanism to modulate the contributions of the vision-centric and dense text retrievers in the fusion process, by learning to minimize the impact of one retriever's weaknesses on the overall fusion result, and encourage the strengths of each retriever to boost the fusion result.
CONTROLS: Compare against the baseline of no attention mechanism, and evaluate the impact of different attention weights and hyperparameter settings.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Adversarial attention improves retrieval quality and reduces the modality gap between the two retrievers, by intelligently managing the contributions of each retriever, but may increase online latency and index memory requirements due to the need to compute attention weights.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: weighted reranking
PROPOSAL: Introduce a weighted reranking approach to reevaluate the ranking of documents based on the fusion results of the two retrievers, using a learned weighting scheme to adjust the importance of each retriever's scores in the final ranking.
CONTROLS: Compare against the baseline of no reranking, and evaluate the impact of different weighting schemes and hyperparameter settings.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Weighted reranking improves retrieval quality and precision by selectively emphasizing the strengths of each retriever in the final ranking, but may increase online latency due to the need for additional computation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: hyperparameter tuning via stochastic optimization
PROPOSAL: Utilize stochastic optimization methods, such as Bayesian optimization or random search, to efficiently tune the hyperparameters of the fusion framework and its individual components, in order to discover the optimal settings that achieve state-of-the-art retrieval quality and efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare against the baseline of grid search or random initialization, and evaluate the impact of different stochastic optimization methods and hyperparameter settings.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (note: this is a computationally intensive proposal)
PREDICTION: Hyperparameter tuning via stochastic optimization significantly improves the performance and efficiency of the fusion framework, by efficiently finding the optimal hyperparameters in a larger search space, but may require substantial computational resources and expertise.

Understanding how a scene has changed and forecasting how it will look next from Satellite Image Time Series (SITS) is fundamental to many critical applications, yet it poses a profound challenge: predicting the future requires a deep understanding of past change. Two tasks are central. In temporal change description, given a sequence of temporally ordered satellite images of the same area, the goal is to generate a natural-language description that accurately summarizes the key dynamic changes that occurred over the observation period, such as urban expansion or agricultural cycles; this requires comprehending the temporal evolution and, ideally, the underlying causal narrative of the changes. In future satellite image forecasting, given the same historical sequence, the goal is to generate a plausible image for the next time point. A critical and often overlooked requirement is that the forecast be temporally consistent: the generated changes should be a logical continuation of the trends and dynamics observed in the historical data, not merely a plausible standalone picture.

Although foundation models such as Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and diffusion-based image generators have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their application to this domain remains fragmented and fundamentally limited. On the understanding side, static image captioning ignores temporal context, while existing temporal change description methods lack the semantic depth of MLLMs: they fuse information across images through simple interactions, their long-range temporal reasoning is limited, and they struggle to capture why changes occur. General-purpose MLLMs, even video-capable ones, are not optimized for this setting either: video-centric models are typically tuned for densely sampled frames with fixed, short intervals, whereas consecutive satellite acquisitions are sparse and irregular, with gaps that can span several years. On the generation side, single-image synthesis cannot model evolution, and temporal forecasting approaches struggle with long-term consistency because they do not grasp the semantic drivers of change: their conditioning is typically low-level (e.g., edge maps), based on simple metadata, or limited to text guidance, and it lacks fine-grained temporal semantic interaction, so they can generate what a scene looks like but cannot reason about why it should look that way given its history. As a result, change understanding and future forecasting have been treated as disjointed tasks, even though both are limited by a common bottleneck: modeling long-range temporal dynamics.

This raises several questions. How can a model reason about why changes occurred across a long, irregularly sampled sequence of satellite images, and describe them accurately? How can such an understanding of past change be used to generate what will happen next, so that the forecast is a temporally consistent continuation of the observed trajectory rather than only a realistic-looking image? Can enhancing long-range temporal understanding improve performance on both tasks simultaneously, with the understanding of past change directly informing the forecast? Finally, how can the temporal consistency of a forecast be rigorously evaluated, given that standard image-quality metrics cannot penalize a prediction that is perceptually realistic but inconsistent with historical trends?

Graphs are powerful abstractions for representing complex relationships between entities, from social networks to molecular structures, and learning effective graph representations is crucial for node classification, graph classification and link prediction. Over the past decade, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become the dominant paradigm for graph representation learning, building representations through a message-passing mechanism that iteratively aggregates local neighborhood information. Despite its success, message passing faces several key limitations, such as limited expressiveness and difficulty in capturing long-range dependencies. Numerous efforts address different aspects of these limitations: graph transformer architectures incorporate long-range interactions across broader graph contexts, positional encodings inject structural priors to improve global topological awareness, and graph rewiring techniques modify the topology to mitigate structural bottlenecks and enhance information diffusion.

However, these advances remain constrained by a cognitive discrepancy. Humans perceive global structure intuitively, following visual Gestalt principles: they understand the whole before analyzing the individual parts. GNNs and their variants, by contrast, operate through bottom-up processing. People instantly recognize ring structures, symmetric structures and critical bridges in a drawing of a graph, yet even advanced architectures struggle with such basic topological understanding: standard message-passing networks provably cannot identify bridges, and graphs that people tell apart at a glance can fool message passing unless sophisticated topological computations are added. Although architectural innovations have made significant theoretical and practical progress, their essence is still to identify and repair different aspects of the inherent defects of message passing. Approaches that perceive graphs visually remain largely unexplored for graph learning, despite their natural alignment with how humans perceive network structures, and despite a flourishing computer vision ecosystem whose models excel at holistic pattern recognition and global structure understanding. Recent work has begun to bring graph drawings into existing architectures, for instance into vision-language models for graph reasoning or into GNNs to enhance expressivity, but it treats graph layouts and vision models as black boxes, without examining how visual and message-passing models fundamentally differ in the way they understand graphs.

A second obstacle is measurement. Established benchmarks built from molecules, citation networks or protein interaction graphs tightly couple domain-specific node features with topology, which makes their separate contributions hard to quantify and can let models succeed through feature-based shortcuts rather than genuine structural understanding. Models that replace the true molecular topology with fixed-structure expander graphs have been shown to match or exceed performance on several molecular benchmarks, suggesting that node features often dominate structural information in standard datasets, potentially masking differences in how models perceive graph topology. The theoretical evaluation of GNNs has centered on the Weisfeiler-Lehman test, which measures the ability to distinguish pairs of non-isomorphic graphs of the same size; valuable for theory, it is limited to binary discrimination between fixed-size graph pairs. Recent graph benchmarks oriented toward large language models focus on structural analysis tasks such as node counting, cycle detection and path finding, and typically rely on a limited set of random graph generators (such as Erdős–Rényi or Watts–Strogatz) that inadequately capture topological diversity. What remains missing is a way to assess human-like graph cognition: the intuitive ability to perceive, abstract and reason about fundamental global graph properties, and to recognize the same connectivity patterns across varying scales and contexts.

This leads to the questions addressed here. Could models designed for visual perception, which carry no graph-specific inductive bias, offer a viable pathway to graph structural understanding, and do they process graph information in the same way as message-passing GNNs or through fundamentally different strategies? How can a model's ability to perceive and abstract global graph properties be evaluated rigorously, in isolation from domain-specific features, including whether it recognizes the same structural pattern regardless of graph size? And what does it take for a graph learning model to acquire the holistic, scale-robust understanding of topology that humans display effortlessly?

Semantic segmentation has improved significantly with recent advances in deep neural networks, but it requires a large volume of fine-grained pixel-level labels, which are time-consuming and labor-intensive to obtain. Because images themselves are readily available, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) and semi-supervised learning (SSL) have been introduced to handle label-scarce scenarios: UDA learns from labeled synthetic data and transfers knowledge to real, unlabeled target domains, while SSL uses a tiny portion of annotated data to generalize to unseen data. Both are gaining attention as promising ways to reduce the reliance on extensive annotation in semantic segmentation.

In both settings, models are trained on annotated and unlabeled data simultaneously. Mainstream methods follow two paradigms. Self-training methods use a temporally smoothed exponential moving average (EMA) model as a teacher to generate stable pseudo-labels for unlabeled data, while consistency regularization methods encourage the model to produce consistent predictions for the same sample under different perturbation views; recent state-of-the-art methods combine the two. Both can be summarized as pseudo-label learning, in which the network's own predictions serve as supervision for unlabeled data. In the widely adopted form of this paradigm, the teacher's prediction is converted into a hard pseudo-label through an argmax and encoded one-hot, a confidence-based quality estimate (threshold filtering or a weighting function) controls how much each pseudo-label contributes, and training uses a cross-entropy loss.

Despite promising results, pseudo-labels inevitably contain errors that mislead training, and these errors are further amplified during training because of the one-hot encoding. Typical remedies use filter-out mechanisms that train only on high-confidence pseudo-labels, but this makes the model focus on easy samples while neglecting difficult ones, resulting in sub-optimal performance. Another alternative assigns weights according to pseudo-label confidence, but such weighting functions require careful design and selection of hyperparameters, which compromises their applicability. Other work designs new optimization criteria, for example inspired by negative learning. Existing work thus concentrates on selection strategies for pseudo-labels and rarely considers the impact of the encoding form assigned to classes.

This omission matters most for confusing classes. For instance, pixels of the class sheep may be confused by the classifier with horse or cow, and the resulting erroneous pseudo-label is encoded one-hot through the argmax, committing the supervision entirely to a wrong class. Similar classes plausibly share common visual attributes (sheep and cows, for example, both have horns and hooves), which leads to confusing pseudo-labels that further misguide training, yet a one-hot target cannot express what the confused classes have in common. How to utilize the shared attributes among confusing classes to design a suitable encoding form for pseudo-label learning remains rarely explored.

This raises several questions. Can the class encoding used by the segmentation model and its pseudo-labels be redesigned so that supervision stays informative even when the class decision for a pixel is wrong? Under such an encoding, how should pseudo-labels be generated from the teacher's predictions so that they introduce less noise than hard one-hot labels, and what training objective is appropriate? Can an alternative encoding be shown, both theoretically and empirically, to match one-hot encoding in the fully supervised setting while being more robust to label noise in pseudo-label learning? Finally, since the encoding form is orthogonal to pseudo-label selection strategies, can such a change be integrated into existing self-training and consistency-regularization frameworks for both UDA and SSL, across different segmentation architectures?

enonce:
Video anomaly analysis is a key application of computer vision for public security. Most early work formulates it as temporal video anomaly detection: marking the segments of a video whose behavior deviates from learned normal patterns, whether with one-class models trained only on normal clips, unsupervised reconstruction or future-frame prediction objectives, or weakly supervised learning from video-level labels. Such detectors have reached high performance on benchmarks, yet they output only frame-wise anomaly scores, without spatial or semantic context, and give no insight into why a segment is abnormal. These limits of interpretability have motivated a shift from temporal detection toward downstream tasks with user-friendly, explainable outputs: spatial video anomaly localization, which predicts bounding boxes around the regions that contain the abnormal activity, and textual video anomaly understanding, which decides whether a video contains an anomaly and produces a human-readable description explaining it, typically with fine-tuned multimodal large language models. Each line of work, however, provides either spatial or textual cues on its own and focuses on a single type of task, so that existing methods offer only an incomplete analysis of video anomalies. A holistic analysis would answer when an anomaly happens, where it is, what it is and why it is abnormal, each of the existing benchmark tasks addressing one of these sub-problems.

A second challenge is the heavy reliance on dataset-specific supervision. Detection and localization models require temporal masks or spatial bounding boxes, yet anomaly definitions vary widely across datasets, so a model tuned on one domain often fails on another and must be retrained for unseen domains or anomaly types. In real-world applications, privacy and security concerns may also make training data unavailable for some sensitive scenes. Open-set detectors that fuse language semantics in order to detect and classify novel anomalies still require task-specific training and give very limited insight into why frames are abnormal. As partial remedies, recent work has explored zero- and few-shot approaches built on frozen vision-language backbones or multimodal large language models, but most of these approaches have a limited task scope and still rely on annotated datasets. The only strictly zero-shot, training-free method addresses temporal detection alone: a frozen vision-language model captions the frames and a prompted large language model converts the captions into frame-wise anomaly scores. It is effective when anomalies are clearly distinguishable from normality but occasionally fails on more complex anomaly types, and it offers neither spatial grounding nor any direct semantic explanation beyond generic captions. Prompt-tuning methods, which optimize textual prompts to guide frozen models, require induction on an annotated training set and pay for it in generality, since the learned prompts tend to be task- or domain-specific. The generality problem is worse still for instruction-tuned multimodal models: they produce rich narrative explanations, but they require extensive annotation and computational resources, lack temporal or spatial coverage, and are optimized to return answers from seen question-answer pairs that describe a closed set of anomaly types.

Multimodal large language models already encode rich visual-semantic priors for commonsense reasoning, which suggests that fine-tuning may not be necessary for every task. This raises the questions addressed here: can temporal detection, spatial localization and textual explanation of video anomalies be delivered together, as one holistic and interpretable analysis, in a strictly zero-shot manner, with frozen pretrained models and without any additional training data, annotations or gradient updates? And can such an analysis remain at least as accurate as existing zero-shot detectors while staying robust across domains whose definitions of anomaly differ?

Recording dynamic scenes from multiple viewpoints has become increasingly common in everyday life. From concerts and sports events to lectures and birthday parties, people often capture the same moment using different handheld devices. These multi-view recordings present a rich opportunity to reconstruct scenes in 4D, enable bullet-time effects, or enhance the capabilities of existing vision models. However, these videos are typically captured independently, without synchronization or known camera poses, making it difficult to align and fuse them coherently.

The task is the following: given a set of asynchronous videos that capture the same dynamic scene from different viewpoints, estimate a time offset for each video, to be applied to its original out-of-sync clock, so that after correction frames sharing the same clock time correspond to the exact same moment across all videos.

Existing synchronization methods rely on controlled environments, manual annotations, specific patterns such as human pose, audio signals such as flashes or claps, or expensive hardware setups such as time-coded devices, none of which are available in casually captured videos. Human-centric approaches, which use body pose as the synchronization signal, are limited by the accuracy of pose estimation and by the number of people present, and they struggle in scenes without prominent human activity. Audio-based approaches only work in quiet environments and do not carry over to in-the-wild settings where audio is noisy or unavailable. Methods that jointly optimize camera poses and temporal offsets within a learned scene representation are often constrained to specific environments or object types. Geometry-based methods estimate temporal offsets from multi-view geometric constraints, but typically assume static scenes or a fixed viewpoint. Meanwhile, structure-from-motion and learned camera-pose estimators recover camera geometry accurately, yet they rely predominantly on static visual cues and therefore fall short of synchronizing dynamic scenes.

Building a practical and robust synchronization system that works on videos in the wild is challenging. Camera poses are unknown and cameras may move, so the geometric relationship between each pair of cameras must itself be estimated reliably. The moving objects that carry the timing information are not known in advance and are generally small and blurry. Associating points across cameras with significantly different viewpoints is difficult. The offsets to be recovered are continuous, while observations arrive only at discrete frame times. Finally, not all views overlap, so some pairs of cameras may share little spatial or temporal overlap.

This raises several questions. How can a set of casually captured, unposed and unsynchronized videos of the same dynamic scene be aligned in time with high precision, without specialized capture, audio, manual correction, or assumptions about the scene content such as the presence of people? Which visual evidence can reliably reveal the temporal offset between two cameras whose poses are unknown and possibly changing over time? And how can a single, globally consistent offset be recovered for every video when the evidence relating some pairs of views is weak, ambiguous or missing? Answering these questions would open the door to scalable, unconstrained multi-view 4D scene understanding and to downstream tasks, such as 4D reconstruction of dynamic scenes, that depend on synchronized input.

Diffusion models have demonstrated a remarkable ability to learn data distributions across many modalities, with strong results in both data generation and image restoration. In medical imaging, they are effective at modeling the distribution of 2D image slices, and by combining these powerful learned priors with conventional optimization frameworks, diffusion-based solvers have reached state-of-the-art performance on medical inverse problems such as accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and undersampled X-ray computed tomography (CT). Such problems are often severely ill-posed: far fewer measurements are acquired than there are unknowns, so the measurements alone cannot determine the image, and the learned prior must fill in what they leave ambiguous. Diffusion-based solvers do so through an iterative reverse sampling process that, at each step, predicts a clean image from the current noisy state, corrects this estimate for consistency with the measurements, and re-noises it to the next timestep, which repeatedly injects random noise.

In clinical practice, however, medical data are fundamentally large 3D volumes. Individual 2D slices matter for review, but a complete and accurate volumetric reconstruction is often essential for downstream tasks such as precise tumor volume assessment, surgical planning, and tracking disease progression over time. Translating the success of 2D diffusion-based solvers to 3D is difficult: because of the curse of dimensionality, the memory, computational, and data requirements of training a diffusion prior directly on volumetric data are prohibitive for most academic and even industrial labs. A common and practical workaround is to train a diffusion model on 2D slices and apply this 2D prior slice by slice to reconstruct the volume.

This workaround eases the training burden but creates a critical new problem: the reconstructed volumes lack consistency along the third dimension (the z-axis). Because each slice is processed independently during the reverse diffusion process, the intrinsic randomness of the sampling procedure leads to severe inter-slice discontinuities and artifacts, degrading the diagnostic and analytical quality of the stacked volume. Existing remedies have important drawbacks. The most direct one augments the 2D prior with a hand-crafted regularizer such as total variation, applied in an additional optimization step to enforce smoothness between adjacent slices. This is effective, but it introduces sensitive hyperparameters that require careful tuning, can over-smooth the volume or produce cartoon-like textures that erase fine diagnostic details, and acts as an external correction that masks the symptoms rather than addressing the intrinsic cause. More principled approaches try to learn a more complete 3D prior, for instance by training on 3D patches or by combining priors from two perpendicular 2D planes, but they increase the complexity of the training or inference pipeline and may impose constraints on the data, such as requiring cubic volumes.

A similar discontinuity arises in video restoration, where applying a pre-trained 2D image diffusion model to video inverse problems often produces temporal flickering across frames. Prior work attributed this flickering to the uncoordinated stochasticity inherent in diffusion sampling and alleviated it by synchronizing the stochastic noise components across frames. Whether the same mechanism is the fundamental cause of inter-slice inconsistency in 3D medical reconstruction, and how such a remedy would transfer from video to volumetric medical data, remains open.

This raises the following questions. How does the stochasticity of independent slice-wise sampling give rise to inter-slice inconsistency when 2D diffusion priors are used for 3D medical reconstruction? Is it possible to enhance inter-slice consistency directly within the diffusion sampling process itself, obviating the need for external, artifact-inducing optimization, ideally without new loss terms, additional sensitive hyperparameters, model retraining, or extra computational cost, so that the remedy could be dropped into existing 2D diffusion-based 3D reconstruction pipelines? And can inter-slice consistency be improved while preserving the natural anatomical variation between slices and fine diagnostic details, rather than trading them away for smoothness?

By comparing these diagnostics across different variants of the solver, including and without the slice synchronization method proposed in our previous experiment, we will analyze the mechanism behind inter-slice inconsistency and provide a deeper understanding of its origin.
CONTROLS: The baseline for our diagnostics will be the existing implementation of the 2D diffusion-based solver without any additional modifications, with details given in the appendix.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The advanced diffusion diagnostics are expected to uncover the inherent stochasticity and its effects on slice consistency, supporting evidence for the potential benefits of our proposed slice synchronization method. However, inconsistent results might challenge our current assumptions and necessitate a reevaluation of the underlying problem.

PROPOSAL: We will adapt the 2D diffusion-based solver to operate within a 2D+1 framework, where each 2D slice is augmented with a per-pixel description of the slice's spatial relationship to adjacent slices in the 3D volume. This framework will be used to train a set of 2D diffusion priors, each conditioned on 3D patches of volume data. During inference, the 2D diffusion model will use the spatial relationship descriptions to predict a clean image slice that is consistent with adjacent slices.

Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly expanded in capability and are now widely used in domains such as conversational agents, healthcare and finance, where they often process sensitive personal information. Early privacy concerns focused mainly on memorization and leakage of training data, but recent studies show that LLMs can also infer private attributes of an author, such as location, identity or demographics, from subtle semantic cues in seemingly innocuous text. With sufficiently capable models, such inferences can be surprisingly accurate and often go undetected by users, who continue to share content unaware of the risk. Moreover, text sent to external services may be intercepted in transit or retained by providers, for example for model training, increasing the risk of misuse or data breaches.

Traditional anonymization methods rely on rule-based de-identification, such as named entity recognition or pattern matching, to remove surface-level identifiers like names, social security numbers or explicit locations. They frequently overlook the context-dependent semantics that LLMs can exploit, so private information that is embedded in context rather than stated explicitly remains inferable. This gap calls for anonymization techniques that account for semantic context and defend against inference-based privacy threats, while preserving the meaning and readability of the text, that is, techniques that achieve a good privacy-utility trade-off.

A growing body of work pursues LLM-based anonymization to protect semantic-level private information from model inference. In feedback-guided adversarial anonymization, an LLM anonymizer rewrites the input text while a second LLM, acting as an adversary, attempts to infer private attributes from the rewritten output; based on this adversarial feedback, the anonymizer iteratively refines its output to prevent the inferences that remain possible. With GPT-4 as both anonymizer and adversary, this approach achieves a substantially better privacy-utility trade-off than traditional industry-grade anonymizers. However, reliance on large proprietary models is costly and requires sending the very text that should be protected to potentially untrusted external systems. Attempts to transfer these anonymization capabilities into smaller models have been explored only to a limited extent, and existing approaches still depend on a proprietary model to provide the adversarial feedback, incurring similar costs and privacy concerns.

The open problem is therefore whether, and how, small language models that can run locally under modest compute budgets can become effective anonymizers that protect semantic-level private information against inference by strong LLM adversaries, without relying on any external model at inference time. Can such models reach a privacy-utility trade-off comparable to, or better than, that of anonymizers built on frontier proprietary LLMs, including on texts where personal information is conveyed by the overall context rather than by explicit mentions, while remaining cheap enough to deploy in settings with strict data-confidentiality requirements?

Predicting the intermediate trajectories between an initial and a target distribution is a central problem in generative modeling. Tasks such as crowd navigation or modeling cell-state transitions under perturbation involve learning a transport map between two empirically observed endpoint distributions, rather than from the noisy prior required by denoising diffusion and flow matching. The Schrödinger bridge problem seeks an optimal stochastic map between a pair of endpoint distributions that minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence to an underlying reference process. Schrödinger bridge matching solves this problem by learning a drift field that matches a mixture of conditional stochastic bridges between endpoint pairs, and generalized Schrödinger bridge formulations add a non-linear state cost, interpretable as the potential energy of the system, to describe systems whose optimal dynamics are not captured by the standard squared-Euclidean cost of entropic optimal transport.

These approaches have important limitations. They typically assume conservation of mass from the initial to the target distribution, which fails to capture dynamical population behaviors such as the growth and destruction of mass that are common in single-cell population data. They also model a single stochastic path: samples are transported from the initial distribution to the target through independent stochastic trajectories, without accounting for branching dynamics, so these methods are inherently limited to unimodal transitions and cannot capture branched or divergent evolution from a common origin to multiple distinct modes. When a system follows a branched trajectory that diverges toward several target modes, approximating the multi-modal target by simulating many independent particles is susceptible to mode collapse, with particles concentrating on dominant high-density modes or traversing only low-energy intermediate paths. Even when particles do reach several modes, counting where they end up gives only an indirect estimate of how mass splits across trajectories: it neither describes how mass is distributed over time nor reveals when the population begins to diverge toward different targets.

Yet branching is central to many real-world systems. When a homogeneous cell population undergoes a perturbation such as a gene knockout or a drug treatment, it frequently undergoes fate bifurcation, splitting into multiple phenotypically distinct outcomes or committing to divergent cell fates. Such trajectories are observable in single-cell RNA sequencing data, where each subpopulation evolves independently and grows or contracts along its trajectory toward a distinct terminal state. Predicting how cell states change after a perturbation is a crucial problem for therapeutic design, but the intermediate states between the unperturbed and perturbed populations are usually unknown, and intermediate snapshots are often sparse or unavailable. Related work leaves this gap open. Branched dynamics have been explored for optimal transport and Brownian motion, but matching one initial distribution to multiple terminal distributions through stochastic bridges has not been explicitly formulated; branching Brownian motion, for instance, describes particles that proliferate in number rather than a fixed population whose mass divides among distinct trajectories with their own terminal states. Some unbalanced transport methods that model growth rely on reconstruction losses on observed intermediate snapshots and fail to learn meaningful trajectories when these snapshots are unavailable, and existing models of perturbation responses either predict only the terminal perturbed state or model a single unimodal trajectory between one pair of boundary distributions.

This raises the following questions. Given samples from an initial population and from a terminal population that has split into several distinct modes, each holding a known share of the total mass, how can one learn a set of energy-minimizing stochastic bridges that represent the divergence of the population from a common origin into multiple distinct terminal states? How can such a model determine when and where branching occurs, and how mass is redistributed among branches over time, so that each terminal mode receives its observed share while trajectories follow low-energy paths under a task-specific state cost? And can such branched dynamics be recovered from initial and terminal snapshots alone, without intermediate-time supervision and without the mode collapse that affects single-path bridge matching?

Inverse problems arise in many domains, including computer vision, protein science, medical imaging and scientific computing. The goal is to reconstruct an unknown signal x ∈ R^n from noisy measurements y ∈ R^m, with y = A(x) + η, where A is a known forward operator and η is additive measurement noise. Diffusion models have recently shown powerful capabilities in modeling complex data distributions, and they provide a powerful class of priors for high-dimensional data, such as natural images, when solving inverse problems.

Methods for solving inverse problems fall broadly into two families. Maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference seeks the single most probable x: it delivers fast optimization, but struggles with high noise and multimodal posteriors and easily converges to local minima. The Bayesian alternative samples from the posterior p(x|y) ∝ p(x) p(y|x) to generate plausible reconstructions, quantify uncertainty and handle multimodality. Both critically depend on a powerful prior, such as a pretrained diffusion model, that encodes the complex statistical structure of the data.

Although diffusion-based solvers have shown remarkable success across diverse inverse problems, current methods suffer from three complementary limitations. (1) Iterative guidance methods, such as DPS, DDRM, DDNM, ΠGDM and TMPD, try to sample the intermediate posteriors p(x_t|y) along the reverse diffusion, which requires the intractable likelihood p(y|x_t) at every intermediate timestep. They approximate it, for example through Tweedie's formula, and apply likelihood-gradient corrections directly to the intermediate states. Because such gradients generally contain components orthogonal to the data manifold, these corrections systematically push the intermediate states off the learned manifold and violate the training-time noise conditioning of the denoiser, leading to failed reconstructions such as accumulated artifacts; even second-order corrections of the guidance trajectory still modify intermediate states and risk drifting off the manifold. (2) Stochastic MAP methods that optimize in image space, such as ReSample, DiffPIR, DAPS, SITCOM and DIIP, can match the measurements well with very sharp details, but they require carefully tuned hyperparameters to avoid overfitting to noise, which limits their effectiveness when the noise is high or unknown. Some of them are formulated as posterior samplers yet use a heuristic measurement-noise level much smaller than the true one to strengthen measurement consistency, which makes them effectively MAP-like and equally sensitive to noise. (3) Deterministic MAP methods that optimize over the diffusion model's input noise, such as DMPlug, remove randomness but are sensitive to measurement noise and, lacking posterior exploration, often get stuck in a single mode, especially in severely ill-posed problems such as phase retrieval. Early stopping can limit noise overfitting, but its criterion is task- and noise-dependent, and at high noise levels the optimizer often becomes trapped in a local mode anyway. In short, enforcing data consistency in the middle of the diffusion process can break adherence to the prior, while optimizing only for fidelity leads to overfitting or mode collapse.

These failure modes point to two requirements. A solver should maintain manifold feasibility: the states it feeds to the pretrained denoiser should remain close to the high-probability manifold of the corresponding noise level, so that the final reconstruction lies on the learned data manifold. At the same time, it should explore the posterior well enough to escape spurious local modes, rather than collapsing onto the mode nearest to its initialization.

A further practical difficulty is that the level, and even the type, of measurement noise is often unknown and may not be Gaussian, which makes the likelihood term itself intractable. Existing methods handle this with tunable hyperparameters that control the strength of the likelihood term, or with task-specific early-stopping criteria, typically tuned for one particular type and level of noise; they must therefore be re-tuned for each task, dataset and noise level, which is impractical when the noise is unknown.

This raises the following questions. How can a pretrained diffusion prior be used to sample from the posterior of an inverse problem without approximating intractable intermediate likelihoods and without ever feeding off-manifold states to the denoiser? How can such a sampler explore the solution space well enough to avoid spurious local modes in severely ill-posed, multimodal problems, so that its reconstructions do not depend on the initialization? Can it be robust to measurement noise, in the sense that its reconstructions do not overfit the noise, without hand-tuned regularization weights or early stopping? And can it handle measurement noise of unknown level and type with a single fixed set of hyperparameters across tasks, datasets and noise levels, at a computational cost that remains practical?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: dynamic consistency and manifold preservation
PROPOSAL: Develop a method called Dynamic Consistency and Manifold Preservation (DCMP), which iteratively updates the diffusion guidance process by matching the intermediate states to the manifold — instead of directly feeding them back to the denoiser. First, we use the learned denoiser to define a manifold — where data likelihood is high — by calculating the mean of the denoiser output for a range of noise inputs. Then, at each timestep, we check if the guidance signal differs significantly from the manifold. If it does, we re-align the guidance trajectory to be closer to the manifold. This should maintain the learned data distribution, avoiding drift off the manifold and guaranteeing manifold feasibility.
CONTROLS: Compare against DPS and DDRM.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: DCMP should significantly reduce the off-manifold drift seen in current methods and maintain reliable reconstructions, even at high noise levels. A minor issue could be that manual tuning of parameters for DCMP would be needed for different noise distributions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: uncertainty-aware reconstruction guidance
PROPOSAL: Introduce an uncertainty-aware variant of the guidance process, Uncertainty-Aware Reconstruction Guidance (UARG), by modelling and learning the compact uncertainty via an ensemble of diffusion models, each with a distinct noise schedule. During the guidance process, we draw samples from the distributions output by the ensemble, and combine them to inform the reconstruction guidance signal. This approach can estimate and incorporate the uncertainty, adapting the guidance process to the inherent uncertainty in the posterior and, consequently, escape spurious modes more effectively.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard guidance methods, and assess the impact of ensemble size on performance.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: UARG would have improved performance over standard guidance methods for challenging inverse problems, but careful ensemble size and model selection could be required, while estimating uncertainty could increase computational cost.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: probabilistic forward mappings
PROPOSAL: To address the intractable likelihoods, develop Probabilistic Forward Mappings (PFM), a probabilistic, invertible, and differentiable approximation of the forward operator A. We achieve this by training a probabilistic neural network that maps the true forward operator to a Gaussian process, allowing us to treat the forward operator as a probabilistic function and comptuted the likelihoods, p(y|x), in closed-form. PFM can be efficiently inverted to produce samples from the intractable forward process.
CONTROLS: Compare against approximate likelihood methods (e.g. Tweedie's formula) and assess the impact of model capacity on performance.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: PFM should provide accurate approximations of the likelihoods without adding additional hyperparameters or prior knowledge, but the performance would heavily depend on the choice of model and capacities.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: uncertainty-aware reconstruction guidance
PROPOSAL: Revising the previous proposal, introduce Uncertainty-Aware Reconstruction Guidance (UARG), but with an additional regularization term that encourages the ensemble of diffusion models to be consistent with the probabilistic forward mappings (PFM) - leading to a framework that simultaneously model the uncertainty of the inverse posterior, and approximates the intractable likelihoods in a probabilistic manner. This synergy can help the guidance process to dichotomize from potential spurious modes more effectively and estimate the noise level adaptively.
CONTROLS: Compare against UARG without the regularization term, standard guidance methods, and assess the impact of model capacity on performance.
COST: 450 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised UARG should improve upon both UARG and PFM individually, offering a more comprehensive approach to uncertainty modelling and probabilistic likelihoods estimation, with the potential downside of increased computational cost.

ACTION: REVISE
 NUMBER: 2
 TITLE: uncertainty-aware reconstruction guidance
PROPOSAL: Revising the previous proposal, introduce Uncertainty-Aware Reconstruction Guidance (UARG), but with an additional emphasis on robustness to noise levels - by learning a noise-adaptive versioning of the guidance process, which monitors the current noise level and weighs its contribution accordingly. To achieve this, we use a neural network that takes both the guidance state and the estimated noise level as inputs and outputs a noise-adaptive guidance signal. This approach can help the guidance process to adapt to the uncertainty in the noise, leveraging this learned noise robustness to supervise spurious modes and produce more accurate reconstructions.
CONTROLS: Compare against UARG without the noise-adaptive term, standard guidance methods, and assess the impact of noise level estimation accuracy on performance.
COST: 375 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised UARG should reduce the need for hand-tuning regularization weights and early stopping, and improve noise robustness, but may increase computational cost due to the additional neural network component.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adaptive diffusion guidance sampling
PROPOSAL: Develop an adaptive sampling method, Adaptive Diffusion Guidance Sampling (ADGS), which dynamically selects the most informative samples from the guided diffusion process, allowing for an efficient exploration of the solution space while maintaining a constrained number of samples. By iteratively Assessing the Information Content (AIC) of the samples and dynamically sampling from the intermediate posteriors, we can estimate which samples contribute most significantly to the reconstruction, and reserve computation resources accordingly.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard sampling methods (e.g. Independent Sampling, Sequential Sampling) and assess the impact of hyperparameters on performance. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ADGS should improve the efficiency of the sampling process while maintaining accurate reconstructions, but its effectiveness might depend heavily on the choice of AIC metric and the specific inverse problem at hand.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: inference-time model distillation
PROPOSAL: Introduce Inference-Time Model Distillation (ITMD), a technique to reduce the computational resources needed for inference by distilling a large diffusion model into a smaller, more efficient version while preserving the accuracy of the original model. Specifically, we use a knowledge distillation framework with the goal of matching the output probabilities of the original model, while minimizing a metric of similarity between the two models' weights.
CONTROLS: Compare against pruning and quantization methods for model size reduction, and assess the impact of hyperparameters on performance.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ITMD should lead to a significant reduction in computational resources required for inference, without a substantial loss in accuracy, making it feasible to deploy the proposed methods on edge devices and for large-scale real-world applications. However, finding the optimal distillation parameter might be challenging.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: manifold-aware reconstruction uncertainties
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to quantify the reconstruction uncertainty in a probabilistic and mathematically grounded manner, by modeling the output variability of a diffusion-based sampler conditioned on the true forward operator and noise, leading to a lognormal distribution over reconstructions. This estimate can be directly mapped back to the original reconstruction problem, unbiasedly estimating the subtle noise artifacts, ill-posedness of images, providing informative information on reconstruction reliability.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing uncertainty estimation methods (e.g. MC dropout, variational inference) and assess the impact of model capacity on performance.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed method should provide a robust and accurate measure of reconstruction uncertainty, capable of distinguishing between low-confidence regions and more reliable areas, but it may be computationally expensive due to the need to condition on the true forward operator.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 6
TITLE: manifold-aware reconstruction uncertainties
PROPOSAL: Revising the previous proposal, refine the method to estimate manifold-aware reconstruction uncertainties by incorporating the probabilistic forward mappings (PFM) estimates directly within the uncertainty estimation process. This allows us to capture the inductive bias and prior knowledge of the diffusion model to directly inject uncertainty information into the reconstruction uncertainty calculations, leading to a more principled and accurate estimate of uncertainties. Additionally, introduce a novel strategy to actively leverage this uncertainty information to actively correct for errors and spurious modes.
CONTROLS: Compare against the previous manifold-aware uncertainty estimation method and assess the impact of incorporating PFM on performance and computational cost.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The refined method should lead to more accurate uncertainty estimates, and the active correction mechanism should help correct for spurious modes, but it remains to be seen whether the increased complexity and computational costs would be justified.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: experimentally validating the approach on challenging inverse problems
PROPOSAL: Develop a comprehensive suite of experiments on a diverse set of real-world inverse problems, including image super-resolution, image inpainting, image deblurring, phase retrieval, and high dynamic range (HDR) image reconstruction. Evaluate the proposed methods' performance on these experiments, assessing both quantitative metrics and qualitative visual inspections, and systematically comparing against state-of-the-art methods. Collectively, these experiments should provide a broad validation of the proposed approach's efficacy across various real-world inverse problems.
CONTROLS: Compare against DPS, DDRM, and other state-of-the-art inverse problem solvers on a diverse range of benchmarks.
COST: 5,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The comprehensive experiments should convincingly demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of the proposed methods on challenging real-world inverse problems, showing that the improvements outweigh the increased complexity.

Grounding procedural steps in videos is crucial for enabling machines to follow along and assist humans in complex tasks such as cooking a recipe, assembling furniture, or performing maintenance work. This ability is particularly valuable for real-time procedural guidance in augmented and extended reality applications, where recognizing task progress allows users wearing headsets or smart glasses to receive timely, step-specific instructions. The task of Video Step Grounding (VSG) takes as input a list of procedural steps extracted from an instructional article (e.g., a recipe or a how-to guide) and a video of the same task, and aims to identify which of the steps are performed in the video, that is, which step, if any, each part of the video depicts (a segment may also show an action outside the listed steps).

Existing VSG approaches align procedural step descriptions with their corresponding video frames. Earlier works relied on weakly-supervised learning from instructional narrations, while more recent methods increasingly leverage language models and large-scale pretraining, for instance using language models to turn noisy narrations or speech transcripts into steps and pseudo-labels for training. These strategies face two key limitations. First, they need a training set, entailing the cost of collecting (and potentially annotating) it; moreover, a training set can bias models toward the specific videos and procedural tasks it depicts, limiting their generalization capability. Second, they assume offline processing, where the entire video is available ahead of time, which makes them unsuitable for real-world applications that process a live video stream and must make decisions as it unfolds.

This calls for addressing VSG online and without training: video segments arrive one after the other, and whether the current segment depicts a given step must be decided using only that segment and the segments preceding it, with no task-specific training data. This setting is challenging. Predictions must be made from partial evidence, and without the task-specific representations that would typically be learned from a dedicated training set. The task also requires fine-grained video understanding, since key steps of instructional tasks often involve similar objects or scenes: "inserting a screw" or "aligning parts" may look alike in tasks such as "Assemble a chair" and "Fix a table", making them hard to distinguish without nuanced semantic understanding. Large pretrained multimodal models have demonstrated impressive zero-shot performance on a wide variety of tasks without further tuning, and work on video-language alignment has moved away from frame-caption embedding similarity, which struggles to capture temporal dynamics, toward such models; yet whether off-the-shelf models can ground procedural steps when they only see the current short segment remains an open question. Moreover, a prediction made from the current segment alone has no memory of what has already happened in the video, so uncertain observations cannot benefit from past evidence, while storing and reprocessing the whole history is impractical on a live stream.

The research questions are therefore: can video step grounding be performed online, on a streaming video and without any training, at a level competitive with training-based offline methods? And how can knowledge from past segments be injected into the prediction for the current segment, without storing the whole history and while preserving a zero-shot, training-free approach?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating baseline models for online video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate a set of strong multimodal model baselines for video step grounding, adapted to process only one video segment at a time. Specifically, we will investigate large-scale multimodal transformer models like CLIP, and recent multimodal variants like OSIM and VisIoL, with a focus on evaluating their zero-shot performance when processing a live video stream one segment at a time. We will measure performance using metrics like accuracy, F1-score, and Hamming loss on real-world video step grounding benchmarks from instructional cooking recipe videos and egocentric procedural activity videos.
CONTROLS: We will compare our zero-shot baseline models to models that have been pre-trained on VSG tasks and fine-tuned on a specific dataset, providing an offline benchmark for comparison. We will also evaluate various ablations of our zero-shot models, including the effect of using different types of multimodal input (e.g., frame, audio, or both) and different window sizes for segmenting video frames
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that competing zero-shot models struggle due to the lack of task-specific information in the model, however strong multimodal models that are not specifically designed for this task can still achieve good performance due to their general-purpose multimodal capabilities, and ablation studies will point towards multimodal input as a key factor for zero-shot performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adding contextualized embeddings for video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will investigate using contextualized embeddings to improve the performance of online video step grounding. Specifically, we will experiment with using pre-trained BERT-like models to generate text embeddings for the step descriptions, and multimodal transformer models to generate visual embeddings for the video frames. We will then use a common encodings space for the step descriptions and video frames to compute similarity scores. This approach aims to capture the nuances of language and visual context that are crucial for accurately grounding video steps.
CONTROLS: We will control for the quality of the step descriptions by evaluating the RAKE (Rapid Automatic Keyword Extraction) score of the text, and we will compare our contextualized embeddings approach to a baseline model that uses keyword matching between step descriptions and video frames. We will also evaluate the effect of using different quality and quantities of step descriptions on model performance, in the same setting as the proposal.
COST: 8000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that using contextualized embeddings improves the performance of video step grounding, especially in scenarios where step descriptions have high RAKE scores, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: revising evaluating baseline models for online video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate a set of strong multimodal model baselines for video step grounding, adapted to process only one video segment at a time, focusing on the use of cross-modal learning. Specifically, we will investigate how different cross-modal fusion methods (e.g., concatenation, attention, and late fusion) can improve the zero-shot performance of large-scale multimodal transformer models like CLIP, and recent multimodal variants like OSIM and VisIoL. We will measure performance using metrics like accuracy, F1-score, and Hamming loss on real-world video step grounding benchmarks from instructional cooking recipe videos and egocentric procedural activity videos.
CONTROLS: We will compare our zero-shot baseline models to models that have been pre-trained on VSG tasks and fine-tuned on a specific dataset, providing an offline benchmark for comparison. We will also evaluate various ablations of our zero-shot models, including the effect of using different types of multimodal input (e.g., frame, audio, or both) and different window sizes for segmenting video frames. Additionally, we will control for the impact of cross-modal learning on model performance by adapting the original two-step fine-tuning approach for cross-modal training in online videos.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that cross-modal learning is a key factor for achieving strong zero-shot performance in video step grounding, and that different cross-modal fusion methods perform differently on various VSG tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: improving adding contextualized embeddings for video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will improve our approach to using contextualized embeddings for video step grounding by incorporating attention mechanisms to dynamically weigh the importance of different tokens in both the step descriptions and video frames. Specifically, we will experiment with using multi-head attention to compute attention weights that align the text and visual embeddings, and use these attention weights to fuse the embeddings. We will explore different options for initialising the attention weights, such as using dominant keywords from the step description or learned weights from the model.
CONTROLS: We will compare our improved contextualized embeddings approach to our previous baseline method, and evaluate its performance with different options for initialising the attention weights. We will also control for the impact of attention mechanisms on model performance by comparing our results with a baseline model that uses a pre-defined fusion scheme, following the setup outlined in the proposal.
COST: 7000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that our improved contextualized embeddings approach with attention mechanisms outperforms our previous baseline method, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: leveraging semantic graph reasoning for video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will investigate using semantic graph reasoning to reason about the relationship between video segments and step descriptions in video step grounding. Specifically, we will construct a knowledge graph that represents the semantic relationships between entities and actions in the step descriptions, and then use a graph neural network to reason about the relevance of the video segments to the step descriptions. We will evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks and compare it to our contextualized embeddings approach.
CONTROLS: We will control for the quality of the knowledge graph by evaluating the accuracy of the entity and action recognition methods used to construct the graph, and we will compare our graph reasoning approach to a baseline model that uses a simple matching scheme between the step descriptions and video segments.
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that semantic graph reasoning can improve the performance of video step grounding by capturing complex relationships between video segments and step descriptions, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: injecting temporal context with transformer encoder layers
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate the impact of injecting temporal context to our baseline models for video step grounding using transformer encoder layers. Specifically, we will modify our multimodal transformer model to include an additional encoder layer that takes into account the temporal relationships between consecutive video frames, and evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks. We will compare our results to our baseline model without temporal context and other state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of the additional encoder layer on model performance by comparing it to a baseline model with a reduced number of layers, and we will evaluate the effect of different window sizes for segmenting video frames on the performance of our model.
COST: 6500
PREDICTION: We expect to find that injecting temporal context improves the performance of our baseline model by capturing the nuances of the video sequence, and that this approach performs well even when the video sequence has a complex structure.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: enhancing leveraging semantic graph reasoning for video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will enhance our approach to using semantic graph reasoning for video step grounding by incorporating a procedure for iteratively refining the knowledge graph and re-reasoning about the relationship between video segments and step descriptions. Specifically, we will experiment with an iterative process that involves re-scoring the relevance of video segments to step descriptions based on the refined knowledge graph, and re-ranking the step descriptions based on their relevance to the video segments. We will evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks and compare it to our previous graph reasoning approach.
CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of the iterative refinement process on model performance by comparing it to a baseline model that uses a simple matching scheme between the step descriptions and video segments, and we will evaluate the effect of different refinement thresholds on the performance of our model.
COST: 8500
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the iterative refinement process improves the performance of our graph reasoning approach by capturing more nuanced relationships between video segments and step descriptions, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: fusing visual and language features with adaptive fusion mechanism
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate the impact of using an adaptive fusion mechanism to fuse the visual and language features extracted from the video frames and step descriptions in video step grounding. Specifically, we will design a mechanism that dynamically adjusts the weighting of the visual and language features based on the contextual information present in the step descriptions and video frames, and evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks.
CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of the adaptive fusion mechanism on model performance by comparing it to a baseline model that uses a fixed weighting scheme for the visual and language features, and we will evaluate the effect of different fusion mechanisms on the performance of our model.
COST: 7200
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the adaptive fusion mechanism improves the performance of our baseline model by capturing the complex relationships between the visual and language features, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating the impact of sample efficiency with few-shot learning
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the impact of sample efficiency on video step grounding using few-shot learning. Specifically, we will experiment with fine-tuning our baseline models using only a few examples of the video and step descriptions, and evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks. We will explore different few-shot learning strategies, such as batch optimization and meta-learning.
CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of the few-shot learning strategy on model performance by comparing it to a baseline model that uses a larger dataset for training. We will also evaluate the effect of different few-shot learning settings, such as the number of episodes and shots per episode, on the performance of our model.
COST: 5800
PREDICTION: We expect to find that our baseline model can achieve good performance with only a few examples, and that the few-shot learning approach improves the sample efficiency of our model without compromising its overall performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: a comprehensive evaluation and analysis of online video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a comprehensive evaluation and analysis of the performance of our existing approaches for online video step grounding, including evaluating the impact of each component on the overall performance, identifying the limitations of our approaches, and exploring potential avenues for future research.
CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of each component by comparing the performance of our baseline models to each of our proposed approaches, in the same setting as the proposal. We will also conduct a qualitative analysis of the performance of our approaches, including an evaluation of the errors made by each approach and the types of errors that are most frequent.
COST: 0 (no additional computation required)
PREDICTION: We expect to identify areas for improvement in our existing approaches, gain a deeper understanding of the challenges and limitations of online video step grounding, and identify potential avenues for future research that can lead to even better performance.

Transformers, powered by attention mechanisms, have become the default backbone for sequence modeling across language, vision, speech, and decision making. Their success is often linked to selective access to an ever-growing key-value cache while retaining parallel training and inference. In large language models, this selective ability, composed across multiple attention layers and residual pathways, supports long-range memory retrieval and the algorithmic behaviors associated with in-context learning (for example induction heads and pattern completion), as shown by empirical and mechanistic studies.

Causal softmax attention combines strong selectivity with parallel efficiency: at each step it forms a distribution over past indices and mixes their values, while all steps can be computed in parallel. Given queries, keys and values $Q,K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}$ with rows $q_t$, $k_i$, $v_i$, define masked scores $s_{t,i}=q_t^\top k_i/\sqrt{d}$ for $i\le t$ and $-\infty$ otherwise, and set $\alpha_{t,\cdot}=\mathrm{softmax}(s_{t,\cdot})$, a probability distribution over $\{1,\dots,t\}$. The step-$t$ read is $o_t=\sum_{i\le t}\alpha_{t,i}v_i$, which lies in the convex hull of $\{v_1,\dots,v_t\}$; stacking all steps yields $O=AV$ with $A_{t,i}=\alpha_{t,i}$, so a single matrix multiply produces all outputs.

This convex-mixture view explains the efficiency of attention, but it also reveals a dilemma between lossless storage and lossy processing. The key-value cache stores the full context, but the read is lossy: each head applies the same weights to all coordinates of $v_i$, so the output lies in the convex hull of the stored values and all channels are synchronized. As a result, even simple per-channel indexing, such as returning $(v_{i_1,1},\dots,v_{i_D,D})$ where each coordinate $j$ is taken from its own past index $i_j$ (for example, a coordinate-wise argmax), cannot be represented unless all chosen indices coincide. This limitation hinders Transformers in long-range modeling with non-sequential or irregular timestep indexing, and in tasks where channel-wise structure is critical, such as multivariate time series modeling.

Most recent advances in attention aim to improve expressivity and efficiency, typically by designing richer selection distributions while still reading values through a token-separable linear combination. These include sparse attention patterns, low-rank projections, and kernelizable variants with normalization or gating. Efficiency-oriented work accelerates attention through factorized implementations, or replaces the cache with streaming state space models and recurrent networks that keep a fixed-size state. Across these lines, computation becomes faster or the distribution richer, but the read remains a linear mix: channels share weights, and even simple per-channel indexing cannot be realized in one step. Some recent works explore more complex combinations, such as nonlinear mixing or hard/top-k selection, yet these mainly target training stability or accuracy in specific cases and do not address the lossy-processing limitation.

This leaves an open problem: how can the read of an attention-style sequence mixer be redesigned to remove this linear read bottleneck and support per-channel, context-dependent selection from memory, so that different channels can retrieve different past indices in the same step, while keeping causal parallelism and the asymptotic time complexity of the underlying selection mechanism (for example, quadratic in sequence length for softmax attention and linear for linear-time variants)? And does closing this gap between lossless storage and lossy processing translate into better sequence modeling in practice?

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: temporal dependency in the selection bottleneck
PROPOSAL: Investigate how much the linear mixing bottleneck in causal softmax attention can be attributed to temporal dependencies in the selection distribution. One approach could be to analyze the structural similarity between the attention weights and the sequence itself. Specifically, we can apply tools from information theory and dynamical systems to study how the selection distribution captures temporal patterns in the input sequence. We hypothesize that a redesigned read function can decouple the selection bias from this temporal structure, leading to improved expressivity.
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard causal softmax attention mechanism, and analyze the results with a baseline that fixes the selection distribution.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to show that temporal dependencies in the selection distribution contribute significantly to the linear mixing bottleneck, and that decoupling these dependencies can improve the expressivity of the attention mechanism. However, we also expect to find that this improvement comes at a cost of requiring more compute during inference.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: hierarchical channel attentions
PROPOSAL: Design and evaluate a variant of causal softmax attention where each output channel has its own dedicated focus selection mechanism, applied on top of the standard causal softmax attention. This hierarchical approach should allow for per-channel selection of past indices, even when the standard attention mechanism cannot. Specifically, we will implement a two-stage selection process where the seeds for the second stage are selected based on pairwise activations or hierarchical pooling operations. This would enable context-dependent channel-wise retrieval of past indices.
CONTROLS: Evaluate against the standard causal softmax attention and compare with an ablation study where only one stage of the hierarchical mechanism is applied.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved performance on tasks with non-sequential or irregular timestep indexing, but may also find increased computational complexity compared to the standard causal softmax attention mechanism.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: factorized causal softmax
PROPOSAL: Modify causal softmax attention to have a factorized structure, where each output channel is represented as a weighted sum of a smaller set of key-value pairs, with coefficients that can be selected independently for each channel. This should reduce the linear mixing bottleneck by allowing per-channel selection from a smaller sparse subset of the key-value pairs. We will apply techniques from compressed sensing and sparse recovery to select the most important key-value pairs and adjust the channel-wise coefficients accordingly.
CONTROLS: Evaluate against standard causal softmax attention and the hierarchical channel attentions from proposal 2, using a baseline that selects the most important key-value pairs based on random sampling.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved performance on tasks with long-range dependencies, as the factorized structure reduces the memory usage and computationally complexity of the selection process. However, the effectiveness of this approach also depends on the choice of sparse recovery techniques and the parameter tuning for the selection coefficients.

ACTION: REVISE 
TITLE: temporal dependency in the selection bottleneck 
PROPOSAL: Refine the investigation of temporal dependencies in the selection distribution by considering the impact of common temporal structures such as autoregressive dependencies or time of arrival, on the selection process. One approach is to use recurrent inductive biases, by using recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or long short-term memory (LSTM) networks to model these temporal dependencies, and then analyze how these dependencies affect the selection distribution. We can use this analysis to inform the design of a more expressive selection mechanism that decouples the selection bias from these temporal structures.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline that fixes the selection distribution and evaluate against a task that emphasizes temporal dependencies.
COST: no additional compute is assumed for this revision
PREDICTION: We expect to better understand the role of temporal dependencies in the selection bottleneck and identify a more robust approach to decoupling the temporal structure from the selection process, leading to improved expressivity and reduced overfitting.
