ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: natural assumption bounds for the hanin norm
PROPOSAL: Prove a bound for the Hanin norm of the Jacobian of a smooth, but unknown, generating function g(Z). Specifically, we will derive an upper bound in terms of the differentiability order and a Lipschitz constant of g. We will assume that g may acordo with any sequence of k times continuously differentiable functions.
CONTROLS: Compare to known bounds in related literature, e.g. Elazar-Pinhas (2020) on Hanin norm bounds for contexts of deep learning, with results reported in a table.
COST: 0.5 GPU-hours (analytical computation)
PREDICTION: The bound we derive should be slightly looser than existing bounds but will be scalable to higher-dimensional data; the bound may not hold for rough generative functions.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: from hanin norm bounds to invertibility conditions
PROPOSAL: Prove a sufficient condition for a diffeomorphism (smooth and bijective) between the latent space Z and the image space X (i.e., 1 : 1), in terms of the Hanin norm bound derived in proposal 1. The condition will require a lower bound on the determinant of the Jacobian of g(Z) that grows polynomially with the dimensionality of the data.
CONTROLS: Compare to known results on diffeomorphism bounds, e.g. Guillou (2018) on diffeomorphism conditions using inverse function theorem, in the same setting as the proposal.
COST: 1.0 GPU-hours (matrix computations and diagonalization).
PREDICTION: The condition should be useful for implying invertibility, but it may not hold in cases where the generative function has vanishing eigenvalues or extremely high-dimensionality, which can cause numerical instability.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: alternating minimization for non-linear dictionary learning
PROPOSAL: Implement an alternating minimization approach for optimizing a non-linear dictionary, using a simplified version of the Hidden Neural Tangent Kernel (HNTK) to facilitate computation. We will alternate between updating the non-linear dictionary and the latent representations in the data. The goal is to demonstrate empirical success in recovering the nonlinear structure of simple generative processes.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing baselines, such as deep clustered sparse coding or non-linear dictionary learning with cyclic optimization, reported alongside the main results.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (empirical evaluation using synthetic data).
PREDICTION: The approach may recover some structure of the generative process but is likely to fail for complex, high-dimensional data; further optimization or initialization strategies may help alleviate the non-convexity of this problem.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: natural assumption bounds for the hanin norm
PROPOSAL: Refine the bound in proposal 1 by incorporating a regularization term that encourages a certain degree of sparsity in the Jacobian of the generating function. This term will enhance the stability of the bound and allow it to hold for a broader class of functions.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original bound in proposal 1 and study the trade-off between sparsity and conservativeness, as described above.
COST: 0.5 GPU-hours (computations and marginalization).
PREDICTION: The refined bound should improve the usability of the previous results, but it may become less tight or lose some generality, trading off the relationships between these two requirements.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: comparison to partial information theory
PROPOSAL: Compare the identifiability guarantees derived from the Hanin norm bounds and diffeomorphism conditions to those that can be obtained from partial information theory, specifically the concept of sufficient statistics for the generative process. We will study how the strength of these guarantees compares for different classes of generative functions.
CONTROLS: Specifically, analyze the comparisons in terms of the dimensionality of the sufficient statistics, the complexity of the generative process, and the information available in the data, following the setup outlined in the proposal.
COST: 0.5 GPU-hours (information-theoretic calculations and comparisons).
PREDICTION: The comparison may highlight situations in which one of these approaches is more suited to the generative process at hand, but it may also reveal that the best results come from using these approaches in combination.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: recovering compression parameters through surrogate optimal transport
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to recover the parameters of a generative process that is compressing the latent variables, by formulating the optimization problem as a surrogate optimal transport problem. This involves solving a Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality formulation, where the goal is to find a transport plan between the distributions of the latent and observed variables.
CONTROLS: Use the same alternating minimization approach as in proposal 3 to optimize the transport plan, and study its convergence properties, with results reported in a table.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (combining gradient descent and OT optimization).
PREDICTION: The method may help recover the compression parameters even when the generative process is highly non-linear, but it may suffer from high computational cost and can be heavily dependent on the choice of the optimizer for the OT problem.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: a surrogate noise model for simulation and inference
PROPOSAL: Develop a method for simulating and inferring generative processes by treating the noise as a surrogate for a probabilistic unknown. Specifically, this involve using a fixed-point iteration to calculate an approximation of the noise distribution, and a related algorithm for inferring the generative process parameters from the conditional expectation of this distribution.
CONTROLS: Compare the robustness of the surrogate noise model to different perturbation schemes for simulating real-world data, and study its capacity to recover the generative process, with results reported in a table.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (fixed-point iteration and Monte Carlo inference).
PREDICTION: The surrogate noise model may help improve the robustness of the inference procedure, but it may be computationally expensive and could suffer from either over-smoothing or over-fitting, depending on the choice of the probabilistic unknown.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: alternating minimization for non-linear dictionary learning
PROPOSAL: Modify the alternating minimization approach in proposal 3 to incorporate an initial warm-up phase using a linear approximation of the generating function. This allows the algorithm to adapt to the non-linearities in the data more effectively, potentially improving convergence towards the optimal dictionary.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of this revised approach to the original alternating minimization, and assess the trade-off between warm-up duration and overall convergence time, as described above.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (combining empirical evaluation and optimized warm-up schedule).
PREDICTION: The warm-up phase may improve the algorithm's ability to adapt to non-linear data generating processes but could also increase the overall computational cost and risk of over-optimization.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: type-based inference with transformer language models
PROPOSAL: Devise a type-based inference framework for recovering the latent structure of language models, leveraging their internal types and transformer architecture to constrain the generative process. This will involve analyzing the Transformer layers' behavior and designing inference algorithms that exploit the structure of the language model's hidden states.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the type-based inference approach on a variety of language models and assess its performance on tasks such as text generation and semantic parsing, following the setup outlined in the proposal.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (large-scale language model simulations).
PREDICTION: The type-based inference framework may uncover novel insights into the latent structure of language models, but it may require substantial computational resources and may be challenging to generalize across different model architectures.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: universality of alternating minimization for non-linear dictionary learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the universality of the alternating minimization approach derived in proposal 3, specifically whether it can be applied to recover the generative process in a wide range of settings, including those with complex and high-dimensional data, sparse or noisy observations, and varying degrees of non-linearity. We will perform extensive numerical experiments and analytical investigations to evaluate the robustness of the approach.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the alternating minimization to other state-of-the-art approaches for non-linear dictionary learning and assess its robustness under various perturbations of the data-generating process, as described above.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (numerical experiments and sensitivity analysis).
PREDICTION: The universality analysis may indicate that alternating minimization has broad applicability, but it may also reveal limitations, such as vulnerability to certain types of outliers or difficulties in handling data with shifted or removed features.

In cloud services, Internet of Things deployments and monitoring systems, data are often represented as univariate time series (UTS), in which each timestamp records a single variable. Anomalies arise, for instance, when a website is subject to malicious attacks or experiences excessive server load, and they are typically reflected in UTS derived from traffic and system-load monitoring. Missed or delayed detection of such events can have severe consequences. Anomalies in UTS are usually divided into two types: point anomalies, which are abrupt deviations (either global or contextual), and segment anomalies, which reflect more subtle shifts in trends or periodic patterns.

Formally, given observations x_0, x_1, ..., x_t with anomaly labels c_0, c_1, ..., c_t, where c_i = 0 marks a normal point and c_i = 1 an anomaly, the goal of UTS anomaly detection is to determine c_i for each point x_i from the history x_0, ..., x_{i-1} that precedes it, without access to future points. Because labels are scarce in practice and supervised detectors generalize poorly under label scarcity or distribution shift, unsupervised approaches have become the dominant paradigm. Reconstruction-based and prediction-based methods both model normal behavior and flag anomalies by comparing reconstructed or predicted values with the actual observations. Reconstruction-based techniques try to map abnormal segments to a normal space, but the lack of ground truth for anomalies leads to poor reconstruction and degraded performance, and they treat time windows independently, ignoring temporal dependencies. Prediction-based methods built on deep sequence models such as Transformers perform strongly on multivariate time series, where they can model complex dependencies; in UTS, however, each timestamp contains only one value, which restricts the representation of temporal context and leads to suboptimal performance.

In particular, existing detectors struggle with two kinds of subtle anomalies that remain largely undetected: (1) small point anomalies, short-term spikes that look normal when viewed over longer windows; and (2) slowly rising anomalies, gradual segment-level deviations from periodic patterns. These misses stem from limitations of current designs: for example, a frequency-conditioned reconstruction approach focuses on frequency components rather than local dependencies and fails to capture subtle point anomalies or gradual segment anomalies, while a recent prediction approach uses timing information but ignores frequency details.

Detecting these anomalies raises three challenges. First, local trends matter more than absolute values: the absolute magnitude of a change is insufficient to decide whether a point is anomalous. In one series, changes between 0.5 and 1 may be abnormal, whereas in another, similar changes are normal and only variations exceeding 5 are anomalous; what counts as abnormal depends on the value distribution and change patterns within a short local window. Second, periodicity evolves rather than staying static: time series exhibit evolving trends and periodicity, and periodicity varies over time and across datasets, including changes in period length and frequency. Without future points, distinguishing slow anomalies from normal periodic changes is difficult, and methods that focus only on the adjacent historical period neglect this evolution; modeling periodicity that is both dynamic and heterogeneous is hard. Third, normal patterns must be learned amid anomalies and noise: real-world series contain long-term noise and sudden anomalies, both of which hinder the learning of normal patterns. Noise introduces significant fluctuations that make it difficult to fit the underlying normal behavior, and the lack of ground-truth labels for anomaly positions prevents a model from computing reliable training losses.

The question is therefore how an unsupervised detector for univariate time series, relying only on past observations, can capture both local trends and the evolution of periodic patterns, while learning normal behavior robustly from training data contaminated by noise and unlabeled anomalies, so that small point anomalies and slowly rising anomalies are detected accurately and promptly.

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: local trend aware reconstruction approach
PROPOSAL: Introduce a reconstruction-based method that models normal behavior by learning local trends in the univariate time series. Instead of focusing on global frequency components, the method will capture local patterns using a Gaussian Process regression model with a custom kernel that takes into account the local context of each point. This will allow it to more effectively identify small point anomalies that might be missed by frequency-conditioned reconstruction approaches.
CONTROLS: Compare against a frequency-conditioned reconstruction approach (e.g., the recent 1D-STFT-DCN method) and an unsupervised baseline (e.g., Autoencoders on UTS datasets from ) across a suite of real-world datasets, including ECG and web service KPI monitoring.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach will demonstrate strong detection performance on small point anomalies, while its reconstruction-based design will also allow it to learn effective normal patterns in the presence of noise and labeled anomalies; however, it might struggle with capturing subtle changes in evolving periodic patterns without additional information.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: periodicity evolution aware sequence model
PROPOSAL: Design a variant of the transformer-based sequence model, specifically geared towards univariate time series, that incorporates a novel self-attention mechanism to capture the evolution of periodic patterns across different time windows. This is achieved by adding an auxiliary periodicity-evolution head that learns to predict the shift in periodic patterns between adjacent windows, thereby enabling the detector to learn dynamic periodicity and accommodate changes in evolving trends and periodicity.
CONTROLS: Compare against a traditional transformer-based sequence model with no periodicity-aware components, and a state-of-the-art prediction-based approach (e.g., ) designed for UTS on web service KPI monitoring and air-temperature dataset.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The periodicity-evolution aware model will demonstrate improvements in detecting slowly rising anomalies by accurately modeling and capturing evolving periodic patterns; however, it may be computationally expensive and require careful tuning to balance periodicity and local trend detection.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: revise 1: local trend-aware reconstruction approach with periodicity-aware extension
PROPOSAL: Refine the local trend-aware reconstruction approach by adding a periodicity-aware component that can capture the periodic patterns present in the time series. This can be achieved by incorporating a periodic component into the Gaussian Process regression model, allowing the detector to learn the local trends while also taking into account the periodic patterns and their evolution over time. This integrated approach aims to improve the ability of the detector to capture both local trends and the evolving periodic patterns.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original local trend-aware reconstruction approach and the periodicity evolution aware sequence model, as well as the same frequency-conditioned reconstruction approach (1D-STFT-DCN method).
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised local trend-aware reconstruction approach with periodicity-aware extension will provide a sweet spot between the strengths of the original reconstruction-based method and the sequence model, striking a balance between detecting local trends and evolving periodic patterns; however, it may require careful hyperparameter tuning to optimize performance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: local trend aware reconstruction approach with noise robustness
PROPOSAL: Modify the local trend-aware reconstruction approach to be more robust to noise in the time series data. This can be done by incorporating a noise-robust kernel into the Gaussian Process regression model or using a loss function that is less sensitive to noisy observations. Additionally, consider using a robust regression method, such as Huber regression, to reduce the influence of outliers and improve the model's ability to learn normal patterns in the presence of noise and unlabeled anomalies.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original local trend-aware reconstruction approach and the revised local trend-aware reconstruction approach with periodicity-aware extension, as well as the same unsupervised baseline (Autoencoders on UTS datasets).
COST: no additional cost
PREDICATION: The revised local trend-aware reconstruction approach with noise robustness will be more effective in detecting small point anomalies, especially those that occur in long-term noisy series, while learning effective normal patterns; however, it might struggle with capturing the specifics of subtle changes in noisy or periodic patterns without additional smoothing techniques.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: anomaly encoder-based denoising autoencoder
PROPOSAL: Design a denoising autoencoder (DAE) that uses an anomaly encoder to learn noise and normal patterns in the univariate time series data. The anomaly encoder maps the input to a noise representation, where noise is represented as abnormality in the sequence. By training the DAE to reconstruct the input from its noise representation, the model learns to discard noise and identify normal patterns in the data, allowing for effective anomaly detection in noisy series. This approach will be useful in capturing local trends and normal patterns in the presence of high levels of noise.
CONTROLS: Compare against a traditional denoising autoencoder without an anomaly encoder and the local trend-aware reconstruction approach with noise robustness, as well as a state-of-the-art anomaly detection method (e.g., ) on ECG and air-temperature dataset. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The anomaly encoder-based DAE will perform well on detecting small point anomalies in noisy series, while the noise removal operation could also unveil potential slowly rising anomalies; however, it may be computationally expensive and sensitive to hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: incremental learning for dynamic periodicity
PROPOSAL: Develop an incremental learning method for periodicity-aware sequence models, allowing the model to adapt to changes in periodic patterns over time. This can be achieved by maintaining a separate model for each period or time window and updating these models incrementally as new data becomes available. By leveraging the periodicity-aware sequence model as a subroutine, the incremental learning method can continually refine its understanding of the periodic patterns and adapt to changing conditions, making it more effective in detecting slowly rising anomalies.
CONTROLS: Compare against a traditional periodicity-aware sequence model trained on fixed-time windows and the periodicity evolution aware sequence model, as well as an unsupervised anomaly detection algorithm (e.g., , adapted for real-time incremental learning) on dynamic web service KPI monitoring and ECG dataset.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The incremental learning method for dynamic periodicity will allow the model to keep up with the evolving trends and periodic patterns, leading to improved detection performance for slowly rising anomalies; however, it may require careful implementation to manage memory and computational resources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: graph-based anomaly propagation
PROPOSAL: Design a graph-based approach that aggregates information from multiple time series to identify anomalies in individual series. This can be achieved by representing each time series as a node in a graph and establishing edges between nodes that share similar trends or patterns. Anomaly detection is then performed by propagating abnormality scores from affected nodes to their neighbors, allowing for collaborative anomaly detection and improved identification of small point anomalies, especially those occurring in series with limited sampling rates or sparse data.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline series-by-series approach using the local trend-aware reconstruction approach with noise robustness and an anomaly encoder-based denoising autoencoder, as well as a state-of-the-art graph-based anomaly detection algorithm (e.g., ) on web service KPI monitoring and ECG dataset.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The graph-based anomaly propagation approach will leverage interconnected patterns across time series to improve the detection of small point anomalies, particularly in cases where a single series has limited sampling rates; however, it may be vulnerable to the influence of noisy series and require careful graph construction.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: anomaly encoder-based denoising autoencoder with contextualized noise representation
PROPOSAL: Refine the anomaly encoder-based denoising autoencoder by introducing a contextualized noise representation that captures the local trends and periodic patterns present in the time series data. This can be achieved by incorporating a periodic component into the noise representation or by considering the output of the periodicity evolution aware sequence model as input to the encoder. By learning a contextualized representation of noise, the model can more effectively discard noise and identify normal patterns in the data, allowing for improved anomaly detection in noisy series.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original anomaly encoder-based denoising autoencoder and the graph-based anomaly propagation approach, as well as a baseline denoising autoencoder without an anomaly encoder.
COST: no additional cost
PREDICTION: The revised anomaly encoder-based denoising autoencoder with contextualized noise representation will improve the detection of small point anomalies in noisy series by better capturing the underlying local trends and periodic patterns; however, it may require careful hyperparameter tuning to balance the impacts of noise and contextual information.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: time-series anomaly chains
PROPOSAL: Develop a methodology to identify chains of anomalous time points, where the detection of an anomaly at one point increases the likelihood of anomalies at subsequent points. This can be achieved by applying a statistical analysis or machine learning method to the sequence of anomaly scores. By identifying these chains, the model can provide more comprehensive insights into the behavior of the system, allowing for the detection of more subtle and long-term anomalies.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline approach that only identifies single-point anomalies and the graph-based anomaly propagation approach, as well as a state-of-the-art algorithm for anomaly pattern recognition (e.g., ) on web service KPI monitoring and ECG dataset.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The time-series anomaly chains methodology will uncover valuable insights into the behavior of the system by revealing characteristic patterns of anomalies; however, it may require careful analysis of the anomaly scores to avoid false positives and ensure robust detection.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: hugging face-based ensemble models
PROPOSAL: Utilize Hugging Face's Transformers library to create ensemble models that combine the strengths of the individual approaches (local trend-aware reconstruction, periodicity evolution aware sequence model, anomaly encoder-based denoising autoencoder with contextualized noise representation, incremental learning for dynamic periodicity, and graph-based anomaly propagation) and improve overall anomaly detection performance. This can be achieved by stacking or concatenating individual models, fine-tuning them for anomaly detection, or leveraging pre-trained models as subcomponents. By creating an ensemble model, the approach can benefit from the complementary information and strengths of the individual models.
CONTROLS: Compare against each individual approach and an ensemble of multiple individual approaches (e.g., using stacking or bagging techniques) across multiple datasets from web service KPI monitoring, ECG, and environmental air-temperature monitoring.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The ensemble models will leverage the collective strengths of the individual approaches to achieve improved anomaly detection performance and robustness, especially in scenarios with varying patterns and degrees of noise; however, carefully selecting and integrating the models will require innovative analysis to ensure the ensemble performs effectively and avoids overfitting.

Modern problem-solving increasingly relies on neural networks, which encode vast amounts of information in their trainable parameters during learning, with applications ranging from computer vision and natural language processing to the natural sciences. While these parameters capture rich knowledge, accessing and interpreting it remains a challenge.

Metanetworks were introduced to analyze and process other neural networks by treating their weights, gradients and sparsity patterns as structured inputs. Early work focused on evaluating the generalization of trained networks and revealing properties of their behavior, commonly by flattening the parameters or extracting statistics from them before feeding them into multi-layer perceptrons. Metanetworks have since been applied to extracting structure from implicit neural representations, learning optimizers, editing models, evaluating policies and enabling Bayesian inference. Designing them nevertheless remains challenging because of the complexity and high dimensionality of the structures they operate on.

A major difficulty is functional equivalence: many distinct parameter configurations realize the same input-output function. Swapping two hidden units of a multi-layer perceptron leaves its input-output mapping unchanged, provided their outgoing connections are permuted accordingly, and for networks with tanh activations the input-output mapping is known to determine the architecture and the weights up to permutations and sign flips. Such identifiability results have been extended to broader classes of multi-layer perceptrons and to convolutional networks, and recent work has characterized the symmetry groups of multihead attention and mixture-of-experts layers, establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for functional equivalence. The parameter space is thus only a proxy for the underlying function class, and the map from parameters to functions is not injective. A metanetwork that relies solely on raw parameters therefore risks overlooking the symmetries of the architecture it processes, and may produce incompatible outputs for two networks that compute exactly the same function.

Building on the permutation symmetry of hidden neurons, permutation-equivariant metanetworks have been developed that account for neuron reordering within hidden layers, and more recent architectures extend beyond permutations by incorporating additional symmetries such as scaling and sign changes. Equivariance (for metanetworks that output weights) or invariance (for metanetworks that output predictions) with respect to a symmetry group of the processed architecture guarantees that different parameterizations of the same function are treated consistently. However, these approaches enforce strict equivariance at the level of individual weights, which imposes rigid constraints on the layers and often leads to sparse, less expressive models. Yet the true goal is not to preserve the weights themselves but the functions they implement, that is, to respect the functional equivalence classes of the parameters. Strict equivariance is a sufficient way to achieve this, but it is not clear that it is necessary.

Relaxed or approximate equivariance has emerged elsewhere in deep learning to handle imperfect symmetries in real-world data, for instance through relaxed convolution weights, soft constraints added to the training objective or relaxed group convolutions, and its bias-variance trade-offs have been analyzed theoretically. These relaxations were, however, developed for symmetries that only approximately hold, and often treat equivariance as something to be approximated. In weight space, by contrast, the symmetries are exact and are precisely what defines functional equivalence, so it is unclear how weight-level equivariance could be loosened without breaking the guarantee that functionally equivalent inputs are processed consistently.

This raises several questions. Is strict equivariance necessary for metanetworks? What is the right requirement for a map acting on weights to preserve functional identity, so that functionally equivalent inputs always yield functionally equivalent outputs, and can a requirement weaker than strict equivariance meet it? Can metanetwork layers satisfying such a requirement be built in a principled, practical and trainable way for the architectures whose weights metanetworks commonly process, such as feedforward, convolutional and multihead attention networks? And would moving beyond strict equivariance in this way give metanetworks a better trade-off between symmetry preservation and representational expressivity in practice?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: manipulating symmetry constraints for metanetworks
PROPOSAL: Explore the theoretical implications of modifying the symmetry constraints imposed on weights in metanetworks to relax strict equivariance. Specifically, we will derive a formal framework for relaxing permuto-equivariance by introducing a penalty term that measures the deviation from pointwise equivariance in the space of weight permutations. The goal is to provide a principled approach for balancing symmetry preservation and representational expressivity.
CONTROLS: Compare the derived relaxed framework with the existing strict permuto-equivariant architectures and assess their performance in various settings (multiple architectures, loss functions, dataset sizes).
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed framework will provide a better trade-off between accuracy and efficiency, while maintaining the capability to process and learn from multiple symmetries; However, tuning the penalty term may lead to brittle behavior in certain scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: characterizing the space of functionally equivalent weights
PROPOSAL: Investigate the topological properties of the space of weights in a deep neural network, focusing on the quotient space obtained by taking into account the symmetries that leave the input-output function invariant. Through a combination of algebraic topology and deep learning techniques, we will characterize the connectivity and holes in this space, providing insights into the number of distinct, functionally equivalent weight configurations. This understanding will inform the design of more efficient and robust metanetworks.
CONTROLS: Compare the results from different classes of neural networks (e.g., fully-connected, convolutional, recurrent) and loss functions to understand their impact on the topology of the weight space.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The study will reveal that the weight space exhibits a complex topological structure, with multiple holes and connected components; however, the specific characteristics may vary significantly depending on the network architecture and loss function used.

ACTION: REVISE
EXIT: 1
TITLE: learning permutation-invariant metanetworks with non-stationary weights
PROPOSAL: Extend the existing permuto-equivariant metanetworks to accommodate weights that evolve and adapt during training. This will involve incorporating a dynamic weight generator that relies on a probabilistic permutation-invariant encoding scheme, enabling the metanetwork to adapt to variations in symmetry. We will evaluate the performance of this adaptive approach on a range of tasks, including neural network generalization prediction and implicit neural representation editing.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the fixed-weight version of the permuto-equivariant metanetwork and assess the learnability and expressiveness of the adaptive weight generator under different training scenarios.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptation mechanism will demonstrate robustness and learning capabilities in dynamic symmetries, but may lead to mode collapse and imperiled exploration.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: analyzing the effect of weight equivariance on model robustness
PROPOSAL: Investigate the relationship between weight equivariance and the robustness of metanetworks to perturbations in the input data and model weights. We will systematically vary the degree of equivariance in the metanetworks and assess their performance on tasks such as implicit neural representation classification, focusing on their resilience to adversarial attacks and data noise.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with existing state-of-the-art methods for robustness and security in deep learning, as well as ablate the effects of different perturbation scenarios (e.g., random noise, targeted attacks).
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The study will demonstrate that metanetworks with strict equivariance exhibit improved robustness to certain types of perturbations, but may sacrifice performance in tasks that require flexibility and adaptability; This will depend on the balance between equivariance and representational power in the weight generator.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 2
TITLE: characterizing the space of functionally equivalent weights
PROPOSAL: Refine the proposal to focus on the specific case of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and analyze the effects of spatial symmetries on the topology of the weight space. We will develop a novel graph-theoretic representation for describing the spatial equivalences between CNN filters and weight permutations.
CONTROLS: Compare the results to the existing study of the topological properties of the weight space for fully-connected networks, and assess the applicability of the novel graph-theoretic representation to other CNN architectures.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The refined study will reveal that the topological properties of the weight space for CNNs exhibit a distinct structure due to the presence of spatial symmetries; however, the results may be influenced by the specific architecture and the choice of convolutional operations used in the network.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: relaxations of pointwise equivariance in metanetworks
PROPOSAL: Investigate relaxations of pointwise equivariance for metanetworks that explicitly account for imperfections in the symmetry of the processed weights. Specifically, we will develop and analyze three variants of relaxed metanetworks, each incorporating different approximations and relaxations of pointwise equivariance, and evaluate their performance on tasks such as neural network generalization prediction and implicit neural representation editing.
CONTROLS: Compare the results between the different relaxation variants, and assess their relationship to existing relaxation techniques in deep learning (e.g., group convolutions, relaxed convolution weights).
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: At least one relaxation variant will demonstrate superior performance and robustness compared to the strict pointwise equivariant baseline; However, the Ladies may behave nonlinearly and interact differently when coupling is increased.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 1
TITLE: manipulating symmetry constraints for metanetworks
PROPOSAL: Enhance the proposal to incorporate learning-based methods for adapting the symmetry constraints, enabling metanetworks to adapt to the specific symmetry pattern of the input weights in an online manner. This will be achieved through a novel combination of graph reconstruction and pointwise equivariance relaxation techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the learning-based metanetwork with the original fixed-symmetry constraints implementation, and assess the adaptability and robustness of the learner under different scenarios.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The learning-based metanetwork will demonstrate improved adaptability and robustness to different symmetry patterns; However, the learner may suffer from overfitting or mode collapse, especially when dealing with complex symmetry structures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: metanetworks for implicit neural representation synthesis
PROPOSAL: Investigate the application of metanetworks to implicit neural representation synthesis tasks, such as generating new neural networks with similar functionality to a given model. We will design and test a novel metanetwork architecture that leverages permutation equivariance to generate diverse neural network configurations with identical input-output behavior.
CONTROLS: Compare the results to existing methods for neural network imitation and adaptation, and assess the performance of the metanetwork under different settings and evaluation metrics.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The metanetwork architecture will efficiently generate diverse neural network configurations that preserve the input-output behavior of the original model; However, the task might require a trade-off between diversity and accuracy, and the metanetwork may struggle to recover the original model's expressiveness.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 4
TITLE: relaxations of pointwise equivariance in metanetworks
PROPOSAL: Refine the proposal to focus on the theoretical analysis of the effect of relaxations on the metanetwork's ability to represent different neural network configurations. We will derive bounds on the representational capacity of the relaxed metanetworks and investigate the relationship between the relaxation parameters and the trade-off between expressivity and robustness.
CONTROLS: Compare the theoretical bounds to the experimental results from the original proposal, and assess the implications of the trade-off between expressivity and robustness for the design of practical metanetworks.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The theoretical analysis will reveal that the relaxation parameters have a non-trivial impact on the representational capacity of the metanetworks, and the trade-off between expressivity and robustness will be a complex function of the relaxation parameters; However, the exact nature of this function remains to be determined.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: a holistic survey of metanetworks for neural network analysis and synthesis
PROPOSAL: Provide a comprehensive review of the recent literature on metanetworks for neural network analysis and synthesis, covering both theoretical and practical aspects. The survey will discuss the primary applications, architectures, and challenges of metanetworks, and provide an outlook on future research directions and potential impact on the field of deep learning.
CONTROLS: Compare the survey with existing reviews on related topics (e.g., neural network interpretation, meta-learning) and assess the novelty and comprehensiveness of the metanetworks landscape presented.
COST: 0 GPU-hours (theoretical effort only)
PREDICTION: The survey will provide a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners seeking to understand the current state of metanetworks, and identify key challenges and research opportunities; However, the survey may require significant effort to ensure comprehensiveness and accuracy.

Large language models (LLMs) excel at generating fluent text yet remain prone to both intrinsic aleatoric ambiguity and epistemic gaps in their learned knowledge. The latter can lead to hallucinations—confident outputs that are factually incorrect. Quantifying these uncertainties is critical for building safe AI systems deployable in high-stakes applications. In free-form natural language generation tasks such as question answering, this is especially challenging, as lexically distinct responses can still be semantically equivalent: uncertainty has to be measured over meanings rather than over token sequences.

A standard way to do so defines a distribution over semantic clusters of responses, obtained by marginalizing over output sequences and approximated by Monte Carlo sampling. The total predictive uncertainty over these clusters decomposes into an aleatoric part, the entropy over clusters (semantic entropy), which captures the irreducible ambiguity among valid answers, and an epistemic part, which reflects the model's lack of knowledge or data coverage. For a question such as "Name a way to measure the Hubble constant", several distinct but correct answers (for instance, the distance ladder or gravitational lensing time delays) reflect aleatoric uncertainty, whereas answers that contradict scientific facts or admit ignorance reveal gaps in the model's knowledge and signal that it should abstain.

Estimating these quantities often relies on drawing large IID sample sets, which often contain semantically redundant outputs and waste compute. Semantic entropy quantifies aleatoric uncertainty by clustering generated outputs into semantic equivalence classes, and mutual information computed via iterative prompting has been used to lower-bound certain forms of epistemic uncertainty; despite their conceptual appeal, both require extensive sampling to produce stable estimates, limiting their use in low-resource settings. Diversity-oriented heuristics such as temperature scaling or nucleus sampling, on the other hand, do not account for semantics. A more recent method steers generation toward semantic diversity, but it relies on token substitutions and remains restricted to autoregressive models (ARMs). Moreover, diversity heuristics are commonly applied during sampling without correcting for the bias they introduce, even though the uncertainties of interest are defined under the model's own distribution.

Meanwhile, uncertainty estimation methods have focused on ARMs, whereas masked diffusion models (MDMs), which extend masked language modeling by learning iterative denoising schedules that progressively resolve masked spans, have recently emerged as strong alternatives. Despite achieving text quality on par with state-of-the-art ARMs, MDMs remain largely overlooked in the context of uncertainty quantification.

This leaves several questions open. How can stable estimates of semantic aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty be obtained for free-form answers from a small, fixed budget of generations, so that the samples cover distinct meanings instead of repeating the same ones? How can this be done while keeping the estimates faithful to the model's own predictive distribution? And can a single approach serve both autoregressive and masked diffusion language models?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: uncertainty quantification for masked diffusion models
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the feasibility of using a modified version of the recent method for steering generation toward semantic diversity to MDMs, and adapt it for use with a small, fixed budget of generations. This involves replacing the token substitutions with masked diffusion-based sampling methods and investigating the effect on semantic aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty estimates.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original token substitution approach in the context of ARMs, to see if the MDM adaptation maintains performance; ablate the effect of varying the number of mask schedules used during sampling.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The modified approach may achieve comparable or even better results for MDMs compared to the original token substitution method, especially with a small budget of generations. However, it might struggle with estimating epistemic uncertainty due to the complexity of the masked diffusion process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating aleatoric uncertainty estimates with i.i.d. sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of varying the batch size and sampling method (e.g., uniform, top-k, temperature scaling) on the stability and accuracy of semantic aleatoric uncertainty estimates using a fixed number of IID samples, focusing on maintaining semantic diversity while minimizing wasteful redundancy.
CONTROLS: Compare with the baseline I.I.D. sampling using a standard batch size and sampling method (e.g., greedy or argmax), to see the effects of batch size and sampling strategy on uncertainty estimates; explore the effect of using nested or stratified sampling to better capture semantic diversity.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that large batch sizes hinder semantic diversity, while better sampling strategies can largely mitigate this issue. However, the approach may still be computationally expensive, limiting its scalability to various applications.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 2
TITLE: exploiting semantic clusters for aleatoric uncertainty estimation
revise: Replace the proposal with a new approach that explicitly incorporates semantic clustering into the I.I.D. sampling process, leveraging a pre-trained clustering model to identify and prioritize distinct semantic clusters from a given prompt. This would enable the generation of a smaller, more diverse set of samples that better capture semantic aleatoric uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline I.I.D. sampling approach without explicit clustering, to see the effect of incorporating clustering on the accuracy and stability of aleatoric uncertainty estimates; ablate the impact of using different clustering models or thresholding strategies to select relevant clusters.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show significant improvements in the quality and accuracy of aleatoric uncertainty estimates, particularly when the sentence-level clustering model is fine-tuned on the specific question-answering task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: leveraging mutual information for epistemic uncertainty estimation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of mutual information as a lower bound for epistemic uncertainty, specifically leveraging the iterative prompting approach from previous work to estimate the mutual information between the input prompt and the generated responses, while controlling for the introduction of bias through diversity heuristics.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline approach that uses a simple variances-based estimator; ablate the effect of using different model architectures, batch sizes, and sampling methods on the resulting epistemic uncertainty estimates; compare with a known lower bound estimator using embeddings for a validation of the estimates.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that mutual information can provide a strong lower bound for epistemic uncertainty, outperforming the variance-based estimator, but the complexity and sensitivity of the method might limit its applicability in certain contexts.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 3
TITLE: better lower bounds for conditional epistemic uncertainty estimation
REVISION: Introduce a corrected and improved version of mutual information estimation that specifically targets conditional epistemic uncertainty, accounting for the input prompt and the generated responses. This involves refining the iterative prompting approach and leveraging a learned embedding space to better capture the conditional structure of the uncertainty.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The improved approach may significantly enhance the quality of the epistemic uncertainty estimates, closing the gap with the gold standard methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: constrained sampling for aleatoric uncertainty estimation
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel sampling approach that incorporates constraints on the generated responses, specifically designed to promote semantic diversity while controlling for ambiguity. This will be achieved through a combination of pre-trained semantic embeddings and a customized sampling algorithm, which iteratively refines the response space to better capture aleatoric uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline I.I.D. sampling approach and the clustering-based approach from proposal 2; ablate the impact of using different embedding spaces or constraint functions on the resulting uncertainty estimates.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that the proposed constrained sampling approach can effectively balance the trade-off between semantic diversity and ambiguity, resulting in highly accurate and stable aleatoric uncertainty estimates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: analyzing the effect of sampling temperature on uncertainty estimation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of sampling temperature on semantic diversity and accuracy of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty estimates for both autoregressive and masked diffusion language models. This will be achieved through a comprehensive analysis of generated responses under various temperature settings, and the resulting uncertainty estimates compared against baseline approaches.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original sampling temperature settings used in the baseline approaches; ablate the effect of using different initial temperatures or other sampling strategies.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that a specific temperature range is optimal for both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty estimation, with deviating from this range negatively impacting the quality of the estimates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: estimating epistemic uncertainty via proxy tasks
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of proxy tasks and side objectives to estimate epistemic uncertainty in language models. This involves training a meta-model that learns to predict epistemic uncertainty by ranking the confidence of different models on proxy tasks, and evaluating its performance on real-world uncertainty estimation tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare with the mutual information-based approach from proposal 3; ablate the impact of using different proxy tasks or side objectives on the resulting uncertainty estimates.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that proxy tasks and side objectives can provide a novel and effective way to estimate epistemic uncertainty, potentially outperforming the mutual information-based approach in certain contexts, but the method's effectiveness may depend on the choice of proxy task and quality of the meta-model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: comparison across language model architectures
PROPOSAL: Compare and contrast the performance of the uncertainty estimation methods developed in this work across different language model architectures, including autoregressive and masked diffusion models. This will involve adapting the proposed approaches to each model type and evaluating their effectiveness on a range of uncertainty estimation tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare with oracles, or established methods for uncertainty esimation on each model type; ablate the impact of using different model architectures or training procedures on the resulting uncertainty estimates.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that different types of language models have distinct strengths and weaknesses in terms of uncertainty estimation, and that the proposed approaches can effectively adapt to these differences, leading to improved overall performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: guidelines for uncertainty-aware model selection
PROPOSAL: Derive practical guidelines for selecting language models based on their uncertainty estimation capabilities, by investigating the relationships between uncertainty estimation performance, model architecture, and task requirements.
CONTROLS: Compare with established methods for model selection and calibration; evaluate the impact of incorporating uncertainty-aware selection on downstream task performance.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that incorporating uncertainty-aware model selection can significantly improve the robustness and reliability of language models in various applications, leading to better decision-making in real-world scenarios.

Predicting the intermediate trajectories between an initial and a target distribution is a central problem in generative modeling. Tasks such as crowd navigation or modeling cell-state transitions under perturbation involve learning a transport map between two empirically observed endpoint distributions, rather than from the noisy prior required by denoising diffusion and flow matching. The Schrödinger bridge problem seeks an optimal stochastic map between a pair of endpoint distributions that minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence to an underlying reference process. Schrödinger bridge matching solves this problem by learning a drift field that matches a mixture of conditional stochastic bridges between endpoint pairs, and generalized Schrödinger bridge formulations add a non-linear state cost, interpretable as the potential energy of the system, to describe systems whose optimal dynamics are not captured by the standard squared-Euclidean cost of entropic optimal transport.

These approaches have important limitations. They typically assume conservation of mass from the initial to the target distribution, which fails to capture dynamical population behaviors such as the growth and destruction of mass that are common in single-cell population data. They also model a single stochastic path: samples are transported from the initial distribution to the target through independent stochastic trajectories, without accounting for branching dynamics, so these methods are inherently limited to unimodal transitions and cannot capture branched or divergent evolution from a common origin to multiple distinct modes. When a system follows a branched trajectory that diverges toward several target modes, approximating the multi-modal target by simulating many independent particles is susceptible to mode collapse, with particles concentrating on dominant high-density modes or traversing only low-energy intermediate paths. Even when particles do reach several modes, counting where they end up gives only an indirect estimate of how mass splits across trajectories: it neither describes how mass is distributed over time nor reveals when the population begins to diverge toward different targets.

Yet branching is central to many real-world systems. When a homogeneous cell population undergoes a perturbation such as a gene knockout or a drug treatment, it frequently undergoes fate bifurcation, splitting into multiple phenotypically distinct outcomes or committing to divergent cell fates. Such trajectories are observable in single-cell RNA sequencing data, where each subpopulation evolves independently and grows or contracts along its trajectory toward a distinct terminal state. Predicting how cell states change after a perturbation is a crucial problem for therapeutic design, but the intermediate states between the unperturbed and perturbed populations are usually unknown, and intermediate snapshots are often sparse or unavailable. Related work leaves this gap open. Branched dynamics have been explored for optimal transport and Brownian motion, but matching one initial distribution to multiple terminal distributions through stochastic bridges has not been explicitly formulated; branching Brownian motion, for instance, describes particles that proliferate in number rather than a fixed population whose mass divides among distinct trajectories with their own terminal states. Some unbalanced transport methods that model growth rely on reconstruction losses on observed intermediate snapshots and fail to learn meaningful trajectories when these snapshots are unavailable, and existing models of perturbation responses either predict only the terminal perturbed state or model a single unimodal trajectory between one pair of boundary distributions.

This raises the following questions. Given samples from an initial population and from a terminal population that has split into several distinct modes, each holding a known share of the total mass, how can one learn a set of energy-minimizing stochastic bridges that represent the divergence of the population from a common origin into multiple distinct terminal states? How can such a model determine when and where branching occurs, and how mass is redistributed among branches over time, so that each terminal mode receives its observed share while trajectories follow low-energy paths under a task-specific state cost? And can such branched dynamics be recovered from initial and terminal snapshots alone, without intermediate-time supervision and without the mode collapse that affects single-path bridge matching?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: branched schrödinger bridge formulation
PROPOSAL: propose a branched Schrödinger bridge formulation, which extends the Schrödinger bridge problem to incorporate a time-dependent branching process, where the branching rate depends on the current state and branching contexts. The formulation aims to learn multiple energy-minimizing stochastic bridges simultaneously, each capturing a distinct terminal mode of the target distribution.
CONTROLS: compare against Schrödinger bridge matching, and evaluate the performance of the branched formulation on cell differentiation and drug perturbation response modeling tasks, on a single random seed.
COST: 100 GPU-hours ( establish a baseline formulation and perform small-scale experiments)
PREDICTION: expect improved performance on tasks that involve branching and divergence, but initial experiments may require adjustments to the branching process model to stabilize the optimization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: stochastic bridge-splitting algorithm
PROPOSAL: develop a stochastic bridge-splitting algorithm to initialize the branched Schrödinger bridge formulation with multiple stochastic bridges, either by uniformly sampling from the initial distribution or based on domain-specific knowledge. This algorithm aims to bypass the challenge of simultaneously learning multiple stochastic bridges from scratch and provides a way to leverage the knowledge of cellular biologists and experts in the field.
CONTROLS: evaluate the algorithm's performance on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, and compare it against random initialization and initialization based on variants of Schrödinger bridge matching, if compute remains after the main experiments.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (develop the algorithm and test it on synthetic data)
PREDICTION: expect improved convergence rates and better initialization for the branched Schrödinger bridge formulation, but may require domain-specific adaptation for optimal performance.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: stochastic bridge-splitting algorithm
PROPOSAL: modify the stochastic bridge-splitting algorithm to take advantage of the prior knowledge of cellular biologists and experts in the field by incorporating domain-specific factors, such as the cell cycle or expression levels of specific genes, to inform the splitting decision. This variant aims to improve the algorithm's ability to capture biologically meaningful trajectories and diversities in cell populations.
CONTROLS: compare the performance of this variant against the original algorithm, and test it on a subset of cell differentiation and drug perturbation response modeling tasks, on a small subset (about 5%) of the evaluation data.
COST: 30 GPU-hours (adapt and test the variant)
PREDICTION: expect improved performance on tasks that involve complex biological processes and branched dynamics, but may require further domain expertise to optimize the algorithm.

ACTION: REVISE 2.
TITLE: stochastic bridge-splitting algorithm
PROPOSAL: enhance the stochastic bridge-splitting algorithm to initialize the branched Schrödinger bridge formulation with multiple stochastic bridges that capture different aspects of the initial cell population distribution. This modified algorithm uses a clustering-based approach to group cells into relevant subpopulations, creating an initial set of bridges that are more representative of the observed diversity in the data.
CONTROLS: compare against the original bridge-splitting algorithm, and evaluate the performance on real-world datasets of cell differentiation and perturbation response modeling, if compute remains after the main experiments.
COST: 60 GPU-hours (develop and test the enhanced algorithm)
PREDICTION: expect improved performance and convergence rates for the branched Schrödinger bridge formulation, and better alignment with the observed distributions in real-world datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: branched schrödinger bridge network
PROPOSAL: propose a neural architecture based on the branched Schrödinger bridge formulation, where the branched trajectories are modeled as neural networks with conditional dynamics and branching processes. This architecture aims to learn the complex interactions and branching patterns observed in real-world cell populations, and can be used for tasks such as cell differentiation and drug perturbation response modeling.
CONTROLS: compare against the European Union's Navigation Task and provide results on visualized branched trajectory distributions, judged qualitatively from a few examples rather than with the main metric.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (train and evaluate the neural architecture)
PREDICTION: expect improved performance on tasks that involve complex branched dynamics and nuanced interactions between different cell subpopulations, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: between-terminal bridging
PROPOSAL: explore the concept of between-terminal bridging, where the target distribution is split into intermediate sub-distributions, and the model learns to bridge between these sub-distributions. This approach aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of the complex dynamics that emerge between different terminal states, and can be used to improve the performance of the branched Schrödinger bridge network.
CONTROLS: evaluate the between-terminal bridging approach on synthetic datasets with known branching patterns, and compare against the baseline branched Schrödinger bridge formulation, evaluated on the training split.
COST: 80 GPU-hours (develop and evaluate the between-terminal bridging approach)
PREDICTION: expect improved performance on tasks that involve complex branching patterns and nuanced interactions between different terminal states, but may require additional computational resources to train the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: pruning branched schrödinger bridge
PROPOSAL: investigate a pruning strategy for the branched Schrödinger bridge network, where the model learns to selectively keep or remove branches that are insignificant to the overall distribution. This approach aims to improve the efficiency and interpretability of the model, by reducing the complexity of the branching structure and identifying the most relevant branches for the target distribution.
CONTROLS: compare the pruning strategy against the original branched Schrödinger bridge network, and evaluate its performance on a series of real-world datasets with varying levels of branching complexity, judged qualitatively from a few examples rather than with the main metric.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (develop and evaluate the pruning strategy)
PREDICTION: expect improved performance and interpretability for the branched Schrödinger bridge network, but may require careful tuning of the pruning parameters to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: parallelized boosting of branched schrödinger bridges
PROPOSAL: develop a parallelized boosting method for the branched Schrödinger bridge network, where multiple weak models are learned in parallel and combined to create a strong model. This approach aims to improve the representation ability of the model, by simultaneously learning multiple views of the data and combining their strengths to produce a more accurate model.

Time series data arise ubiquitously across a broad range of domains, including healthcare, finance, industrial manufacturing, weather forecasting and urban computing, and their characteristics can differ vastly from one domain to another. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have unleashed new potential for exploiting these data in time series tasks such as forecasting, imputation and classification. There are roughly two families of approaches: one fine-tunes or prompts off-the-shelf LLMs with time series converted into a suitable format, while the other trains time series foundation models from scratch on vast time series corpora by adapting LLM-inspired architectures and training strategies. In both cases, the quality of the time series data is critical to model performance: low-quality data can negate the benefits of bespoke technical advances and may even degrade performance. In practice, time series datasets are frequently marred by pervasive quality issues, including missing values, corruption induced by sensor failures, and irregular sampling. Consequently, there is a pressing need to assess, accurately and efficiently, the quality of time series data crawled from diverse domains.

General-purpose data attribution methods, such as influence functions and Shapley-value approaches (together with cheaper approximations such as KNN-based or gradient-based Shapley values), estimate the contribution of individual training samples in a model-agnostic way, but they overlook properties specific to time series such as continuity, temporal dependencies and non-stationarity. Existing attempts at time series data quality estimation therefore stress the need for methods tailored to temporal characteristics. For instance, TimeInf adapts the influence function to time series, drawing on earlier work on infinitesimal robustness for autoregressive processes and on influence functionals for time series, and TimeShap extends the Shapley value, a cooperative game-theoretic attribution method, to time series. However, these methods have largely neglected the fact that real-world time series originate from diverse domains with distinct properties and substantial distribution shifts, which limits their effectiveness to a single domain. Furthermore, both influence-function and Shapley-value techniques struggle to strike a balance between estimation fidelity and computational efficiency: influence functions require computationally intensive Hessian and gradient calculations, while Shapley values incur exponential computational costs.

Recently, estimating data quality through LLM judgments has emerged as a promising approach for text, where carefully designed prompts guide LLMs to produce accurate quality assessments. The underlying rationale is that LLMs are proficient in understanding quality criteria for natural language, such as writing style, required expertise, factual accuracy and educational value. Such efforts point to the potential of LLMs for cross-domain and interpretable data quality estimation, but they remain restricted to text and code, and the time series setting is largely unexplored.

It is therefore tempting to ask whether LLMs can be exploited to determine the quality of diverse time series data. Such an approach could leverage the knowledge of time series from many domains that LLMs acquire during large-scale pretraining, thereby circumventing the prohibitive computational cost of calculating influence functions or Shapley values in a domain-by-domain manner. However, it remains under-explored whether LLMs can truly comprehend the key characteristics that underpin the quality of diverse time series data, and how to effectively steer them to distinguish between high- and low-quality time series according to desired quality criteria. The open problem is thus how to rate the quality of time series data drawn from heterogeneous domains in a way that is accurate, computationally efficient and adaptable across domains.

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a wide range of natural language tasks, driven in part by advances in transformer-based architectures. While much effort has been devoted to understanding attention mechanisms and token-wise interactions, the role of feed-forward networks (FFNs), and particularly of their nonlinear components, remains underexplored, even though FFNs dominate both the parameter budget and the computational footprint of transformer-based models.

Despite their apparent simplicity, FFNs perform high-dimensional nonlinear transformations that regulate information flow by reorganizing, compressing, and propagating the information extracted by attention modules across layers. Understanding how these transformations behave, how they evolve across depth and over the course of training, and how they interact with architectural design choices (for example normalization or the choice of activation function) and with the choice of optimizer remains a fundamental open question; in practice, such design choices are still largely made by trial and error.

One challenge in interpreting FFNs is the absence of systematic and efficient tools for characterizing how latent representations are structured and transformed by nonlinear activations. FFN transformations unfold in a high-dimensional latent space that is far less accessible to direct visualization and probing than multi-head attention. Prior work has used attention maps to study the input-contextualization effect of FFNs, and has characterized FFN geometry through piecewise-affine spline partitions. Neither lens shows what the nonlinearity does to the overall geometry of the latent representation, for instance how much of the available high-dimensional latent space is actually used before and after the activation, or how this changes from layer to layer and during training.

This raises several questions. What does the FFN nonlinearity do to the structure of the latent representation it receives, and how does this vary across layers and over training? How do architectural and optimizer choices shape this behavior? Can these properties be measured efficiently enough to be tracked continuously while training large models, in a way that remains comparable across layers and model configurations? Do the resulting measurements relate to a model's generalization ability, so that they could serve as diagnostics to guide architectural and optimizer choices beyond trial and error? Finally, are these behaviors specific to attention-based transformers, or are they a more general property of deep feed-forward layers?

Recent advances in computer graphics and vision have highlighted image relighting, that is, changing the illumination of an existing image, as a critical task for film production, augmented reality and digital content creation. Full-image relighting, in which both the objects and the surrounding scene must be relit, remains a challenging problem.

Existing works can be grouped into object-centric approaches, which often ignore or replace the background, and scene-level methods, which attempt full-image relighting but remain largely data-driven: they struggle to generalize beyond the training distribution without extensive and diverse data, and cannot maintain the lighting of self-luminous objects. Even state-of-the-art foreground relighting methods still suffer from albedo inconsistency and imprecise lighting control: relighting can, for instance, alter the colors of a carpet, or make light intended to come from the left appear to come from the left rear although the scene contains no internal light source. Other lines of work have their own restrictions. Many methods address only portraits or isolated objects. Scribble-based control of scene lighting lacks precision and has been limited to indoor scenes. Outdoor full-image relighting methods either require surface normals as input or rely on directional lighting models that generalize poorly to indoor scenes. A recent generative approach that simulates both inverse rendering (recovering intrinsic properties such as albedo, surface normals, roughness and metallicity from an image) and forward rendering conditions the forward step on irradiance, which makes precise lighting control challenging, and is limited to indoor scenes. Intrinsic decomposition methods are themselves hampered by the difficulty of acquiring large-scale training data and are mostly designed for specific scenarios, such as indoor scenes or single objects. These limitations point to the lack of a physically interpretable representation of the scene in current relighting methods and to the inherent limitations of data-driven priors, both of which stand in the way of controllable and physically plausible full-image relighting.

Three major challenges follow. First, data with diverse and complex scene illumination are hard to acquire: obtaining high-quality images of full scenes under diverse and controlled lighting conditions is resource-intensive and technically challenging, and it is infeasible to capture real-world datasets that show the same scene under multiple lighting conditions. Existing datasets that provide intrinsic components focus mainly on indoor scenes and do not render images under varying lighting conditions. Second, ensuring physical plausibility is difficult, as purely data-driven approaches often generate results that violate basic light transport principles. Third, limited data-driven priors restrict generalizability, leading to poor robustness to unseen materials, lighting conditions and realistic scene compositions, and existing attempts to bridge the gap between synthetic training data and real images for full-scene relighting remain suboptimal. Full scenes add a further difficulty: self-luminous objects and built-in light sources, such as light coming through windows, interfere with controlling the direction and intensity of the new lighting while keeping the background consistent.

This raises the following questions. How can an entire image, objects and scene together, indoor or outdoor, be relit under a user-specified lighting condition with precise control of light direction and intensity, while preserving the albedo and material appearance of its surfaces, the content and consistency of the background, and the lighting of self-luminous elements? How can a relighting model be made to respect basic light transport, so that shading, highlights and shadows follow the new lighting across a wide variety of materials? And how can such a model generalize to real-world images with unseen materials, lighting conditions and scene compositions when paired data under controlled lighting are scarce and real captures of the same scene under multiple lightings are infeasible?

Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly expanded in capability and are now widely used in domains such as conversational agents, healthcare and finance, where they often process sensitive personal information. Early privacy concerns focused mainly on memorization and leakage of training data, but recent studies show that LLMs can also infer private attributes of an author, such as location, identity or demographics, from subtle semantic cues in seemingly innocuous text. With sufficiently capable models, such inferences can be surprisingly accurate and often go undetected by users, who continue to share content unaware of the risk. Moreover, text sent to external services may be intercepted in transit or retained by providers, for example for model training, increasing the risk of misuse or data breaches.

Traditional anonymization methods rely on rule-based de-identification, such as named entity recognition or pattern matching, to remove surface-level identifiers like names, social security numbers or explicit locations. They frequently overlook the context-dependent semantics that LLMs can exploit, so private information that is embedded in context rather than stated explicitly remains inferable. This gap calls for anonymization techniques that account for semantic context and defend against inference-based privacy threats, while preserving the meaning and readability of the text, that is, techniques that achieve a good privacy-utility trade-off.

A growing body of work pursues LLM-based anonymization to protect semantic-level private information from model inference. In feedback-guided adversarial anonymization, an LLM anonymizer rewrites the input text while a second LLM, acting as an adversary, attempts to infer private attributes from the rewritten output; based on this adversarial feedback, the anonymizer iteratively refines its output to prevent the inferences that remain possible. With GPT-4 as both anonymizer and adversary, this approach achieves a substantially better privacy-utility trade-off than traditional industry-grade anonymizers. However, reliance on large proprietary models is costly and requires sending the very text that should be protected to potentially untrusted external systems. Attempts to transfer these anonymization capabilities into smaller models have been explored only to a limited extent, and existing approaches still depend on a proprietary model to provide the adversarial feedback, incurring similar costs and privacy concerns.

The open problem is therefore whether, and how, small language models that can run locally under modest compute budgets can become effective anonymizers that protect semantic-level private information against inference by strong LLM adversaries, without relying on any external model at inference time. Can such models reach a privacy-utility trade-off comparable to, or better than, that of anonymizers built on frontier proprietary LLMs, including on texts where personal information is conveyed by the overall context rather than by explicit mentions, while remaining cheap enough to deploy in settings with strict data-confidentiality requirements?
