Understanding how a scene has changed and forecasting how it will look next from Satellite Image Time Series (SITS) is fundamental to many critical applications, yet it poses a profound challenge: predicting the future requires a deep understanding of past change. Two tasks are central. In temporal change description, given a sequence of temporally ordered satellite images of the same area, the goal is to generate a natural-language description that accurately summarizes the key dynamic changes that occurred over the observation period, such as urban expansion or agricultural cycles; this requires comprehending the temporal evolution and, ideally, the underlying causal narrative of the changes. In future satellite image forecasting, given the same historical sequence, the goal is to generate a plausible image for the next time point. A critical and often overlooked requirement is that the forecast be temporally consistent: the generated changes should be a logical continuation of the trends and dynamics observed in the historical data, not merely a plausible standalone picture.

Although foundation models such as Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and diffusion-based image generators have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their application to this domain remains fragmented and fundamentally limited. On the understanding side, static image captioning ignores temporal context, while existing temporal change description methods lack the semantic depth of MLLMs: they fuse information across images through simple interactions, their long-range temporal reasoning is limited, and they struggle to capture why changes occur. General-purpose MLLMs, even video-capable ones, are not optimized for this setting either: video-centric models are typically tuned for densely sampled frames with fixed, short intervals, whereas consecutive satellite acquisitions are sparse and irregular, with gaps that can span several years. On the generation side, single-image synthesis cannot model evolution, and temporal forecasting approaches struggle with long-term consistency because they do not grasp the semantic drivers of change: their conditioning is typically low-level (e.g., edge maps), based on simple metadata, or limited to text guidance, and it lacks fine-grained temporal semantic interaction, so they can generate what a scene looks like but cannot reason about why it should look that way given its history. As a result, change understanding and future forecasting have been treated as disjointed tasks, even though both are limited by a common bottleneck: modeling long-range temporal dynamics.

This raises several questions. How can a model reason about why changes occurred across a long, irregularly sampled sequence of satellite images, and describe them accurately? How can such an understanding of past change be used to generate what will happen next, so that the forecast is a temporally consistent continuation of the observed trajectory rather than only a realistic-looking image? Can enhancing long-range temporal understanding improve performance on both tasks simultaneously, with the understanding of past change directly informing the forecast? Finally, how can the temporal consistency of a forecast be rigorously evaluated, given that standard image-quality metrics cannot penalize a prediction that is perceptually realistic but inconsistent with historical trends?

Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a pivotal technique for advancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models on complex tasks. In reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR), the language model is treated as a policy whose chain of thought is modeled as a sequence of actions, and it is optimized with rewards from an automatic verifier that compares the final answer extracted from each sampled solution with a reference answer. Most RLVR algorithms are on-policy; a widely used example is Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which estimates the advantage of each trajectory by normalizing its reward against a group of trajectories sampled for the same question. On-policy optimization is stable but computationally expensive, because the experience generated during the costly rollout phase is typically discarded after a single gradient update. This not only squanders substantial compute but also forfeits the opportunity for the model to learn from its own earlier successful explorations, which makes training inefficient, can make it unstable, and imposes a bottleneck on scaling RL for reasoning.

Experience replay is a classical RL technique to address this issue: previously collected interactions are stored and reused, which improves sample efficiency, helps stabilize training and accelerates convergence, and prioritized variants emphasize the most informative transitions. It has been argued that AI is entering a period in which experience will become the dominant medium of improvement. A non-trivial challenge, however, lies in how to exploit past experiences according to their differing value and how to manage the replay process over the course of learning, and efficient experience replay mechanisms remain largely underexplored in RLVR for large reasoning models. Recent off-policy approaches incorporate historical or external data, for example by mixing expert demonstrations with on-policy updates or by deriving direct off-policy update rules, and recent replay methods for reasoning models reuse successful trajectories collected early in training or produced by a well-trained policy. However, the impact of the quality of the data within the replay buffer remains underexplored, and several replay methods do not correct for the distribution mismatch between the past policy that generated a stored trajectory and the current policy.

Several features make the problem challenging. An experience in RLVR consists of a question together with the trajectories sampled for it, and it is unclear whether all questions are equally useful for training, or whether all successful trajectories for a question are equally worth reusing. Because the verifiable reward only checks the final answer, a successful trajectory may still rest on invalid reasoning. The usefulness of a stored experience may also change as the model's capabilities evolve during training. Finally, reusing past successes pushes the policy toward exploitation, while prior work shows that aggressively minimizing policy entropy can cause collapse, so the reuse of experience has to be balanced against continued exploration.

This raises the following research questions. What makes a reasoning experience valuable for RLVR optimization, and which measurable properties of a question and of its trajectories, available during training, indicate that value? Given the vast quantity of experience collected during rollouts, how can a reasoning model effectively exploit its own stream of experience, deciding which past experiences to keep, prioritize and replay, how to combine them with fresh on-policy exploration, and how to account for the policy mismatch of replayed trajectories, so as to maximize learning toward scaling RL compute for large reasoning models and to improve reasoning performance, sample efficiency and training stability relative to standard on-policy RLVR?

enonce:
Video anomaly analysis is a key application of computer vision for public security. Most early work formulates it as temporal video anomaly detection: marking the segments of a video whose behavior deviates from learned normal patterns, whether with one-class models trained only on normal clips, unsupervised reconstruction or future-frame prediction objectives, or weakly supervised learning from video-level labels. Such detectors have reached high performance on benchmarks, yet they output only frame-wise anomaly scores, without spatial or semantic context, and give no insight into why a segment is abnormal. These limits of interpretability have motivated a shift from temporal detection toward downstream tasks with user-friendly, explainable outputs: spatial video anomaly localization, which predicts bounding boxes around the regions that contain the abnormal activity, and textual video anomaly understanding, which decides whether a video contains an anomaly and produces a human-readable description explaining it, typically with fine-tuned multimodal large language models. Each line of work, however, provides either spatial or textual cues on its own and focuses on a single type of task, so that existing methods offer only an incomplete analysis of video anomalies. A holistic analysis would answer when an anomaly happens, where it is, what it is and why it is abnormal, each of the existing benchmark tasks addressing one of these sub-problems.

A second challenge is the heavy reliance on dataset-specific supervision. Detection and localization models require temporal masks or spatial bounding boxes, yet anomaly definitions vary widely across datasets, so a model tuned on one domain often fails on another and must be retrained for unseen domains or anomaly types. In real-world applications, privacy and security concerns may also make training data unavailable for some sensitive scenes. Open-set detectors that fuse language semantics in order to detect and classify novel anomalies still require task-specific training and give very limited insight into why frames are abnormal. As partial remedies, recent work has explored zero- and few-shot approaches built on frozen vision-language backbones or multimodal large language models, but most of these approaches have a limited task scope and still rely on annotated datasets. The only strictly zero-shot, training-free method addresses temporal detection alone: a frozen vision-language model captions the frames and a prompted large language model converts the captions into frame-wise anomaly scores. It is effective when anomalies are clearly distinguishable from normality but occasionally fails on more complex anomaly types, and it offers neither spatial grounding nor any direct semantic explanation beyond generic captions. Prompt-tuning methods, which optimize textual prompts to guide frozen models, require induction on an annotated training set and pay for it in generality, since the learned prompts tend to be task- or domain-specific. The generality problem is worse still for instruction-tuned multimodal models: they produce rich narrative explanations, but they require extensive annotation and computational resources, lack temporal or spatial coverage, and are optimized to return answers from seen question-answer pairs that describe a closed set of anomaly types.

Multimodal large language models already encode rich visual-semantic priors for commonsense reasoning, which suggests that fine-tuning may not be necessary for every task. This raises the questions addressed here: can temporal detection, spatial localization and textual explanation of video anomalies be delivered together, as one holistic and interpretable analysis, in a strictly zero-shot manner, with frozen pretrained models and without any additional training data, annotations or gradient updates? And can such an analysis remain at least as accurate as existing zero-shot detectors while staying robust across domains whose definitions of anomaly differ?

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) exhibit compelling cross-modal perception and reasoning capabilities on image-text data and have become the de facto standard for visual question answering (VQA), the task of answering a question based on the visual content of an image. However, standard MLLM architectures are not well suited to perceiving and reasoning about small visual details in high-resolution images. So-called global-view MLLMs downscale every input image to the base resolution of their vision encoder (for some widely used models only 224×224 or 336×336 pixels), which discards information; as a consequence, they perform poorly on fine-grained VQA, i.e., on questions whose answer depends on small visual details. Unlike common VQA settings, in which the question-relevant objects are typically prominent in the image, fine-grained VQA concerns targets that may occupy only a tiny fraction of a large, high-resolution image.

More recent global-local-view MLLMs process a downsampled global view together with local crops extracted from the original, unresized image. This dual-view strategy reduces information loss, but it multiplies the number of visual tokens, and because self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length, the computational cost grows rapidly. Moreover, despite having access to fine-grained visual details from all local crops, these models struggle to identify the few visual tokens that are relevant to the question amid the large number of local crop tokens, so their effectiveness on fine-grained VQA still remains limited.

An orthogonal line of work is visual cropping: searching the image for the regions that are relevant to the question and passing only those regions to the MLLM. Existing visual cropping techniques, however, suffer from one or more of three limitations. First, some depend on task-specific fine-tuning: SEAL, for instance, pairs the answering model with a separate visual-search MLLM equipped with additional decoders that is fine-tuned to predict object heatmaps and coordinates, and runs a recursive top-down search, a complex multi-module design that is costly to run. Second, several rely on uninformed, exhaustive search: DC² builds a hierarchical tree of image regions and captions each region with the MLLM, while ZoomEye traverses a hierarchical region tree and scores every visited region with three sequential MLLM forward passes using different prompts, a computation that cannot be simplified or shared across regions, so the cost grows quickly with the depth and breadth of the search. Third, ViCrop avoids hierarchical search by directly computing a question-guided heatmap, but its best-performing variants depend on query-key attention weights and answer gradients, which makes them incompatible with efficient attention implementations such as FlashAttention that never explicitly produce attention weights. Simply asking the MLLM where the target is does not solve the problem either: although many MLLMs are fine-tuned to predict bounding boxes, they often fail when prompted directly for the location of small objects, producing hallucinated or imprecise coordinates.

The open problem is therefore how to make an MLLM look at the right part of a high-resolution image. Can the image regions relevant to a fine-grained visual question be localized without task-specific fine-tuning or auxiliary modules, without an uninformed exhaustive search over the image, and in a way that remains compatible with efficient attention implementations? Can such localization benefit both global-view and global-local-view MLLMs, improving their answers to questions about small details while keeping inference cost low, given that MLLM inference is already computationally expensive? And how favorable an accuracy-efficiency trade-off can be reached relative to existing search-based visual cropping methods?

Knowledge distillation is a fundamental technique in machine learning, widely used for model compression, transfer learning, and improving generalization. Its core idea is to transfer knowledge from a "teacher" model to a (typically smaller) "student" model by training the student to match the teacher's output probabilities rather than categorical one-hot labels. This softened supervision has been shown to improve performance across a range of tasks. Consequently, a substantial body of research has focused on designing distillation mechanisms, such as dynamic temperature scaling, feature-based distillation, and task-aware teacher-student matching, typically assuming a large teacher that is optimized to maximize its own performance.

Despite its widespread adoption, the theoretical foundations of knowledge distillation remain only partially understood. In particular, the impact of the teacher's output probabilities on the student's optimization trajectory and generalization has not been fully characterized. Existing explanations attribute the usefulness of distillation to the regularizing effect of the teacher's soft estimates, to trade-offs such as precision versus recall or knowledge inheritance versus exploration, or to factors such as data geometry and optimization bias. Insights into how distillation affects the optimization itself have been developed only for special cases, such as self-distillation or a student that is a compressed version of the teacher, and rely on dedicated gradient approximations. A principled understanding of how distillation affects common learning algorithms, such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants, for arbitrary teachers, is still lacking.

Recent works have begun to view distillation through a Bayesian lens, interpreting the teacher's outputs as (possibly noisy) estimates of the true class posterior probabilities of the data-generating distribution. From this statistical viewpoint, learning from accurate class posteriors has been argued to reduce the variance of the student's objective, and excess-risk and generalization bounds have been derived in terms of the distance between the teacher's predictions and the true posteriors. These analyses, however, characterize the statistical properties of the risk rather than the behavior of the learning algorithm that actually trains the student. The probabilistic perspective thus opens relatively unexplored questions about the dynamics of SGD-based learning under probabilistic supervision, and about how the statistical calibration of the teacher influences the student. Teacher calibration has been recognized as a key driver of distillation, but it remains unclear how the quality of the teacher's probability estimates should guide the way teachers are built.

This raises several questions. How does supervising a student with the exact class posterior probabilities, instead of one-hot labels, change the convergence behavior and stability of SGD-based learning and the generalization of the resulting student? In the realistic case where the teacher provides only imperfect, noisy estimates of these posteriors, how does the level of estimation error affect the student's convergence, generalization and accuracy, and under what conditions does probabilistic supervision remain preferable to one-hot labels? Finally, what practical guidelines follow for designing or choosing teacher models, beyond maximizing the teacher's own accuracy, so that their outputs provide better supervision for students trained with SGD-based optimizers?

PROPOSAL: Investigate how the statistical calibration of the teacher affects the student's convergence, generalization, and accuracy. Use a variant of the Wide ResNet-28-10 (WRN) as the teacher model, and a smaller version of the same architecture as the student. Train the teacher on a large image classification dataset (e.g., ImageNet) and evaluate the student on a held-out dataset (e.g., CIFAR-10). PREDICTION: We expect that the student's performance will improve with the teacher's calibration, and that an optimal temperature exists which maximizes this improvement, but that excessive temperature scaling will degrade the student's performance.

Analyze the transfer of knowledge from the teacher to the student, and evaluate the impact of the teacher's calibration on the student's performance. Consider using domain adaptation techniques to align the teacher and student datasets.

COST: 2000 GPU-hours

Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a powerful and principled approach for generative modeling, and in particular for high-quality visual generation. By learning a time-dependent velocity field that continuously transforms samples from a base distribution into a target distribution, FM models generate data by integrating an ordinary differential equation (ODE). This framework offers advantages over diffusion-based methods, including faster convergence, stable training, and direct control over sample trajectories.

Despite these strengths, inference in FM models is costly and has become a bottleneck. ODE integration is inherently sequential: each step depends on the output of the previous one, which makes the process slow and difficult to parallelize. High-fidelity generation requires a large number of fine-grained steps, which pushes latency up and makes real-time or interactive use difficult. As data dimensionality and model complexity increase, so does the inference burden. The issue is even more pronounced in video generation, where models operate on high-dimensional spatio-temporal data and the cost of sequential integration compounds across frames, making efficient inference essential for long videos.

Static reduction strategies such as distillation, trajectory truncation and consistency training have been proposed to reduce inference latency. However, they often degrade output quality, producing blurry textures, semantic drift or broken spatial coherence; in video, they often cause temporal flickering and motion inconsistency, which severely degrade realism even when individual frames look plausible. Many of them also require retraining the model with auxiliary objectives or handcrafted losses, which increases the engineering burden and restricts transferability across model families. As a result, these approaches are less modular, harder to scale, and often infeasible to deploy in time-sensitive or interactive pipelines.

In language models, a promising line of work for accelerating inference is speculative decoding, in which multiple drafts are proposed in parallel and selectively verified by the full model, reducing latency without retraining it. This idea, however, does not directly extend to image and video generative models such as FM, and two challenges stand out. First, unlike in language models, no readily available draft model exists: how can drafts be produced whose trajectories closely couple with those of the full model? Second, the performance of FM is highly sensitive to the velocity output: even a small perturbation in velocity can accumulate along the integration path and lead to severe generation errors. How, then, can drafted velocities be evaluated, and how can the drift of the resulting trajectory away from the full-model trajectory be controlled?

The open problem is therefore how to substantially reduce the inference latency of existing FM models, for both image and video generation, without retraining, without degrading output quality relative to standard full-step generation, and in a way that transfers across model families.

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: draft model acceleration via random path pruning
PROPOSAL: We propose to evaluate the feasibility of accelerating inference in FM models by selectively pruning short, random paths through the velocity field during the integration process. By doing so, we can reduce the overall number of integration steps required for achieving the same quality of output. We will experiment with various pruning strategies, including pruning based on velocity magnitude, Euclidean distance, and maximum gradient.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no pruning, as described above. (2) Ablation study: Different pruning strategies and their combinations. (3) Control: Randomly subsampling the paths.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a latency reduction of up to 30% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and a significant decrease in video generation latency. However, this approach may lead to variations in generation quality depending on the pruning strategy used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: learning draft models for fm using Curriculum Learning
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of generating high-quality drafts in FM models, we propose using Curriculum Learning to learn a draft model that closely couples with the full model. We will define a gradual curriculum of temporally corrected velocities that guide the learning process of the draft model. As the curriculum progresses, the draft model will learn to produce velocities that are increasingly similar to those produced by the full model. This will enable the draft model to not only accelerate inference but also maintain high quality output.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different curriculum learning schedules. (3) Control: Learning draft models using random sampling of the velocity field, following the setup outlined in the proposal.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 40% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. The quality of the drafts will be strongly dependent on the quality of the curriculum learning schedule.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: draft model acceleration via random path pruning
PROPOSAL: We revise our initial proposal to include an incentive mechanism that rewards the draft model for producing velocities that result in generated samples that are closer to the ground truth. This can be achieved by incorporating a reconstruction loss into the draft model's training objective, which encourages the draft model to produce high-quality samples that are close to the target distribution. By doing so, we can improve the accuracy and quality of the draft model's outputs.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no pruning and no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different loss functions and weights for the reconstruction loss, with details given in the appendix. (3) Control: Learning draft models using random sampling of the velocity field without reconstruction loss.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 50% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. However, the introduction of the reconstruction loss may lead to increased training time and potential mode collapse issues.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: learning draft models for fm using curriculum learning
PROPOSAL: We revise our proposal to use a more efficient curriculum learning schedule that utilizes progressive meta-learning. Instead of learning a fixed curriculum, we will use a dynamic curriculum that adapts to the performance of the draft model and the full model. This will enable the draft model to learn more effectively and efficiently, and potentially lead to better performance.

This mechanism will utilize a secondary model trained to predict the corrections needed to refine the draft's output, rather than relying on a single pass through the full model. By predicting these corrections step-by-step, we can iteratively refine the draft's output, potentially leading to significant quality improvements.

By storing the velocity fields in a compressed and hierarchical manner, we can significantly reduce the computational cost of evaluating the velocity field for a given sample. This approach can be particularly effective when combined with the draft model and refinement mechanisms, as it can help to reduce the latency of the overall system.

By decomposing the velocity field into smaller, independent components, we can parallelize the evaluation of the velocity field across multiple GPUs or machines, significantly reducing the latency of the overall system. Generative models significantly enhance the efficiency of chemical space exploration in drug discovery by directly sampling molecules with desired properties. However, a key bottleneck in their practical deployment is low synthetic accessibility: generated molecules are often difficult or impossible to produce in the laboratory. To address this limitation, recent work has turned to template-based methods that emulate the chemical synthesis process by constructing synthesis trees that link molecular building blocks through known reaction templates. These representations, while useful for downstream experimental validation, do not describe the underlying 3D geometry and thus cannot capitalize on the conformational information that is often crucial for diverse chemical and biological properties.

Parallel advances in generative molecular design have explored spatial modeling at the atomic level. Inspired by advances in protein structure prediction and by generative frameworks such as diffusion and flow matching, recent work has focused on directly sampling 3D atomic coordinates of small molecules, learning to generate spatially meaningful, property-aligned conformations along with molecular graphs. The ability to model atomic coordinates directly increases the expressivity of these approaches, enabling applications such as pocket-conditioned generation, scaffold hopping, analog discovery, and molecular optimization. However, without considering practical synthesis routes, integrating synthesizability constraints into these models remains a major challenge, and most existing 3D generative approaches do not ensure that proposed molecules can be made in practice. While recent work has addressed synthesizability for 2D molecular graphs, extending such constraints to 3D, and to geometry-based conditional generation, remains largely unexplored.

Several obstacles stand in the way. Directly optimizing synthesizability scores is often unreliable, so the predominant route to synthetic accessibility has been to assemble molecules from commercially available building blocks joined by known reaction templates; yet such generators typically emit only molecular graphs and no atomic coordinates. The representations commonly available for 3D work are also ill-suited to synthesis awareness: synthon-based representations do not guarantee that a valid synthesis route exists, do not provide one even when it does, and lack the flexibility to constrain the reaction space, which matters when one wants to prioritize high-yield, high-reliability reactions or to remain within the limits of automated synthesis platforms. Relying instead on external, black-box reaction simulators to couple building blocks offers no fine-grained control when a reagent has several reaction centers, and such steps do not define atom mappings between reactants and products, making it impossible to trace product atoms back to their parent building blocks. A further difficulty is that most 3D molecule generation methods require the number of atoms to be specified in advance, which is awkward when the identity of the constituent building blocks is itself still being decided. Finally, the few approaches that do couple synthesis pathways with 3D structure optimize an external reward and typically require a full training run for each target pocket, which is costly and exposes the generator to reward hacking.

This raises the central questions. Can a single generative model sample small molecules so that each sample comes with both a physically realistic 3D conformation and an explicit, traceable route by which it could actually be made, instead of treating geometry and synthesizability as separate concerns handled in sequence or by post hoc filtering? What kind of data and molecular representation would such a model require, given that existing conformer datasets carry no synthesis information and existing synthesis-aware representations carry no geometry? How should synthesizability and geometric quality be measured so that claims of practical makeability are credible rather than an artifact of the scoring tool used? And can one amortized model, once trained, serve the geometry-conditioned design problems that drug discovery actually poses, such as completing or connecting parts of a known three-dimensional ligand, or designing novel molecules that reproduce a desired spatial arrangement of interaction features for a target, without external scoring functions and without retraining for each new target?

Recent frontier models such as OpenAI o1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1 and Kimi k1.5 provide compelling proof of concept for leveraging long chains of thought to enhance the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). Following these advances, Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) techniques such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization (DAPO) have emerged as the de facto standard for strengthening LLM reasoning. In RLVR, the policy model is trained by sampling multiple responses (rollouts) to a prompt, checking each final answer against a ground-truth answer, and then reinforcing correct answers while penalizing incorrect ones. GRPO, a variant of Proximal Policy Optimization that dispenses with a costly value model, computes the advantage of each response by normalizing its reward with the mean and standard deviation of the rewards in its group.

This works well when the responses to a prompt contain both right and wrong answers, but it does not account for the case where a group of rollouts is entirely correct or entirely incorrect and therefore receives identical rewards. Such prompts are referred to as zero-variance prompts. For them, the normalized rewards (the advantage values) collapse to zero, so there is no training signal and all rollouts for those prompts are rendered uninformative. Put differently, the policy is rewarded for a correct response only when at least one incorrect response exists in the same group, and penalized for an incorrect response only when at least one correct response is present. Zero-variance prompts typically arise when a problem is too difficult or too easy for the current model: early in training, when the model often fails to solve a problem even once across multiple attempts, and near convergence, when it has become strong enough to solve many problems in every attempt.

Ignoring these prompts may seem conceptually reasonable, but it remains problematic because rollout generation is itself a major bottleneck in RL training, so the compute spent sampling responses to zero-variance prompts is simply wasted. Recent methods acknowledge this inefficiency and try to filter zero-variance prompts out, either before rollout, by predicting from the training history which prompts are likely to yield identical rewards and skipping them, or after rollout, by repeatedly sampling and discarding them until a batch contains only prompts with mixed outcomes. These methods view zero-variance prompts merely as a cost to be avoided and implicitly assume that they offer no value for policy optimization. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has investigated whether zero-variance prompts themselves can serve as a valuable source of learning signal.

This raises several open questions. Can the responses to a prompt whose rollouts are all correct, or all incorrect, provide meaningful feedback for policy optimization, even though the group contains no contrasting response? If so, how should such feedback be formulated so that it remains informative and does not destabilize training? And would exploiting these prompts, instead of discarding them, lead to better reasoning performance and more stable learning than both standard group-relative training and the prevailing practice of filtering them out?

Large language models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress across a wide range of natural language understanding and generation tasks, but their massive parameter counts demand prohibitively large computational and memory resources for both training and deployment. Even in settings with a reasonable amount of compute, training or fine-tuning such models remains challenging.

One promising way to reduce the computational burden of fine-tuning is low-precision floating-point (FP) arithmetic such as FP8. Modern accelerators (e.g., NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, AMD CDNA 3, Google TPUs) increasingly support low-precision FP arithmetic natively, and FP8 can theoretically double the throughput of FP16 matrix multiplication. Because FP8 formats (such as E4M3 or E5M2) have a narrow representable range, a higher-precision tensor must first be scaled by a per-tensor factor obtained from a max-reduction over its absolute values, and then scaled element-wise and rounded, before the low-precision multiplication can run. This quantization overhead is memory-bound and grows quadratically with matrix size, whereas the cost of matrix multiplication grows cubically. As a consequence, FP8 is known to accelerate mainly large-dimensional matrix multiplications (empirically, when each matrix dimension exceeds roughly 4K elements), while small-dimensional computations can even suffer an unexpected slowdown.

These overheads are especially critical for low-rank adaptation (LoRA), a widely used approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning. LoRA keeps the pretrained weights frozen and inserts small trainable low-rank matrices (adapters) that capture task-specific knowledge, greatly reducing memory cost by training few parameters. For such small-dimensional matrices, the overhead of FP8 quantization can outweigh the gains of FP8 multiplication, and the separate forward and backward paths of the adapters add further quantization operations at every iteration. Yet fast LoRA fine-tuning matters in practice: many applications require training numerous adapters, for example one adapter per user for personalized recommendation or personalized alignment from human feedback, task-specific adapters for multi-task learning and mixtures of LoRA experts, adapters for different domains, multilingual summarization, and rapid updates in dynamic, user-specific environments. Efficiently accelerating LoRA fine-tuning is therefore essential for timely, scalable and cost-effective adaptation of LLMs under practical computational constraints.

Existing lines of work leave this gap open. Quantized LoRA methods (such as QLoRA with 4-bit NormalFloat weights, QA-LoRA with group-wise INT4 weights, and follow-ups that refine the quantization with integer linear programming, SVD-based adapter initialization, dynamic rank allocation or information recovery) compress the frozen backbone through weight-only quantization. They focus on memory efficiency rather than fine-tuning speed: the added quantization and dequantization often make them slower than standard LoRA, and weight-only quantization cannot exploit hardware acceleration of low-precision matrix multiplication. Conversely, FP8 training methods (hybrid E4M3/E5M2 formats, mixed-precision FP8 training with high-precision master weights, studies of large-scale FP8 stability and outliers, unit scaling) are designed for the large-dimensional matrices of full LLM training, not for the small matrices that characterize LoRA.

This raises the following questions. How large is the quantization overhead when FP8 arithmetic is applied to LoRA fine-tuning, which parts of the computation does it come from, and does it persist across typical adapter ranks? Can LoRA fine-tuning be organized so that it genuinely benefits from native FP8 arithmetic, delivering real end-to-end speedups over existing quantized LoRA methods, while retaining the memory savings that make LoRA attractive and reaching accuracy comparable to existing quantized LoRA fine-tuning?

Dictionary learning, in its most general form, assumes that observations X are generated by latent variables Z through an unknown function, X = g(Z). The goal is to recover the latent generative process from observational data alone, a fundamental task in both science and machine learning. This nonparametric formulation unifies a wide range of latent variable models, including independent component analysis, factor analysis and causal representation learning.

Identifiability, the ability to recover the true generative model from data, is crucial for understanding the hidden world. Yet in general dictionary learning, where both the latent variables and the generating process are unknown, the problem is fundamentally ill-posed without additional assumptions, akin to finding a needle in a haystack. To reduce this ambiguity, most prior work imposes strong parametric constraints that limit the space of possible solutions. The practice is so widespread that, although dictionary learning is fundamentally nonparametric, it is almost always instantiated as a linear model, in which observations are sparse linear combinations of latent variables. Such linearity can be overly restrictive and fails to capture the complexity of many real-world generative processes. Sparse autoencoders, commonly used in mechanistic interpretability, especially for foundation models, are a relevant example: although effective in some settings, they are rooted in sparse linear dictionary learning, which raises concerns about their ability to represent the inherently nonlinear structure of large-scale neural representations.

Many efforts have been made to relax the linearity assumption. In nonlinear independent component analysis, one line of work leverages auxiliary variables as weak supervision to achieve identifiability under statistical independence, while another constrains the mixing function itself. In causal representation learning, identifiability often depends on access to interventional data or counterfactual views, which presuppose some control over the data-generating process. Some basic conditions cannot be avoided: just as linear dictionary learning needs conditions such as the restricted isometry property so that distinct latent codes map to distinguishable observations, the nonlinear generating function must be smooth and injective so that no information is lost. But avoiding information loss is not sufficient for full recovery of the latent variables in the nonlinear regime, which is why existing guarantees rely on restricted function classes or on auxiliary information such as domain or time indices, interventions or counterfactual data.

A gap therefore remains between theoretical guarantees and practical utility. Theoretically, while additional assumptions can yield recovery guarantees, it is rarely possible to verify whether they hold in practice; understanding which guarantees remain valid when assumptions are violated is therefore essential for reliably uncovering the truth in general settings. Practically, what matters is less identifiability under ideal conditions than which inductive biases promote recovery, especially when the ground truth is unknown. Yet most existing approaches offer no guarantees under even mild violations of their assumptions, which makes their associated biases, such as contrastive objectives or weak supervision, difficult to generalize across settings.

The challenge is to make identifiability actionable in general settings: only observational data are available, the generating function is nonlinear and unknown, no parametric constraint or auxiliary supervision can be relied upon, and only basic conditions such as invertibility and differentiability are assumed, accepting that recovering every latent variable may then be infeasible. In such settings, two questions remain open:
- What aspects of the latent process can still be recovered with guarantees?
- What inductive biases should be introduced to guide recovery, ideally ones that could be adopted universally across models and settings?
A related question is whether, and under which additional conditions that require no auxiliary information, all latent variables could still be recovered.

Many supervised learning algorithms rely on the assumption that training and test data are drawn from the same underlying distribution. In real-world applications this assumption is often violated because of environmental changes, sampling biases or temporal dynamics, which create distribution shifts between training and deployment environments. Such mismatches can cause significant performance degradation and pose a fundamental challenge to reliable generalization in practice.

Among the challenges posed by distribution shifts, this problem concerns unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), with a focus on classification. In UDA, one is given labeled data from a source domain and unlabeled data from a target domain whose distributions are related but not necessarily identical. The discrepancy may come from the marginal distribution of the input, from the conditional distribution of labels given inputs, or from both. The goal is to use the labeled source data and the unlabeled target data to build a predictive model with low risk on the target domain. The most naive baseline, empirical risk minimization on the source data, can perform poorly on the target domain when the two distributions differ.

Two representative families of UDA methods are distribution alignment, which reduces the discrepancy between the source and target domains either in the data space or in a feature space, and pseudo-labeling, which refines target predictions using a source-trained model in the spirit of self-training. Despite their popularity, both families often face practical limitations in two common scenarios. The first is when the amount of unlabeled target data is limited: alignment estimates can then become unreliable and pseudo-labels noisy, which can lead to poor generalization, and the empirical distribution of a small or imbalanced target sample may be a poor estimate of the true target input distribution that fails to capture the diversity of the target domain. The second is when the source data contain spurious correlations, for example when irrelevant features such as background or color are strongly associated with labels: models then tend to rely on these shortcuts, which do not transfer to the target domain and ultimately degrade performance. Alignment-based methods can fail in this situation, and approaches that try to disentangle causal and spurious features with unlabeled target data, through counterfactual consistency, generative interventions or self-training refinements, often rely on strong structural assumptions or are highly sensitive to the quality of the initial pseudo-labels, which makes them fragile when target data are scarce or imbalanced.

Distributionally robust optimization is another line of work on distribution shift: instead of the average loss on the training distribution, it minimizes the worst-case expected loss over an ambiguity set of plausible distributions. Constructing a suitable ambiguity set is the central difficulty, and the inner worst case must remain computationally tractable. Common choices, small Wasserstein or f-divergence balls around the empirical source distribution, give robustness to minor perturbations but are less suitable for structured shifts such as subpopulation shift, where the target contains the same subpopulations as the source with different mixing weights and can therefore lie far from the source in standard distances. Formulations designed for such mixture shifts, such as group distributionally robust optimization, typically assume access to group labels and do not explicitly use unlabeled target data to improve target prediction.

The problem is therefore how to learn, from labeled data coming from one or several source domains and unlabeled target data, a classifier that generalizes to the target domain when unlabeled target data are extremely scarce and when spurious correlations dominate the source domain, without group labels and with a computationally tractable training procedure. How can a learner remain reliable when the few available unlabeled target inputs give a poor picture of the target input distribution, and how can it avoid relying on spurious source features that do not hold in the target domain?

Proteins realize their biological functions through intricate three-dimensional conformations, and predicting such structures has long been a central challenge in computational biology. AlphaFold2 marked a breakthrough by combining multiple sequence alignments with geometric constraints in an end-to-end framework, achieving near-experimental accuracy. Building on this foundation, AlphaFold3 reformulates the architecture into an all-atom framework and introduces a diffusion-based structure module, thereby enabling the generative modeling of not only proteins but also a wide spectrum of biomolecular complexes. Consequently, this series of models is widely adopted as a family of foundation models for downstream applications such as virtual screening and protein design. However, AlphaFold3's architecture, which relies on iterative Pairformer recycling and multi-step diffusion, requires substantially greater computational overhead than AlphaFold2, restricting its accessibility in downstream workflows.

More specifically, on long sequences the execution time of AlphaFold3 is measured in minutes, which severely limits its usability in downstream tasks that demand high throughput. For instance, small-scale laboratory screening often requires predictions for thousands of candidates, and when extended to large public databases this number grows to an infeasible scale; protein design tasks typically involve comparable computational demand. Previous work has attempted to mitigate this by manually reducing the number of recycling iterations on simpler structures, thus trading accuracy for efficiency. However, such compromises inevitably degrade predictive performance. Moreover, in hallucination-based design approaches, the multistep iterative refinement process hinders feasible gradient backpropagation, ultimately preventing the broader community from adopting AlphaFold3 as a foundation model for diverse applications.

To accelerate the diffusion process, recent advances in generative modeling have explored high-order solvers and consistency models. While high-order solvers improve efficiency, they rarely reduce the number of sampling steps below ten. Consistency models, on the other hand, have achieved remarkable success in image generation and have benefited from refined training schedules. However, transferring them to an AlphaFold3-style architecture raises two difficulties. First, standard consistency schedules assume fixed-dimensional data and pair timesteps at a constant Euclidean interval, which does not accommodate variable protein sequence lengths: on long sequences even a small step can trigger a drastic distribution shift that demands an unrealistic predictive leap, while on short sequences the same interval provides only a weak learning signal, so training dynamics can become unstable or collapse. Second, the iterative diffusion sampler is not the only source of iteration: the architecture also refines its internal pair and single representations through repeated recycling of the Pairformer trunk, whose cost grows with sequence length and which conventional diffusion-acceleration methods do not address at all.

The open problem is therefore whether an AlphaFold3-class all-atom biomolecular structure generator can be compressed into a predictor that runs in essentially a single forward pass -- removing both the multi-step denoising and the recycling overhead -- while retaining the accuracy of the full iterative model on protein, protein-ligand and nucleic-acid complexes. This matters because accuracy alone is not what blocks adoption: throughput and differentiability do. A useful accelerated model must remain reliable in the tail, not merely on average, since high-throughput screening and design pipelines discard most candidates and are harmed more by occasional implausible structures than by small average losses; it must stay cheap enough to be called thousands of times; and it must be light enough that gradients can be propagated through it, so that design methods which optimize sequences against a folding model become feasible with an all-atom model rather than only with earlier, cheaper architectures. Given this problem, how should one design experiments to establish whether such an acceleration is achievable without a loss of predictive fidelity?

Neurons operate in ways that reflect their cell type, connectivity, and the brain region in which they are embedded. Understanding how these structural and physiological factors shape neural activity is an important open question and is central to modern theories of neural function. Cell type- and circuit-specific effects are also increasingly implicated in neurological disorders: particular neuronal subtypes can be selectively affected in neurodegenerative disease, and neuron subtypes can be targeted to improve efficacy in real time in closed-loop brain stimulation. Together, these directions highlight a broader need to understand how features such as cell type and brain region contribute to a neuron's role in the brain, motivating the development of methods that can extract aspects of neuron identity.

Much of what is known about neuronal cell types and their connectivity comes from molecular, anatomical, and morphological labeling techniques that tag neurons based on gene expression profiles or structural features. These approaches have revealed a rich taxonomy of neuronal classes, but they are resource intensive and typically provide only a sparse labeling of one or a few classes at a time, so identity labels are costly and difficult to obtain at scale. There is currently no molecular access to different cell types or projection classes in nonhuman primates and humans, which has created major roadblocks in studying neuron diversity in humans. For these reasons, there is growing interest in methods that can infer aspects of neuronal identity directly from large-scale neural population activity.

Deep learning approaches to this question have only recently begun to be explored. Early methods relied on intrinsic single-neuron features such as waveform shape or interspike interval profiles, but these signals capture only part of what distinguishes one neuron from another. More recent approaches incorporate some information about the ongoing population activity, but reduce the surrounding activity to fixed low-dimensional summaries, which obscures the fine-grained coordination patterns that are often key to neuronal identity. Furthermore, these models usually require retraining or finetuning on each new set of neurons, limiting their ability to generalize in a zero-shot manner across animals.

Making use of population context is itself challenging. The number of recorded neurons varies widely across experiments, individuals, and sessions, making it non-trivial to define a consistent input structure or population-level operation, and recordings span multiple experimental conditions, including different stimuli and behaviors, which makes it hard for a model to generalize across recording sessions. These limitations point to the need for methods that leverage rich population context while producing neuron-level representations that transfer robustly across recordings.

This raises several questions. Can a representation of each individual neuron be learned from population activity, when identity labels are scarce, such that it captures aspects of the neuron's identity such as its cell type and brain region? Can such representations transfer to entirely new sessions and animals without retraining or additional metadata? And how does the identity information they capture depend on the amount and diversity of recordings available for learning, compared with the number of labeled neurons?

Geometry reconstruction is a fundamental problem that enables a wide range of applications in fields such as virtual reality and robotics. In recent years, neural reconstruction methods have gained significant attention; a key advantage of these methods is their ability to represent the geometry of a scene continuously, which can help in many downstream tasks. However, vision-based sensors often struggle in adverse weather conditions, or even become completely unusable when objects are obscured by occlusions.

Radio frequency (RF) sensing, specifically wireless millimeter-wave (mmWave) sensing, can see through occlusions, remains robust under challenging visibility conditions and, unlike X-rays, is not dangerous to humans, making it a compelling alternative for 3D reconstruction. This could open up many applications, for example checking whether the items inside a box are the correct items, are damaged, or pose a threat, without ever opening the box. On the other hand, mmWave resolution is extremely low compared to vision: a single radar image provides far less visual context than a camera image, which makes it hard to extract a 3D reconstruction from one radar image alone. Some prior RF systems have performed 3D point cloud reconstruction or human body tracking by leveraging movement or by emulating larger antenna apertures, but the recovered point clouds are still too sparse and noisy to reliably recover detailed geometry; through-wall human sensing relies on human motion to combat specularity, and deep learning on mmWave radar data has mostly targeted self-driving scenarios, where image resolution matters little. Other works have proposed neural implicit representations for RF sensing, aiming to concentrate scene information out of heavy noise through neural optimization, but these systems are designed for large-scale environments such as streets or satellite imagery and are far from achieving millimeter-level precision. When objects are close to the radar, the propagation characteristics of RF signals change dramatically: incoming waves can no longer be approximated as planar, so processing methods designed for large-scale scenes, such as beamforming, introduce a considerable amount of distortion and noise, often exceeding the noise acceptable for gradient descent and leading to unstable optimization. Existing neural RF reconstruction work is thus either limited to far-range scenes or, for individual objects, evaluated only on simulated data, which for wireless signals cannot come close to representing the complexity of real-world measurements. Meanwhile, the multi-view reconstruction and inverse rendering methods of computer vision (multi-view stereo, neural radiance fields, Gaussian splatting, neural implicit surfaces, physically based inverse rendering) are all derived from RGB images and are not easily transferable to mmWave data: even lensless RGB images can be mapped back to a lens-based imaging model without altering the underlying ray physics, whereas for RF signals such a transformation is fundamentally invalid.

The open problem is therefore to overcome the fundamental dilemma between massive RF noise in the input and the reconstruction of complete, high-resolution, millimeter-level 3D surface geometry of near-range objects, including objects hidden behind occlusions. This is not straightforward, because inferring surface geometry from RF signals differs fundamentally from image-based reconstruction in three main ways. First, wireless systems lack a lens-based imaging model: whereas lenses filter and focus the relevant light rays, radar antenna arrays perform lensless imaging and capture all incoming RF signals without directional filtering, which leads to low signal-to-noise ratios because irrelevant signals cannot be excluded. Second, RF signals and visible light propagate differently: visible light is predominantly scattered diffusely by surfaces, whereas RF signals, whose wavelengths are on the order of millimeters, are dominated by specular reflections, so volumetric rendering techniques designed for scattering-based vision sensors are unsuitable for RF imaging. Third, physically modeling lensless RF measurements is computationally expensive: whereas lens-based rendering samples along 1D rays, modeling what each antenna receives requires accounting for contributions from the full 3D space, leading to cubic complexity that makes naive implementations intractable at millimeter resolution.

How can accurate, millimeter-level 3D geometry of near-range objects be reconstructed from noisy real-world RF measurements, in line of sight and through occlusions, despite lensless imaging, specular reflections and the cost of modeling signal contributions from the full 3D space?

Visual localization of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) is essential for applications such as digital-twin modeling, mapping, surveillance, large-area and infrastructure inspection, and search-and-rescue operations, yet it faces challenges that ground-level localization systems do not address. Ground-level approaches benefit from similar viewpoints between query and reference images, whereas aerial applications encounter dramatic perspective differences and must scale to large areas. In many scenarios, these systems require high-precision localization while operating with limited resources, for example without an internet connection or without GNSS/GPS support, which makes large image databases or heavy 3D models impractical.

Current UAV localization algorithms either retrieve the closest match from a database of posed images, which is inaccurate, or rely on 3D models of the scene, which are expensive in memory and computation; in resource-limited settings, such as connectivity-limited environments, this can degrade accuracy. Image retrieval methods based on global descriptors struggle with the large viewpoint and illumination changes of UAV imagery, and even with view synthesis or self-supervised learning their performance drops under extreme perspective shifts, so retrieval alone remains insufficient for accurate 6-DoF localization. Structure-based methods build a 3D model with structure-from-motion, establish 2D-3D correspondences against meshes or dense depth maps, and estimate the pose with PnP solvers inside RANSAC, but such complete 3D models require extensive manual effort to create for each operational area. Most UAV-specific positioning methods estimate only 2-DoF or 3-DoF poses rather than the full 6-DoF pose required by advanced applications. Recent approaches based on level-of-detail (LoD) city models improve storage efficiency, but they still assume unchanged environments, perform poorly in building-sparse areas such as highways, and depend on positioning sensors for initialization.

A compelling alternative is geodata, such as orthographic aerial views (digital orthophotos) and elevation maps (digital surface models). Such data are lightweight, scalable and better suited to low-resource settings, and they are increasingly accessible through free releases from government geoportals, for instance in the European Union; where public access is limited, they can be synthesized with photogrammetric tools. For example, covering an area of approximately 0.265 km² can require a 3D model of around 8 GB, whereas geodata require about 30 times less memory. Surprisingly, no existing UAV localization approach seems to fully leverage these data sources: previous work has not used the combination of orthophotos and elevation models for UAV pose estimation, so no existing method is directly applicable to this scenario. Modern feature matchers (dense, semi-dense, sparse, and geometry-aware) perform robustly in many scenarios, but their effectiveness with orthographic geodata remains unexplored. A major reason for this gap is the absence of aligned cross-domain datasets and of full-pose, paired, large-scale benchmarks designed for localization with these types of geodata. Existing UAV localization datasets provide only partial pose information (2-DoF or 3-DoF), feature predominantly nadir views with limited viewpoint diversity, rely on entirely synthetic environments or synthetically rendered views that introduce domain gaps, or lack integrated geodata; the one concurrent collection that includes orthographic geodata focuses its pose evaluation on 3-DoF and suffers from a misalignment between its low-resolution satellite imagery and its aerial photogrammetry data. Furthermore, visual localization methods often need to solve image retrieval before estimating the pose; because these two steps are coupled, it is difficult to disentangle the contribution of each component to the final error.

The problem is therefore the following: given an orthophoto raster, an elevation raster, and a query UAV image taken from an arbitrary viewpoint, determine the georeferenced 6-DoF pose of the camera (localization) and, optionally, its intrinsic parameters (calibration). The key challenge is bridging two fundamentally different projection models: perspective projection for UAV imagery and orthographic projection for geodata. This difference creates a domain gap that is particularly pronounced in oblique views, where perspective distortion is significant. A second domain gap arises from visual and structural discrepancies between query and reference data caused by differences in acquisition time: reference geodata may have been collected months or years before a flight, so orthophotos differ in appearance (color shifts, illumination variations, seasonal differences) and elevation models differ in geometry (construction changes, vegetation growth, infrastructure evolution). These changes vary unpredictably across locations and seasons, cannot easily be addressed through simple data augmentation or domain adaptation, and cannot be faithfully replicated by synthetic alternatives.

This raises several open questions. Can lightweight 2.5D orthographic geodata serve as the only reference for accurate full 6-DoF UAV pose estimation and camera calibration? Can state-of-the-art feature matchers, designed largely for perspective imagery, bridge the perspective-orthographic gap, especially for oblique viewpoints, and how can the perspective disparity between query and reference be reduced? How difficult is it to recover camera intrinsics from aerial imagery in this setting? And how do characteristics of the reference data, namely temporal visual and structural domain shifts, data resolution, and the covisibility between the query image and the reference area (which depends on imperfect upstream retrieval), affect localization accuracy?

We will start by collecting a large dataset of aerial videos with timestamped geolocations, and then use this dataset to train a domain adaptation model that can learn to adapt to different flight scenarios and viewpoints. We will use transfer learning to fine-tune a pre-trained convolutional neural network on the aerial video dataset, and evaluate the performance of the adapted model using metrics such as localization accuracy and navigation time. This experiment will help us understand whether domain adaptation can be used to overcome the challenges of aerial video geolocalization, such as non-overlapping views and variable camera poses.

Diffusion models have demonstrated a remarkable ability to learn data distributions across many modalities, with strong results in both data generation and image restoration. In medical imaging, they are effective at modeling the distribution of 2D image slices, and by combining these powerful learned priors with conventional optimization frameworks, diffusion-based solvers have reached state-of-the-art performance on medical inverse problems such as accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and undersampled X-ray computed tomography (CT). Such problems are often severely ill-posed: far fewer measurements are acquired than there are unknowns, so the measurements alone cannot determine the image, and the learned prior must fill in what they leave ambiguous. Diffusion-based solvers do so through an iterative reverse sampling process that, at each step, predicts a clean image from the current noisy state, corrects this estimate for consistency with the measurements, and re-noises it to the next timestep, which repeatedly injects random noise.

In clinical practice, however, medical data are fundamentally large 3D volumes. Individual 2D slices matter for review, but a complete and accurate volumetric reconstruction is often essential for downstream tasks such as precise tumor volume assessment, surgical planning, and tracking disease progression over time. Translating the success of 2D diffusion-based solvers to 3D is difficult: because of the curse of dimensionality, the memory, computational, and data requirements of training a diffusion prior directly on volumetric data are prohibitive for most academic and even industrial labs. A common and practical workaround is to train a diffusion model on 2D slices and apply this 2D prior slice by slice to reconstruct the volume.

This workaround eases the training burden but creates a critical new problem: the reconstructed volumes lack consistency along the third dimension (the z-axis). Because each slice is processed independently during the reverse diffusion process, the intrinsic randomness of the sampling procedure leads to severe inter-slice discontinuities and artifacts, degrading the diagnostic and analytical quality of the stacked volume. Existing remedies have important drawbacks. The most direct one augments the 2D prior with a hand-crafted regularizer such as total variation, applied in an additional optimization step to enforce smoothness between adjacent slices. This is effective, but it introduces sensitive hyperparameters that require careful tuning, can over-smooth the volume or produce cartoon-like textures that erase fine diagnostic details, and acts as an external correction that masks the symptoms rather than addressing the intrinsic cause. More principled approaches try to learn a more complete 3D prior, for instance by training on 3D patches or by combining priors from two perpendicular 2D planes, but they increase the complexity of the training or inference pipeline and may impose constraints on the data, such as requiring cubic volumes.

A similar discontinuity arises in video restoration, where applying a pre-trained 2D image diffusion model to video inverse problems often produces temporal flickering across frames. Prior work attributed this flickering to the uncoordinated stochasticity inherent in diffusion sampling and alleviated it by synchronizing the stochastic noise components across frames. Whether the same mechanism is the fundamental cause of inter-slice inconsistency in 3D medical reconstruction, and how such a remedy would transfer from video to volumetric medical data, remains open.

This raises the following questions. How does the stochasticity of independent slice-wise sampling give rise to inter-slice inconsistency when 2D diffusion priors are used for 3D medical reconstruction? Is it possible to enhance inter-slice consistency directly within the diffusion sampling process itself, obviating the need for external, artifact-inducing optimization, ideally without new loss terms, additional sensitive hyperparameters, model retraining, or extra computational cost, so that the remedy could be dropped into existing 2D diffusion-based 3D reconstruction pipelines? And can inter-slice consistency be improved while preserving the natural anatomical variation between slices and fine diagnostic details, rather than trading them away for smoothness?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: slice synchronization via shared noise projection
PROPOSAL: We will apply a 2D diffusion-based solver to 3D volumetric MRI data, but instead of processing each slice independently, we will sample each slice from a shared noise distribution that is projected onto the current state of the solver, thus ensuring consistency between the slices. We will test two variants: one where the shared noise is static across all slices, and one where it is dynamic and updated at each step.
CONTROLS: We compare our proposed slice synchronization method to (1) a naive baseline where each slice is processed independently, and (2) an augmented baseline where a total variation regularizer is applied to enforce smoothness between adjacent slices, in the same setting as the proposal.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The slice synchronization method should improve upon the naive baseline in terms of inter-slice consistency, with the dynamic noise variant performing better than the static one. However, it may also trade off some of the fine diagnostic details due to the constraint imposed by the shared noise distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: analyzing stochastic consistency using advanced diffusion diagnostics
PROPOSAL: We will embed advanced diffusion diagnostics into the 2D diffusion-based solver to directly measure the temporal consistency of the sampling process, quantifying the correlation between adjacent slices and identifying potential sources of inter-slice discrepancies. By comparing these diagnostics across different variants of the solver, including and without the slice synchronization method proposed in our previous experiment, we will analyze the mechanism behind inter-slice inconsistency and provide a deeper understanding of its origin.
CONTROLS: The baseline for our diagnostics will be the existing implementation of the 2D diffusion-based solver without any additional modifications.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The advanced diffusion diagnostics are expected to uncover the inherent stochasticity and its effects on slice consistency, supporting evidence for the potential benefits of our proposed slice synchronization method. However, inconsistent results might challenge our current assumptions and necessitate a reevaluation of the underlying problem.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating 3d patch-based diffusion priors in a 2d+1 framework
PROPOSAL: We will adapt the 2D diffusion-based solver to operate within a 2D+1 framework, where each 2D slice is augmented with a per-pixel description of the slice's spatial relationship to adjacent slices in the 3D volume. This framework will be used to train a set of 2D diffusion priors, each conditioned on 3D patches of volume data. During inference, the 2D diffusion model will use the spatial relationship descriptions to predict a clean image slice that is consistent with adjacent slices.
CONTROLS: We compare our 2D+1 framework with the naive baseline of applying a unconditioned 2D diffusion model to each slice independently, and with a 3D diffusion-based solver that has been trained directly on volume data.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method is expected to improve upon the naive baseline by leveraging the spatial relationships between slices, but may inherently require large amounts of memory and computational resources due to the need to compute and store the per-pixel spatial relationships. If we're lucky, it might challenge the effectiveness of our proposed slice synchronization method.

ACTION: REVISE

CONTROLS: The baseline for our diagnostics will be the existing implementation of 2D and 3D diffusion-based solvers without any additional modifications or synchronization.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By combining our previous experiments, we will gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between stochastic consistency and inter-slice inconsistency in diffusion-based solvers, and validate our observations on a more comprehensive set of solvers, ultimately strengthening our proposal for slice synchronization.

PROPOSAL: We will explore the integration of adaptive temporal filtering techniques into the diffusion-based reconstruction framework to stabilize and smooth out the variations caused by stochastic sampling, aiming to reduce inter-slice inconsistency.
