ACTION: ADD
TITLE: low-nfe consistency for large multi-modal models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the feasibility of consistency-based models for single-function or very low-NFE generation, by adapting the any-step training objective of [1] to constrain the output of the generator to a function of the input, plus a small, learnable residual. Evaluate the performance of this "residual-constrained" consistency model on a range of large text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard unconditional flow-based model variant, and with a separately-trained student teacher model with 5 iterations of progressive distillation.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The residual-constrained consistency model should provide a quality drop of less than 1.5 points on the MSMFT metric, compared to the unconditional flow-based model, while achieving a reduction in NFEs. However, very large models may still face training instability due to the use of large learnable residuals.

References:
[1] any-step training objective (not specified reference)
[2] DALL-E 2 dataset
[3] MSMFT metric (not specified reference)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adversarial-free distilled sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate a method for distilled sampling without adversarial losses, by computing the output of a given step through a combination of its own knowledge up to that point and the cached output from the preceding steps. Implement this method using a non-adversarial student-teacher approach, where the teacher is a frozen version of the model and the student takes fewer steps to sample an image. Evaluate this "distilled samplifier" on a set of large text-to-image models, using the COCO dataset [4] and the Inception score [5].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard progressive distillation approach and a baseline of the full model taking 5-10 steps.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The distilled samplifier should achieve a quality improvement of more than 1 point in Inception score, even when the teacher model is frozen, while reducing the number of NFEs significantly. However, evaluation metrics may become less reliable at very low NFEs, making quality assessment challenging.

References:
[4] COCO dataset
[5] Inception score

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: adversarial-free distilled sampling (not changed)
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 2 to include an evaluation of the training time of the distilled samplifier, and investigate its impact on model capacity. Add an experiment where the student model and teacher model have the same capacity, but the student is trained with a reduced number of iterations, and another where the student model has a significantly reduced capacity compared to the teacher model, to analyze its effects on training time and inference quality.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The evaluation of training time and capacity will show that the distilled samplifier achieves a significant reduction in training time and enables the use of smaller models, but may come at the cost of reduced inference quality if the student and teacher models have significantly different capacities.

Note: This is a refinement of the original proposal, rather than a completely new one. It incorporates additional evaluation and analysis, and expands on the original ideas.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: adverse-free distilled sampling
PROPOSAL: Modify the architecture of the distilled sampler to use a denoising autoencoder instead of a simple student model, which will allow it to learn the structure of the data distribution directly from the teacher model. This will reduce the need for pre-training the student model and improve its ability to generalize to new input distributions. Evaluate the performance of this "autoencoder-based distilled sampler" on the same COCO dataset [4] and Inception score [5] as before.
COST: 1400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The autoencoder-based distilled sampler should achieve significant improvements in Inception score and reduce the number of NFEs, with better generalization capabilities compared to the original student-teacher approach. However, it may be more sensitive to the configuration of the teacher model and the pre-training stage.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: momentum-guided consistency
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new variant of the consistency model, where the generator is trained to produce output that not only matches the input, but also a momentum-buffered version of the input. This momentum buffer is initialized with a value close to zero and updated on each iteration of the training process. Evaluate the performance of this "momentum-guided consistency model" on a range of large text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard unconditional flow-based model variant and the residual-constrained consistency model from proposal 1.
COST: 1100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The momentum-guided consistency model should stabilize the training dynamics and improve the quality of generated images, especially when the input sequence has a strong temporal structure. However, it may increase the number of NFEs required for convergence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: conditional pre-training for low-nfe models
PROPOSAL: Investigate a method to improve the performance of low-NFE models by pre-training them on a large dataset with conditional inputs and then fine-tuning them on a smaller dataset with the target format of images or text. This will allow the model to learn a richer representation of the data distribution and improve its ability to generate high-quality output in a single function evaluation. Evaluate the performance of this "conditionally pre-trained low-NFE model" on a range of text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with unconditional pre-training and the residual-constrained consistency model from proposal 1.
COST: 1600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The conditionally pre-trained low-NFE model should achieve significant improvements in MSMFT score and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, but the fine-tuning stage may require careful hyperparameter tuning to maintain performance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: low-nfe consistency for large multi-modal models
PROPOSAL: Refine the residual-constrained consistency model by splitting the residual into two parts: a shared residual that is conditioned on the input sequence, and a private residual that is specific to each instance of the input sequence. This will allow the model to learn more robust and transferable representations of the data distribution. Evaluate the performance of this "split-residual consistency model" on a range of large text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
COST: 1300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The split-residual consistency model should achieve improved MSMFT scores and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, especially when evaluated on diverse and out-of-distribution test sets. However, it may be more challenging to train due to the increased complexity of the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: constructive diffusion initialization
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of constructive diffusion initialization to improve the performance of low-NFE models. This involves pre-training a large model using reversible denoising diffusion [6] and then initializing the lower-capacity model with the final stage of the diffusion process. Evaluate the performance of this "constructively initialized low-NFE model" on a range of text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with standard random initialization and the split-residual consistency model from proposal 1.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The constructively initialized low-NFE model should achieve improved MSMFT scores and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, due to the more effective initialization of the model weights. However, it may require careful tuning of the diffusion process and initialization hyperparameters.

Reference:
[6] reversible denoising diffusion

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: attention-augmented low-nfe models
PROPOSAL: Modify the architecture of the low-NFE models by adding self-attention layers to allow for more flexible and adaptive interactions between different parts of the input sequence. This will enable the model to better capture long-range dependencies and generate more coherent and detailed output in a single function evaluation. Evaluate the performance of this "attention-augmented low-NFE model" on a range of text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard model architecture and the split-residual consistency model from proposal 1.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The attention-augmented low-NFE model should achieve improved MSMFT scores and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, especially when the input sequence has complex and long-range dependencies. However, it may be more challenging to train due to the increased complexity of the model and the potential for catastrophic forgetting of important features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: early-stopped multi-sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of early-stopped multi-sampling as a final stage of the inference process for low-NFE models. This involves sampling multiple times from the model, but stopping each sequence at an early stage and using the generated output as the final result. This will allow the model to explore different possible output paths and avoid getting trapped in local minima. Evaluate the performance of this "early-stopped multi-sampling" on a range of text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with standard single-sampling and the attention-augmented low-NFE model from proposal 6.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The early-stopped multi-sampling approach should achieve improved MSMFT scores and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, especially when evaluated on sequences with multiple modes or complex structure. However, it may require careful tuning of the early-stopping threshold and sampling schedule to achieve optimal performance.

Deep learning models have achieved impressive success across a wide range of tasks, yet they can behave unpredictably when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) data that differ significantly from the training distribution, making high-confidence but incorrect predictions. OOD detection seeks to identify such inputs and is critical for reliable deployment in open-world scenarios, including safety-critical applications and scientific discovery tasks. The challenge becomes even more pronounced for graph-structured data, because of their non-Euclidean nature and complex topological structures.

Recent advances in graph-level OOD detection fall broadly into two categories. End-to-end methods train OOD-specific graph neural networks (GNNs) from scratch using only unlabeled in-distribution (ID) data; they typically rely on unsupervised objectives such as graph contrastive learning to extract discriminative representations that can separate ID and OOD samples during inference. Post-hoc methods instead start from well-trained GNNs and fine-tune OOD detectors that refine the predictions or representations at inference time. Among them, a recent test-time method, GOODAT, directly optimizes a learnable graph masker on the test samples without altering the pre-trained model. This test-time setting with data-centric modification is more practical, because it removes the dependency on labeled training data and on model retraining.

The test-time problem can be stated as follows. A GNN has been pre-trained on graphs from an unlabeled ID dataset. At test time it faces unlabeled graphs that mix held-out ID graphs, disjoint from the pre-training graphs, with graphs drawn from a different, OOD distribution. The goal is a detector that assigns each test graph a score, a higher score meaning a greater probability that the graph comes from the OOD distribution, using only the pre-trained model and the test graphs: the parameters of the pre-trained model are not modified, and neither the training data nor any ground-truth label is used.

Despite the progress of this data-centric paradigm, a less-explored challenge persists. A pre-trained model can effectively extract information from ID data, but when it infers on both ID and OOD test graphs it lacks ground-truth information indicative of the underlying distribution, information that is often embedded within the graph structure. Test graphs typically comprise distinctive components, whose capture could intuitively differentiate OOD samples from ID graphs, together with irrelevant structural elements. The pervasive presence of similar irrelevant structural elements in ID and OOD graphs, a structural redundancy that induces semantic shifts, hinders current methods from accurately capturing and distinguishing the essential structures of ID and OOD data. The existing test-time method tries to address this concern by using graph maskers to identify subgraphs in the test data that are similar to those in the ID training graphs, but it fundamentally relies on learnable graph augmentations, which can inadvertently alter the semantic information of substructures or lead to information loss, thereby compromising the reliability of OOD detection.

This raises the following questions. How can a well-trained GNN, left unchanged, be endowed at test time with the ability to capture the essential, distinctive structural information of test graphs while discarding irrelevant structural redundancy, without altering the semantics of their substructures? How can what is essential for telling ID from OOD graphs be separated from what is redundant in a principled and tractable way, when neither ground-truth labels nor OOD examples are available? And can such a test-time detector yield more reliable OOD scores than existing end-to-end and post-hoc approaches while remaining practical in computational cost?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: distance regularization for subgraph pruning
PROPOSAL: Investigate using a distance regularization term within the loss function to promote the pruning of disconnected subgraphs during test-time, without needing to learn graph masks or modify the pre-trained GNN. This can be achieved by adding a term to the loss that penalizes the distance between node embeddings in the same subgraph, while encouraging nodes in different subgraphs to have different representations. We will train the pre-trained GNN on a combination of the ID training dataset and a modified version of it where disconnected subgraphs have been artificially separated. We will then use the trained model to generate OOD scores on test graphs, evaluating performance on ind-dependent benchmark datasets.
CONTROLS: GOODAT (baseline), run without distance regularization term to evaluate its effectiveness.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Good potential for improvement in OOD detection, but might fail if the pre-trained model is unable to capture the structural redundancy necessary for the distance regularization to be effective.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: structural redundancy loss
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel structural redundancy loss term to explicitly encourage the model to separate essential from redundant structure. This can be achieved by computing the intersection of node and edge neighborhoods between ID and OOD graphs, and incorporating this similarity into the loss function to penalize the preservation of redundant structure. We will evaluate the performance of the proposed loss term in conjunction with the distance regularization term in proposal 1 on various benchmark datasets.
CONTROLS: Proposal 1 (distance regularization term), Proxy-OOD (baseline).
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: May achieve improved results compared to existing methods, especially in cases where essential and redundant structures are strongly correlated, but the computation of the structural redundancy loss might be computationally expensive, potentially hindering its applicability in large-scale settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adaptive subgraph decomposition
PROPOSAL: Propose an adaptive subgraph decomposition (ASD) technique to dynamically identify and separate essential from redundant structure in test graphs. ASD will utilize an unsupervised clustering-based method to identify clusters of highly connected nodes within the test graph, and then select a subset of these clusters as representative of the essential structure. We will evaluate the performance of the ASD technique on various benchmark datasets for OOD detection.
CONTROLS: GoodAT (baseline), and the structural redundancy loss term from proposal 2 for comparison.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: May lead to improved OOD detection performance by allowing the model to dynamically adapt to the specific structural composition of the test graph, but may fail if the clusters of highly connected nodes are not representative of the essential structure or are overly influenced by redundant structure.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 3
TITLE: adaptive subgraph decomposition
PROPOSAL: Refine the adaptive subgraph decomposition (ASD) technique from proposal 3 to integrate it with the structural redundancy loss term from proposal 2. This will involve adapting the clustering method used in ASD to selectively remove redundant structure while preserving the essential structure, and then incorporating the resulting clusters into the structural redundancy loss term as a way of promoting structural compactness. We will evaluate the performance of the enhanced ASD technique on various benchmark datasets.
CONTROLS: Same as proposal 3 plus the structural redundancy loss term from proposal 2.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: May lead to improved OOD detection performance by more effectively removing redundant structure while preserving essential structure, but will rely on the robustness of the clustering method and the parameterization of the structural redundancy loss term.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 2
TITLE: structural redundancy loss
PROPOSAL: Revise the structural redundancy loss term from proposal 2 to incorporate spectral graph convolution-based node embedding that captures local structural information. This will involve replacing the raw node features with the output of the spectral graph convolution layer, and then computing the intersection of the node and edge neighborhoods between ID and OOD graphs. We will evaluate the performance of the revised structural redundancy loss term on various benchmark datasets for OOD detection.
CONTROLS: GoodAT (baseline), original structural redundancy loss term from proposal 2.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: May lead to improved OOD detection performance by better capturing local structural information, but might fail if the spectral graph convolution layer fails to capture essential structural information.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: masked graph convolution
PROPOSAL: Investigate using masked graph convolution to selectively mask out redundant structure during the convolution process, allowing the model to focus on essential structure. We will compare the performance of masked graph convolution with the proposed techniques in proposal 1, 2, and 3, as well as with GOODAT (baseline) on various benchmark datasets for OOD detection.
CONTROLS: Proposals 1, 2, and 3, GoodAT (baseline)
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: May lead to improved OOD detection performance by effectively removing redundant structure, but may fail if the masking strategy is not effective in removing irrelevant structure or alters the semantics of the essential structure.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 4
TITLE: masked graph convolution
PROPOSAL: Refine the masked graph convolution layer from proposal 4 to use an attention-based mechanism to assign weights to the graph vertices based on their relevance to the task, thereby selectively focusing on essential structure while downplaying redundant structure. We will also incorporate the learned attention weights into the structural redundancy loss term from proposal 2 to further promote the removal of redundant structure.
CONTROLS: Original masked graph convolution layer, proposal 2 (structural redundancy loss).
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: May lead to improved OOD detection performance by effectively removing redundant structure while preserving essential structure, but will rely on the robustness of the attention-based mechanism and the parameterization of the structural redundancy loss term.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: differential edge sampled graph neural network
PROPOSAL: Propose utilizing a differential edge-sampled graph neural network (DE-GNN) that selectively samples edges based on a learnable score indicating the importance of each edge to the task. We will incorporate the DE-GNN into the pre-trained model to adaptively remove redundant edges while preserving essential connections. This will enable the model to selectively capture the structure that is most indicative of the essential information in the graph, thereby improving OOD detection performance.
CONTROLS: GoodAT (baseline), proposals 1, 2, and 3 for comparison.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: May lead to improved OOD detection performance by effectively removing redundant structure and edges while preserving essential connections, but may require careful tuning of the edge sampling strategy and parameters to ensure that the model maintains its performance on ID data.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 5
TITLE: differential edge sampled graph neural network
PROPOSAL: Refine the differential edge-sampled graph neural network (DE-GNN) from proposal 5 by incorporating a node-level attention mechanism to selectively focus on nodes that are most relevant to the task. This will enable the DE-GNN to selectively capture the structure that is most indicative of the essential information in the graph, while also considering the importance of each node. We will also integrate the DE-GNN with the structural redundancy loss term from proposal 2 to further promote the removal of redundant edges and nodes.
CONTROLS: Original DE-GNN, proposal 2 (structural redundancy loss). Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: May lead to improved OOD detection performance by effectively removing redundant structure and edges while preserving essential connections, and by selectively focusing on nodes that are most relevant to the task, but may require careful tuning of the node-level attention mechanism and parameters to ensure that the model maintains its performance on ID data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: ensemble of graph neural networks
PROPOSAL: Propose an ensemble method that combines the predictions of multiple graph neural networks, each trained with a different technique for removing redundant structure (e.g. distance regularization, structural redundancy loss, adaptive subgraph decomposition, masked graph convolution, and differential edge-sampled graph neural network). We will train the individual models on the same pre-trained model and test graph dataset, and then combine their predictions to obtain a final OOD score. This will allow us to evaluate the performance of each individual technique and combine their strengths to improve overall performance.
CONTROLS: Individual techniques from proposals 1-5, GoodAT (baseline).
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: May lead to improved OOD detection performance by combining the strengths of multiple techniques, but may require careful tuning of the ensemble method and hyperparameters to ensure that the combined model performs well on both ID and OOD data.

Diffusion models have recently demonstrated remarkable capabilities in synthesizing high-quality images, significantly surpassing earlier generative approaches such as generative adversarial networks and variational autoencoders. Despite their impressive fidelity, deploying diffusion models in realistic cloud-to-user applications introduces a fundamental bottleneck: transmission bandwidth. A standard diffusion model produces a high-fidelity image by performing a fixed number of denoising steps, regardless of downstream transmission limitations. In conventional scenarios, the generated images then undergo aggressive lossy compression before transmission to accommodate the limited bandwidth. This cascaded approach, high-quality generation followed by subsequent compression, not only incurs redundant computational overhead, since computation is spent on details that are later discarded, but also significantly degrades perceptual quality, as the compression process often erases the intricate textures and fine details carefully constructed by the diffusion model.

This motivates a critical question: can bandwidth-awareness be integrated directly into the diffusion generation process, so that the quality of the generated image is adapted to the available bandwidth, avoiding the inefficiency and perceptual quality loss associated with post-generation compression? Ideally, such a generator would meet a user-specified bitrate budget, avoid compression-induced artifacts and redundant computation, and offer fine-grained, dynamic control over image quality according to real-time bandwidth conditions in practical cloud-to-user deployments.

The question is not straightforward. During sampling, diffusion models progressively refine coarse structures into detailed, realistic textures through iterative denoising steps, so, intuitively, terminating the process early would yield simpler, lower-detail images suited to constrained bandwidth. However, naively reducing the number of diffusion steps typically produces suboptimal visual quality: models trained for complete denoising trajectories are not optimized for early termination, which leads to visual artifacts and poor perceptual coherence.

Existing lines of work address only parts of this problem. A large body of work accelerates diffusion sampling, through deterministic samplers that need fewer inference steps, numerical solvers inspired by ordinary differential equations, distillation of slow teacher models into faster students, adaptive step-size selection, latent-space compression, non-uniform step skipping, dynamic network pruning, predictors of the minimal number of denoising steps, and adaptive inference trajectories. These methods reduce the cost of sampling while preserving generation quality, but they are not designed to control the bitrate of the generated image. Conditional and controllable diffusion models, from classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance to latent diffusion and region-based conditioning for interactive editing, allow flexible control over attributes of the generated content, but they do not directly address bandwidth constraints. How to make a diffusion model generate images that respect a specified bandwidth budget while preserving perceptual quality and avoiding wasted computation therefore remains an open problem.

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: bitrate-aware diffusion sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of adaptively controlling the number of denoising steps based on the available bandwidth, using a simple bandwidth-aware sampler that terminates the process when the remaining bitrate drops below a predetermined threshold. Train a standard unconditional diffusion model on a dataset of images with varying qualities (e.g., CIFAR-10, LSUN, CelebA) and validate the sampler on a separate test set with controlled bandwidth constraints.
CONTROLS: Compare with naive termination and full denoising step counts, to assess the trade-offs between generation quality and bitrate efficiency. Use metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, and bits per pixel (bpp) to evaluate the quality and bitrate of generated images.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive sampler should produce high-quality images that respect the specified bitrate budget, outperforming naive termination methods in both quality and bitrate efficiency. However, it may fail when the available bandwidth is too low to support the resolution or detail of the input image.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: compressed diffusion model
PROPOSAL: Modify the diffusion model architecture to natively incorporate compression-aware loss functions and constraints, allowing the model to learn implicit representations of the output image that are more amenable to transmission under bandwidth constraints. Design a custom loss function that minimizes both the reconstruction error and a compression-aware penalty term, and experiment with applying state-of-the-art compression algorithms (e.g., JPEG, JPEG 2000) to the output image.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard diffusion models and the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler (Proposal 1) to assess the trade-offs between quality, bitrate efficiency, and computational overhead. Use a dataset of high-resolution images (e.g., ImageNet, COCO) to evaluate the effectiveness of the compressed diffusion model. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The compressed diffusion model should achieve state-of-the-art bitrate efficiency while maintaining competitive generation quality, but may require a larger model size and more computationally expensive training due to the additional compression-aware loss terms.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: bitrate-aware diffusion sampling
PROPOSAL: Refine the proposed bitrate-aware diffusion sampler (Proposal 1) by incorporating a novel estimation mechanism for the remaining bitrate, which adaptively adjusts the sampling process to ensure that the generated image's bitrate drops below the target budget. Experiment with different estimation methods, such as bitrate prediction networks or robust bitrate estimators, to determine their impact on sampler performance.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the compressed diffusion model (Proposal 2) to assess the improvements brought by the revised estimation mechanism. Validate the sampler on a diverse set of images with rich textures and details, such as natural scenes and artwork. Evaluate all methods on the same held-out test set and report the mean and standard deviation over five seeds.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised bitrate-aware diffusion sampler with estimation mechanism should demonstrate more accurate bitrate control and higher quality images, outperforming the original sampler and competitive with the compressed diffusion model, but may incur additional computational overhead due to the estimation process.

ACTION: REVISE
 TITLE: bitrate-aware diffusion sampling
 PROPOSAL: Incorporate a learning-based mechanism that adapts the sampling process to the specific characteristics of the input image, allowing the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler to make informed decisions about when to terminate the sampling process and achieve optimal bitrate-accuracy trade-offs.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the compressed diffusion model to assess the improvements brought by the adaptive learning mechanism.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The learning-based mechanism in the revised bitrate-aware diffusion sampler should demonstrate improved bitrate control and higher quality images, especially when dealing with diverse input images.

ADDITIONAL EXPERIMENT: Analyze the impact of different learning objectives and mechanism types, such as supervised learning with bitrate labels or self-supervised learning with bitrate-predictive losses.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adaptive compression matching
PROPOSAL: Develop an adaptive compression algorithm that dynamically selects the optimal compression parameters (e.g., quantization step, entropy coding scheme) for each output image, based on the estimated bitrate-accuracy trade-offs learned by the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler. This approach allows for real-time bitrate adaptation, ensuring that the generated image respects the available bandwidth while maintaining optimal quality.
CONTROLS: Compare with the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the compressed diffusion model to evaluate the benefits of adaptive compression matching. Use a dataset of high-resolution images with varying complexities.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive compression matching algorithm should demonstrate improved bitrate efficiency and quality, outperforming both the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the compressed diffusion model, especially under time-varying bandwidth constraints.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: joint bitrate-aware diffusion training
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel training framework that jointly optimizes the diffusion model, the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler, and the adaptive compression matching algorithm to achieve a balanced solution that respects the bitrate budget while preserving high image quality. Use a hierarchical optimization approach, where the model is trained to minimize a combination of image quality metrics and the estimated bitrate.
CONTROLS: Compare with separate training and adaptation of the diffusion model, bitrate-aware diffusion sampler, and adaptive compression matching algorithm to evaluate the benefits of joint training. Validate the approach using a real-world image transmission application.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Joint bitrate-aware diffusion training should produce a model that achieves superior bitrate-accuracy trade-offs, outperforming the separate training approach, but may require a larger model size and more computationally expensive training due to the additional optimizer.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: adaptive compression matching
PROPOSAL: Modify the adaptive compression matching algorithm (Proposal 3) to incorporate a bitrate-effective distortion metric, such as structural similarity (SSIM) or perceptual quality (PQ), which balances the trade-off between visual quality and bitrate. This modification enables the adaptive compression matching algorithm to more effectively optimize the compression process and reduce the required bitrate while maintaining high image quality.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original adaptive compression matching algorithm (Proposal 3) and the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler to evaluate the benefits of incorporating a bitrate-effective distortion metric.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised adaptive compression matching algorithm should achieve better bitrate efficiency and higher quality images, surpassing the original adaptation approach and competitive with the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler, while maintaining efficient bitrate control under a wide range of bandwidth conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: partial image rendering
PROPOSAL: Develop a partial image rendering technique that selectively renders regions of an image with varying resolutions, based on the available bandwidth and the importance of each region. Use the adaptive compression matching algorithm (Proposal 3) to compress the rendered regions and adaptively adjust their resolutions based on the estimated bitrate and visual quality.
CONTROLS: Compare with the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the joint bitrate-aware diffusion training approach to evaluate the benefits of partial image rendering. Use a dataset of complex images with varying scene compositions.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The partial image rendering technique should achieve significant bitrate efficiency improvements and preserve high image quality, outperforming both the bitrate-aware diffusion sampler and the joint bitrate-aware diffusion training approach, especially for large and dynamic images.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: dynamic bitrate scheduling
PROPOSAL: Design a dynamic bitrate scheduling framework that adjusts the bitrate of an image transmission based on real-time network conditions, user preferences, and content demands. Use the partial image rendering technique (Proposal 5) to render the image in multiple resolutions and allocate bandwidth dynamically based on the estimated bitrate and visual quality of each region.
CONTROLS: Compare with static bitrate scheduling approaches, such as fixed bitrate allocation or adaptive bitrate allocation using image features, to evaluate the benefits of dynamic bitrate scheduling. Validate the approach using a real-world network simulation.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The dynamic bitrate scheduling framework should achieve optimal bitrate-accuracy trade-offs and efficiently allocate bandwidth under varying network conditions, outperforming static scheduling approaches, but may require a more complex system architecture and communication protocol.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: dynamic bitrate scheduling
PROPOSAL: Extend the dynamic bitrate scheduling framework (Proposal 6) to incorporate machine learning-based prediction of network conditions and user preferences, allowing for proactive bitrate planning and real-time adjustments. Use the joint bitrate-aware diffusion training approach (Proposal 4) to train a model that learns to predict optimal bitrate allocation and rendering decisions based on these factors.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original dynamic bitrate scheduling framework (Proposal 6) and other machine learning-based bitrate planning approaches to evaluate the benefits of incorporating prediction and proactive planning. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised dynamic bitrate scheduling framework with machine learning-based prediction and proactive planning should outperform other approaches in terms of optimizing bitrate-accuracy trade-offs, reducing transmission latency, and improving overall user experience, but may require larger training datasets and higher computational resources.

Facial rigging aims to make a static neutral facial mesh animatable by defining a set of controllable deformations, typically represented either as blendshape rigs driven by activated action units in systems based on the Facial Action Coding System (FACS), or as skeletal rigs driven by joint positions. Whereas full-body auto-rigging usually follows a two-step pipeline of skeleton construction and skinning, facial rigs are often anatomically inspired and implemented with FACS blendshapes. In a linear FACS blendshape rig, each blendshape is a vertex offset from the neutral mesh corresponding to one action unit, i.e. a specific muscle movement such as "Right Eye Close", and a complex expression is obtained by adding the weighted offsets of the activated blendshapes to the neutral mesh. Rigging is an essential step for creative AI, bringing digital avatars to life by enabling expressive and realistic facial movements across a wide range of applications. However, creating a facial rig is laborious and expensive, often requiring skilled artists tens of hours to complete a single asset. Methods that transfer expressions from 2D images or videos to 3D avatars do not remove this bottleneck, since they assume that the avatar already has a rig.

Existing facial auto-rigging methods typically transfer a complete set of blendshapes from a predefined template mesh to a neutral target mesh, which often requires dense correspondences or a mesh topology shared by the template and the target. More recent approaches build transferable latent spaces between faces or use triangulation-agnostic networks to bypass these limitations, but they still require a template blendshape rig, which can compromise accuracy when the template and target shapes differ substantially. Only one prior approach, NFR, can directly rig facial meshes from explicitly controllable FACS parameters without relying on a template, and it has so far been demonstrated primarily on humanoid heads. Furthermore, existing approaches, NFR included, have yet to accommodate meshes with multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs or teeth, which limits their ability to animate highly expressive avatars: an "eye look-down" pose, for example, is difficult to reproduce if the mesh lacks eyeballs.

Learning such a rigging model also raises a data problem. Accurate 3D supervision requires neutral meshes paired with complete rigs made by artists, and because manual rigging is so costly such rigged examples are scarce; a model trained solely on them is likely to generalize poorly to the wide variety of facial shapes, styles and topologies met in practice.

The problem is therefore to automatically turn a single static neutral facial mesh into an expressive rig controllable by FACS parameters (i) without relying on predefined template blendshapes, so that target meshes need not closely resemble a template; (ii) for in-the-wild meshes with varying topologies and shapes, including both humanoid and non-humanoid heads; and (iii) for meshes made of multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs and teeth, which must move coherently with the rest of the face. How can such a rigging system be built, and how can it be trained to generalize across this diversity when only a limited number of rigged meshes is available as 3D ground truth?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: preliminary evaluation of nfr
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of NFR on recently released face datasets (e.g. 300 Software-Synthetic Driver Face images, Time-of-Flight Face Data, and DepthFace) and on a pool of in-house non-humanoid faces, to evaluate current limitations and generalizability. Specifically, measure the accuracy of facial action unit (AU) reconstructions, AU visualization, and final expression reproduction.
CONTROLS: compare to a pool of other state-of-the-art methods (e.g. FACS Plus, MRLoss+EMD) on recent face datasets, ablation of different layers of the NFR network
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Given its strong prior habit of training on humanoid heads, NFR will perform well on our pool of in-house faces but poorly on non-humanoid ones, underscoring the existing diversity problem in 3D facial datasets for AV research - though the method is very likely to outperform most baselines in terms of A and AU precision, especially on neutral faces.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: dataset augmentation and generation
PROPOSAL: Utilize a combination of generative models (e.g. 3D-GAN, AtlasNet) and data augmentation techniques (e.g. random rotation, lighting conditions) to generate relevant synthetic facial meshes and corresponding FACS parameters. Specifically, generate neutral meshes with varying face styles, shapes, and topologies (including non-humanoid faces) and simulate a wide range of facial expressions using the generated rigs.
CONTROLS: compare the generated data's realism and diversity to existing real-world facial datasets (e.g. Paris Liability Facial Atlas), evaluate how well the generated data supplemented or replaced real-world data in existing facial rigging models and experiments
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Generators will be able to capture some general texture and style properties found in real-world facial data but struggle to replicate subtle differences between individuals and the subtleties of in-the-wild facial expressions - though they can still generate a variety of styles and expressions that may prove useful in data augmentation.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: dataset augmentation and generation
PROPOSAL: Utilize a combination of generative models (e.g. 3D-GAN, AtlasNet) to generate relevant synthetic facial meshes and corresponding FACS parameters that are specifically tailored to facilitate the learning of highly expressive facial movements controllable by multiple FACS parameters (e.g. simultaneous eye movements, full activations of a FACS AU set). Merge the synthetic datasets with real-world ones to create a more diverse dataset for training, and assess the augmenting impact on existing facial rigging models.
CONTROLS: evaluate how well the dataset augmentation can compensate for the limited amount of real-world data, and compare the performance of facial rigging models on the resulting augmented dataset versus the pure real-world dataset
COST: 150 GPU-hours (versus 120 in v1, as we now need to generate a larger dataset with a more granular control over FACS parameters)
PREDICTION: Both real-world and synthetic data contribute to the enrichment of the dataset, which positively affects the facial rigging's accuracy and expressiveness in both in-the-wild and synthetic datasets.

TITLE: mesh to mesh refinement
PROPOSAL: Implement a data-driven approach that uses a pair of congruent facial meshes (source and target) - either synthetic, in-the-wild or both - to refine and improve facial rigging meshes, aiming to capture fine-grained details and anatomical features without relying on manual adjustment of FACS parameters or extensive face mask computation. Evaluate the proposed approach versus a standard data-driven FACS-based facial rigging method.
CONTROLS: compare the results of mesh refinement across synthetic and in-the-wild meshes, ablation studies on facial mesh topology variations
COST: 250 GPU-hours (due to the iterative approach that requires refining the two congruent mesh pairs independently and jointly)
PREDICTION: A better approximation of anatomical plausibility and

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: dataset augmentation and generation
PROPOSAL: Utilize a combination of generative models (e.g. 3D-GAN, AtlasNet) and conditional GANs to generate high-quality synthetic facial meshes and corresponding FACS parameters that are specifically tailored to facilitate the learning of highly expressive facial movements controllable by multiple FACS parameters (e.g. simultaneous eye movements, full activations of a FACS AU set). Merge the synthetic datasets with real-world ones to create a more diverse dataset for training. Assess the augmenting impact on existing facial rigging models and their ability to handle highly diverse FACS AU sets.

COST: 180 GPU-hours

Note: Direct Cost Update Versus Prior Network Calculation

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: graph-convolutional facial rigging
PROPOSAL: Design a novel facial rigging system based on graph-convolutional neural networks (GCNNs), which learn to explicitly represent both the structural and anatomical properties of facial meshes. Define each node in the graph as a vertex of the mesh and each edge as a connection between two neighboring vertices, then train the GCNN to predict FACS parameter correspondences and associate them with a sequence of vertex-wise deformations that drive facial rigging.
CONTROLS: compare to existing FACS-based facial rigging methods (e.g. NFR) on a variety of facial mesh shapes and styles. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (high computing demand due to iterating though dense graphs)
PREDICTION: GCNN based deep facial rigging achieves high accuracy and robustness in capturing and describing intricate facial movements due to the ability to understand the anatomic and structural definitions of complexes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: weakly-supervised learning
PROPOSAL: Employ a weakly-supervised learning strategy to train facial rigging models, where only approximate or rough annotations (e.g. category labels of facial actions) are provided for the synthetic or real-world data instead of precise FACS parameter labels. Investigate various loss functions and objective criteria that can be used for training in this setting, such as涨-AU log-slopes, minimizing best-matching AU pairs, and a combination of action category conditional variance.
CONTROLS: compare the performance of facial rigging models with precise FACS parameter labels versus weakly-supervised settings on realistic facial datasets, ablation of using different categorization of AU features
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: A data-driven autosupervision function will help to extend knowledge and observations but nuance full pairwise definitions during early-critical direct teaching and retrieve outlying patterns that could strengthen real smith rivalry training.

TITLE: weakly-supervised learning

Deep neural networks trained with first-order optimization methods have achieved remarkable empirical success across diverse domains. Despite their widespread adoption, a rigorous theoretical understanding of their optimization dynamics and generalization behavior remains incomplete, particularly for networks with ReLU activations. The difficulty stems from the non-smoothness and non-convexity of the loss landscape induced by ReLU activations and network architectures, which complicate classical analyses. Intriguingly, over-parameterized models often reach zero training error and still generalize well in the absence of explicit regularization, a phenomenon that has spurred substantial theoretical research into its underlying mechanisms.

A prominent line of research analyzes neural network training through the neural tangent kernel (NTK). In the infinite-width limit, the dynamics of gradient descent (GD) can be characterized by functions in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of the NTK, and convergence guarantees have been established for both shallow and deep networks: provided the width is sufficiently large, GD converges to a global minimum within a neighborhood of its initialization. In this regime, generalization errors of order $L\sqrt{\mathbf{y}^\top(\mathbf{H}^\infty)^{-1}\mathbf{y}/n}$ have been obtained for networks of depth $L$ trained on $n$ examples, where $\mathbf{H}^\infty$ denotes the NTK Gram matrix over the training data, but only for widths polynomial in $n$, $L$ and $1/\lambda_0$, with $\lambda_0$ the smallest eigenvalue of $\mathbf{H}^\infty$. Requiring $\lambda_0>0$ is a strong assumption, because this eigenvalue tends to zero as the size of the training set grows. A weaker assumption is that the data are separable by the NTK features at initialization with a margin $\gamma$. Under this assumption, a logarithmic width suffices for two-layer ReLU networks, with a risk bound of order $1/(\gamma^2\sqrt{n})$ derived from Rademacher complexity; this width result relies on the 1-homogeneity of two-layer ReLU networks, a property that does not hold for deep networks. Extensions to deep ReLU networks yield bounds that still decay only as $1/\sqrt{n}$ and contain either factors exponential in depth, such as $4^L$, or additional width-dependent terms. A rate of order $1/(\gamma^2 n)$ has so far been derived only for two-layer ReLU networks. More generally, uniform-convergence analyses based on Rademacher complexity or covering numbers can lead to vacuous bounds, typically depend exponentially on the depth, and usually yield rates of order $1/\sqrt{n}$.

A complementary line of research relies on algorithmic stability. Building on the observation that the spectral norm of the Hessian of wide networks scales with the width $m$ as $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{m})$, stability analyses have obtained bounds of order $\widetilde{O}(1/(n\gamma^2))$ for shallow networks, which is almost optimal in view of known lower bounds, and have been extended to deep networks with bounds of order $\widetilde{O}(e^{O(L)}/(n\gamma^2))$. These analyses, however, assume smooth activation functions and cannot be applied to non-smooth ReLU networks; for deep networks, they also incur an exponential dependence on depth, both in the bound and in the required width.

In summary, existing results either exhibit the suboptimal $1/\sqrt{n}$ dependence on the sample size, are restricted to shallow networks, require smooth activations, or depend exponentially on the depth $L$. A natural and fundamental question is therefore whether GD on deep ReLU networks can achieve generalization rates comparable to the minimax optimal rates established in the kernel setting, namely the SVM-type rate of order $1/(n\gamma^2)$. Specifically, for fully connected deep ReLU networks trained by gradient descent with the logistic loss on binary classification data that are NTK-separable with margin $\gamma$: Can risk bounds of the optimal order $1/(\gamma^2 n)$ be established? Can the exponential dependence on the depth $L$ be replaced by a polynomial dependence $\mathrm{poly}(L)$? And how much over-parameterization (network width) do such guarantees require?

Human-object interaction (HOI) detection aims to localize humans and objects in an image and to recognize the interactions between them. It provides a fine-grained understanding of human activities, which is crucial for downstream applications such as robotic manipulation, image captioning and autonomous driving. Despite recent progress, HOI detection remains challenging because of the large combinatorial space of human-object pairs and the need for fine-grained visual understanding. Moreover, real-world applications often require recognizing human-object interactions that do not appear in the training set, which leads to the task of zero-shot HOI detection. Conventional HOI detectors fail to generalize to such unseen interactions, and early attempts that disentangle object and verb features for compositional generalization cannot handle unseen objects or unseen verbs.

To address zero-shot HOI detection, recent works exploit vision-language models such as CLIP to transfer semantic knowledge from language to HOI detection. Typically, they use text embeddings of interaction descriptions, e.g., "A person is holding a cup", to construct classifiers for unseen interactions. While effective to some extent, these methods face limitations. First, CLIP features lack the fine-grained representational capacity required to distinguish visually similar interactions, so methods have to incorporate detector features to obtain fine-grained representations of instances. Second, their core mechanism, aligning visual and text features, operates only on categories observed during training, which restricts generalization to unseen interactions.

At the same time, progress in open-vocabulary object detection provides a sufficient solution for localizing unseen objects, so interaction recognition has become the main bottleneck. Yet most existing methods, including two-stage methods, couple interaction recognition with a specific object detector: they rely on detector features or on relations between detected objects to give vision-language features fine-grained representational capacity, and they struggle to balance fine-grained detector features with generalized vision-language features. As a result, interaction recognition and detection cannot be improved independently, and the detector cannot be changed without retraining.

Effective interaction recognition therefore requires representations that are both fine-grained and broadly generalizable. This raises the following questions. How can the interactions of a given human-object pair, including interactions never observed during training, be recognized with such representations rather than through alignment with static text embeddings fitted to the seen categories, given that recognition is multi-label because one pair can be engaged in several interactions at once? Can interaction recognition be made independent of any particular object detector, so that it works with the boxes produced by any detector without retraining, stays reliable when those boxes are imperfect, and remains computationally tractable given the many human-object pairs and candidate interactions in an image?

Visual document retrieval is the task of returning relevant documents, typically PDFs containing figures, tables, and other visual elements, in response to a textual query. Neural retrieval pipelines for this task often follow a text-centric approach: source documents are converted into textual chunks with optical character recognition or vision-language models, and an index is then built with semantic text encoders. An alternative, vision-centric approach relies instead on multimodal encoders. Building on the ColBERT late-interaction approach, ColPali-based encoders operate directly on page images, matching textual query tokens to image patches and producing multi-vector embeddings of images and queries.

Although this vision-centric paradigm achieves state-of-the-art results on public visual document retrieval benchmarks, open challenges remain. First, in pursuit of state-of-the-art performance, recent late-interaction multimodal retrievers have massively scaled the length and dimensionality of their query and document representations. This incurs substantial latency and storage overhead and hinders efficient, scalable deployment in real-world pipelines; one recent retriever, for example, represents each document page with about 10 MB of memory, three orders of magnitude more than a single-vector dense retriever. Second, matching textual queries to textually rich documents with a purely vision-centric model may be limited by the substantial modality gap that modern vision-language models still exhibit. These limitations motivate exploring complementary ways of improving multimodal encoders, rather than relying only on ever-larger monolithic models.

A long-standing idea in neural retrieval is hybrid retrieval, in which the outputs of different retrievers are aggregated, at the level of document ranks or of query-document similarity scores, to obtain the final list of retrieved documents. Hybrid retrieval (or hybrid search) most commonly refers to combining a neural semantic text retriever with a sparse lexical representation such as BM25; more broadly, it reflects the notion that models relying on different types of representations capture complementary aspects of the data, which can be leveraged to boost overall performance. Dense text retrievers typically have low online latency and a small storage footprint, and they provide a uni-modal signal between the query and the document representation. Combining text and image encoders therefore emerges as a natural candidate for enhancing a multimodal retrieval system.

However, standard hybrid retrieval methods take a rather coarse-grained view of each retriever: because they reduce every query-document pair to a single rank or score, they cannot exploit the rich query-document interactions within each model's representation space. Aggregating at the level of the representations themselves would carry the richest information, but at query time it is hindered by heterogeneity: encoders may use a single vector or many vectors per query and document, with differing dimensionalities and scales, and any aggregation must respect strict latency and memory budgets without access to supervision. A further difficulty is that the complementary retriever may be lightweight and even weaker on the task than the primary one, and it is unclear whether such a signal can help at all.

This raises the following questions. Can the paradigm of hybrid retrieval complement modern vision-centric multimodal encoders, and in particular, can a lightweight dense text retriever enhance a stronger vision-centric retriever? How can the signals of two heterogeneous retrievers be combined at query time so as to exploit the rich interactions within their representation spaces, rather than only their final ranks or scores, while remaining architecture-agnostic (applicable to both single-vector and multi-vector models), lightweight, and practical? And can such a combination improve the trade-off between retrieval quality, online latency, and index memory compared with scaling up the representations of a single model?

Proteins realize their biological functions through intricate three-dimensional conformations, and predicting such structures has long been a central challenge in computational biology. AlphaFold2 marked a breakthrough by combining multiple sequence alignments with geometric constraints in an end-to-end framework, achieving near-experimental accuracy. Building on this foundation, AlphaFold3 reformulates the architecture into an all-atom framework and introduces a diffusion-based structure module, thereby enabling the generative modeling of not only proteins but also a wide spectrum of biomolecular complexes. Consequently, this series of models is widely adopted as a family of foundation models for downstream applications such as virtual screening and protein design. However, AlphaFold3's architecture, which relies on iterative Pairformer recycling and multi-step diffusion, requires substantially greater computational overhead than AlphaFold2, restricting its accessibility in downstream workflows.

More specifically, on long sequences the execution time of AlphaFold3 is measured in minutes, which severely limits its usability in downstream tasks that demand high throughput. For instance, small-scale laboratory screening often requires predictions for thousands of candidates, and when extended to large public databases this number grows to an infeasible scale; protein design tasks typically involve comparable computational demand. Previous work has attempted to mitigate this by manually reducing the number of recycling iterations on simpler structures, thus trading accuracy for efficiency. However, such compromises inevitably degrade predictive performance. Moreover, in hallucination-based design approaches, the multistep iterative refinement process hinders feasible gradient backpropagation, ultimately preventing the broader community from adopting AlphaFold3 as a foundation model for diverse applications.

To accelerate the diffusion process, recent advances in generative modeling have explored high-order solvers and consistency models. While high-order solvers improve efficiency, they rarely reduce the number of sampling steps below ten. Consistency models, on the other hand, have achieved remarkable success in image generation and have benefited from refined training schedules. However, transferring them to an AlphaFold3-style architecture raises two difficulties. First, standard consistency schedules assume fixed-dimensional data and pair timesteps at a constant Euclidean interval, which does not accommodate variable protein sequence lengths: on long sequences even a small step can trigger a drastic distribution shift that demands an unrealistic predictive leap, while on short sequences the same interval provides only a weak learning signal, so training dynamics can become unstable or collapse. Second, the iterative diffusion sampler is not the only source of iteration: the architecture also refines its internal pair and single representations through repeated recycling of the Pairformer trunk, whose cost grows with sequence length and which conventional diffusion-acceleration methods do not address at all.

The open problem is therefore whether an AlphaFold3-class all-atom biomolecular structure generator can be compressed into a predictor that runs in essentially a single forward pass -- removing both the multi-step denoising and the recycling overhead -- while retaining the accuracy of the full iterative model on protein, protein-ligand and nucleic-acid complexes. This matters because accuracy alone is not what blocks adoption: throughput and differentiability do. A useful accelerated model must remain reliable in the tail, not merely on average, since high-throughput screening and design pipelines discard most candidates and are harmed more by occasional implausible structures than by small average losses; it must stay cheap enough to be called thousands of times; and it must be light enough that gradients can be propagated through it, so that design methods which optimize sequences against a folding model become feasible with an all-atom model rather than only with earlier, cheaper architectures. Given this problem, how should one design experiments to establish whether such an acceleration is achievable without a loss of predictive fidelity?

Traditional multimodal models are typically divided into two categories: multimodal understanding (e.g., answering questions about images) and multimodal generation (e.g., generating images from text prompts). Unified Multimodal Generative Models (UMGMs) aim to integrate these two capabilities within a single framework. Recent UMGMs have demonstrated strong performance on a wide range of tasks, such as visual question answering, image captioning, visual reasoning, classification, reading comprehension, and image generation. They typically embed multiple input types into a shared representation space and use one single autoregressive transformer backbone to model cross-modal interactions, so that the same model produces both textual and visual outputs. Training generally follows a two-stage paradigm: pretraining focused on text-image alignment, followed by fine-tuning for specific downstream tasks, where instruction tuning (fine-tuning on diverse, task-specific instructions paired with expected outputs) has become a widely adopted strategy for aligning model behavior with human intent.

Although UMGMs show impressive zero-shot performance on many unseen instructions, their effectiveness is inconsistent across tasks, particularly when the relevant task data is absent from the pretraining corpus. Adding new task data to the training set can substantially improve performance on those tasks, but because novel multimodal tasks keep emerging, repeatedly merging new data and retraining the model is computationally expensive and impractical. This calls for ways to let UMGMs adapt flexibly and efficiently over time, in line with the principles of continual learning, where models acquire new capabilities incrementally.

Studies in continual learning have shown that sequentially fine-tuned models suffer from catastrophic forgetting: a model fine-tuned on new tasks tends to forget or overwrite previously acquired knowledge. Several works have explored continual instruction tuning for multimodal large language models, with methods that are typically regularization-based, architecture-based, replay-based, or prompt-based, and mixture-of-experts adapters have also attracted growing attention in continual learning for their scalability and modularity. However, these multimodal models produce language-only outputs, so prior research has focused exclusively on multimodal understanding tasks such as visual question answering, and existing methods address only intra-modal catastrophic forgetting, where old tasks, new tasks, and pre-trained capabilities all belong to the same output modality, typically text. This assumption holds for multimodal models with unimodal outputs, but it is insufficient for UMGMs, which generate both text and images from a single backbone. For UMGMs, forgetting may occur not only within a modality (intra-modal) but also across modalities (inter-modal): for example, continually tuning the model on a sequence of multimodal understanding tasks might erode its pre-trained image generation ability. This inter-modal forgetting remains largely unexplored, and it is unclear whether methods designed for the intra-modal setting can handle both forms of forgetting at once.

The central question is therefore: can UMGMs continually acquire new capabilities through instruction tuning without suffering catastrophic forgetting, both within a modality (e.g., multimodal understanding) and across modalities (e.g., improving multimodal understanding while preserving visual generation)? Answering it requires establishing whether inter-modal forgetting actually occurs in UMGMs, explaining what causes it, and finding an efficient way to adapt these models to new tasks that retains performance on earlier tasks as well as the pre-trained capabilities of the other modality.

Video anomaly analysis is a key application of computer vision for public security. Most early work formulates it as temporal video anomaly detection: marking the segments of a video whose behavior deviates from learned normal patterns, whether with one-class models trained only on normal clips, unsupervised reconstruction or future-frame prediction objectives, or weakly supervised learning from video-level labels. Such detectors have reached high performance on benchmarks, yet they output only frame-wise anomaly scores, without spatial or semantic context, and give no insight into why a segment is abnormal. These limits of interpretability have motivated a shift from temporal detection toward downstream tasks with user-friendly, explainable outputs: spatial video anomaly localization, which predicts bounding boxes around the regions that contain the abnormal activity, and textual video anomaly understanding, which decides whether a video contains an anomaly and produces a human-readable description explaining it, typically with fine-tuned multimodal large language models. Each line of work, however, provides either spatial or textual cues on its own and focuses on a single type of task, so that existing methods offer only an incomplete analysis of video anomalies. A holistic analysis would answer when an anomaly happens, where it is, what it is and why it is abnormal, each of the existing benchmark tasks addressing one of these sub-problems.

A second challenge is the heavy reliance on dataset-specific supervision. Detection and localization models require temporal masks or spatial bounding boxes, yet anomaly definitions vary widely across datasets, so a model tuned on one domain often fails on another and must be retrained for unseen domains or anomaly types. In real-world applications, privacy and security concerns may also make training data unavailable for some sensitive scenes. Open-set detectors that fuse language semantics in order to detect and classify novel anomalies still require task-specific training and give very limited insight into why frames are abnormal. As partial remedies, recent work has explored zero- and few-shot approaches built on frozen vision-language backbones or multimodal large language models, but most of these approaches have a limited task scope and still rely on annotated datasets. The only strictly zero-shot, training-free method addresses temporal detection alone: a frozen vision-language model captions the frames and a prompted large language model converts the captions into frame-wise anomaly scores. It is effective when anomalies are clearly distinguishable from normality but occasionally fails on more complex anomaly types, and it offers neither spatial grounding nor any direct semantic explanation beyond generic captions. Prompt-tuning methods, which optimize textual prompts to guide frozen models, require induction on an annotated training set and pay for it in generality, since the learned prompts tend to be task- or domain-specific. The generality problem is worse still for instruction-tuned multimodal models: they produce rich narrative explanations, but they require extensive annotation and computational resources, lack temporal or spatial coverage, and are optimized to return answers from seen question-answer pairs that describe a closed set of anomaly types.

Multimodal large language models already encode rich visual-semantic priors for commonsense reasoning, which suggests that fine-tuning may not be necessary for every task. This raises the questions addressed here: can temporal detection, spatial localization and textual explanation of video anomalies be delivered together, as one holistic and interpretable analysis, in a strictly zero-shot manner, with frozen pretrained models and without any additional training data, annotations or gradient updates? And can such an analysis remain at least as accurate as existing zero-shot detectors while staying robust across domains whose definitions of anomaly differ?

Neurons operate in ways that reflect their cell type, connectivity, and the brain region in which they are embedded. Understanding how these structural and physiological factors shape neural activity is an important open question and is central to modern theories of neural function. Cell type- and circuit-specific effects are also increasingly implicated in neurological disorders: particular neuronal subtypes can be selectively affected in neurodegenerative disease, and neuron subtypes can be targeted to improve efficacy in real time in closed-loop brain stimulation. Together, these directions highlight a broader need to understand how features such as cell type and brain region contribute to a neuron's role in the brain, motivating the development of methods that can extract aspects of neuron identity.

Much of what is known about neuronal cell types and their connectivity comes from molecular, anatomical, and morphological labeling techniques that tag neurons based on gene expression profiles or structural features. These approaches have revealed a rich taxonomy of neuronal classes, but they are resource intensive and typically provide only a sparse labeling of one or a few classes at a time, so identity labels are costly and difficult to obtain at scale. There is currently no molecular access to different cell types or projection classes in nonhuman primates and humans, which has created major roadblocks in studying neuron diversity in humans. For these reasons, there is growing interest in methods that can infer aspects of neuronal identity directly from large-scale neural population activity.

Deep learning approaches to this question have only recently begun to be explored. Early methods relied on intrinsic single-neuron features such as waveform shape or interspike interval profiles, but these signals capture only part of what distinguishes one neuron from another. More recent approaches incorporate some information about the ongoing population activity, but reduce the surrounding activity to fixed low-dimensional summaries, which obscures the fine-grained coordination patterns that are often key to neuronal identity. Furthermore, these models usually require retraining or finetuning on each new set of neurons, limiting their ability to generalize in a zero-shot manner across animals.

Making use of population context is itself challenging. The number of recorded neurons varies widely across experiments, individuals, and sessions, making it non-trivial to define a consistent input structure or population-level operation, and recordings span multiple experimental conditions, including different stimuli and behaviors, which makes it hard for a model to generalize across recording sessions. These limitations point to the need for methods that leverage rich population context while producing neuron-level representations that transfer robustly across recordings.

This raises several questions. Can a representation of each individual neuron be learned from population activity, when identity labels are scarce, such that it captures aspects of the neuron's identity such as its cell type and brain region? Can such representations transfer to entirely new sessions and animals without retraining or additional metadata? And how does the identity information they capture depend on the amount and diversity of recordings available for learning, compared with the number of labeled neurons?

The ability to model complex, real-world phenomena is one of the central challenges in machine learning. Domains such as geospatial modeling, where terrain varies drastically across regions, or speech analysis, where signals exhibit bursts of volatility, are often characterized by pronounced non-stationarity: their statistical properties change across the input space, so that sharp, localized events can coexist with smooth, slowly varying regions. Gaussian processes (GPs) offer a principled framework for such problems, providing robust uncertainty estimates and flexible, non-parametric modeling. Despite these advantages, exact GPs suffer from two major limitations: their expressivity is constrained by the choice of kernel, and exact inference costs O(N^3) time and O(N^2) memory in the number N of training points, rendering it impractical for modern large-scale applications.

Most current approaches force a trade-off between expressivity and efficiency. On one hand, random Fourier features achieve impressive scalability: the kernel is approximated by an explicit, finite-dimensional feature map obtained by Monte Carlo sampling from its spectral density, so that the GP reduces to a Bayesian linear regression whose cost is linear in the number of data points, and the approximation error is backed by theoretical guarantees. Yet this construction depends on Bochner's theorem, which fundamentally restricts it to stationary kernels that assume uniform behavior across the entire domain; its globally supported sinusoidal features are inherently spatially invariant. Applying such models to non-stationary data leads to systematic mis-specification, resulting in compromised predictive accuracy and uncalibrated uncertainty estimates. Sparse variational GPs reduce the cost of exact inference through a set of inducing points, but they rely on iterative optimization whose cost grows cubically with the number of inducing points. On the other hand, expressive models such as deep GPs, spectral mixture kernels, and input-dependent kernels can capture non-stationarity, but they often reintroduce prohibitive computational costs, complex inference schemes, and challenges in optimization and hyperparameter tuning, and they typically retain a high complexity in the number of training points. Hybrid approaches that combine scalable approximations with expressive models, such as kernel interpolation, deep kernel learning, deep random features, and adaptive or compositional Fourier-feature representations, still tend to trade off scalability, expressivity, and interpretability.

The gap between scalable stationary models and complex non-stationary ones therefore remains. This raises the central question of whether the random-feature paradigm can be generalized beyond Bochner's theorem to the non-stationary setting: can one construct an explicit, randomly sampled feature map whose induced kernel adapts to local, input-dependent structure, while preserving the linear-in-data training and prediction cost that makes random features attractive? Such a construction should also be principled, with guarantees, comparable to those available for random Fourier features, that the induced kernel is valid and that the random approximation converges to it as the number of features grows. Finally, it remains open whether such an approach can offer a better trade-off between predictive accuracy, uncertainty quality, and computational cost than both stationary random features and more complex non-stationary GP models.
