Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a powerful and principled approach for generative modeling, and in particular for high-quality visual generation. By learning a time-dependent velocity field that continuously transforms samples from a base distribution into a target distribution, FM models generate data by integrating an ordinary differential equation (ODE). This framework offers advantages over diffusion-based methods, including faster convergence, stable training, and direct control over sample trajectories.

Despite these strengths, inference in FM models is costly and has become a bottleneck. ODE integration is inherently sequential: each step depends on the output of the previous one, which makes the process slow and difficult to parallelize. High-fidelity generation requires a large number of fine-grained steps, which pushes latency up and makes real-time or interactive use difficult. As data dimensionality and model complexity increase, so does the inference burden. The issue is even more pronounced in video generation, where models operate on high-dimensional spatio-temporal data and the cost of sequential integration compounds across frames, making efficient inference essential for long videos.

Static reduction strategies such as distillation, trajectory truncation and consistency training have been proposed to reduce inference latency. However, they often degrade output quality, producing blurry textures, semantic drift or broken spatial coherence; in video, they often cause temporal flickering and motion inconsistency, which severely degrade realism even when individual frames look plausible. Many of them also require retraining the model with auxiliary objectives or handcrafted losses, which increases the engineering burden and restricts transferability across model families. As a result, these approaches are less modular, harder to scale, and often infeasible to deploy in time-sensitive or interactive pipelines.

In language models, a promising line of work for accelerating inference is speculative decoding, in which multiple drafts are proposed in parallel and selectively verified by the full model, reducing latency without retraining it. This idea, however, does not directly extend to image and video generative models such as FM, and two challenges stand out. First, unlike in language models, no readily available draft model exists: how can drafts be produced whose trajectories closely couple with those of the full model? Second, the performance of FM is highly sensitive to the velocity output: even a small perturbation in velocity can accumulate along the integration path and lead to severe generation errors. How, then, can drafted velocities be evaluated, and how can the drift of the resulting trajectory away from the full-model trajectory be controlled?

The open problem is therefore how to substantially reduce the inference latency of existing FM models, for both image and video generation, without retraining, without degrading output quality relative to standard full-step generation, and in a way that transfers across model families.

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: draft model acceleration via random path pruning
PROPOSAL: We propose to evaluate the feasibility of accelerating inference in FM models by selectively pruning short, random paths through the velocity field during the integration process. By doing so, we can reduce the overall number of integration steps required for achieving the same quality of output. We will experiment with various pruning strategies, including pruning based on velocity magnitude, Euclidean distance, and maximum gradient.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no pruning. (2) Ablation study: Different pruning strategies and their combinations. (3) Control: Randomly subsampling the paths. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a latency reduction of up to 30% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and a significant decrease in video generation latency. However, this approach may lead to variations in generation quality depending on the pruning strategy used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: learning draft models for fm using Curriculum Learning
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of generating high-quality drafts in FM models, we propose using Curriculum Learning to learn a draft model that closely couples with the full model. We will define a gradual curriculum of temporally corrected velocities that guide the learning process of the draft model. As the curriculum progresses, the draft model will learn to produce velocities that are increasingly similar to those produced by the full model. This will enable the draft model to not only accelerate inference but also maintain high quality output.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different curriculum learning schedules. (3) Control: Learning draft models using random sampling of the velocity field. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 40% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. The quality of the drafts will be strongly dependent on the quality of the curriculum learning schedule.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: draft model acceleration via random path pruning
PROPOSAL: We revise our initial proposal to include an incentive mechanism that rewards the draft model for producing velocities that result in generated samples that are closer to the ground truth. This can be achieved by incorporating a reconstruction loss into the draft model's training objective, which encourages the draft model to produce high-quality samples that are close to the target distribution. By doing so, we can improve the accuracy and quality of the draft model's outputs.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no pruning and no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different loss functions and weights for the reconstruction loss. (3) Control: Learning draft models using random sampling of the velocity field without reconstruction loss. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 50% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. However, the introduction of the reconstruction loss may lead to increased training time and potential mode collapse issues.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: learning draft models for fm using curriculum learning
PROPOSAL: We revise our proposal to use a more efficient curriculum learning schedule that utilizes progressive meta-learning. Instead of learning a fixed curriculum, we will use a dynamic curriculum that adapts to the performance of the draft model and the full model. This will enable the draft model to learn more effectively and efficiently, and potentially lead to better performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different progressive meta-learning schedules. (3) Control: Using a fixed curriculum learning schedule. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 45% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. The progressive meta-learning schedule may lead to improved performance, but it may also increase computational costs due to the need to adapt the curriculum during training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: draft refinement via multi-step prediction
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-step prediction mechanism to refine the outputs of the draft model. This mechanism will utilize a secondary model trained to predict the corrections needed to refine the draft's output, rather than relying on a single pass through the full model. By predicting these corrections step-by-step, we can iteratively refine the draft's output, potentially leading to significant quality improvements.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different numbers of refinement steps and secondary model architectures. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve high-quality outputs comparable to the full model, with a latency reduction of up to 40% in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. However, the multiple steps of refinement may lead to increased training time and potential issues with convergence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: lazy evaluation of fm velocity fields
PROPOSAL: We propose a lazy evaluation approach for the velocity fields used in FM models. By storing the velocity fields in a compressed and hierarchical manner, we can significantly reduce the computational cost of evaluating the velocity field for a given sample. This approach can be particularly effective when combined with the draft model and refinement mechanisms, as it can help to reduce the latency of the overall system.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no lazy evaluation. (2) Ablation study: Different compression techniques and hierarchical representations. Evaluate all methods on the same held-out test set and report the mean and standard deviation over five seeds.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a significant reduction in computational cost, with a latency reduction of up to 25% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the compressed representation may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or discontinuities in the velocity field.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: model-parallelizable fm through decomposition
PROPOSAL: We propose a decomposition-based approach to make FM models parallelizable. By decomposing the velocity field into smaller, independent components, we can parallelize the evaluation of the velocity field across multiple GPUs or machines, significantly reducing the latency of the overall system. This approach can be particularly effective for large-scale FM models and video generation tasks.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no decomposition. (2) Ablation study: Different decomposition techniques and parallelization strategies. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a significant reduction in latency, with a speedup of up to 4x in text-to-image generation, and an even larger speedup in video generation. However, the decomposition may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or discontinuities in the velocity field, and complex decomposition strategies may increase engineering burden.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: uncertainty-based draft model deployment
PROPOSAL: We propose an uncertainty-based approach for deploying draft models, where the draft model is only used to generate samples when the uncertainty in the velocity field is high, and the full model is used otherwise. This approach can help to mitigate potential quality degradation issues and reduce the overall latency of the system.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different uncertainty measures and threshold values for draft model deployment. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 30% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the deployment strategy may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or inconsistent behavior at high uncertainty values.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adaptive draft model switching
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive approach for switching between the draft model and the full model based on the performance of the system. By continuously monitoring the quality and latency of the generated samples, we can dynamically switch between the two models to achieve the optimal trade-off between quality and latency. This approach can help to adapt to changing system conditions and optimize performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different switching policies and performance metrics. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 110 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 35% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the adaptive switching strategy may lead to potential issues with instability or mode collapse.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: hybrid fm architectures
PROPOSAL: We propose a hybrid approach that combines the strengths of multiple architectures to achieve improved performance in FM models. By combining the draft model, full model, and lazy evaluation, we can create a flexible and adaptable architecture that can dynamically adjust to changing system conditions and optimize performance. This approach can help to achieve the optimal trade-off between quality, latency, and computational cost.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model. (2) Ablation study: Different combinations of draft model, full model, and lazy evaluation. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 50% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation, while maintaining high quality and performance. However, the hybrid architecture may lead to potential issues with complexity, overhead, and stability.

Large language models can be knowledge edited, that is, updated to incorporate new or corrected facts without retraining from scratch. This capability is crucial for keeping models up to date with evolving information and for correcting errors on the fly. Large vision-language models (LVLMs), which combine textual and visual understanding, make knowledge editing even more challenging: they encode factual knowledge in both their textual and their visual pathways, and they require mechanisms that update the knowledge of both modalities consistently. Efficiently editing LVLMs is crucial for real-world applications, such as swiftly correcting critical visual recognition errors (e.g., a model misidentifying Donald Trump as Boris Johnson). However, research on multimodal knowledge editing remains scarce compared with the extensive studies on text-only language models.

Existing benchmarks for LVLM knowledge editing are limited in scope. They typically focus only on visual knowledge updates, such as changing the identity that an image is recognized as, and overlook scenarios in which textual facts about an entity (e.g., its attributes, roles or affiliations) must also be updated. Furthermore, they do not evaluate continual editing, in which multiple knowledge updates are performed sequentially, nor do they test a model's ability to reason compositionally over edited facts. This is a critical gap, because real-world knowledge updates often arrive incrementally and involve intertwined visual and textual information: once a model has been corrected about who appears in a photo and, separately, updated with a new fact about that person, a question about the person in the photo can only be answered correctly by combining both edits.

Existing editing approaches face fundamental difficulties in this setting. External-memory editors store edited knowledge outside the model and retrieve relevant information at inference time without modifying model parameters, which makes them suitable for long-term retention. However, they typically transplant text-based retrieval strategies from language models directly, ignoring visual cues that are necessary for matching multimodal queries to the right edits, which can reduce retrieval accuracy. They also face an internalization issue: the model may over-rely on its stale internal knowledge, especially when the retrieved information conflicts with what it has learned, leading to incorrect answers. Conversely, internal-memory editors embed edits directly into model parameters via fine-tuning or low-rank adaptation, viewing the feed-forward network as a key-value memory that stores in-model knowledge. Although beneficial for internalizing edits, these methods typically store visual and textual edits within a unified representation space, risking cross-modal interference and representation collapse; moreover, sequential internal edits suffer from catastrophic forgetting, degrading previously stored knowledge with successive updates.

This raises several questions. How can an LVLM accommodate a continual sequence of interleaved visual and textual edits so that each new edit takes effect while earlier edits are retained, without interference between modalities? How can separately edited visual and textual facts be integrated to answer compositional queries that require both, even when externally retrieved evidence and the model's internal knowledge disagree? And how can editors be evaluated in this continual and compositional setting, which existing benchmarks do not cover?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: unified multimodal editing via policy updating
PROPOSAL: We will design a mechanism that updates the knowledge network of an LVLM by integrating visual and textual edits. Specifically, we will utilize a policy-based approach, where the model learns to update its knowledge by consuming policy embeddings that encode the edits. This allows the model to learn a consensual representation of the edits and integrate them seamlessly into its existing knowledge network. We will employ a transformer-based encoder-decoder framework, fine-tune on a set of multimodal datasets, and evaluate on a range of tasks including knowledge-based visual question answering and text-image retrieval.
CONTROLS: baseline comparison with traditional external-memory editing strategies, ablation study on the importance of policy embeddings, fine-tuning without policy embeddings
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this approach should outperform traditional external-memory editors in multimodal knowledge editing tasks, and potentially provide more robust and flexible updates. However, it may struggle with catastrophic forgetting if not properly regularized.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: testing catastrophic forgetting resistance in multimodal editing
PROPOSAL: Given the concerns about catastrophic forgetting in internal-memory editors, we will introduce a regularized training objective that encourages the model to retain previously updated knowledge while incorporating new edits. Specifically, we will propose a knowledge distillation objective that emphasizes the retention of salient information from the model's initial knowledge state, which we will then blend with the information from the latest edit. We hypothesize that this approach will improve the model's ability to retain previously updated knowledge.
CONTROLS: quantitative evaluation of catastrophic forgetting, comparison with other regularization schemes (e.g., L1/L2 penalty, gradient regularization), ablation study on the importance of the knowledge distillation objective
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this approach should significantly reduce catastrophic forgetting in multimodal editing tasks, but may come at the expense of slower convergence rates or decreased model accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: multi-step evaluation methodology for multimodal knowledge editors
PROPOSAL: To better assess the performance of multimodal knowledge editors, we will propose a multi-step evaluation methodology that measures their performance over a series of incremental update steps. Specifically, we will evaluate the model's accuracy on a range of tasks (e.g., visual question answering, text-image retrieval) across multiple update steps, using metrics that capture both short-term and long-term recall. This will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the model's ability to retain previously updated knowledge over time.
CONTROLS: comparisons with existing evaluation methodologies (e.g., one-shot update, batch update), ablation study on the importance of evaluating model performance over multiple update steps
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this evaluation methodology should provide a more nuanced understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of moment-to-moment performance of multimodal editors but may require an additional increase in data annotation and new evaluation frameworks.

ACTION: REVISE
number: 3
TITLE: refined multi-step evaluation methodology for multimodal knowledge editors
PROPOSAL: To further refine our multi-step evaluation methodology, we will introduce a difficulty metric that measures the average difficulty of the tasks presented to the model over multiple update steps. This metric will be used to normalize the model's performance across different difficulty levels, allowing for a more fair comparison between models. Additionally, we will also track the model's performance on a set of compositional questions that require integrating previously updated knowledge with new information.
CONTROLS: comparison with the original multi-step evaluation methodology, ablation study on the importance of the difficulty metric and compositional questions
COST: no additional compute, modification of existing proposal
PREDICTION: the refined methodology should provide a more robust and nuanced understanding of the model's performance, but may require careful tuning of the difficulty metric to ensure it accurately captures the model's abilities.

number: 3

ACTION: REVISE
number: 1
TITLE: unified multimodal editing via policy updating for realistic image editing
PROPOSAL: We will extend our policy-based editing approach to handle more realistic image editing tasks, such as object removal, object insertion, and image inpainting. We will use synthetic datasets with variable image complexity, pose, and occlusions to simulate real-world scenarios. Our goal is to demonstrate that our policy-based editing framework can successfully update LVLMs to handle such complex image editing tasks.
CONTROLS: comparison with state-of-the-art image editing methodologies (e.g., DeepFill v2), evaluation of the model's ability to generalize to new, unseen scenarios
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this extension should enable our policy-based editing framework to handle more complex and realistic image editing tasks, but may require careful tuning of the model's architecture and the policy updates to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adversarial evaluation of multimodal knowledge editors
PROPOSAL: To provide a more comprehensive assessment of multimodal knowledge editors, we will introduce an adversarial evaluation framework that tests the model's resilience tocrafted attacks designed to compromise its performance. Specifically, we will use strong and strategic attacks (e.g., semantic adversarial examples, multi-step attacks) to probe the model's vulnerabilities and evaluate its robustness.

Diffusion models have demonstrated a remarkable ability to learn data distributions across many modalities, with strong results in both data generation and image restoration. In medical imaging, they are effective at modeling the distribution of 2D image slices, and by combining these powerful learned priors with conventional optimization frameworks, diffusion-based solvers have reached state-of-the-art performance on medical inverse problems such as accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and undersampled X-ray computed tomography (CT). Such problems are often severely ill-posed: far fewer measurements are acquired than there are unknowns, so the measurements alone cannot determine the image, and the learned prior must fill in what they leave ambiguous. Diffusion-based solvers do so through an iterative reverse sampling process that, at each step, predicts a clean image from the current noisy state, corrects this estimate for consistency with the measurements, and re-noises it to the next timestep, which repeatedly injects random noise.

In clinical practice, however, medical data are fundamentally large 3D volumes. Individual 2D slices matter for review, but a complete and accurate volumetric reconstruction is often essential for downstream tasks such as precise tumor volume assessment, surgical planning, and tracking disease progression over time. Translating the success of 2D diffusion-based solvers to 3D is difficult: because of the curse of dimensionality, the memory, computational, and data requirements of training a diffusion prior directly on volumetric data are prohibitive for most academic and even industrial labs. A common and practical workaround is to train a diffusion model on 2D slices and apply this 2D prior slice by slice to reconstruct the volume.

This workaround eases the training burden but creates a critical new problem: the reconstructed volumes lack consistency along the third dimension (the z-axis). Because each slice is processed independently during the reverse diffusion process, the intrinsic randomness of the sampling procedure leads to severe inter-slice discontinuities and artifacts, degrading the diagnostic and analytical quality of the stacked volume. Existing remedies have important drawbacks. The most direct one augments the 2D prior with a hand-crafted regularizer such as total variation, applied in an additional optimization step to enforce smoothness between adjacent slices. This is effective, but it introduces sensitive hyperparameters that require careful tuning, can over-smooth the volume or produce cartoon-like textures that erase fine diagnostic details, and acts as an external correction that masks the symptoms rather than addressing the intrinsic cause. More principled approaches try to learn a more complete 3D prior, for instance by training on 3D patches or by combining priors from two perpendicular 2D planes, but they increase the complexity of the training or inference pipeline and may impose constraints on the data, such as requiring cubic volumes.

A similar discontinuity arises in video restoration, where applying a pre-trained 2D image diffusion model to video inverse problems often produces temporal flickering across frames. Prior work attributed this flickering to the uncoordinated stochasticity inherent in diffusion sampling and alleviated it by synchronizing the stochastic noise components across frames. Whether the same mechanism is the fundamental cause of inter-slice inconsistency in 3D medical reconstruction, and how such a remedy would transfer from video to volumetric medical data, remains open.

This raises the following questions. How does the stochasticity of independent slice-wise sampling give rise to inter-slice inconsistency when 2D diffusion priors are used for 3D medical reconstruction? Is it possible to enhance inter-slice consistency directly within the diffusion sampling process itself, obviating the need for external, artifact-inducing optimization, ideally without new loss terms, additional sensitive hyperparameters, model retraining, or extra computational cost, so that the remedy could be dropped into existing 2D diffusion-based 3D reconstruction pipelines? And can inter-slice consistency be improved while preserving the natural anatomical variation between slices and fine diagnostic details, rather than trading them away for smoothness?

PREDICTION: The slice synchronization method should improve upon the naive baseline in terms of inter-slice consistency, with the dynamic noise variant performing better than the static one. Geometry reconstruction is a fundamental problem that enables a wide range of applications in fields such as virtual reality and robotics. In recent years, neural reconstruction methods have gained significant attention; a key advantage of these methods is their ability to represent the geometry of a scene continuously, which can help in many downstream tasks. However, vision-based sensors often struggle in adverse weather conditions, or even become completely unusable when objects are obscured by occlusions.

Radio frequency (RF) sensing, specifically wireless millimeter-wave (mmWave) sensing, can see through occlusions, remains robust under challenging visibility conditions and, unlike X-rays, is not dangerous to humans, making it a compelling alternative for 3D reconstruction. This could open up many applications, for example checking whether the items inside a box are the correct items, are damaged, or pose a threat, without ever opening the box. On the other hand, mmWave resolution is extremely low compared to vision: a single radar image provides far less visual context than a camera image, which makes it hard to extract a 3D reconstruction from one radar image alone. Some prior RF systems have performed 3D point cloud reconstruction or human body tracking by leveraging movement or by emulating larger antenna apertures, but the recovered point clouds are still too sparse and noisy to reliably recover detailed geometry; through-wall human sensing relies on human motion to combat specularity, and deep learning on mmWave radar data has mostly targeted self-driving scenarios, where image resolution matters little. Other works have proposed neural implicit representations for RF sensing, aiming to concentrate scene information out of heavy noise through neural optimization, but these systems are designed for large-scale environments such as streets or satellite imagery and are far from achieving millimeter-level precision. When objects are close to the radar, the propagation characteristics of RF signals change dramatically: incoming waves can no longer be approximated as planar, so processing methods designed for large-scale scenes, such as beamforming, introduce a considerable amount of distortion and noise, often exceeding the noise acceptable for gradient descent and leading to unstable optimization. Existing neural RF reconstruction work is thus either limited to far-range scenes or, for individual objects, evaluated only on simulated data, which for wireless signals cannot come close to representing the complexity of real-world measurements. Meanwhile, the multi-view reconstruction and inverse rendering methods of computer vision (multi-view stereo, neural radiance fields, Gaussian splatting, neural implicit surfaces, physically based inverse rendering) are all derived from RGB images and are not easily transferable to mmWave data: even lensless RGB images can be mapped back to a lens-based imaging model without altering the underlying ray physics, whereas for RF signals such a transformation is fundamentally invalid.

The open problem is therefore to overcome the fundamental dilemma between massive RF noise in the input and the reconstruction of complete, high-resolution, millimeter-level 3D surface geometry of near-range objects, including objects hidden behind occlusions. This is not straightforward, because inferring surface geometry from RF signals differs fundamentally from image-based reconstruction in three main ways. First, wireless systems lack a lens-based imaging model: whereas lenses filter and focus the relevant light rays, radar antenna arrays perform lensless imaging and capture all incoming RF signals without directional filtering, which leads to low signal-to-noise ratios because irrelevant signals cannot be excluded. Second, RF signals and visible light propagate differently: visible light is predominantly scattered diffusely by surfaces, whereas RF signals, whose wavelengths are on the order of millimeters, are dominated by specular reflections, so volumetric rendering techniques designed for scattering-based vision sensors are unsuitable for RF imaging. Third, physically modeling lensless RF measurements is computationally expensive: whereas lens-based rendering samples along 1D rays, modeling what each antenna receives requires accounting for contributions from the full 3D space, leading to cubic complexity that makes naive implementations intractable at millimeter resolution.

How can accurate, millimeter-level 3D geometry of near-range objects be reconstructed from noisy real-world RF measurements, in line of sight and through occlusions, despite lensless imaging, specular reflections and the cost of modeling signal contributions from the full 3D space?

enonce:
Transformers, powered by attention mechanisms, have become the default backbone for sequence modeling across language, vision, speech, and decision making. Their success is often linked to selective access to an ever-growing key-value cache while retaining parallel training and inference. In large language models, this selective ability, composed across multiple attention layers and residual pathways, supports long-range memory retrieval and the algorithmic behaviors associated with in-context learning (for example induction heads and pattern completion), as shown by empirical and mechanistic studies.

Causal softmax attention combines strong selectivity with parallel efficiency: at each step it forms a distribution over past indices and mixes their values, while all steps can be computed in parallel. Given queries, keys and values $Q,K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}$ with rows $q_t$, $k_i$, $v_i$, define masked scores $s_{t,i}=q_t^\top k_i/\sqrt{d}$ for $i\le t$ and $-\infty$ otherwise, and set $\alpha_{t,\cdot}=\mathrm{softmax}(s_{t,\cdot})$, a probability distribution over $\{1,\dots,t\}$. The step-$t$ read is $o_t=\sum_{i\le t}\alpha_{t,i}v_i$, which lies in the convex hull of $\{v_1,\dots,v_t\}$; stacking all steps yields $O=AV$ with $A_{t,i}=\alpha_{t,i}$, so a single matrix multiply produces all outputs.

This convex-mixture view explains the efficiency of attention, but it also reveals a dilemma between lossless storage and lossy processing. The key-value cache stores the full context, but the read is lossy: each head applies the same weights to all coordinates of $v_i$, so the output lies in the convex hull of the stored values and all channels are synchronized. As a result, even simple per-channel indexing, such as returning $(v_{i_1,1},\dots,v_{i_D,D})$ where each coordinate $j$ is taken from its own past index $i_j$ (for example, a coordinate-wise argmax), cannot be represented unless all chosen indices coincide. This limitation hinders Transformers in long-range modeling with non-sequential or irregular timestep indexing, and in tasks where channel-wise structure is critical, such as multivariate time series modeling.

Most recent advances in attention aim to improve expressivity and efficiency, typically by designing richer selection distributions while still reading values through a token-separable linear combination. These include sparse attention patterns, low-rank projections, and kernelizable variants with normalization or gating. Efficiency-oriented work accelerates attention through factorized implementations, or replaces the cache with streaming state space models and recurrent networks that keep a fixed-size state. Across these lines, computation becomes faster or the distribution richer, but the read remains a linear mix: channels share weights, and even simple per-channel indexing cannot be realized in one step. Some recent works explore more complex combinations, such as nonlinear mixing or hard/top-k selection, yet these mainly target training stability or accuracy in specific cases and do not address the lossy-processing limitation.

This leaves an open problem: how can the read of an attention-style sequence mixer be redesigned to remove this linear read bottleneck and support per-channel, context-dependent selection from memory, so that different channels can retrieve different past indices in the same step, while keeping causal parallelism and the asymptotic time complexity of the underlying selection mechanism (for example, quadratic in sequence length for softmax attention and linear for linear-time variants)? And does closing this gap between lossless storage and lossy processing translate into better sequence modeling in practice?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: temporal dependency in the selection bottleneck
PROPOSAL: Investigate how much the linear mixing bottleneck in causal softmax attention can be attributed to temporal dependencies in the selection distribution. One approach could be to analyze the structural similarity between the attention weights and the sequence itself. Specifically, we can apply tools from information theory and dynamical systems to study how the selection distribution captures temporal patterns in the input sequence. We hypothesize that a redesigned read function can decouple the selection bias from this temporal structure, leading to improved expressivity.
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard causal softmax attention mechanism, and analyze the results with a baseline that fixes the selection distribution, with details given in the appendix.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to show that temporal dependencies in the selection distribution contribute significantly to the linear mixing bottleneck, and that decoupling these dependencies can improve the expressivity of the attention mechanism. However, we also expect to find that this improvement comes at a cost of requiring more compute during inference.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: hierarchical channel attentions
PROPOSAL: Design and evaluate a variant of causal softmax attention where each output channel has its own dedicated focus selection mechanism, applied on top of the standard causal softmax attention. This hierarchical approach should allow for per-channel selection of past indices, even when the standard attention mechanism cannot. Specifically, we will implement a two-stage selection process where the seeds for the second stage are selected based on pairwise activations or hierarchical pooling operations. This would enable context-dependent channel-wise retrieval of past indices.
CONTROLS: Evaluate against the standard causal softmax attention and compare with an ablation study where only one stage of the hierarchical mechanism is applied, with details given in the appendix.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved performance on tasks with non-sequential or irregular timestep indexing, but may also find increased computational complexity compared to the standard causal softmax attention mechanism.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: factorized causal softmax
PROPOSAL: Modify causal softmax attention to have a factorized structure, where each output channel is represented as a weighted sum of a smaller set of key-value pairs, with coefficients that can be selected independently for each channel. This should reduce the linear mixing bottleneck by allowing per-channel selection from a smaller sparse subset of the key-value pairs. We will apply techniques from compressed sensing and sparse recovery to select the most important key-value pairs and adjust the channel-wise coefficients accordingly.
CONTROLS: Evaluate against standard causal softmax attention and the hierarchical channel attentions from proposal 2, using a baseline that selects the most important key-value pairs based on random sampling, following the setup outlined in the proposal.

In cloud services, Internet of Things deployments and monitoring systems, data are often represented as univariate time series (UTS), in which each timestamp records a single variable. Anomalies arise, for instance, when a website is subject to malicious attacks or experiences excessive server load, and they are typically reflected in UTS derived from traffic and system-load monitoring. Missed or delayed detection of such events can have severe consequences. Anomalies in UTS are usually divided into two types: point anomalies, which are abrupt deviations (either global or contextual), and segment anomalies, which reflect more subtle shifts in trends or periodic patterns.

Formally, given observations x_0, x_1, ..., x_t with anomaly labels c_0, c_1, ..., c_t, where c_i = 0 marks a normal point and c_i = 1 an anomaly, the goal of UTS anomaly detection is to determine c_i for each point x_i from the history x_0, ..., x_{i-1} that precedes it, without access to future points. Because labels are scarce in practice and supervised detectors generalize poorly under label scarcity or distribution shift, unsupervised approaches have become the dominant paradigm. Reconstruction-based and prediction-based methods both model normal behavior and flag anomalies by comparing reconstructed or predicted values with the actual observations. Reconstruction-based techniques try to map abnormal segments to a normal space, but the lack of ground truth for anomalies leads to poor reconstruction and degraded performance, and they treat time windows independently, ignoring temporal dependencies. Prediction-based methods built on deep sequence models such as Transformers perform strongly on multivariate time series, where they can model complex dependencies; in UTS, however, each timestamp contains only one value, which restricts the representation of temporal context and leads to suboptimal performance.

In particular, existing detectors struggle with two kinds of subtle anomalies that remain largely undetected: (1) small point anomalies, short-term spikes that look normal when viewed over longer windows; and (2) slowly rising anomalies, gradual segment-level deviations from periodic patterns. These misses stem from limitations of current designs: for example, a frequency-conditioned reconstruction approach focuses on frequency components rather than local dependencies and fails to capture subtle point anomalies or gradual segment anomalies, while a recent prediction approach uses timing information but ignores frequency details.

Detecting these anomalies raises three challenges. First, local trends matter more than absolute values: the absolute magnitude of a change is insufficient to decide whether a point is anomalous. In one series, changes between 0.5 and 1 may be abnormal, whereas in another, similar changes are normal and only variations exceeding 5 are anomalous; what counts as abnormal depends on the value distribution and change patterns within a short local window. Second, periodicity evolves rather than staying static: time series exhibit evolving trends and periodicity, and periodicity varies over time and across datasets, including changes in period length and frequency. Without future points, distinguishing slow anomalies from normal periodic changes is difficult, and methods that focus only on the adjacent historical period neglect this evolution; modeling periodicity that is both dynamic and heterogeneous is hard. Third, normal patterns must be learned amid anomalies and noise: real-world series contain long-term noise and sudden anomalies, both of which hinder the learning of normal patterns. Noise introduces significant fluctuations that make it difficult to fit the underlying normal behavior, and the lack of ground-truth labels for anomaly positions prevents a model from computing reliable training losses.

The question is therefore how an unsupervised detector for univariate time series, relying only on past observations, can capture both local trends and the evolution of periodic patterns, while learning normal behavior robustly from training data contaminated by noise and unlabeled anomalies, so that small point anomalies and slowly rising anomalies are detected accurately and promptly.

PROPOSAL: Introduce a reconstruction-based method that models normal behavior by learning local trends in the univariate time series. Instead of focusing on global frequency components, the method will capture local patterns using a Gaussian Process regression model with a custom kernel that takes into account the local context of each point. This will allow it to more effectively identify small point anomalies that might be missed by frequency-conditioned reconstruction approaches.

Diffusion models have catalyzed an enormous research wave in generative modeling. Conceptually, they couple a stochastic forward noising process with a reverse-time ordinary or stochastic differential equation whose density evolution is governed by the Fokker–Planck equation, a linear second-order parabolic partial differential equation. Learning consists of estimating time-indexed scores or velocities and integrating them for sampling. A growing body of work also explores probability-flow backbones: deterministic flows trained via flow matching and its optimal-transport variants, rectified flows, and stochastic interpolants that bridge flows and diffusion.

Yet the partial-differential-equation lens on generative modeling need not be limited to Fokker–Planck. Other classical linear second-order equations, elliptic and hyperbolic, offer different structural advantages but remain comparatively underexplored; Poisson flow models, for instance, recast generation through electrostatics-inspired fields. On the hyperbolic side, recent work has replaced the Fokker–Planck equation with the telegrapher equation (the one-dimensional damped wave equation) and its stochastic Kac representation, in which a particle moves at constant speed and reverses direction at the jump times of a Poisson process. A network is fit by regression to a closed-form conditional velocity of this process and integrated backward in time from noise to data, with each image coordinate following an independent one-dimensional Kac process. The resulting probability flows have a finite propagation speed: starting from localized mass, the distribution remains inside a causal cone, the flow is Lipschitz in Wasserstein distance, and velocity norms, hence kinetic energy, stay globally bounded. Diffusion, by contrast, spreads mass instantaneously with effectively infinite propagation speed, which manifests as stiff, rapidly growing reverse-time velocities and as ill-conditioned fields with Lipschitz blow-ups near the end of denoising; indeed, diffusion arises as a limit of the damped wave equation as the damping and the propagation speed tend to infinity. A finite speed cap thus acts like a built-in stability constraint: trajectories cannot accelerate without bound, and late-time integration is less stiff.

So far, however, these finite-speed flows have been developed only for unconditional image generation, and they lack two ingredients that make diffusion-style generators practical. The first is guided conditional generation. Classifier-free guidance, which mixes conditional and unconditional predictions to steer samples toward a condition, is a standard tool for diffusion models, but it is unclear whether guidance can be carried over to finite-speed dynamics without losing the bounded-energy property that distinguishes them from diffusion, whose kinetic energy can diverge near data time. The second is fast sampling. Practical generators are expected to deliver high-quality samples with very few network evaluations, yet it is unknown whether finite-speed flows can be brought down to a handful of sampling steps, or even a single one, without a severe loss of sample quality, and whether their finite-speed, bounded-energy structure can explain, and ideally guarantee, that a coarse few-step sampler stays close to the full sampling trajectory.

This leads to three questions. How can guided conditional generation be built on finite-speed Kac flows while provably keeping the guided velocity field at finite kinetic energy? How can such flows be turned into few-step, ideally one-step, image generators that preserve both sample quality and the numerical stability benefits of finite-speed probability flows? And can the finite-speed structure provide theoretical guarantees that a few-step sampler remains close to the full flow along the entire generation path, not only in its final samples? Answering them would show whether hyperbolic, finite-speed dynamics can be a credible alternative to diffusion for fast image generation.

Modern problem-solving increasingly relies on neural networks, which encode vast amounts of information in their trainable parameters during learning, with applications ranging from computer vision and natural language processing to the natural sciences. While these parameters capture rich knowledge, accessing and interpreting it remains a challenge.

Metanetworks were introduced to analyze and process other neural networks by treating their weights, gradients and sparsity patterns as structured inputs. Early work focused on evaluating the generalization of trained networks and revealing properties of their behavior, commonly by flattening the parameters or extracting statistics from them before feeding them into multi-layer perceptrons. Metanetworks have since been applied to extracting structure from implicit neural representations, learning optimizers, editing models, evaluating policies and enabling Bayesian inference. Designing them nevertheless remains challenging because of the complexity and high dimensionality of the structures they operate on.

A major difficulty is functional equivalence: many distinct parameter configurations realize the same input-output function. Swapping two hidden units of a multi-layer perceptron leaves its input-output mapping unchanged, provided their outgoing connections are permuted accordingly, and for networks with tanh activations the input-output mapping is known to determine the architecture and the weights up to permutations and sign flips. Such identifiability results have been extended to broader classes of multi-layer perceptrons and to convolutional networks, and recent work has characterized the symmetry groups of multihead attention and mixture-of-experts layers, establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for functional equivalence. The parameter space is thus only a proxy for the underlying function class, and the map from parameters to functions is not injective. A metanetwork that relies solely on raw parameters therefore risks overlooking the symmetries of the architecture it processes, and may produce incompatible outputs for two networks that compute exactly the same function.

Building on the permutation symmetry of hidden neurons, permutation-equivariant metanetworks have been developed that account for neuron reordering within hidden layers, and more recent architectures extend beyond permutations by incorporating additional symmetries such as scaling and sign changes. Equivariance (for metanetworks that output weights) or invariance (for metanetworks that output predictions) with respect to a symmetry group of the processed architecture guarantees that different parameterizations of the same function are treated consistently. However, these approaches enforce strict equivariance at the level of individual weights, which imposes rigid constraints on the layers and often leads to sparse, less expressive models. Yet the true goal is not to preserve the weights themselves but the functions they implement, that is, to respect the functional equivalence classes of the parameters. Strict equivariance is a sufficient way to achieve this, but it is not clear that it is necessary.

Relaxed or approximate equivariance has emerged elsewhere in deep learning to handle imperfect symmetries in real-world data, for instance through relaxed convolution weights, soft constraints added to the training objective or relaxed group convolutions, and its bias-variance trade-offs have been analyzed theoretically. These relaxations were, however, developed for symmetries that only approximately hold, and often treat equivariance as something to be approximated. In weight space, by contrast, the symmetries are exact and are precisely what defines functional equivalence, so it is unclear how weight-level equivariance could be loosened without breaking the guarantee that functionally equivalent inputs are processed consistently.

This raises several questions. Is strict equivariance necessary for metanetworks? What is the right requirement for a map acting on weights to preserve functional identity, so that functionally equivalent inputs always yield functionally equivalent outputs, and can a requirement weaker than strict equivariance meet it? Can metanetwork layers satisfying such a requirement be built in a principled, practical and trainable way for the architectures whose weights metanetworks commonly process, such as feedforward, convolutional and multihead attention networks? And would moving beyond strict equivariance in this way give metanetworks a better trade-off between symmetry preservation and representational expressivity in practice?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: manipulating symmetry constraints for metanetworks
PROPOSAL: Explore the theoretical implications of modifying the symmetry constraints imposed on weights in metanetworks to relax strict equivariance. Specifically, we will derive a formal framework for relaxing permuto-equivariance by introducing a penalty term that measures the deviation from pointwise equivariance in the space of weight permutations. The goal is to provide a principled approach for balancing symmetry preservation and representational expressivity.
CONTROLS: Compare the derived relaxed framework with the existing strict permuto-equivariant architectures and assess their performance in various settings (multiple architectures, loss functions, dataset sizes).
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed framework will provide a better trade-off between accuracy and efficiency, while maintaining the capability to process and learn from multiple symmetries; However, tuning the penalty term may lead to brittle behavior in certain scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: characterizing the space of functionally equivalent weights
PROPOSAL: Investigate the topological properties of the space of weights in a deep neural network, focusing on the quotient space obtained by taking into account the symmetries that leave the input-output function invariant. Through a combination of algebraic topology and deep learning techniques, we will characterize the connectivity and holes in this space, providing insights into the number of distinct, functionally equivalent weight configurations. This understanding will inform the design of more efficient and robust metanetworks.
CONTROLS: Compare the results from different classes of neural networks (e.g., fully-connected, convolutional, recurrent) and loss functions to understand their impact on the topology of the weight space. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The study will reveal that the weight space exhibits a complex topological structure, with multiple holes and connected components; however, the specific characteristics may vary significantly depending on the network architecture and loss function used.

ACTION: REVISE
EXIT: 1
TITLE: learning permutation-invariant metanetworks with non-stationary weights
PROPOSAL: Extend the existing permuto-equivariant metanetworks to accommodate weights that evolve and adapt during training. This will involve incorporating a dynamic weight generator that relies on a probabilistic permutation-invariant encoding scheme, enabling the metanetwork to adapt to variations in symmetry. We will evaluate the performance of this adaptive approach on a range of tasks, including neural network generalization prediction and implicit neural representation editing.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the fixed-weight version of the permuto-equivariant metanetwork and assess the learnability and expressiveness of the adaptive weight generator under different training scenarios.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptation mechanism will demonstrate robustness and learning capabilities in dynamic symmetries, but may lead to mode collapse and imperiled exploration.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: analyzing the effect of weight equivariance on model robustness
PROPOSAL: Investigate the relationship between weight equivariance and the robustness of metanetworks to perturbations in the input data and model weights. We will systematically vary the degree of equivariance in the metanetworks and assess their performance on tasks such as implicit neural representation classification, focusing on their resilience to adversarial attacks and data noise.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with existing state-of-the-art methods for robustness and security in deep learning, as well as ablate the effects of different perturbation scenarios (e.g., random noise, targeted attacks).
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The study will demonstrate that metanetworks with strict equivariance exhibit improved robustness to certain types of perturbations, but may sacrifice performance in tasks that require flexibility and adaptability; This will depend on the balance between equivariance and representational power in the weight generator.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 2
TITLE: characterizing the space of functionally equivalent weights
PROPOSAL: Refine the proposal to focus on the specific case of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and analyze the effects of spatial symmetries on the topology of the weight space. We will develop a novel graph-theoretic representation for describing the spatial equivalences between CNN filters and weight permutations.
CONTROLS: Compare the results to the existing study of the topological properties of the weight space for fully-connected networks, and assess the applicability of the novel graph-theoretic representation to other CNN architectures. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The refined study will reveal that the topological properties of the weight space for CNNs exhibit a distinct structure due to the presence of spatial symmetries; however, the results may be influenced by the specific architecture and the choice of convolutional operations used in the network.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: relaxations of pointwise equivariance in metanetworks
PROPOSAL: Investigate relaxations of pointwise equivariance for metanetworks that explicitly account for imperfections in the symmetry of the processed weights. Specifically, we will develop and analyze three variants of relaxed metanetworks, each incorporating different approximations and relaxations of pointwise equivariance, and evaluate their performance on tasks such as neural network generalization prediction and implicit neural representation editing.
CONTROLS: Compare the results between the different relaxation variants, and assess their relationship to existing relaxation techniques in deep learning (e.g., group convolutions, relaxed convolution weights).
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: At least one relaxation variant will demonstrate superior performance and robustness compared to the strict pointwise equivariant baseline; However, the Ladies may behave nonlinearly and interact differently when coupling is increased.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 1
TITLE: manipulating symmetry constraints for metanetworks
PROPOSAL: Enhance the proposal to incorporate learning-based methods for adapting the symmetry constraints, enabling metanetworks to adapt to the specific symmetry pattern of the input weights in an online manner. This will be achieved through a novel combination of graph reconstruction and pointwise equivariance relaxation techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the learning-based metanetwork with the original fixed-symmetry constraints implementation, and assess the adaptability and robustness of the learner under different scenarios.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The learning-based metanetwork will demonstrate improved adaptability and robustness to different symmetry patterns; However, the learner may suffer from overfitting or mode collapse, especially when dealing with complex symmetry structures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: metanetworks for implicit neural representation synthesis
PROPOSAL: Investigate the application of metanetworks to implicit neural representation synthesis tasks, such as generating new neural networks with similar functionality to a given model. We will design and test a novel metanetwork architecture that leverages permutation equivariance to generate diverse neural network configurations with identical input-output behavior.
CONTROLS: Compare the results to existing methods for neural network imitation and adaptation, and assess the performance of the metanetwork under different settings and evaluation metrics.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The metanetwork architecture will efficiently generate diverse neural network configurations that preserve the input-output behavior of the original model; However, the task might require a trade-off between diversity and accuracy, and the metanetwork may struggle to recover the original model's expressiveness.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 4
TITLE: relaxations of pointwise equivariance in metanetworks
PROPOSAL: Refine the proposal to focus on the theoretical analysis of the effect of relaxations on the metanetwork's ability to represent different neural network configurations. We will derive bounds on the representational capacity of the relaxed metanetworks and investigate the relationship between the relaxation parameters and the trade-off between expressivity and robustness.
CONTROLS: Compare the theoretical bounds to the experimental results from the original proposal, and assess the implications of the trade-off between expressivity and robustness for the design of practical metanetworks. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The theoretical analysis will reveal that the relaxation parameters have a non-trivial impact on the representational capacity of the metanetworks, and the trade-off between expressivity and robustness will be a complex function of the relaxation parameters; However, the exact nature of this function remains to be determined.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: a holistic survey of metanetworks for neural network analysis and synthesis
PROPOSAL: Provide a comprehensive review of the recent literature on metanetworks for neural network analysis and synthesis, covering both theoretical and practical aspects. The survey will discuss the primary applications, architectures, and challenges of metanetworks, and provide an outlook on future research directions and potential impact on the field of deep learning.
CONTROLS: Compare the survey with existing reviews on related topics (e.g., neural network interpretation, meta-learning) and assess the novelty and comprehensiveness of the metanetworks landscape presented.
COST: 0 GPU-hours (theoretical effort only)
PREDICTION: The survey will provide a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners seeking to understand the current state of metanetworks, and identify key challenges and research opportunities; However, the survey may require significant effort to ensure comprehensiveness and accuracy.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a pivotal technique for advancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models on complex tasks. In reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR), the language model is treated as a policy whose chain of thought is modeled as a sequence of actions, and it is optimized with rewards from an automatic verifier that compares the final answer extracted from each sampled solution with a reference answer. Most RLVR algorithms are on-policy; a widely used example is Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which estimates the advantage of each trajectory by normalizing its reward against a group of trajectories sampled for the same question. On-policy optimization is stable but computationally expensive, because the experience generated during the costly rollout phase is typically discarded after a single gradient update. This not only squanders substantial compute but also forfeits the opportunity for the model to learn from its own earlier successful explorations, which makes training inefficient, can make it unstable, and imposes a bottleneck on scaling RL for reasoning.

Experience replay is a classical RL technique to address this issue: previously collected interactions are stored and reused, which improves sample efficiency, helps stabilize training and accelerates convergence, and prioritized variants emphasize the most informative transitions. It has been argued that AI is entering a period in which experience will become the dominant medium of improvement. A non-trivial challenge, however, lies in how to exploit past experiences according to their differing value and how to manage the replay process over the course of learning, and efficient experience replay mechanisms remain largely underexplored in RLVR for large reasoning models. Recent off-policy approaches incorporate historical or external data, for example by mixing expert demonstrations with on-policy updates or by deriving direct off-policy update rules, and recent replay methods for reasoning models reuse successful trajectories collected early in training or produced by a well-trained policy. However, the impact of the quality of the data within the replay buffer remains underexplored, and several replay methods do not correct for the distribution mismatch between the past policy that generated a stored trajectory and the current policy.

Several features make the problem challenging. An experience in RLVR consists of a question together with the trajectories sampled for it, and it is unclear whether all questions are equally useful for training, or whether all successful trajectories for a question are equally worth reusing. Because the verifiable reward only checks the final answer, a successful trajectory may still rest on invalid reasoning. The usefulness of a stored experience may also change as the model's capabilities evolve during training. Finally, reusing past successes pushes the policy toward exploitation, while prior work shows that aggressively minimizing policy entropy can cause collapse, so the reuse of experience has to be balanced against continued exploration.

This raises the following research questions. What makes a reasoning experience valuable for RLVR optimization, and which measurable properties of a question and of its trajectories, available during training, indicate that value? Given the vast quantity of experience collected during rollouts, how can a reasoning model effectively exploit its own stream of experience, deciding which past experiences to keep, prioritize and replay, how to combine them with fresh on-policy exploration, and how to account for the policy mismatch of replayed trajectories, so as to maximize learning toward scaling RL compute for large reasoning models and to improve reasoning performance, sample efficiency and training stability relative to standard on-policy RLVR?

Diffusion models have recently demonstrated remarkable capabilities in synthesizing high-quality images, significantly surpassing earlier generative approaches such as generative adversarial networks and variational autoencoders. Despite their impressive fidelity, deploying diffusion models in realistic cloud-to-user applications introduces a fundamental bottleneck: transmission bandwidth. A standard diffusion model produces a high-fidelity image by performing a fixed number of denoising steps, regardless of downstream transmission limitations. In conventional scenarios, the generated images then undergo aggressive lossy compression before transmission to accommodate the limited bandwidth. This cascaded approach, high-quality generation followed by subsequent compression, not only incurs redundant computational overhead, since computation is spent on details that are later discarded, but also significantly degrades perceptual quality, as the compression process often erases the intricate textures and fine details carefully constructed by the diffusion model.

This motivates a critical question: can bandwidth-awareness be integrated directly into the diffusion generation process, so that the quality of the generated image is adapted to the available bandwidth, avoiding the inefficiency and perceptual quality loss associated with post-generation compression? Ideally, such a generator would meet a user-specified bitrate budget, avoid compression-induced artifacts and redundant computation, and offer fine-grained, dynamic control over image quality according to real-time bandwidth conditions in practical cloud-to-user deployments.

The question is not straightforward. During sampling, diffusion models progressively refine coarse structures into detailed, realistic textures through iterative denoising steps, so, intuitively, terminating the process early would yield simpler, lower-detail images suited to constrained bandwidth. However, naively reducing the number of diffusion steps typically produces suboptimal visual quality: models trained for complete denoising trajectories are not optimized for early termination, which leads to visual artifacts and poor perceptual coherence.

Existing lines of work address only parts of this problem. A large body of work accelerates diffusion sampling, through deterministic samplers that need fewer inference steps, numerical solvers inspired by ordinary differential equations, distillation of slow teacher models into faster students, adaptive step-size selection, latent-space compression, non-uniform step skipping, dynamic network pruning, predictors of the minimal number of denoising steps, and adaptive inference trajectories. These methods reduce the cost of sampling while preserving generation quality, but they are not designed to control the bitrate of the generated image. Conditional and controllable diffusion models, from classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance to latent diffusion and region-based conditioning for interactive editing, allow flexible control over attributes of the generated content, but they do not directly address bandwidth constraints. How to make a diffusion model generate images that respect a specified bandwidth budget while preserving perceptual quality and avoiding wasted computation therefore remains an open problem.

Facial rigging aims to make a static neutral facial mesh animatable by defining a set of controllable deformations, typically represented either as blendshape rigs driven by activated action units in systems based on the Facial Action Coding System (FACS), or as skeletal rigs driven by joint positions. Whereas full-body auto-rigging usually follows a two-step pipeline of skeleton construction and skinning, facial rigs are often anatomically inspired and implemented with FACS blendshapes. In a linear FACS blendshape rig, each blendshape is a vertex offset from the neutral mesh corresponding to one action unit, i.e. a specific muscle movement such as "Right Eye Close", and a complex expression is obtained by adding the weighted offsets of the activated blendshapes to the neutral mesh. Rigging is an essential step for creative AI, bringing digital avatars to life by enabling expressive and realistic facial movements across a wide range of applications. However, creating a facial rig is laborious and expensive, often requiring skilled artists tens of hours to complete a single asset. Methods that transfer expressions from 2D images or videos to 3D avatars do not remove this bottleneck, since they assume that the avatar already has a rig.

Existing facial auto-rigging methods typically transfer a complete set of blendshapes from a predefined template mesh to a neutral target mesh, which often requires dense correspondences or a mesh topology shared by the template and the target. More recent approaches build transferable latent spaces between faces or use triangulation-agnostic networks to bypass these limitations, but they still require a template blendshape rig, which can compromise accuracy when the template and target shapes differ substantially. Only one prior approach, NFR, can directly rig facial meshes from explicitly controllable FACS parameters without relying on a template, and it has so far been demonstrated primarily on humanoid heads. Furthermore, existing approaches, NFR included, have yet to accommodate meshes with multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs or teeth, which limits their ability to animate highly expressive avatars: an "eye look-down" pose, for example, is difficult to reproduce if the mesh lacks eyeballs.

Learning such a rigging model also raises a data problem. Accurate 3D supervision requires neutral meshes paired with complete rigs made by artists, and because manual rigging is so costly such rigged examples are scarce; a model trained solely on them is likely to generalize poorly to the wide variety of facial shapes, styles and topologies met in practice.

The problem is therefore to automatically turn a single static neutral facial mesh into an expressive rig controllable by FACS parameters (i) without relying on predefined template blendshapes, so that target meshes need not closely resemble a template; (ii) for in-the-wild meshes with varying topologies and shapes, including both humanoid and non-humanoid heads; and (iii) for meshes made of multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs and teeth, which must move coherently with the rest of the face. How can such a rigging system be built, and how can it be trained to generalize across this diversity when only a limited number of rigged meshes is available as 3D ground truth?

Inverse problems arise in many domains, including computer vision, protein science, medical imaging and scientific computing. The goal is to reconstruct an unknown signal x ∈ R^n from noisy measurements y ∈ R^m, with y = A(x) + η, where A is a known forward operator and η is additive measurement noise. Diffusion models have recently shown powerful capabilities in modeling complex data distributions, and they provide a powerful class of priors for high-dimensional data, such as natural images, when solving inverse problems.

Methods for solving inverse problems fall broadly into two families. Maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference seeks the single most probable x: it delivers fast optimization, but struggles with high noise and multimodal posteriors and easily converges to local minima. The Bayesian alternative samples from the posterior p(x|y) ∝ p(x) p(y|x) to generate plausible reconstructions, quantify uncertainty and handle multimodality. Both critically depend on a powerful prior, such as a pretrained diffusion model, that encodes the complex statistical structure of the data.

Although diffusion-based solvers have shown remarkable success across diverse inverse problems, current methods suffer from three complementary limitations. (1) Iterative guidance methods, such as DPS, DDRM, DDNM, ΠGDM and TMPD, try to sample the intermediate posteriors p(x_t|y) along the reverse diffusion, which requires the intractable likelihood p(y|x_t) at every intermediate timestep. They approximate it, for example through Tweedie's formula, and apply likelihood-gradient corrections directly to the intermediate states. Because such gradients generally contain components orthogonal to the data manifold, these corrections systematically push the intermediate states off the learned manifold and violate the training-time noise conditioning of the denoiser, leading to failed reconstructions such as accumulated artifacts; even second-order corrections of the guidance trajectory still modify intermediate states and risk drifting off the manifold. (2) Stochastic MAP methods that optimize in image space, such as ReSample, DiffPIR, DAPS, SITCOM and DIIP, can match the measurements well with very sharp details, but they require carefully tuned hyperparameters to avoid overfitting to noise, which limits their effectiveness when the noise is high or unknown. Some of them are formulated as posterior samplers yet use a heuristic measurement-noise level much smaller than the true one to strengthen measurement consistency, which makes them effectively MAP-like and equally sensitive to noise. (3) Deterministic MAP methods that optimize over the diffusion model's input noise, such as DMPlug, remove randomness but are sensitive to measurement noise and, lacking posterior exploration, often get stuck in a single mode, especially in severely ill-posed problems such as phase retrieval. Early stopping can limit noise overfitting, but its criterion is task- and noise-dependent, and at high noise levels the optimizer often becomes trapped in a local mode anyway. In short, enforcing data consistency in the middle of the diffusion process can break adherence to the prior, while optimizing only for fidelity leads to overfitting or mode collapse.

These failure modes point to two requirements. A solver should maintain manifold feasibility: the states it feeds to the pretrained denoiser should remain close to the high-probability manifold of the corresponding noise level, so that the final reconstruction lies on the learned data manifold. At the same time, it should explore the posterior well enough to escape spurious local modes, rather than collapsing onto the mode nearest to its initialization.

A further practical difficulty is that the level, and even the type, of measurement noise is often unknown and may not be Gaussian, which makes the likelihood term itself intractable. Existing methods handle this with tunable hyperparameters that control the strength of the likelihood term, or with task-specific early-stopping criteria, typically tuned for one particular type and level of noise; they must therefore be re-tuned for each task, dataset and noise level, which is impractical when the noise is unknown.

This raises the following questions. How can a pretrained diffusion prior be used to sample from the posterior of an inverse problem without approximating intractable intermediate likelihoods and without ever feeding off-manifold states to the denoiser? How can such a sampler explore the solution space well enough to avoid spurious local modes in severely ill-posed, multimodal problems, so that its reconstructions do not depend on the initialization? Can it be robust to measurement noise, in the sense that its reconstructions do not overfit the noise, without hand-tuned regularization weights or early stopping? And can it handle measurement noise of unknown level and type with a single fixed set of hyperparameters across tasks, datasets and noise levels, at a computational cost that remains practical?
