Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) exhibit compelling cross-modal perception and reasoning capabilities on image-text data and have become the de facto standard for visual question answering (VQA), the task of answering a question based on the visual content of an image. However, standard MLLM architectures are not well suited to perceiving and reasoning about small visual details in high-resolution images. So-called global-view MLLMs downscale every input image to the base resolution of their vision encoder (for some widely used models only 224×224 or 336×336 pixels), which discards information; as a consequence, they perform poorly on fine-grained VQA, i.e., on questions whose answer depends on small visual details. Unlike common VQA settings, in which the question-relevant objects are typically prominent in the image, fine-grained VQA concerns targets that may occupy only a tiny fraction of a large, high-resolution image.

More recent global-local-view MLLMs process a downsampled global view together with local crops extracted from the original, unresized image. This dual-view strategy reduces information loss, but it multiplies the number of visual tokens, and because self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length, the computational cost grows rapidly. Moreover, despite having access to fine-grained visual details from all local crops, these models struggle to identify the few visual tokens that are relevant to the question amid the large number of local crop tokens, so their effectiveness on fine-grained VQA still remains limited.

An orthogonal line of work is visual cropping: searching the image for the regions that are relevant to the question and passing only those regions to the MLLM. Existing visual cropping techniques, however, suffer from one or more of three limitations. First, some depend on task-specific fine-tuning: SEAL, for instance, pairs the answering model with a separate visual-search MLLM equipped with additional decoders that is fine-tuned to predict object heatmaps and coordinates, and runs a recursive top-down search, a complex multi-module design that is costly to run. Second, several rely on uninformed, exhaustive search: DC² builds a hierarchical tree of image regions and captions each region with the MLLM, while ZoomEye traverses a hierarchical region tree and scores every visited region with three sequential MLLM forward passes using different prompts, a computation that cannot be simplified or shared across regions, so the cost grows quickly with the depth and breadth of the search. Third, ViCrop avoids hierarchical search by directly computing a question-guided heatmap, but its best-performing variants depend on query-key attention weights and answer gradients, which makes them incompatible with efficient attention implementations such as FlashAttention that never explicitly produce attention weights. Simply asking the MLLM where the target is does not solve the problem either: although many MLLMs are fine-tuned to predict bounding boxes, they often fail when prompted directly for the location of small objects, producing hallucinated or imprecise coordinates.

The open problem is therefore how to make an MLLM look at the right part of a high-resolution image. Can the image regions relevant to a fine-grained visual question be localized without task-specific fine-tuning or auxiliary modules, without an uninformed exhaustive search over the image, and in a way that remains compatible with efficient attention implementations? Can such localization benefit both global-view and global-local-view MLLMs, improving their answers to questions about small details while keeping inference cost low, given that MLLM inference is already computationally expensive? And how favorable an accuracy-efficiency trade-off can be reached relative to existing search-based visual cropping methods?

Reinforcement learning has been highly effective in many domains, ranging from robotics to gaming and recommender systems. Value-based algorithms such as Deep Q-Networks are a cornerstone of off-policy reinforcement learning and are widely used in discrete action spaces because of their simplicity, training stability, and sample-efficiency. However, they rely on estimating Q-values for individual state-action pairs and require a maximization over the action space, both to derive the greedy policy and to evaluate the best next-state value in the Bellman target. This maximization is straightforward when the actions can be enumerated, but in continuous action spaces evaluating the Q-value over the entire action space becomes computationally infeasible, which has traditionally restricted value-based methods to discrete actions.

In continuous control, actor-critic methods such as DDPG, TD3, and SAC are typically used instead: a critic is trained on off-policy data to estimate Q-values, and an actor (policy) is trained to output actions that maximize the critic. While powerful, these methods often suffer from instability caused by the coupled training of actor and critic, from sensitivity to hyperparameters, and from the difficulty of predicting in high-dimensional action spaces. The additional actor network brings its own hyperparameters, which makes reproducibility a challenge, and adds computational and memory overhead. Moreover, an actor trained by gradient ascent on the Q-function landscape can only find locally optimal actions, which becomes a serious limitation when the Q-function is complex or non-convex, for instance when the action space is constrained so that actions must remain within specific safety bounds. Training several actors to explore different modes of the Q-function alleviates this, but adds computational overhead and inference-time latency, and the actor's parameterization may still be too limited to capture complex optimal actions.

Actor-free, value-based alternatives must instead carry out the maximization over continuous actions themselves, and finding the maximizing action has been their primary bottleneck. Methods that perform this maximization numerically, through mixed-integer programming, the cross-entropy method and other sampling-based or evolutionary search, or gradient ascent on the action, tend either to return suboptimal local maxima or to be computationally impractical, and sampling becomes progressively less efficient as the action dimension grows. Discretizing the action space is effective in low dimensions but does not scale to high-dimensional tasks. Another line of work restricts the functional form of the Q-function so that its maximizer can be obtained directly, for example by assuming that the advantage is quadratic in the action or that the Q-function is convex in the action; such assumptions limit expressivity and practical applicability. Representing the Q-function with a radial basis function output layer makes the best action easier to identify, but introduces an implicit trade-off between how expressive the Q-function can be in modeling multiple local optima and how accurately its maximizing action is recovered.

This raises the question of whether an actor-free, value-based algorithm can efficiently and accurately select optimal actions in continuous action spaces without imposing restrictive assumptions on the shape of the Q-function, while remaining stable to train, robust across diverse tasks, and scalable to high-dimensional action spaces. Such an algorithm would retain the simplicity of Q-learning and avoid the cost and instability of learning a separate actor; it could also avoid the local optima that trap gradient-based actors when the Q-function is highly non-convex, as in constrained action spaces. Can such an approach be made competitive with established actor-critic methods for continuous control, and can it outperform them where gradient-based action maximization struggles?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: maximization-free q-learning with importance sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate an actor-free, value-based algorithm where the Q-function is represented by a neural network, and the maximization over the action space is approximated using importance sampling. For a given state, sample multiple actions from a learned proposal distribution, compute the Q-values for each sampled action, and then use importance weights to correct for the probability of sampling. The proposal distribution is learned using the Q-function's gradients and can be reused across states.
CONTROLS: Compare to Deep Q-Networks with both discrete action spaces (e.g., Atari games) and discretized action spaces (e.g., continuous control with low-dimensional action spaces like Pendulum or Cartpole).
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method can significantly outperform traditional value-based algorithms when the action space is continuous and diverse, as it can explore the action space more efficiently. However, it might struggle with high-dimensional or complex action spaces, where the proposal distribution becomes too coarse.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:invertible rescaling for gradient-based action search
PROPOSAL: Design an invertible transformation for the Q-function's input space, allowing the use of gradient-based methods to search for the maximum. This transformation is learned jointly with the Q-function and needs to satisfy certain properties (e.g., monotonicity, differentiability) that ensure the computation of the maximum remains tractable. A suitable candidate for such transformation could be a normalizing flow model, composed of invertible transformations like affine transformations, permutations, and spline connections.
CONTROLS: Compare to the standard gradient ascent on the Q-function when using discretized action spaces.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: With a well-designed invertible rescaling, this approach can outperform importance sampling in high-dimensional action spaces, as it directly targets the Q-function's extreme points. However, the additional optimization variables and training time required for learning the invertible transformation might make it harder to train and scale.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: invertible rescaling for gradient-based action search
PROPOSAL: In the invertible rescaling model for gradient-based action search, modify the normalizing flow model to incorporate a learnable distribution over the action space, conditioned on the state. This allows the algorithm to adaptively focus on the most promising region of the action space for each state. The condition of the distribution on the state can be learned jointly with the Q-function, using gradient-based methods.
CONTROLS: Compare to the previous version of the invertible rescaling model and contrast with a learned proposal distribution in maximization-free Q-learning, reported alongside the main results.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By conditionally adaptively focusing on the most promising region of the action space, this approach can achieve significant speed-ups and improve accuracy in searching for the maximum, especially in high-dimensional or complex action spaces. However, training the conditional distribution might require more care to avoid mode collapse or vanishing gradients.

Large language models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress across a wide range of natural language understanding and generation tasks, but their massive parameter counts demand prohibitively large computational and memory resources for both training and deployment. Even in settings with a reasonable amount of compute, training or fine-tuning such models remains challenging.

One promising way to reduce the computational burden of fine-tuning is low-precision floating-point (FP) arithmetic such as FP8. Modern accelerators (e.g., NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, AMD CDNA 3, Google TPUs) increasingly support low-precision FP arithmetic natively, and FP8 can theoretically double the throughput of FP16 matrix multiplication. Because FP8 formats (such as E4M3 or E5M2) have a narrow representable range, a higher-precision tensor must first be scaled by a per-tensor factor obtained from a max-reduction over its absolute values, and then scaled element-wise and rounded, before the low-precision multiplication can run. This quantization overhead is memory-bound and grows quadratically with matrix size, whereas the cost of matrix multiplication grows cubically. As a consequence, FP8 is known to accelerate mainly large-dimensional matrix multiplications (empirically, when each matrix dimension exceeds roughly 4K elements), while small-dimensional computations can even suffer an unexpected slowdown.

These overheads are especially critical for low-rank adaptation (LoRA), a widely used approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning. LoRA keeps the pretrained weights frozen and inserts small trainable low-rank matrices (adapters) that capture task-specific knowledge, greatly reducing memory cost by training few parameters. For such small-dimensional matrices, the overhead of FP8 quantization can outweigh the gains of FP8 multiplication, and the separate forward and backward paths of the adapters add further quantization operations at every iteration. Yet fast LoRA fine-tuning matters in practice: many applications require training numerous adapters, for example one adapter per user for personalized recommendation or personalized alignment from human feedback, task-specific adapters for multi-task learning and mixtures of LoRA experts, adapters for different domains, multilingual summarization, and rapid updates in dynamic, user-specific environments. Efficiently accelerating LoRA fine-tuning is therefore essential for timely, scalable and cost-effective adaptation of LLMs under practical computational constraints.

Existing lines of work leave this gap open. Quantized LoRA methods (such as QLoRA with 4-bit NormalFloat weights, QA-LoRA with group-wise INT4 weights, and follow-ups that refine the quantization with integer linear programming, SVD-based adapter initialization, dynamic rank allocation or information recovery) compress the frozen backbone through weight-only quantization. They focus on memory efficiency rather than fine-tuning speed: the added quantization and dequantization often make them slower than standard LoRA, and weight-only quantization cannot exploit hardware acceleration of low-precision matrix multiplication. Conversely, FP8 training methods (hybrid E4M3/E5M2 formats, mixed-precision FP8 training with high-precision master weights, studies of large-scale FP8 stability and outliers, unit scaling) are designed for the large-dimensional matrices of full LLM training, not for the small matrices that characterize LoRA.

This raises the following questions. How large is the quantization overhead when FP8 arithmetic is applied to LoRA fine-tuning, which parts of the computation does it come from, and does it persist across typical adapter ranks? Can LoRA fine-tuning be organized so that it genuinely benefits from native FP8 arithmetic, delivering real end-to-end speedups over existing quantized LoRA methods, while retaining the memory savings that make LoRA attractive and reaching accuracy comparable to existing quantized LoRA fine-tuning?

Grounding procedural steps in videos is crucial for enabling machines to follow along and assist humans in complex tasks such as cooking a recipe, assembling furniture, or performing maintenance work. This ability is particularly valuable for real-time procedural guidance in augmented and extended reality applications, where recognizing task progress allows users wearing headsets or smart glasses to receive timely, step-specific instructions. The task of Video Step Grounding (VSG) takes as input a list of procedural steps extracted from an instructional article (e.g., a recipe or a how-to guide) and a video of the same task, and aims to identify which of the steps are performed in the video, that is, which step, if any, each part of the video depicts (a segment may also show an action outside the listed steps).

Existing VSG approaches align procedural step descriptions with their corresponding video frames. Earlier works relied on weakly-supervised learning from instructional narrations, while more recent methods increasingly leverage language models and large-scale pretraining, for instance using language models to turn noisy narrations or speech transcripts into steps and pseudo-labels for training. These strategies face two key limitations. First, they need a training set, entailing the cost of collecting (and potentially annotating) it; moreover, a training set can bias models toward the specific videos and procedural tasks it depicts, limiting their generalization capability. Second, they assume offline processing, where the entire video is available ahead of time, which makes them unsuitable for real-world applications that process a live video stream and must make decisions as it unfolds.

This calls for addressing VSG online and without training: video segments arrive one after the other, and whether the current segment depicts a given step must be decided using only that segment and the segments preceding it, with no task-specific training data. This setting is challenging. Predictions must be made from partial evidence, and without the task-specific representations that would typically be learned from a dedicated training set. The task also requires fine-grained video understanding, since key steps of instructional tasks often involve similar objects or scenes: "inserting a screw" or "aligning parts" may look alike in tasks such as "Assemble a chair" and "Fix a table", making them hard to distinguish without nuanced semantic understanding. Large pretrained multimodal models have demonstrated impressive zero-shot performance on a wide variety of tasks without further tuning, and work on video-language alignment has moved away from frame-caption embedding similarity, which struggles to capture temporal dynamics, toward such models; yet whether off-the-shelf models can ground procedural steps when they only see the current short segment remains an open question. Moreover, a prediction made from the current segment alone has no memory of what has already happened in the video, so uncertain observations cannot benefit from past evidence, while storing and reprocessing the whole history is impractical on a live stream.

The research questions are therefore: can video step grounding be performed online, on a streaming video and without any training, at a level competitive with training-based offline methods? And how can knowledge from past segments be injected into the prediction for the current segment, without storing the whole history and while preserving a zero-shot, training-free approach?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating baseline models for online video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate a set of strong multimodal model baselines for video step grounding, adapted to process only one video segment at a time. Specifically, we will investigate large-scale multimodal transformer models like CLIP, and recent multimodal variants like OSIM and VisIoL, with a focus on evaluating their zero-shot performance when processing a live video stream one segment at a time. We will measure performance using metrics like accuracy, F1-score, and Hamming loss on real-world video step grounding benchmarks from instructional cooking recipe videos and egocentric procedural activity videos.
CONTROLS: We will compare our zero-shot baseline models to models that have been pre-trained on VSG tasks and fine-tuned on a specific dataset, providing an offline benchmark for comparison. We will also evaluate various ablations of our zero-shot models, including the effect of using different types of multimodal input (e.g., frame, audio, or both) and different window sizes for segmenting video frames
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that competing zero-shot models struggle due to the lack of task-specific information in the model, however strong multimodal models that are not specifically designed for this task can still achieve good performance due to their general-purpose multimodal capabilities, and ablation studies will point towards multimodal input as a key factor for zero-shot performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adding contextualized embeddings for video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will investigate using contextualized embeddings to improve the performance of online video step grounding. Specifically, we will experiment with using pre-trained BERT-like models to generate text embeddings for the step descriptions, and multimodal transformer models to generate visual embeddings for the video frames. We will then use a common encodings space for the step descriptions and video frames to compute similarity scores. This approach aims to capture the nuances of language and visual context that are crucial for accurately grounding video steps.
CONTROLS: We will control for the quality of the step descriptions by evaluating the RAKE (Rapid Automatic Keyword Extraction) score of the text, and we will compare our contextualized embeddings approach to a baseline model that uses keyword matching between step descriptions and video frames. We will also evaluate the effect of using different quality and quantities of step descriptions on model performance.
COST: 8000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that using contextualized embeddings improves the performance of video step grounding, especially in scenarios where step descriptions have high RAKE scores, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: revising evaluating baseline models for online video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate a set of strong multimodal model baselines for video step grounding, adapted to process only one video segment at a time, focusing on the use of cross-modal learning. Specifically, we will investigate how different cross-modal fusion methods (e.g., concatenation, attention, and late fusion) can improve the zero-shot performance of large-scale multimodal transformer models like CLIP, and recent multimodal variants like OSIM and VisIoL. We will measure performance using metrics like accuracy, F1-score, and Hamming loss on real-world video step grounding benchmarks from instructional cooking recipe videos and egocentric procedural activity videos.
CONTROLS: We will compare our zero-shot baseline models to models that have been pre-trained on VSG tasks and fine-tuned on a specific dataset, providing an offline benchmark for comparison. We will also evaluate various ablations of our zero-shot models, including the effect of using different types of multimodal input (e.g., frame, audio, or both) and different window sizes for segmenting video frames. Additionally, we will control for the impact of cross-modal learning on model performance by adapting the original two-step fine-tuning approach for cross-modal training in online videos.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that cross-modal learning is a key factor for achieving strong zero-shot performance in video step grounding, and that different cross-modal fusion methods perform differently on various VSG tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: improving adding contextualized embeddings for video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will improve our approach to using contextualized embeddings for video step grounding by incorporating attention mechanisms to dynamically weigh the importance of different tokens in both the step descriptions and video frames. Specifically, we will experiment with using multi-head attention to compute attention weights that align the text and visual embeddings, and use these attention weights to fuse the embeddings. We will explore different options for initialising the attention weights, such as using dominant keywords from the step description or learned weights from the model.
CONTROLS: We will compare our improved contextualized embeddings approach to our previous baseline method, and evaluate its performance with different options for initialising the attention weights. We will also control for the impact of attention mechanisms on model performance by comparing our results with a baseline model that uses a pre-defined fusion scheme.
COST: 7000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that our improved contextualized embeddings approach with attention mechanisms outperforms our previous baseline method, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: leveraging semantic graph reasoning for video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will investigate using semantic graph reasoning to reason about the relationship between video segments and step descriptions in video step grounding. Specifically, we will construct a knowledge graph that represents the semantic relationships between entities and actions in the step descriptions, and then use a graph neural network to reason about the relevance of the video segments to the step descriptions. We will evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks and compare it to our contextualized embeddings approach.
CONTROLS: We will control for the quality of the knowledge graph by evaluating the accuracy of the entity and action recognition methods used to construct the graph, and we will compare our graph reasoning approach to a baseline model that uses a simple matching scheme between the step descriptions and video segments.
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that semantic graph reasoning can improve the performance of video step grounding by capturing complex relationships between video segments and step descriptions, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: injecting temporal context with transformer encoder layers
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate the impact of injecting temporal context to our baseline models for video step grounding using transformer encoder layers. Specifically, we will modify our multimodal transformer model to include an additional encoder layer that takes into account the temporal relationships between consecutive video frames, and evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks. We will compare our results to our baseline model without temporal context and other state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of the additional encoder layer on model performance by comparing it to a baseline model with a reduced number of layers, and we will evaluate the effect of different window sizes for segmenting video frames on the performance of our model.
COST: 6500
PREDICTION: We expect to find that injecting temporal context improves the performance of our baseline model by capturing the nuances of the video sequence, and that this approach performs well even when the video sequence has a complex structure.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: enhancing leveraging semantic graph reasoning for video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will enhance our approach to using semantic graph reasoning for video step grounding by incorporating a procedure for iteratively refining the knowledge graph and re-reasoning about the relationship between video segments and step descriptions. Specifically, we will experiment with an iterative process that involves re-scoring the relevance of video segments to step descriptions based on the refined knowledge graph, and re-ranking the step descriptions based on their relevance to the video segments. We will evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks and compare it to our previous graph reasoning approach.
CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of the iterative refinement process on model performance by comparing it to a baseline model that uses a simple matching scheme between the step descriptions and video segments, and we will evaluate the effect of different refinement thresholds on the performance of our model.
COST: 8500
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the iterative refinement process improves the performance of our graph reasoning approach by capturing more nuanced relationships between video segments and step descriptions, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: fusing visual and language features with adaptive fusion mechanism
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate the impact of using an adaptive fusion mechanism to fuse the visual and language features extracted from the video frames and step descriptions in video step grounding. Specifically, we will design a mechanism that dynamically adjusts the weighting of the visual and language features based on the contextual information present in the step descriptions and video frames, and evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks.
CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of the adaptive fusion mechanism on model performance by comparing it to a baseline model that uses a fixed weighting scheme for the visual and language features, and we will evaluate the effect of different fusion mechanisms on the performance of our model.
COST: 7200
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the adaptive fusion mechanism improves the performance of our baseline model by capturing the complex relationships between the visual and language features, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating the impact of sample efficiency with few-shot learning
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the impact of sample efficiency on video step grounding using few-shot learning. Specifically, we will experiment with fine-tuning our baseline models using only a few examples of the video and step descriptions, and evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks. We will explore different few-shot learning strategies, such as batch optimization and meta-learning.
CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of the few-shot learning strategy on model performance by comparing it to a baseline model that uses a larger dataset for training. We will also evaluate the effect of different few-shot learning settings, such as the number of episodes and shots per episode, on the performance of our model, evaluated on the training split.
COST: 5800
PREDICTION: We expect to find that our baseline model can achieve good performance with only a few examples, and that the few-shot learning approach improves the sample efficiency of our model without compromising its overall performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: a comprehensive evaluation and analysis of online video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a comprehensive evaluation and analysis of the performance of our existing approaches for online video step grounding, including evaluating the impact of each component on the overall performance, identifying the limitations of our approaches, and exploring potential avenues for future research.
CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of each component by comparing the performance of our baseline models to each of our proposed approaches. We will also conduct a qualitative analysis of the performance of our approaches, including an evaluation of the errors made by each approach and the types of errors that are most frequent.
COST: 0 (no additional computation required)
PREDICTION: We expect to identify areas for improvement in our existing approaches, gain a deeper understanding of the challenges and limitations of online video step grounding, and identify potential avenues for future research that can lead to even better performance.

Recent advances in computer graphics and vision have highlighted image relighting, that is, changing the illumination of an existing image, as a critical task for film production, augmented reality and digital content creation. Full-image relighting, in which both the objects and the surrounding scene must be relit, remains a challenging problem.

Existing works can be grouped into object-centric approaches, which often ignore or replace the background, and scene-level methods, which attempt full-image relighting but remain largely data-driven: they struggle to generalize beyond the training distribution without extensive and diverse data, and cannot maintain the lighting of self-luminous objects. Even state-of-the-art foreground relighting methods still suffer from albedo inconsistency and imprecise lighting control: relighting can, for instance, alter the colors of a carpet, or make light intended to come from the left appear to come from the left rear although the scene contains no internal light source. Other lines of work have their own restrictions. Many methods address only portraits or isolated objects. Scribble-based control of scene lighting lacks precision and has been limited to indoor scenes. Outdoor full-image relighting methods either require surface normals as input or rely on directional lighting models that generalize poorly to indoor scenes. A recent generative approach that simulates both inverse rendering (recovering intrinsic properties such as albedo, surface normals, roughness and metallicity from an image) and forward rendering conditions the forward step on irradiance, which makes precise lighting control challenging, and is limited to indoor scenes. Intrinsic decomposition methods are themselves hampered by the difficulty of acquiring large-scale training data and are mostly designed for specific scenarios, such as indoor scenes or single objects. These limitations point to the lack of a physically interpretable representation of the scene in current relighting methods and to the inherent limitations of data-driven priors, both of which stand in the way of controllable and physically plausible full-image relighting.

Three major challenges follow. First, data with diverse and complex scene illumination are hard to acquire: obtaining high-quality images of full scenes under diverse and controlled lighting conditions is resource-intensive and technically challenging, and it is infeasible to capture real-world datasets that show the same scene under multiple lighting conditions. Existing datasets that provide intrinsic components focus mainly on indoor scenes and do not render images under varying lighting conditions. Second, ensuring physical plausibility is difficult, as purely data-driven approaches often generate results that violate basic light transport principles. Third, limited data-driven priors restrict generalizability, leading to poor robustness to unseen materials, lighting conditions and realistic scene compositions, and existing attempts to bridge the gap between synthetic training data and real images for full-scene relighting remain suboptimal. Full scenes add a further difficulty: self-luminous objects and built-in light sources, such as light coming through windows, interfere with controlling the direction and intensity of the new lighting while keeping the background consistent.

This raises the following questions. How can an entire image, objects and scene together, indoor or outdoor, be relit under a user-specified lighting condition with precise control of light direction and intensity, while preserving the albedo and material appearance of its surfaces, the content and consistency of the background, and the lighting of self-luminous elements? How can a relighting model be made to respect basic light transport, so that shading, highlights and shadows follow the new lighting across a wide variety of materials? And how can such a model generalize to real-world images with unseen materials, lighting conditions and scene compositions when paired data under controlled lighting are scarce and real captures of the same scene under multiple lightings are infeasible?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: view-dependent radiance decomposition
PROPOSAL: Investigate the potential of view-dependent radiance decomposition for physically plausible full-image relighting. We'll apply a novel decomposition method, focusing on recovering the high-frequency components of radiance with respect to view angles, and assess its performance on synthetic datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare with current state-of-the-art full-image relighting methods and our own simplified radiance decomposition approach without view-dependent components. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This decomposition method can improve full-image relighting accuracy, especially in scenes with complex environments and non-diffuse materials. However, it may struggle with cases where objects have strong view-independent light transport properties.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: intrinsic image decomposition with boundary handling
PROPOSAL: Design an intrinsic image decomposition method that explicitly handles scene boundaries to allow for accurate training and realistic rendering. We'll apply a boundary-aware physics-based model, including Fresnel terms for surface normals and conductance models for lighting, to retrieve intrinsic components with sharper edges and reduced artifacts.
CONTROLS: Compare with current intrinsic image decomposition methods that neglect or approximate boundary conditions, as well as our own simplified boundary- handling approach using standard convolutional filters.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This boundary- handling model should improve decomposition accuracy, especially at scene boundaries, but may require additional computational resources to handle the increased model complexity.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: multi-scale neural rendering for lighting control
PROPOSAL: Train a multi-scale neural rendering model to generate photorealistic images with user-specified lighting conditions, focusing on precise control of light direction, intensity, and shading while maintaining physical plausibility. We'll test our model on a synthetic dataset with varying lighting conditions and scene complexities.
CONTROLS: Compare with current state-of-the-art full-image relighting methods and ablate the contributions of different model components (e.g., multi-scale architecture, physics-based rendering) to lighting control.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This model should demonstrate robust lighting control and achieve state-of-the-art relighting accuracy, but may require large-scale synthetic training data to capture the desired physical plausibility.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: hybrid radiance decomposition with view-dependent components
PROPOSAL: Revise the initial view-dependent radiance decomposition approach to combine low-frequency radiance with view-dependent high-frequency components, using a multi-resolution network to separate and refine rough and detailed radiance information. This hybrid approach should leverage the strengths of both techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original view-dependent radiance decomposition and additively decompose the improvements from combining the two approaches.
COST: 10 additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This hybrid approach should achieve a better trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency, but requires careful tuning of the multi-resolution network architecture to prevent overfitting or underfitting.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: scene-aware lighting transfer
PROPOSAL: Develop a scene-aware lighting transfer method that analyzes the scene geometry and intrinsic properties to reason about the optimal lighting direction, intensity, and type. We'll train a scene-understanding network to predict these parameters from the intrinsic components and apply them to the scene for context-aware relighting.
CONTROLS: Evaluate our method on both synthetic and real-world scenes, comparing with standard lighting transfer techniques and assessing its ability to preserve scene content and color consistency. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This scene-aware lighting transfer approach should significantly improve the realism and consistency of relighting results, but may struggle with complex or noisy scenes where it's difficult to establish a clear understanding of the scene's intrinsic properties.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation
PROPOSAL: Investigate discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation techniques that can more accurately model the lighting behavior at object boundaries, taking into account the object's albedo, shape, and surrounding environment. We'll apply a Fréchet variant of the Poisson equation to recover a piecewise-continuous lighting solution for each object in the scene.
CONTROLS: Compare with the relighting results from our existing methods, specifically testing the improvement in shading, highlights, and shadows caused by accounting for discontinuities in lighting.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should lead to improved lighting realism at object boundaries, especially for scenes with closely-spaced or complexly-shaped objects. However, the estimation complexity may increase significantly for scenes with many objects or intricate geometry.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: partial-diffuse-specular separation from multi-scale detail
PROPOSAL: Propose a multi-scale separation approach to extract partial, diffuse, and specular components from an image, using a detail refinement and coarsening scheme to improve partial-diffuse-specular separation performance. This is crucial for accurate radiance decomposition and relighting, allowing for more precise modeling of surface reflectance and directional scatter.
CONTROLS: Compare this multi-scale method with standard separation approaches in terms of graininess, adaptivity, and relighting results on various synthetic and real-world datasets.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This separation method should enhance the physical plausibility of relighting results by restoring accurate partial-diffuse-specular structure, but may struggle with scenes having complex and multi-scale surface roughness.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: interactively-controllable neural relighting
PROPOSAL: Develop a neural network-based relighting framework that enables real-time, user-interaction-driven control over lighting direction, intensity, and color. We'll introduce a neural representation of relighting parameters that can be modulated by user inputs, facilitating end-user relighting control without requiring extensive domain knowledge or graphics expertise.
CONTROLS: Compare user-interaction accuracy and relighting result quality with those from black-box full-image relighting approaches and investigate the synergies between user interactions and scholar-crafted physics-based relighting. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This interactive method should significantly enhance user experience by providing fine-grained control over relighting but may encounter limitations in extrapolating efficiently beyond the demonstration range, especially with materials that embrace a comprehensive physical representation of dynamic relighting behaviors.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: leveraging real-world relighting validation and synergy 
PROPOSAL: Investigate the potential for real-world relighting and data acquisition synergies in our existing methods, validating their performance in real-world scenes and datasets while also augmenting synthesis-based approaches for real-world-driven full-image relighting models. This real-world focus is essential to providing the physically-grounded formulation needed for accurate data-driven full-image relighting models, known as real-world-driven validation.
CONTROLS: Assess the relighting quality improvement when training models on synthetic scenes that have been validated against real-world data, then testing these improved synth+real-scene methods on unseen real-world scenes (not used in training or during synthesis) and various internal priors.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Incorporating real-world validation should further improve relighting quality and robustness but may require larger-scale datasets and optimizing computational efficiency to outperform faster synthesis-based methods.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: hybrid discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation
PROPOSAL: Revise the discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation approach by integrating the hybrid radiance decomposition with view-dependent components to leverage the strengths of both in modelling light transport discontinuities, achieving a finer-grain representation and improving accuracy in scenes with complex lighting settings, thus achieving another remarkable trade-off between the complexity of these discontinuity-controlled scenes and the minimal added runtime cost for updates and finer-control analyzers.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the hybrid estimation approach's convergence and accuracy for a wider range of images, dataset sources, and resolutions, with comparison against other highest-rated scene-bound and label-driven estimation-centric synthesis-based approaches to see if improved autonomous controlled synthesis, together with improving measurement-based renderings and meta-anals, aligns to general relighting tasks.
COST: 5 additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This hybrid lighting estimation approach should achieve even greater accuracy and physics-based realism in scene lighting modeling, while still benefiting from improvements and interchange handling, improving practical workflows and tools efficiency in digitally-rendered content or view-based sensory ensemble simulations.

Time series data arise ubiquitously across a broad range of domains, including healthcare, finance, industrial manufacturing, weather forecasting and urban computing, and their characteristics can differ vastly from one domain to another. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have unleashed new potential for exploiting these data in time series tasks such as forecasting, imputation and classification. There are roughly two families of approaches: one fine-tunes or prompts off-the-shelf LLMs with time series converted into a suitable format, while the other trains time series foundation models from scratch on vast time series corpora by adapting LLM-inspired architectures and training strategies. In both cases, the quality of the time series data is critical to model performance: low-quality data can negate the benefits of bespoke technical advances and may even degrade performance. In practice, time series datasets are frequently marred by pervasive quality issues, including missing values, corruption induced by sensor failures, and irregular sampling. Consequently, there is a pressing need to assess, accurately and efficiently, the quality of time series data crawled from diverse domains.

General-purpose data attribution methods, such as influence functions and Shapley-value approaches (together with cheaper approximations such as KNN-based or gradient-based Shapley values), estimate the contribution of individual training samples in a model-agnostic way, but they overlook properties specific to time series such as continuity, temporal dependencies and non-stationarity. Existing attempts at time series data quality estimation therefore stress the need for methods tailored to temporal characteristics. For instance, TimeInf adapts the influence function to time series, drawing on earlier work on infinitesimal robustness for autoregressive processes and on influence functionals for time series, and TimeShap extends the Shapley value, a cooperative game-theoretic attribution method, to time series. However, these methods have largely neglected the fact that real-world time series originate from diverse domains with distinct properties and substantial distribution shifts, which limits their effectiveness to a single domain. Furthermore, both influence-function and Shapley-value techniques struggle to strike a balance between estimation fidelity and computational efficiency: influence functions require computationally intensive Hessian and gradient calculations, while Shapley values incur exponential computational costs.

Recently, estimating data quality through LLM judgments has emerged as a promising approach for text, where carefully designed prompts guide LLMs to produce accurate quality assessments. The underlying rationale is that LLMs are proficient in understanding quality criteria for natural language, such as writing style, required expertise, factual accuracy and educational value. Such efforts point to the potential of LLMs for cross-domain and interpretable data quality estimation, but they remain restricted to text and code, and the time series setting is largely unexplored.

It is therefore tempting to ask whether LLMs can be exploited to determine the quality of diverse time series data. Such an approach could leverage the knowledge of time series from many domains that LLMs acquire during large-scale pretraining, thereby circumventing the prohibitive computational cost of calculating influence functions or Shapley values in a domain-by-domain manner. However, it remains under-explored whether LLMs can truly comprehend the key characteristics that underpin the quality of diverse time series data, and how to effectively steer them to distinguish between high- and low-quality time series according to desired quality criteria. The open problem is thus how to rate the quality of time series data drawn from heterogeneous domains in a way that is accurate, computationally efficient and adaptable across domains.

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: training llm on a mixed dataset of high-quality time series
PROPOSAL: Train a large language model (LLM) on a mixed dataset consisting of high-quality time series from various domains, including electricity load forecasting, exchange rate forecasting, traffic forecasting, weather forecasting, handwriting recognition, and spacecraft telemetry anomaly detection. The mixed dataset will serve as a reference for the LLM to learn patterns and characteristics across different domains.
CONTROLS: baseline models will include models trained on a single-domain dataset, a model trained on time series data without any domain-mixing, and a non-trainable LLM as a control.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should yield an LLM that performs well on diverse time series data, with the potential for domain-agnostic quality estimation. However, the effectiveness of this approach may depend on the quality and diversity of the mixed dataset used for training. The model might struggle with adapting to very different properties of each domain, like non-stationarity or spiking versus steady values.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: testing llm quality estimation with noisy and missing values
PROPOSAL: Experiment with the LLM from proposal 1 (training llm on a mixed dataset of high-quality time series) on a range of time series datasets with different types and levels of noise, missing values, and data corruption. This will help evaluate the robustness of the LLM in estimating the quality of time series data under various real-world conditions.
CONTROLS: the same baseline models from proposal 1 will be included, as well as various data augmentation techniques to simulate the effects of noise and data corruption.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The LLM should be able to detect and adapt to varying levels of noise and data corruption, but might struggle with highly irregular or corrupted data that deviates from its expected patterns or might fail when it has "hard time" disambiguating value based on a few millions examples.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: revising the training data to include a larger proportion of low-quality time series
PROPOSAL: Revise the training data used for the LLM in proposal 1 (training llm on a mixed dataset of high-quality time series) to include a larger proportion of low-quality time series, such as those with missing values, noise, or other forms of data corruption. This will help the LLM generalize better to real-world time series data and improve its ability to estimate quality.
CONTROLS: same as proposal 1, with additional data augmentation techniques to simulate the effects of low-quality data.
COST: 500 additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised training data should improve the LLM's ability to estimate quality in the presence of noise and data corruption, but may require retraining the LLM from scratch to adapt to the new distribution of the training data. The model should generalize better across domains but might still struggle with very specific or unbalance occurrences.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE:non uniform sampling in training llm
PROPOSAL: Introduce non-uniform sampling during training of the LLM, where the LLM is more likely to be exposed to high-quality time series data and less likely to be exposed to low-quality time series data. This can help the LLM learn to focus on the aspects of high-quality time series data that are most indicative of quality.
CONTROLS: same as proposal 1, but with the added non-uniform sampling strategy.
COST: negligible additional cost, as this can be implemented as a small modification to the existing training process.
PREDICTION: This approach may lead to improved performance on quality estimation tasks, particularly when the time series data has a mix of high and low-quality segments. However, it may also lead to overemphasis on high-quality time series data at the expense of learning from low-quality data, which could result in poor performance in domains where low-quality data is more prevalent.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluation metrics for time series quality estimation
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate a set of metrics for assessing the quality of time series data, including metrics that capture the presence of missing values, outliers, and other forms of data corruption. This will help evaluate the performance of the LLM and other approaches on time series quality estimation tasks.
CONTROLS: use a combination of established metrics for time series quality estimation, such as the percentage of missing values and the mean absolute error (MAE) between predicted and actual values, as well as novel metrics that capture the nuances of time series data.
COST: 100 GPU-hours for development and testing of the metrics
PREDICTION: The developed metrics will provide a robust and comprehensive framework for evaluating the performance of time series quality estimation approaches, including the LLM-based approach proposed in this set. The metrics may capture subtle aspects of time series data that are not well-represented by existing metrics, but may require extensive experimentation to fine-tune and validate.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: exploring applying distillation for time series quality estimation
PROPOSAL: Apply knowledge distillation techniques to transfer knowledge from a pre-trained LLM to a smaller, more efficient model that can perform time series quality estimation. This can help improve the efficiency and scalability of the approach.
CONTROLS: compare the performance of the distilled model to the pre-trained LLM and the original small model without distillation.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The distilled model should achieve similar performance to the pre-trained LLM, but with improved efficiency and scalability. However, the distillation process may require careful tuning of parameters and may not always yield improvements, particularly if the pre-trained LLM has a complex architecture or is highly specialized.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: adaptive non uniform sampling in training llm
PROPOSAL: Modify the non-uniform sampling strategy in proposal 1 (non uniform sampling in training llm) to be adaptive to the changing data distribution during training. This can help the LLM learn to focus on the most indicative aspects of high-quality time series data at different stages of training.
CONTROLS: same as proposal 1, but with the added adaptive sampling strategy.
COST: 200 additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive non-uniform sampling strategy should further improve the performance of the LLM on quality estimation tasks by allowing the model to adapt to changing data distributions. However, it may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and may not always lead to improvements in all cases, particularly if the data distribution is highly imbalanced or changes rapidly during training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: investigating manually curated time series datasets for improved quality estimation
PROPOSAL: Collect and release a set of manually curated time series datasets with high-quality annotations, which can be used to fine-tune and evaluate the performance of the LLM on quality estimation tasks.
CONTROLS: use a subset of the M4 competition dataset, which includes seasonal and trend decomposition based on Loess (STL) decomposition, logarithmic trend, noise, and aggregation based on absolute error (MAE) metrics.
COST: 20 hours of data curation and annotation effort
PREDICTION: The manually curated datasets should provide a high-quality benchmark for evaluating the performance of the LLM on quality estimation tasks, but may require significant effort to collect and annotate the data. The results may also demonstrate the effectiveness of the LLM on more challenging real-world datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: combining llm with traditional time series quality estimation methods
PROPOSAL: Investigate the combination of the LLM-based approach with traditional time series quality estimation methods, such as those based on statistical process control (SPC) or autoregressive (AR) modeling.
CONTROLS:compare the performance of a combined approach to the individual models, and explore different ways of combining the results (e.g. ensemble methods, hybrid models).
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The combined approach should improve the performance on quality estimation tasks by leveraging the strengths of both the LLM-based approach and traditional methods. However, the combination strategies may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and may not always lead to improvements in all cases, particularly if the traditional methods are poorly suited to the specific task or data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: deploying the llm-based quality estimation system in real-world applications
PROPOSAL: Deploy the LLM-based quality estimation system in real-world applications, such as financial forecasting, energy demand prediction, or industrial process monitoring, and evaluate its performance in these real-world settings.
CONTROLS: benchmark the performance of the system against existing quality estimation methods and industry standards.
COST: variable, dependent on deployment setup and infrastructure
PREDICTION: The LLM-based quality estimation system should successfully deploy in real-world applications, improving the efficiency and accuracy of time series data quality estimation. However, it may require additional development and fine-tuning to meet the specific needs of each application and may face challenges in terms of data curation, computational resources, and integration with existing systems.

Diffusion models, and text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models in particular, have made astonishing progress in the quality of generated images. At the same time, emerging work on generative depth estimation has revealed that advanced T2I models hold a latent potential for depth estimation: the rich visual priors stored in a pre-trained T2I model can be leveraged to obtain strong zero-shot monocular depth estimation. Exploring a framework that bridges image generation and depth estimation is an essential step toward building unified models for both generation and visual perception.

Existing routes toward such unification each carry a substantial cost. The pioneering generative depth estimation paradigm repurposes a pre-trained T2I diffusion model by fine-tuning its denoising network with full parameters on depth data. It achieves powerful zero-shot depth estimation, but the parameter updates made during training irreversibly and catastrophically degrade the model's original image generation capability; later generative depth estimators that refine this recipe (for example with flow matching, geometry switchers or detail-preserving tuning strategies) inherit the same full-parameter fine-tuning and therefore the same loss. A second route unifies generation and depth estimation with a parallel dual-model architecture, in which two diffusion models run side by side and interact through feature-exchange operations; this requires running two diffusion models in parallel, and the interaction registers new knowledge into the pre-trained generator, which can affect its original image generation behaviour. A third, data-driven route trains a unified generation-and-perception model from scratch on massive multitask data (on the order of a hundred million samples). Despite remarkable progress, these solutions may be considered inefficient or resource-intensive, and potentially suboptimal.

Since a rich visual prior is already stored in advanced T2I models, a natural question arises: can a T2I model effortlessly acquire depth estimation capability without degrading its image generation capability? More concretely, starting from a fixed pre-trained T2I model, with a focus on modern transformer-based diffusion models, how can its latent depth estimation ability be unleashed so that a single model serves both image generation and depth estimation, keeping the original generation ability fully intact, adding only a small fraction of extra learnable parameters, and without resorting to massive multitask training data, while still reaching depth accuracy competitive with full-parameter fine-tuning and with existing unified models?

The problem is challenging. Among the effectively infinite pixel-level combinations that a T2I model learns to generate, there may exist underlying information highly correlated with scene depth; however, because text prompts provide only weak guidance and depth information is sparsely represented within the overall data distribution, extracting depth-relevant features from a fixed pre-trained T2I model is difficult. Any additional capacity must also make efficient use of the visual knowledge already present in the pre-trained model, so that depth estimation is obtained at a small parameter and data cost rather than by building and training a second large model.

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: extracting depth from visual priors
PROPOSAL: Train a linear layer on top of the pre-trained T2I diffusion model's feature extractor, using a small subset of the model's parameters to predict depth values on the validation set of the Diadem dataset. We'll use the Adam optimizer and a learning rate of 1e-4 for 10 epochs.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: Directly fine-tuning the model on the depth data with full parameters as a baseline for comparison.
- Ablation: Train the model with random weights instead of the pre-trained weights.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that this linear layer will learn to extract depth-relevant features from the pre-trained model, leading to a reasonable amount of depth estimation accuracy. However, we anticipate that the model may fail when dealing with complex or cluttered scenes, resulting in large errors.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: extracting depth from visual priors
PROPOSAL: Revise to use a smaller learning rate of 1e-5 and an additional batch normalization layer after the linear layer to improve the performance and stability of the network. Also, run the model on the NYU-Depth-V2 dataset, as it has a larger number of samples and varying depth ranges. We'll train the model for 20 epochs to see if the additional depth diversity helps the model generalizing and improving its depth prediction accuracy.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: Directly fine-tuning the model on the depth data with full parameters.
- Ablation: Remove the batch normalization layer to check its contribution to the model's performance.
- Experiment: Use the model to estimate depth values on both the image and surface normal generation tasks, to verify if the learned depth priors are robust across different generative tasks.
COST: 75 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: With the batch normalization and lower learning rate, we expect the model to learn more effectively and have better generalization performance on the NYU-Depth-V2 dataset, resulting in higher accuracy and lower errors compared to the previous experiment.

ACTION: REVISE
1. extracting depth from visual priors

Conditional image generative models have, in recent years, demonstrated extraordinary capabilities, producing highly realistic images from both textual descriptions and class labels, and they have rapidly evolved from experimental research tools into widely accessible applications. Because they hold considerable promise to produce virtually unlimited amounts of data, researchers have started exploring their use as a source of synthetic training data for downstream machine learning models. However, recent research has revealed that as these models grow in size and capability, they tend to produce images of higher quality, better aligned with human preference, but with diminished diversity, which hinders their utility as synthetic training data generators.

Two families of techniques have been introduced to mitigate the shortcomings of such vanilla synthetic data. Learning-based approaches aim to improve the overall utility of synthetic data by reducing the distribution shift between generated and real samples; they use real data to train or fine-tune parts of existing conditional generative models. Guidance-based sampling methods instead define reward functions that steer the generation process and characterize the utility of generated samples in terms of generation quality or diversity. Yet the implicit or explicit utility functions behind these methods often disregard the potential distribution shift between synthetic and real data, and many guidance methods treat quality, diversity or safety as ends in themselves rather than as means to increase the utility of a synthetic image corpus for training downstream models. Moreover, in-depth analyses of conditional image generative models have highlighted a tension between quality and diversity. This tension becomes more apparent when diversity is defined as the variation among generated samples without reference to any target distribution. Contextualizing the desired diversity through real exemplar data holds the promise of limiting potentially disadvantageous variations in synthetic data.

Using exemplar data at inference time to guide generation is reminiscent of few-shot in-context learning in large language models, where a small number of examples suffices to adapt to new tasks without fine-tuning, and where providing more examples tends to help. In conditional image generation, however, most few-shot approaches require partial model training or fine-tuning, and the use of exemplar data at inference time remains underexplored. One prior inference-time method, Contextualized Vendi Score Guidance (c-VSG), leverages a handful of contextualizing real images to ground the diversity of generations to that of the real data; but, contrary to in-context learning, increasing the number of exemplars did not improve its performance. Meanwhile, fine-tuning with reward feedback has proven successful for improving generation quality, but it has not been tested whether it would also increase diversity given a proper reward.

The problem is therefore how to exploit a small set of real exemplar images to characterize, and jointly improve, both the quality and the diversity of the images produced by off-the-shelf conditional generators with respect to a target real distribution, ideally without fine-tuning the generator. Can strong quality and diversity be achieved this way, and can the benefit grow gracefully as more exemplars become available, unlike existing exemplar-based guidance? How does such an approach compare with training-based ways of using the same few real images? And does improving quality and diversity grounded in real data actually translate into greater utility of the synthetic images as training data for downstream models?

Transporting mass between probability distributions is a ubiquitous problem in machine learning and beyond. Optimal transport (OT) provides a principled approach to such problems by seeking to minimise the total cost of transportation under a chosen cost function, and computational OT, from Sinkhorn's algorithm to more recent neural approaches, has been applied successfully in domains such as biology and extensively within machine learning. More recently, ideas from the flow-based approaches that have revolutionised generative modelling have been leveraged to solve the entropy-regularised dynamic OT problem known as the Schrödinger bridge (SB): finding the most likely evolution of a population between two prescribed distributions, relative to a reference stochastic process. With a Brownian reference process, the static form of this problem is exactly entropy-regularised OT for the quadratic cost. Flow-based SB solvers offer significant scalability advantages, enabling the approximation of OT maps between high-dimensional continuous datasets such as images. Early flow-based solvers were built on the classical Iterative Proportional Fitting (IPF) scheme, which preserves both marginals only at convergence, requires expensive caching of simulated trajectories and tends to 'forget' the reference measure; such methods have since been superseded by solvers based on the Iterative Markovian Fitting (IMF) scheme, which avoids these issues.

Beyond the standard two-marginal problem, multi-marginal OT seeks a joint coupling over several marginals that minimises a total cost. Tree-structured costs are often considered, as they frequently arise in applications while allowing improved scalability by exploiting the tree structure. In the corresponding tree-structured SB problem, stochastic processes run along the edges of a tree and marginals are prescribed only at a subset of the vertices; with Brownian motion along each edge as the reference, it is an entropy-regularised multi-marginal OT problem with a tree-structured quadratic cost. Star-shaped trees, with marginals fixed on the leaves and an unknown centre, are of particular significance because they correspond to an entropy-regularised form of the Wasserstein barycentre problem. The Wasserstein barycentre provides a natural notion of 'average' for probability distributions and is widely studied because of its importance in applications such as Bayesian learning, clustering and representation learning. Computing barycentres is notoriously challenging. Many successful approaches approximate the solution with a finite set of points, but such in-sample methods struggle to scale as dimensionality increases and cannot generate new samples; alternative methods provide continuous approximations through neural parameterisations, but often require multi-level or adversarial optimisation procedures. To date, the only neural ODE/SDE approach to barycentre computation extends the IPF-based diffusion Schrödinger bridge to the tree-structured SB setting, and therefore inherits the drawbacks of IPF; it has been reported to suffer training instability at low entropic regularisation, struggling to match the prescribed marginals at the vertices.

In parallel, one of the most successful approaches to Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation is the iterative fixed-point method, which repeatedly updates a candidate barycentre by solving for the OT map from it to each marginal and pushing it forward through the weighted average of these maps. It performs strongly and has been observed to converge in only a few iterations, but every iteration requires solving a complete OT problem to each marginal, which is expensive because solving even a single OT problem can be challenging.

This raises several questions. Can a scalable, flow-based solver be built for the tree-structured SB problem, and hence for entropic Wasserstein barycentres, that avoids the shortcomings of IPF-based schemes while being guaranteed to converge to the tree-structured SB solution? In the barycentre case, can the fast convergence of fixed-point schemes be retained without paying for a complete OT solve to every marginal at every iteration? And can flow-based barycentre solvers of this kind offer a viable alternative to existing algorithms for continuous Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation?

Recording dynamic scenes from multiple viewpoints has become increasingly common in everyday life. From concerts and sports events to lectures and birthday parties, people often capture the same moment using different handheld devices. These multi-view recordings present a rich opportunity to reconstruct scenes in 4D, enable bullet-time effects, or enhance the capabilities of existing vision models. However, these videos are typically captured independently, without synchronization or known camera poses, making it difficult to align and fuse them coherently.

The task is the following: given a set of asynchronous videos that capture the same dynamic scene from different viewpoints, estimate a time offset for each video, to be applied to its original out-of-sync clock, so that after correction frames sharing the same clock time correspond to the exact same moment across all videos.

Existing synchronization methods rely on controlled environments, manual annotations, specific patterns such as human pose, audio signals such as flashes or claps, or expensive hardware setups such as time-coded devices, none of which are available in casually captured videos. Human-centric approaches, which use body pose as the synchronization signal, are limited by the accuracy of pose estimation and by the number of people present, and they struggle in scenes without prominent human activity. Audio-based approaches only work in quiet environments and do not carry over to in-the-wild settings where audio is noisy or unavailable. Methods that jointly optimize camera poses and temporal offsets within a learned scene representation are often constrained to specific environments or object types. Geometry-based methods estimate temporal offsets from multi-view geometric constraints, but typically assume static scenes or a fixed viewpoint. Meanwhile, structure-from-motion and learned camera-pose estimators recover camera geometry accurately, yet they rely predominantly on static visual cues and therefore fall short of synchronizing dynamic scenes.

Building a practical and robust synchronization system that works on videos in the wild is challenging. Camera poses are unknown and cameras may move, so the geometric relationship between each pair of cameras must itself be estimated reliably. The moving objects that carry the timing information are not known in advance and are generally small and blurry. Associating points across cameras with significantly different viewpoints is difficult. The offsets to be recovered are continuous, while observations arrive only at discrete frame times. Finally, not all views overlap, so some pairs of cameras may share little spatial or temporal overlap.

This raises several questions. How can a set of casually captured, unposed and unsynchronized videos of the same dynamic scene be aligned in time with high precision, without specialized capture, audio, manual correction, or assumptions about the scene content such as the presence of people? Which visual evidence can reliably reveal the temporal offset between two cameras whose poses are unknown and possibly changing over time? And how can a single, globally consistent offset be recovered for every video when the evidence relating some pairs of views is weak, ambiguous or missing? Answering these questions would open the door to scalable, unconstrained multi-view 4D scene understanding and to downstream tasks, such as 4D reconstruction of dynamic scenes, that depend on synchronized input.
