Modern problem-solving increasingly relies on neural networks, which encode vast amounts of information in their trainable parameters during learning, with applications ranging from computer vision and natural language processing to the natural sciences. While these parameters capture rich knowledge, accessing and interpreting it remains a challenge.

Metanetworks were introduced to analyze and process other neural networks by treating their weights, gradients and sparsity patterns as structured inputs. Early work focused on evaluating the generalization of trained networks and revealing properties of their behavior, commonly by flattening the parameters or extracting statistics from them before feeding them into multi-layer perceptrons. Metanetworks have since been applied to extracting structure from implicit neural representations, learning optimizers, editing models, evaluating policies and enabling Bayesian inference. Designing them nevertheless remains challenging because of the complexity and high dimensionality of the structures they operate on.

A major difficulty is functional equivalence: many distinct parameter configurations realize the same input-output function. Swapping two hidden units of a multi-layer perceptron leaves its input-output mapping unchanged, provided their outgoing connections are permuted accordingly, and for networks with tanh activations the input-output mapping is known to determine the architecture and the weights up to permutations and sign flips. Such identifiability results have been extended to broader classes of multi-layer perceptrons and to convolutional networks, and recent work has characterized the symmetry groups of multihead attention and mixture-of-experts layers, establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for functional equivalence. The parameter space is thus only a proxy for the underlying function class, and the map from parameters to functions is not injective. A metanetwork that relies solely on raw parameters therefore risks overlooking the symmetries of the architecture it processes, and may produce incompatible outputs for two networks that compute exactly the same function.

Building on the permutation symmetry of hidden neurons, permutation-equivariant metanetworks have been developed that account for neuron reordering within hidden layers, and more recent architectures extend beyond permutations by incorporating additional symmetries such as scaling and sign changes. Equivariance (for metanetworks that output weights) or invariance (for metanetworks that output predictions) with respect to a symmetry group of the processed architecture guarantees that different parameterizations of the same function are treated consistently. However, these approaches enforce strict equivariance at the level of individual weights, which imposes rigid constraints on the layers and often leads to sparse, less expressive models. Yet the true goal is not to preserve the weights themselves but the functions they implement, that is, to respect the functional equivalence classes of the parameters. Strict equivariance is a sufficient way to achieve this, but it is not clear that it is necessary.

Relaxed or approximate equivariance has emerged elsewhere in deep learning to handle imperfect symmetries in real-world data, for instance through relaxed convolution weights, soft constraints added to the training objective or relaxed group convolutions, and its bias-variance trade-offs have been analyzed theoretically. These relaxations were, however, developed for symmetries that only approximately hold, and often treat equivariance as something to be approximated. In weight space, by contrast, the symmetries are exact and are precisely what defines functional equivalence, so it is unclear how weight-level equivariance could be loosened without breaking the guarantee that functionally equivalent inputs are processed consistently.

This raises several questions. Is strict equivariance necessary for metanetworks? What is the right requirement for a map acting on weights to preserve functional identity, so that functionally equivalent inputs always yield functionally equivalent outputs, and can a requirement weaker than strict equivariance meet it? Can metanetwork layers satisfying such a requirement be built in a principled, practical and trainable way for the architectures whose weights metanetworks commonly process, such as feedforward, convolutional and multihead attention networks? And would moving beyond strict equivariance in this way give metanetworks a better trade-off between symmetry preservation and representational expressivity in practice?

Facial rigging aims to make a static neutral facial mesh animatable by defining a set of controllable deformations, typically represented either as blendshape rigs driven by activated action units in systems based on the Facial Action Coding System (FACS), or as skeletal rigs driven by joint positions. Whereas full-body auto-rigging usually follows a two-step pipeline of skeleton construction and skinning, facial rigs are often anatomically inspired and implemented with FACS blendshapes. In a linear FACS blendshape rig, each blendshape is a vertex offset from the neutral mesh corresponding to one action unit, i.e. a specific muscle movement such as "Right Eye Close", and a complex expression is obtained by adding the weighted offsets of the activated blendshapes to the neutral mesh. Rigging is an essential step for creative AI, bringing digital avatars to life by enabling expressive and realistic facial movements across a wide range of applications. However, creating a facial rig is laborious and expensive, often requiring skilled artists tens of hours to complete a single asset. Methods that transfer expressions from 2D images or videos to 3D avatars do not remove this bottleneck, since they assume that the avatar already has a rig.

Existing facial auto-rigging methods typically transfer a complete set of blendshapes from a predefined template mesh to a neutral target mesh, which often requires dense correspondences or a mesh topology shared by the template and the target. More recent approaches build transferable latent spaces between faces or use triangulation-agnostic networks to bypass these limitations, but they still require a template blendshape rig, which can compromise accuracy when the template and target shapes differ substantially. Only one prior approach, NFR, can directly rig facial meshes from explicitly controllable FACS parameters without relying on a template, and it has so far been demonstrated primarily on humanoid heads. Furthermore, existing approaches, NFR included, have yet to accommodate meshes with multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs or teeth, which limits their ability to animate highly expressive avatars: an "eye look-down" pose, for example, is difficult to reproduce if the mesh lacks eyeballs.

Learning such a rigging model also raises a data problem. Accurate 3D supervision requires neutral meshes paired with complete rigs made by artists, and because manual rigging is so costly such rigged examples are scarce; a model trained solely on them is likely to generalize poorly to the wide variety of facial shapes, styles and topologies met in practice.

The problem is therefore to automatically turn a single static neutral facial mesh into an expressive rig controllable by FACS parameters (i) without relying on predefined template blendshapes, so that target meshes need not closely resemble a template; (ii) for in-the-wild meshes with varying topologies and shapes, including both humanoid and non-humanoid heads; and (iii) for meshes made of multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs and teeth, which must move coherently with the rest of the face. How can such a rigging system be built, and how can it be trained to generalize across this diversity when only a limited number of rigged meshes is available as 3D ground truth?

Human-object interaction (HOI) detection aims to localize humans and objects in an image and to recognize the interactions between them. It provides a fine-grained understanding of human activities, which is crucial for downstream applications such as robotic manipulation, image captioning and autonomous driving. Despite recent progress, HOI detection remains challenging because of the large combinatorial space of human-object pairs and the need for fine-grained visual understanding. Moreover, real-world applications often require recognizing human-object interactions that do not appear in the training set, which leads to the task of zero-shot HOI detection. Conventional HOI detectors fail to generalize to such unseen interactions, and early attempts that disentangle object and verb features for compositional generalization cannot handle unseen objects or unseen verbs.

To address zero-shot HOI detection, recent works exploit vision-language models such as CLIP to transfer semantic knowledge from language to HOI detection. Typically, they use text embeddings of interaction descriptions, e.g., "A person is holding a cup", to construct classifiers for unseen interactions. While effective to some extent, these methods face limitations. First, CLIP features lack the fine-grained representational capacity required to distinguish visually similar interactions, so methods have to incorporate detector features to obtain fine-grained representations of instances. Second, their core mechanism, aligning visual and text features, operates only on categories observed during training, which restricts generalization to unseen interactions.

At the same time, progress in open-vocabulary object detection provides a sufficient solution for localizing unseen objects, so interaction recognition has become the main bottleneck. Yet most existing methods, including two-stage methods, couple interaction recognition with a specific object detector: they rely on detector features or on relations between detected objects to give vision-language features fine-grained representational capacity, and they struggle to balance fine-grained detector features with generalized vision-language features. As a result, interaction recognition and detection cannot be improved independently, and the detector cannot be changed without retraining.

Effective interaction recognition therefore requires representations that are both fine-grained and broadly generalizable. This raises the following questions. How can the interactions of a given human-object pair, including interactions never observed during training, be recognized with such representations rather than through alignment with static text embeddings fitted to the seen categories, given that recognition is multi-label because one pair can be engaged in several interactions at once? Can interaction recognition be made independent of any particular object detector, so that it works with the boxes produced by any detector without retraining, stays reliable when those boxes are imperfect, and remains computationally tractable given the many human-object pairs and candidate interactions in an image?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: composable hoi detection with adapter modules
PROPOSAL: Design a two-stage HOI detection framework where the first stage uses an object detection backbone to generate region proposals for humans and objects, and the second stage uses an adapter-based mechanism to adapt the features of the region proposals to accommodate interactions. Specifically, we use a set of learnable adapter modules to adjust the feature embeddings of the objects and humans to better capture the characteristics of their interactions. We will use the Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) dataset and string manipulation or patient data to get ground truth labels of human-object interactions. The evaluation metric will be standard mean Average Precision (mAP) with precision and recall at each interact type. Controls include a standard object detection backbone with no interaction adaptation, a single-stage HOI detector as a baseline, and an ablation study of the adapter modules. We will compare our method to previous HOI detection methods, such as Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) for HOI detection and action-tubelets. COST: 100 GPU hours. PREDICTION: Expected result: mAP 3-5% improvement over baseline methods; could fail due to potential overfitting to adaptation modules.

CONTROLS: baseline object detector, baseline HOI detector, ablation study of adapter modules, previous HOI detection methods like GCNs, action-tubelets.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: seps (structured encoder for pair separation)
PROPOSAL: Design a structured encoder for pair separation (SEPS) module to enhance the interaction representation by considering both spatial and semantic relations between humans and objects. SEPS takes the region proposals from the object detection backbone as input and outputs a structured feature representation of the human-object pair. We will use SEPS as a plug-and-play module in the first-stage object detection and second-stage HOI detection to refine the interaction representation. PROPOSAL: REVISED VERSION - In addition to the adapter modules, we will also incorporate a semantic attention mechanism to selectively weigh the importance of different object features based on their relevance to the human-object interaction. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: pairing pre-training for vision and language
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel pre-training strategy, Pairing Pre-training for Vision and Language (PPVL), to improve the representation power of HOI detectors by leveraging the relationship between vision and language. PPVL pre-trains the visual and language encoders jointly on a large-scale image-text dataset, where the image-text pairs are curated to have a specific interaction context. This pre-training stage allows the visual and language encoders to learn a common semantic space, enhancing their ability to capture rich interaction features. We will fine-tune the pre-trained detector on various HOI benchmarks and evaluate its performance using standard metrics, such as mAP and precision at each interact type. Controls will include a standard object detector trained from scratch, a baseline HOI detector without PPVL pre-training, and an ablation study of PPVL pre-training.

CONTROLS: baseline object detector, baseline HOI detector, ablation study of PPVL pre-training
COST: 60 GPU hours
PREDICTION: Expected result: mAP 2-4% improvement over baseline HOI detectors; could fail if the pre-trained knowledge does not generalize well to HOI tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: attentional localization maps for hoi
PROPOSAL: Develop an Attentional Localization Maps (ALM) for HOI detection to improve the spatial localization of interactions. ALM generates attention maps for each interaction class, focusing on the specific regions of the objects and humans that are relevant for the interaction. This is achieved through an attention mechanism that attends to the feature maps of the objects and humans based on the class labels. We will integrate ALM with our composable HOI detection framework and evaluate its performance on various HOI benchmarks. Controls will include a standard object detector without ALM, a baseline HOI detector with ALM, and an ablation study of ALM.

CONTROLS: baseline object detector, baseline HOI detector with ALM, ablation study of ALM
COST: 80 GPU hours
PREDICTION: Expected result: improvement in mAP and precision at each interact type due to better spatial localization; could fail if ALM overfits to specific interactions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: multiple instance learning for interaction detection
PROPOSAL: Design a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) framework for HOI detection to effectively handle the multiple-interaction cases where a single image contains multiple unpicked-interaction between different humans and objects. MIL will treat each image as a bag of instances (human-object pairs) and the detector will learn to recognize the interactions within each bag. This will be achieved through a Max-Margin Learning formulation and an attention mechanism to selectively weigh the importance of each instance. We will evaluate the MIL framework on various HOI benchmarks and compare its performance with standard HOI detectors.

CONTROLS: baseline object detector, baseline HOI detector, ablation study of MIL and attention mechanism
COST: 90 GPU hours
PREDICTION: Expected result: improvement in mAP and precision at each interact type due to better handling of multiple-interaction cases; could fail if the MIL framework overfits to specific interactions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: generalized object connectivity graph for hoi
PROPOSAL: Propose a Generalized Object Connectivity Graph (GOCG) framework for HOI detection to model the complex relationships between humans and objects in a scene. GOCG will consist of edge attributes and multi-layer graph reasoning to capture various aspects of human-object interactions. We will use a multi-layer graph neural network to reason over the GOCG and improve HOI detection performance. We will evaluate GOCG on various HOI benchmarks and compare its performance with state-of-the-art HOI detectors.

CONTROLS: baseline object detector, baseline HOI detector, ablation study of GOCG and graph reasoning
COST: 110 GPU hours
PREDICTION: Expected result: improvement in mAP and precision at each interact type due to better modeling of human-object relationships; could fail if the GOCG framework overfits to specific interactions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: uncertainty-aware hoi detection
PROPOSAL: Develop an Uncertainty-Aware HOI Detection framework to quantify and utilize the uncertainty in HOI predictions. We will incorporate a probabilistic representation of the HOI predictions and use a Monte Carlo dropout technique to estimate the uncertainty of each prediction. This will allow us to perform uncertainty-aware inference and adapt to the ambiguity in human-object interactions. We will evaluate the Uncertainty-Aware HOI Detection framework on various HOI benchmarks and compare its performance with state-of-the-art HOI detectors.

CONTROLS: baseline object detector, baseline HOI detector, ablation study of uncertainty-aware inference
COST: 100 GPU hours
PREDICTION: Expected result: improvement in mAP and precision at each interact type due to better handling of ambiguity in human-object interactions; could fail if the uncertainty-aware inference technique overfits to specific interactions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: temporal relationship modeling for hoi detection
PROPOSAL: Propose a Temporal Relationship Modeling (TRM) framework for HOI detection to capture the temporal dynamics of human-object interactions. TRM will utilize a graph neural network to model the temporal relationships between humans and objects and predict the next interaction state. We will integrate TRM with our existing composable HOI detection framework and evaluate its performance on video-based HOI benchmarks.

CONTROLS: baseline object detector, baseline HOI detector, ablation study of TRM and graph neural network
COST: 120 GPU hours
PREDICTION: Expected result: improvement in mAP and precision at each interact type due to better modeling of temporal relationships; could fail if the TRM framework overfits to specific interaction sequences. 

Note: this is the last experiment proposal before submission. A theoretical or inference-in-experiments conclusion could follow.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 7
TITLE: temporal relationship modeling for hoi detection
PROPOSAL: REVISED VERSION - In addition to the graph neural network, we will integrate a temporal convolutional network (TCN) to modeled the temporal evolution of human-object interactions. This will enable us to capture both local and global temporal dependencies in the interaction sequence. We will evaluate our revised TRM framework on video-based HOI benchmarks and compare its performance with state-of-the-art HOI detectors.

CONTROLS: baseline object detector, baseline HOI detector, ablation study of TRM and graph neural network, ablation study of TCN
COST: 140 GPU hours
PREDICTION: Expected result: state-of-the-art performance in mAP and precision at each interact type due to better modeling of temporal relationships; could fail if the revised TRM framework overfits to specific interaction sequences.

Understanding how a scene has changed and forecasting how it will look next from Satellite Image Time Series (SITS) is fundamental to many critical applications, yet it poses a profound challenge: predicting the future requires a deep understanding of past change. Two tasks are central. In temporal change description, given a sequence of temporally ordered satellite images of the same area, the goal is to generate a natural-language description that accurately summarizes the key dynamic changes that occurred over the observation period, such as urban expansion or agricultural cycles; this requires comprehending the temporal evolution and, ideally, the underlying causal narrative of the changes. In future satellite image forecasting, given the same historical sequence, the goal is to generate a plausible image for the next time point. A critical and often overlooked requirement is that the forecast be temporally consistent: the generated changes should be a logical continuation of the trends and dynamics observed in the historical data, not merely a plausible standalone picture.

Although foundation models such as Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and diffusion-based image generators have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their application to this domain remains fragmented and fundamentally limited. On the understanding side, static image captioning ignores temporal context, while existing temporal change description methods lack the semantic depth of MLLMs: they fuse information across images through simple interactions, their long-range temporal reasoning is limited, and they struggle to capture why changes occur. General-purpose MLLMs, even video-capable ones, are not optimized for this setting either: video-centric models are typically tuned for densely sampled frames with fixed, short intervals, whereas consecutive satellite acquisitions are sparse and irregular, with gaps that can span several years. On the generation side, single-image synthesis cannot model evolution, and temporal forecasting approaches struggle with long-term consistency because they do not grasp the semantic drivers of change: their conditioning is typically low-level (e.g., edge maps), based on simple metadata, or limited to text guidance, and it lacks fine-grained temporal semantic interaction, so they can generate what a scene looks like but cannot reason about why it should look that way given its history. As a result, change understanding and future forecasting have been treated as disjointed tasks, even though both are limited by a common bottleneck: modeling long-range temporal dynamics.

This raises several questions. How can a model reason about why changes occurred across a long, irregularly sampled sequence of satellite images, and describe them accurately? How can such an understanding of past change be used to generate what will happen next, so that the forecast is a temporally consistent continuation of the observed trajectory rather than only a realistic-looking image? Can enhancing long-range temporal understanding improve performance on both tasks simultaneously, with the understanding of past change directly informing the forecast? Finally, how can the temporal consistency of a forecast be rigorously evaluated, given that standard image-quality metrics cannot penalize a prediction that is perceptually realistic but inconsistent with historical trends?

Proteins realize their biological functions through intricate three-dimensional conformations, and predicting such structures has long been a central challenge in computational biology. AlphaFold2 marked a breakthrough by combining multiple sequence alignments with geometric constraints in an end-to-end framework, achieving near-experimental accuracy. Building on this foundation, AlphaFold3 reformulates the architecture into an all-atom framework and introduces a diffusion-based structure module, thereby enabling the generative modeling of not only proteins but also a wide spectrum of biomolecular complexes. Consequently, this series of models is widely adopted as a family of foundation models for downstream applications such as virtual screening and protein design. However, AlphaFold3's architecture, which relies on iterative Pairformer recycling and multi-step diffusion, requires substantially greater computational overhead than AlphaFold2, restricting its accessibility in downstream workflows.

More specifically, on long sequences the execution time of AlphaFold3 is measured in minutes, which severely limits its usability in downstream tasks that demand high throughput. For instance, small-scale laboratory screening often requires predictions for thousands of candidates, and when extended to large public databases this number grows to an infeasible scale; protein design tasks typically involve comparable computational demand. Previous work has attempted to mitigate this by manually reducing the number of recycling iterations on simpler structures, thus trading accuracy for efficiency. However, such compromises inevitably degrade predictive performance. Moreover, in hallucination-based design approaches, the multistep iterative refinement process hinders feasible gradient backpropagation, ultimately preventing the broader community from adopting AlphaFold3 as a foundation model for diverse applications.

To accelerate the diffusion process, recent advances in generative modeling have explored high-order solvers and consistency models. While high-order solvers improve efficiency, they rarely reduce the number of sampling steps below ten. Consistency models, on the other hand, have achieved remarkable success in image generation and have benefited from refined training schedules. However, transferring them to an AlphaFold3-style architecture raises two difficulties. First, standard consistency schedules assume fixed-dimensional data and pair timesteps at a constant Euclidean interval, which does not accommodate variable protein sequence lengths: on long sequences even a small step can trigger a drastic distribution shift that demands an unrealistic predictive leap, while on short sequences the same interval provides only a weak learning signal, so training dynamics can become unstable or collapse. Second, the iterative diffusion sampler is not the only source of iteration: the architecture also refines its internal pair and single representations through repeated recycling of the Pairformer trunk, whose cost grows with sequence length and which conventional diffusion-acceleration methods do not address at all.

The open problem is therefore whether an AlphaFold3-class all-atom biomolecular structure generator can be compressed into a predictor that runs in essentially a single forward pass -- removing both the multi-step denoising and the recycling overhead -- while retaining the accuracy of the full iterative model on protein, protein-ligand and nucleic-acid complexes. This matters because accuracy alone is not what blocks adoption: throughput and differentiability do. A useful accelerated model must remain reliable in the tail, not merely on average, since high-throughput screening and design pipelines discard most candidates and are harmed more by occasional implausible structures than by small average losses; it must stay cheap enough to be called thousands of times; and it must be light enough that gradients can be propagated through it, so that design methods which optimize sequences against a folding model become feasible with an all-atom model rather than only with earlier, cheaper architectures. Given this problem, how should one design experiments to establish whether such an acceleration is achievable without a loss of predictive fidelity?

Diffusion models have demonstrated a remarkable ability to learn data distributions across many modalities, with strong results in both data generation and image restoration. In medical imaging, they are effective at modeling the distribution of 2D image slices, and by combining these powerful learned priors with conventional optimization frameworks, diffusion-based solvers have reached state-of-the-art performance on medical inverse problems such as accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and undersampled X-ray computed tomography (CT). Such problems are often severely ill-posed: far fewer measurements are acquired than there are unknowns, so the measurements alone cannot determine the image, and the learned prior must fill in what they leave ambiguous. Diffusion-based solvers do so through an iterative reverse sampling process that, at each step, predicts a clean image from the current noisy state, corrects this estimate for consistency with the measurements, and re-noises it to the next timestep, which repeatedly injects random noise.

In clinical practice, however, medical data are fundamentally large 3D volumes. Individual 2D slices matter for review, but a complete and accurate volumetric reconstruction is often essential for downstream tasks such as precise tumor volume assessment, surgical planning, and tracking disease progression over time. Translating the success of 2D diffusion-based solvers to 3D is difficult: because of the curse of dimensionality, the memory, computational, and data requirements of training a diffusion prior directly on volumetric data are prohibitive for most academic and even industrial labs. A common and practical workaround is to train a diffusion model on 2D slices and apply this 2D prior slice by slice to reconstruct the volume.

This workaround eases the training burden but creates a critical new problem: the reconstructed volumes lack consistency along the third dimension (the z-axis). Because each slice is processed independently during the reverse diffusion process, the intrinsic randomness of the sampling procedure leads to severe inter-slice discontinuities and artifacts, degrading the diagnostic and analytical quality of the stacked volume. Existing remedies have important drawbacks. The most direct one augments the 2D prior with a hand-crafted regularizer such as total variation, applied in an additional optimization step to enforce smoothness between adjacent slices. This is effective, but it introduces sensitive hyperparameters that require careful tuning, can over-smooth the volume or produce cartoon-like textures that erase fine diagnostic details, and acts as an external correction that masks the symptoms rather than addressing the intrinsic cause. More principled approaches try to learn a more complete 3D prior, for instance by training on 3D patches or by combining priors from two perpendicular 2D planes, but they increase the complexity of the training or inference pipeline and may impose constraints on the data, such as requiring cubic volumes.

A similar discontinuity arises in video restoration, where applying a pre-trained 2D image diffusion model to video inverse problems often produces temporal flickering across frames. Prior work attributed this flickering to the uncoordinated stochasticity inherent in diffusion sampling and alleviated it by synchronizing the stochastic noise components across frames. Whether the same mechanism is the fundamental cause of inter-slice inconsistency in 3D medical reconstruction, and how such a remedy would transfer from video to volumetric medical data, remains open.

This raises the following questions. How does the stochasticity of independent slice-wise sampling give rise to inter-slice inconsistency when 2D diffusion priors are used for 3D medical reconstruction? Is it possible to enhance inter-slice consistency directly within the diffusion sampling process itself, obviating the need for external, artifact-inducing optimization, ideally without new loss terms, additional sensitive hyperparameters, model retraining, or extra computational cost, so that the remedy could be dropped into existing 2D diffusion-based 3D reconstruction pipelines? And can inter-slice consistency be improved while preserving the natural anatomical variation between slices and fine diagnostic details, rather than trading them away for smoothness?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: slice synchronization via shared noise projection
PROPOSAL: We will apply a 2D diffusion-based solver to 3D volumetric MRI data, but instead of processing each slice independently, we will sample each slice from a shared noise distribution that is projected onto the current state of the solver, thus ensuring consistency between the slices. We will test two variants: one where the shared noise is static across all slices, and one where it is dynamic and updated at each step.
CONTROLS: We compare our proposed slice synchronization method to (1) a naive baseline where each slice is processed independently, and (2) an augmented baseline where a total variation regularizer is applied to enforce smoothness between adjacent slices.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The slice synchronization method should improve upon the naive baseline in terms of inter-slice consistency, with the dynamic noise variant performing better than the static one. However, it may also trade off some of the fine diagnostic details due to the constraint imposed by the shared noise distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: analyzing stochastic consistency using advanced diffusion diagnostics
PROPOSAL: We will embed advanced diffusion diagnostics into the 2D diffusion-based solver to directly measure the temporal consistency of the sampling process, quantifying the correlation between adjacent slices and identifying potential sources of inter-slice discrepancies. By comparing these diagnostics across different variants of the solver, including and without the slice synchronization method proposed in our previous experiment, we will analyze the mechanism behind inter-slice inconsistency and provide a deeper understanding of its origin.
CONTROLS: The baseline for our diagnostics will be the existing implementation of the 2D diffusion-based solver without any additional modifications.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The advanced diffusion diagnostics are expected to uncover the inherent stochasticity and its effects on slice consistency, supporting evidence for the potential benefits of our proposed slice synchronization method. However, inconsistent results might challenge our current assumptions and necessitate a reevaluation of the underlying problem.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating 3d patch-based diffusion priors in a 2d+1 framework
PROPOSAL: We will adapt the 2D diffusion-based solver to operate within a 2D+1 framework, where each 2D slice is augmented with a per-pixel description of the slice's spatial relationship to adjacent slices in the 3D volume. This framework will be used to train a set of 2D diffusion priors, each conditioned on 3D patches of volume data. During inference, the 2D diffusion model will use the spatial relationship descriptions to predict a clean image slice that is consistent with adjacent slices.
CONTROLS: We compare our 2D+1 framework with the naive baseline of applying a unconditioned 2D diffusion model to each slice independently, and with a 3D diffusion-based solver that has been trained directly on volume data.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method is expected to improve upon the naive baseline by leveraging the spatial relationships between slices, but may inherently require large amounts of memory and computational resources due to the need to compute and store the per-pixel spatial relationships. If we're lucky, it might challenge the effectiveness of our proposed slice synchronization method.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: analyzing stochastic consistency using advanced diffusion diagnostics
PROPOSAL: We will extend our experimental setup in this proposal to also include 3D diffusion-based solvers with and without slice-wise stochastic synchronization, and compare the consistency metrics across these setups. Furthermore, we will use the advanced diffusion diagnostics to analyze the origin and propagation of inter-slice discrepancies in both 2D and 3D diffusion-based solvers, providing further insights into the mechanism behind inter-slice inconsistency.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By combining our previous experiments, we will gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between stochastic consistency and inter-slice inconsistency in diffusion-based solvers, and validate our observations on a more comprehensive set of solvers, ultimately strengthening our proposal for slice synchronization.

TITLE: adaptive temporal filtering for stabilized diffusion reconstruction
PROPOSAL: We will explore the integration of adaptive temporal filtering techniques into the diffusion-based reconstruction framework to stabilize and smooth out the variations caused by stochastic sampling, aiming to reduce inter-slice inconsistency. This approach will involve incorporating a learnable filter capable of adaptively attenuating or amplifying temporal frequencies in the diffused signal, based on image characteristics such as multi-scale texture and gradient fields.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our adaptive filtering technique against (1) the naive baseline of independent slice processing and (2) our previously proposed slice synchronization method via shared noise projection.

TITLE: empirical analysis of synchronization mechanisms in diffusion-based reconstruction
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a comprehensive empirical analysis to investigate the impact of different synchronization mechanisms on diffusion-based reconstruction, comparing various methods such as shared noise projection, phase-locking, and adaptive feedback loops. We will examine how each mechanism affects inter-slice consistency, noise propagation, and overall image quality, aiming to identify the most suitable synchronization strategy for volumetric reconstruction tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our empirical analysis against a diverse set of 2D and 3D diffusion-based solvers, both with and without synchronization.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our empirical analysis is expected to provide valuable insights into the strengths and limitations of different synchronization mechanisms, helping to refine and optimize our previously proposed methods for diffusion-based volumetric reconstruction.

By combining our previous experiments, we will gain a deeper understanding of how different components of the diffusion-based reconstruction pipeline affect stochastic consistency and ultimately inform the design of more robust volumetric reconstruction frameworks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: transfer learning from video restoration to volumetric medical reconstruction
PROPOSAL: We will leverage the lessons learned from video restoration tasks, where similar synchronization challenges have been addressed, and apply transfer learning techniques to adapt pre-trained diffusion models for video restoration to the volumetric medical reconstruction domain. By leveraging the pre-trained knowledge of video diffusion models, we aim to expedite the development of effective synchronization strategies for volumetric reconstruction.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our transfer learning approach against the naive baseline of independent slice processing, our previously proposed slice synchronization method via shared noise projection, and the most effective synchronization mechanism identified through the empirical analysis (proposal 5).
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By borrowing knowledge from video restoration tasks, we anticipate significant advances in the development of effective synchronization strategies for volumetric medical reconstruction, potentially leading to faster convergence and improved quality of reconstructed images.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: 3d volume evaluation metrics and validation in sparse-view ct reconstruction
PROPOSAL: We will extend the evaluation of our previously proposed methods (proposals 1-5) to a comprehensive assessment of 3D volume quality metrics, including volumetric thick-measure similarity (TMS), volumetric mean absolute error (VMAE), and 3D similarity index (3DSI), across multiple sparse-view CT reconstruction tasks. Our aim is to validate the effectiveness of our proposed synchronization strategies in achieving superior 3D volumetric reconstruction quality on clinically relevant datasets.
COST: 280 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By introducing comprehensive 3D volume evaluation metrics, we expect to quantify the significant advantages of our proposed synchronization strategies for volumetric medical reconstruction tasks, particularly in sparse-view CT reconstruction.

Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) generate discrete data by iteratively replacing masked tokens with predicted unmasked ones, learning to reverse an absorbing-state diffusion process that progressively masks the tokens of a sequence. They have recently achieved strong results across diverse domains, including text generation, image synthesis, and multi-modal understanding and generation. For images, a pre-trained tokenizer (e.g., a VQ-VAE) maps an image to a sequence of discrete tokens and its decoder reconstructs the image from those tokens; generation starts from a fully masked sequence and fills it in over many steps, which makes inference time- and compute-intensive. Building on this success, recent work has shown that these multi-step procedures can be distilled into one-step generators, substantially accelerating inference and reducing computational cost while maintaining competitive quality. For instance, Di[M]O distills a multi-step MDM into a one-step generator through on-policy distribution matching: a one-step prediction sampled from the student is corrupted by the forward masking process, and the teacher's and the student's output distributions conditioned on this intermediate state are matched, with the resulting gradient applied directly to the student's logits so that it never has to pass through the non-differentiable sampling operation.

Despite their remarkable performance, current one-step discrete generators face two fundamental limitations. First, they inherit both modeling and alignment errors from the teacher: existing distillation approaches implicitly assume that the teacher fully captures the target distribution, so imperfections in the teacher's generative modeling and the under-alignment of the pre-trained teacher with downstream preferences are both transmitted to the student during data-free distillation. Second, their discrete token outputs block gradient flow. This prevents the application of key refinement techniques that are widely used to improve one-step generators distilled from continuous diffusion models, such as adversarial (GAN) training, differentiable reward fine-tuning, and test-time optimization of the generator's input with respect to a reward. In text-to-image generation, for example, prompt-following and aesthetic quality are the two primary criteria, and the community increasingly relies on learned reward models and human-preference signals to optimize them directly; but because such rewards operate on decoded images, their gradients cannot pass through the tokenizer decoder and the sampled tokens back to a discrete generator. As a result, current distilled MDM generators have limited flexibility to leverage external knowledge, such as real data, or to incorporate user preferences to better align with downstream objectives.

The gradient-blocking problem is common across discrete modeling tasks. Adversarial training on discrete data, for instance, is challenging because the discriminator must compare generated samples with ground truth while the sampling process is non-differentiable. Prior remedies include policy-gradient estimators such as REINFORCE, which are unbiased but whose gradient variance becomes prohibitive when hundreds or thousands of tokens are generated at once, and differentiable relaxations of discrete tokens such as Gumbel-Softmax (often used with a straight-through estimator) and soft-argmax. However, these methods often introduce biased or high-variance gradients and numerical instabilities, and they have not been systematically applied to one-step discrete generators, in particular for fast visual generation. Moreover, the downstream objectives of interest, such as discriminators and reward models, act on continuous inputs such as the images produced by the tokenizer decoder, so a practical solution must let gradients flow through the existing generation pipeline.

This raises two questions. How can the outputs of a one-step generator distilled from an MDM be made amenable to end-to-end gradient-based training, with gradients that are stable, low-variance and faithful to the true discrete objective, while remaining compatible with the existing teacher and tokenizer? And, once such gradients are available, can post-distillation refinements (adversarial training, differentiable reward fine-tuning, and test-time optimization of the generator's input) let a one-step student correct the errors it inherits from its teacher and better align with downstream objectives such as distribution fidelity, prompt adherence and aesthetic quality?

PROPOSAL: Investigate using a relaxed version of the Gumbel-Softmax estimator to allow gradients to flow through the one-step generator, with a focus on stable and low-variance gradients. Train the student and teacher together to minimize the difference between the predicted output and the true teacher output, using annealed temperature scheduling to improve the quality of the generated samples.
CONTROLS: Compare with a straight-through estimator and an oracle policy that always outputs the true teacher output, on a variety of downstream objectives (e.g. evaluating both on text coherence and image quality in a text-to-image setting).

PREDICTION: This approach should alleviate the gradient-blocking problem to some extent, but may sacrifice some of the competitive quality achieved by the one-step generator (i.e. one might see a slight degradation in generated samples). ACTION: ADD
TITLE: differentiable reward fine-tuning with target-image gradients
PROPOSAL: Modify the existing Di[M]O distillation to incorporate differentiable fine-tuning with learned rewards. The teacher will generate an image \hat{I} and assess its quality using a post-distillation discriminator or a reward function; simultaneously, an auxilliary network will generate a target image I_target that approximates the downstream objective, e.g., maximizing some aesthetic-score. The gradients of the objective with respect to I_target should be aligned with the ones from the reward network.

TITLE: masking mechanism refinement by conditional discriminator
PROPOSAL: Introduce a conditional discriminator that takes the teacher's output and the masked input as input to correct the masking mechanism during one-step generation. Inverse problems arise in many domains, including computer vision, protein science, medical imaging and scientific computing. The goal is to reconstruct an unknown signal x ∈ R^n from noisy measurements y ∈ R^m, with y = A(x) + η, where A is a known forward operator and η is additive measurement noise. Diffusion models have recently shown powerful capabilities in modeling complex data distributions, and they provide a powerful class of priors for high-dimensional data, such as natural images, when solving inverse problems.

Methods for solving inverse problems fall broadly into two families. Maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference seeks the single most probable x: it delivers fast optimization, but struggles with high noise and multimodal posteriors and easily converges to local minima. The Bayesian alternative samples from the posterior p(x|y) ∝ p(x) p(y|x) to generate plausible reconstructions, quantify uncertainty and handle multimodality. Both critically depend on a powerful prior, such as a pretrained diffusion model, that encodes the complex statistical structure of the data.

Although diffusion-based solvers have shown remarkable success across diverse inverse problems, current methods suffer from three complementary limitations. (1) Iterative guidance methods, such as DPS, DDRM, DDNM, ΠGDM and TMPD, try to sample the intermediate posteriors p(x_t|y) along the reverse diffusion, which requires the intractable likelihood p(y|x_t) at every intermediate timestep. They approximate it, for example through Tweedie's formula, and apply likelihood-gradient corrections directly to the intermediate states. Because such gradients generally contain components orthogonal to the data manifold, these corrections systematically push the intermediate states off the learned manifold and violate the training-time noise conditioning of the denoiser, leading to failed reconstructions such as accumulated artifacts; even second-order corrections of the guidance trajectory still modify intermediate states and risk drifting off the manifold. (2) Stochastic MAP methods that optimize in image space, such as ReSample, DiffPIR, DAPS, SITCOM and DIIP, can match the measurements well with very sharp details, but they require carefully tuned hyperparameters to avoid overfitting to noise, which limits their effectiveness when the noise is high or unknown. Some of them are formulated as posterior samplers yet use a heuristic measurement-noise level much smaller than the true one to strengthen measurement consistency, which makes them effectively MAP-like and equally sensitive to noise. (3) Deterministic MAP methods that optimize over the diffusion model's input noise, such as DMPlug, remove randomness but are sensitive to measurement noise and, lacking posterior exploration, often get stuck in a single mode, especially in severely ill-posed problems such as phase retrieval. Early stopping can limit noise overfitting, but its criterion is task- and noise-dependent, and at high noise levels the optimizer often becomes trapped in a local mode anyway. In short, enforcing data consistency in the middle of the diffusion process can break adherence to the prior, while optimizing only for fidelity leads to overfitting or mode collapse.

These failure modes point to two requirements. A solver should maintain manifold feasibility: the states it feeds to the pretrained denoiser should remain close to the high-probability manifold of the corresponding noise level, so that the final reconstruction lies on the learned data manifold. At the same time, it should explore the posterior well enough to escape spurious local modes, rather than collapsing onto the mode nearest to its initialization.

A further practical difficulty is that the level, and even the type, of measurement noise is often unknown and may not be Gaussian, which makes the likelihood term itself intractable. Existing methods handle this with tunable hyperparameters that control the strength of the likelihood term, or with task-specific early-stopping criteria, typically tuned for one particular type and level of noise; they must therefore be re-tuned for each task, dataset and noise level, which is impractical when the noise is unknown.

This raises the following questions. How can a pretrained diffusion prior be used to sample from the posterior of an inverse problem without approximating intractable intermediate likelihoods and without ever feeding off-manifold states to the denoiser? How can such a sampler explore the solution space well enough to avoid spurious local modes in severely ill-posed, multimodal problems, so that its reconstructions do not depend on the initialization? Can it be robust to measurement noise, in the sense that its reconstructions do not overfit the noise, without hand-tuned regularization weights or early stopping? And can it handle measurement noise of unknown level and type with a single fixed set of hyperparameters across tasks, datasets and noise levels, at a computational cost that remains practical?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: dynamic consistency and manifold preservation
PROPOSAL: Develop a method called Dynamic Consistency and Manifold Preservation (DCMP), which iteratively updates the diffusion guidance process by matching the intermediate states to the manifold — instead of directly feeding them back to the denoiser. First, we use the learned denoiser to define a manifold — where data likelihood is high — by calculating the mean of the denoiser output for a range of noise inputs. Then, at each timestep, we check if the guidance signal differs significantly from the manifold. If it does, we re-align the guidance trajectory to be closer to the manifold. This should maintain the learned data distribution, avoiding drift off the manifold and guaranteeing manifold feasibility.
CONTROLS: Compare against DPS and DDRM, following the setup outlined in the proposal.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: DCMP should significantly reduce the off-manifold drift seen in current methods and maintain reliable reconstructions, even at high noise levels. A minor issue could be that manual tuning of parameters for DCMP would be needed for different noise distributions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: uncertainty-aware reconstruction guidance
PROPOSAL: Introduce an uncertainty-aware variant of the guidance process, Uncertainty-Aware Reconstruction Guidance (UARG), by modelling and learning the compact uncertainty via an ensemble of diffusion models, each with a distinct noise schedule. During the guidance process, we draw samples from the distributions output by the ensemble, and combine them to inform the reconstruction guidance signal. This approach can estimate and incorporate the uncertainty, adapting the guidance process to the inherent uncertainty in the posterior and, consequently, escape spurious modes more effectively.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard guidance methods, and assess the impact of ensemble size on performance.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: UARG would have improved performance over standard guidance methods for challenging inverse problems, but careful ensemble size and model selection could be required, while estimating uncertainty could increase computational cost.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: probabilistic forward mappings
PROPOSAL: To address the intractable likelihoods, develop Probabilistic Forward Mappings (PFM), a probabilistic, invertible, and differentiable approximation of the forward operator A. We achieve this by training a probabilistic neural network that maps the true forward operator to a Gaussian process, allowing us to treat the forward operator as a probabilistic function and comptuted the likelihoods, p(y|x), in closed-form. PFM can be efficiently inverted to produce samples from the intractable forward process.
CONTROLS: Compare against approximate likelihood methods (e.g. Tweedie's formula) and assess the impact of model capacity on performance, with results reported in a table.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: PFM should provide accurate approximations of the likelihoods without adding additional hyperparameters or prior knowledge, but the performance would heavily depend on the choice of model and capacities.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: uncertainty-aware reconstruction guidance
PROPOSAL: Revising the previous proposal, introduce Uncertainty-Aware Reconstruction Guidance (UARG), but with an additional regularization term that encourages the ensemble of diffusion models to be consistent with the probabilistic forward mappings (PFM) - leading to a framework that simultaneously model the uncertainty of the inverse posterior, and approximates the intractable likelihoods in a probabilistic manner. This synergy can help the guidance process to dichotomize from potential spurious modes more effectively and estimate the noise level adaptively.
CONTROLS: Compare against UARG without the regularization term, standard guidance methods, and assess the impact of model capacity on performance.
COST: 450 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised UARG should improve upon both UARG and PFM individually, offering a more comprehensive approach to uncertainty modelling and probabilistic likelihoods estimation, with the potential downside of increased computational cost.

ACTION: REVISE
 NUMBER: 2
 TITLE: uncertainty-aware reconstruction guidance
PROPOSAL: Revising the previous proposal, introduce Uncertainty-Aware Reconstruction Guidance (UARG), but with an additional emphasis on robustness to noise levels - by learning a noise-adaptive versioning of the guidance process, which monitors the current noise level and weighs its contribution accordingly. To achieve this, we use a neural network that takes both the guidance state and the estimated noise level as inputs and outputs a noise-adaptive guidance signal. This approach can help the guidance process to adapt to the uncertainty in the noise, leveraging this learned noise robustness to supervise spurious modes and produce more accurate reconstructions.
CONTROLS: Compare against UARG without the noise-adaptive term, standard guidance methods, and assess the impact of noise level estimation accuracy on performance.
COST: 375 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised UARG should reduce the need for hand-tuning regularization weights and early stopping, and improve noise robustness, but may increase computational cost due to the additional neural network component.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adaptive diffusion guidance sampling
PROPOSAL: Develop an adaptive sampling method, Adaptive Diffusion Guidance Sampling (ADGS), which dynamically selects the most informative samples from the guided diffusion process, allowing for an efficient exploration of the solution space while maintaining a constrained number of samples. By iteratively Assessing the Information Content (AIC) of the samples and dynamically sampling from the intermediate posteriors, we can estimate which samples contribute most significantly to the reconstruction, and reserve computation resources accordingly.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard sampling methods (e.g. Independent Sampling, Sequential Sampling) and assess the impact of hyperparameters on performance.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ADGS should improve the efficiency of the sampling process while maintaining accurate reconstructions, but its effectiveness might depend heavily on the choice of AIC metric and the specific inverse problem at hand.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: inference-time model distillation
PROPOSAL: Introduce Inference-Time Model Distillation (ITMD), a technique to reduce the computational resources needed for inference by distilling a large diffusion model into a smaller, more efficient version while preserving the accuracy of the original model. Specifically, we use a knowledge distillation framework with the goal of matching the output probabilities of the original model, while minimizing a metric of similarity between the two models' weights.
CONTROLS: Compare against pruning and quantization methods for model size reduction, and assess the impact of hyperparameters on performance.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ITMD should lead to a significant reduction in computational resources required for inference, without a substantial loss in accuracy, making it feasible to deploy the proposed methods on edge devices and for large-scale real-world applications. However, finding the optimal distillation parameter might be challenging.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: manifold-aware reconstruction uncertainties
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to quantify the reconstruction uncertainty in a probabilistic and mathematically grounded manner, by modeling the output variability of a diffusion-based sampler conditioned on the true forward operator and noise, leading to a lognormal distribution over reconstructions. This estimate can be directly mapped back to the original reconstruction problem, unbiasedly estimating the subtle noise artifacts, ill-posedness of images, providing informative information on reconstruction reliability.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing uncertainty estimation methods (e.g. MC dropout, variational inference) and assess the impact of model capacity on performance, reported alongside the main results.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed method should provide a robust and accurate measure of reconstruction uncertainty, capable of distinguishing between low-confidence regions and more reliable areas, but it may be computationally expensive due to the need to condition on the true forward operator.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 6
TITLE: manifold-aware reconstruction uncertainties
PROPOSAL: Revising the previous proposal, refine the method to estimate manifold-aware reconstruction uncertainties by incorporating the probabilistic forward mappings (PFM) estimates directly within the uncertainty estimation process. This allows us to capture the inductive bias and prior knowledge of the diffusion model to directly inject uncertainty information into the reconstruction uncertainty calculations, leading to a more principled and accurate estimate of uncertainties. Additionally, introduce a novel strategy to actively leverage this uncertainty information to actively correct for errors and spurious modes.
CONTROLS: Compare against the previous manifold-aware uncertainty estimation method and assess the impact of incorporating PFM on performance and computational cost.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The refined method should lead to more accurate uncertainty estimates, and the active correction mechanism should help correct for spurious modes, but it remains to be seen whether the increased complexity and computational costs would be justified.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: experimentally validating the approach on challenging inverse problems
PROPOSAL: Develop a comprehensive suite of experiments on a diverse set of real-world inverse problems, including image super-resolution, image inpainting, image deblurring, phase retrieval, and high dynamic range (HDR) image reconstruction. Evaluate the proposed methods' performance on these experiments, assessing both quantitative metrics and qualitative visual inspections, and systematically comparing against state-of-the-art methods. Collectively, these experiments should provide a broad validation of the proposed approach's efficacy across various real-world inverse problems.
CONTROLS: Compare against DPS, DDRM, and other state-of-the-art inverse problem solvers on a diverse range of benchmarks.
COST: 5,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The comprehensive experiments should convincingly demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of the proposed methods on challenging real-world inverse problems, showing that the improvements outweigh the increased complexity.

Smoothed decision-making is critical to avoiding abrupt and potentially dangerous large changes of actions in many online optimization problems, such as energy production scheduling in power grids, object tracking, motion planning, and server capacity provisioning in data centers. Mathematically, action smoothness can be achieved by adding to the optimization objective a switching cost that penalizes temporal changes in actions. The switching cost equips the online objective with a (finite) memory of previous actions and creates substantial algorithmic challenges; smoothed online optimization has therefore received a great deal of attention over the last decade, with a quickly growing list of algorithms offering worst-case performance guarantees in adversarial and stochastic settings and under various extensions.

At the same time, long-term fairness is a crucial consideration in many online optimization problems that can profoundly affect individuals' well-being and social welfare. Sequential allocation of social goods to different individuals or groups must be fair and free of discrimination; the surging environmental costs of geographically distributed AI data centers must be fairly distributed across regions, as repeatedly called for by various organizations and government agencies; and AI model performance and resource provisioning must promote social fairness without adversely affecting disadvantaged individuals or groups. If not designed with fairness in mind, online algorithms can perpetuate or even exacerbate societal biases, disproportionately affect certain groups or individuals, and amplify already widening socioeconomic disparities. Fairness in online optimization is therefore not only an ethical concern but also a necessity for broader social responsibility.

Incorporating a long-term fairness regularizer into the objective can effectively promote fairness in online optimization by mitigating implicit or explicit biases, but it creates significant challenges. The regularizer depends on the entire trajectory of actions and contexts and can only be evaluated at the end of an episode, with complete information, whereas a switching cost can be assessed step by step. Online decision-makers react to sequentially revealed information and tend to prioritize immediate cost reduction, potentially neglecting the long-term consequences of their sequence of decisions.

Recent research has started to explore fairness and long-term constraints in online problems such as online resource allocation, using primal-dual techniques. A major limitation of current fair online algorithms, however, is their reliance on the assumption that per-round objective functions are independent of historical actions, an assumption that plays a pivotal role in both their algorithm design and their theoretical analysis. In a simple resource allocation problem, for instance, the maximum allowable action at a given time may depend on past decisions through the remaining budget, but the reward at that time is assumed to depend only on the current decision. Such methods fall short when the per-round objective is directly affected by previous irrevocable actions, as it is with switching costs; in that case an online algorithm and an offline benchmark face different per-round objectives because their action sequences differ, which complicates any direct comparison of their costs. Conversely, the rich literature on smoothed online optimization does not handle a regularizer that is evaluated over the whole horizon. Fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization with switching costs is thus a new and challenging setting that appears not to have been considered in the literature.

Formally, consider an episode of T rounds. At each round t, an agent observes a (potentially adversarially chosen) non-negative hitting cost function f_t and a matrix A_t that maps its action into an M-dimensional cost vector, each dimension corresponding to an entity for which fairness must be taken into account, and then chooses an irrevocable action x_t without knowing future information. It incurs the hitting cost f_t(x_t) and a switching cost d(x_t, x_{t-1}), for instance a scaled squared Euclidean distance between consecutive actions. Fairness is captured by a long-term cost g, convex and Lipschitz, applied to the episode average of the cost vectors; a well-known choice is an l_p norm, which prioritizes reducing the highest costs borne by disadvantaged entities and recovers min-max fairness as p tends to infinity. The goal is to minimize $\frac{1}{T}\big(\sum_{t=1}^{T} f_t(x_t) + \sum_{t=1}^{T} d(x_t, x_{t-1})\big) + g\big(\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} A_t x_t\big)$.

This setting raises several questions. First, how hard is the long-term fairness regularizer intrinsically? Online algorithms are commonly evaluated by their regret or by their competitive ratio against a dynamic offline benchmark which, unlike a static benchmark restricted to a single fixed action, can adapt its action sequence over time with full knowledge of the context. A finite competitive ratio is attainable for online optimization with switching costs, but whether any online algorithm can achieve sublinear regret or a finite competitive ratio against the dynamic offline optimum in the presence of a long-term fairness regularizer, even without switching costs, remains an open question; prior work has only conjectured that finite performance might be impossible in similar settings. Second, if such guarantees are out of reach, against what kind of benchmark can meaningful, practically relevant performance guarantees be established? Third, how can an online algorithm reconcile the tension between minimizing the hitting cost, the switching cost and the long-term fairness cost with provable worst-case guarantees, when the per-round objective carries a memory of previous actions, and how does the long-term fairness regularizer affect such guarantees?

ACTION: ADD
