Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a powerful and principled approach for generative modeling, and in particular for high-quality visual generation. By learning a time-dependent velocity field that continuously transforms samples from a base distribution into a target distribution, FM models generate data by integrating an ordinary differential equation (ODE). This framework offers advantages over diffusion-based methods, including faster convergence, stable training, and direct control over sample trajectories.

Despite these strengths, inference in FM models is costly and has become a bottleneck. ODE integration is inherently sequential: each step depends on the output of the previous one, which makes the process slow and difficult to parallelize. High-fidelity generation requires a large number of fine-grained steps, which pushes latency up and makes real-time or interactive use difficult. As data dimensionality and model complexity increase, so does the inference burden. The issue is even more pronounced in video generation, where models operate on high-dimensional spatio-temporal data and the cost of sequential integration compounds across frames, making efficient inference essential for long videos.

Static reduction strategies such as distillation, trajectory truncation and consistency training have been proposed to reduce inference latency. However, they often degrade output quality, producing blurry textures, semantic drift or broken spatial coherence; in video, they often cause temporal flickering and motion inconsistency, which severely degrade realism even when individual frames look plausible. Many of them also require retraining the model with auxiliary objectives or handcrafted losses, which increases the engineering burden and restricts transferability across model families. As a result, these approaches are less modular, harder to scale, and often infeasible to deploy in time-sensitive or interactive pipelines.

In language models, a promising line of work for accelerating inference is speculative decoding, in which multiple drafts are proposed in parallel and selectively verified by the full model, reducing latency without retraining it. This idea, however, does not directly extend to image and video generative models such as FM, and two challenges stand out. First, unlike in language models, no readily available draft model exists: how can drafts be produced whose trajectories closely couple with those of the full model? Second, the performance of FM is highly sensitive to the velocity output: even a small perturbation in velocity can accumulate along the integration path and lead to severe generation errors. How, then, can drafted velocities be evaluated, and how can the drift of the resulting trajectory away from the full-model trajectory be controlled?

The open problem is therefore how to substantially reduce the inference latency of existing FM models, for both image and video generation, without retraining, without degrading output quality relative to standard full-step generation, and in a way that transfers across model families.

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: draft model acceleration via random path pruning
PROPOSAL: We propose to evaluate the feasibility of accelerating inference in FM models by selectively pruning short, random paths through the velocity field during the integration process. By doing so, we can reduce the overall number of integration steps required for achieving the same quality of output. We will experiment with various pruning strategies, including pruning based on velocity magnitude, Euclidean distance, and maximum gradient.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no pruning. (2) Ablation study: Different pruning strategies and their combinations. (3) Control: Randomly subsampling the paths.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a latency reduction of up to 30% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and a significant decrease in video generation latency. However, this approach may lead to variations in generation quality depending on the pruning strategy used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: learning draft models for fm using Curriculum Learning
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of generating high-quality drafts in FM models, we propose using Curriculum Learning to learn a draft model that closely couples with the full model. We will define a gradual curriculum of temporally corrected velocities that guide the learning process of the draft model. As the curriculum progresses, the draft model will learn to produce velocities that are increasingly similar to those produced by the full model. This will enable the draft model to not only accelerate inference but also maintain high quality output.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different curriculum learning schedules. (3) Control: Learning draft models using random sampling of the velocity field.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 40% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. The quality of the drafts will be strongly dependent on the quality of the curriculum learning schedule.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: draft model acceleration via random path pruning
PROPOSAL: We revise our initial proposal to include an incentive mechanism that rewards the draft model for producing velocities that result in generated samples that are closer to the ground truth. This can be achieved by incorporating a reconstruction loss into the draft model's training objective, which encourages the draft model to produce high-quality samples that are close to the target distribution. By doing so, we can improve the accuracy and quality of the draft model's outputs.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no pruning and no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different loss functions and weights for the reconstruction loss. (3) Control: Learning draft models using random sampling of the velocity field without reconstruction loss.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 50% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. However, the introduction of the reconstruction loss may lead to increased training time and potential mode collapse issues.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: learning draft models for fm using curriculum learning
PROPOSAL: We revise our proposal to use a more efficient curriculum learning schedule that utilizes progressive meta-learning. Instead of learning a fixed curriculum, we will use a dynamic curriculum that adapts to the performance of the draft model and the full model. This will enable the draft model to learn more effectively and efficiently, and potentially lead to better performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different progressive meta-learning schedules. (3) Control: Using a fixed curriculum learning schedule.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 45% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. The progressive meta-learning schedule may lead to improved performance, but it may also increase computational costs due to the need to adapt the curriculum during training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: draft refinement via multi-step prediction
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-step prediction mechanism to refine the outputs of the draft model. This mechanism will utilize a secondary model trained to predict the corrections needed to refine the draft's output, rather than relying on a single pass through the full model. By predicting these corrections step-by-step, we can iteratively refine the draft's output, potentially leading to significant quality improvements.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different numbers of refinement steps and secondary model architectures.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve high-quality outputs comparable to the full model, with a latency reduction of up to 40% in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. However, the multiple steps of refinement may lead to increased training time and potential issues with convergence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: lazy evaluation of fm velocity fields
PROPOSAL: We propose a lazy evaluation approach for the velocity fields used in FM models. By storing the velocity fields in a compressed and hierarchical manner, we can significantly reduce the computational cost of evaluating the velocity field for a given sample. This approach can be particularly effective when combined with the draft model and refinement mechanisms, as it can help to reduce the latency of the overall system.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a significant reduction in computational cost, with a latency reduction of up to 25% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the compressed representation may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or discontinuities in the velocity field.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: model-parallelizable fm through decomposition
PROPOSAL: We propose a decomposition-based approach to make FM models parallelizable. By decomposing the velocity field into smaller, independent components, we can parallelize the evaluation of the velocity field across multiple GPUs or machines, significantly reducing the latency of the overall system. This approach can be particularly effective for large-scale FM models and video generation tasks.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no decomposition. (2) Ablation study: Different decomposition techniques and parallelization strategies.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a significant reduction in latency, with a speedup of up to 4x in text-to-image generation, and an even larger speedup in video generation. However, the decomposition may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or discontinuities in the velocity field, and complex decomposition strategies may increase engineering burden.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: uncertainty-based draft model deployment
PROPOSAL: We propose an uncertainty-based approach for deploying draft models, where the draft model is only used to generate samples when the uncertainty in the velocity field is high, and the full model is used otherwise. This approach can help to mitigate potential quality degradation issues and reduce the overall latency of the system.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different uncertainty measures and threshold values for draft model deployment.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 30% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the deployment strategy may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or inconsistent behavior at high uncertainty values.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adaptive draft model switching
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive approach for switching between the draft model and the full model based on the performance of the system. By continuously monitoring the quality and latency of the generated samples, we can dynamically switch between the two models to achieve the optimal trade-off between quality and latency. This approach can help to adapt to changing system conditions and optimize performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different switching policies and performance metrics.
COST: 110 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 35% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the adaptive switching strategy may lead to potential issues with instability or mode collapse.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: hybrid fm architectures
PROPOSAL: We propose a hybrid approach that combines the strengths of multiple architectures to achieve improved performance in FM models. By combining the draft model, full model, and lazy evaluation, we can create a flexible and adaptable architecture that can dynamically adjust to changing system conditions and optimize performance. This approach can help to achieve the optimal trade-off between quality, latency, and computational cost.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model. (2) Ablation study: Different combinations of draft model, full model, and lazy evaluation.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 50% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation, while maintaining high quality and performance. However, the hybrid architecture may lead to potential issues with complexity, overhead, and stability.

Many supervised learning algorithms rely on the assumption that training and test data are drawn from the same underlying distribution. In real-world applications this assumption is often violated because of environmental changes, sampling biases or temporal dynamics, which create distribution shifts between training and deployment environments. Such mismatches can cause significant performance degradation and pose a fundamental challenge to reliable generalization in practice.

Among the challenges posed by distribution shifts, this problem concerns unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), with a focus on classification. In UDA, one is given labeled data from a source domain and unlabeled data from a target domain whose distributions are related but not necessarily identical. The discrepancy may come from the marginal distribution of the input, from the conditional distribution of labels given inputs, or from both. The goal is to use the labeled source data and the unlabeled target data to build a predictive model with low risk on the target domain. The most naive baseline, empirical risk minimization on the source data, can perform poorly on the target domain when the two distributions differ.

Two representative families of UDA methods are distribution alignment, which reduces the discrepancy between the source and target domains either in the data space or in a feature space, and pseudo-labeling, which refines target predictions using a source-trained model in the spirit of self-training. Despite their popularity, both families often face practical limitations in two common scenarios. The first is when the amount of unlabeled target data is limited: alignment estimates can then become unreliable and pseudo-labels noisy, which can lead to poor generalization, and the empirical distribution of a small or imbalanced target sample may be a poor estimate of the true target input distribution that fails to capture the diversity of the target domain. The second is when the source data contain spurious correlations, for example when irrelevant features such as background or color are strongly associated with labels: models then tend to rely on these shortcuts, which do not transfer to the target domain and ultimately degrade performance. Alignment-based methods can fail in this situation, and approaches that try to disentangle causal and spurious features with unlabeled target data, through counterfactual consistency, generative interventions or self-training refinements, often rely on strong structural assumptions or are highly sensitive to the quality of the initial pseudo-labels, which makes them fragile when target data are scarce or imbalanced.

Distributionally robust optimization is another line of work on distribution shift: instead of the average loss on the training distribution, it minimizes the worst-case expected loss over an ambiguity set of plausible distributions. Constructing a suitable ambiguity set is the central difficulty, and the inner worst case must remain computationally tractable. Common choices, small Wasserstein or f-divergence balls around the empirical source distribution, give robustness to minor perturbations but are less suitable for structured shifts such as subpopulation shift, where the target contains the same subpopulations as the source with different mixing weights and can therefore lie far from the source in standard distances. Formulations designed for such mixture shifts, such as group distributionally robust optimization, typically assume access to group labels and do not explicitly use unlabeled target data to improve target prediction.

The problem is therefore how to learn, from labeled data coming from one or several source domains and unlabeled target data, a classifier that generalizes to the target domain when unlabeled target data are extremely scarce and when spurious correlations dominate the source domain, without group labels and with a computationally tractable training procedure. How can a learner remain reliable when the few available unlabeled target inputs give a poor picture of the target input distribution, and how can it avoid relying on spurious source features that do not hold in the target domain?

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: dimensionality reduction for distribution alignment
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of using dimensionality reduction techniques (e.g., PCA, t-SNE) to align the feature spaces of the source and target domains in UDA. Specifically, we will apply dimensionality reduction to the labeled source data and test its transferability to the unlabeled target data, exploring combinations of techniques and hyperparameter settings. We will use the Ladybug and CIFAR-10 datasets for digit recognition, as well as the CelebA dataset for facial attribute classification.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Empirical risk minimization on the source data; Baseline 2: State-of-the-art UDA methods (e.g.,/domain adversarial neural network, adversarial deep domain confusion network). Ablation 1: No dimensionality reduction; Ablation 2: Using dimensionality reduction on target data alone.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours ( exploratory experiments with small models)
PREDICTION: We anticipate that dimensionality reduction will improve alignment, especially when combined with other methods (e.g., adversarial training), but may not be sufficient to handle extreme distribution shifts or spurious correlations. The combination of techniques and hyperparameter tuning is likely crucial for best performance.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: self-training with robust source classifiers
PROPOSAL: Modify the self-training paradigm to improve robustness against spurious correlations in the source data. Specifically, we will use robust source classifiers trained with input and label perturbations, such as adversarial training and data augmentation. We will also use these robust source models to generate pseudo-labels for the target data. The goal is to build a more reliable self-training pipeline that focuses on the most informative features and reduces the impact of spurious correlations.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: counterfactual reasoning with limited target data
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of counterfactual reasoning to improve UDA performance when target data is scarce. Specifically, we will adapt the counterfactual decision network framework to use limited target samples to infer latent counterfactual variables. We will then train a UDA model to predict on these counterfactuals, aiming to improve generalizability and reduce reliance on spurious correlations. As a starting point, we will use the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for digit recognition.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: dimensionality reduction for distribution alignment
PROPOSAL: Expand the dimensionality reduction approach (1) by combining it with other methods for aligning the source and target domains. Specifically, we will explore the use of adversarial training and pseudo-labeling to further improve alignment, using dimensionality reduction as a preprocessing step to reduce the impact of spurious correlations. We will apply this combined approach to the Ladybug and CIFAR-10 datasets for digit recognition, as well as the CelebA dataset for facial attribute classification.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Empirical risk minimization on the source data; Baseline 2: State-of-the-art UDA methods (e.g., domain adversarial neural network, adversarial deep domain confusion network). Ablation 1: Using dimensionality reduction alone; Ablation 2: Using adversarial training and pseudo-labeling without dimensionality reduction.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours (combining with other methods, but maintaining moderate complexity)
PREDICTION: The combination of dimensionality reduction and other methods should improve alignment and reduce the reliance on spurious correlations, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to optimize performance. The method may struggle with extremely different input distributions or very scarce target data.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: robustness regularization for self-training
PROPOSAL: Regularize the self-training process to improve robustness against spurious correlations in the source data. Specifically, we will add a regularization term to the self-training loss that encourages the model to focus on informative features and avoid relying on spurious correlations. We will implement this regularization using techniques such as dropout, weight decay, or early stopping. As a starting point, we will use the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for digit recognition.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Standard self-training; Ablation 1: No regularization; Ablation 2: Using dropout regularization. Benchmark comparison: a teacher-student setup on the Fashion-MNIST dataset.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours (moderate-scale experiments with regularized models)
PREDICTION: Regularization should improve the robustness of self-training by reducing overfitting to spurious correlations, but may compromise performance on data-rich scenarios or scenarios where the model can handle spurious correlations without regularization. The optimal regularization technique and strength may depend on the specific dataset and model architecture.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: sample selection for robust UDA
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of sample selection methods to improve robustness of UDA in scenarios where target data is scarce or imbalanced. Specifically, we will adapt sample selection methods (e.g., coherence-based sampling, density-based sampling) to select the most informative target samples for UDA. We will then train a UDA model using these selected samples and compare the results to baseline models trained on the full target dataset. We will apply this approach to the Ladybug and CIFAR-10 datasets for bird image classification.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Standard UDA on the full target dataset; Ablation 1: No sample selection; Ablation 2: Using a random sample selection method.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours (large-scale experiments with selected samples)
PREDICTION: Sample selection should improve the robustness of UDA by focusing on the most informative target samples, but may compromise performance if the selected samples are not representative of the target distribution. The choice of sample selection method may depend on the specific dataset and UDA model architecture.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: self-training with robust source classifiers
PROPOSAL: Expand the self-training approach (2) to incorporate multiple levels of robustness and regularization. Specifically, we will combine the robust source classifier with robustness regularization (4) and sample selection (5) to improve the robustness of self-training. We will also explore the use of robust multi-instance learning to handle diverse and noisy target samples. We will apply this combined approach to the CelebA dataset for facial attribute classification and other datasets.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Standard self-training with a standard source classifier; Ablation 1: No robust source classifier; Ablation 2: Using robust multi-instance learning without sample selection. Benchmark comparison: a vanilla teacher-student setup on the head bird category.
COST: 2200 GPU-hours (moderate-scale experiments with robust models)
PREDICTION: The combined approach should significantly improve the robustness of self-training by reducing overfitting to spurious correlations and handling noisy and diverse target samples, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to optimize performance. The method may be sensitive to the choice of robustness regularization technique and sample selection method.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: uncertainty-based pseudo-labeling for uda
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of uncertainty-based pseudo-labeling to improve UDA in scenarios where target data is scarce or imbalanced. Specifically, we will adapt Bayesian neural networks or Monte Carlo dropout to estimate the uncertainty of target predictions, and then use these uncertainty estimates to select high-confidence pseudo-labels for fine-tuning. We will compare the results to baseline models trained with standard pseudo-labeling and evaluate the impact of uncertainty-based pseudo-labeling on robustness and generalization. We will apply this approach to the CIFAR-10 and Ladybug datasets for image classification.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: transferable features selection for uda
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of transferable features selection to improve UDA in scenarios where the source and target domains have different feature distributions. Specifically, we will use feature selection techniques (e.g., mutual information, L1 regularization) to identify transferable features that are robust across domains. We will then train a UDA model using only these transferable features and evaluate its performance on the target domain. As a starting point, we will use the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for image classification.

The choice of feature selection method may depend on the specific dataset and UDA model architecture.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: hierarchical adaptability for domain adaptation
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of hierarchical adaptability to improve UDA in scenarios where the source and target domains have different sub-populations or sub-tasks. Specifically, we will use a hierarchical neural architecture to adapt to multiple sub-populations or sub-tasks in a single model, rather than requiring separate models for each one. We will then evaluate the performance of this hierarchical approach on a range of UDA benchmarks, including the CIFAR-10 and Ladybug datasets.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Standard UDA; Ablation 1: No hierarchical adaptability; Ablation 2: Using only one level of adaptability. Evaluate all methods on the same held-out test set and report the mean and standard deviation over five seeds.
COST: 4000 GPU-hours (large-scale experiments with hierarchical models)

Diffusion models have recently demonstrated remarkable capabilities in synthesizing high-quality images, significantly surpassing earlier generative approaches such as generative adversarial networks and variational autoencoders. Despite their impressive fidelity, deploying diffusion models in realistic cloud-to-user applications introduces a fundamental bottleneck: transmission bandwidth. A standard diffusion model produces a high-fidelity image by performing a fixed number of denoising steps, regardless of downstream transmission limitations. In conventional scenarios, the generated images then undergo aggressive lossy compression before transmission to accommodate the limited bandwidth. This cascaded approach, high-quality generation followed by subsequent compression, not only incurs redundant computational overhead, since computation is spent on details that are later discarded, but also significantly degrades perceptual quality, as the compression process often erases the intricate textures and fine details carefully constructed by the diffusion model.

This motivates a critical question: can bandwidth-awareness be integrated directly into the diffusion generation process, so that the quality of the generated image is adapted to the available bandwidth, avoiding the inefficiency and perceptual quality loss associated with post-generation compression? Ideally, such a generator would meet a user-specified bitrate budget, avoid compression-induced artifacts and redundant computation, and offer fine-grained, dynamic control over image quality according to real-time bandwidth conditions in practical cloud-to-user deployments.

The question is not straightforward. During sampling, diffusion models progressively refine coarse structures into detailed, realistic textures through iterative denoising steps, so, intuitively, terminating the process early would yield simpler, lower-detail images suited to constrained bandwidth. However, naively reducing the number of diffusion steps typically produces suboptimal visual quality: models trained for complete denoising trajectories are not optimized for early termination, which leads to visual artifacts and poor perceptual coherence.

Existing lines of work address only parts of this problem. A large body of work accelerates diffusion sampling, through deterministic samplers that need fewer inference steps, numerical solvers inspired by ordinary differential equations, distillation of slow teacher models into faster students, adaptive step-size selection, latent-space compression, non-uniform step skipping, dynamic network pruning, predictors of the minimal number of denoising steps, and adaptive inference trajectories. These methods reduce the cost of sampling while preserving generation quality, but they are not designed to control the bitrate of the generated image. Conditional and controllable diffusion models, from classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance to latent diffusion and region-based conditioning for interactive editing, allow flexible control over attributes of the generated content, but they do not directly address bandwidth constraints. How to make a diffusion model generate images that respect a specified bandwidth budget while preserving perceptual quality and avoiding wasted computation therefore remains an open problem.

Semantic segmentation has improved significantly with recent advances in deep neural networks, but it requires a large volume of fine-grained pixel-level labels, which are time-consuming and labor-intensive to obtain. Because images themselves are readily available, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) and semi-supervised learning (SSL) have been introduced to handle label-scarce scenarios: UDA learns from labeled synthetic data and transfers knowledge to real, unlabeled target domains, while SSL uses a tiny portion of annotated data to generalize to unseen data. Both are gaining attention as promising ways to reduce the reliance on extensive annotation in semantic segmentation.

In both settings, models are trained on annotated and unlabeled data simultaneously. Mainstream methods follow two paradigms. Self-training methods use a temporally smoothed exponential moving average (EMA) model as a teacher to generate stable pseudo-labels for unlabeled data, while consistency regularization methods encourage the model to produce consistent predictions for the same sample under different perturbation views; recent state-of-the-art methods combine the two. Both can be summarized as pseudo-label learning, in which the network's own predictions serve as supervision for unlabeled data. In the widely adopted form of this paradigm, the teacher's prediction is converted into a hard pseudo-label through an argmax and encoded one-hot, a confidence-based quality estimate (threshold filtering or a weighting function) controls how much each pseudo-label contributes, and training uses a cross-entropy loss.

Despite promising results, pseudo-labels inevitably contain errors that mislead training, and these errors are further amplified during training because of the one-hot encoding. Typical remedies use filter-out mechanisms that train only on high-confidence pseudo-labels, but this makes the model focus on easy samples while neglecting difficult ones, resulting in sub-optimal performance. Another alternative assigns weights according to pseudo-label confidence, but such weighting functions require careful design and selection of hyperparameters, which compromises their applicability. Other work designs new optimization criteria, for example inspired by negative learning. Existing work thus concentrates on selection strategies for pseudo-labels and rarely considers the impact of the encoding form assigned to classes.

This omission matters most for confusing classes. For instance, pixels of the class sheep may be confused by the classifier with horse or cow, and the resulting erroneous pseudo-label is encoded one-hot through the argmax, committing the supervision entirely to a wrong class. Similar classes plausibly share common visual attributes (sheep and cows, for example, both have horns and hooves), which leads to confusing pseudo-labels that further misguide training, yet a one-hot target cannot express what the confused classes have in common. How to utilize the shared attributes among confusing classes to design a suitable encoding form for pseudo-label learning remains rarely explored.

This raises several questions. Can the class encoding used by the segmentation model and its pseudo-labels be redesigned so that supervision stays informative even when the class decision for a pixel is wrong? Under such an encoding, how should pseudo-labels be generated from the teacher's predictions so that they introduce less noise than hard one-hot labels, and what training objective is appropriate? Can an alternative encoding be shown, both theoretically and empirically, to match one-hot encoding in the fully supervised setting while being more robust to label noise in pseudo-label learning? Finally, since the encoding form is orthogonal to pseudo-label selection strategies, can such a change be integrated into existing self-training and consistency-regularization frameworks for both UDA and SSL, across different segmentation architectures?

enonce:
Diffusion models have catalyzed an enormous research wave in generative modeling. Conceptually, they couple a stochastic forward noising process with a reverse-time ordinary or stochastic differential equation whose density evolution is governed by the Fokker–Planck equation, a linear second-order parabolic partial differential equation. Learning consists of estimating time-indexed scores or velocities and integrating them for sampling. A growing body of work also explores probability-flow backbones: deterministic flows trained via flow matching and its optimal-transport variants, rectified flows, and stochastic interpolants that bridge flows and diffusion.

Yet the partial-differential-equation lens on generative modeling need not be limited to Fokker–Planck. Other classical linear second-order equations, elliptic and hyperbolic, offer different structural advantages but remain comparatively underexplored; Poisson flow models, for instance, recast generation through electrostatics-inspired fields. On the hyperbolic side, recent work has replaced the Fokker–Planck equation with the telegrapher equation (the one-dimensional damped wave equation) and its stochastic Kac representation, in which a particle moves at constant speed and reverses direction at the jump times of a Poisson process. A network is fit by regression to a closed-form conditional velocity of this process and integrated backward in time from noise to data, with each image coordinate following an independent one-dimensional Kac process. The resulting probability flows have a finite propagation speed: starting from localized mass, the distribution remains inside a causal cone, the flow is Lipschitz in Wasserstein distance, and velocity norms, hence kinetic energy, stay globally bounded. Diffusion, by contrast, spreads mass instantaneously with effectively infinite propagation speed, which manifests as stiff, rapidly growing reverse-time velocities and as ill-conditioned fields with Lipschitz blow-ups near the end of denoising; indeed, diffusion arises as a limit of the damped wave equation as the damping and the propagation speed tend to infinity. A finite speed cap thus acts like a built-in stability constraint: trajectories cannot accelerate without bound, and late-time integration is less stiff.

So far, however, these finite-speed flows have been developed only for unconditional image generation, and they lack two ingredients that make diffusion-style generators practical. The first is guided conditional generation. Classifier-free guidance, which mixes conditional and unconditional predictions to steer samples toward a condition, is a standard tool for diffusion models, but it is unclear whether guidance can be carried over to finite-speed dynamics without losing the bounded-energy property that distinguishes them from diffusion, whose kinetic energy can diverge near data time. The second is fast sampling. Practical generators are expected to deliver high-quality samples with very few network evaluations, yet it is unknown whether finite-speed flows can be brought down to a handful of sampling steps, or even a single one, without a severe loss of sample quality, and whether their finite-speed, bounded-energy structure can explain, and ideally guarantee, that a coarse few-step sampler stays close to the full sampling trajectory.

This leads to three questions. How can guided conditional generation be built on finite-speed Kac flows while provably keeping the guided velocity field at finite kinetic energy? How can such flows be turned into few-step, ideally one-step, image generators that preserve both sample quality and the numerical stability benefits of finite-speed probability flows? And can the finite-speed structure provide theoretical guarantees that a few-step sampler remains close to the full flow along the entire generation path, not only in its final samples? Answering them would show whether hyperbolic, finite-speed dynamics can be a credible alternative to diffusion for fast image generation.

enonce:
Recording dynamic scenes from multiple viewpoints has become increasingly common in everyday life. From concerts and sports events to lectures and birthday parties, people often capture the same moment using different handheld devices. These multi-view recordings present a rich opportunity to reconstruct scenes in 4D, enable bullet-time effects, or enhance the capabilities of existing vision models. However, these videos are typically captured independently, without synchronization or known camera poses, making it difficult to align and fuse them coherently.

The task is the following: given a set of asynchronous videos that capture the same dynamic scene from different viewpoints, estimate a time offset for each video, to be applied to its original out-of-sync clock, so that after correction frames sharing the same clock time correspond to the exact same moment across all videos.

Existing synchronization methods rely on controlled environments, manual annotations, specific patterns such as human pose, audio signals such as flashes or claps, or expensive hardware setups such as time-coded devices, none of which are available in casually captured videos. Human-centric approaches, which use body pose as the synchronization signal, are limited by the accuracy of pose estimation and by the number of people present, and they struggle in scenes without prominent human activity. Audio-based approaches only work in quiet environments and do not carry over to in-the-wild settings where audio is noisy or unavailable. Methods that jointly optimize camera poses and temporal offsets within a learned scene representation are often constrained to specific environments or object types. Geometry-based methods estimate temporal offsets from multi-view geometric constraints, but typically assume static scenes or a fixed viewpoint. Meanwhile, structure-from-motion and learned camera-pose estimators recover camera geometry accurately, yet they rely predominantly on static visual cues and therefore fall short of synchronizing dynamic scenes.

Building a practical and robust synchronization system that works on videos in the wild is challenging. Camera poses are unknown and cameras may move, so the geometric relationship between each pair of cameras must itself be estimated reliably. The moving objects that carry the timing information are not known in advance and are generally small and blurry. Associating points across cameras with significantly different viewpoints is difficult. The offsets to be recovered are continuous, while observations arrive only at discrete frame times. Finally, not all views overlap, so some pairs of cameras may share little spatial or temporal overlap.

This raises several questions. How can a set of casually captured, unposed and unsynchronized videos of the same dynamic scene be aligned in time with high precision, without specialized capture, audio, manual correction, or assumptions about the scene content such as the presence of people? Which visual evidence can reliably reveal the temporal offset between two cameras whose poses are unknown and possibly changing over time? And how can a single, globally consistent offset be recovered for every video when the evidence relating some pairs of views is weak, ambiguous or missing? Answering these questions would open the door to scalable, unconstrained multi-view 4D scene understanding and to downstream tasks, such as 4D reconstruction of dynamic scenes, that depend on synchronized input.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: shallow networks for temporal alignment
PROPOSAL: Design a simple neural network architecture that learns to predict temporal offsets between video frames from different viewpoints, using multi-view video sequences captured in dynamic scenes and a novel dataset that includes videos with varying difficulty levels and noisy audio. Train the network on a subset of the videos with clear synchronization signals and evaluate its performance on the rest using metrics such as mean absolute error and frame-to-frame alignment accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of a deep neural network (e.g., ResNet) against the shallow architecture on the same task, and test the effect of different network designs, such as adding more layers or using different activation functions.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The shallow network might perform surprisingly well on simple scenes, but its accuracy could degrade when handling complex or dynamic scenes where audio and visual features fail to align.

Generative models significantly enhance the efficiency of chemical space exploration in drug discovery by directly sampling molecules with desired properties. However, a key bottleneck in their practical deployment is low synthetic accessibility: generated molecules are often difficult or impossible to produce in the laboratory. To address this limitation, recent work has turned to template-based methods that emulate the chemical synthesis process by constructing synthesis trees that link molecular building blocks through known reaction templates. These representations, while useful for downstream experimental validation, do not describe the underlying 3D geometry and thus cannot capitalize on the conformational information that is often crucial for diverse chemical and biological properties.

Parallel advances in generative molecular design have explored spatial modeling at the atomic level. Inspired by advances in protein structure prediction and by generative frameworks such as diffusion and flow matching, recent work has focused on directly sampling 3D atomic coordinates of small molecules, learning to generate spatially meaningful, property-aligned conformations along with molecular graphs. The ability to model atomic coordinates directly increases the expressivity of these approaches, enabling applications such as pocket-conditioned generation, scaffold hopping, analog discovery, and molecular optimization. However, without considering practical synthesis routes, integrating synthesizability constraints into these models remains a major challenge, and most existing 3D generative approaches do not ensure that proposed molecules can be made in practice. While recent work has addressed synthesizability for 2D molecular graphs, extending such constraints to 3D, and to geometry-based conditional generation, remains largely unexplored.

Several obstacles stand in the way. Directly optimizing synthesizability scores is often unreliable, so the predominant route to synthetic accessibility has been to assemble molecules from commercially available building blocks joined by known reaction templates; yet such generators typically emit only molecular graphs and no atomic coordinates. The representations commonly available for 3D work are also ill-suited to synthesis awareness: synthon-based representations do not guarantee that a valid synthesis route exists, do not provide one even when it does, and lack the flexibility to constrain the reaction space, which matters when one wants to prioritize high-yield, high-reliability reactions or to remain within the limits of automated synthesis platforms. Relying instead on external, black-box reaction simulators to couple building blocks offers no fine-grained control when a reagent has several reaction centers, and such steps do not define atom mappings between reactants and products, making it impossible to trace product atoms back to their parent building blocks. A further difficulty is that most 3D molecule generation methods require the number of atoms to be specified in advance, which is awkward when the identity of the constituent building blocks is itself still being decided. Finally, the few approaches that do couple synthesis pathways with 3D structure optimize an external reward and typically require a full training run for each target pocket, which is costly and exposes the generator to reward hacking.

This raises the central questions. Can a single generative model sample small molecules so that each sample comes with both a physically realistic 3D conformation and an explicit, traceable route by which it could actually be made, instead of treating geometry and synthesizability as separate concerns handled in sequence or by post hoc filtering? What kind of data and molecular representation would such a model require, given that existing conformer datasets carry no synthesis information and existing synthesis-aware representations carry no geometry? How should synthesizability and geometric quality be measured so that claims of practical makeability are credible rather than an artifact of the scoring tool used? And can one amortized model, once trained, serve the geometry-conditioned design problems that drug discovery actually poses, such as completing or connecting parts of a known three-dimensional ligand, or designing novel molecules that reproduce a desired spatial arrangement of interaction features for a target, without external scoring functions and without retraining for each new target?

Time series data arise ubiquitously across a broad range of domains, including healthcare, finance, industrial manufacturing, weather forecasting and urban computing, and their characteristics can differ vastly from one domain to another. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have unleashed new potential for exploiting these data in time series tasks such as forecasting, imputation and classification. There are roughly two families of approaches: one fine-tunes or prompts off-the-shelf LLMs with time series converted into a suitable format, while the other trains time series foundation models from scratch on vast time series corpora by adapting LLM-inspired architectures and training strategies. In both cases, the quality of the time series data is critical to model performance: low-quality data can negate the benefits of bespoke technical advances and may even degrade performance. In practice, time series datasets are frequently marred by pervasive quality issues, including missing values, corruption induced by sensor failures, and irregular sampling. Consequently, there is a pressing need to assess, accurately and efficiently, the quality of time series data crawled from diverse domains.

General-purpose data attribution methods, such as influence functions and Shapley-value approaches (together with cheaper approximations such as KNN-based or gradient-based Shapley values), estimate the contribution of individual training samples in a model-agnostic way, but they overlook properties specific to time series such as continuity, temporal dependencies and non-stationarity. Existing attempts at time series data quality estimation therefore stress the need for methods tailored to temporal characteristics. For instance, TimeInf adapts the influence function to time series, drawing on earlier work on infinitesimal robustness for autoregressive processes and on influence functionals for time series, and TimeShap extends the Shapley value, a cooperative game-theoretic attribution method, to time series. However, these methods have largely neglected the fact that real-world time series originate from diverse domains with distinct properties and substantial distribution shifts, which limits their effectiveness to a single domain. Furthermore, both influence-function and Shapley-value techniques struggle to strike a balance between estimation fidelity and computational efficiency: influence functions require computationally intensive Hessian and gradient calculations, while Shapley values incur exponential computational costs.

Recently, estimating data quality through LLM judgments has emerged as a promising approach for text, where carefully designed prompts guide LLMs to produce accurate quality assessments. The underlying rationale is that LLMs are proficient in understanding quality criteria for natural language, such as writing style, required expertise, factual accuracy and educational value. Such efforts point to the potential of LLMs for cross-domain and interpretable data quality estimation, but they remain restricted to text and code, and the time series setting is largely unexplored.

It is therefore tempting to ask whether LLMs can be exploited to determine the quality of diverse time series data. Such an approach could leverage the knowledge of time series from many domains that LLMs acquire during large-scale pretraining, thereby circumventing the prohibitive computational cost of calculating influence functions or Shapley values in a domain-by-domain manner. However, it remains under-explored whether LLMs can truly comprehend the key characteristics that underpin the quality of diverse time series data, and how to effectively steer them to distinguish between high- and low-quality time series according to desired quality criteria. The open problem is thus how to rate the quality of time series data drawn from heterogeneous domains in a way that is accurate, computationally efficient and adaptable across domains.

Humans naturally parse scenes into coherent objects (e.g., grouping features such as a rounded shape, a smooth surface and a muted color into the mug) and further ground their identities in context (e.g., recognizing my coffee mug on the desk rather than just a mug). This is assumed to be made possible by what cognitive scientists call object binding, the brain's ability to group an object's low-level features (color, shape, motion, etc.) into a unified representation. This in turn enables objects to be stored efficiently and compositionally in memory and used as high-level symbols for reasoning about individual object instances. The binding problem is a genuine computational challenge, as evidenced by humans' limited competence in conjunction-search tasks and by clinical dissociations such as Balint's syndrome, where feature perception remains intact but binding breaks down. If AI systems could replicate the human ability for object binding, that may help them ground symbols in perception and exploit compositionality. The key question is: do current AI systems solve the binding problem?

Object binding has received little attention in mainstream AI research. Cognition-inspired models build in human-like object-based attention. By contrast, mainstream vision models are assumed to learn implicitly to handle multiple objects from training data, yet empirical studies show that they often "attend" only to the most salient regions and overlook the rest. While the attention scores of Vision Transformers (ViTs) can capture global image structure and salient regions (often corresponding to target objects), empirical evidence shows that self-attention tends to group patches by low-level feature similarity rather than reliably producing object-level binding. Object-centric methods such as Slot Attention fix this by allocating a small set of learnable slots that compete for token features, enforcing binding by design; however, because such modules are added externally rather than integrated into the transformer architecture, they introduce additional challenges for scaling and training. Other work has assumed that ViTs already carry implicit object-level structure and has tried to group patches into objects directly from their activations or attention maps. Binding failures are also seen as a source of performance breakdowns in modern transformer-based systems: text-to-image diffusion models suffer attribute leakage between entities (e.g., both a dog and a cat end up wearing sunglasses and a sun-hat), and vision-language models struggle to differentiate multiple objects defined by feature conjunctions. Despite these failures, transformers still demonstrate some binding capability, yet the underlying mechanism is not well understood: binding has started to be characterized in language models, but binding mechanisms in vision transformers remain unexplored. Whether AI vision models, especially leading ViTs, can achieve robust object binding without explicit mechanisms therefore remains an open question.

Cognitive scientists have questioned whether ViTs can bind objects at all, arguing that they lack mechanisms for dynamically and flexibly grouping features, that they lack the recurrence necessary for iterative refinement of object representations, and that, as purely connectionist models, they appear incapable of true symbolic processing. However, these architectural limitations do not preclude binding from emerging through learning. ViTs share several computational parallels with the mammalian visual system: both rely on parallel, distributed and hierarchical processing; explicit position embeddings resemble the spatial tagging and spatiotopic organization observed in the ventral stream; and self-attention is akin to the dynamic tuning and attentional modulation thought to be primary mechanisms of binding in the brain. Moreover, knowing which patches belong to the same object would be useful for prediction and could guide attention, and human-labeled data also reflects object-level structure, so ViTs could acquire binding by imitation. ViTs may therefore learn to bind objects directly from large-scale training data, without requiring explicit architectural inductive biases.

This raises the question of whether object binding naturally emerges in large, pretrained Vision Transformers, a question that matters for both cognitive science and AI. Answering it requires establishing whether the internal representations of such models reliably encode which parts of an image belong to the same object; and, if they do, how this information is represented, whether it reflects an ability acquired through learning rather than a trivial artifact of the architecture, and whether the model actually makes functional use of it.

Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly expanded in capability and are now widely used in domains such as conversational agents, healthcare and finance, where they often process sensitive personal information. Early privacy concerns focused mainly on memorization and leakage of training data, but recent studies show that LLMs can also infer private attributes of an author, such as location, identity or demographics, from subtle semantic cues in seemingly innocuous text. With sufficiently capable models, such inferences can be surprisingly accurate and often go undetected by users, who continue to share content unaware of the risk. Moreover, text sent to external services may be intercepted in transit or retained by providers, for example for model training, increasing the risk of misuse or data breaches.

Traditional anonymization methods rely on rule-based de-identification, such as named entity recognition or pattern matching, to remove surface-level identifiers like names, social security numbers or explicit locations. They frequently overlook the context-dependent semantics that LLMs can exploit, so private information that is embedded in context rather than stated explicitly remains inferable. This gap calls for anonymization techniques that account for semantic context and defend against inference-based privacy threats, while preserving the meaning and readability of the text, that is, techniques that achieve a good privacy-utility trade-off.

A growing body of work pursues LLM-based anonymization to protect semantic-level private information from model inference. In feedback-guided adversarial anonymization, an LLM anonymizer rewrites the input text while a second LLM, acting as an adversary, attempts to infer private attributes from the rewritten output; based on this adversarial feedback, the anonymizer iteratively refines its output to prevent the inferences that remain possible. With GPT-4 as both anonymizer and adversary, this approach achieves a substantially better privacy-utility trade-off than traditional industry-grade anonymizers. However, reliance on large proprietary models is costly and requires sending the very text that should be protected to potentially untrusted external systems. Attempts to transfer these anonymization capabilities into smaller models have been explored only to a limited extent, and existing approaches still depend on a proprietary model to provide the adversarial feedback, incurring similar costs and privacy concerns.

The open problem is therefore whether, and how, small language models that can run locally under modest compute budgets can become effective anonymizers that protect semantic-level private information against inference by strong LLM adversaries, without relying on any external model at inference time. Can such models reach a privacy-utility trade-off comparable to, or better than, that of anonymizers built on frontier proprietary LLMs, including on texts where personal information is conveyed by the overall context rather than by explicit mentions, while remaining cheap enough to deploy in settings with strict data-confidentiality requirements?

Visual localization of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) is essential for applications such as digital-twin modeling, mapping, surveillance, large-area and infrastructure inspection, and search-and-rescue operations, yet it faces challenges that ground-level localization systems do not address. Ground-level approaches benefit from similar viewpoints between query and reference images, whereas aerial applications encounter dramatic perspective differences and must scale to large areas. In many scenarios, these systems require high-precision localization while operating with limited resources, for example without an internet connection or without GNSS/GPS support, which makes large image databases or heavy 3D models impractical.

Current UAV localization algorithms either retrieve the closest match from a database of posed images, which is inaccurate, or rely on 3D models of the scene, which are expensive in memory and computation; in resource-limited settings, such as connectivity-limited environments, this can degrade accuracy. Image retrieval methods based on global descriptors struggle with the large viewpoint and illumination changes of UAV imagery, and even with view synthesis or self-supervised learning their performance drops under extreme perspective shifts, so retrieval alone remains insufficient for accurate 6-DoF localization. Structure-based methods build a 3D model with structure-from-motion, establish 2D-3D correspondences against meshes or dense depth maps, and estimate the pose with PnP solvers inside RANSAC, but such complete 3D models require extensive manual effort to create for each operational area. Most UAV-specific positioning methods estimate only 2-DoF or 3-DoF poses rather than the full 6-DoF pose required by advanced applications. Recent approaches based on level-of-detail (LoD) city models improve storage efficiency, but they still assume unchanged environments, perform poorly in building-sparse areas such as highways, and depend on positioning sensors for initialization.

A compelling alternative is geodata, such as orthographic aerial views (digital orthophotos) and elevation maps (digital surface models). Such data are lightweight, scalable and better suited to low-resource settings, and they are increasingly accessible through free releases from government geoportals, for instance in the European Union; where public access is limited, they can be synthesized with photogrammetric tools. For example, covering an area of approximately 0.265 km² can require a 3D model of around 8 GB, whereas geodata require about 30 times less memory. Surprisingly, no existing UAV localization approach seems to fully leverage these data sources: previous work has not used the combination of orthophotos and elevation models for UAV pose estimation, so no existing method is directly applicable to this scenario. Modern feature matchers (dense, semi-dense, sparse, and geometry-aware) perform robustly in many scenarios, but their effectiveness with orthographic geodata remains unexplored. A major reason for this gap is the absence of aligned cross-domain datasets and of full-pose, paired, large-scale benchmarks designed for localization with these types of geodata. Existing UAV localization datasets provide only partial pose information (2-DoF or 3-DoF), feature predominantly nadir views with limited viewpoint diversity, rely on entirely synthetic environments or synthetically rendered views that introduce domain gaps, or lack integrated geodata; the one concurrent collection that includes orthographic geodata focuses its pose evaluation on 3-DoF and suffers from a misalignment between its low-resolution satellite imagery and its aerial photogrammetry data. Furthermore, visual localization methods often need to solve image retrieval before estimating the pose; because these two steps are coupled, it is difficult to disentangle the contribution of each component to the final error.

The problem is therefore the following: given an orthophoto raster, an elevation raster, and a query UAV image taken from an arbitrary viewpoint, determine the georeferenced 6-DoF pose of the camera (localization) and, optionally, its intrinsic parameters (calibration). The key challenge is bridging two fundamentally different projection models: perspective projection for UAV imagery and orthographic projection for geodata. This difference creates a domain gap that is particularly pronounced in oblique views, where perspective distortion is significant. A second domain gap arises from visual and structural discrepancies between query and reference data caused by differences in acquisition time: reference geodata may have been collected months or years before a flight, so orthophotos differ in appearance (color shifts, illumination variations, seasonal differences) and elevation models differ in geometry (construction changes, vegetation growth, infrastructure evolution). These changes vary unpredictably across locations and seasons, cannot easily be addressed through simple data augmentation or domain adaptation, and cannot be faithfully replicated by synthetic alternatives.

This raises several open questions. Can lightweight 2.5D orthographic geodata serve as the only reference for accurate full 6-DoF UAV pose estimation and camera calibration? Can state-of-the-art feature matchers, designed largely for perspective imagery, bridge the perspective-orthographic gap, especially for oblique viewpoints, and how can the perspective disparity between query and reference be reduced? How difficult is it to recover camera intrinsics from aerial imagery in this setting? And how do characteristics of the reference data, namely temporal visual and structural domain shifts, data resolution, and the covisibility between the query image and the reference area (which depends on imperfect upstream retrieval), affect localization accuracy?

In cloud services, Internet of Things deployments and monitoring systems, data are often represented as univariate time series (UTS), in which each timestamp records a single variable. Anomalies arise, for instance, when a website is subject to malicious attacks or experiences excessive server load, and they are typically reflected in UTS derived from traffic and system-load monitoring. Missed or delayed detection of such events can have severe consequences. Anomalies in UTS are usually divided into two types: point anomalies, which are abrupt deviations (either global or contextual), and segment anomalies, which reflect more subtle shifts in trends or periodic patterns.

Formally, given observations x_0, x_1, ..., x_t with anomaly labels c_0, c_1, ..., c_t, where c_i = 0 marks a normal point and c_i = 1 an anomaly, the goal of UTS anomaly detection is to determine c_i for each point x_i from the history x_0, ..., x_{i-1} that precedes it, without access to future points. Because labels are scarce in practice and supervised detectors generalize poorly under label scarcity or distribution shift, unsupervised approaches have become the dominant paradigm. Reconstruction-based and prediction-based methods both model normal behavior and flag anomalies by comparing reconstructed or predicted values with the actual observations. Reconstruction-based techniques try to map abnormal segments to a normal space, but the lack of ground truth for anomalies leads to poor reconstruction and degraded performance, and they treat time windows independently, ignoring temporal dependencies. Prediction-based methods built on deep sequence models such as Transformers perform strongly on multivariate time series, where they can model complex dependencies; in UTS, however, each timestamp contains only one value, which restricts the representation of temporal context and leads to suboptimal performance.

In particular, existing detectors struggle with two kinds of subtle anomalies that remain largely undetected: (1) small point anomalies, short-term spikes that look normal when viewed over longer windows; and (2) slowly rising anomalies, gradual segment-level deviations from periodic patterns. These misses stem from limitations of current designs: for example, a frequency-conditioned reconstruction approach focuses on frequency components rather than local dependencies and fails to capture subtle point anomalies or gradual segment anomalies, while a recent prediction approach uses timing information but ignores frequency details.

Detecting these anomalies raises three challenges. First, local trends matter more than absolute values: the absolute magnitude of a change is insufficient to decide whether a point is anomalous. In one series, changes between 0.5 and 1 may be abnormal, whereas in another, similar changes are normal and only variations exceeding 5 are anomalous; what counts as abnormal depends on the value distribution and change patterns within a short local window. Second, periodicity evolves rather than staying static: time series exhibit evolving trends and periodicity, and periodicity varies over time and across datasets, including changes in period length and frequency. Without future points, distinguishing slow anomalies from normal periodic changes is difficult, and methods that focus only on the adjacent historical period neglect this evolution; modeling periodicity that is both dynamic and heterogeneous is hard. Third, normal patterns must be learned amid anomalies and noise: real-world series contain long-term noise and sudden anomalies, both of which hinder the learning of normal patterns. Noise introduces significant fluctuations that make it difficult to fit the underlying normal behavior, and the lack of ground-truth labels for anomaly positions prevents a model from computing reliable training losses.

The question is therefore how an unsupervised detector for univariate time series, relying only on past observations, can capture both local trends and the evolution of periodic patterns, while learning normal behavior robustly from training data contaminated by noise and unlabeled anomalies, so that small point anomalies and slowly rising anomalies are detected accurately and promptly.

Recent advances in computer graphics and vision have highlighted image relighting, that is, changing the illumination of an existing image, as a critical task for film production, augmented reality and digital content creation. Full-image relighting, in which both the objects and the surrounding scene must be relit, remains a challenging problem.

Existing works can be grouped into object-centric approaches, which often ignore or replace the background, and scene-level methods, which attempt full-image relighting but remain largely data-driven: they struggle to generalize beyond the training distribution without extensive and diverse data, and cannot maintain the lighting of self-luminous objects. Even state-of-the-art foreground relighting methods still suffer from albedo inconsistency and imprecise lighting control: relighting can, for instance, alter the colors of a carpet, or make light intended to come from the left appear to come from the left rear although the scene contains no internal light source. Other lines of work have their own restrictions. Many methods address only portraits or isolated objects. Scribble-based control of scene lighting lacks precision and has been limited to indoor scenes. Outdoor full-image relighting methods either require surface normals as input or rely on directional lighting models that generalize poorly to indoor scenes. A recent generative approach that simulates both inverse rendering (recovering intrinsic properties such as albedo, surface normals, roughness and metallicity from an image) and forward rendering conditions the forward step on irradiance, which makes precise lighting control challenging, and is limited to indoor scenes. Intrinsic decomposition methods are themselves hampered by the difficulty of acquiring large-scale training data and are mostly designed for specific scenarios, such as indoor scenes or single objects. These limitations point to the lack of a physically interpretable representation of the scene in current relighting methods and to the inherent limitations of data-driven priors, both of which stand in the way of controllable and physically plausible full-image relighting.

Three major challenges follow. First, data with diverse and complex scene illumination are hard to acquire: obtaining high-quality images of full scenes under diverse and controlled lighting conditions is resource-intensive and technically challenging, and it is infeasible to capture real-world datasets that show the same scene under multiple lighting conditions. Existing datasets that provide intrinsic components focus mainly on indoor scenes and do not render images under varying lighting conditions. Second, ensuring physical plausibility is difficult, as purely data-driven approaches often generate results that violate basic light transport principles. Third, limited data-driven priors restrict generalizability, leading to poor robustness to unseen materials, lighting conditions and realistic scene compositions, and existing attempts to bridge the gap between synthetic training data and real images for full-scene relighting remain suboptimal. Full scenes add a further difficulty: self-luminous objects and built-in light sources, such as light coming through windows, interfere with controlling the direction and intensity of the new lighting while keeping the background consistent.

This raises the following questions. How can an entire image, objects and scene together, indoor or outdoor, be relit under a user-specified lighting condition with precise control of light direction and intensity, while preserving the albedo and material appearance of its surfaces, the content and consistency of the background, and the lighting of self-luminous elements? How can a relighting model be made to respect basic light transport, so that shading, highlights and shadows follow the new lighting across a wide variety of materials? And how can such a model generalize to real-world images with unseen materials, lighting conditions and scene compositions when paired data under controlled lighting are scarce and real captures of the same scene under multiple lightings are infeasible?

Knowledge distillation is a fundamental technique in machine learning, widely used for model compression, transfer learning, and improving generalization. Its core idea is to transfer knowledge from a "teacher" model to a (typically smaller) "student" model by training the student to match the teacher's output probabilities rather than categorical one-hot labels. This softened supervision has been shown to improve performance across a range of tasks. Consequently, a substantial body of research has focused on designing distillation mechanisms, such as dynamic temperature scaling, feature-based distillation, and task-aware teacher-student matching, typically assuming a large teacher that is optimized to maximize its own performance.

Despite its widespread adoption, the theoretical foundations of knowledge distillation remain only partially understood. In particular, the impact of the teacher's output probabilities on the student's optimization trajectory and generalization has not been fully characterized. Existing explanations attribute the usefulness of distillation to the regularizing effect of the teacher's soft estimates, to trade-offs such as precision versus recall or knowledge inheritance versus exploration, or to factors such as data geometry and optimization bias. Insights into how distillation affects the optimization itself have been developed only for special cases, such as self-distillation or a student that is a compressed version of the teacher, and rely on dedicated gradient approximations. A principled understanding of how distillation affects common learning algorithms, such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants, for arbitrary teachers, is still lacking.

Recent works have begun to view distillation through a Bayesian lens, interpreting the teacher's outputs as (possibly noisy) estimates of the true class posterior probabilities of the data-generating distribution. From this statistical viewpoint, learning from accurate class posteriors has been argued to reduce the variance of the student's objective, and excess-risk and generalization bounds have been derived in terms of the distance between the teacher's predictions and the true posteriors. These analyses, however, characterize the statistical properties of the risk rather than the behavior of the learning algorithm that actually trains the student. The probabilistic perspective thus opens relatively unexplored questions about the dynamics of SGD-based learning under probabilistic supervision, and about how the statistical calibration of the teacher influences the student. Teacher calibration has been recognized as a key driver of distillation, but it remains unclear how the quality of the teacher's probability estimates should guide the way teachers are built.

This raises several questions. How does supervising a student with the exact class posterior probabilities, instead of one-hot labels, change the convergence behavior and stability of SGD-based learning and the generalization of the resulting student? In the realistic case where the teacher provides only imperfect, noisy estimates of these posteriors, how does the level of estimation error affect the student's convergence, generalization and accuracy, and under what conditions does probabilistic supervision remain preferable to one-hot labels? Finally, what practical guidelines follow for designing or choosing teacher models, beyond maximizing the teacher's own accuracy, so that their outputs provide better supervision for students trained with SGD-based optimizers?
