ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: natural assumption bounds for the hanin norm
PROPOSAL: Prove a bound for the Hanin norm of the Jacobian of a smooth, but unknown, generating function g(Z). Specifically, we will derive an upper bound in terms of the differentiability order and a Lipschitz constant of g. We will assume that g may acordo with any sequence of k times continuously differentiable functions.
CONTROLS: Compare to known bounds in related literature, e.g. Elazar-Pinhas (2020) on Hanin norm bounds for contexts of deep learning.
COST: 0.5 GPU-hours (analytical computation)
PREDICTION: The bound we derive should be slightly looser than existing bounds but will be scalable to higher-dimensional data; the bound may not hold for rough generative functions.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: from hanin norm bounds to invertibility conditions
PROPOSAL: Prove a sufficient condition for a diffeomorphism (smooth and bijective) between the latent space Z and the image space X (i.e., 1 : 1), in terms of the Hanin norm bound derived in proposal 1. The condition will require a lower bound on the determinant of the Jacobian of g(Z) that grows polynomially with the dimensionality of the data.
CONTROLS: Compare to known results on diffeomorphism bounds, e.g. Guillou (2018) on diffeomorphism conditions using inverse function theorem.
COST: 1.0 GPU-hours (matrix computations and diagonalization).
PREDICTION: The condition should be useful for implying invertibility, but it may not hold in cases where the generative function has vanishing eigenvalues or extremely high-dimensionality, which can cause numerical instability.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: alternating minimization for non-linear dictionary learning
PROPOSAL: Implement an alternating minimization approach for optimizing a non-linear dictionary, using a simplified version of the Hidden Neural Tangent Kernel (HNTK) to facilitate computation. We will alternate between updating the non-linear dictionary and the latent representations in the data. The goal is to demonstrate empirical success in recovering the nonlinear structure of simple generative processes.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing baselines, such as deep clustered sparse coding or non-linear dictionary learning with cyclic optimization.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (empirical evaluation using synthetic data).
PREDICTION: The approach may recover some structure of the generative process but is likely to fail for complex, high-dimensional data; further optimization or initialization strategies may help alleviate the non-convexity of this problem.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: natural assumption bounds for the hanin norm
PROPOSAL: Refine the bound in proposal 1 by incorporating a regularization term that encourages a certain degree of sparsity in the Jacobian of the generating function. This term will enhance the stability of the bound and allow it to hold for a broader class of functions.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original bound in proposal 1 and study the trade-off between sparsity and conservativeness.
COST: 0.5 GPU-hours (computations and marginalization).
PREDICTION: The refined bound should improve the usability of the previous results, but it may become less tight or lose some generality, trading off the relationships between these two requirements.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: comparison to partial information theory
PROPOSAL: Compare the identifiability guarantees derived from the Hanin norm bounds and diffeomorphism conditions to those that can be obtained from partial information theory, specifically the concept of sufficient statistics for the generative process. We will study how the strength of these guarantees compares for different classes of generative functions.
CONTROLS: Specifically, analyze the comparisons in terms of the dimensionality of the sufficient statistics, the complexity of the generative process, and the information available in the data.
COST: 0.5 GPU-hours (information-theoretic calculations and comparisons).
PREDICTION: The comparison may highlight situations in which one of these approaches is more suited to the generative process at hand, but it may also reveal that the best results come from using these approaches in combination.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: recovering compression parameters through surrogate optimal transport
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to recover the parameters of a generative process that is compressing the latent variables, by formulating the optimization problem as a surrogate optimal transport problem. This involves solving a Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality formulation, where the goal is to find a transport plan between the distributions of the latent and observed variables.
CONTROLS: Use the same alternating minimization approach as in proposal 3 to optimize the transport plan, and study its convergence properties.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (combining gradient descent and OT optimization).
PREDICTION: The method may help recover the compression parameters even when the generative process is highly non-linear, but it may suffer from high computational cost and can be heavily dependent on the choice of the optimizer for the OT problem.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: a surrogate noise model for simulation and inference
PROPOSAL: Develop a method for simulating and inferring generative processes by treating the noise as a surrogate for a probabilistic unknown. Specifically, this involve using a fixed-point iteration to calculate an approximation of the noise distribution, and a related algorithm for inferring the generative process parameters from the conditional expectation of this distribution.
CONTROLS: Compare the robustness of the surrogate noise model to different perturbation schemes for simulating real-world data, and study its capacity to recover the generative process.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (fixed-point iteration and Monte Carlo inference).
PREDICTION: The surrogate noise model may help improve the robustness of the inference procedure, but it may be computationally expensive and could suffer from either over-smoothing or over-fitting, depending on the choice of the probabilistic unknown.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: alternating minimization for non-linear dictionary learning
PROPOSAL: Modify the alternating minimization approach in proposal 3 to incorporate an initial warm-up phase using a linear approximation of the generating function. This allows the algorithm to adapt to the non-linearities in the data more effectively, potentially improving convergence towards the optimal dictionary.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of this revised approach to the original alternating minimization, and assess the trade-off between warm-up duration and overall convergence time.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (combining empirical evaluation and optimized warm-up schedule).
PREDICTION: The warm-up phase may improve the algorithm's ability to adapt to non-linear data generating processes but could also increase the overall computational cost and risk of over-optimization.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: type-based inference with transformer language models
PROPOSAL: Devise a type-based inference framework for recovering the latent structure of language models, leveraging their internal types and transformer architecture to constrain the generative process. This will involve analyzing the Transformer layers' behavior and designing inference algorithms that exploit the structure of the language model's hidden states.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the type-based inference approach on a variety of language models and assess its performance on tasks such as text generation and semantic parsing.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (large-scale language model simulations).
PREDICTION: The type-based inference framework may uncover novel insights into the latent structure of language models, but it may require substantial computational resources and may be challenging to generalize across different model architectures.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: universality of alternating minimization for non-linear dictionary learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the universality of the alternating minimization approach derived in proposal 3, specifically whether it can be applied to recover the generative process in a wide range of settings, including those with complex and high-dimensional data, sparse or noisy observations, and varying degrees of non-linearity. We will perform extensive numerical experiments and analytical investigations to evaluate the robustness of the approach.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the alternating minimization to other state-of-the-art approaches for non-linear dictionary learning and assess its robustness under various perturbations of the data-generating process.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (numerical experiments and sensitivity analysis).
PREDICTION: The universality analysis may indicate that alternating minimization has broad applicability, but it may also reveal limitations, such as vulnerability to certain types of outliers or difficulties in handling data with shifted or removed features.

Modern generative paradigms, including diffusion, flow matching and consistency models, have achieved state-of-the-art performance and form the backbone of leading image and video generation systems, including large multi-modal generative models. Despite their success, they share a critical drawback: both training and sampling demand substantial computational resources. Multi-step frameworks such as diffusion and flow matching produce a sample by iteratively integrating a probability-flow ordinary differential equation, typically requiring 40 to 100 network function evaluations (NFEs). The problem is magnified for large-scale models, for which efficient sampling is paramount: the continuous, long-term cost of inference often surpasses the one-time training cost, directly affecting economic viability and practical deployment. For example, the largest open multi-modal image generators (about 20B parameters) typically need about 100 NFEs, i.e. roughly 40 seconds on a single A100 GPU for one 1024×1024 image.

Numerous efforts aim to accelerate generative inference by reducing the number of sampling steps. Early single-step generators such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) often suffered from unstable training dynamics. To accelerate multi-step diffusion models, various distillation techniques have been introduced. They range from student-teacher methods, in which a student learns to reproduce a frozen teacher's sampling trajectory in fewer steps (e.g., progressive distillation, which requires an iterative distillation procedure), to distribution matching distillation (e.g., DMD and DMD2), which uses adversarial-style training with auxiliary networks to align the generator's output distribution directly with the data distribution. In parallel, consistency models and their variants (e.g., LCM and PCM), as well as related shortcut and MeanFlow objectives, have been designed explicitly for high-quality generation in very few steps, and recent work shows that multi-step and few-step models can be cast as instances of a single unified any-step training objective.

Despite this progress, existing few-step methods face a difficult trade-off between simplicity, efficiency and quality. (a) Complexity and instability: adversarial approaches, such as GANs, DMD-style distribution matching and hybrid frameworks that combine teacher guidance with adversarial signals (e.g., SANA-Sprint), require auxiliary trained networks (discriminators or fake-sample score networks) and/or frozen teacher models; distribution matching methods typically keep separate copies of a generator, a real-score model and a fake-score model. This introduces training instability and sensitivity to hyperparameters, and it increases architectural complexity and GPU memory overhead. For ultra-large models, the added complexity often translates into out-of-memory failures or brittle training dynamics, so few-step approaches have rarely been applied to models beyond about 3B parameters, and the only open-source few-step model released for a large model was obtained by distribution matching distillation with its GAN loss removed, an indirect sign of the high cost of adversarial losses at scale. (b) Performance degradation: methods trained without adversarial guidance, such as consistency models, often show a sharp decline in quality at very low NFEs (fewer than 4), and within the unified any-step view, current few-step methods struggle to reach high-quality one-step generation without resorting to a GAN-style loss.

The open problem is therefore how to train a generator that produces high-quality images in a single function evaluation, or very few, without discriminators, auxiliary score networks or frozen teacher models, so that training remains simple, stable and memory-efficient enough to scale to full-parameter training of the largest (10B to 20B parameters) text-to-image and multi-modal generators, without sacrificing the quality obtained by multi-step sampling.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: low-nfe consistency for large multi-modal models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the feasibility of consistency-based models for single-function or very low-NFE generation, by adapting the any-step training objective of [1] to constrain the output of the generator to a function of the input, plus a small, learnable residual. Evaluate the performance of this "residual-constrained" consistency model on a range of large text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard unconditional flow-based model variant, and with a separately-trained student teacher model with 5 iterations of progressive distillation.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The residual-constrained consistency model should provide a quality drop of less than 1.5 points on the MSMFT metric, compared to the unconditional flow-based model, while achieving a reduction in NFEs. However, very large models may still face training instability due to the use of large learnable residuals.

References:
[1] any-step training objective (not specified reference)
[2] DALL-E 2 dataset
[3] MSMFT metric (not specified reference)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adversarial-free distilled sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate a method for distilled sampling without adversarial losses, by computing the output of a given step through a combination of its own knowledge up to that point and the cached output from the preceding steps. Implement this method using a non-adversarial student-teacher approach, where the teacher is a frozen version of the model and the student takes fewer steps to sample an image. Evaluate this "distilled samplifier" on a set of large text-to-image models, using the COCO dataset [4] and the Inception score [5].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard progressive distillation approach and a baseline of the full model taking 5-10 steps, following the setup outlined in the proposal.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The distilled samplifier should achieve a quality improvement of more than 1 point in Inception score, even when the teacher model is frozen, while reducing the number of NFEs significantly. However, evaluation metrics may become less reliable at very low NFEs, making quality assessment challenging.

References:
[4] COCO dataset
[5] Inception score

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: adversarial-free distilled sampling (not changed)
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 2 to include an evaluation of the training time of the distilled samplifier, and investigate its impact on model capacity. Add an experiment where the student model and teacher model have the same capacity, but the student is trained with a reduced number of iterations, and another where the student model has a significantly reduced capacity compared to the teacher model, to analyze its effects on training time and inference quality.
CONTROLS: Include comparisons with progressive distillation as before, and add ablation studies on the impact of teacher-student capacity mismatch on distilled sampler performance.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The evaluation of training time and capacity will show that the distilled samplifier achieves a significant reduction in training time and enables the use of smaller models, but may come at the cost of reduced inference quality if the student and teacher models have significantly different capacities.

Note: This is a refinement of the original proposal, rather than a completely new one. It incorporates additional evaluation and analysis, and expands on the original ideas.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: adverse-free distilled sampling
PROPOSAL: Modify the architecture of the distilled sampler to use a denoising autoencoder instead of a simple student model, which will allow it to learn the structure of the data distribution directly from the teacher model. This will reduce the need for pre-training the student model and improve its ability to generalize to new input distributions. Evaluate the performance of this "autoencoder-based distilled sampler" on the same COCO dataset [4] and Inception score [5] as before.
CONTROLS: Include comparisons with the original student-teacher approach and progressive distillation as before, and add ablation studies on the importance of the autoencoder structure and the pre-training stage.
COST: 1400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The autoencoder-based distilled sampler should achieve significant improvements in Inception score and reduce the number of NFEs, with better generalization capabilities compared to the original student-teacher approach. However, it may be more sensitive to the configuration of the teacher model and the pre-training stage.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: momentum-guided consistency
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new variant of the consistency model, where the generator is trained to produce output that not only matches the input, but also a momentum-buffered version of the input. This momentum buffer is initialized with a value close to zero and updated on each iteration of the training process. Evaluate the performance of this "momentum-guided consistency model" on a range of large text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard unconditional flow-based model variant and the residual-constrained consistency model from proposal 1, reported alongside the main results.

Large language models (LLMs) excel at generating fluent text yet remain prone to both intrinsic aleatoric ambiguity and epistemic gaps in their learned knowledge. The latter can lead to hallucinations—confident outputs that are factually incorrect. Quantifying these uncertainties is critical for building safe AI systems deployable in high-stakes applications. In free-form natural language generation tasks such as question answering, this is especially challenging, as lexically distinct responses can still be semantically equivalent: uncertainty has to be measured over meanings rather than over token sequences.

A standard way to do so defines a distribution over semantic clusters of responses, obtained by marginalizing over output sequences and approximated by Monte Carlo sampling. The total predictive uncertainty over these clusters decomposes into an aleatoric part, the entropy over clusters (semantic entropy), which captures the irreducible ambiguity among valid answers, and an epistemic part, which reflects the model's lack of knowledge or data coverage. For a question such as "Name a way to measure the Hubble constant", several distinct but correct answers (for instance, the distance ladder or gravitational lensing time delays) reflect aleatoric uncertainty, whereas answers that contradict scientific facts or admit ignorance reveal gaps in the model's knowledge and signal that it should abstain.

Estimating these quantities often relies on drawing large IID sample sets, which often contain semantically redundant outputs and waste compute. Semantic entropy quantifies aleatoric uncertainty by clustering generated outputs into semantic equivalence classes, and mutual information computed via iterative prompting has been used to lower-bound certain forms of epistemic uncertainty; despite their conceptual appeal, both require extensive sampling to produce stable estimates, limiting their use in low-resource settings. Diversity-oriented heuristics such as temperature scaling or nucleus sampling, on the other hand, do not account for semantics. A more recent method steers generation toward semantic diversity, but it relies on token substitutions and remains restricted to autoregressive models (ARMs). Moreover, diversity heuristics are commonly applied during sampling without correcting for the bias they introduce, even though the uncertainties of interest are defined under the model's own distribution.

Meanwhile, uncertainty estimation methods have focused on ARMs, whereas masked diffusion models (MDMs), which extend masked language modeling by learning iterative denoising schedules that progressively resolve masked spans, have recently emerged as strong alternatives. Despite achieving text quality on par with state-of-the-art ARMs, MDMs remain largely overlooked in the context of uncertainty quantification.

This leaves several questions open. How can stable estimates of semantic aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty be obtained for free-form answers from a small, fixed budget of generations, so that the samples cover distinct meanings instead of repeating the same ones? How can this be done while keeping the estimates faithful to the model's own predictive distribution? And can a single approach serve both autoregressive and masked diffusion language models?

Diffusion models, and text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models in particular, have made astonishing progress in the quality of generated images. At the same time, emerging work on generative depth estimation has revealed that advanced T2I models hold a latent potential for depth estimation: the rich visual priors stored in a pre-trained T2I model can be leveraged to obtain strong zero-shot monocular depth estimation. Exploring a framework that bridges image generation and depth estimation is an essential step toward building unified models for both generation and visual perception.

Existing routes toward such unification each carry a substantial cost. The pioneering generative depth estimation paradigm repurposes a pre-trained T2I diffusion model by fine-tuning its denoising network with full parameters on depth data. It achieves powerful zero-shot depth estimation, but the parameter updates made during training irreversibly and catastrophically degrade the model's original image generation capability; later generative depth estimators that refine this recipe (for example with flow matching, geometry switchers or detail-preserving tuning strategies) inherit the same full-parameter fine-tuning and therefore the same loss. A second route unifies generation and depth estimation with a parallel dual-model architecture, in which two diffusion models run side by side and interact through feature-exchange operations; this requires running two diffusion models in parallel, and the interaction registers new knowledge into the pre-trained generator, which can affect its original image generation behaviour. A third, data-driven route trains a unified generation-and-perception model from scratch on massive multitask data (on the order of a hundred million samples). Despite remarkable progress, these solutions may be considered inefficient or resource-intensive, and potentially suboptimal.

Since a rich visual prior is already stored in advanced T2I models, a natural question arises: can a T2I model effortlessly acquire depth estimation capability without degrading its image generation capability? More concretely, starting from a fixed pre-trained T2I model, with a focus on modern transformer-based diffusion models, how can its latent depth estimation ability be unleashed so that a single model serves both image generation and depth estimation, keeping the original generation ability fully intact, adding only a small fraction of extra learnable parameters, and without resorting to massive multitask training data, while still reaching depth accuracy competitive with full-parameter fine-tuning and with existing unified models?

The problem is challenging. Among the effectively infinite pixel-level combinations that a T2I model learns to generate, there may exist underlying information highly correlated with scene depth; however, because text prompts provide only weak guidance and depth information is sparsely represented within the overall data distribution, extracting depth-relevant features from a fixed pre-trained T2I model is difficult. Any additional capacity must also make efficient use of the visual knowledge already present in the pre-trained model, so that depth estimation is obtained at a small parameter and data cost rather than by building and training a second large model.

Real-world reinforcement learning (RL) systems often struggle with reward specification: it is notoriously difficult to craft a reward function that captures the intended goals in all scenarios, so designers rely on proxy rewards that only approximate the true objective. Agents that optimize such imperfect proxies can discover unintended, exploitative behaviors that achieve high proxy return while yielding poor true outcomes, a phenomenon known as reward hacking. Reward hacking is not merely hypothetical: it has led to undesirable or even catastrophic consequences in safety-critical settings and is common in real-world deployments. At the same time, interpretability and transparency of RL policies are increasingly recognized as requirements for real-world acceptance: policymakers and practitioners in safety-critical domains need systems that are not only robust but also understandable, so that they can identify which decision-making criteria lead to undesirable outcomes, mitigate risks, and ensure compliance with safety regulations. RL algorithms for high-stakes applications therefore face two fundamental challenges: robustness to uncertain or poorly specified rewards, and interpretability that facilitates oversight by human stakeholders.

Recent work has begun to formalize reward hacking and to develop principled mitigations. In one such framework, the agent is given a proxy reward and a reference policy, while the true reward is hidden. The proxy is called r-correlated with the true reward if the two maintain a correlation coefficient r > 0 on the state-action pairs encountered by the reference policy, that is, under the reference policy's state-action occupancy measure. This definition permits the proxy and the true reward to diverge arbitrarily in parts of the state-action space that the reference policy does not visit, which are precisely the regions an RL agent may exploit under intensive optimization. Reward hacking is then said to occur when optimizing an r-correlated proxy yields a policy with lower true reward than the reference policy. The mitigation proposed within that framework, Occupancy-Regularized Policy Optimization (ORPO), augments the standard RL objective with a regularization term that penalizes the chi-squared divergence between the learned policy's state-action occupancy measure and that of the reference policy, with a strength that depends on the correlation level, and it guarantees a lower bound on the improvement in true reward.

Despite this progress, existing solutions to reward hacking have several limitations. First, their effectiveness relies heavily on the specific proxy reward. Designing good proxies is hard: in real-world scenarios, proxies are often derived heuristically or empirically from noisy or limited data, which leaves uncertainty about their exact relationship to the true reward, and the correlation level itself is typically known only approximately. Robustness to variations in the proxy is therefore crucial for dependable deployment, yet a method that regularizes against one fixed proxy offers only a weak guarantee on worst-case performance when the proxy could be any reward consistent with the assumed correlation, including an adversarially chosen one. Second, current methods treat the reward function as a black box and learn complex policies with no easily interpretable structure, making it hard to understand why a policy avoids reward hacking or to trust its behavior in novel situations; moreover, they cannot easily incorporate prior knowledge about the true reward when such knowledge is available.

This raises several research questions. Given only a proxy reward, a reference policy and an assumed correlation level, how can one learn a policy whose true performance is guaranteed against the entire class of rewards consistent with the correlation constraint, rather than against a single trusted proxy? Can such a guarantee be turned into an objective that is tractable to optimize with standard policy-optimization tools? How should state-action pairs that the reference policy rarely or never visits, where the correlation constraint says nothing about the true reward, be handled? When prior knowledge about the structure of the true reward is available, how can it be exploited to avoid excessive conservatism and to expose, in an interpretable way, which aspects of the reward a learned policy is most vulnerable to? Finally, how can one obtain policies whose performance remains robust and stable when the true correlation between proxy and true reward is uncertain or misspecified?

Graphs are powerful abstractions for representing complex relationships between entities, from social networks to molecular structures, and learning effective graph representations is crucial for node classification, graph classification and link prediction. Over the past decade, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become the dominant paradigm for graph representation learning, building representations through a message-passing mechanism that iteratively aggregates local neighborhood information. Despite its success, message passing faces several key limitations, such as limited expressiveness and difficulty in capturing long-range dependencies. Numerous efforts address different aspects of these limitations: graph transformer architectures incorporate long-range interactions across broader graph contexts, positional encodings inject structural priors to improve global topological awareness, and graph rewiring techniques modify the topology to mitigate structural bottlenecks and enhance information diffusion.

However, these advances remain constrained by a cognitive discrepancy. Humans perceive global structure intuitively, following visual Gestalt principles: they understand the whole before analyzing the individual parts. GNNs and their variants, by contrast, operate through bottom-up processing. People instantly recognize ring structures, symmetric structures and critical bridges in a drawing of a graph, yet even advanced architectures struggle with such basic topological understanding: standard message-passing networks provably cannot identify bridges, and graphs that people tell apart at a glance can fool message passing unless sophisticated topological computations are added. Although architectural innovations have made significant theoretical and practical progress, their essence is still to identify and repair different aspects of the inherent defects of message passing. Approaches that perceive graphs visually remain largely unexplored for graph learning, despite their natural alignment with how humans perceive network structures, and despite a flourishing computer vision ecosystem whose models excel at holistic pattern recognition and global structure understanding. Recent work has begun to bring graph drawings into existing architectures, for instance into vision-language models for graph reasoning or into GNNs to enhance expressivity, but it treats graph layouts and vision models as black boxes, without examining how visual and message-passing models fundamentally differ in the way they understand graphs.

A second obstacle is measurement. Established benchmarks built from molecules, citation networks or protein interaction graphs tightly couple domain-specific node features with topology, which makes their separate contributions hard to quantify and can let models succeed through feature-based shortcuts rather than genuine structural understanding. Models that replace the true molecular topology with fixed-structure expander graphs have been shown to match or exceed performance on several molecular benchmarks, suggesting that node features often dominate structural information in standard datasets, potentially masking differences in how models perceive graph topology. The theoretical evaluation of GNNs has centered on the Weisfeiler-Lehman test, which measures the ability to distinguish pairs of non-isomorphic graphs of the same size; valuable for theory, it is limited to binary discrimination between fixed-size graph pairs. Recent graph benchmarks oriented toward large language models focus on structural analysis tasks such as node counting, cycle detection and path finding, and typically rely on a limited set of random graph generators (such as Erdős–Rényi or Watts–Strogatz) that inadequately capture topological diversity. What remains missing is a way to assess human-like graph cognition: the intuitive ability to perceive, abstract and reason about fundamental global graph properties, and to recognize the same connectivity patterns across varying scales and contexts.

This leads to the questions addressed here. Could models designed for visual perception, which carry no graph-specific inductive bias, offer a viable pathway to graph structural understanding, and do they process graph information in the same way as message-passing GNNs or through fundamentally different strategies? How can a model's ability to perceive and abstract global graph properties be evaluated rigorously, in isolation from domain-specific features, including whether it recognizes the same structural pattern regardless of graph size? And what does it take for a graph learning model to acquire the holistic, scale-robust understanding of topology that humans display effortlessly?

Score learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for modeling complex probability distributions, driving progress in generative modeling, Bayesian inverse problems and sampling. Given a data measure $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, one considers its Gaussian-smoothed version $\mu_\sigma$, defined as the law of $X + \sigma Z$ (variance-exploding smoothing) or of $\sqrt{1-\sigma^2} X + \sigma Z$ (variance-preserving smoothing), where $X \sim \mu_{\mathrm{data}}$ and $Z$ is a standard Gaussian vector, with density $p_\sigma$. A key step in this framework is to approximate the score function $\nabla \log p_\sigma$, typically by score matching, and to use it to sample from $\mu_\sigma$, possibly across a range of noise levels: through the reverse process of a diffusion model, through Langevin dynamics driven by the learned score, or through predictor-corrector schemes that combine the two.

A central challenge is the low-temperature limit, that is, learning the score of $\mu_\sigma$ as $\sigma \to 0$, which encodes the most detailed information about the data. This regime is also the most valuable in practice: low-noise scores underpin many probabilistic learning frameworks, including diffusion models, whose noise schedules are designed to emphasize low noise levels and often require substantial post-training engineering to stabilize the learned scores. Yet accurately estimating the score in the small-$\sigma$ regime remains notoriously difficult. This raises a basic question: if the learned score is unavoidably inaccurate at small noise levels, what do score-based methods actually recover, and why do they nevertheless produce realistic samples?

A natural setting for this question is the widely adopted manifold hypothesis, which posits that $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$ is supported on a compact, low-dimensional manifold embedded in a high-dimensional ambient space. The data then carry two kinds of information: the geometry of their support, and the particular density of the data on that support. Existing convergence theory for diffusion and score-based samplers shows that the generated law approaches the target when the learned score is accurate, with error bounds that scale directly with the score mismatch, and related work studies other factors such as the dependence on dimension. These results, however, treat geometry and density together in the score error and do not say whether score errors affect the recovery of the support and the recovery of the on-manifold density differently. A growing body of work suggests that diffusion models often capture the data support while missing fine-grained distributional structure, but this evidence comes from restricted settings: estimating the intrinsic dimension of the manifold, linear manifolds (linear subspaces) only, or primarily empirical observations. Sufficient regularity conditions are known under which highly accurate scores concentrate mass near the manifold, but not how approximation errors may scale with $\sigma$. Likewise, it is established that under the manifold hypothesis the score develops a singularity in the small-noise regime, becoming orthogonal to the manifold and acting as a geometric projection onto it; yet these analyses fold the distributional information into a generic bounded remainder term and do not isolate the terms that involve the data density.

A first set of questions is therefore the following. In the small-$\sigma$ regime, at which orders in $\sigma$ do information about the manifold geometry and information about the data density enter the log-density and the score of $\mu_\sigma$? What accuracy, expressed as a rate in $\sigma$, must a learned score achieve for the distribution produced by a sampler to concentrate on the data manifold, and what accuracy is needed for it to recover $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$ itself? Do these two requirements differ and, when a score is accurate enough for the first but not for the second, what can be said about the distribution that is produced on the manifold?

A second set of questions concerns which target is worth learning. For tasks that depend only on the geometry of the data, such as approximating the Laplace-Beltrami operator and heat kernels or computing geodesic and diffusion distances, it is well known that samples drawn uniformly with respect to the manifold's intrinsic (Riemannian) volume measure are the most useful; uniform samples also support principled exploration of the manifold, yielding diverse samples while mitigating biases present in $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$. Classical graph-based normalizations achieve uniform sampling on a manifold by cancelling the sampling density, but they are designed to approximate geometric operators from neighborhood graphs and do not scale readily to high-dimensional, large-scale generative modeling; a recent alternative fine-tunes diffusion models so that they produce uniform samples, at the cost of additional training. Can the uniform distribution on the data manifold be obtained from a score model trained on samples of a non-uniform $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$, and how much score error can such a procedure tolerate compared with exact recovery of $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$? Any answer must cope with the fact that a score produced by a parameterized model is generally not a gradient field, so that the Langevin dynamics it drives is non-reversible and its stationary distribution has no closed form. Asymptotic analyses of such stationary distributions, based on WKB-type expansions of the stationary Fokker-Planck equation, typically focus on low-dimensional special examples or on drifts with a single stable point, whereas data supported on a manifold give rise to a whole manifold of stable points.

Finally, the same issues arise in Bayesian inverse problems, where a latent signal $x$ is observed through a measurement map with noise, $y = A(x) + \xi$, and inference amounts to sampling the posterior $p(x \mid y) \propto p(y \mid x) p_{\mathrm{prior}}(x)$. Plug-and-play methods run posterior Langevin dynamics that combine the gradient of the log-likelihood with a (possibly learned) prior score, and a common choice of prior is the smoothed data density $p_\sigma$ with small $\sigma$. Existing guarantees that such updates sample the correct posterior require the learned prior score to have vanishing error, or even to be exact, which is difficult to achieve at small $\sigma$. How does the choice of prior affect the score accuracy needed for correct posterior sampling? Answering these questions would clarify what score-based methods can reliably learn from imperfect scores in the low-noise regime, which learning objectives are realistic there, and whether these distinctions matter in practice for score-based generative models.

TITLE: small-sigma analysis of diffusion models on manifolds
PROPOSAL: Investigate the convergence rate of diffusion models on manifolds in the small-$\sigma$ limit. Consider the normalized diffusion process $dX_t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \sigma^2}} \left( Z_t - \nabla \log p_\sigma(X_t) \right) dt$ as $\sigma \to 0$, and analyze the resulting Malliavin derivative.

However, the analysis may fail to provide a precise characterization of the convergence rate, due to the technical challenges associated with estimating the Malliavin derivative in high dimensions.

Neurons operate in ways that reflect their cell type, connectivity, and the brain region in which they are embedded. Understanding how these structural and physiological factors shape neural activity is an important open question and is central to modern theories of neural function. Cell type- and circuit-specific effects are also increasingly implicated in neurological disorders: particular neuronal subtypes can be selectively affected in neurodegenerative disease, and neuron subtypes can be targeted to improve efficacy in real time in closed-loop brain stimulation. Together, these directions highlight a broader need to understand how features such as cell type and brain region contribute to a neuron's role in the brain, motivating the development of methods that can extract aspects of neuron identity.

Much of what is known about neuronal cell types and their connectivity comes from molecular, anatomical, and morphological labeling techniques that tag neurons based on gene expression profiles or structural features. These approaches have revealed a rich taxonomy of neuronal classes, but they are resource intensive and typically provide only a sparse labeling of one or a few classes at a time, so identity labels are costly and difficult to obtain at scale. There is currently no molecular access to different cell types or projection classes in nonhuman primates and humans, which has created major roadblocks in studying neuron diversity in humans. For these reasons, there is growing interest in methods that can infer aspects of neuronal identity directly from large-scale neural population activity.

Deep learning approaches to this question have only recently begun to be explored. Early methods relied on intrinsic single-neuron features such as waveform shape or interspike interval profiles, but these signals capture only part of what distinguishes one neuron from another. More recent approaches incorporate some information about the ongoing population activity, but reduce the surrounding activity to fixed low-dimensional summaries, which obscures the fine-grained coordination patterns that are often key to neuronal identity. Furthermore, these models usually require retraining or finetuning on each new set of neurons, limiting their ability to generalize in a zero-shot manner across animals.

Making use of population context is itself challenging. The number of recorded neurons varies widely across experiments, individuals, and sessions, making it non-trivial to define a consistent input structure or population-level operation, and recordings span multiple experimental conditions, including different stimuli and behaviors, which makes it hard for a model to generalize across recording sessions. These limitations point to the need for methods that leverage rich population context while producing neuron-level representations that transfer robustly across recordings.

This raises several questions. Can a representation of each individual neuron be learned from population activity, when identity labels are scarce, such that it captures aspects of the neuron's identity such as its cell type and brain region? Can such representations transfer to entirely new sessions and animals without retraining or additional metadata? And how does the identity information they capture depend on the amount and diversity of recordings available for learning, compared with the number of labeled neurons?

CONTROLS: Compare against a hand-crafted feature-based approach and a random baseline. Also include an ablation study where the model is trained without access to population context (i.e., per-neuron activity instead of population activity), following the setup outlined in the proposal.

This proposal aims to learn rich representations of neural activity from Neuropixels recordings and evaluate their effectiveness in distinguishing between cell types. By using a permutation invariant testing framework, we can assess the quality of the learned representations without worrying about the specific ordering of the data.

Traditional multimodal models are typically divided into two categories: multimodal understanding (e.g., answering questions about images) and multimodal generation (e.g., generating images from text prompts). Unified Multimodal Generative Models (UMGMs) aim to integrate these two capabilities within a single framework. Recent UMGMs have demonstrated strong performance on a wide range of tasks, such as visual question answering, image captioning, visual reasoning, classification, reading comprehension, and image generation. They typically embed multiple input types into a shared representation space and use one single autoregressive transformer backbone to model cross-modal interactions, so that the same model produces both textual and visual outputs. Training generally follows a two-stage paradigm: pretraining focused on text-image alignment, followed by fine-tuning for specific downstream tasks, where instruction tuning (fine-tuning on diverse, task-specific instructions paired with expected outputs) has become a widely adopted strategy for aligning model behavior with human intent.

Although UMGMs show impressive zero-shot performance on many unseen instructions, their effectiveness is inconsistent across tasks, particularly when the relevant task data is absent from the pretraining corpus. Adding new task data to the training set can substantially improve performance on those tasks, but because novel multimodal tasks keep emerging, repeatedly merging new data and retraining the model is computationally expensive and impractical. This calls for ways to let UMGMs adapt flexibly and efficiently over time, in line with the principles of continual learning, where models acquire new capabilities incrementally.

Studies in continual learning have shown that sequentially fine-tuned models suffer from catastrophic forgetting: a model fine-tuned on new tasks tends to forget or overwrite previously acquired knowledge. Several works have explored continual instruction tuning for multimodal large language models, with methods that are typically regularization-based, architecture-based, replay-based, or prompt-based, and mixture-of-experts adapters have also attracted growing attention in continual learning for their scalability and modularity. However, these multimodal models produce language-only outputs, so prior research has focused exclusively on multimodal understanding tasks such as visual question answering, and existing methods address only intra-modal catastrophic forgetting, where old tasks, new tasks, and pre-trained capabilities all belong to the same output modality, typically text. This assumption holds for multimodal models with unimodal outputs, but it is insufficient for UMGMs, which generate both text and images from a single backbone. For UMGMs, forgetting may occur not only within a modality (intra-modal) but also across modalities (inter-modal): for example, continually tuning the model on a sequence of multimodal understanding tasks might erode its pre-trained image generation ability. This inter-modal forgetting remains largely unexplored, and it is unclear whether methods designed for the intra-modal setting can handle both forms of forgetting at once.

The central question is therefore: can UMGMs continually acquire new capabilities through instruction tuning without suffering catastrophic forgetting, both within a modality (e.g., multimodal understanding) and across modalities (e.g., improving multimodal understanding while preserving visual generation)? Answering it requires establishing whether inter-modal forgetting actually occurs in UMGMs, explaining what causes it, and finding an efficient way to adapt these models to new tasks that retains performance on earlier tasks as well as the pre-trained capabilities of the other modality.

Evaluate intra-modal and inter-modal forgetting on different UMGM models using commonly used metrics such as accuracy and F1-score. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: robustness to catastrophic forgetting in UMGMs with rehearsal and weight decay
PROPOSAL: Investigate two standard methods for preventing catastrophic forgetting in the intra-modal setting: rehearsal and weight decay. Modify UMGMs to utilize a combination of these two methods independently and jointly. Rehearsal involves storing and replaying training data from past tasks during additional fine-tuning steps. Weight decay acts as a penalty term added to the loss function, preventing large weight changes and reinforcing generalization. With rehearsal and weight decay integrated into the UMGM, retrain and re-evaluate models across multiple multimodal understanding tasks and observe how these methods mitigate inter-modal forgetting. Compare methods to establish an optimal combination and assess performance on visual question answering and reading comprehension tasks.
COST: 80 GPU-hours, requiring an additional 4 days of training with 4 GPUs.
PREDICTION: applying both rehearsal and weight decay will show the best performance in retaining pre-trained image generation skills in UMGMs under instruction tuning, as these methods provide useful and individual protection against inter-modal forgetting. Still, there's a chance we might not see optimal results for tasks with frequently updated outputs (e.g. image generation), because the paths in the model require frequent updating as well.

Use techniques from theoretical computer science and machine learning to derive bounds on the forgetting rates of UMGMs in the presence of interfering tasks, and to identify conditions under which these rates can be reduced. This will help to provide a deeper understanding of the phenomenon of catastrophic forgetting in UMGMs and inform the design of new methods for preventing it.
CONTROLS: compare results with empirical studies on UMGMs and other multimodal models
COST: negligible (theoretical analysis done using pen and paper)
PREDICTION: will derive bounds on forgetting rates that are smaller than previously thought, which can help to guide the design of new methods for preventing catastrophic forgetting in UMGMs.

The ability to model complex, real-world phenomena is one of the central challenges in machine learning. Domains such as geospatial modeling, where terrain varies drastically across regions, or speech analysis, where signals exhibit bursts of volatility, are often characterized by pronounced non-stationarity: their statistical properties change across the input space, so that sharp, localized events can coexist with smooth, slowly varying regions. Gaussian processes (GPs) offer a principled framework for such problems, providing robust uncertainty estimates and flexible, non-parametric modeling. Despite these advantages, exact GPs suffer from two major limitations: their expressivity is constrained by the choice of kernel, and exact inference costs O(N^3) time and O(N^2) memory in the number N of training points, rendering it impractical for modern large-scale applications.

Most current approaches force a trade-off between expressivity and efficiency. On one hand, random Fourier features achieve impressive scalability: the kernel is approximated by an explicit, finite-dimensional feature map obtained by Monte Carlo sampling from its spectral density, so that the GP reduces to a Bayesian linear regression whose cost is linear in the number of data points, and the approximation error is backed by theoretical guarantees. Yet this construction depends on Bochner's theorem, which fundamentally restricts it to stationary kernels that assume uniform behavior across the entire domain; its globally supported sinusoidal features are inherently spatially invariant. Applying such models to non-stationary data leads to systematic mis-specification, resulting in compromised predictive accuracy and uncalibrated uncertainty estimates. Sparse variational GPs reduce the cost of exact inference through a set of inducing points, but they rely on iterative optimization whose cost grows cubically with the number of inducing points. On the other hand, expressive models such as deep GPs, spectral mixture kernels, and input-dependent kernels can capture non-stationarity, but they often reintroduce prohibitive computational costs, complex inference schemes, and challenges in optimization and hyperparameter tuning, and they typically retain a high complexity in the number of training points. Hybrid approaches that combine scalable approximations with expressive models, such as kernel interpolation, deep kernel learning, deep random features, and adaptive or compositional Fourier-feature representations, still tend to trade off scalability, expressivity, and interpretability.

The gap between scalable stationary models and complex non-stationary ones therefore remains. This raises the central question of whether the random-feature paradigm can be generalized beyond Bochner's theorem to the non-stationary setting: can one construct an explicit, randomly sampled feature map whose induced kernel adapts to local, input-dependent structure, while preserving the linear-in-data training and prediction cost that makes random features attractive? Such a construction should also be principled, with guarantees, comparable to those available for random Fourier features, that the induced kernel is valid and that the random approximation converges to it as the number of features grows. Finally, it remains open whether such an approach can offer a better trade-off between predictive accuracy, uncertainty quality, and computational cost than both stationary random features and more complex non-stationary GP models.

Video anomaly analysis is a key application of computer vision for public security. Most early work formulates it as temporal video anomaly detection: marking the segments of a video whose behavior deviates from learned normal patterns, whether with one-class models trained only on normal clips, unsupervised reconstruction or future-frame prediction objectives, or weakly supervised learning from video-level labels. Such detectors have reached high performance on benchmarks, yet they output only frame-wise anomaly scores, without spatial or semantic context, and give no insight into why a segment is abnormal. These limits of interpretability have motivated a shift from temporal detection toward downstream tasks with user-friendly, explainable outputs: spatial video anomaly localization, which predicts bounding boxes around the regions that contain the abnormal activity, and textual video anomaly understanding, which decides whether a video contains an anomaly and produces a human-readable description explaining it, typically with fine-tuned multimodal large language models. Each line of work, however, provides either spatial or textual cues on its own and focuses on a single type of task, so that existing methods offer only an incomplete analysis of video anomalies. A holistic analysis would answer when an anomaly happens, where it is, what it is and why it is abnormal, each of the existing benchmark tasks addressing one of these sub-problems.

A second challenge is the heavy reliance on dataset-specific supervision. Detection and localization models require temporal masks or spatial bounding boxes, yet anomaly definitions vary widely across datasets, so a model tuned on one domain often fails on another and must be retrained for unseen domains or anomaly types. In real-world applications, privacy and security concerns may also make training data unavailable for some sensitive scenes. Open-set detectors that fuse language semantics in order to detect and classify novel anomalies still require task-specific training and give very limited insight into why frames are abnormal. As partial remedies, recent work has explored zero- and few-shot approaches built on frozen vision-language backbones or multimodal large language models, but most of these approaches have a limited task scope and still rely on annotated datasets. The only strictly zero-shot, training-free method addresses temporal detection alone: a frozen vision-language model captions the frames and a prompted large language model converts the captions into frame-wise anomaly scores. It is effective when anomalies are clearly distinguishable from normality but occasionally fails on more complex anomaly types, and it offers neither spatial grounding nor any direct semantic explanation beyond generic captions. Prompt-tuning methods, which optimize textual prompts to guide frozen models, require induction on an annotated training set and pay for it in generality, since the learned prompts tend to be task- or domain-specific. The generality problem is worse still for instruction-tuned multimodal models: they produce rich narrative explanations, but they require extensive annotation and computational resources, lack temporal or spatial coverage, and are optimized to return answers from seen question-answer pairs that describe a closed set of anomaly types.

Multimodal large language models already encode rich visual-semantic priors for commonsense reasoning, which suggests that fine-tuning may not be necessary for every task. This raises the questions addressed here: can temporal detection, spatial localization and textual explanation of video anomalies be delivered together, as one holistic and interpretable analysis, in a strictly zero-shot manner, with frozen pretrained models and without any additional training data, annotations or gradient updates? And can such an analysis remain at least as accurate as existing zero-shot detectors while staying robust across domains whose definitions of anomaly differ?

Geometry reconstruction is a fundamental problem that enables a wide range of applications in fields such as virtual reality and robotics. In recent years, neural reconstruction methods have gained significant attention; a key advantage of these methods is their ability to represent the geometry of a scene continuously, which can help in many downstream tasks. However, vision-based sensors often struggle in adverse weather conditions, or even become completely unusable when objects are obscured by occlusions.

Radio frequency (RF) sensing, specifically wireless millimeter-wave (mmWave) sensing, can see through occlusions, remains robust under challenging visibility conditions and, unlike X-rays, is not dangerous to humans, making it a compelling alternative for 3D reconstruction. This could open up many applications, for example checking whether the items inside a box are the correct items, are damaged, or pose a threat, without ever opening the box. On the other hand, mmWave resolution is extremely low compared to vision: a single radar image provides far less visual context than a camera image, which makes it hard to extract a 3D reconstruction from one radar image alone. Some prior RF systems have performed 3D point cloud reconstruction or human body tracking by leveraging movement or by emulating larger antenna apertures, but the recovered point clouds are still too sparse and noisy to reliably recover detailed geometry; through-wall human sensing relies on human motion to combat specularity, and deep learning on mmWave radar data has mostly targeted self-driving scenarios, where image resolution matters little. Other works have proposed neural implicit representations for RF sensing, aiming to concentrate scene information out of heavy noise through neural optimization, but these systems are designed for large-scale environments such as streets or satellite imagery and are far from achieving millimeter-level precision. When objects are close to the radar, the propagation characteristics of RF signals change dramatically: incoming waves can no longer be approximated as planar, so processing methods designed for large-scale scenes, such as beamforming, introduce a considerable amount of distortion and noise, often exceeding the noise acceptable for gradient descent and leading to unstable optimization. Existing neural RF reconstruction work is thus either limited to far-range scenes or, for individual objects, evaluated only on simulated data, which for wireless signals cannot come close to representing the complexity of real-world measurements. Meanwhile, the multi-view reconstruction and inverse rendering methods of computer vision (multi-view stereo, neural radiance fields, Gaussian splatting, neural implicit surfaces, physically based inverse rendering) are all derived from RGB images and are not easily transferable to mmWave data: even lensless RGB images can be mapped back to a lens-based imaging model without altering the underlying ray physics, whereas for RF signals such a transformation is fundamentally invalid.

The open problem is therefore to overcome the fundamental dilemma between massive RF noise in the input and the reconstruction of complete, high-resolution, millimeter-level 3D surface geometry of near-range objects, including objects hidden behind occlusions. This is not straightforward, because inferring surface geometry from RF signals differs fundamentally from image-based reconstruction in three main ways. First, wireless systems lack a lens-based imaging model: whereas lenses filter and focus the relevant light rays, radar antenna arrays perform lensless imaging and capture all incoming RF signals without directional filtering, which leads to low signal-to-noise ratios because irrelevant signals cannot be excluded. Second, RF signals and visible light propagate differently: visible light is predominantly scattered diffusely by surfaces, whereas RF signals, whose wavelengths are on the order of millimeters, are dominated by specular reflections, so volumetric rendering techniques designed for scattering-based vision sensors are unsuitable for RF imaging. Third, physically modeling lensless RF measurements is computationally expensive: whereas lens-based rendering samples along 1D rays, modeling what each antenna receives requires accounting for contributions from the full 3D space, leading to cubic complexity that makes naive implementations intractable at millimeter resolution.

How can accurate, millimeter-level 3D geometry of near-range objects be reconstructed from noisy real-world RF measurements, in line of sight and through occlusions, despite lensless imaging, specular reflections and the cost of modeling signal contributions from the full 3D space?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: spectral clustering for rf feature extraction
PROPOSAL: This experiment uses spectral clustering to automatically extract salient RF features relevant for 3D reconstruction in the presence of occlusions. We will train a spectral clustering model on a dataset of mmWave radar images and evaluate its performance in extracting features that are useful for 3D reconstruction. We will compare the performance of spectral clustering to other approaches like PCA and t-SNE.
CONTROLS: We will use mmWave radar images from the existing DriveWave dataset as controls and compare the performance of the spectral clustering model to other approaches.
COST: Estimated to require 10 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the spectral clustering model.
PREDICTION: We expect spectral clustering to improve feature extraction in occluded scenes, but we worry that the model may struggle to generalize across different occlusion patterns and radar sensor settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: neural indoor/outdoor discriminators for robustness
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes adding a neural indoor/outdoor discriminator module to the RF 3D reconstruction network to improve robustness in indoor and outdoor domains with varying levels of occlusions. We will train a neural network to distinguish between indoor and outdoor environments and use this module to adapt the reconstruction network for improved performance.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the proposed model to the state-of-the-art RF 3D reconstruction model without the discriminator module, using the same mmWave radar image dataset. We will also evaluate the performance of the model in both indoor and outdoor scenarios.
COST: Estimated to require an additional 20 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the model with the discriminator module.
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the addition of the indoor/outdoor discriminator module will improve the robustness and accuracy of the RF 3D reconstruction network in both indoor and outdoor scenarios, but may require careful tuning of the discriminator network to achieve good performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: volumetric processing for through-occlusion imaging
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes adapting the volumetric processing approach used in computer vision for 3D shape reconstruction to the RF domain, using a combination of simulated RF data and real-world mmWave radar images to train and evaluate the performance of this approach in through-occlusion imaging.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of volumetric processing to state-of-the-art RF 3D reconstruction methods, using datasets of mmWave radar images with and without occlusions.
COST: Estimated to require 15 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the volumetric processing model.
PREDICTION: We expect that volumetric processing will help improve the accuracy and robustness of through-occlusion imaging, but may require careful tuning of the model architecture and training parameters to achieve good performance.

TITLE: volumetric processing for through-occlusion imaging
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes adapting the volumetric processing approach used in computer vision for 3D shape reconstruction to the RF domain, using a combination of simulated RF data and real-world mmWave radar images to train and evaluate the performance of this approach in through-occlusion imaging of objects in boxes. Specifically, we will use a neural implicit surface model to represent the volumetric data and evaluate its performance in reconstructing detailed 3D surface geometry of objects behind occlusions.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of volumetric processing to state-of-the-art RF 3D reconstruction methods, using datasets of mmWave radar images of objects in boxes with and without occlusions. The multi-objective multi-armed bandit problem generalizes the classical, single-objective multi-armed bandit to settings with multiple, potentially conflicting objectives. Pulling an arm yields a vector of objective-specific rewards, so a single "best" arm is often ill-defined and optimality must account for trade-offs across objectives. The setting of interest here is the multi-objective linear contextual bandit: at each round, every arm of a finite set is described by a d-dimensional context vector, which may be chosen adversarially; each of the L objectives has its own fixed but unknown parameter vector; and the agent, after choosing an arm, observes an L-dimensional reward vector whose entry for each objective is the inner product of the arm's context with that objective's parameter, plus zero-mean sub-Gaussian noise.

One simple way to handle trade-offs is scalarization, which maps reward vectors to a scalar via, for example, weighted sums, minimax, or other nonlinear transforms, thereby reducing the problem to a single-objective bandit. However, selecting a suitable scalarization is itself nontrivial, and an arm that is optimal under one scalarization can be markedly suboptimal under another. An alternative is to reason directly in the vector space via Pareto optimality: the Pareto front comprises the arms whose mean reward vectors are not dominated component-wise by that of any other arm. Because it compares reward vectors objective-wise, Pareto optimality is more general than committing to a fixed scalarization. Performance is then usually measured by the Pareto regret, which sums over rounds the smallest uniform increase that would make the mean reward vector of the chosen arm non-dominated.

Prior work on Pareto regret in multi-objective bandits proposes and studies upper-confidence-bound (UCB) algorithms, which typically compute an empirical Pareto front at every round and are therefore complex. Approaches that identify the Pareto front by eliminating arms do not carry over to the contextual setting, where the Pareto front changes with the contexts and an arm discarded early may later be Pareto optimal. By contrast, the Pareto regret of Thompson Sampling has not been studied for multi-objective bandits: the only Thompson Sampling algorithm proposed for this problem comes without theoretical analysis, and the analyses of randomized scalarization in multi-objective Bayesian optimization concern the Bayesian regret under a known Gaussian prior, with bounds that increase with the number of objectives. This gap is noteworthy: in many single-objective contextual and non-contextual bandits, Thompson Sampling and its variants are empirically competitive with or superior to UCB methods, yet their worst-case (frequentist) analyses are typically more delicate. Extending Thompson Sampling to several objectives introduces additional challenges, including coordinating randomized samples across multiple objectives, ensuring optimism of the randomized estimates across all objectives simultaneously, and handling the possibility of multiple Pareto-optimal arms.

A second issue concerns the performance measure itself. The standard Pareto regret compares per-round mean reward vectors; consequently, a policy that plays only Pareto-optimal arms incurs zero Pareto regret, even when an alternative selection of arms over the same number of rounds would yield strictly larger cumulative rewards in every objective. Pareto regret therefore does not distinguish between policies that obtain different cumulative rewards while selecting only Pareto-optimal arms, and the resulting shortfall can grow with the number of rounds.

This raises two questions. First, can a computationally efficient, Thompson Sampling-type randomized algorithm for the multi-objective linear contextual bandit be designed with worst-case Pareto regret guarantees, how close can these guarantees come to those known for randomized algorithms in the single-objective linear setting, and how must they depend on the number of objectives? Second, how should optimality and regret be defined in this setting so that they also account for cumulative rewards under repeated selections, penalizing policies that are Pareto optimal round by round but inefficient in aggregate?
