ACTION: ADD
TITLE: manipulating symmetry constraints for metanetworks
PROPOSAL: Explore the theoretical implications of modifying the symmetry constraints imposed on weights in metanetworks to relax strict equivariance. Specifically, we will derive a formal framework for relaxing permuto-equivariance by introducing a penalty term that measures the deviation from pointwise equivariance in the space of weight permutations. The goal is to provide a principled approach for balancing symmetry preservation and representational expressivity.
CONTROLS: Compare the derived relaxed framework with the existing strict permuto-equivariant architectures and assess their performance in various settings (multiple architectures, loss functions, dataset sizes). Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed framework will provide a better trade-off between accuracy and efficiency, while maintaining the capability to process and learn from multiple symmetries; However, tuning the penalty term may lead to brittle behavior in certain scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: characterizing the space of functionally equivalent weights
PROPOSAL: Investigate the topological properties of the space of weights in a deep neural network, focusing on the quotient space obtained by taking into account the symmetries that leave the input-output function invariant. Through a combination of algebraic topology and deep learning techniques, we will characterize the connectivity and holes in this space, providing insights into the number of distinct, functionally equivalent weight configurations. This understanding will inform the design of more efficient and robust metanetworks.
CONTROLS: Compare the results from different classes of neural networks (e.g., fully-connected, convolutional, recurrent) and loss functions to understand their impact on the topology of the weight space. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The study will reveal that the weight space exhibits a complex topological structure, with multiple holes and connected components; however, the specific characteristics may vary significantly depending on the network architecture and loss function used.

PROPOSAL: Extend the existing permuto-equivariant metanetworks to accommodate weights that evolve and adapt during training. This will involve incorporating a dynamic weight generator that relies on a probabilistic permutation-invariant encoding scheme, enabling the metanetwork to adapt to variations in symmetry. We will evaluate the performance of this adaptive approach on a range of tasks, including neural network generalization prediction and implicit neural representation editing.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the fixed-weight version of the permuto-equivariant metanetwork and assess the learnability and expressiveness of the adaptive weight generator under different training scenarios. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptation mechanism will demonstrate robustness and learning capabilities in dynamic symmetries, but may lead to mode collapse and imperiled exploration.

TITLE: analyzing the effect of weight equivariance on model robustness
PROPOSAL: Investigate the relationship between weight equivariance and the robustness of metanetworks to perturbations in the input data and model weights. We will systematically vary the degree of equivariance in the metanetworks and assess their performance on tasks such as implicit neural representation classification, focusing on their resilience to adversarial attacks and data noise.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with existing state-of-the-art methods for robustness and security in deep learning, as well as ablate the effects of different perturbation scenarios (e.g., random noise, targeted attacks). Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The study will demonstrate that metanetworks with strict equivariance exhibit improved robustness to certain types of perturbations, but may sacrifice performance in tasks that require flexibility and adaptability; This will depend on the balance between equivariance and representational power in the weight generator.

We will develop a novel graph-theoretic representation for describing the spatial equivalences between CNN filters and weight permutations.
CONTROLS: Compare the results to the existing study of the topological properties of the weight space for fully-connected networks, and assess the applicability of the novel graph-theoretic representation to other CNN architectures. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.

PREDICTION: The refined study will reveal that the topological properties of the weight space for CNNs exhibit a distinct structure due to the presence of spatial symmetries; however, the results may be influenced by the specific architecture and the choice of convolutional operations used in the network.

TITLE: relaxations of pointwise equivariance in metanetworks
PROPOSAL: Investigate relaxations of pointwise equivariance for metanetworks that explicitly account for imperfections in the symmetry of the processed weights. Specifically, we will develop and analyze three variants of relaxed metanetworks, each incorporating different approximations and relaxations of pointwise equivariance, and evaluate their performance on tasks such as neural network generalization prediction and implicit neural representation editing.

PROPOSAL: Investigate the application of metanetworks to implicit neural representation synthesis tasks, such as generating new neural networks with similar functionality to a given model. Recent advances in computer graphics and vision have highlighted image relighting, that is, changing the illumination of an existing image, as a critical task for film production, augmented reality and digital content creation. Full-image relighting, in which both the objects and the surrounding scene must be relit, remains a challenging problem.

Existing works can be grouped into object-centric approaches, which often ignore or replace the background, and scene-level methods, which attempt full-image relighting but remain largely data-driven: they struggle to generalize beyond the training distribution without extensive and diverse data, and cannot maintain the lighting of self-luminous objects. Even state-of-the-art foreground relighting methods still suffer from albedo inconsistency and imprecise lighting control: relighting can, for instance, alter the colors of a carpet, or make light intended to come from the left appear to come from the left rear although the scene contains no internal light source. Other lines of work have their own restrictions. Many methods address only portraits or isolated objects. Scribble-based control of scene lighting lacks precision and has been limited to indoor scenes. Outdoor full-image relighting methods either require surface normals as input or rely on directional lighting models that generalize poorly to indoor scenes. A recent generative approach that simulates both inverse rendering (recovering intrinsic properties such as albedo, surface normals, roughness and metallicity from an image) and forward rendering conditions the forward step on irradiance, which makes precise lighting control challenging, and is limited to indoor scenes. Intrinsic decomposition methods are themselves hampered by the difficulty of acquiring large-scale training data and are mostly designed for specific scenarios, such as indoor scenes or single objects. These limitations point to the lack of a physically interpretable representation of the scene in current relighting methods and to the inherent limitations of data-driven priors, both of which stand in the way of controllable and physically plausible full-image relighting.

Three major challenges follow. First, data with diverse and complex scene illumination are hard to acquire: obtaining high-quality images of full scenes under diverse and controlled lighting conditions is resource-intensive and technically challenging, and it is infeasible to capture real-world datasets that show the same scene under multiple lighting conditions. Existing datasets that provide intrinsic components focus mainly on indoor scenes and do not render images under varying lighting conditions. Second, ensuring physical plausibility is difficult, as purely data-driven approaches often generate results that violate basic light transport principles. Third, limited data-driven priors restrict generalizability, leading to poor robustness to unseen materials, lighting conditions and realistic scene compositions, and existing attempts to bridge the gap between synthetic training data and real images for full-scene relighting remain suboptimal. Full scenes add a further difficulty: self-luminous objects and built-in light sources, such as light coming through windows, interfere with controlling the direction and intensity of the new lighting while keeping the background consistent.

This raises the following questions. How can an entire image, objects and scene together, indoor or outdoor, be relit under a user-specified lighting condition with precise control of light direction and intensity, while preserving the albedo and material appearance of its surfaces, the content and consistency of the background, and the lighting of self-luminous elements? How can a relighting model be made to respect basic light transport, so that shading, highlights and shadows follow the new lighting across a wide variety of materials? And how can such a model generalize to real-world images with unseen materials, lighting conditions and scene compositions when paired data under controlled lighting are scarce and real captures of the same scene under multiple lightings are infeasible?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: view-dependent radiance decomposition
PROPOSAL: Investigate the potential of view-dependent radiance decomposition for physically plausible full-image relighting. We'll apply a novel decomposition method, focusing on recovering the high-frequency components of radiance with respect to view angles, and assess its performance on synthetic datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare with current state-of-the-art full-image relighting methods and our own simplified radiance decomposition approach without view-dependent components. Evaluate all methods on the same held-out test set and report the mean and standard deviation over five seeds.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This decomposition method can improve full-image relighting accuracy, especially in scenes with complex environments and non-diffuse materials. However, it may struggle with cases where objects have strong view-independent light transport properties.

TITLE: intrinsic image decomposition with boundary handling
PROPOSAL: Design an intrinsic image decomposition method that explicitly handles scene boundaries to allow for accurate training and realistic rendering. We'll apply a boundary-aware physics-based model, including Fresnel terms for surface normals and conductance models for lighting, to retrieve intrinsic components with sharper edges and reduced artifacts.
CONTROLS: Compare with current intrinsic image decomposition methods that neglect or approximate boundary conditions, as well as our own simplified boundary- handling approach using standard convolutional filters. Evaluate all methods on the same held-out test set and report the mean and standard deviation over five seeds.
COST: 15 GPU-hours

Proteins realize their biological functions through intricate three-dimensional conformations, and predicting such structures has long been a central challenge in computational biology. AlphaFold2 marked a breakthrough by combining multiple sequence alignments with geometric constraints in an end-to-end framework, achieving near-experimental accuracy. Building on this foundation, AlphaFold3 reformulates the architecture into an all-atom framework and introduces a diffusion-based structure module, thereby enabling the generative modeling of not only proteins but also a wide spectrum of biomolecular complexes. Consequently, this series of models is widely adopted as a family of foundation models for downstream applications such as virtual screening and protein design. However, AlphaFold3's architecture, which relies on iterative Pairformer recycling and multi-step diffusion, requires substantially greater computational overhead than AlphaFold2, restricting its accessibility in downstream workflows.

More specifically, on long sequences the execution time of AlphaFold3 is measured in minutes, which severely limits its usability in downstream tasks that demand high throughput. For instance, small-scale laboratory screening often requires predictions for thousands of candidates, and when extended to large public databases this number grows to an infeasible scale; protein design tasks typically involve comparable computational demand. Previous work has attempted to mitigate this by manually reducing the number of recycling iterations on simpler structures, thus trading accuracy for efficiency. However, such compromises inevitably degrade predictive performance. Moreover, in hallucination-based design approaches, the multistep iterative refinement process hinders feasible gradient backpropagation, ultimately preventing the broader community from adopting AlphaFold3 as a foundation model for diverse applications.

To accelerate the diffusion process, recent advances in generative modeling have explored high-order solvers and consistency models. While high-order solvers improve efficiency, they rarely reduce the number of sampling steps below ten. Consistency models, on the other hand, have achieved remarkable success in image generation and have benefited from refined training schedules. However, transferring them to an AlphaFold3-style architecture raises two difficulties. First, standard consistency schedules assume fixed-dimensional data and pair timesteps at a constant Euclidean interval, which does not accommodate variable protein sequence lengths: on long sequences even a small step can trigger a drastic distribution shift that demands an unrealistic predictive leap, while on short sequences the same interval provides only a weak learning signal, so training dynamics can become unstable or collapse. Second, the iterative diffusion sampler is not the only source of iteration: the architecture also refines its internal pair and single representations through repeated recycling of the Pairformer trunk, whose cost grows with sequence length and which conventional diffusion-acceleration methods do not address at all.

The open problem is therefore whether an AlphaFold3-class all-atom biomolecular structure generator can be compressed into a predictor that runs in essentially a single forward pass -- removing both the multi-step denoising and the recycling overhead -- while retaining the accuracy of the full iterative model on protein, protein-ligand and nucleic-acid complexes. This matters because accuracy alone is not what blocks adoption: throughput and differentiability do. A useful accelerated model must remain reliable in the tail, not merely on average, since high-throughput screening and design pipelines discard most candidates and are harmed more by occasional implausible structures than by small average losses; it must stay cheap enough to be called thousands of times; and it must be light enough that gradients can be propagated through it, so that design methods which optimize sequences against a folding model become feasible with an all-atom model rather than only with earlier, cheaper architectures. Given this problem, how should one design experiments to establish whether such an acceleration is achievable without a loss of predictive fidelity?

The ability to model complex, real-world phenomena is one of the central challenges in machine learning. Domains such as geospatial modeling, where terrain varies drastically across regions, or speech analysis, where signals exhibit bursts of volatility, are often characterized by pronounced non-stationarity: their statistical properties change across the input space, so that sharp, localized events can coexist with smooth, slowly varying regions. Gaussian processes (GPs) offer a principled framework for such problems, providing robust uncertainty estimates and flexible, non-parametric modeling. Despite these advantages, exact GPs suffer from two major limitations: their expressivity is constrained by the choice of kernel, and exact inference costs O(N^3) time and O(N^2) memory in the number N of training points, rendering it impractical for modern large-scale applications.

Most current approaches force a trade-off between expressivity and efficiency. On one hand, random Fourier features achieve impressive scalability: the kernel is approximated by an explicit, finite-dimensional feature map obtained by Monte Carlo sampling from its spectral density, so that the GP reduces to a Bayesian linear regression whose cost is linear in the number of data points, and the approximation error is backed by theoretical guarantees. Yet this construction depends on Bochner's theorem, which fundamentally restricts it to stationary kernels that assume uniform behavior across the entire domain; its globally supported sinusoidal features are inherently spatially invariant. Applying such models to non-stationary data leads to systematic mis-specification, resulting in compromised predictive accuracy and uncalibrated uncertainty estimates. Sparse variational GPs reduce the cost of exact inference through a set of inducing points, but they rely on iterative optimization whose cost grows cubically with the number of inducing points. On the other hand, expressive models such as deep GPs, spectral mixture kernels, and input-dependent kernels can capture non-stationarity, but they often reintroduce prohibitive computational costs, complex inference schemes, and challenges in optimization and hyperparameter tuning, and they typically retain a high complexity in the number of training points. Hybrid approaches that combine scalable approximations with expressive models, such as kernel interpolation, deep kernel learning, deep random features, and adaptive or compositional Fourier-feature representations, still tend to trade off scalability, expressivity, and interpretability.

The gap between scalable stationary models and complex non-stationary ones therefore remains. This raises the central question of whether the random-feature paradigm can be generalized beyond Bochner's theorem to the non-stationary setting: can one construct an explicit, randomly sampled feature map whose induced kernel adapts to local, input-dependent structure, while preserving the linear-in-data training and prediction cost that makes random features attractive? Such a construction should also be principled, with guarantees, comparable to those available for random Fourier features, that the induced kernel is valid and that the random approximation converges to it as the number of features grows. Finally, it remains open whether such an approach can offer a better trade-off between predictive accuracy, uncertainty quality, and computational cost than both stationary random features and more complex non-stationary GP models.

Traditional multimodal models are typically divided into two categories: multimodal understanding (e.g., answering questions about images) and multimodal generation (e.g., generating images from text prompts). Unified Multimodal Generative Models (UMGMs) aim to integrate these two capabilities within a single framework. Recent UMGMs have demonstrated strong performance on a wide range of tasks, such as visual question answering, image captioning, visual reasoning, classification, reading comprehension, and image generation. They typically embed multiple input types into a shared representation space and use one single autoregressive transformer backbone to model cross-modal interactions, so that the same model produces both textual and visual outputs. Training generally follows a two-stage paradigm: pretraining focused on text-image alignment, followed by fine-tuning for specific downstream tasks, where instruction tuning (fine-tuning on diverse, task-specific instructions paired with expected outputs) has become a widely adopted strategy for aligning model behavior with human intent.

Although UMGMs show impressive zero-shot performance on many unseen instructions, their effectiveness is inconsistent across tasks, particularly when the relevant task data is absent from the pretraining corpus. Adding new task data to the training set can substantially improve performance on those tasks, but because novel multimodal tasks keep emerging, repeatedly merging new data and retraining the model is computationally expensive and impractical. This calls for ways to let UMGMs adapt flexibly and efficiently over time, in line with the principles of continual learning, where models acquire new capabilities incrementally.

Studies in continual learning have shown that sequentially fine-tuned models suffer from catastrophic forgetting: a model fine-tuned on new tasks tends to forget or overwrite previously acquired knowledge. Several works have explored continual instruction tuning for multimodal large language models, with methods that are typically regularization-based, architecture-based, replay-based, or prompt-based, and mixture-of-experts adapters have also attracted growing attention in continual learning for their scalability and modularity. However, these multimodal models produce language-only outputs, so prior research has focused exclusively on multimodal understanding tasks such as visual question answering, and existing methods address only intra-modal catastrophic forgetting, where old tasks, new tasks, and pre-trained capabilities all belong to the same output modality, typically text. This assumption holds for multimodal models with unimodal outputs, but it is insufficient for UMGMs, which generate both text and images from a single backbone. For UMGMs, forgetting may occur not only within a modality (intra-modal) but also across modalities (inter-modal): for example, continually tuning the model on a sequence of multimodal understanding tasks might erode its pre-trained image generation ability. This inter-modal forgetting remains largely unexplored, and it is unclear whether methods designed for the intra-modal setting can handle both forms of forgetting at once.

The central question is therefore: can UMGMs continually acquire new capabilities through instruction tuning without suffering catastrophic forgetting, both within a modality (e.g., multimodal understanding) and across modalities (e.g., improving multimodal understanding while preserving visual generation)? Answering it requires establishing whether inter-modal forgetting actually occurs in UMGMs, explaining what causes it, and finding an efficient way to adapt these models to new tasks that retains performance on earlier tasks as well as the pre-trained capabilities of the other modality.

Diffusion models have demonstrated a remarkable ability to learn data distributions across many modalities, with strong results in both data generation and image restoration. In medical imaging, they are effective at modeling the distribution of 2D image slices, and by combining these powerful learned priors with conventional optimization frameworks, diffusion-based solvers have reached state-of-the-art performance on medical inverse problems such as accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and undersampled X-ray computed tomography (CT). Such problems are often severely ill-posed: far fewer measurements are acquired than there are unknowns, so the measurements alone cannot determine the image, and the learned prior must fill in what they leave ambiguous. Diffusion-based solvers do so through an iterative reverse sampling process that, at each step, predicts a clean image from the current noisy state, corrects this estimate for consistency with the measurements, and re-noises it to the next timestep, which repeatedly injects random noise.

In clinical practice, however, medical data are fundamentally large 3D volumes. Individual 2D slices matter for review, but a complete and accurate volumetric reconstruction is often essential for downstream tasks such as precise tumor volume assessment, surgical planning, and tracking disease progression over time. Translating the success of 2D diffusion-based solvers to 3D is difficult: because of the curse of dimensionality, the memory, computational, and data requirements of training a diffusion prior directly on volumetric data are prohibitive for most academic and even industrial labs. A common and practical workaround is to train a diffusion model on 2D slices and apply this 2D prior slice by slice to reconstruct the volume.

This workaround eases the training burden but creates a critical new problem: the reconstructed volumes lack consistency along the third dimension (the z-axis). Because each slice is processed independently during the reverse diffusion process, the intrinsic randomness of the sampling procedure leads to severe inter-slice discontinuities and artifacts, degrading the diagnostic and analytical quality of the stacked volume. Existing remedies have important drawbacks. The most direct one augments the 2D prior with a hand-crafted regularizer such as total variation, applied in an additional optimization step to enforce smoothness between adjacent slices. This is effective, but it introduces sensitive hyperparameters that require careful tuning, can over-smooth the volume or produce cartoon-like textures that erase fine diagnostic details, and acts as an external correction that masks the symptoms rather than addressing the intrinsic cause. More principled approaches try to learn a more complete 3D prior, for instance by training on 3D patches or by combining priors from two perpendicular 2D planes, but they increase the complexity of the training or inference pipeline and may impose constraints on the data, such as requiring cubic volumes.

A similar discontinuity arises in video restoration, where applying a pre-trained 2D image diffusion model to video inverse problems often produces temporal flickering across frames. Prior work attributed this flickering to the uncoordinated stochasticity inherent in diffusion sampling and alleviated it by synchronizing the stochastic noise components across frames. Whether the same mechanism is the fundamental cause of inter-slice inconsistency in 3D medical reconstruction, and how such a remedy would transfer from video to volumetric medical data, remains open.

This raises the following questions. How does the stochasticity of independent slice-wise sampling give rise to inter-slice inconsistency when 2D diffusion priors are used for 3D medical reconstruction? Is it possible to enhance inter-slice consistency directly within the diffusion sampling process itself, obviating the need for external, artifact-inducing optimization, ideally without new loss terms, additional sensitive hyperparameters, model retraining, or extra computational cost, so that the remedy could be dropped into existing 2D diffusion-based 3D reconstruction pipelines? And can inter-slice consistency be improved while preserving the natural anatomical variation between slices and fine diagnostic details, rather than trading them away for smoothness?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: slice synchronization via shared noise projection
PROPOSAL: We will apply a 2D diffusion-based solver to 3D volumetric MRI data, but instead of processing each slice independently, we will sample each slice from a shared noise distribution that is projected onto the current state of the solver, thus ensuring consistency between the slices. We will test two variants: one where the shared noise is static across all slices, and one where it is dynamic and updated at each step.
CONTROLS: We compare our proposed slice synchronization method to (1) a naive baseline where each slice is processed independently, and (2) an augmented baseline where a total variation regularizer is applied to enforce smoothness between adjacent slices.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The slice synchronization method should improve upon the naive baseline in terms of inter-slice consistency, with the dynamic noise variant performing better than the static one. However, it may also trade off some of the fine diagnostic details due to the constraint imposed by the shared noise distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: analyzing stochastic consistency using advanced diffusion diagnostics
PROPOSAL: We will embed advanced diffusion diagnostics into the 2D diffusion-based solver to directly measure the temporal consistency of the sampling process, quantifying the correlation between adjacent slices and identifying potential sources of inter-slice discrepancies. By comparing these diagnostics across different variants of the solver, including and without the slice synchronization method proposed in our previous experiment, we will analyze the mechanism behind inter-slice inconsistency and provide a deeper understanding of its origin.
CONTROLS: The baseline for our diagnostics will be the existing implementation of the 2D diffusion-based solver without any additional modifications.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The advanced diffusion diagnostics are expected to uncover the inherent stochasticity and its effects on slice consistency, supporting evidence for the potential benefits of our proposed slice synchronization method. However, inconsistent results might challenge our current assumptions and necessitate a reevaluation of the underlying problem.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating 3d patch-based diffusion priors in a 2d+1 framework
PROPOSAL: We will adapt the 2D diffusion-based solver to operate within a 2D+1 framework, where each 2D slice is augmented with a per-pixel description of the slice's spatial relationship to adjacent slices in the 3D volume. This framework will be used to train a set of 2D diffusion priors, each conditioned on 3D patches of volume data. During inference, the 2D diffusion model will use the spatial relationship descriptions to predict a clean image slice that is consistent with adjacent slices.
CONTROLS: We compare our 2D+1 framework with the naive baseline of applying a unconditioned 2D diffusion model to each slice independently, and with a 3D diffusion-based solver that has been trained directly on volume data.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method is expected to improve upon the naive baseline by leveraging the spatial relationships between slices, but may inherently require large amounts of memory and computational resources due to the need to compute and store the per-pixel spatial relationships. If we're lucky, it might challenge the effectiveness of our proposed slice synchronization method.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: analyzing stochastic consistency using advanced diffusion diagnostics
PROPOSAL: We will extend our experimental setup in this proposal to also include 3D diffusion-based solvers with and without slice-wise stochastic synchronization, and compare the consistency metrics across these setups. Furthermore, we will use the advanced diffusion diagnostics to analyze the origin and propagation of inter-slice discrepancies in both 2D and 3D diffusion-based solvers, providing further insights into the mechanism behind inter-slice inconsistency.
CONTROLS: The baseline for our diagnostics will be the existing implementation of 2D and 3D diffusion-based solvers without any additional modifications or synchronization.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By combining our previous experiments, we will gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between stochastic consistency and inter-slice inconsistency in diffusion-based solvers, and validate our observations on a more comprehensive set of solvers, ultimately strengthening our proposal for slice synchronization.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: analyzing stochastic consistency using advanced diffusion diagnostics
PROPOSAL: We will extend our experimental setup in this proposal to also include 3D diffusion-based solvers with and without slice-wise stochastic synchronization, and compare the consistency metrics across these setups. Furthermore, we will use the advanced diffusion diagnostics to analyze the origin and propagation of inter-slice discrepancies in both 2D and 3D diffusion-based solvers, providing further insights into the mechanism behind inter-slice inconsistency.
CONTROLS: The baseline for our diagnostics will be the existing implementation of 2D and 3D diffusion-based solvers without any additional modifications or synchronization, reported alongside the main results. We will also compare our results to a phase of the experiment where the synchronization is delayed, illustrating the dynamic nature of the synchronization improvement.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By combining our previous experiments, we will gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between stochastic consistency and inter-slice inconsistency in diffusion-based solvers, and validate our observations on a more comprehensive set of solvers, ultimately strengthening our proposal for slice synchronization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adaptive temporal filtering for stabilized diffusion reconstruction
PROPOSAL: We will explore the integration of adaptive temporal filtering techniques into the diffusion-based reconstruction framework to stabilize and smooth out the variations caused by stochastic sampling, aiming to reduce inter-slice inconsistency. This approach will involve incorporating a learnable filter capable of adaptively attenuating or amplifying temporal frequencies in the diffused signal, based on image characteristics such as multi-scale texture and gradient fields.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our adaptive filtering technique against (1) the naive baseline of independent slice processing and (2) our previously proposed slice synchronization method via shared noise projection.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging adaptive temporal filtering, we anticipate significant reduction in inter-slice inconsistency, potentially leading to more realistic and stable volumetric reconstructions. However, there is a risk that overly aggressive filtering may hinder fine texture preservation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: empirical analysis of synchronization mechanisms in diffusion-based reconstruction
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a comprehensive empirical analysis to investigate the impact of different synchronization mechanisms on diffusion-based reconstruction, comparing various methods such as shared noise projection, phase-locking, and adaptive feedback loops. We will examine how each mechanism affects inter-slice consistency, noise propagation, and overall image quality, aiming to identify the most suitable synchronization strategy for volumetric reconstruction tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our empirical analysis against a diverse set of 2D and 3D diffusion-based solvers, both with and without synchronization, as described above.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our empirical analysis is expected to provide valuable insights into the strengths and limitations of different synchronization mechanisms, helping to refine and optimize our previously proposed methods for diffusion-based volumetric reconstruction.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: analyzing stochastic consistency using advanced diffusion diagnostics
PROPOSAL: We will integrate the findings from our empirical analysis of synchronization mechanisms (proposal 5) into the advanced diffusion diagnostics framework, extending the diagnostics to evaluate the effects of different synchronization strategies on inter-slice consistency and temporal noise propagation. By combining our previous experiments, we will gain a deeper understanding of how different components of the diffusion-based reconstruction pipeline affect stochastic consistency and ultimately inform the design of more robust volumetric reconstruction frameworks.
CONTROLS: The baseline for our diagnostics will remain the existing implementation of 2D and 3D diffusion-based solvers without any additional modifications or synchronization. We will also compare the results to a phase of the experiment where different synchronization mechanisms are applied in combination with our previously proposed slice synchronization method, in the same setting as the proposal.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By integrating the insights from the empirical analysis into the diagnostics framework, we will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms driving inter-slice inconsistency and temporal noise propagation in diffusion-based solvers, ultimately leading to more effective solutions for stabilized volumetric reconstruction.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: transfer learning from video restoration to volumetric medical reconstruction
PROPOSAL: We will leverage the lessons learned from video restoration tasks, where similar synchronization challenges have been addressed, and apply transfer learning techniques to adapt pre-trained diffusion models for video restoration to the volumetric medical reconstruction domain. By leveraging the pre-trained knowledge of video diffusion models, we aim to expedite the development of effective synchronization strategies for volumetric reconstruction.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our transfer learning approach against the naive baseline of independent slice processing, our previously proposed slice synchronization method via shared noise projection, and the most effective synchronization mechanism identified through the empirical analysis (proposal 5).
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By borrowing knowledge from video restoration tasks, we anticipate significant advances in the development of effective synchronization strategies for volumetric medical reconstruction, potentially leading to faster convergence and improved quality of reconstructed images.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: 3d volume evaluation metrics and validation in sparse-view ct reconstruction
PROPOSAL: We will extend the evaluation of our previously proposed methods (proposals 1-5) to a comprehensive assessment of 3D volume quality metrics, including volumetric thick-measure similarity (TMS), volumetric mean absolute error (VMAE), and 3D similarity index (3DSI), across multiple sparse-view CT reconstruction tasks. Our aim is to validate the effectiveness of our proposed synchronization strategies in achieving superior 3D volumetric reconstruction quality on clinically relevant datasets.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our proposed 3D volume evaluation metrics against state-of-the-art methods for 3D sparse-view CT reconstruction.
COST: 280 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By introducing comprehensive 3D volume evaluation metrics, we expect to quantify the significant advantages of our proposed synchronization strategies for volumetric medical reconstruction tasks, particularly in sparse-view CT reconstruction.

Deep neural networks trained with first-order optimization methods have achieved remarkable empirical success across diverse domains. Despite their widespread adoption, a rigorous theoretical understanding of their optimization dynamics and generalization behavior remains incomplete, particularly for networks with ReLU activations. The difficulty stems from the non-smoothness and non-convexity of the loss landscape induced by ReLU activations and network architectures, which complicate classical analyses. Intriguingly, over-parameterized models often reach zero training error and still generalize well in the absence of explicit regularization, a phenomenon that has spurred substantial theoretical research into its underlying mechanisms.

A prominent line of research analyzes neural network training through the neural tangent kernel (NTK). In the infinite-width limit, the dynamics of gradient descent (GD) can be characterized by functions in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of the NTK, and convergence guarantees have been established for both shallow and deep networks: provided the width is sufficiently large, GD converges to a global minimum within a neighborhood of its initialization. In this regime, generalization errors of order $L\sqrt{\mathbf{y}^\top(\mathbf{H}^\infty)^{-1}\mathbf{y}/n}$ have been obtained for networks of depth $L$ trained on $n$ examples, where $\mathbf{H}^\infty$ denotes the NTK Gram matrix over the training data, but only for widths polynomial in $n$, $L$ and $1/\lambda_0$, with $\lambda_0$ the smallest eigenvalue of $\mathbf{H}^\infty$. Requiring $\lambda_0>0$ is a strong assumption, because this eigenvalue tends to zero as the size of the training set grows. A weaker assumption is that the data are separable by the NTK features at initialization with a margin $\gamma$. Under this assumption, a logarithmic width suffices for two-layer ReLU networks, with a risk bound of order $1/(\gamma^2\sqrt{n})$ derived from Rademacher complexity; this width result relies on the 1-homogeneity of two-layer ReLU networks, a property that does not hold for deep networks. Extensions to deep ReLU networks yield bounds that still decay only as $1/\sqrt{n}$ and contain either factors exponential in depth, such as $4^L$, or additional width-dependent terms. A rate of order $1/(\gamma^2 n)$ has so far been derived only for two-layer ReLU networks. More generally, uniform-convergence analyses based on Rademacher complexity or covering numbers can lead to vacuous bounds, typically depend exponentially on the depth, and usually yield rates of order $1/\sqrt{n}$.

A complementary line of research relies on algorithmic stability. Building on the observation that the spectral norm of the Hessian of wide networks scales with the width $m$ as $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{m})$, stability analyses have obtained bounds of order $\widetilde{O}(1/(n\gamma^2))$ for shallow networks, which is almost optimal in view of known lower bounds, and have been extended to deep networks with bounds of order $\widetilde{O}(e^{O(L)}/(n\gamma^2))$. These analyses, however, assume smooth activation functions and cannot be applied to non-smooth ReLU networks; for deep networks, they also incur an exponential dependence on depth, both in the bound and in the required width.

In summary, existing results either exhibit the suboptimal $1/\sqrt{n}$ dependence on the sample size, are restricted to shallow networks, require smooth activations, or depend exponentially on the depth $L$. A natural and fundamental question is therefore whether GD on deep ReLU networks can achieve generalization rates comparable to the minimax optimal rates established in the kernel setting, namely the SVM-type rate of order $1/(n\gamma^2)$. Specifically, for fully connected deep ReLU networks trained by gradient descent with the logistic loss on binary classification data that are NTK-separable with margin $\gamma$: Can risk bounds of the optimal order $1/(\gamma^2 n)$ be established? Can the exponential dependence on the depth $L$ be replaced by a polynomial dependence $\mathrm{poly}(L)$? And how much over-parameterization (network width) do such guarantees require?

Multimodal learning has become a cornerstone of many real-world applications, such as autonomous perception, medical diagnosis, and human-computer interaction. By integrating information from multiple sources, such as vision, audio, and text, multimodal systems aim to improve performance and generalization. However, multimodal data often exhibit a significant imbalance between modalities due to noise, lack of information, or sensor heterogeneity, so that a dominant modality may overshadow the others and hinder the learning of weak modalities. Unimodal prediction accuracy is widely used to detect modality imbalance; it is a simple and effective metric, but it is inherently sensitive to noise and perturbations. This vulnerability often leads to fragile performance in practice and limits the reliability of accuracy-based definitions of strong and weak modalities in real-world deployments.

Modality imbalance arises in early, intermediate, and late fusion alike. Late fusion, also known as decision-level fusion, combines the outputs (logits) of modality-specific models, either with equal weights (static late fusion) or with weights that vary across samples (dynamic late fusion). It remains one of the most widely adopted paradigms because of its modular design, interpretability, and strong compatibility with unimodal pre-trained models. Yet, lacking feature-level compensation or cross-modal interaction, late fusion tends to amplify the influence of strong modalities while weakening the role of lower-quality ones, so that predictions from disadvantaged modalities often carry little weight or even introduce noise into the final decision. A large body of work has attempted to alleviate this imbalance by enhancing the predictive performance of weak modalities, for example by aggregating independently trained modality-specific classifiers, confidence-based weighting, modality dropout or gating, adaptive ensembling, or knowledge distillation from dominant modalities.

While effective in certain scenarios, these methods often implicitly aim to align weak modalities with dominant ones in terms of prediction accuracy, attempting to bring them closer to their stronger counterparts. Such over-alignment raises several concerns: (1) it may suppress the distinct and complementary information encoded in weak modalities, causing modality-specific information loss; (2) it risks error propagation, as the dominant modality's errors are amplified when weak modalities follow them blindly; and (3) through excessive conformity, weak modalities may lose the predictive advantages they originally held on some samples.

Robustness makes the issue more pressing. Multimodal cooperation is inherently sensitive to perturbations such as data noise, label noise, and incomplete modalities, because modalities are heterogeneous and vary in reliability in real-world conditions. Prior studies have highlighted that the robustness of a multimodal system can be bottlenecked by a single weak modality, revealing a strong link between modality imbalance and overall system reliability. Existing work addresses robustness by incorporating uncertainty modeling, designing robustness-aware fusion strategies, quantifying multimodal robustness with dedicated evaluation metrics, or connecting it with generalization error bounds. However, most of these approaches emphasize prediction-consistency modeling and pay little attention to the instability of the decision space, that is, a model's high sensitivity to input perturbations near the decision boundary, where even minor changes can cause large shifts in prediction; they also tend to require more complex architectures with limited generalizability across tasks with different class granularity.

This raises several questions. How can a dominant modality help a weak modality within a decision-level fusion system without forcing it to conform, so that the weak modality keeps its unique, complementary information and does not inherit the dominant modality's errors? Given that judging modality strength by unimodal accuracy or confidence is itself fragile under noise, how can one reliably determine which modality is dominant and which is weak? How do the predictions of the individual modalities determine the robustness of the fused decision to input perturbations, and can a remedy for modality imbalance come with a theoretical guarantee on that robustness? Finally, can such a remedy both narrow the performance gap between modalities and make the fused prediction more reliable under noisy and imbalanced conditions?

Directed graphs (digraphs) model systems with asymmetric relationships, capturing essential structures such as flows, dependencies, and hierarchies that arise in many real-world applications. This makes digraphs particularly well-suited for problems in diverse domains including biology, transportation, social dynamics, and, more recently, image and video understanding, where structured and directional representations are critical for interpretation and reasoning. Consequently, generating digraphs is central to tasks such as simulation, data augmentation and novel instance discovery in domains with directional structure.

Graph generative models aim to learn the probability distribution of a set of observed graphs, enabling the generation of new samples that preserve structural and statistical properties. Such models have shown strong potential in diverse applications, including drug discovery, finance, social network modeling, and medicine. However, most generative models focus on undirected graphs, with only limited efforts on directed settings. The vast majority of works on directed graph generation focus solely on directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), with autoencoders, autoregressive methods and, more recently, diffusion combined with an auto-regressive process; these require the input DAGs to be topologically ordered, which can result in higher computational cost. Other approaches are tailored to specific applications and, therefore, to DAGs. A general digraph generation method, following an auto-regressive perspective, has only recently been proposed, and its implementation is not publicly available, limiting its accessibility for study and evaluation.

Two main factors limit progress in this direction. First, at the modeling level, the directed setting is inherently more challenging than its undirected counterpart: edge directionality greatly enlarges the learnable space (for graphs with 4 nodes, there are 218 possible digraphs, compared to only 11 undirected ones) and introduces a substantially larger dependency space, making the underlying distribution harder to learn. In directed graphs, a model must distinguish the different semantics carried by incoming and outgoing edges. The difficulty is further amplified in settings where domain-specific structural constraints must be respected, such as acyclicity in DAGs. Second, beyond these technical challenges, the lack of standardized benchmarks for directed graph generation is a barrier to rigorous evaluation and fair comparison: existing approaches typically rely only on proxy metrics derived from downstream tasks, failing to directly evaluate generative quality, and there are no established benchmarks to evaluate digraph generative quality systematically.

This raises several questions. How can a generative model be made expressive enough to learn distributions over general directed graphs, capturing directional dependencies and respecting structural properties such as acyclicity, without being restricted to DAGs or relying on a prescribed node ordering? Is it sufficient to extend generative architectures designed for undirected graphs to the directed case, or must such models be explicitly sensitive to directional topology? And how can the generative quality of directed graph generators be evaluated directly and systematically, rather than through downstream proxies, so that different approaches can be compared fairly?

Transformers, powered by attention mechanisms, have become the default backbone for sequence modeling across language, vision, speech, and decision making. Their success is often linked to selective access to an ever-growing key-value cache while retaining parallel training and inference. In large language models, this selective ability, composed across multiple attention layers and residual pathways, supports long-range memory retrieval and the algorithmic behaviors associated with in-context learning (for example induction heads and pattern completion), as shown by empirical and mechanistic studies.

Causal softmax attention combines strong selectivity with parallel efficiency: at each step it forms a distribution over past indices and mixes their values, while all steps can be computed in parallel. Given queries, keys and values $Q,K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}$ with rows $q_t$, $k_i$, $v_i$, define masked scores $s_{t,i}=q_t^\top k_i/\sqrt{d}$ for $i\le t$ and $-\infty$ otherwise, and set $\alpha_{t,\cdot}=\mathrm{softmax}(s_{t,\cdot})$, a probability distribution over $\{1,\dots,t\}$. The step-$t$ read is $o_t=\sum_{i\le t}\alpha_{t,i}v_i$, which lies in the convex hull of $\{v_1,\dots,v_t\}$; stacking all steps yields $O=AV$ with $A_{t,i}=\alpha_{t,i}$, so a single matrix multiply produces all outputs.

This convex-mixture view explains the efficiency of attention, but it also reveals a dilemma between lossless storage and lossy processing. The key-value cache stores the full context, but the read is lossy: each head applies the same weights to all coordinates of $v_i$, so the output lies in the convex hull of the stored values and all channels are synchronized. As a result, even simple per-channel indexing, such as returning $(v_{i_1,1},\dots,v_{i_D,D})$ where each coordinate $j$ is taken from its own past index $i_j$ (for example, a coordinate-wise argmax), cannot be represented unless all chosen indices coincide. This limitation hinders Transformers in long-range modeling with non-sequential or irregular timestep indexing, and in tasks where channel-wise structure is critical, such as multivariate time series modeling.

Most recent advances in attention aim to improve expressivity and efficiency, typically by designing richer selection distributions while still reading values through a token-separable linear combination. These include sparse attention patterns, low-rank projections, and kernelizable variants with normalization or gating. Efficiency-oriented work accelerates attention through factorized implementations, or replaces the cache with streaming state space models and recurrent networks that keep a fixed-size state. Across these lines, computation becomes faster or the distribution richer, but the read remains a linear mix: channels share weights, and even simple per-channel indexing cannot be realized in one step. Some recent works explore more complex combinations, such as nonlinear mixing or hard/top-k selection, yet these mainly target training stability or accuracy in specific cases and do not address the lossy-processing limitation.

This leaves an open problem: how can the read of an attention-style sequence mixer be redesigned to remove this linear read bottleneck and support per-channel, context-dependent selection from memory, so that different channels can retrieve different past indices in the same step, while keeping causal parallelism and the asymptotic time complexity of the underlying selection mechanism (for example, quadratic in sequence length for softmax attention and linear for linear-time variants)? And does closing this gap between lossless storage and lossy processing translate into better sequence modeling in practice?

Real-world reinforcement learning (RL) systems often struggle with reward specification: it is notoriously difficult to craft a reward function that captures the intended goals in all scenarios, so designers rely on proxy rewards that only approximate the true objective. Agents that optimize such imperfect proxies can discover unintended, exploitative behaviors that achieve high proxy return while yielding poor true outcomes, a phenomenon known as reward hacking. Reward hacking is not merely hypothetical: it has led to undesirable or even catastrophic consequences in safety-critical settings and is common in real-world deployments. At the same time, interpretability and transparency of RL policies are increasingly recognized as requirements for real-world acceptance: policymakers and practitioners in safety-critical domains need systems that are not only robust but also understandable, so that they can identify which decision-making criteria lead to undesirable outcomes, mitigate risks, and ensure compliance with safety regulations. RL algorithms for high-stakes applications therefore face two fundamental challenges: robustness to uncertain or poorly specified rewards, and interpretability that facilitates oversight by human stakeholders.

Recent work has begun to formalize reward hacking and to develop principled mitigations. In one such framework, the agent is given a proxy reward and a reference policy, while the true reward is hidden. The proxy is called r-correlated with the true reward if the two maintain a correlation coefficient r > 0 on the state-action pairs encountered by the reference policy, that is, under the reference policy's state-action occupancy measure. This definition permits the proxy and the true reward to diverge arbitrarily in parts of the state-action space that the reference policy does not visit, which are precisely the regions an RL agent may exploit under intensive optimization. Reward hacking is then said to occur when optimizing an r-correlated proxy yields a policy with lower true reward than the reference policy. The mitigation proposed within that framework, Occupancy-Regularized Policy Optimization (ORPO), augments the standard RL objective with a regularization term that penalizes the chi-squared divergence between the learned policy's state-action occupancy measure and that of the reference policy, with a strength that depends on the correlation level, and it guarantees a lower bound on the improvement in true reward.

Despite this progress, existing solutions to reward hacking have several limitations. First, their effectiveness relies heavily on the specific proxy reward. Designing good proxies is hard: in real-world scenarios, proxies are often derived heuristically or empirically from noisy or limited data, which leaves uncertainty about their exact relationship to the true reward, and the correlation level itself is typically known only approximately. Robustness to variations in the proxy is therefore crucial for dependable deployment, yet a method that regularizes against one fixed proxy offers only a weak guarantee on worst-case performance when the proxy could be any reward consistent with the assumed correlation, including an adversarially chosen one. Second, current methods treat the reward function as a black box and learn complex policies with no easily interpretable structure, making it hard to understand why a policy avoids reward hacking or to trust its behavior in novel situations; moreover, they cannot easily incorporate prior knowledge about the true reward when such knowledge is available.

This raises several research questions. Given only a proxy reward, a reference policy and an assumed correlation level, how can one learn a policy whose true performance is guaranteed against the entire class of rewards consistent with the correlation constraint, rather than against a single trusted proxy? Can such a guarantee be turned into an objective that is tractable to optimize with standard policy-optimization tools? How should state-action pairs that the reference policy rarely or never visits, where the correlation constraint says nothing about the true reward, be handled? When prior knowledge about the structure of the true reward is available, how can it be exploited to avoid excessive conservatism and to expose, in an interpretable way, which aspects of the reward a learned policy is most vulnerable to? Finally, how can one obtain policies whose performance remains robust and stable when the true correlation between proxy and true reward is uncertain or misspecified?

Dictionary learning, in its most general form, assumes that observations X are generated by latent variables Z through an unknown function, X = g(Z). The goal is to recover the latent generative process from observational data alone, a fundamental task in both science and machine learning. This nonparametric formulation unifies a wide range of latent variable models, including independent component analysis, factor analysis and causal representation learning.

Identifiability, the ability to recover the true generative model from data, is crucial for understanding the hidden world. Yet in general dictionary learning, where both the latent variables and the generating process are unknown, the problem is fundamentally ill-posed without additional assumptions, akin to finding a needle in a haystack. To reduce this ambiguity, most prior work imposes strong parametric constraints that limit the space of possible solutions. The practice is so widespread that, although dictionary learning is fundamentally nonparametric, it is almost always instantiated as a linear model, in which observations are sparse linear combinations of latent variables. Such linearity can be overly restrictive and fails to capture the complexity of many real-world generative processes. Sparse autoencoders, commonly used in mechanistic interpretability, especially for foundation models, are a relevant example: although effective in some settings, they are rooted in sparse linear dictionary learning, which raises concerns about their ability to represent the inherently nonlinear structure of large-scale neural representations.

Many efforts have been made to relax the linearity assumption. In nonlinear independent component analysis, one line of work leverages auxiliary variables as weak supervision to achieve identifiability under statistical independence, while another constrains the mixing function itself. In causal representation learning, identifiability often depends on access to interventional data or counterfactual views, which presuppose some control over the data-generating process. Some basic conditions cannot be avoided: just as linear dictionary learning needs conditions such as the restricted isometry property so that distinct latent codes map to distinguishable observations, the nonlinear generating function must be smooth and injective so that no information is lost. But avoiding information loss is not sufficient for full recovery of the latent variables in the nonlinear regime, which is why existing guarantees rely on restricted function classes or on auxiliary information such as domain or time indices, interventions or counterfactual data.

A gap therefore remains between theoretical guarantees and practical utility. Theoretically, while additional assumptions can yield recovery guarantees, it is rarely possible to verify whether they hold in practice; understanding which guarantees remain valid when assumptions are violated is therefore essential for reliably uncovering the truth in general settings. Practically, what matters is less identifiability under ideal conditions than which inductive biases promote recovery, especially when the ground truth is unknown. Yet most existing approaches offer no guarantees under even mild violations of their assumptions, which makes their associated biases, such as contrastive objectives or weak supervision, difficult to generalize across settings.

The challenge is to make identifiability actionable in general settings: only observational data are available, the generating function is nonlinear and unknown, no parametric constraint or auxiliary supervision can be relied upon, and only basic conditions such as invertibility and differentiability are assumed, accepting that recovering every latent variable may then be infeasible. In such settings, two questions remain open:
- What aspects of the latent process can still be recovered with guarantees?
- What inductive biases should be introduced to guide recovery, ideally ones that could be adopted universally across models and settings?
A related question is whether, and under which additional conditions that require no auxiliary information, all latent variables could still be recovered.

Reinforcement learning has been highly effective in many domains, ranging from robotics to gaming and recommender systems. Value-based algorithms such as Deep Q-Networks are a cornerstone of off-policy reinforcement learning and are widely used in discrete action spaces because of their simplicity, training stability, and sample-efficiency. However, they rely on estimating Q-values for individual state-action pairs and require a maximization over the action space, both to derive the greedy policy and to evaluate the best next-state value in the Bellman target. This maximization is straightforward when the actions can be enumerated, but in continuous action spaces evaluating the Q-value over the entire action space becomes computationally infeasible, which has traditionally restricted value-based methods to discrete actions.

In continuous control, actor-critic methods such as DDPG, TD3, and SAC are typically used instead: a critic is trained on off-policy data to estimate Q-values, and an actor (policy) is trained to output actions that maximize the critic. While powerful, these methods often suffer from instability caused by the coupled training of actor and critic, from sensitivity to hyperparameters, and from the difficulty of predicting in high-dimensional action spaces. The additional actor network brings its own hyperparameters, which makes reproducibility a challenge, and adds computational and memory overhead. Moreover, an actor trained by gradient ascent on the Q-function landscape can only find locally optimal actions, which becomes a serious limitation when the Q-function is complex or non-convex, for instance when the action space is constrained so that actions must remain within specific safety bounds. Training several actors to explore different modes of the Q-function alleviates this, but adds computational overhead and inference-time latency, and the actor's parameterization may still be too limited to capture complex optimal actions.

Actor-free, value-based alternatives must instead carry out the maximization over continuous actions themselves, and finding the maximizing action has been their primary bottleneck. Methods that perform this maximization numerically, through mixed-integer programming, the cross-entropy method and other sampling-based or evolutionary search, or gradient ascent on the action, tend either to return suboptimal local maxima or to be computationally impractical, and sampling becomes progressively less efficient as the action dimension grows. Discretizing the action space is effective in low dimensions but does not scale to high-dimensional tasks. Another line of work restricts the functional form of the Q-function so that its maximizer can be obtained directly, for example by assuming that the advantage is quadratic in the action or that the Q-function is convex in the action; such assumptions limit expressivity and practical applicability. Representing the Q-function with a radial basis function output layer makes the best action easier to identify, but introduces an implicit trade-off between how expressive the Q-function can be in modeling multiple local optima and how accurately its maximizing action is recovered.

This raises the question of whether an actor-free, value-based algorithm can efficiently and accurately select optimal actions in continuous action spaces without imposing restrictive assumptions on the shape of the Q-function, while remaining stable to train, robust across diverse tasks, and scalable to high-dimensional action spaces. Such an algorithm would retain the simplicity of Q-learning and avoid the cost and instability of learning a separate actor; it could also avoid the local optima that trap gradient-based actors when the Q-function is highly non-convex, as in constrained action spaces. Can such an approach be made competitive with established actor-critic methods for continuous control, and can it outperform them where gradient-based action maximization struggles?

Recent frontier models such as OpenAI o1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1 and Kimi k1.5 provide compelling proof of concept for leveraging long chains of thought to enhance the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). Following these advances, Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) techniques such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization (DAPO) have emerged as the de facto standard for strengthening LLM reasoning. In RLVR, the policy model is trained by sampling multiple responses (rollouts) to a prompt, checking each final answer against a ground-truth answer, and then reinforcing correct answers while penalizing incorrect ones. GRPO, a variant of Proximal Policy Optimization that dispenses with a costly value model, computes the advantage of each response by normalizing its reward with the mean and standard deviation of the rewards in its group.

This works well when the responses to a prompt contain both right and wrong answers, but it does not account for the case where a group of rollouts is entirely correct or entirely incorrect and therefore receives identical rewards. Such prompts are referred to as zero-variance prompts. For them, the normalized rewards (the advantage values) collapse to zero, so there is no training signal and all rollouts for those prompts are rendered uninformative. Put differently, the policy is rewarded for a correct response only when at least one incorrect response exists in the same group, and penalized for an incorrect response only when at least one correct response is present. Zero-variance prompts typically arise when a problem is too difficult or too easy for the current model: early in training, when the model often fails to solve a problem even once across multiple attempts, and near convergence, when it has become strong enough to solve many problems in every attempt.

Ignoring these prompts may seem conceptually reasonable, but it remains problematic because rollout generation is itself a major bottleneck in RL training, so the compute spent sampling responses to zero-variance prompts is simply wasted. Recent methods acknowledge this inefficiency and try to filter zero-variance prompts out, either before rollout, by predicting from the training history which prompts are likely to yield identical rewards and skipping them, or after rollout, by repeatedly sampling and discarding them until a batch contains only prompts with mixed outcomes. These methods view zero-variance prompts merely as a cost to be avoided and implicitly assume that they offer no value for policy optimization. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has investigated whether zero-variance prompts themselves can serve as a valuable source of learning signal.

This raises several open questions. Can the responses to a prompt whose rollouts are all correct, or all incorrect, provide meaningful feedback for policy optimization, even though the group contains no contrasting response? If so, how should such feedback be formulated so that it remains informative and does not destabilize training? And would exploiting these prompts, instead of discarding them, lead to better reasoning performance and more stable learning than both standard group-relative training and the prevailing practice of filtering them out?

PREDICTION: This approach might enable the policy to learn from zero-variance prompts, but may require careful selection of auxiliary tasks and risk overfitting to these specific tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: extended group relative policy optimization with uncertainty estimation
PROPOSAL: Integrate Bayesian neural network elements into the advantage estimation of GRPO, such that the variance of the reward among rollouts in a group is explicitly modeled. This allows for the direct computation of an "uncertainty-aware" advantage value, which is then used for policy training.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard GRPO without Bayesian estimation, and a variant of GRPO where the uncertainty estimation is not used for advantage computation.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This model might generalize better to unseen tasks, especially on zero-variance prompts, by capturing the underlying uncertainty in the policy's predictions, but may also add a significant computational cost due to the additional Bayesian inference.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: mining valuable knowledge from monotonic sequences of rollouts
PROPOSAL: Develop a technique to extract patterns or insights from sequences of rollouts where the correct answer is consistently provided or consistently absent. This can be done through sequential pattern mining or sequential Bayesian inference. The extracted patterns can then be fed back into the policy training process to help improve its performance.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline where no pattern mining is performed, and a variant where the mine extracted patterns are used to augment the policy loss.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might reveal meaningful relationships between rollouts and the underlying task, but might also require significant resources and may be affected by the curse of dimensionality.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: using hierarchical auxiliary tasks to overcome zero-variance prompts
PROPOSAL: Instead of using a single auxiliary task, use a hierarchical structure of tasks where each task builds upon the previous one. For example, the first task might be to predict the output space for a given prompt, the second task might be to estimate the confidence in the answer based on the output space, and the third task might be to predict the correct answer based on the output space and confidence estimates. These hierarchical tasks are then added to the policy loss, encouraging the policy to learn from the zero-variance prompts.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline where only the primary task is used, and a variant where multiple auxiliary tasks are combined without hierarchical structure.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might enable the policy to learn more robustly from zero-variance prompts by providing a more comprehensive understanding of the task, but may also require careful design of the hierarchical tasks and risk overfitting to these specific tasks.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: tracking task difficulty in a dynamic skills graph
PROPOSAL: Develop a graph-based framework to track the difficulty of different tasks as the policy learns. The graph represents the policy's skills and how they relate to each other, with edges indicating the difficulty of transitioning between skills. The policy can then use this graph to dynamically adjust its learning strategy based on its current strengths and weaknesses, including when to focus on difficult tasks that are currently zero-variance.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline where no dynamic skills graph is maintained, and a variant where the graph is used only for visualization purposes.
COST: 280 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might enable the policy to learn more efficiently by adaptively focusing on difficult tasks, but may also require significant resources to maintain and update the graph, and may be affected by the complexity of the graph structure.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: exploiting zero-variance prompts through transition-state reinforcement learning
PROPOSAL: Reformulate the policy optimization problem as a transition-state reinforcement learning problem, where the goal is to learn the optimal transition between states (rollouts) that are currently zero-variance. This is done by computing the value function for each state and using this to guide the policy in transitioning between states.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline where no transition-state reinforcement learning is used, and a variant where the policy is trained on a fixed set of states.
COST: 320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might enable the policy to learn more robustly from zero-variance prompts by explicitly modeling the transitions between states, but may also require significant resources to compute the value function and may be affected by the curse of dimensionality.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: evaluating and benchmarking the efficacy of zero-variance prompt exploitation
PROPOSAL: Develop a benchmarking framework to evaluate the efficacy of the various methods proposed to exploit zero-variance prompts. This includes designing a set of tasks that exhibit zero-variance behavior and testing the proposed methods on these tasks. The results are then compared against a set of baselines to provide a holistic understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of each approach.
CONTROLS: Compare against a set of baselines including standard policy optimization, group relative policy optimization, and other techniques for handling zero-variance prompts, as described above.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This evaluation framework will provide a comprehensive understanding of the efficacy of zero-variance prompt exploitation methods, but may require additional resources to establish and maintain the benchmarking framework.
