Visual localization of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) is essential for applications such as digital-twin modeling, mapping, surveillance, large-area and infrastructure inspection, and search-and-rescue operations, yet it faces challenges that ground-level localization systems do not address. Ground-level approaches benefit from similar viewpoints between query and reference images, whereas aerial applications encounter dramatic perspective differences and must scale to large areas. In many scenarios, these systems require high-precision localization while operating with limited resources, for example without an internet connection or without GNSS/GPS support, which makes large image databases or heavy 3D models impractical.

Current UAV localization algorithms either retrieve the closest match from a database of posed images, which is inaccurate, or rely on 3D models of the scene, which are expensive in memory and computation; in resource-limited settings, such as connectivity-limited environments, this can degrade accuracy. Image retrieval methods based on global descriptors struggle with the large viewpoint and illumination changes of UAV imagery, and even with view synthesis or self-supervised learning their performance drops under extreme perspective shifts, so retrieval alone remains insufficient for accurate 6-DoF localization. Structure-based methods build a 3D model with structure-from-motion, establish 2D-3D correspondences against meshes or dense depth maps, and estimate the pose with PnP solvers inside RANSAC, but such complete 3D models require extensive manual effort to create for each operational area. Most UAV-specific positioning methods estimate only 2-DoF or 3-DoF poses rather than the full 6-DoF pose required by advanced applications. Recent approaches based on level-of-detail (LoD) city models improve storage efficiency, but they still assume unchanged environments, perform poorly in building-sparse areas such as highways, and depend on positioning sensors for initialization.

A compelling alternative is geodata, such as orthographic aerial views (digital orthophotos) and elevation maps (digital surface models). Such data are lightweight, scalable and better suited to low-resource settings, and they are increasingly accessible through free releases from government geoportals, for instance in the European Union; where public access is limited, they can be synthesized with photogrammetric tools. For example, covering an area of approximately 0.265 km² can require a 3D model of around 8 GB, whereas geodata require about 30 times less memory. Surprisingly, no existing UAV localization approach seems to fully leverage these data sources: previous work has not used the combination of orthophotos and elevation models for UAV pose estimation, so no existing method is directly applicable to this scenario. Modern feature matchers (dense, semi-dense, sparse, and geometry-aware) perform robustly in many scenarios, but their effectiveness with orthographic geodata remains unexplored. A major reason for this gap is the absence of aligned cross-domain datasets and of full-pose, paired, large-scale benchmarks designed for localization with these types of geodata. Existing UAV localization datasets provide only partial pose information (2-DoF or 3-DoF), feature predominantly nadir views with limited viewpoint diversity, rely on entirely synthetic environments or synthetically rendered views that introduce domain gaps, or lack integrated geodata; the one concurrent collection that includes orthographic geodata focuses its pose evaluation on 3-DoF and suffers from a misalignment between its low-resolution satellite imagery and its aerial photogrammetry data. Furthermore, visual localization methods often need to solve image retrieval before estimating the pose; because these two steps are coupled, it is difficult to disentangle the contribution of each component to the final error.

The problem is therefore the following: given an orthophoto raster, an elevation raster, and a query UAV image taken from an arbitrary viewpoint, determine the georeferenced 6-DoF pose of the camera (localization) and, optionally, its intrinsic parameters (calibration). The key challenge is bridging two fundamentally different projection models: perspective projection for UAV imagery and orthographic projection for geodata. This difference creates a domain gap that is particularly pronounced in oblique views, where perspective distortion is significant. A second domain gap arises from visual and structural discrepancies between query and reference data caused by differences in acquisition time: reference geodata may have been collected months or years before a flight, so orthophotos differ in appearance (color shifts, illumination variations, seasonal differences) and elevation models differ in geometry (construction changes, vegetation growth, infrastructure evolution). These changes vary unpredictably across locations and seasons, cannot easily be addressed through simple data augmentation or domain adaptation, and cannot be faithfully replicated by synthetic alternatives.

This raises several open questions. Can lightweight 2.5D orthographic geodata serve as the only reference for accurate full 6-DoF UAV pose estimation and camera calibration? Can state-of-the-art feature matchers, designed largely for perspective imagery, bridge the perspective-orthographic gap, especially for oblique viewpoints, and how can the perspective disparity between query and reference be reduced? How difficult is it to recover camera intrinsics from aerial imagery in this setting? And how do characteristics of the reference data, namely temporal visual and structural domain shifts, data resolution, and the covisibility between the query image and the reference area (which depends on imperfect upstream retrieval), affect localization accuracy?

Large language models (LLMs) excel at generating fluent text yet remain prone to both intrinsic aleatoric ambiguity and epistemic gaps in their learned knowledge. The latter can lead to hallucinations—confident outputs that are factually incorrect. Quantifying these uncertainties is critical for building safe AI systems deployable in high-stakes applications. In free-form natural language generation tasks such as question answering, this is especially challenging, as lexically distinct responses can still be semantically equivalent: uncertainty has to be measured over meanings rather than over token sequences.

A standard way to do so defines a distribution over semantic clusters of responses, obtained by marginalizing over output sequences and approximated by Monte Carlo sampling. The total predictive uncertainty over these clusters decomposes into an aleatoric part, the entropy over clusters (semantic entropy), which captures the irreducible ambiguity among valid answers, and an epistemic part, which reflects the model's lack of knowledge or data coverage. For a question such as "Name a way to measure the Hubble constant", several distinct but correct answers (for instance, the distance ladder or gravitational lensing time delays) reflect aleatoric uncertainty, whereas answers that contradict scientific facts or admit ignorance reveal gaps in the model's knowledge and signal that it should abstain.

Estimating these quantities often relies on drawing large IID sample sets, which often contain semantically redundant outputs and waste compute. Semantic entropy quantifies aleatoric uncertainty by clustering generated outputs into semantic equivalence classes, and mutual information computed via iterative prompting has been used to lower-bound certain forms of epistemic uncertainty; despite their conceptual appeal, both require extensive sampling to produce stable estimates, limiting their use in low-resource settings. Diversity-oriented heuristics such as temperature scaling or nucleus sampling, on the other hand, do not account for semantics. A more recent method steers generation toward semantic diversity, but it relies on token substitutions and remains restricted to autoregressive models (ARMs). Moreover, diversity heuristics are commonly applied during sampling without correcting for the bias they introduce, even though the uncertainties of interest are defined under the model's own distribution.

Meanwhile, uncertainty estimation methods have focused on ARMs, whereas masked diffusion models (MDMs), which extend masked language modeling by learning iterative denoising schedules that progressively resolve masked spans, have recently emerged as strong alternatives. Despite achieving text quality on par with state-of-the-art ARMs, MDMs remain largely overlooked in the context of uncertainty quantification.

This leaves several questions open. How can stable estimates of semantic aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty be obtained for free-form answers from a small, fixed budget of generations, so that the samples cover distinct meanings instead of repeating the same ones? How can this be done while keeping the estimates faithful to the model's own predictive distribution? And can a single approach serve both autoregressive and masked diffusion language models?

Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) generate discrete data by iteratively replacing masked tokens with predicted unmasked ones, learning to reverse an absorbing-state diffusion process that progressively masks the tokens of a sequence. They have recently achieved strong results across diverse domains, including text generation, image synthesis, and multi-modal understanding and generation. For images, a pre-trained tokenizer (e.g., a VQ-VAE) maps an image to a sequence of discrete tokens and its decoder reconstructs the image from those tokens; generation starts from a fully masked sequence and fills it in over many steps, which makes inference time- and compute-intensive. Building on this success, recent work has shown that these multi-step procedures can be distilled into one-step generators, substantially accelerating inference and reducing computational cost while maintaining competitive quality. For instance, Di[M]O distills a multi-step MDM into a one-step generator through on-policy distribution matching: a one-step prediction sampled from the student is corrupted by the forward masking process, and the teacher's and the student's output distributions conditioned on this intermediate state are matched, with the resulting gradient applied directly to the student's logits so that it never has to pass through the non-differentiable sampling operation.

Despite their remarkable performance, current one-step discrete generators face two fundamental limitations. First, they inherit both modeling and alignment errors from the teacher: existing distillation approaches implicitly assume that the teacher fully captures the target distribution, so imperfections in the teacher's generative modeling and the under-alignment of the pre-trained teacher with downstream preferences are both transmitted to the student during data-free distillation. Second, their discrete token outputs block gradient flow. This prevents the application of key refinement techniques that are widely used to improve one-step generators distilled from continuous diffusion models, such as adversarial (GAN) training, differentiable reward fine-tuning, and test-time optimization of the generator's input with respect to a reward. In text-to-image generation, for example, prompt-following and aesthetic quality are the two primary criteria, and the community increasingly relies on learned reward models and human-preference signals to optimize them directly; but because such rewards operate on decoded images, their gradients cannot pass through the tokenizer decoder and the sampled tokens back to a discrete generator. As a result, current distilled MDM generators have limited flexibility to leverage external knowledge, such as real data, or to incorporate user preferences to better align with downstream objectives.

The gradient-blocking problem is common across discrete modeling tasks. Adversarial training on discrete data, for instance, is challenging because the discriminator must compare generated samples with ground truth while the sampling process is non-differentiable. Prior remedies include policy-gradient estimators such as REINFORCE, which are unbiased but whose gradient variance becomes prohibitive when hundreds or thousands of tokens are generated at once, and differentiable relaxations of discrete tokens such as Gumbel-Softmax (often used with a straight-through estimator) and soft-argmax. However, these methods often introduce biased or high-variance gradients and numerical instabilities, and they have not been systematically applied to one-step discrete generators, in particular for fast visual generation. Moreover, the downstream objectives of interest, such as discriminators and reward models, act on continuous inputs such as the images produced by the tokenizer decoder, so a practical solution must let gradients flow through the existing generation pipeline.

This raises two questions. How can the outputs of a one-step generator distilled from an MDM be made amenable to end-to-end gradient-based training, with gradients that are stable, low-variance and faithful to the true discrete objective, while remaining compatible with the existing teacher and tokenizer? And, once such gradients are available, can post-distillation refinements (adversarial training, differentiable reward fine-tuning, and test-time optimization of the generator's input) let a one-step student correct the errors it inherits from its teacher and better align with downstream objectives such as distribution fidelity, prompt adherence and aesthetic quality?

Smoothed decision-making is critical to avoiding abrupt and potentially dangerous large changes of actions in many online optimization problems, such as energy production scheduling in power grids, object tracking, motion planning, and server capacity provisioning in data centers. Mathematically, action smoothness can be achieved by adding to the optimization objective a switching cost that penalizes temporal changes in actions. The switching cost equips the online objective with a (finite) memory of previous actions and creates substantial algorithmic challenges; smoothed online optimization has therefore received a great deal of attention over the last decade, with a quickly growing list of algorithms offering worst-case performance guarantees in adversarial and stochastic settings and under various extensions.

At the same time, long-term fairness is a crucial consideration in many online optimization problems that can profoundly affect individuals' well-being and social welfare. Sequential allocation of social goods to different individuals or groups must be fair and free of discrimination; the surging environmental costs of geographically distributed AI data centers must be fairly distributed across regions, as repeatedly called for by various organizations and government agencies; and AI model performance and resource provisioning must promote social fairness without adversely affecting disadvantaged individuals or groups. If not designed with fairness in mind, online algorithms can perpetuate or even exacerbate societal biases, disproportionately affect certain groups or individuals, and amplify already widening socioeconomic disparities. Fairness in online optimization is therefore not only an ethical concern but also a necessity for broader social responsibility.

Incorporating a long-term fairness regularizer into the objective can effectively promote fairness in online optimization by mitigating implicit or explicit biases, but it creates significant challenges. The regularizer depends on the entire trajectory of actions and contexts and can only be evaluated at the end of an episode, with complete information, whereas a switching cost can be assessed step by step. Online decision-makers react to sequentially revealed information and tend to prioritize immediate cost reduction, potentially neglecting the long-term consequences of their sequence of decisions.

Recent research has started to explore fairness and long-term constraints in online problems such as online resource allocation, using primal-dual techniques. A major limitation of current fair online algorithms, however, is their reliance on the assumption that per-round objective functions are independent of historical actions, an assumption that plays a pivotal role in both their algorithm design and their theoretical analysis. In a simple resource allocation problem, for instance, the maximum allowable action at a given time may depend on past decisions through the remaining budget, but the reward at that time is assumed to depend only on the current decision. Such methods fall short when the per-round objective is directly affected by previous irrevocable actions, as it is with switching costs; in that case an online algorithm and an offline benchmark face different per-round objectives because their action sequences differ, which complicates any direct comparison of their costs. Conversely, the rich literature on smoothed online optimization does not handle a regularizer that is evaluated over the whole horizon. Fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization with switching costs is thus a new and challenging setting that appears not to have been considered in the literature.

Formally, consider an episode of T rounds. At each round t, an agent observes a (potentially adversarially chosen) non-negative hitting cost function f_t and a matrix A_t that maps its action into an M-dimensional cost vector, each dimension corresponding to an entity for which fairness must be taken into account, and then chooses an irrevocable action x_t without knowing future information. It incurs the hitting cost f_t(x_t) and a switching cost d(x_t, x_{t-1}), for instance a scaled squared Euclidean distance between consecutive actions. Fairness is captured by a long-term cost g, convex and Lipschitz, applied to the episode average of the cost vectors; a well-known choice is an l_p norm, which prioritizes reducing the highest costs borne by disadvantaged entities and recovers min-max fairness as p tends to infinity. The goal is to minimize $\frac{1}{T}\big(\sum_{t=1}^{T} f_t(x_t) + \sum_{t=1}^{T} d(x_t, x_{t-1})\big) + g\big(\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} A_t x_t\big)$.

This setting raises several questions. First, how hard is the long-term fairness regularizer intrinsically? Online algorithms are commonly evaluated by their regret or by their competitive ratio against a dynamic offline benchmark which, unlike a static benchmark restricted to a single fixed action, can adapt its action sequence over time with full knowledge of the context. A finite competitive ratio is attainable for online optimization with switching costs, but whether any online algorithm can achieve sublinear regret or a finite competitive ratio against the dynamic offline optimum in the presence of a long-term fairness regularizer, even without switching costs, remains an open question; prior work has only conjectured that finite performance might be impossible in similar settings. Second, if such guarantees are out of reach, against what kind of benchmark can meaningful, practically relevant performance guarantees be established? Third, how can an online algorithm reconcile the tension between minimizing the hitting cost, the switching cost and the long-term fairness cost with provable worst-case guarantees, when the per-round objective carries a memory of previous actions, and how does the long-term fairness regularizer affect such guarantees?

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) exhibit compelling cross-modal perception and reasoning capabilities on image-text data and have become the de facto standard for visual question answering (VQA), the task of answering a question based on the visual content of an image. However, standard MLLM architectures are not well suited to perceiving and reasoning about small visual details in high-resolution images. So-called global-view MLLMs downscale every input image to the base resolution of their vision encoder (for some widely used models only 224×224 or 336×336 pixels), which discards information; as a consequence, they perform poorly on fine-grained VQA, i.e., on questions whose answer depends on small visual details. Unlike common VQA settings, in which the question-relevant objects are typically prominent in the image, fine-grained VQA concerns targets that may occupy only a tiny fraction of a large, high-resolution image.

More recent global-local-view MLLMs process a downsampled global view together with local crops extracted from the original, unresized image. This dual-view strategy reduces information loss, but it multiplies the number of visual tokens, and because self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length, the computational cost grows rapidly. Moreover, despite having access to fine-grained visual details from all local crops, these models struggle to identify the few visual tokens that are relevant to the question amid the large number of local crop tokens, so their effectiveness on fine-grained VQA still remains limited.

An orthogonal line of work is visual cropping: searching the image for the regions that are relevant to the question and passing only those regions to the MLLM. Existing visual cropping techniques, however, suffer from one or more of three limitations. First, some depend on task-specific fine-tuning: SEAL, for instance, pairs the answering model with a separate visual-search MLLM equipped with additional decoders that is fine-tuned to predict object heatmaps and coordinates, and runs a recursive top-down search, a complex multi-module design that is costly to run. Second, several rely on uninformed, exhaustive search: DC² builds a hierarchical tree of image regions and captions each region with the MLLM, while ZoomEye traverses a hierarchical region tree and scores every visited region with three sequential MLLM forward passes using different prompts, a computation that cannot be simplified or shared across regions, so the cost grows quickly with the depth and breadth of the search. Third, ViCrop avoids hierarchical search by directly computing a question-guided heatmap, but its best-performing variants depend on query-key attention weights and answer gradients, which makes them incompatible with efficient attention implementations such as FlashAttention that never explicitly produce attention weights. Simply asking the MLLM where the target is does not solve the problem either: although many MLLMs are fine-tuned to predict bounding boxes, they often fail when prompted directly for the location of small objects, producing hallucinated or imprecise coordinates.

The open problem is therefore how to make an MLLM look at the right part of a high-resolution image. Can the image regions relevant to a fine-grained visual question be localized without task-specific fine-tuning or auxiliary modules, without an uninformed exhaustive search over the image, and in a way that remains compatible with efficient attention implementations? Can such localization benefit both global-view and global-local-view MLLMs, improving their answers to questions about small details while keeping inference cost low, given that MLLM inference is already computationally expensive? And how favorable an accuracy-efficiency trade-off can be reached relative to existing search-based visual cropping methods?

Grounding procedural steps in videos is crucial for enabling machines to follow along and assist humans in complex tasks such as cooking a recipe, assembling furniture, or performing maintenance work. This ability is particularly valuable for real-time procedural guidance in augmented and extended reality applications, where recognizing task progress allows users wearing headsets or smart glasses to receive timely, step-specific instructions. The task of Video Step Grounding (VSG) takes as input a list of procedural steps extracted from an instructional article (e.g., a recipe or a how-to guide) and a video of the same task, and aims to identify which of the steps are performed in the video, that is, which step, if any, each part of the video depicts (a segment may also show an action outside the listed steps).

Existing VSG approaches align procedural step descriptions with their corresponding video frames. Earlier works relied on weakly-supervised learning from instructional narrations, while more recent methods increasingly leverage language models and large-scale pretraining, for instance using language models to turn noisy narrations or speech transcripts into steps and pseudo-labels for training. These strategies face two key limitations. First, they need a training set, entailing the cost of collecting (and potentially annotating) it; moreover, a training set can bias models toward the specific videos and procedural tasks it depicts, limiting their generalization capability. Second, they assume offline processing, where the entire video is available ahead of time, which makes them unsuitable for real-world applications that process a live video stream and must make decisions as it unfolds.

This calls for addressing VSG online and without training: video segments arrive one after the other, and whether the current segment depicts a given step must be decided using only that segment and the segments preceding it, with no task-specific training data. This setting is challenging. Predictions must be made from partial evidence, and without the task-specific representations that would typically be learned from a dedicated training set. The task also requires fine-grained video understanding, since key steps of instructional tasks often involve similar objects or scenes: "inserting a screw" or "aligning parts" may look alike in tasks such as "Assemble a chair" and "Fix a table", making them hard to distinguish without nuanced semantic understanding. Large pretrained multimodal models have demonstrated impressive zero-shot performance on a wide variety of tasks without further tuning, and work on video-language alignment has moved away from frame-caption embedding similarity, which struggles to capture temporal dynamics, toward such models; yet whether off-the-shelf models can ground procedural steps when they only see the current short segment remains an open question. Moreover, a prediction made from the current segment alone has no memory of what has already happened in the video, so uncertain observations cannot benefit from past evidence, while storing and reprocessing the whole history is impractical on a live stream.

The research questions are therefore: can video step grounding be performed online, on a streaming video and without any training, at a level competitive with training-based offline methods? And how can knowledge from past segments be injected into the prediction for the current segment, without storing the whole history and while preserving a zero-shot, training-free approach?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating baseline models for online video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate a set of strong multimodal model baselines for video step grounding, adapted to process only one video segment at a time. Specifically, we will investigate large-scale multimodal transformer models like CLIP, and recent multimodal variants like OSIM and VisIoL, with a focus on evaluating their zero-shot performance when processing a live video stream one segment at a time. We will measure performance using metrics like accuracy, F1-score, and Hamming loss on real-world video step grounding benchmarks from instructional cooking recipe videos and egocentric procedural activity videos.
CONTROLS: We will compare our zero-shot baseline models to models that have been pre-trained on VSG tasks and fine-tuned on a specific dataset, providing an offline benchmark for comparison. We will also evaluate various ablations of our zero-shot models, including the effect of using different types of multimodal input (e.g., frame, audio, or both) and different window sizes for segmenting video frames
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that competing zero-shot models struggle due to the lack of task-specific information in the model, however strong multimodal models that are not specifically designed for this task can still achieve good performance due to their general-purpose multimodal capabilities, and ablation studies will point towards multimodal input as a key factor for zero-shot performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adding contextualized embeddings for video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will investigate using contextualized embeddings to improve the performance of online video step grounding. Specifically, we will experiment with using pre-trained BERT-like models to generate text embeddings for the step descriptions, and multimodal transformer models to generate visual embeddings for the video frames. We will then use a common encodings space for the step descriptions and video frames to compute similarity scores. This approach aims to capture the nuances of language and visual context that are crucial for accurately grounding video steps.
CONTROLS: We will control for the quality of the step descriptions by evaluating the RAKE (Rapid Automatic Keyword Extraction) score of the text, and we will compare our contextualized embeddings approach to a baseline model that uses keyword matching between step descriptions and video frames, as described above. We will also evaluate the effect of using different quality and quantities of step descriptions on model performance.
COST: 8000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that using contextualized embeddings improves the performance of video step grounding, especially in scenarios where step descriptions have high RAKE scores, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: revising evaluating baseline models for online video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate a set of strong multimodal model baselines for video step grounding, adapted to process only one video segment at a time, focusing on the use of cross-modal learning. Specifically, we will investigate how different cross-modal fusion methods (e.g., concatenation, attention, and late fusion) can improve the zero-shot performance of large-scale multimodal transformer models like CLIP, and recent multimodal variants like OSIM and VisIoL. We will measure performance using metrics like accuracy, F1-score, and Hamming loss on real-world video step grounding benchmarks from instructional cooking recipe videos and egocentric procedural activity videos.
CONTROLS: We will compare our zero-shot baseline models to models that have been pre-trained on VSG tasks and fine-tuned on a specific dataset, providing an offline benchmark for comparison. We will also evaluate various ablations of our zero-shot models, including the effect of using different types of multimodal input (e.g., frame, audio, or both) and different window sizes for segmenting video frames. Additionally, we will control for the impact of cross-modal learning on model performance by adapting the original two-step fine-tuning approach for cross-modal training in online videos.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that cross-modal learning is a key factor for achieving strong zero-shot performance in video step grounding, and that different cross-modal fusion methods perform differently on various VSG tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: improving adding contextualized embeddings for video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will improve our approach to using contextualized embeddings for video step grounding by incorporating attention mechanisms to dynamically weigh the importance of different tokens in both the step descriptions and video frames. Specifically, we will experiment with using multi-head attention to compute attention weights that align the text and visual embeddings, and use these attention weights to fuse the embeddings. We will explore different options for initialising the attention weights, such as using dominant keywords from the step description or learned weights from the model.
CONTROLS: We will compare our improved contextualized embeddings approach to our previous baseline method, and evaluate its performance with different options for initialising the attention weights. We will also control for the impact of attention mechanisms on model performance by comparing our results with a baseline model that uses a pre-defined fusion scheme.
COST: 7000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that our improved contextualized embeddings approach with attention mechanisms outperforms our previous baseline method, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: leveraging semantic graph reasoning for video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will investigate using semantic graph reasoning to reason about the relationship between video segments and step descriptions in video step grounding. Specifically, we will construct a knowledge graph that represents the semantic relationships between entities and actions in the step descriptions, and then use a graph neural network to reason about the relevance of the video segments to the step descriptions. We will evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks and compare it to our contextualized embeddings approach.
CONTROLS: We will control for the quality of the knowledge graph by evaluating the accuracy of the entity and action recognition methods used to construct the graph, and we will compare our graph reasoning approach to a baseline model that uses a simple matching scheme between the step descriptions and video segments.
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that semantic graph reasoning can improve the performance of video step grounding by capturing complex relationships between video segments and step descriptions, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: injecting temporal context with transformer encoder layers
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate the impact of injecting temporal context to our baseline models for video step grounding using transformer encoder layers. Specifically, we will modify our multimodal transformer model to include an additional encoder layer that takes into account the temporal relationships between consecutive video frames, and evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks. We will compare our results to our baseline model without temporal context and other state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of the additional encoder layer on model performance by comparing it to a baseline model with a reduced number of layers, and we will evaluate the effect of different window sizes for segmenting video frames on the performance of our model.
COST: 6500
PREDICTION: We expect to find that injecting temporal context improves the performance of our baseline model by capturing the nuances of the video sequence, and that this approach performs well even when the video sequence has a complex structure.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: enhancing leveraging semantic graph reasoning for video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will enhance our approach to using semantic graph reasoning for video step grounding by incorporating a procedure for iteratively refining the knowledge graph and re-reasoning about the relationship between video segments and step descriptions. Specifically, we will experiment with an iterative process that involves re-scoring the relevance of video segments to step descriptions based on the refined knowledge graph, and re-ranking the step descriptions based on their relevance to the video segments. We will evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks and compare it to our previous graph reasoning approach.
CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of the iterative refinement process on model performance by comparing it to a baseline model that uses a simple matching scheme between the step descriptions and video segments, and we will evaluate the effect of different refinement thresholds on the performance of our model.
COST: 8500
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the iterative refinement process improves the performance of our graph reasoning approach by capturing more nuanced relationships between video segments and step descriptions, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: fusing visual and language features with adaptive fusion mechanism
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate the impact of using an adaptive fusion mechanism to fuse the visual and language features extracted from the video frames and step descriptions in video step grounding. Specifically, we will design a mechanism that dynamically adjusts the weighting of the visual and language features based on the contextual information present in the step descriptions and video frames, and evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks.
CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of the adaptive fusion mechanism on model performance by comparing it to a baseline model that uses a fixed weighting scheme for the visual and language features, and we will evaluate the effect of different fusion mechanisms on the performance of our model.
COST: 7200
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the adaptive fusion mechanism improves the performance of our baseline model by capturing the complex relationships between the visual and language features, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating the impact of sample efficiency with few-shot learning
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the impact of sample efficiency on video step grounding using few-shot learning. Specifically, we will experiment with fine-tuning our baseline models using only a few examples of the video and step descriptions, and evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks. We will explore different few-shot learning strategies, such as batch optimization and meta-learning.
CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of the few-shot learning strategy on model performance by comparing it to a baseline model that uses a larger dataset for training. We will also evaluate the effect of different few-shot learning settings, such as the number of episodes and shots per episode, on the performance of our model.
COST: 5800
PREDICTION: We expect to find that our baseline model can achieve good performance with only a few examples, and that the few-shot learning approach improves the sample efficiency of our model without compromising its overall performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: a comprehensive evaluation and analysis of online video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a comprehensive evaluation and analysis of the performance of our existing approaches for online video step grounding, including evaluating the impact of each component on the overall performance, identifying the limitations of our approaches, and exploring potential avenues for future research.
CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of each component by comparing the performance of our baseline models to each of our proposed approaches. We will also conduct a qualitative analysis of the performance of our approaches, including an evaluation of the errors made by each approach and the types of errors that are most frequent.
COST: 0 (no additional computation required)
PREDICTION: We expect to identify areas for improvement in our existing approaches, gain a deeper understanding of the challenges and limitations of online video step grounding, and identify potential avenues for future research that can lead to even better performance.

Graphs are powerful abstractions for representing complex relationships between entities, from social networks to molecular structures, and learning effective graph representations is crucial for node classification, graph classification and link prediction. Over the past decade, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become the dominant paradigm for graph representation learning, building representations through a message-passing mechanism that iteratively aggregates local neighborhood information. Despite its success, message passing faces several key limitations, such as limited expressiveness and difficulty in capturing long-range dependencies. Numerous efforts address different aspects of these limitations: graph transformer architectures incorporate long-range interactions across broader graph contexts, positional encodings inject structural priors to improve global topological awareness, and graph rewiring techniques modify the topology to mitigate structural bottlenecks and enhance information diffusion.

However, these advances remain constrained by a cognitive discrepancy. Humans perceive global structure intuitively, following visual Gestalt principles: they understand the whole before analyzing the individual parts. GNNs and their variants, by contrast, operate through bottom-up processing. People instantly recognize ring structures, symmetric structures and critical bridges in a drawing of a graph, yet even advanced architectures struggle with such basic topological understanding: standard message-passing networks provably cannot identify bridges, and graphs that people tell apart at a glance can fool message passing unless sophisticated topological computations are added. Although architectural innovations have made significant theoretical and practical progress, their essence is still to identify and repair different aspects of the inherent defects of message passing. Approaches that perceive graphs visually remain largely unexplored for graph learning, despite their natural alignment with how humans perceive network structures, and despite a flourishing computer vision ecosystem whose models excel at holistic pattern recognition and global structure understanding. Recent work has begun to bring graph drawings into existing architectures, for instance into vision-language models for graph reasoning or into GNNs to enhance expressivity, but it treats graph layouts and vision models as black boxes, without examining how visual and message-passing models fundamentally differ in the way they understand graphs.

A second obstacle is measurement. Established benchmarks built from molecules, citation networks or protein interaction graphs tightly couple domain-specific node features with topology, which makes their separate contributions hard to quantify and can let models succeed through feature-based shortcuts rather than genuine structural understanding. Models that replace the true molecular topology with fixed-structure expander graphs have been shown to match or exceed performance on several molecular benchmarks, suggesting that node features often dominate structural information in standard datasets, potentially masking differences in how models perceive graph topology. The theoretical evaluation of GNNs has centered on the Weisfeiler-Lehman test, which measures the ability to distinguish pairs of non-isomorphic graphs of the same size; valuable for theory, it is limited to binary discrimination between fixed-size graph pairs. Recent graph benchmarks oriented toward large language models focus on structural analysis tasks such as node counting, cycle detection and path finding, and typically rely on a limited set of random graph generators (such as Erdős–Rényi or Watts–Strogatz) that inadequately capture topological diversity. What remains missing is a way to assess human-like graph cognition: the intuitive ability to perceive, abstract and reason about fundamental global graph properties, and to recognize the same connectivity patterns across varying scales and contexts.

This leads to the questions addressed here. Could models designed for visual perception, which carry no graph-specific inductive bias, offer a viable pathway to graph structural understanding, and do they process graph information in the same way as message-passing GNNs or through fundamentally different strategies? How can a model's ability to perceive and abstract global graph properties be evaluated rigorously, in isolation from domain-specific features, including whether it recognizes the same structural pattern regardless of graph size? And what does it take for a graph learning model to acquire the holistic, scale-robust understanding of topology that humans display effortlessly?

Humans naturally parse scenes into coherent objects (e.g., grouping features such as a rounded shape, a smooth surface and a muted color into the mug) and further ground their identities in context (e.g., recognizing my coffee mug on the desk rather than just a mug). This is assumed to be made possible by what cognitive scientists call object binding, the brain's ability to group an object's low-level features (color, shape, motion, etc.) into a unified representation. This in turn enables objects to be stored efficiently and compositionally in memory and used as high-level symbols for reasoning about individual object instances. The binding problem is a genuine computational challenge, as evidenced by humans' limited competence in conjunction-search tasks and by clinical dissociations such as Balint's syndrome, where feature perception remains intact but binding breaks down. If AI systems could replicate the human ability for object binding, that may help them ground symbols in perception and exploit compositionality. The key question is: do current AI systems solve the binding problem?

Object binding has received little attention in mainstream AI research. Cognition-inspired models build in human-like object-based attention. By contrast, mainstream vision models are assumed to learn implicitly to handle multiple objects from training data, yet empirical studies show that they often "attend" only to the most salient regions and overlook the rest. While the attention scores of Vision Transformers (ViTs) can capture global image structure and salient regions (often corresponding to target objects), empirical evidence shows that self-attention tends to group patches by low-level feature similarity rather than reliably producing object-level binding. Object-centric methods such as Slot Attention fix this by allocating a small set of learnable slots that compete for token features, enforcing binding by design; however, because such modules are added externally rather than integrated into the transformer architecture, they introduce additional challenges for scaling and training. Other work has assumed that ViTs already carry implicit object-level structure and has tried to group patches into objects directly from their activations or attention maps. Binding failures are also seen as a source of performance breakdowns in modern transformer-based systems: text-to-image diffusion models suffer attribute leakage between entities (e.g., both a dog and a cat end up wearing sunglasses and a sun-hat), and vision-language models struggle to differentiate multiple objects defined by feature conjunctions. Despite these failures, transformers still demonstrate some binding capability, yet the underlying mechanism is not well understood: binding has started to be characterized in language models, but binding mechanisms in vision transformers remain unexplored. Whether AI vision models, especially leading ViTs, can achieve robust object binding without explicit mechanisms therefore remains an open question.

Cognitive scientists have questioned whether ViTs can bind objects at all, arguing that they lack mechanisms for dynamically and flexibly grouping features, that they lack the recurrence necessary for iterative refinement of object representations, and that, as purely connectionist models, they appear incapable of true symbolic processing. However, these architectural limitations do not preclude binding from emerging through learning. ViTs share several computational parallels with the mammalian visual system: both rely on parallel, distributed and hierarchical processing; explicit position embeddings resemble the spatial tagging and spatiotopic organization observed in the ventral stream; and self-attention is akin to the dynamic tuning and attentional modulation thought to be primary mechanisms of binding in the brain. Moreover, knowing which patches belong to the same object would be useful for prediction and could guide attention, and human-labeled data also reflects object-level structure, so ViTs could acquire binding by imitation. ViTs may therefore learn to bind objects directly from large-scale training data, without requiring explicit architectural inductive biases.

This raises the question of whether object binding naturally emerges in large, pretrained Vision Transformers, a question that matters for both cognitive science and AI. Answering it requires establishing whether the internal representations of such models reliably encode which parts of an image belong to the same object; and, if they do, how this information is represented, whether it reflects an ability acquired through learning rather than a trivial artifact of the architecture, and whether the model actually makes functional use of it.

Diffusion models have catalyzed an enormous research wave in generative modeling. Conceptually, they couple a stochastic forward noising process with a reverse-time ordinary or stochastic differential equation whose density evolution is governed by the Fokker–Planck equation, a linear second-order parabolic partial differential equation. Learning consists of estimating time-indexed scores or velocities and integrating them for sampling. A growing body of work also explores probability-flow backbones: deterministic flows trained via flow matching and its optimal-transport variants, rectified flows, and stochastic interpolants that bridge flows and diffusion.

Yet the partial-differential-equation lens on generative modeling need not be limited to Fokker–Planck. Other classical linear second-order equations, elliptic and hyperbolic, offer different structural advantages but remain comparatively underexplored; Poisson flow models, for instance, recast generation through electrostatics-inspired fields. On the hyperbolic side, recent work has replaced the Fokker–Planck equation with the telegrapher equation (the one-dimensional damped wave equation) and its stochastic Kac representation, in which a particle moves at constant speed and reverses direction at the jump times of a Poisson process. A network is fit by regression to a closed-form conditional velocity of this process and integrated backward in time from noise to data, with each image coordinate following an independent one-dimensional Kac process. The resulting probability flows have a finite propagation speed: starting from localized mass, the distribution remains inside a causal cone, the flow is Lipschitz in Wasserstein distance, and velocity norms, hence kinetic energy, stay globally bounded. Diffusion, by contrast, spreads mass instantaneously with effectively infinite propagation speed, which manifests as stiff, rapidly growing reverse-time velocities and as ill-conditioned fields with Lipschitz blow-ups near the end of denoising; indeed, diffusion arises as a limit of the damped wave equation as the damping and the propagation speed tend to infinity. A finite speed cap thus acts like a built-in stability constraint: trajectories cannot accelerate without bound, and late-time integration is less stiff.

So far, however, these finite-speed flows have been developed only for unconditional image generation, and they lack two ingredients that make diffusion-style generators practical. The first is guided conditional generation. Classifier-free guidance, which mixes conditional and unconditional predictions to steer samples toward a condition, is a standard tool for diffusion models, but it is unclear whether guidance can be carried over to finite-speed dynamics without losing the bounded-energy property that distinguishes them from diffusion, whose kinetic energy can diverge near data time. The second is fast sampling. Practical generators are expected to deliver high-quality samples with very few network evaluations, yet it is unknown whether finite-speed flows can be brought down to a handful of sampling steps, or even a single one, without a severe loss of sample quality, and whether their finite-speed, bounded-energy structure can explain, and ideally guarantee, that a coarse few-step sampler stays close to the full sampling trajectory.

This leads to three questions. How can guided conditional generation be built on finite-speed Kac flows while provably keeping the guided velocity field at finite kinetic energy? How can such flows be turned into few-step, ideally one-step, image generators that preserve both sample quality and the numerical stability benefits of finite-speed probability flows? And can the finite-speed structure provide theoretical guarantees that a few-step sampler remains close to the full flow along the entire generation path, not only in its final samples? Answering them would show whether hyperbolic, finite-speed dynamics can be a credible alternative to diffusion for fast image generation.

Video anomaly analysis is a key application of computer vision for public security. Most early work formulates it as temporal video anomaly detection: marking the segments of a video whose behavior deviates from learned normal patterns, whether with one-class models trained only on normal clips, unsupervised reconstruction or future-frame prediction objectives, or weakly supervised learning from video-level labels. Such detectors have reached high performance on benchmarks, yet they output only frame-wise anomaly scores, without spatial or semantic context, and give no insight into why a segment is abnormal. These limits of interpretability have motivated a shift from temporal detection toward downstream tasks with user-friendly, explainable outputs: spatial video anomaly localization, which predicts bounding boxes around the regions that contain the abnormal activity, and textual video anomaly understanding, which decides whether a video contains an anomaly and produces a human-readable description explaining it, typically with fine-tuned multimodal large language models. Each line of work, however, provides either spatial or textual cues on its own and focuses on a single type of task, so that existing methods offer only an incomplete analysis of video anomalies. A holistic analysis would answer when an anomaly happens, where it is, what it is and why it is abnormal, each of the existing benchmark tasks addressing one of these sub-problems.

A second challenge is the heavy reliance on dataset-specific supervision. Detection and localization models require temporal masks or spatial bounding boxes, yet anomaly definitions vary widely across datasets, so a model tuned on one domain often fails on another and must be retrained for unseen domains or anomaly types. In real-world applications, privacy and security concerns may also make training data unavailable for some sensitive scenes. Open-set detectors that fuse language semantics in order to detect and classify novel anomalies still require task-specific training and give very limited insight into why frames are abnormal. As partial remedies, recent work has explored zero- and few-shot approaches built on frozen vision-language backbones or multimodal large language models, but most of these approaches have a limited task scope and still rely on annotated datasets. The only strictly zero-shot, training-free method addresses temporal detection alone: a frozen vision-language model captions the frames and a prompted large language model converts the captions into frame-wise anomaly scores. It is effective when anomalies are clearly distinguishable from normality but occasionally fails on more complex anomaly types, and it offers neither spatial grounding nor any direct semantic explanation beyond generic captions. Prompt-tuning methods, which optimize textual prompts to guide frozen models, require induction on an annotated training set and pay for it in generality, since the learned prompts tend to be task- or domain-specific. The generality problem is worse still for instruction-tuned multimodal models: they produce rich narrative explanations, but they require extensive annotation and computational resources, lack temporal or spatial coverage, and are optimized to return answers from seen question-answer pairs that describe a closed set of anomaly types.

Multimodal large language models already encode rich visual-semantic priors for commonsense reasoning, which suggests that fine-tuning may not be necessary for every task. This raises the questions addressed here: can temporal detection, spatial localization and textual explanation of video anomalies be delivered together, as one holistic and interpretable analysis, in a strictly zero-shot manner, with frozen pretrained models and without any additional training data, annotations or gradient updates? And can such an analysis remain at least as accurate as existing zero-shot detectors while staying robust across domains whose definitions of anomaly differ?

Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a powerful and principled approach for generative modeling, and in particular for high-quality visual generation. By learning a time-dependent velocity field that continuously transforms samples from a base distribution into a target distribution, FM models generate data by integrating an ordinary differential equation (ODE). This framework offers advantages over diffusion-based methods, including faster convergence, stable training, and direct control over sample trajectories.

Despite these strengths, inference in FM models is costly and has become a bottleneck. ODE integration is inherently sequential: each step depends on the output of the previous one, which makes the process slow and difficult to parallelize. High-fidelity generation requires a large number of fine-grained steps, which pushes latency up and makes real-time or interactive use difficult. As data dimensionality and model complexity increase, so does the inference burden. The issue is even more pronounced in video generation, where models operate on high-dimensional spatio-temporal data and the cost of sequential integration compounds across frames, making efficient inference essential for long videos.

Static reduction strategies such as distillation, trajectory truncation and consistency training have been proposed to reduce inference latency. However, they often degrade output quality, producing blurry textures, semantic drift or broken spatial coherence; in video, they often cause temporal flickering and motion inconsistency, which severely degrade realism even when individual frames look plausible. Many of them also require retraining the model with auxiliary objectives or handcrafted losses, which increases the engineering burden and restricts transferability across model families. As a result, these approaches are less modular, harder to scale, and often infeasible to deploy in time-sensitive or interactive pipelines.

In language models, a promising line of work for accelerating inference is speculative decoding, in which multiple drafts are proposed in parallel and selectively verified by the full model, reducing latency without retraining it. This idea, however, does not directly extend to image and video generative models such as FM, and two challenges stand out. First, unlike in language models, no readily available draft model exists: how can drafts be produced whose trajectories closely couple with those of the full model? Second, the performance of FM is highly sensitive to the velocity output: even a small perturbation in velocity can accumulate along the integration path and lead to severe generation errors. How, then, can drafted velocities be evaluated, and how can the drift of the resulting trajectory away from the full-model trajectory be controlled?

The open problem is therefore how to substantially reduce the inference latency of existing FM models, for both image and video generation, without retraining, without degrading output quality relative to standard full-step generation, and in a way that transfers across model families.

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: draft model acceleration via random path pruning
PROPOSAL: We propose to evaluate the feasibility of accelerating inference in FM models by selectively pruning short, random paths through the velocity field during the integration process. By doing so, we can reduce the overall number of integration steps required for achieving the same quality of output. We will experiment with various pruning strategies, including pruning based on velocity magnitude, Euclidean distance, and maximum gradient.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no pruning. (2) Ablation study: Different pruning strategies and their combinations. (3) Control: Randomly subsampling the paths.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a latency reduction of up to 30% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and a significant decrease in video generation latency. However, this approach may lead to variations in generation quality depending on the pruning strategy used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: learning draft models for fm using Curriculum Learning
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of generating high-quality drafts in FM models, we propose using Curriculum Learning to learn a draft model that closely couples with the full model. We will define a gradual curriculum of temporally corrected velocities that guide the learning process of the draft model. As the curriculum progresses, the draft model will learn to produce velocities that are increasingly similar to those produced by the full model. This will enable the draft model to not only accelerate inference but also maintain high quality output.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different curriculum learning schedules. (3) Control: Learning draft models using random sampling of the velocity field.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 40% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. The quality of the drafts will be strongly dependent on the quality of the curriculum learning schedule.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: draft model acceleration via random path pruning
PROPOSAL: We revise our initial proposal to include an incentive mechanism that rewards the draft model for producing velocities that result in generated samples that are closer to the ground truth. This can be achieved by incorporating a reconstruction loss into the draft model's training objective, which encourages the draft model to produce high-quality samples that are close to the target distribution. By doing so, we can improve the accuracy and quality of the draft model's outputs.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no pruning and no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different loss functions and weights for the reconstruction loss. (3) Control: Learning draft models using random sampling of the velocity field without reconstruction loss. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 50% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. However, the introduction of the reconstruction loss may lead to increased training time and potential mode collapse issues.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: learning draft models for fm using curriculum learning
PROPOSAL: We revise our proposal to use a more efficient curriculum learning schedule that utilizes progressive meta-learning. Instead of learning a fixed curriculum, we will use a dynamic curriculum that adapts to the performance of the draft model and the full model. This will enable the draft model to learn more effectively and efficiently, and potentially lead to better performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different progressive meta-learning schedules. (3) Control: Using a fixed curriculum learning schedule.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 45% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. The progressive meta-learning schedule may lead to improved performance, but it may also increase computational costs due to the need to adapt the curriculum during training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: draft refinement via multi-step prediction
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-step prediction mechanism to refine the outputs of the draft model. This mechanism will utilize a secondary model trained to predict the corrections needed to refine the draft's output, rather than relying on a single pass through the full model. By predicting these corrections step-by-step, we can iteratively refine the draft's output, potentially leading to significant quality improvements.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different numbers of refinement steps and secondary model architectures.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve high-quality outputs comparable to the full model, with a latency reduction of up to 40% in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. However, the multiple steps of refinement may lead to increased training time and potential issues with convergence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: lazy evaluation of fm velocity fields
PROPOSAL: We propose a lazy evaluation approach for the velocity fields used in FM models. By storing the velocity fields in a compressed and hierarchical manner, we can significantly reduce the computational cost of evaluating the velocity field for a given sample. This approach can be particularly effective when combined with the draft model and refinement mechanisms, as it can help to reduce the latency of the overall system.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no lazy evaluation. (2) Ablation study: Different compression techniques and hierarchical representations.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a significant reduction in computational cost, with a latency reduction of up to 25% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the compressed representation may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or discontinuities in the velocity field.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: model-parallelizable fm through decomposition
PROPOSAL: We propose a decomposition-based approach to make FM models parallelizable. By decomposing the velocity field into smaller, independent components, we can parallelize the evaluation of the velocity field across multiple GPUs or machines, significantly reducing the latency of the overall system. This approach can be particularly effective for large-scale FM models and video generation tasks.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no decomposition. (2) Ablation study: Different decomposition techniques and parallelization strategies.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a significant reduction in latency, with a speedup of up to 4x in text-to-image generation, and an even larger speedup in video generation. However, the decomposition may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or discontinuities in the velocity field, and complex decomposition strategies may increase engineering burden.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: uncertainty-based draft model deployment
PROPOSAL: We propose an uncertainty-based approach for deploying draft models, where the draft model is only used to generate samples when the uncertainty in the velocity field is high, and the full model is used otherwise. This approach can help to mitigate potential quality degradation issues and reduce the overall latency of the system.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different uncertainty measures and threshold values for draft model deployment.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 30% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the deployment strategy may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or inconsistent behavior at high uncertainty values.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adaptive draft model switching
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive approach for switching between the draft model and the full model based on the performance of the system. By continuously monitoring the quality and latency of the generated samples, we can dynamically switch between the two models to achieve the optimal trade-off between quality and latency. This approach can help to adapt to changing system conditions and optimize performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different switching policies and performance metrics.
COST: 110 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 35% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the adaptive switching strategy may lead to potential issues with instability or mode collapse.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: hybrid fm architectures
PROPOSAL: We propose a hybrid approach that combines the strengths of multiple architectures to achieve improved performance in FM models. By combining the draft model, full model, and lazy evaluation, we can create a flexible and adaptable architecture that can dynamically adjust to changing system conditions and optimize performance. This approach can help to achieve the optimal trade-off between quality, latency, and computational cost.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model. (2) Ablation study: Different combinations of draft model, full model, and lazy evaluation.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 50% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation, while maintaining high quality and performance. However, the hybrid architecture may lead to potential issues with complexity, overhead, and stability.
