In cloud services, Internet of Things deployments and monitoring systems, data are often represented as univariate time series (UTS), in which each timestamp records a single variable. Anomalies arise, for instance, when a website is subject to malicious attacks or experiences excessive server load, and they are typically reflected in UTS derived from traffic and system-load monitoring. Missed or delayed detection of such events can have severe consequences. Anomalies in UTS are usually divided into two types: point anomalies, which are abrupt deviations (either global or contextual), and segment anomalies, which reflect more subtle shifts in trends or periodic patterns.

Formally, given observations x_0, x_1, ..., x_t with anomaly labels c_0, c_1, ..., c_t, where c_i = 0 marks a normal point and c_i = 1 an anomaly, the goal of UTS anomaly detection is to determine c_i for each point x_i from the history x_0, ..., x_{i-1} that precedes it, without access to future points. Because labels are scarce in practice and supervised detectors generalize poorly under label scarcity or distribution shift, unsupervised approaches have become the dominant paradigm. Reconstruction-based and prediction-based methods both model normal behavior and flag anomalies by comparing reconstructed or predicted values with the actual observations. Reconstruction-based techniques try to map abnormal segments to a normal space, but the lack of ground truth for anomalies leads to poor reconstruction and degraded performance, and they treat time windows independently, ignoring temporal dependencies. Prediction-based methods built on deep sequence models such as Transformers perform strongly on multivariate time series, where they can model complex dependencies; in UTS, however, each timestamp contains only one value, which restricts the representation of temporal context and leads to suboptimal performance.

In particular, existing detectors struggle with two kinds of subtle anomalies that remain largely undetected: (1) small point anomalies, short-term spikes that look normal when viewed over longer windows; and (2) slowly rising anomalies, gradual segment-level deviations from periodic patterns. These misses stem from limitations of current designs: for example, a frequency-conditioned reconstruction approach focuses on frequency components rather than local dependencies and fails to capture subtle point anomalies or gradual segment anomalies, while a recent prediction approach uses timing information but ignores frequency details.

Detecting these anomalies raises three challenges. First, local trends matter more than absolute values: the absolute magnitude of a change is insufficient to decide whether a point is anomalous. In one series, changes between 0.5 and 1 may be abnormal, whereas in another, similar changes are normal and only variations exceeding 5 are anomalous; what counts as abnormal depends on the value distribution and change patterns within a short local window. Second, periodicity evolves rather than staying static: time series exhibit evolving trends and periodicity, and periodicity varies over time and across datasets, including changes in period length and frequency. Without future points, distinguishing slow anomalies from normal periodic changes is difficult, and methods that focus only on the adjacent historical period neglect this evolution; modeling periodicity that is both dynamic and heterogeneous is hard. Third, normal patterns must be learned amid anomalies and noise: real-world series contain long-term noise and sudden anomalies, both of which hinder the learning of normal patterns. Noise introduces significant fluctuations that make it difficult to fit the underlying normal behavior, and the lack of ground-truth labels for anomaly positions prevents a model from computing reliable training losses.

The question is therefore how an unsupervised detector for univariate time series, relying only on past observations, can capture both local trends and the evolution of periodic patterns, while learning normal behavior robustly from training data contaminated by noise and unlabeled anomalies, so that small point anomalies and slowly rising anomalies are detected accurately and promptly.

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: local trend aware reconstruction approach
PROPOSAL: Introduce a reconstruction-based method that models normal behavior by learning local trends in the univariate time series. Instead of focusing on global frequency components, the method will capture local patterns using a Gaussian Process regression model with a custom kernel that takes into account the local context of each point. This will allow it to more effectively identify small point anomalies that might be missed by frequency-conditioned reconstruction approaches.
CONTROLS: Compare against a frequency-conditioned reconstruction approach (e.g., the recent 1D-STFT-DCN method) and an unsupervised baseline (e.g., Autoencoders on UTS datasets from ) across a suite of real-world datasets, including ECG and web service KPI monitoring.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach will demonstrate strong detection performance on small point anomalies, while its reconstruction-based design will also allow it to learn effective normal patterns in the presence of noise and labeled anomalies; however, it might struggle with capturing subtle changes in evolving periodic patterns without additional information.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: periodicity evolution aware sequence model
PROPOSAL: Design a variant of the transformer-based sequence model, specifically geared towards univariate time series, that incorporates a novel self-attention mechanism to capture the evolution of periodic patterns across different time windows. This is achieved by adding an auxiliary periodicity-evolution head that learns to predict the shift in periodic patterns between adjacent windows, thereby enabling the detector to learn dynamic periodicity and accommodate changes in evolving trends and periodicity.
CONTROLS: Compare against a traditional transformer-based sequence model with no periodicity-aware components, and a state-of-the-art prediction-based approach (e.g., ) designed for UTS on web service KPI monitoring and air-temperature dataset.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The periodicity-evolution aware model will demonstrate improvements in detecting slowly rising anomalies by accurately modeling and capturing evolving periodic patterns; however, it may be computationally expensive and require careful tuning to balance periodicity and local trend detection.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: revise 1: local trend-aware reconstruction approach with periodicity-aware extension
PROPOSAL: Refine the local trend-aware reconstruction approach by adding a periodicity-aware component that can capture the periodic patterns present in the time series. This can be achieved by incorporating a periodic component into the Gaussian Process regression model, allowing the detector to learn the local trends while also taking into account the periodic patterns and their evolution over time. This integrated approach aims to improve the ability of the detector to capture both local trends and the evolving periodic patterns.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original local trend-aware reconstruction approach and the periodicity evolution aware sequence model, as well as the same frequency-conditioned reconstruction approach (1D-STFT-DCN method).
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised local trend-aware reconstruction approach with periodicity-aware extension will provide a sweet spot between the strengths of the original reconstruction-based method and the sequence model, striking a balance between detecting local trends and evolving periodic patterns; however, it may require careful hyperparameter tuning to optimize performance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: local trend aware reconstruction approach with noise robustness
PROPOSAL: Modify the local trend-aware reconstruction approach to be more robust to noise in the time series data. This can be done by incorporating a noise-robust kernel into the Gaussian Process regression model or using a loss function that is less sensitive to noisy observations. Additionally, consider using a robust regression method, such as Huber regression, to reduce the influence of outliers and improve the model's ability to learn normal patterns in the presence of noise and unlabeled anomalies.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original local trend-aware reconstruction approach and the revised local trend-aware reconstruction approach with periodicity-aware extension, as well as the same unsupervised baseline (Autoencoders on UTS datasets).
COST: no additional cost
PREDICATION: The revised local trend-aware reconstruction approach with noise robustness will be more effective in detecting small point anomalies, especially those that occur in long-term noisy series, while learning effective normal patterns; however, it might struggle with capturing the specifics of subtle changes in noisy or periodic patterns without additional smoothing techniques.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: anomaly encoder-based denoising autoencoder
PROPOSAL: Design a denoising autoencoder (DAE) that uses an anomaly encoder to learn noise and normal patterns in the univariate time series data. The anomaly encoder maps the input to a noise representation, where noise is represented as abnormality in the sequence. By training the DAE to reconstruct the input from its noise representation, the model learns to discard noise and identify normal patterns in the data, allowing for effective anomaly detection in noisy series. This approach will be useful in capturing local trends and normal patterns in the presence of high levels of noise.
CONTROLS: Compare against a traditional denoising autoencoder without an anomaly encoder and the local trend-aware reconstruction approach with noise robustness, as well as a state-of-the-art anomaly detection method (e.g., ) on ECG and air-temperature dataset.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The anomaly encoder-based DAE will perform well on detecting small point anomalies in noisy series, while the noise removal operation could also unveil potential slowly rising anomalies; however, it may be computationally expensive and sensitive to hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: incremental learning for dynamic periodicity
PROPOSAL: Develop an incremental learning method for periodicity-aware sequence models, allowing the model to adapt to changes in periodic patterns over time. This can be achieved by maintaining a separate model for each period or time window and updating these models incrementally as new data becomes available. By leveraging the periodicity-aware sequence model as a subroutine, the incremental learning method can continually refine its understanding of the periodic patterns and adapt to changing conditions, making it more effective in detecting slowly rising anomalies.
CONTROLS: Compare against a traditional periodicity-aware sequence model trained on fixed-time windows and the periodicity evolution aware sequence model, as well as an unsupervised anomaly detection algorithm (e.g., , adapted for real-time incremental learning) on dynamic web service KPI monitoring and ECG dataset.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The incremental learning method for dynamic periodicity will allow the model to keep up with the evolving trends and periodic patterns, leading to improved detection performance for slowly rising anomalies; however, it may require careful implementation to manage memory and computational resources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: graph-based anomaly propagation
PROPOSAL: Design a graph-based approach that aggregates information from multiple time series to identify anomalies in individual series. This can be achieved by representing each time series as a node in a graph and establishing edges between nodes that share similar trends or patterns. Anomaly detection is then performed by propagating abnormality scores from affected nodes to their neighbors, allowing for collaborative anomaly detection and improved identification of small point anomalies, especially those occurring in series with limited sampling rates or sparse data.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline series-by-series approach using the local trend-aware reconstruction approach with noise robustness and an anomaly encoder-based denoising autoencoder, as well as a state-of-the-art graph-based anomaly detection algorithm (e.g., ) on web service KPI monitoring and ECG dataset.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The graph-based anomaly propagation approach will leverage interconnected patterns across time series to improve the detection of small point anomalies, particularly in cases where a single series has limited sampling rates; however, it may be vulnerable to the influence of noisy series and require careful graph construction.

This can be achieved by incorporating a periodic component into the noise representation or by considering the output of the periodicity evolution aware sequence model as input to the encoder. By learning a contextualized representation of noise, the model can more effectively discard noise and identify normal patterns in the data, allowing for improved anomaly detection in noisy series.

PREDICTION: The revised anomaly encoder-based denoising autoencoder with contextualized noise representation will improve the detection of small point anomalies in noisy series by better capturing the underlying local trends and periodic patterns; however, it may require careful hyperparameter tuning to balance the impacts of noise and contextual information.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: time-series anomaly chains
PROPOSAL: Develop a methodology to identify chains of anomalous time points, where the detection of an anomaly at one point increases the likelihood of anomalies at subsequent points. This can be achieved by applying a statistical analysis or machine learning method to the sequence of anomaly scores. By identifying these chains, the model can provide more comprehensive insights into the behavior of the system, allowing for the detection of more subtle and long-term anomalies.

PREDICTION: The time-series anomaly chains methodology will uncover valuable insights into the behavior of the system by revealing characteristic patterns of anomalies; however, it may require careful analysis of the anomaly scores to avoid false positives and ensure robust detection.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: hugging face-based ensemble models
PROPOSAL: Utilize Hugging Face's Transformers library to create ensemble models that combine the strengths of the individual approaches (local trend-aware reconstruction, periodicity evolution aware sequence model, anomaly encoder-based denoising autoencoder with contextualized noise representation, incremental learning for dynamic periodicity, and graph-based anomaly propagation) and improve overall anomaly detection performance. This can be achieved by stacking or concatenating individual models, fine-tuning them for anomaly detection, or leveraging pre-trained models as subcomponents. By creating an ensemble model, the approach can benefit from the complementary information and strengths of the individual models.
CONTROLS: Compare against each individual approach and an ensemble of multiple individual approaches (e.g., using stacking or bagging techniques) across multiple datasets from web service KPI monitoring, ECG, and environmental air-temperature monitoring.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The ensemble models will leverage the collective strengths of the individual approaches to achieve improved anomaly detection performance and robustness, especially in scenarios with varying patterns and degrees of noise; however, carefully selecting and integrating the models will require innovative analysis to ensure the ensemble performs effectively and avoids overfitting.

Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly expanded in capability and are now widely used in domains such as conversational agents, healthcare and finance, where they often process sensitive personal information. Early privacy concerns focused mainly on memorization and leakage of training data, but recent studies show that LLMs can also infer private attributes of an author, such as location, identity or demographics, from subtle semantic cues in seemingly innocuous text. With sufficiently capable models, such inferences can be surprisingly accurate and often go undetected by users, who continue to share content unaware of the risk. Moreover, text sent to external services may be intercepted in transit or retained by providers, for example for model training, increasing the risk of misuse or data breaches.

Traditional anonymization methods rely on rule-based de-identification, such as named entity recognition or pattern matching, to remove surface-level identifiers like names, social security numbers or explicit locations. They frequently overlook the context-dependent semantics that LLMs can exploit, so private information that is embedded in context rather than stated explicitly remains inferable. This gap calls for anonymization techniques that account for semantic context and defend against inference-based privacy threats, while preserving the meaning and readability of the text, that is, techniques that achieve a good privacy-utility trade-off.

A growing body of work pursues LLM-based anonymization to protect semantic-level private information from model inference. In feedback-guided adversarial anonymization, an LLM anonymizer rewrites the input text while a second LLM, acting as an adversary, attempts to infer private attributes from the rewritten output; based on this adversarial feedback, the anonymizer iteratively refines its output to prevent the inferences that remain possible. With GPT-4 as both anonymizer and adversary, this approach achieves a substantially better privacy-utility trade-off than traditional industry-grade anonymizers. However, reliance on large proprietary models is costly and requires sending the very text that should be protected to potentially untrusted external systems. Attempts to transfer these anonymization capabilities into smaller models have been explored only to a limited extent, and existing approaches still depend on a proprietary model to provide the adversarial feedback, incurring similar costs and privacy concerns.

The open problem is therefore whether, and how, small language models that can run locally under modest compute budgets can become effective anonymizers that protect semantic-level private information against inference by strong LLM adversaries, without relying on any external model at inference time. Can such models reach a privacy-utility trade-off comparable to, or better than, that of anonymizers built on frontier proprietary LLMs, including on texts where personal information is conveyed by the overall context rather than by explicit mentions, while remaining cheap enough to deploy in settings with strict data-confidentiality requirements?

Inverse problems arise in many domains, including computer vision, protein science, medical imaging and scientific computing. The goal is to reconstruct an unknown signal x ∈ R^n from noisy measurements y ∈ R^m, with y = A(x) + η, where A is a known forward operator and η is additive measurement noise. Diffusion models have recently shown powerful capabilities in modeling complex data distributions, and they provide a powerful class of priors for high-dimensional data, such as natural images, when solving inverse problems.

Methods for solving inverse problems fall broadly into two families. Maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference seeks the single most probable x: it delivers fast optimization, but struggles with high noise and multimodal posteriors and easily converges to local minima. The Bayesian alternative samples from the posterior p(x|y) ∝ p(x) p(y|x) to generate plausible reconstructions, quantify uncertainty and handle multimodality. Both critically depend on a powerful prior, such as a pretrained diffusion model, that encodes the complex statistical structure of the data.

Although diffusion-based solvers have shown remarkable success across diverse inverse problems, current methods suffer from three complementary limitations. (1) Iterative guidance methods, such as DPS, DDRM, DDNM, ΠGDM and TMPD, try to sample the intermediate posteriors p(x_t|y) along the reverse diffusion, which requires the intractable likelihood p(y|x_t) at every intermediate timestep. They approximate it, for example through Tweedie's formula, and apply likelihood-gradient corrections directly to the intermediate states. Because such gradients generally contain components orthogonal to the data manifold, these corrections systematically push the intermediate states off the learned manifold and violate the training-time noise conditioning of the denoiser, leading to failed reconstructions such as accumulated artifacts; even second-order corrections of the guidance trajectory still modify intermediate states and risk drifting off the manifold. (2) Stochastic MAP methods that optimize in image space, such as ReSample, DiffPIR, DAPS, SITCOM and DIIP, can match the measurements well with very sharp details, but they require carefully tuned hyperparameters to avoid overfitting to noise, which limits their effectiveness when the noise is high or unknown. Some of them are formulated as posterior samplers yet use a heuristic measurement-noise level much smaller than the true one to strengthen measurement consistency, which makes them effectively MAP-like and equally sensitive to noise. (3) Deterministic MAP methods that optimize over the diffusion model's input noise, such as DMPlug, remove randomness but are sensitive to measurement noise and, lacking posterior exploration, often get stuck in a single mode, especially in severely ill-posed problems such as phase retrieval. Early stopping can limit noise overfitting, but its criterion is task- and noise-dependent, and at high noise levels the optimizer often becomes trapped in a local mode anyway. In short, enforcing data consistency in the middle of the diffusion process can break adherence to the prior, while optimizing only for fidelity leads to overfitting or mode collapse.

These failure modes point to two requirements. A solver should maintain manifold feasibility: the states it feeds to the pretrained denoiser should remain close to the high-probability manifold of the corresponding noise level, so that the final reconstruction lies on the learned data manifold. At the same time, it should explore the posterior well enough to escape spurious local modes, rather than collapsing onto the mode nearest to its initialization.

A further practical difficulty is that the level, and even the type, of measurement noise is often unknown and may not be Gaussian, which makes the likelihood term itself intractable. Existing methods handle this with tunable hyperparameters that control the strength of the likelihood term, or with task-specific early-stopping criteria, typically tuned for one particular type and level of noise; they must therefore be re-tuned for each task, dataset and noise level, which is impractical when the noise is unknown.

This raises the following questions. How can a pretrained diffusion prior be used to sample from the posterior of an inverse problem without approximating intractable intermediate likelihoods and without ever feeding off-manifold states to the denoiser? How can such a sampler explore the solution space well enough to avoid spurious local modes in severely ill-posed, multimodal problems, so that its reconstructions do not depend on the initialization? Can it be robust to measurement noise, in the sense that its reconstructions do not overfit the noise, without hand-tuned regularization weights or early stopping? And can it handle measurement noise of unknown level and type with a single fixed set of hyperparameters across tasks, datasets and noise levels, at a computational cost that remains practical?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: dynamic consistency and manifold preservation
PROPOSAL: Develop a method called Dynamic Consistency and Manifold Preservation (DCMP), which iteratively updates the diffusion guidance process by matching the intermediate states to the manifold — instead of directly feeding them back to the denoiser. First, we use the learned denoiser to define a manifold — where data likelihood is high — by calculating the mean of the denoiser output for a range of noise inputs. Then, at each timestep, we check if the guidance signal differs significantly from the manifold. If it does, we re-align the guidance trajectory to be closer to the manifold. This should maintain the learned data distribution, avoiding drift off the manifold and guaranteeing manifold feasibility.
CONTROLS: Compare against DPS and DDRM.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: DCMP should significantly reduce the off-manifold drift seen in current methods and maintain reliable reconstructions, even at high noise levels. A minor issue could be that manual tuning of parameters for DCMP would be needed for different noise distributions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: uncertainty-aware reconstruction guidance
PROPOSAL: Introduce an uncertainty-aware variant of the guidance process, Uncertainty-Aware Reconstruction Guidance (UARG), by modelling and learning the compact uncertainty via an ensemble of diffusion models, each with a distinct noise schedule. During the guidance process, we draw samples from the distributions output by the ensemble, and combine them to inform the reconstruction guidance signal. This approach can estimate and incorporate the uncertainty, adapting the guidance process to the inherent uncertainty in the posterior and, consequently, escape spurious modes more effectively.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard guidance methods, and assess the impact of ensemble size on performance.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: UARG would have improved performance over standard guidance methods for challenging inverse problems, but careful ensemble size and model selection could be required, while estimating uncertainty could increase computational cost.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: probabilistic forward mappings
PROPOSAL: To address the intractable likelihoods, develop Probabilistic Forward Mappings (PFM), a probabilistic, invertible, and differentiable approximation of the forward operator A. We achieve this by training a probabilistic neural network that maps the true forward operator to a Gaussian process, allowing us to treat the forward operator as a probabilistic function and comptuted the likelihoods, p(y|x), in closed-form. PFM can be efficiently inverted to produce samples from the intractable forward process.
CONTROLS: Compare against approximate likelihood methods (e.g. Tweedie's formula) and assess the impact of model capacity on performance. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: PFM should provide accurate approximations of the likelihoods without adding additional hyperparameters or prior knowledge, but the performance would heavily depend on the choice of model and capacities.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: uncertainty-aware reconstruction guidance
PROPOSAL: Revising the previous proposal, introduce Uncertainty-Aware Reconstruction Guidance (UARG), but with an additional regularization term that encourages the ensemble of diffusion models to be consistent with the probabilistic forward mappings (PFM) - leading to a framework that simultaneously model the uncertainty of the inverse posterior, and approximates the intractable likelihoods in a probabilistic manner. This synergy can help the guidance process to dichotomize from potential spurious modes more effectively and estimate the noise level adaptively.
CONTROLS: Compare against UARG without the regularization term, standard guidance methods, and assess the impact of model capacity on performance.
COST: 450 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised UARG should improve upon both UARG and PFM individually, offering a more comprehensive approach to uncertainty modelling and probabilistic likelihoods estimation, with the potential downside of increased computational cost.

ACTION: REVISE
 NUMBER: 2
 TITLE: uncertainty-aware reconstruction guidance
PROPOSAL: Revising the previous proposal, introduce Uncertainty-Aware Reconstruction Guidance (UARG), but with an additional emphasis on robustness to noise levels - by learning a noise-adaptive versioning of the guidance process, which monitors the current noise level and weighs its contribution accordingly. To achieve this, we use a neural network that takes both the guidance state and the estimated noise level as inputs and outputs a noise-adaptive guidance signal. This approach can help the guidance process to adapt to the uncertainty in the noise, leveraging this learned noise robustness to supervise spurious modes and produce more accurate reconstructions.
CONTROLS: Compare against UARG without the noise-adaptive term, standard guidance methods, and assess the impact of noise level estimation accuracy on performance. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 375 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised UARG should reduce the need for hand-tuning regularization weights and early stopping, and improve noise robustness, but may increase computational cost due to the additional neural network component.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adaptive diffusion guidance sampling
PROPOSAL: Develop an adaptive sampling method, Adaptive Diffusion Guidance Sampling (ADGS), which dynamically selects the most informative samples from the guided diffusion process, allowing for an efficient exploration of the solution space while maintaining a constrained number of samples. By iteratively Assessing the Information Content (AIC) of the samples and dynamically sampling from the intermediate posteriors, we can estimate which samples contribute most significantly to the reconstruction, and reserve computation resources accordingly.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard sampling methods (e.g. Independent Sampling, Sequential Sampling) and assess the impact of hyperparameters on performance.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ADGS should improve the efficiency of the sampling process while maintaining accurate reconstructions, but its effectiveness might depend heavily on the choice of AIC metric and the specific inverse problem at hand.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: inference-time model distillation
PROPOSAL: Introduce Inference-Time Model Distillation (ITMD), a technique to reduce the computational resources needed for inference by distilling a large diffusion model into a smaller, more efficient version while preserving the accuracy of the original model. Specifically, we use a knowledge distillation framework with the goal of matching the output probabilities of the original model, while minimizing a metric of similarity between the two models' weights.
CONTROLS: Compare against pruning and quantization methods for model size reduction, and assess the impact of hyperparameters on performance.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ITMD should lead to a significant reduction in computational resources required for inference, without a substantial loss in accuracy, making it feasible to deploy the proposed methods on edge devices and for large-scale real-world applications. However, finding the optimal distillation parameter might be challenging.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: manifold-aware reconstruction uncertainties
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to quantify the reconstruction uncertainty in a probabilistic and mathematically grounded manner, by modeling the output variability of a diffusion-based sampler conditioned on the true forward operator and noise, leading to a lognormal distribution over reconstructions. This estimate can be directly mapped back to the original reconstruction problem, unbiasedly estimating the subtle noise artifacts, ill-posedness of images, providing informative information on reconstruction reliability.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing uncertainty estimation methods (e.g. MC dropout, variational inference) and assess the impact of model capacity on performance.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed method should provide a robust and accurate measure of reconstruction uncertainty, capable of distinguishing between low-confidence regions and more reliable areas, but it may be computationally expensive due to the need to condition on the true forward operator.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 6
TITLE: manifold-aware reconstruction uncertainties
PROPOSAL: Revising the previous proposal, refine the method to estimate manifold-aware reconstruction uncertainties by incorporating the probabilistic forward mappings (PFM) estimates directly within the uncertainty estimation process. This allows us to capture the inductive bias and prior knowledge of the diffusion model to directly inject uncertainty information into the reconstruction uncertainty calculations, leading to a more principled and accurate estimate of uncertainties. Additionally, introduce a novel strategy to actively leverage this uncertainty information to actively correct for errors and spurious modes.
CONTROLS: Compare against the previous manifold-aware uncertainty estimation method and assess the impact of incorporating PFM on performance and computational cost.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The refined method should lead to more accurate uncertainty estimates, and the active correction mechanism should help correct for spurious modes, but it remains to be seen whether the increased complexity and computational costs would be justified.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: experimentally validating the approach on challenging inverse problems
PROPOSAL: Develop a comprehensive suite of experiments on a diverse set of real-world inverse problems, including image super-resolution, image inpainting, image deblurring, phase retrieval, and high dynamic range (HDR) image reconstruction. Evaluate the proposed methods' performance on these experiments, assessing both quantitative metrics and qualitative visual inspections, and systematically comparing against state-of-the-art methods. Collectively, these experiments should provide a broad validation of the proposed approach's efficacy across various real-world inverse problems.
CONTROLS: Compare against DPS, DDRM, and other state-of-the-art inverse problem solvers on a diverse range of benchmarks. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 5,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The comprehensive experiments should convincingly demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of the proposed methods on challenging real-world inverse problems, showing that the improvements outweigh the increased complexity.

Diffusion models, and text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models in particular, have made astonishing progress in the quality of generated images. At the same time, emerging work on generative depth estimation has revealed that advanced T2I models hold a latent potential for depth estimation: the rich visual priors stored in a pre-trained T2I model can be leveraged to obtain strong zero-shot monocular depth estimation. Exploring a framework that bridges image generation and depth estimation is an essential step toward building unified models for both generation and visual perception.

Existing routes toward such unification each carry a substantial cost. The pioneering generative depth estimation paradigm repurposes a pre-trained T2I diffusion model by fine-tuning its denoising network with full parameters on depth data. It achieves powerful zero-shot depth estimation, but the parameter updates made during training irreversibly and catastrophically degrade the model's original image generation capability; later generative depth estimators that refine this recipe (for example with flow matching, geometry switchers or detail-preserving tuning strategies) inherit the same full-parameter fine-tuning and therefore the same loss. A second route unifies generation and depth estimation with a parallel dual-model architecture, in which two diffusion models run side by side and interact through feature-exchange operations; this requires running two diffusion models in parallel, and the interaction registers new knowledge into the pre-trained generator, which can affect its original image generation behaviour. A third, data-driven route trains a unified generation-and-perception model from scratch on massive multitask data (on the order of a hundred million samples). Despite remarkable progress, these solutions may be considered inefficient or resource-intensive, and potentially suboptimal.

Since a rich visual prior is already stored in advanced T2I models, a natural question arises: can a T2I model effortlessly acquire depth estimation capability without degrading its image generation capability? More concretely, starting from a fixed pre-trained T2I model, with a focus on modern transformer-based diffusion models, how can its latent depth estimation ability be unleashed so that a single model serves both image generation and depth estimation, keeping the original generation ability fully intact, adding only a small fraction of extra learnable parameters, and without resorting to massive multitask training data, while still reaching depth accuracy competitive with full-parameter fine-tuning and with existing unified models?

The problem is challenging. Among the effectively infinite pixel-level combinations that a T2I model learns to generate, there may exist underlying information highly correlated with scene depth; however, because text prompts provide only weak guidance and depth information is sparsely represented within the overall data distribution, extracting depth-relevant features from a fixed pre-trained T2I model is difficult. Any additional capacity must also make efficient use of the visual knowledge already present in the pre-trained model, so that depth estimation is obtained at a small parameter and data cost rather than by building and training a second large model.

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: extracting depth from visual priors
PROPOSAL: Train a linear layer on top of the pre-trained T2I diffusion model's feature extractor, using a small subset of the model's parameters to predict depth values on the validation set of the Diadem dataset. We'll use the Adam optimizer and a learning rate of 1e-4 for 10 epochs.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: Directly fine-tuning the model on the depth data with full parameters as a baseline for comparison.
- Ablation: Train the model with random weights instead of the pre-trained weights, with details given in the appendix.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that this linear layer will learn to extract depth-relevant features from the pre-trained model, leading to a reasonable amount of depth estimation accuracy. However, we anticipate that the model may fail when dealing with complex or cluttered scenes, resulting in large errors.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: extracting depth from visual priors
PROPOSAL: Revise to use a smaller learning rate of 1e-5 and an additional batch normalization layer after the linear layer to improve the performance and stability of the network. Also, run the model on the NYU-Depth-V2 dataset, as it has a larger number of samples and varying depth ranges. We'll train the model for 20 epochs to see if the additional depth diversity helps the model generalizing and improving its depth prediction accuracy.

Understanding how a scene has changed and forecasting how it will look next from Satellite Image Time Series (SITS) is fundamental to many critical applications, yet it poses a profound challenge: predicting the future requires a deep understanding of past change. Two tasks are central. In temporal change description, given a sequence of temporally ordered satellite images of the same area, the goal is to generate a natural-language description that accurately summarizes the key dynamic changes that occurred over the observation period, such as urban expansion or agricultural cycles; this requires comprehending the temporal evolution and, ideally, the underlying causal narrative of the changes. In future satellite image forecasting, given the same historical sequence, the goal is to generate a plausible image for the next time point. A critical and often overlooked requirement is that the forecast be temporally consistent: the generated changes should be a logical continuation of the trends and dynamics observed in the historical data, not merely a plausible standalone picture.

Although foundation models such as Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and diffusion-based image generators have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their application to this domain remains fragmented and fundamentally limited. On the understanding side, static image captioning ignores temporal context, while existing temporal change description methods lack the semantic depth of MLLMs: they fuse information across images through simple interactions, their long-range temporal reasoning is limited, and they struggle to capture why changes occur. General-purpose MLLMs, even video-capable ones, are not optimized for this setting either: video-centric models are typically tuned for densely sampled frames with fixed, short intervals, whereas consecutive satellite acquisitions are sparse and irregular, with gaps that can span several years. On the generation side, single-image synthesis cannot model evolution, and temporal forecasting approaches struggle with long-term consistency because they do not grasp the semantic drivers of change: their conditioning is typically low-level (e.g., edge maps), based on simple metadata, or limited to text guidance, and it lacks fine-grained temporal semantic interaction, so they can generate what a scene looks like but cannot reason about why it should look that way given its history. As a result, change understanding and future forecasting have been treated as disjointed tasks, even though both are limited by a common bottleneck: modeling long-range temporal dynamics.

This raises several questions. How can a model reason about why changes occurred across a long, irregularly sampled sequence of satellite images, and describe them accurately? How can such an understanding of past change be used to generate what will happen next, so that the forecast is a temporally consistent continuation of the observed trajectory rather than only a realistic-looking image? Can enhancing long-range temporal understanding improve performance on both tasks simultaneously, with the understanding of past change directly informing the forecast? Finally, how can the temporal consistency of a forecast be rigorously evaluated, given that standard image-quality metrics cannot penalize a prediction that is perceptually realistic but inconsistent with historical trends?

Conditional image generative models have, in recent years, demonstrated extraordinary capabilities, producing highly realistic images from both textual descriptions and class labels, and they have rapidly evolved from experimental research tools into widely accessible applications. Because they hold considerable promise to produce virtually unlimited amounts of data, researchers have started exploring their use as a source of synthetic training data for downstream machine learning models. However, recent research has revealed that as these models grow in size and capability, they tend to produce images of higher quality, better aligned with human preference, but with diminished diversity, which hinders their utility as synthetic training data generators.

Two families of techniques have been introduced to mitigate the shortcomings of such vanilla synthetic data. Learning-based approaches aim to improve the overall utility of synthetic data by reducing the distribution shift between generated and real samples; they use real data to train or fine-tune parts of existing conditional generative models. Guidance-based sampling methods instead define reward functions that steer the generation process and characterize the utility of generated samples in terms of generation quality or diversity. Yet the implicit or explicit utility functions behind these methods often disregard the potential distribution shift between synthetic and real data, and many guidance methods treat quality, diversity or safety as ends in themselves rather than as means to increase the utility of a synthetic image corpus for training downstream models. Moreover, in-depth analyses of conditional image generative models have highlighted a tension between quality and diversity. This tension becomes more apparent when diversity is defined as the variation among generated samples without reference to any target distribution. Contextualizing the desired diversity through real exemplar data holds the promise of limiting potentially disadvantageous variations in synthetic data.

Using exemplar data at inference time to guide generation is reminiscent of few-shot in-context learning in large language models, where a small number of examples suffices to adapt to new tasks without fine-tuning, and where providing more examples tends to help. In conditional image generation, however, most few-shot approaches require partial model training or fine-tuning, and the use of exemplar data at inference time remains underexplored. One prior inference-time method, Contextualized Vendi Score Guidance (c-VSG), leverages a handful of contextualizing real images to ground the diversity of generations to that of the real data; but, contrary to in-context learning, increasing the number of exemplars did not improve its performance. Meanwhile, fine-tuning with reward feedback has proven successful for improving generation quality, but it has not been tested whether it would also increase diversity given a proper reward.

The problem is therefore how to exploit a small set of real exemplar images to characterize, and jointly improve, both the quality and the diversity of the images produced by off-the-shelf conditional generators with respect to a target real distribution, ideally without fine-tuning the generator. Can strong quality and diversity be achieved this way, and can the benefit grow gracefully as more exemplars become available, unlike existing exemplar-based guidance? How does such an approach compare with training-based ways of using the same few real images? And does improving quality and diversity grounded in real data actually translate into greater utility of the synthetic images as training data for downstream models?

Modern generative paradigms, including diffusion, flow matching and consistency models, have achieved state-of-the-art performance and form the backbone of leading image and video generation systems, including large multi-modal generative models. Despite their success, they share a critical drawback: both training and sampling demand substantial computational resources. Multi-step frameworks such as diffusion and flow matching produce a sample by iteratively integrating a probability-flow ordinary differential equation, typically requiring 40 to 100 network function evaluations (NFEs). The problem is magnified for large-scale models, for which efficient sampling is paramount: the continuous, long-term cost of inference often surpasses the one-time training cost, directly affecting economic viability and practical deployment. For example, the largest open multi-modal image generators (about 20B parameters) typically need about 100 NFEs, i.e. roughly 40 seconds on a single A100 GPU for one 1024×1024 image.

Numerous efforts aim to accelerate generative inference by reducing the number of sampling steps. Early single-step generators such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) often suffered from unstable training dynamics. To accelerate multi-step diffusion models, various distillation techniques have been introduced. They range from student-teacher methods, in which a student learns to reproduce a frozen teacher's sampling trajectory in fewer steps (e.g., progressive distillation, which requires an iterative distillation procedure), to distribution matching distillation (e.g., DMD and DMD2), which uses adversarial-style training with auxiliary networks to align the generator's output distribution directly with the data distribution. In parallel, consistency models and their variants (e.g., LCM and PCM), as well as related shortcut and MeanFlow objectives, have been designed explicitly for high-quality generation in very few steps, and recent work shows that multi-step and few-step models can be cast as instances of a single unified any-step training objective.

Despite this progress, existing few-step methods face a difficult trade-off between simplicity, efficiency and quality. (a) Complexity and instability: adversarial approaches, such as GANs, DMD-style distribution matching and hybrid frameworks that combine teacher guidance with adversarial signals (e.g., SANA-Sprint), require auxiliary trained networks (discriminators or fake-sample score networks) and/or frozen teacher models; distribution matching methods typically keep separate copies of a generator, a real-score model and a fake-score model. This introduces training instability and sensitivity to hyperparameters, and it increases architectural complexity and GPU memory overhead. For ultra-large models, the added complexity often translates into out-of-memory failures or brittle training dynamics, so few-step approaches have rarely been applied to models beyond about 3B parameters, and the only open-source few-step model released for a large model was obtained by distribution matching distillation with its GAN loss removed, an indirect sign of the high cost of adversarial losses at scale. (b) Performance degradation: methods trained without adversarial guidance, such as consistency models, often show a sharp decline in quality at very low NFEs (fewer than 4), and within the unified any-step view, current few-step methods struggle to reach high-quality one-step generation without resorting to a GAN-style loss.

The open problem is therefore how to train a generator that produces high-quality images in a single function evaluation, or very few, without discriminators, auxiliary score networks or frozen teacher models, so that training remains simple, stable and memory-efficient enough to scale to full-parameter training of the largest (10B to 20B parameters) text-to-image and multi-modal generators, without sacrificing the quality obtained by multi-step sampling.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: low-nfe consistency for large multi-modal models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the feasibility of consistency-based models for single-function or very low-NFE generation, by adapting the any-step training objective of [1] to constrain the output of the generator to a function of the input, plus a small, learnable residual. Evaluate the performance of this "residual-constrained" consistency model on a range of large text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard unconditional flow-based model variant, and with a separately-trained student teacher model with 5 iterations of progressive distillation.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The residual-constrained consistency model should provide a quality drop of less than 1.5 points on the MSMFT metric, compared to the unconditional flow-based model, while achieving a reduction in NFEs. However, very large models may still face training instability due to the use of large learnable residuals.

References:
[1] any-step training objective (not specified reference)
[2] DALL-E 2 dataset
[3] MSMFT metric (not specified reference)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adversarial-free distilled sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate a method for distilled sampling without adversarial losses, by computing the output of a given step through a combination of its own knowledge up to that point and the cached output from the preceding steps. Implement this method using a non-adversarial student-teacher approach, where the teacher is a frozen version of the model and the student takes fewer steps to sample an image. Evaluate this "distilled samplifier" on a set of large text-to-image models, using the COCO dataset [4] and the Inception score [5].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard progressive distillation approach and a baseline of the full model taking 5-10 steps.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The distilled samplifier should achieve a quality improvement of more than 1 point in Inception score, even when the teacher model is frozen, while reducing the number of NFEs significantly. However, evaluation metrics may become less reliable at very low NFEs, making quality assessment challenging.

References:
[4] COCO dataset
[5] Inception score

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: adversarial-free distilled sampling (not changed)
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 2 to include an evaluation of the training time of the distilled samplifier, and investigate its impact on model capacity. Add an experiment where the student model and teacher model have the same capacity, but the student is trained with a reduced number of iterations, and another where the student model has a significantly reduced capacity compared to the teacher model, to analyze its effects on training time and inference quality.
CONTROLS: Include comparisons with progressive distillation as before, and add ablation studies on the impact of teacher-student capacity mismatch on distilled sampler performance.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The evaluation of training time and capacity will show that the distilled samplifier achieves a significant reduction in training time and enables the use of smaller models, but may come at the cost of reduced inference quality if the student and teacher models have significantly different capacities.

Note: This is a refinement of the original proposal, rather than a completely new one. It incorporates additional evaluation and analysis, and expands on the original ideas.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: adverse-free distilled sampling
PROPOSAL: Modify the architecture of the distilled sampler to use a denoising autoencoder instead of a simple student model, which will allow it to learn the structure of the data distribution directly from the teacher model. This will reduce the need for pre-training the student model and improve its ability to generalize to new input distributions. Evaluate the performance of this "autoencoder-based distilled sampler" on the same COCO dataset [4] and Inception score [5] as before.
CONTROLS: Include comparisons with the original student-teacher approach and progressive distillation as before, and add ablation studies on the importance of the autoencoder structure and the pre-training stage.
COST: 1400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The autoencoder-based distilled sampler should achieve significant improvements in Inception score and reduce the number of NFEs, with better generalization capabilities compared to the original student-teacher approach. However, it may be more sensitive to the configuration of the teacher model and the pre-training stage.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: momentum-guided consistency
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new variant of the consistency model, where the generator is trained to produce output that not only matches the input, but also a momentum-buffered version of the input. This momentum buffer is initialized with a value close to zero and updated on each iteration of the training process. Evaluate the performance of this "momentum-guided consistency model" on a range of large text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard unconditional flow-based model variant and the residual-constrained consistency model from proposal 1.
COST: 1100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The momentum-guided consistency model should stabilize the training dynamics and improve the quality of generated images, especially when the input sequence has a strong temporal structure. However, it may increase the number of NFEs required for convergence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: conditional pre-training for low-nfe models
PROPOSAL: Investigate a method to improve the performance of low-NFE models by pre-training them on a large dataset with conditional inputs and then fine-tuning them on a smaller dataset with the target format of images or text. This will allow the model to learn a richer representation of the data distribution and improve its ability to generate high-quality output in a single function evaluation. Evaluate the performance of this "conditionally pre-trained low-NFE model" on a range of text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with unconditional pre-training and the residual-constrained consistency model from proposal 1.
COST: 1600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The conditionally pre-trained low-NFE model should achieve significant improvements in MSMFT score and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, but the fine-tuning stage may require careful hyperparameter tuning to maintain performance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: low-nfe consistency for large multi-modal models
PROPOSAL: Refine the residual-constrained consistency model by splitting the residual into two parts: a shared residual that is conditioned on the input sequence, and a private residual that is specific to each instance of the input sequence. This will allow the model to learn more robust and transferable representations of the data distribution. Evaluate the performance of this "split-residual consistency model" on a range of large text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard unconditional flow-based model variant and the momentum-guided consistency model.
COST: 1300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The split-residual consistency model should achieve improved MSMFT scores and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, especially when evaluated on diverse and out-of-distribution test sets. However, it may be more challenging to train due to the increased complexity of the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: constructive diffusion initialization
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of constructive diffusion initialization to improve the performance of low-NFE models. This involves pre-training a large model using reversible denoising diffusion [6] and then initializing the lower-capacity model with the final stage of the diffusion process. Evaluate the performance of this "constructively initialized low-NFE model" on a range of text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with standard random initialization and the split-residual consistency model from proposal 1.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The constructively initialized low-NFE model should achieve improved MSMFT scores and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, due to the more effective initialization of the model weights. However, it may require careful tuning of the diffusion process and initialization hyperparameters.

Reference:
[6] reversible denoising diffusion

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: attention-augmented low-nfe models
PROPOSAL: Modify the architecture of the low-NFE models by adding self-attention layers to allow for more flexible and adaptive interactions between different parts of the input sequence. This will enable the model to better capture long-range dependencies and generate more coherent and detailed output in a single function evaluation. Evaluate the performance of this "attention-augmented low-NFE model" on a range of text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard model architecture and the split-residual consistency model from proposal 1, on a small subset (about 5%) of the evaluation data.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The attention-augmented low-NFE model should achieve improved MSMFT scores and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, especially when the input sequence has complex and long-range dependencies. However, it may be more challenging to train due to the increased complexity of the model and the potential for catastrophic forgetting of important features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: early-stopped multi-sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of early-stopped multi-sampling as a final stage of the inference process for low-NFE models. This involves sampling multiple times from the model, but stopping each sequence at an early stage and using the generated output as the final result. This will allow the model to explore different possible output paths and avoid getting trapped in local minima. Evaluate the performance of this "early-stopped multi-sampling" on a range of text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with standard single-sampling and the attention-augmented low-NFE model from proposal 6.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The early-stopped multi-sampling approach should achieve improved MSMFT scores and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, especially when evaluated on sequences with multiple modes or complex structure. However, it may require careful tuning of the early-stopping threshold and sampling schedule to achieve optimal performance.

Facial rigging aims to make a static neutral facial mesh animatable by defining a set of controllable deformations, typically represented either as blendshape rigs driven by activated action units in systems based on the Facial Action Coding System (FACS), or as skeletal rigs driven by joint positions. Whereas full-body auto-rigging usually follows a two-step pipeline of skeleton construction and skinning, facial rigs are often anatomically inspired and implemented with FACS blendshapes. In a linear FACS blendshape rig, each blendshape is a vertex offset from the neutral mesh corresponding to one action unit, i.e. a specific muscle movement such as "Right Eye Close", and a complex expression is obtained by adding the weighted offsets of the activated blendshapes to the neutral mesh. Rigging is an essential step for creative AI, bringing digital avatars to life by enabling expressive and realistic facial movements across a wide range of applications. However, creating a facial rig is laborious and expensive, often requiring skilled artists tens of hours to complete a single asset. Methods that transfer expressions from 2D images or videos to 3D avatars do not remove this bottleneck, since they assume that the avatar already has a rig.

Existing facial auto-rigging methods typically transfer a complete set of blendshapes from a predefined template mesh to a neutral target mesh, which often requires dense correspondences or a mesh topology shared by the template and the target. More recent approaches build transferable latent spaces between faces or use triangulation-agnostic networks to bypass these limitations, but they still require a template blendshape rig, which can compromise accuracy when the template and target shapes differ substantially. Only one prior approach, NFR, can directly rig facial meshes from explicitly controllable FACS parameters without relying on a template, and it has so far been demonstrated primarily on humanoid heads. Furthermore, existing approaches, NFR included, have yet to accommodate meshes with multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs or teeth, which limits their ability to animate highly expressive avatars: an "eye look-down" pose, for example, is difficult to reproduce if the mesh lacks eyeballs.

Learning such a rigging model also raises a data problem. Accurate 3D supervision requires neutral meshes paired with complete rigs made by artists, and because manual rigging is so costly such rigged examples are scarce; a model trained solely on them is likely to generalize poorly to the wide variety of facial shapes, styles and topologies met in practice.

The problem is therefore to automatically turn a single static neutral facial mesh into an expressive rig controllable by FACS parameters (i) without relying on predefined template blendshapes, so that target meshes need not closely resemble a template; (ii) for in-the-wild meshes with varying topologies and shapes, including both humanoid and non-humanoid heads; and (iii) for meshes made of multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs and teeth, which must move coherently with the rest of the face. How can such a rigging system be built, and how can it be trained to generalize across this diversity when only a limited number of rigged meshes is available as 3D ground truth?

The multi-objective multi-armed bandit problem generalizes the classical, single-objective multi-armed bandit to settings with multiple, potentially conflicting objectives. Pulling an arm yields a vector of objective-specific rewards, so a single "best" arm is often ill-defined and optimality must account for trade-offs across objectives. The setting of interest here is the multi-objective linear contextual bandit: at each round, every arm of a finite set is described by a d-dimensional context vector, which may be chosen adversarially; each of the L objectives has its own fixed but unknown parameter vector; and the agent, after choosing an arm, observes an L-dimensional reward vector whose entry for each objective is the inner product of the arm's context with that objective's parameter, plus zero-mean sub-Gaussian noise.

One simple way to handle trade-offs is scalarization, which maps reward vectors to a scalar via, for example, weighted sums, minimax, or other nonlinear transforms, thereby reducing the problem to a single-objective bandit. However, selecting a suitable scalarization is itself nontrivial, and an arm that is optimal under one scalarization can be markedly suboptimal under another. An alternative is to reason directly in the vector space via Pareto optimality: the Pareto front comprises the arms whose mean reward vectors are not dominated component-wise by that of any other arm. Because it compares reward vectors objective-wise, Pareto optimality is more general than committing to a fixed scalarization. Performance is then usually measured by the Pareto regret, which sums over rounds the smallest uniform increase that would make the mean reward vector of the chosen arm non-dominated.

Prior work on Pareto regret in multi-objective bandits proposes and studies upper-confidence-bound (UCB) algorithms, which typically compute an empirical Pareto front at every round and are therefore complex. Approaches that identify the Pareto front by eliminating arms do not carry over to the contextual setting, where the Pareto front changes with the contexts and an arm discarded early may later be Pareto optimal. By contrast, the Pareto regret of Thompson Sampling has not been studied for multi-objective bandits: the only Thompson Sampling algorithm proposed for this problem comes without theoretical analysis, and the analyses of randomized scalarization in multi-objective Bayesian optimization concern the Bayesian regret under a known Gaussian prior, with bounds that increase with the number of objectives. This gap is noteworthy: in many single-objective contextual and non-contextual bandits, Thompson Sampling and its variants are empirically competitive with or superior to UCB methods, yet their worst-case (frequentist) analyses are typically more delicate. Extending Thompson Sampling to several objectives introduces additional challenges, including coordinating randomized samples across multiple objectives, ensuring optimism of the randomized estimates across all objectives simultaneously, and handling the possibility of multiple Pareto-optimal arms.

A second issue concerns the performance measure itself. The standard Pareto regret compares per-round mean reward vectors; consequently, a policy that plays only Pareto-optimal arms incurs zero Pareto regret, even when an alternative selection of arms over the same number of rounds would yield strictly larger cumulative rewards in every objective. Pareto regret therefore does not distinguish between policies that obtain different cumulative rewards while selecting only Pareto-optimal arms, and the resulting shortfall can grow with the number of rounds.

This raises two questions. First, can a computationally efficient, Thompson Sampling-type randomized algorithm for the multi-objective linear contextual bandit be designed with worst-case Pareto regret guarantees, how close can these guarantees come to those known for randomized algorithms in the single-objective linear setting, and how must they depend on the number of objectives? Second, how should optimality and regret be defined in this setting so that they also account for cumulative rewards under repeated selections, penalizing policies that are Pareto optimal round by round but inefficient in aggregate?

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: maximum likelihood simulation
PROPOSAL: design a simulation-based framework to provide maximum likelihood estimates for the unknown objective parameter vectors in the multi-objective linear contextual bandit setting. we will generate synthetic contexts and rewards using a chosen distribution (e.g., standard normal) and the multiplier travel method to fit the reward functions to the data, for various setting parameters and numbers of objectives.
CONTROLS: ablation study of using different distributions and reward function estimation methods, comparison with the oracle knowledge scenario where the objective parameters are known, following the setup outlined in the proposal.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this approach will provide a fast and efficient method to estimate objective parameters, but may struggle with small sample sizes or complex reward relationships.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: thompson sampling with pareto-conditional utility
PROPOSAL: investigate a Thompson Sampling algorithm that directly estimates the Pareto front using a utility function that conditions on the current Pareto set. at each round, the algorithm generates a set of candidate arms based on an empirical Pareto set, estimates the posterior distribution of the rewards for each arm using Thompson Sampling, and selects the arm with the highest estimated utility. the utility function compares the estimated rewards with the current Pareto front.
CONTROLS: comparison with UCB algorithms, ablation study of the utility function and the empirical Pareto set estimation, with details given in the appendix.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this approach will be able to adapt to changing Pareto sets, but may require a large number of samples to accurately estimate the posterior distributions, and may struggle with large numbers of objectives or complex reward relationships.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: no update to prior proposal
REVISED TITLE: maximum likelihood simulation
PROPOSAL: extend the simulation-based framework to provide confidence intervals for the estimated objective parameter vectors, and analyze the convergence rate of the estimates as a function of the number of samples and the dimensionality of the context space. we will use bootstrapping to compute the standard errors of the estimates, and use the law of the iterated logarithm to establish a bound on the estimation error.
CONTROLS: comparison with the oracle knowledge scenario where the objective parameters are known, ablation study of different bootstrapping methods, following the setup outlined in the proposal.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this updated proposal will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the simulation-based framework, but may require significant computational resources to analyze the convergence rate.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: pareto regret relaxation
PROPOSAL: propose a relaxation of the Pareto regret metric that accounts for cumulative rewards, by introducing a "discounted Pareto regret" metric that weights the regret at each round by the average cumulative reward obtained by the policy up to that round. we will analyze the optimality gap of a greedy algorithm that optimizes the discounted Pareto regret metric.
CONTROLS: comparison with the standard Pareto regret metric, analysis of the effect of the discount factor on the optimality gap, following the setup outlined in the proposal.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this relaxation may provide a more nuanced understanding of the trade-offs between Pareto optimality and cumulative rewards, but may require careful tuning of the discount factor.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: pareto regret relaxation
PROPOSAL: refine the discounted Pareto regret metric by using a more sophisticated discounting strategy, such as a weighted average of the cumulative rewards obtained by the policy at different time horizons. we will analyze the effect of different weighting schemes on the optimality gap and the relative performance of different policies.
CONTROLS: comparison with the standard pareto regret metric, analysis of the effect of different weighting schemes on policy performance, following the setup outlined in the proposal.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this refined metric may provide a more robust understanding of the trade-offs between Pareto optimality and cumulative rewards, but may require extensive computational resources to analyze the effect of different weighting schemes.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: bound on pareto regret
PROPOSAL: provide a high-probability bound on the Pareto regret of an arbitrary bandit algorithm, in terms of the number of samples, the dimensionality of the context space, and the number of objectives. we will use a combination of concentration inequalities and martingale techniques to derive a tight bound on the Pareto regret.
CONTROLS: comparison with existing bounds on single-objective bandits, analysis of the effect of the number of objectives on the bound, reported alongside the main results.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this bound may provide a fundamental understanding of the Pareto regret metric, but may be challenging to derive and may not provide a good approximation for small sample sizes or complex reward relationships.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: thompson sampling with pareto-conditional utility
PROPOSAL: extend the Thompson Sampling algorithm with Pareto-conditional utility to handle multiple Pareto-optimal arms by introducing a hierarchical decision-making process. at each round, the algorithm will generate multiple candidate arms based on an empirical Pareto set, estimate the posterior distribution of the rewards for each arm using Thompson Sampling, and select the arm with the highest estimated utility. however, if multiple arms are tied for the highest utility, the algorithm will use a secondary selection criterion to break ties, such as the maximum estimated reward across all objectives.
CONTROLS: comparison with standard UCB algorithms, analysis of the effect of the hierarchical decision-making process on policy performance, with results reported in a table.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this extended algorithm may be able to handle multiple Pareto-optimal arms more effectively than standard algorithms, but may require additional computational resources and may be more challenging to analyze theoretically.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: regularization of the empirical pareto set
PROPOSAL: introduce regularization techniques to stabilize the empirical Pareto set estimation in the multi-objective bandit setting. we will use L1 or L2 regularization to penalize the empirical Pareto set based on a chosen regularizer, and analyze the effect of regularization on the policy performance and regret.
CONTROLS: comparison with standard empirical Pareto set estimation, analysis of the effect of regularization on the robustness of the policy to outliers and noise, with details given in the appendix.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this regularization approach may improve the stability and robustness of the policy, but may also increase the risk of over-smoothing the empirical Pareto set and sacrificing optimality.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: no update to prior proposal
PROPOSAL: extend the maximum likelihood simulation to estimate the cumulative rewards under repeated selections, by running multiple episodes of the simulation with different initial arm selections and averaging the cumulative rewards across episodes. we will use this approach to evaluate the performance of different policies on cumulative rewards, and analyze the effect of the number of episodes on the accuracy of the estimation.
CONTROLS: comparison with oracle knowledge scenario where the objective parameters are known, analysis of the effect of the number of episodes on the accuracy of the estimation, with results reported in a table.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this extension will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the simulation-based framework, but may require additional computational resources to estimate the cumulative rewards accurately.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: instrumental rewards for multi-objective bandits
PROPOSAL: develop an instrumental rewards approach to handle multi-objective bandits by learning an intermediate representation of the rewards that can be used to optimize a single objective function. we will use a combination of neural networks and reinforcement learning to learn the instrumental rewards, and analyze the effect of the instrumental rewards on the policy performance and regret.
CONTROLS: comparison with direct optimization of the multi-objective function, analysis of the effect of the number of objectives on the accuracy of the instrumental rewards, with results reported in a table.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this instrumental rewards approach may provide a more efficient and scalable solution to multi-objective bandits, but may also introduce additional challenges such as learning the instrumental rewards and handling the trade-offs between objectives.
