Large language models have recently improved their reasoning by spending more test-time compute, generating more tokens before producing a final answer. Extended sequential scaling has limits, however: beyond a certain length, performance can decrease because of "overthinking", and long sequential reasoning can be sensitive to the order of reasoning steps. A complementary scaling dimension, repeated parallel sampling followed by aggregation, as in self-consistency (majority voting) or Best-of-N selection, has further boosted reasoning performance. These parallel methods rely on the model generating solutions that are both diverse and correct, and as tasks become harder, some mechanism for increasing diversity becomes necessary.

Obtaining such diversity is difficult. Only a minority of tokens in a chain of thought act as forking tokens that lead to distinct reasoning modes, so as problems become harder and generations longer, these tokens become substantially harder to sample. The common practice for encouraging diversity, raising the sampling temperature, inherently entails a diversity-accuracy trade-off, because the forking tokens that trigger diverse yet correct reasoning modes typically lie deep within the sampling tree. Theoretical work further shows that increasing the temperature alone does not necessarily yield greater diversity unless the model has been explicitly trained to ensure coverage. Search-based alternatives such as Monte Carlo tree search or Tree of Thoughts increase coverage through heuristic-guided search with an external verifier, but their reliance on heuristics and domain-specific knowledge limits the tasks to which they apply. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is not a complete answer either: it requires a strong base model, and recent work suggests that it does not by itself instill new capabilities, so what a model learns during fine-tuning matters.

At the same time, several distinct and correct reasoning traces per question can be obtained at low cost and without human annotation, for instance by distilling from different teacher models, sampling repeatedly, and filtering with a verifiable correctness check. This suggests training models for coverage directly from such diverse traces, but how to do so is unclear. Standard supervised fine-tuning treats each trace as an independent example and has no explicit mechanism for keeping different reasoning modes apart: it is an open question whether the modes are preserved or merged into one, and whether a particular mode can later be deliberately elicited. Recent efforts to train models natively for parallel reasoning, by converting sequential chains of thought into parallel ones or by training on multiple traces distilled from teachers, show that native parallel scaling can surpass sequential scaling within certain token limits, but they leave open whether the distinct reasoning modes present in the training traces are actually retained and can be reliably triggered.

The problem is therefore how to fine-tune a language model on a set of diverse, correct reasoning traces per question so that it retains their distinct reasoning modes rather than collapsing them, and so that diverse yet accurate reasoning paths can be reliably triggered when sampling in parallel, instead of depending on sampling rare forking tokens deep inside a generation. Can such training improve both the accuracy of a single generation and the accuracy and coverage obtained by aggregating a small number of parallel generations?

COST: 100 GPU-hours (using a batch size of 16 and 5 teacher models)
PREDICTION: We expect the sampling universality proposal to yield better accuracy and a more diverse range of correct reasoning paths compared to Baseline 1 and Baseline 2, particularly in harder, more complex tasks such as competition mathematics and graduate-level science question answering. However, the improved diversity may come at the cost of a slight decrease in accuracy for simpler tasks. This approach may fail if the diverse sampling schedules lead to significantly more mode collapse, erasing diversity in favor of convergence to a single high-accuracy mode.

Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly expanded in capability and are now widely used in domains such as conversational agents, healthcare and finance, where they often process sensitive personal information. Early privacy concerns focused mainly on memorization and leakage of training data, but recent studies show that LLMs can also infer private attributes of an author, such as location, identity or demographics, from subtle semantic cues in seemingly innocuous text. With sufficiently capable models, such inferences can be surprisingly accurate and often go undetected by users, who continue to share content unaware of the risk. Moreover, text sent to external services may be intercepted in transit or retained by providers, for example for model training, increasing the risk of misuse or data breaches.

Traditional anonymization methods rely on rule-based de-identification, such as named entity recognition or pattern matching, to remove surface-level identifiers like names, social security numbers or explicit locations. They frequently overlook the context-dependent semantics that LLMs can exploit, so private information that is embedded in context rather than stated explicitly remains inferable. This gap calls for anonymization techniques that account for semantic context and defend against inference-based privacy threats, while preserving the meaning and readability of the text, that is, techniques that achieve a good privacy-utility trade-off.

A growing body of work pursues LLM-based anonymization to protect semantic-level private information from model inference. In feedback-guided adversarial anonymization, an LLM anonymizer rewrites the input text while a second LLM, acting as an adversary, attempts to infer private attributes from the rewritten output; based on this adversarial feedback, the anonymizer iteratively refines its output to prevent the inferences that remain possible. With GPT-4 as both anonymizer and adversary, this approach achieves a substantially better privacy-utility trade-off than traditional industry-grade anonymizers. However, reliance on large proprietary models is costly and requires sending the very text that should be protected to potentially untrusted external systems. Attempts to transfer these anonymization capabilities into smaller models have been explored only to a limited extent, and existing approaches still depend on a proprietary model to provide the adversarial feedback, incurring similar costs and privacy concerns.

The open problem is therefore whether, and how, small language models that can run locally under modest compute budgets can become effective anonymizers that protect semantic-level private information against inference by strong LLM adversaries, without relying on any external model at inference time. Can such models reach a privacy-utility trade-off comparable to, or better than, that of anonymizers built on frontier proprietary LLMs, including on texts where personal information is conveyed by the overall context rather than by explicit mentions, while remaining cheap enough to deploy in settings with strict data-confidentiality requirements?

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: evaluating the impact of feedback granularity on adversarial anonymization
PROPOSAL: Investigate how different levels of feedback granularity from the adversary affect the convergence rate and final performance of feedback-guided adversarial anonymization, using a small language model (e.g. BART) as the anonymizer and a strong LLM adversarial model (e.g. LaMDA) on a synthetic dataset of online comments.
CONTROLS: Compare the anonymizer's performance with and without feedback from the adversary, and evaluate the effects of refining feedback granularity on test accuracy, precision, recall and F1 score against a baseline LLM's ability to infer personal attributes from the anonymized text, following the setup outlined in the proposal.
COST: 100 GPU-hours to train and test.
PREDICTION: Expected result is that higher feedback granularity will improve anonymizer performance, particularly against stronger adversaries, but with diminishing returns, until diagnosis via a grid search to determine the optimal feedback granularity value, where further experimentation may show it’ll be result in a failing dependency if granularity is reduced any lower than we arrive at.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: analyzing the trade-offs between anonymizer capacity and adversary strength
PROPOSAL: Explore whether small language models of varying capacities (e.g. RoBERTa, ALBERT) can become effective anonymizers by evaluating their performance on a diverse set of synthetic online comment datasets against strong, moderate, and weak LLM adversaries (e.g. using LaMDA, BART, and T5, respectively).
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of anonymizers with different capacities on a range of metrics, including test accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and the amount of information they require to maintain a good privacy-utility trade-off, with results reported in a table.
COST: 200 GPU-hours to train and test, plus synthetic data generation.
PREDICTION: Expected result is that an anonymizer capacity of at least 300M parameters is necessary to match the performance of GPT-4 on the task, but we should find a more modest capacity model, e.g., T5 with 220M parameters, reaches a trade-off that’s competitive for lower data governance costs.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: evaluating the impact of adaptable anonymizer capacity on adversarial anonymization
PROPOSAL: Revise the anonymizer capacity experiment (formerly 2) to dynamically adapt the anonymizer's capacity during the iteration process using an evolutionary algorithm, allowing it to optimize its capacity in response to the adversary's feedback and the task's requirements.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the adaptive anonymizer to the fixed-capacity anonymizers, and evaluate the impact of the adaptation process on the final performance, data governance, and anonymizer stability.
COST: 250 GPU-hours to train and test, plus synthetic data generation.
PREDICTION: Expected result is that an adaptive anonymizer will outperform fixed-capacity anonymizers in scenarios with changing task or adversary characteristics, although we may find instances where the data governance impact is outweighed by the performance risks of the evolving model so at times failing, and needing further deployment calibration.

PROPOSAL: Prove lower bounds on the maximum achievable privacy-utility trade-off for local adversarial anonymization, demonstrating the inherent limitations of small language models in protecting private information in the presence of strong adversaries, and quantify the resilience of our methods to these bounds.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: evaluating the impact of feedback frequency on adversarial anonymization
PROPOSAL: Modify the experiment (1) to investigate how the frequency of feedback from the adversary affects the convergence rate and final performance of feedback-guided adversarial anonymization, using a small language model (e.g. BART) as the anonymizer and a strong LLM adversarial model (e.g. LaMDA) on a synthetic dataset of online comments.

PROPOSAL: Refine the adaptive anonymizer capacity experiment (formerly 2) to scale its design for efficient and practical evaluation, incorporating a grid search over a reasonable range of anonymizer capacity configurations, and leveraging ensemble methods to estimate the performance of the adaptive anonymizer on a larger set of real-world online comment datasets.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: optimizing model size for local adversarial anonymization in low-resource settings
PROPOSAL: Investigate the trade-offs between model size and anonymity performance of local adversarial anonymization in low-resource settings, where computational resources are limited, and propose an efficient pruning technique to reduce the size of the anonymizer model without compromising its performance.
CONTROLS: Compare the anonymity performance of the pruned model with the original model on a subset of low-resource online comment datasets, and evaluate the efficiency of the pruning technique in terms of computational cost and data governance requirements.
COST: 250 GPU-hours to train and test on low-resource data.
PREDICTION: Expected result is that the pruning technique effectively reduces the model size without significantly compromising anonymity performance, making local adversarial anonymization more deployable in low-resource settings.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: robust evaluation of local adversarial anonymization in varying environmental conditions
PROPOSAL: Assess the resilience of local adversarial anonymization to adversarial attacks, model updates, and varying network conditions, to ensure its robustness in practical deployment scenarios, by evaluating its performance on a diverse set of real-world online comment datasets under different levels of noise, attack severity, and network latency.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of local adversarial anonymization with state-of-the-art anonymization methods on a subset of real-world online comment datasets under varying environmental conditions, and evaluate the robustness of its design to different types of attacks and system perturbations.
COST: 800 GPU-hours to train and test on diverse datasets.
PREDICTION: Expected result is that local adversarial anonymization demonstrates robust performance across different environmental conditions, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in some cases, but with areas for improvement in addressing specific types of attacks and system perturbations.

Time series data arise ubiquitously across a broad range of domains, including healthcare, finance, industrial manufacturing, weather forecasting and urban computing, and their characteristics can differ vastly from one domain to another. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have unleashed new potential for exploiting these data in time series tasks such as forecasting, imputation and classification. There are roughly two families of approaches: one fine-tunes or prompts off-the-shelf LLMs with time series converted into a suitable format, while the other trains time series foundation models from scratch on vast time series corpora by adapting LLM-inspired architectures and training strategies. In both cases, the quality of the time series data is critical to model performance: low-quality data can negate the benefits of bespoke technical advances and may even degrade performance. In practice, time series datasets are frequently marred by pervasive quality issues, including missing values, corruption induced by sensor failures, and irregular sampling. Consequently, there is a pressing need to assess, accurately and efficiently, the quality of time series data crawled from diverse domains.

General-purpose data attribution methods, such as influence functions and Shapley-value approaches (together with cheaper approximations such as KNN-based or gradient-based Shapley values), estimate the contribution of individual training samples in a model-agnostic way, but they overlook properties specific to time series such as continuity, temporal dependencies and non-stationarity. Existing attempts at time series data quality estimation therefore stress the need for methods tailored to temporal characteristics. For instance, TimeInf adapts the influence function to time series, drawing on earlier work on infinitesimal robustness for autoregressive processes and on influence functionals for time series, and TimeShap extends the Shapley value, a cooperative game-theoretic attribution method, to time series. However, these methods have largely neglected the fact that real-world time series originate from diverse domains with distinct properties and substantial distribution shifts, which limits their effectiveness to a single domain. Furthermore, both influence-function and Shapley-value techniques struggle to strike a balance between estimation fidelity and computational efficiency: influence functions require computationally intensive Hessian and gradient calculations, while Shapley values incur exponential computational costs.

Recently, estimating data quality through LLM judgments has emerged as a promising approach for text, where carefully designed prompts guide LLMs to produce accurate quality assessments. The underlying rationale is that LLMs are proficient in understanding quality criteria for natural language, such as writing style, required expertise, factual accuracy and educational value. Such efforts point to the potential of LLMs for cross-domain and interpretable data quality estimation, but they remain restricted to text and code, and the time series setting is largely unexplored.

It is therefore tempting to ask whether LLMs can be exploited to determine the quality of diverse time series data. Such an approach could leverage the knowledge of time series from many domains that LLMs acquire during large-scale pretraining, thereby circumventing the prohibitive computational cost of calculating influence functions or Shapley values in a domain-by-domain manner. However, it remains under-explored whether LLMs can truly comprehend the key characteristics that underpin the quality of diverse time series data, and how to effectively steer them to distinguish between high- and low-quality time series according to desired quality criteria. The open problem is thus how to rate the quality of time series data drawn from heterogeneous domains in a way that is accurate, computationally efficient and adaptable across domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: training llm on a mixed dataset of high-quality time series
PROPOSAL: Train a large language model (LLM) on a mixed dataset consisting of high-quality time series from various domains, including electricity load forecasting, exchange rate forecasting, traffic forecasting, weather forecasting, handwriting recognition, and spacecraft telemetry anomaly detection. The mixed dataset will serve as a reference for the LLM to learn patterns and characteristics across different domains.
CONTROLS: baseline models will include models trained on a single-domain dataset, a model trained on time series data without any domain-mixing, and a non-trainable LLM as a control, in the same setting as the proposal.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should yield an LLM that performs well on diverse time series data, with the potential for domain-agnostic quality estimation. However, the effectiveness of this approach may depend on the quality and diversity of the mixed dataset used for training. The model might struggle with adapting to very different properties of each domain, like non-stationarity or spiking versus steady values.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: testing llm quality estimation with noisy and missing values
PROPOSAL: Experiment with the LLM from proposal 1 (training llm on a mixed dataset of high-quality time series) on a range of time series datasets with different types and levels of noise, missing values, and data corruption. This will help evaluate the robustness of the LLM in estimating the quality of time series data under various real-world conditions.
CONTROLS: the same baseline models from proposal 1 will be included, as well as various data augmentation techniques to simulate the effects of noise and data corruption.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The LLM should be able to detect and adapt to varying levels of noise and data corruption, but might struggle with highly irregular or corrupted data that deviates from its expected patterns or might fail when it has "hard time" disambiguating value based on a few millions examples.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: revising the training data to include a larger proportion of low-quality time series
PROPOSAL: Revise the training data used for the LLM in proposal 1 (training llm on a mixed dataset of high-quality time series) to include a larger proportion of low-quality time series, such as those with missing values, noise, or other forms of data corruption. This will help the LLM generalize better to real-world time series data and improve its ability to estimate quality.
CONTROLS: same as proposal 1, with additional data augmentation techniques to simulate the effects of low-quality data.
COST: 500 additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised training data should improve the LLM's ability to estimate quality in the presence of noise and data corruption, but may require retraining the LLM from scratch to adapt to the new distribution of the training data. The model should generalize better across domains but might still struggle with very specific or unbalance occurrences.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE:non uniform sampling in training llm
PROPOSAL: Introduce non-uniform sampling during training of the LLM, where the LLM is more likely to be exposed to high-quality time series data and less likely to be exposed to low-quality time series data. This can help the LLM learn to focus on the aspects of high-quality time series data that are most indicative of quality.
CONTROLS: same as proposal 1, but with the added non-uniform sampling strategy.
COST: negligible additional cost, as this can be implemented as a small modification to the existing training process.
PREDICTION: This approach may lead to improved performance on quality estimation tasks, particularly when the time series data has a mix of high and low-quality segments. However, it may also lead to overemphasis on high-quality time series data at the expense of learning from low-quality data, which could result in poor performance in domains where low-quality data is more prevalent.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluation metrics for time series quality estimation
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate a set of metrics for assessing the quality of time series data, including metrics that capture the presence of missing values, outliers, and other forms of data corruption. This will help evaluate the performance of the LLM and other approaches on time series quality estimation tasks.
CONTROLS: use a combination of established metrics for time series quality estimation, such as the percentage of missing values and the mean absolute error (MAE) between predicted and actual values, as well as novel metrics that capture the nuances of time series data, as described above.
COST: 100 GPU-hours for development and testing of the metrics
PREDICTION: The developed metrics will provide a robust and comprehensive framework for evaluating the performance of time series quality estimation approaches, including the LLM-based approach proposed in this set. The metrics may capture subtle aspects of time series data that are not well-represented by existing metrics, but may require extensive experimentation to fine-tune and validate.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: exploring applying distillation for time series quality estimation
PROPOSAL: Apply knowledge distillation techniques to transfer knowledge from a pre-trained LLM to a smaller, more efficient model that can perform time series quality estimation. This can help improve the efficiency and scalability of the approach.
CONTROLS: compare the performance of the distilled model to the pre-trained LLM and the original small model without distillation.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The distilled model should achieve similar performance to the pre-trained LLM, but with improved efficiency and scalability. However, the distillation process may require careful tuning of parameters and may not always yield improvements, particularly if the pre-trained LLM has a complex architecture or is highly specialized.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: adaptive non uniform sampling in training llm
PROPOSAL: Modify the non-uniform sampling strategy in proposal 1 (non uniform sampling in training llm) to be adaptive to the changing data distribution during training. This can help the LLM learn to focus on the most indicative aspects of high-quality time series data at different stages of training.
CONTROLS: same as proposal 1, but with the added adaptive sampling strategy.
COST: 200 additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive non-uniform sampling strategy should further improve the performance of the LLM on quality estimation tasks by allowing the model to adapt to changing data distributions. However, it may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and may not always lead to improvements in all cases, particularly if the data distribution is highly imbalanced or changes rapidly during training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: investigating manually curated time series datasets for improved quality estimation
PROPOSAL: Collect and release a set of manually curated time series datasets with high-quality annotations, which can be used to fine-tune and evaluate the performance of the LLM on quality estimation tasks.
CONTROLS: use a subset of the M4 competition dataset, which includes seasonal and trend decomposition based on Loess (STL) decomposition, logarithmic trend, noise, and aggregation based on absolute error (MAE) metrics.
COST: 20 hours of data curation and annotation effort
PREDICTION: The manually curated datasets should provide a high-quality benchmark for evaluating the performance of the LLM on quality estimation tasks, but may require significant effort to collect and annotate the data. The results may also demonstrate the effectiveness of the LLM on more challenging real-world datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: combining llm with traditional time series quality estimation methods
PROPOSAL: Investigate the combination of the LLM-based approach with traditional time series quality estimation methods, such as those based on statistical process control (SPC) or autoregressive (AR) modeling.
CONTROLS:compare the performance of a combined approach to the individual models, and explore different ways of combining the results (e.g. ensemble methods, hybrid models), reported alongside the main results.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The combined approach should improve the performance on quality estimation tasks by leveraging the strengths of both the LLM-based approach and traditional methods. However, the combination strategies may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and may not always lead to improvements in all cases, particularly if the traditional methods are poorly suited to the specific task or data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: deploying the llm-based quality estimation system in real-world applications
PROPOSAL: Deploy the LLM-based quality estimation system in real-world applications, such as financial forecasting, energy demand prediction, or industrial process monitoring, and evaluate its performance in these real-world settings.
CONTROLS: benchmark the performance of the system against existing quality estimation methods and industry standards.
COST: variable, dependent on deployment setup and infrastructure
PREDICTION: The LLM-based quality estimation system should successfully deploy in real-world applications, improving the efficiency and accuracy of time series data quality estimation. However, it may require additional development and fine-tuning to meet the specific needs of each application and may face challenges in terms of data curation, computational resources, and integration with existing systems.

Traditional multimodal models are typically divided into two categories: multimodal understanding (e.g., answering questions about images) and multimodal generation (e.g., generating images from text prompts). Unified Multimodal Generative Models (UMGMs) aim to integrate these two capabilities within a single framework. Recent UMGMs have demonstrated strong performance on a wide range of tasks, such as visual question answering, image captioning, visual reasoning, classification, reading comprehension, and image generation. They typically embed multiple input types into a shared representation space and use one single autoregressive transformer backbone to model cross-modal interactions, so that the same model produces both textual and visual outputs. Training generally follows a two-stage paradigm: pretraining focused on text-image alignment, followed by fine-tuning for specific downstream tasks, where instruction tuning (fine-tuning on diverse, task-specific instructions paired with expected outputs) has become a widely adopted strategy for aligning model behavior with human intent.

Although UMGMs show impressive zero-shot performance on many unseen instructions, their effectiveness is inconsistent across tasks, particularly when the relevant task data is absent from the pretraining corpus. Adding new task data to the training set can substantially improve performance on those tasks, but because novel multimodal tasks keep emerging, repeatedly merging new data and retraining the model is computationally expensive and impractical. This calls for ways to let UMGMs adapt flexibly and efficiently over time, in line with the principles of continual learning, where models acquire new capabilities incrementally.

Studies in continual learning have shown that sequentially fine-tuned models suffer from catastrophic forgetting: a model fine-tuned on new tasks tends to forget or overwrite previously acquired knowledge. Several works have explored continual instruction tuning for multimodal large language models, with methods that are typically regularization-based, architecture-based, replay-based, or prompt-based, and mixture-of-experts adapters have also attracted growing attention in continual learning for their scalability and modularity. However, these multimodal models produce language-only outputs, so prior research has focused exclusively on multimodal understanding tasks such as visual question answering, and existing methods address only intra-modal catastrophic forgetting, where old tasks, new tasks, and pre-trained capabilities all belong to the same output modality, typically text. This assumption holds for multimodal models with unimodal outputs, but it is insufficient for UMGMs, which generate both text and images from a single backbone. For UMGMs, forgetting may occur not only within a modality (intra-modal) but also across modalities (inter-modal): for example, continually tuning the model on a sequence of multimodal understanding tasks might erode its pre-trained image generation ability. This inter-modal forgetting remains largely unexplored, and it is unclear whether methods designed for the intra-modal setting can handle both forms of forgetting at once.

The central question is therefore: can UMGMs continually acquire new capabilities through instruction tuning without suffering catastrophic forgetting, both within a modality (e.g., multimodal understanding) and across modalities (e.g., improving multimodal understanding while preserving visual generation)? Answering it requires establishing whether inter-modal forgetting actually occurs in UMGMs, explaining what causes it, and finding an efficient way to adapt these models to new tasks that retains performance on earlier tasks as well as the pre-trained capabilities of the other modality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: comparing catastrophic forgetting across intra-modal and inter-modal tasks
PROPOSAL: Design an experiment to assess the extent of catastrophic forgetting in UMGMs across various multimodal tasks, including visual question answering and text-to-image generation. Evaluate intra-modal and inter-modal forgetting on different UMGM models using commonly used metrics such as accuracy and F1-score. Compare forgetting rates on individual intra-modal and inter-modal tasks to quantify inter-modal interactions. Collect results on 5 multimodal tasks, including some tasks not used during pretraining. Controls will be variants of standard UMGMs with different fine-tuning schedules or use of contrastive loss.
COST: 100 GPU-hours, assuming about 40 tasks to train across 4 GPUs for 5 days.
PREDICTION: will show significant inter-modal forgetting in UMGMs, confirming our research hypothesis, and demonstrate that intra-modal tasks tend to degrade pre-trained image generation skills more significantly than multimodal understanding abilities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: robustness to catastrophic forgetting in UMGMs with rehearsal and weight decay
PROPOSAL: Investigate two standard methods for preventing catastrophic forgetting in the intra-modal setting: rehearsal and weight decay. Modify UMGMs to utilize a combination of these two methods independently and jointly. Rehearsal involves storing and replaying training data from past tasks during additional fine-tuning steps. Weight decay acts as a penalty term added to the loss function, preventing large weight changes and reinforcing generalization. With rehearsal and weight decay integrated into the UMGM, retrain and re-evaluate models across multiple multimodal understanding tasks and observe how these methods mitigate inter-modal forgetting. Compare methods to establish an optimal combination and assess performance on visual question answering and reading comprehension tasks.
COST: 80 GPU-hours, requiring an additional 4 days of training with 4 GPUs.
PREDICTION: applying both rehearsal and weight decay will show the best performance in retaining pre-trained image generation skills in UMGMs under instruction tuning, as these methods provide useful and individual protection against inter-modal forgetting. Still, there's a chance we might not see optimal results for tasks with frequently updated outputs (e.g. image generation), because the paths in the model require frequent updating as well.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 2
TITLE: robustness to catastrophic forgetting in UMGMs with rehearsal and differential weight decay
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 2 by incorporating differential weight decay (DWD) specifically for the visual generation module to retain pre-trained image generation capabilities. This approach involves applying a separate weight decay factor to the visual generator's weights, allowing it to learn and adapt at a different rate than the rest of the model. Test DWD against rehearsal, weight decay, and the combination of rehearsal and weight decay under UMGM instruction tuning. Based on previous work showing that varying learning rates and parameters have different effects on task-specific vs general knowledge in models. Evaluate performance on reading comprehension, visual question answering, and text-to-image generation tasks with pre-training objectives calibrated for this revised fine-tuning schedule.
CONTROLS: compare results with standard models with standard fine-tuning. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: Additional 40 GPU-hours, approximately two more days of training on 4 GPUs.
PREDICTION: introducing differential weight decay will yield the highest retention of pre-trained image generation abilities, giving evidence for the flexibility in fine-tuning of seemingly conflicting reporting directions from other researchers to potentially leverage both preservation techniques to overcome image generation's poorer roaming-зBelow of overall language model features.

TITLE: robustness to catastrophic forgetting in UMGMs with rehearsal and differential weight decay

Recent advances in computer graphics and vision have highlighted image relighting, that is, changing the illumination of an existing image, as a critical task for film production, augmented reality and digital content creation. Full-image relighting, in which both the objects and the surrounding scene must be relit, remains a challenging problem.

Existing works can be grouped into object-centric approaches, which often ignore or replace the background, and scene-level methods, which attempt full-image relighting but remain largely data-driven: they struggle to generalize beyond the training distribution without extensive and diverse data, and cannot maintain the lighting of self-luminous objects. Even state-of-the-art foreground relighting methods still suffer from albedo inconsistency and imprecise lighting control: relighting can, for instance, alter the colors of a carpet, or make light intended to come from the left appear to come from the left rear although the scene contains no internal light source. Other lines of work have their own restrictions. Many methods address only portraits or isolated objects. Scribble-based control of scene lighting lacks precision and has been limited to indoor scenes. Outdoor full-image relighting methods either require surface normals as input or rely on directional lighting models that generalize poorly to indoor scenes. A recent generative approach that simulates both inverse rendering (recovering intrinsic properties such as albedo, surface normals, roughness and metallicity from an image) and forward rendering conditions the forward step on irradiance, which makes precise lighting control challenging, and is limited to indoor scenes. Intrinsic decomposition methods are themselves hampered by the difficulty of acquiring large-scale training data and are mostly designed for specific scenarios, such as indoor scenes or single objects. These limitations point to the lack of a physically interpretable representation of the scene in current relighting methods and to the inherent limitations of data-driven priors, both of which stand in the way of controllable and physically plausible full-image relighting.

Three major challenges follow. First, data with diverse and complex scene illumination are hard to acquire: obtaining high-quality images of full scenes under diverse and controlled lighting conditions is resource-intensive and technically challenging, and it is infeasible to capture real-world datasets that show the same scene under multiple lighting conditions. Existing datasets that provide intrinsic components focus mainly on indoor scenes and do not render images under varying lighting conditions. Second, ensuring physical plausibility is difficult, as purely data-driven approaches often generate results that violate basic light transport principles. Third, limited data-driven priors restrict generalizability, leading to poor robustness to unseen materials, lighting conditions and realistic scene compositions, and existing attempts to bridge the gap between synthetic training data and real images for full-scene relighting remain suboptimal. Full scenes add a further difficulty: self-luminous objects and built-in light sources, such as light coming through windows, interfere with controlling the direction and intensity of the new lighting while keeping the background consistent.

This raises the following questions. How can an entire image, objects and scene together, indoor or outdoor, be relit under a user-specified lighting condition with precise control of light direction and intensity, while preserving the albedo and material appearance of its surfaces, the content and consistency of the background, and the lighting of self-luminous elements? How can a relighting model be made to respect basic light transport, so that shading, highlights and shadows follow the new lighting across a wide variety of materials? And how can such a model generalize to real-world images with unseen materials, lighting conditions and scene compositions when paired data under controlled lighting are scarce and real captures of the same scene under multiple lightings are infeasible?

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: view-dependent radiance decomposition
PROPOSAL: Investigate the potential of view-dependent radiance decomposition for physically plausible full-image relighting. We'll apply a novel decomposition method, focusing on recovering the high-frequency components of radiance with respect to view angles, and assess its performance on synthetic datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare with current state-of-the-art full-image relighting methods and our own simplified radiance decomposition approach without view-dependent components.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This decomposition method can improve full-image relighting accuracy, especially in scenes with complex environments and non-diffuse materials. However, it may struggle with cases where objects have strong view-independent light transport properties.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: intrinsic image decomposition with boundary handling
PROPOSAL: Design an intrinsic image decomposition method that explicitly handles scene boundaries to allow for accurate training and realistic rendering. We'll apply a boundary-aware physics-based model, including Fresnel terms for surface normals and conductance models for lighting, to retrieve intrinsic components with sharper edges and reduced artifacts.
CONTROLS: Compare with current intrinsic image decomposition methods that neglect or approximate boundary conditions, as well as our own simplified boundary- handling approach using standard convolutional filters.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This boundary- handling model should improve decomposition accuracy, especially at scene boundaries, but may require additional computational resources to handle the increased model complexity.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: multi-scale neural rendering for lighting control
PROPOSAL: Train a multi-scale neural rendering model to generate photorealistic images with user-specified lighting conditions, focusing on precise control of light direction, intensity, and shading while maintaining physical plausibility. We'll test our model on a synthetic dataset with varying lighting conditions and scene complexities.
CONTROLS: Compare with current state-of-the-art full-image relighting methods and ablate the contributions of different model components (e.g., multi-scale architecture, physics-based rendering) to lighting control.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This model should demonstrate robust lighting control and achieve state-of-the-art relighting accuracy, but may require large-scale synthetic training data to capture the desired physical plausibility.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: hybrid radiance decomposition with view-dependent components
PROPOSAL: Revise the initial view-dependent radiance decomposition approach to combine low-frequency radiance with view-dependent high-frequency components, using a multi-resolution network to separate and refine rough and detailed radiance information. This hybrid approach should leverage the strengths of both techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original view-dependent radiance decomposition and additively decompose the improvements from combining the two approaches.
COST: 10 additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This hybrid approach should achieve a better trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency, but requires careful tuning of the multi-resolution network architecture to prevent overfitting or underfitting.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: scene-aware lighting transfer
PROPOSAL: Develop a scene-aware lighting transfer method that analyzes the scene geometry and intrinsic properties to reason about the optimal lighting direction, intensity, and type. We'll train a scene-understanding network to predict these parameters from the intrinsic components and apply them to the scene for context-aware relighting.
CONTROLS: Evaluate our method on both synthetic and real-world scenes, comparing with standard lighting transfer techniques and assessing its ability to preserve scene content and color consistency.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This scene-aware lighting transfer approach should significantly improve the realism and consistency of relighting results, but may struggle with complex or noisy scenes where it's difficult to establish a clear understanding of the scene's intrinsic properties.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation
PROPOSAL: Investigate discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation techniques that can more accurately model the lighting behavior at object boundaries, taking into account the object's albedo, shape, and surrounding environment. We'll apply a Fréchet variant of the Poisson equation to recover a piecewise-continuous lighting solution for each object in the scene.
CONTROLS: Compare with the relighting results from our existing methods, specifically testing the improvement in shading, highlights, and shadows caused by accounting for discontinuities in lighting.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should lead to improved lighting realism at object boundaries, especially for scenes with closely-spaced or complexly-shaped objects. However, the estimation complexity may increase significantly for scenes with many objects or intricate geometry.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: partial-diffuse-specular separation from multi-scale detail
PROPOSAL: Propose a multi-scale separation approach to extract partial, diffuse, and specular components from an image, using a detail refinement and coarsening scheme to improve partial-diffuse-specular separation performance. This is crucial for accurate radiance decomposition and relighting, allowing for more precise modeling of surface reflectance and directional scatter.
CONTROLS: Compare this multi-scale method with standard separation approaches in terms of graininess, adaptivity, and relighting results on various synthetic and real-world datasets, with results reported in a table.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This separation method should enhance the physical plausibility of relighting results by restoring accurate partial-diffuse-specular structure, but may struggle with scenes having complex and multi-scale surface roughness.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: interactively-controllable neural relighting
PROPOSAL: Develop a neural network-based relighting framework that enables real-time, user-interaction-driven control over lighting direction, intensity, and color. We'll introduce a neural representation of relighting parameters that can be modulated by user inputs, facilitating end-user relighting control without requiring extensive domain knowledge or graphics expertise.
CONTROLS: Compare user-interaction accuracy and relighting result quality with those from black-box full-image relighting approaches and investigate the synergies between user interactions and scholar-crafted physics-based relighting.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This interactive method should significantly enhance user experience by providing fine-grained control over relighting but may encounter limitations in extrapolating efficiently beyond the demonstration range, especially with materials that embrace a comprehensive physical representation of dynamic relighting behaviors.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: leveraging real-world relighting validation and synergy 
PROPOSAL: Investigate the potential for real-world relighting and data acquisition synergies in our existing methods, validating their performance in real-world scenes and datasets while also augmenting synthesis-based approaches for real-world-driven full-image relighting models. This real-world focus is essential to providing the physically-grounded formulation needed for accurate data-driven full-image relighting models, known as real-world-driven validation.
CONTROLS: Assess the relighting quality improvement when training models on synthetic scenes that have been validated against real-world data, then testing these improved synth+real-scene methods on unseen real-world scenes (not used in training or during synthesis) and various internal priors.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Incorporating real-world validation should further improve relighting quality and robustness but may require larger-scale datasets and optimizing computational efficiency to outperform faster synthesis-based methods.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: hybrid discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation
PROPOSAL: Revise the discontinuity-sensitive lighting estimation approach by integrating the hybrid radiance decomposition with view-dependent components to leverage the strengths of both in modelling light transport discontinuities, achieving a finer-grain representation and improving accuracy in scenes with complex lighting settings, thus achieving another remarkable trade-off between the complexity of these discontinuity-controlled scenes and the minimal added runtime cost for updates and finer-control analyzers.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the hybrid estimation approach's convergence and accuracy for a wider range of images, dataset sources, and resolutions, with comparison against other highest-rated scene-bound and label-driven estimation-centric synthesis-based approaches to see if improved autonomous controlled synthesis, together with improving measurement-based renderings and meta-anals, aligns to general relighting tasks.
COST: 5 additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This hybrid lighting estimation approach should achieve even greater accuracy and physics-based realism in scene lighting modeling, while still benefiting from improvements and interchange handling, improving practical workflows and tools efficiency in digitally-rendered content or view-based sensory ensemble simulations.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a pivotal technique for advancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models on complex tasks. In reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR), the language model is treated as a policy whose chain of thought is modeled as a sequence of actions, and it is optimized with rewards from an automatic verifier that compares the final answer extracted from each sampled solution with a reference answer. Most RLVR algorithms are on-policy; a widely used example is Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which estimates the advantage of each trajectory by normalizing its reward against a group of trajectories sampled for the same question. On-policy optimization is stable but computationally expensive, because the experience generated during the costly rollout phase is typically discarded after a single gradient update. This not only squanders substantial compute but also forfeits the opportunity for the model to learn from its own earlier successful explorations, which makes training inefficient, can make it unstable, and imposes a bottleneck on scaling RL for reasoning.

Experience replay is a classical RL technique to address this issue: previously collected interactions are stored and reused, which improves sample efficiency, helps stabilize training and accelerates convergence, and prioritized variants emphasize the most informative transitions. It has been argued that AI is entering a period in which experience will become the dominant medium of improvement. A non-trivial challenge, however, lies in how to exploit past experiences according to their differing value and how to manage the replay process over the course of learning, and efficient experience replay mechanisms remain largely underexplored in RLVR for large reasoning models. Recent off-policy approaches incorporate historical or external data, for example by mixing expert demonstrations with on-policy updates or by deriving direct off-policy update rules, and recent replay methods for reasoning models reuse successful trajectories collected early in training or produced by a well-trained policy. However, the impact of the quality of the data within the replay buffer remains underexplored, and several replay methods do not correct for the distribution mismatch between the past policy that generated a stored trajectory and the current policy.

Several features make the problem challenging. An experience in RLVR consists of a question together with the trajectories sampled for it, and it is unclear whether all questions are equally useful for training, or whether all successful trajectories for a question are equally worth reusing. Because the verifiable reward only checks the final answer, a successful trajectory may still rest on invalid reasoning. The usefulness of a stored experience may also change as the model's capabilities evolve during training. Finally, reusing past successes pushes the policy toward exploitation, while prior work shows that aggressively minimizing policy entropy can cause collapse, so the reuse of experience has to be balanced against continued exploration.

This raises the following research questions. What makes a reasoning experience valuable for RLVR optimization, and which measurable properties of a question and of its trajectories, available during training, indicate that value? Given the vast quantity of experience collected during rollouts, how can a reasoning model effectively exploit its own stream of experience, deciding which past experiences to keep, prioritize and replay, how to combine them with fresh on-policy exploration, and how to account for the policy mismatch of replayed trajectories, so as to maximize learning toward scaling RL compute for large reasoning models and to improve reasoning performance, sample efficiency and training stability relative to standard on-policy RLVR?

Large language models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress across a wide range of natural language understanding and generation tasks, but their massive parameter counts demand prohibitively large computational and memory resources for both training and deployment. Even in settings with a reasonable amount of compute, training or fine-tuning such models remains challenging.

One promising way to reduce the computational burden of fine-tuning is low-precision floating-point (FP) arithmetic such as FP8. Modern accelerators (e.g., NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, AMD CDNA 3, Google TPUs) increasingly support low-precision FP arithmetic natively, and FP8 can theoretically double the throughput of FP16 matrix multiplication. Because FP8 formats (such as E4M3 or E5M2) have a narrow representable range, a higher-precision tensor must first be scaled by a per-tensor factor obtained from a max-reduction over its absolute values, and then scaled element-wise and rounded, before the low-precision multiplication can run. This quantization overhead is memory-bound and grows quadratically with matrix size, whereas the cost of matrix multiplication grows cubically. As a consequence, FP8 is known to accelerate mainly large-dimensional matrix multiplications (empirically, when each matrix dimension exceeds roughly 4K elements), while small-dimensional computations can even suffer an unexpected slowdown.

These overheads are especially critical for low-rank adaptation (LoRA), a widely used approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning. LoRA keeps the pretrained weights frozen and inserts small trainable low-rank matrices (adapters) that capture task-specific knowledge, greatly reducing memory cost by training few parameters. For such small-dimensional matrices, the overhead of FP8 quantization can outweigh the gains of FP8 multiplication, and the separate forward and backward paths of the adapters add further quantization operations at every iteration. Yet fast LoRA fine-tuning matters in practice: many applications require training numerous adapters, for example one adapter per user for personalized recommendation or personalized alignment from human feedback, task-specific adapters for multi-task learning and mixtures of LoRA experts, adapters for different domains, multilingual summarization, and rapid updates in dynamic, user-specific environments. Efficiently accelerating LoRA fine-tuning is therefore essential for timely, scalable and cost-effective adaptation of LLMs under practical computational constraints.

Existing lines of work leave this gap open. Quantized LoRA methods (such as QLoRA with 4-bit NormalFloat weights, QA-LoRA with group-wise INT4 weights, and follow-ups that refine the quantization with integer linear programming, SVD-based adapter initialization, dynamic rank allocation or information recovery) compress the frozen backbone through weight-only quantization. They focus on memory efficiency rather than fine-tuning speed: the added quantization and dequantization often make them slower than standard LoRA, and weight-only quantization cannot exploit hardware acceleration of low-precision matrix multiplication. Conversely, FP8 training methods (hybrid E4M3/E5M2 formats, mixed-precision FP8 training with high-precision master weights, studies of large-scale FP8 stability and outliers, unit scaling) are designed for the large-dimensional matrices of full LLM training, not for the small matrices that characterize LoRA.

This raises the following questions. How large is the quantization overhead when FP8 arithmetic is applied to LoRA fine-tuning, which parts of the computation does it come from, and does it persist across typical adapter ranks? Can LoRA fine-tuning be organized so that it genuinely benefits from native FP8 arithmetic, delivering real end-to-end speedups over existing quantized LoRA methods, while retaining the memory savings that make LoRA attractive and reaching accuracy comparable to existing quantized LoRA fine-tuning?

Facial rigging aims to make a static neutral facial mesh animatable by defining a set of controllable deformations, typically represented either as blendshape rigs driven by activated action units in systems based on the Facial Action Coding System (FACS), or as skeletal rigs driven by joint positions. Whereas full-body auto-rigging usually follows a two-step pipeline of skeleton construction and skinning, facial rigs are often anatomically inspired and implemented with FACS blendshapes. In a linear FACS blendshape rig, each blendshape is a vertex offset from the neutral mesh corresponding to one action unit, i.e. a specific muscle movement such as "Right Eye Close", and a complex expression is obtained by adding the weighted offsets of the activated blendshapes to the neutral mesh. Rigging is an essential step for creative AI, bringing digital avatars to life by enabling expressive and realistic facial movements across a wide range of applications. However, creating a facial rig is laborious and expensive, often requiring skilled artists tens of hours to complete a single asset. Methods that transfer expressions from 2D images or videos to 3D avatars do not remove this bottleneck, since they assume that the avatar already has a rig.

Existing facial auto-rigging methods typically transfer a complete set of blendshapes from a predefined template mesh to a neutral target mesh, which often requires dense correspondences or a mesh topology shared by the template and the target. More recent approaches build transferable latent spaces between faces or use triangulation-agnostic networks to bypass these limitations, but they still require a template blendshape rig, which can compromise accuracy when the template and target shapes differ substantially. Only one prior approach, NFR, can directly rig facial meshes from explicitly controllable FACS parameters without relying on a template, and it has so far been demonstrated primarily on humanoid heads. Furthermore, existing approaches, NFR included, have yet to accommodate meshes with multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs or teeth, which limits their ability to animate highly expressive avatars: an "eye look-down" pose, for example, is difficult to reproduce if the mesh lacks eyeballs.

Learning such a rigging model also raises a data problem. Accurate 3D supervision requires neutral meshes paired with complete rigs made by artists, and because manual rigging is so costly such rigged examples are scarce; a model trained solely on them is likely to generalize poorly to the wide variety of facial shapes, styles and topologies met in practice.

The problem is therefore to automatically turn a single static neutral facial mesh into an expressive rig controllable by FACS parameters (i) without relying on predefined template blendshapes, so that target meshes need not closely resemble a template; (ii) for in-the-wild meshes with varying topologies and shapes, including both humanoid and non-humanoid heads; and (iii) for meshes made of multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs and teeth, which must move coherently with the rest of the face. How can such a rigging system be built, and how can it be trained to generalize across this diversity when only a limited number of rigged meshes is available as 3D ground truth?

Many supervised learning algorithms rely on the assumption that training and test data are drawn from the same underlying distribution. In real-world applications this assumption is often violated because of environmental changes, sampling biases or temporal dynamics, which create distribution shifts between training and deployment environments. Such mismatches can cause significant performance degradation and pose a fundamental challenge to reliable generalization in practice.

Among the challenges posed by distribution shifts, this problem concerns unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), with a focus on classification. In UDA, one is given labeled data from a source domain and unlabeled data from a target domain whose distributions are related but not necessarily identical. The discrepancy may come from the marginal distribution of the input, from the conditional distribution of labels given inputs, or from both. The goal is to use the labeled source data and the unlabeled target data to build a predictive model with low risk on the target domain. The most naive baseline, empirical risk minimization on the source data, can perform poorly on the target domain when the two distributions differ.

Two representative families of UDA methods are distribution alignment, which reduces the discrepancy between the source and target domains either in the data space or in a feature space, and pseudo-labeling, which refines target predictions using a source-trained model in the spirit of self-training. Despite their popularity, both families often face practical limitations in two common scenarios. The first is when the amount of unlabeled target data is limited: alignment estimates can then become unreliable and pseudo-labels noisy, which can lead to poor generalization, and the empirical distribution of a small or imbalanced target sample may be a poor estimate of the true target input distribution that fails to capture the diversity of the target domain. The second is when the source data contain spurious correlations, for example when irrelevant features such as background or color are strongly associated with labels: models then tend to rely on these shortcuts, which do not transfer to the target domain and ultimately degrade performance. Alignment-based methods can fail in this situation, and approaches that try to disentangle causal and spurious features with unlabeled target data, through counterfactual consistency, generative interventions or self-training refinements, often rely on strong structural assumptions or are highly sensitive to the quality of the initial pseudo-labels, which makes them fragile when target data are scarce or imbalanced.

Distributionally robust optimization is another line of work on distribution shift: instead of the average loss on the training distribution, it minimizes the worst-case expected loss over an ambiguity set of plausible distributions. Constructing a suitable ambiguity set is the central difficulty, and the inner worst case must remain computationally tractable. Common choices, small Wasserstein or f-divergence balls around the empirical source distribution, give robustness to minor perturbations but are less suitable for structured shifts such as subpopulation shift, where the target contains the same subpopulations as the source with different mixing weights and can therefore lie far from the source in standard distances. Formulations designed for such mixture shifts, such as group distributionally robust optimization, typically assume access to group labels and do not explicitly use unlabeled target data to improve target prediction.

The problem is therefore how to learn, from labeled data coming from one or several source domains and unlabeled target data, a classifier that generalizes to the target domain when unlabeled target data are extremely scarce and when spurious correlations dominate the source domain, without group labels and with a computationally tractable training procedure. How can a learner remain reliable when the few available unlabeled target inputs give a poor picture of the target input distribution, and how can it avoid relying on spurious source features that do not hold in the target domain?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: dimensionality reduction for distribution alignment
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of using dimensionality reduction techniques (e.g., PCA, t-SNE) to align the feature spaces of the source and target domains in UDA. Specifically, we will apply dimensionality reduction to the labeled source data and test its transferability to the unlabeled target data, exploring combinations of techniques and hyperparameter settings. We will use the Ladybug and CIFAR-10 datasets for digit recognition, as well as the CelebA dataset for facial attribute classification.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Empirical risk minimization on the source data; Baseline 2: State-of-the-art UDA methods (e.g.,/domain adversarial neural network, adversarial deep domain confusion network). Ablation 1: No dimensionality reduction; Ablation 2: Using dimensionality reduction on target data alone. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours ( exploratory experiments with small models)
PREDICTION: We anticipate that dimensionality reduction will improve alignment, especially when combined with other methods (e.g., adversarial training), but may not be sufficient to handle extreme distribution shifts or spurious correlations. The combination of techniques and hyperparameter tuning is likely crucial for best performance.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: self-training with robust source classifiers
PROPOSAL: Modify the self-training paradigm to improve robustness against spurious correlations in the source data. Specifically, we will use robust source classifiers trained with input and label perturbations, such as adversarial training and data augmentation. We will also use these robust source models to generate pseudo-labels for the target data. Smoothed decision-making is critical to avoiding abrupt and potentially dangerous large changes of actions in many online optimization problems, such as energy production scheduling in power grids, object tracking, motion planning, and server capacity provisioning in data centers. Mathematically, action smoothness can be achieved by adding to the optimization objective a switching cost that penalizes temporal changes in actions. The switching cost equips the online objective with a (finite) memory of previous actions and creates substantial algorithmic challenges; smoothed online optimization has therefore received a great deal of attention over the last decade, with a quickly growing list of algorithms offering worst-case performance guarantees in adversarial and stochastic settings and under various extensions.

At the same time, long-term fairness is a crucial consideration in many online optimization problems that can profoundly affect individuals' well-being and social welfare. Sequential allocation of social goods to different individuals or groups must be fair and free of discrimination; the surging environmental costs of geographically distributed AI data centers must be fairly distributed across regions, as repeatedly called for by various organizations and government agencies; and AI model performance and resource provisioning must promote social fairness without adversely affecting disadvantaged individuals or groups. If not designed with fairness in mind, online algorithms can perpetuate or even exacerbate societal biases, disproportionately affect certain groups or individuals, and amplify already widening socioeconomic disparities. Fairness in online optimization is therefore not only an ethical concern but also a necessity for broader social responsibility.

Incorporating a long-term fairness regularizer into the objective can effectively promote fairness in online optimization by mitigating implicit or explicit biases, but it creates significant challenges. The regularizer depends on the entire trajectory of actions and contexts and can only be evaluated at the end of an episode, with complete information, whereas a switching cost can be assessed step by step. Online decision-makers react to sequentially revealed information and tend to prioritize immediate cost reduction, potentially neglecting the long-term consequences of their sequence of decisions.

Recent research has started to explore fairness and long-term constraints in online problems such as online resource allocation, using primal-dual techniques. A major limitation of current fair online algorithms, however, is their reliance on the assumption that per-round objective functions are independent of historical actions, an assumption that plays a pivotal role in both their algorithm design and their theoretical analysis. In a simple resource allocation problem, for instance, the maximum allowable action at a given time may depend on past decisions through the remaining budget, but the reward at that time is assumed to depend only on the current decision. Such methods fall short when the per-round objective is directly affected by previous irrevocable actions, as it is with switching costs; in that case an online algorithm and an offline benchmark face different per-round objectives because their action sequences differ, which complicates any direct comparison of their costs. Conversely, the rich literature on smoothed online optimization does not handle a regularizer that is evaluated over the whole horizon. Fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization with switching costs is thus a new and challenging setting that appears not to have been considered in the literature.

Formally, consider an episode of T rounds. At each round t, an agent observes a (potentially adversarially chosen) non-negative hitting cost function f_t and a matrix A_t that maps its action into an M-dimensional cost vector, each dimension corresponding to an entity for which fairness must be taken into account, and then chooses an irrevocable action x_t without knowing future information. It incurs the hitting cost f_t(x_t) and a switching cost d(x_t, x_{t-1}), for instance a scaled squared Euclidean distance between consecutive actions. Fairness is captured by a long-term cost g, convex and Lipschitz, applied to the episode average of the cost vectors; a well-known choice is an l_p norm, which prioritizes reducing the highest costs borne by disadvantaged entities and recovers min-max fairness as p tends to infinity. The goal is to minimize $\frac{1}{T}\big(\sum_{t=1}^{T} f_t(x_t) + \sum_{t=1}^{T} d(x_t, x_{t-1})\big) + g\big(\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} A_t x_t\big)$.

This setting raises several questions. First, how hard is the long-term fairness regularizer intrinsically? Online algorithms are commonly evaluated by their regret or by their competitive ratio against a dynamic offline benchmark which, unlike a static benchmark restricted to a single fixed action, can adapt its action sequence over time with full knowledge of the context. A finite competitive ratio is attainable for online optimization with switching costs, but whether any online algorithm can achieve sublinear regret or a finite competitive ratio against the dynamic offline optimum in the presence of a long-term fairness regularizer, even without switching costs, remains an open question; prior work has only conjectured that finite performance might be impossible in similar settings. Second, if such guarantees are out of reach, against what kind of benchmark can meaningful, practically relevant performance guarantees be established? Third, how can an online algorithm reconcile the tension between minimizing the hitting cost, the switching cost and the long-term fairness cost with provable worst-case guarantees, when the per-round objective carries a memory of previous actions, and how does the long-term fairness regularizer affect such guarantees?

Geometry reconstruction is a fundamental problem that enables a wide range of applications in fields such as virtual reality and robotics. In recent years, neural reconstruction methods have gained significant attention; a key advantage of these methods is their ability to represent the geometry of a scene continuously, which can help in many downstream tasks. However, vision-based sensors often struggle in adverse weather conditions, or even become completely unusable when objects are obscured by occlusions.

Radio frequency (RF) sensing, specifically wireless millimeter-wave (mmWave) sensing, can see through occlusions, remains robust under challenging visibility conditions and, unlike X-rays, is not dangerous to humans, making it a compelling alternative for 3D reconstruction. This could open up many applications, for example checking whether the items inside a box are the correct items, are damaged, or pose a threat, without ever opening the box. On the other hand, mmWave resolution is extremely low compared to vision: a single radar image provides far less visual context than a camera image, which makes it hard to extract a 3D reconstruction from one radar image alone. Some prior RF systems have performed 3D point cloud reconstruction or human body tracking by leveraging movement or by emulating larger antenna apertures, but the recovered point clouds are still too sparse and noisy to reliably recover detailed geometry; through-wall human sensing relies on human motion to combat specularity, and deep learning on mmWave radar data has mostly targeted self-driving scenarios, where image resolution matters little. Other works have proposed neural implicit representations for RF sensing, aiming to concentrate scene information out of heavy noise through neural optimization, but these systems are designed for large-scale environments such as streets or satellite imagery and are far from achieving millimeter-level precision. When objects are close to the radar, the propagation characteristics of RF signals change dramatically: incoming waves can no longer be approximated as planar, so processing methods designed for large-scale scenes, such as beamforming, introduce a considerable amount of distortion and noise, often exceeding the noise acceptable for gradient descent and leading to unstable optimization. Existing neural RF reconstruction work is thus either limited to far-range scenes or, for individual objects, evaluated only on simulated data, which for wireless signals cannot come close to representing the complexity of real-world measurements. Meanwhile, the multi-view reconstruction and inverse rendering methods of computer vision (multi-view stereo, neural radiance fields, Gaussian splatting, neural implicit surfaces, physically based inverse rendering) are all derived from RGB images and are not easily transferable to mmWave data: even lensless RGB images can be mapped back to a lens-based imaging model without altering the underlying ray physics, whereas for RF signals such a transformation is fundamentally invalid.

The open problem is therefore to overcome the fundamental dilemma between massive RF noise in the input and the reconstruction of complete, high-resolution, millimeter-level 3D surface geometry of near-range objects, including objects hidden behind occlusions. This is not straightforward, because inferring surface geometry from RF signals differs fundamentally from image-based reconstruction in three main ways. First, wireless systems lack a lens-based imaging model: whereas lenses filter and focus the relevant light rays, radar antenna arrays perform lensless imaging and capture all incoming RF signals without directional filtering, which leads to low signal-to-noise ratios because irrelevant signals cannot be excluded. Second, RF signals and visible light propagate differently: visible light is predominantly scattered diffusely by surfaces, whereas RF signals, whose wavelengths are on the order of millimeters, are dominated by specular reflections, so volumetric rendering techniques designed for scattering-based vision sensors are unsuitable for RF imaging. Third, physically modeling lensless RF measurements is computationally expensive: whereas lens-based rendering samples along 1D rays, modeling what each antenna receives requires accounting for contributions from the full 3D space, leading to cubic complexity that makes naive implementations intractable at millimeter resolution.

How can accurate, millimeter-level 3D geometry of near-range objects be reconstructed from noisy real-world RF measurements, in line of sight and through occlusions, despite lensless imaging, specular reflections and the cost of modeling signal contributions from the full 3D space?
