Visual document retrieval is the task of returning relevant documents, typically PDFs containing figures, tables, and other visual elements, in response to a textual query. Neural retrieval pipelines for this task often follow a text-centric approach: source documents are converted into textual chunks with optical character recognition or vision-language models, and an index is then built with semantic text encoders. An alternative, vision-centric approach relies instead on multimodal encoders. Building on the ColBERT late-interaction approach, ColPali-based encoders operate directly on page images, matching textual query tokens to image patches and producing multi-vector embeddings of images and queries.

Although this vision-centric paradigm achieves state-of-the-art results on public visual document retrieval benchmarks, open challenges remain. First, in pursuit of state-of-the-art performance, recent late-interaction multimodal retrievers have massively scaled the length and dimensionality of their query and document representations. This incurs substantial latency and storage overhead and hinders efficient, scalable deployment in real-world pipelines; one recent retriever, for example, represents each document page with about 10 MB of memory, three orders of magnitude more than a single-vector dense retriever. Second, matching textual queries to textually rich documents with a purely vision-centric model may be limited by the substantial modality gap that modern vision-language models still exhibit. These limitations motivate exploring complementary ways of improving multimodal encoders, rather than relying only on ever-larger monolithic models.

A long-standing idea in neural retrieval is hybrid retrieval, in which the outputs of different retrievers are aggregated, at the level of document ranks or of query-document similarity scores, to obtain the final list of retrieved documents. Hybrid retrieval (or hybrid search) most commonly refers to combining a neural semantic text retriever with a sparse lexical representation such as BM25; more broadly, it reflects the notion that models relying on different types of representations capture complementary aspects of the data, which can be leveraged to boost overall performance. Dense text retrievers typically have low online latency and a small storage footprint, and they provide a uni-modal signal between the query and the document representation. Combining text and image encoders therefore emerges as a natural candidate for enhancing a multimodal retrieval system.

However, standard hybrid retrieval methods take a rather coarse-grained view of each retriever: because they reduce every query-document pair to a single rank or score, they cannot exploit the rich query-document interactions within each model's representation space. Aggregating at the level of the representations themselves would carry the richest information, but at query time it is hindered by heterogeneity: encoders may use a single vector or many vectors per query and document, with differing dimensionalities and scales, and any aggregation must respect strict latency and memory budgets without access to supervision. A further difficulty is that the complementary retriever may be lightweight and even weaker on the task than the primary one, and it is unclear whether such a signal can help at all.

This raises the following questions. Can the paradigm of hybrid retrieval complement modern vision-centric multimodal encoders, and in particular, can a lightweight dense text retriever enhance a stronger vision-centric retriever? How can the signals of two heterogeneous retrievers be combined at query time so as to exploit the rich interactions within their representation spaces, rather than only their final ranks or scores, while remaining architecture-agnostic (applicable to both single-vector and multi-vector models), lightweight, and practical? And can such a combination improve the trade-off between retrieval quality, online latency, and index memory compared with scaling up the representations of a single model?

enonce:
Multimodal learning has become a cornerstone of many real-world applications, such as autonomous perception, medical diagnosis, and human-computer interaction. By integrating information from multiple sources, such as vision, audio, and text, multimodal systems aim to improve performance and generalization. However, multimodal data often exhibit a significant imbalance between modalities due to noise, lack of information, or sensor heterogeneity, so that a dominant modality may overshadow the others and hinder the learning of weak modalities. Unimodal prediction accuracy is widely used to detect modality imbalance; it is a simple and effective metric, but it is inherently sensitive to noise and perturbations. This vulnerability often leads to fragile performance in practice and limits the reliability of accuracy-based definitions of strong and weak modalities in real-world deployments.

Modality imbalance arises in early, intermediate, and late fusion alike. Late fusion, also known as decision-level fusion, combines the outputs (logits) of modality-specific models, either with equal weights (static late fusion) or with weights that vary across samples (dynamic late fusion). It remains one of the most widely adopted paradigms because of its modular design, interpretability, and strong compatibility with unimodal pre-trained models. Yet, lacking feature-level compensation or cross-modal interaction, late fusion tends to amplify the influence of strong modalities while weakening the role of lower-quality ones, so that predictions from disadvantaged modalities often carry little weight or even introduce noise into the final decision. A large body of work has attempted to alleviate this imbalance by enhancing the predictive performance of weak modalities, for example by aggregating independently trained modality-specific classifiers, confidence-based weighting, modality dropout or gating, adaptive ensembling, or knowledge distillation from dominant modalities.

While effective in certain scenarios, these methods often implicitly aim to align weak modalities with dominant ones in terms of prediction accuracy, attempting to bring them closer to their stronger counterparts. Such over-alignment raises several concerns: (1) it may suppress the distinct and complementary information encoded in weak modalities, causing modality-specific information loss; (2) it risks error propagation, as the dominant modality's errors are amplified when weak modalities follow them blindly; and (3) through excessive conformity, weak modalities may lose the predictive advantages they originally held on some samples.

Robustness makes the issue more pressing. Multimodal cooperation is inherently sensitive to perturbations such as data noise, label noise, and incomplete modalities, because modalities are heterogeneous and vary in reliability in real-world conditions. Prior studies have highlighted that the robustness of a multimodal system can be bottlenecked by a single weak modality, revealing a strong link between modality imbalance and overall system reliability. Existing work addresses robustness by incorporating uncertainty modeling, designing robustness-aware fusion strategies, quantifying multimodal robustness with dedicated evaluation metrics, or connecting it with generalization error bounds. However, most of these approaches emphasize prediction-consistency modeling and pay little attention to the instability of the decision space, that is, a model's high sensitivity to input perturbations near the decision boundary, where even minor changes can cause large shifts in prediction; they also tend to require more complex architectures with limited generalizability across tasks with different class granularity.

This raises several questions. How can a dominant modality help a weak modality within a decision-level fusion system without forcing it to conform, so that the weak modality keeps its unique, complementary information and does not inherit the dominant modality's errors? Given that judging modality strength by unimodal accuracy or confidence is itself fragile under noise, how can one reliably determine which modality is dominant and which is weak? How do the predictions of the individual modalities determine the robustness of the fused decision to input perturbations, and can a remedy for modality imbalance come with a theoretical guarantee on that robustness? Finally, can such a remedy both narrow the performance gap between modalities and make the fused prediction more reliable under noisy and imbalanced conditions?

Diffusion models have recently demonstrated remarkable capabilities in synthesizing high-quality images, significantly surpassing earlier generative approaches such as generative adversarial networks and variational autoencoders. Despite their impressive fidelity, deploying diffusion models in realistic cloud-to-user applications introduces a fundamental bottleneck: transmission bandwidth. A standard diffusion model produces a high-fidelity image by performing a fixed number of denoising steps, regardless of downstream transmission limitations. In conventional scenarios, the generated images then undergo aggressive lossy compression before transmission to accommodate the limited bandwidth. This cascaded approach, high-quality generation followed by subsequent compression, not only incurs redundant computational overhead, since computation is spent on details that are later discarded, but also significantly degrades perceptual quality, as the compression process often erases the intricate textures and fine details carefully constructed by the diffusion model.

This motivates a critical question: can bandwidth-awareness be integrated directly into the diffusion generation process, so that the quality of the generated image is adapted to the available bandwidth, avoiding the inefficiency and perceptual quality loss associated with post-generation compression? Ideally, such a generator would meet a user-specified bitrate budget, avoid compression-induced artifacts and redundant computation, and offer fine-grained, dynamic control over image quality according to real-time bandwidth conditions in practical cloud-to-user deployments.

The question is not straightforward. During sampling, diffusion models progressively refine coarse structures into detailed, realistic textures through iterative denoising steps, so, intuitively, terminating the process early would yield simpler, lower-detail images suited to constrained bandwidth. However, naively reducing the number of diffusion steps typically produces suboptimal visual quality: models trained for complete denoising trajectories are not optimized for early termination, which leads to visual artifacts and poor perceptual coherence.

Existing lines of work address only parts of this problem. A large body of work accelerates diffusion sampling, through deterministic samplers that need fewer inference steps, numerical solvers inspired by ordinary differential equations, distillation of slow teacher models into faster students, adaptive step-size selection, latent-space compression, non-uniform step skipping, dynamic network pruning, predictors of the minimal number of denoising steps, and adaptive inference trajectories. These methods reduce the cost of sampling while preserving generation quality, but they are not designed to control the bitrate of the generated image. Conditional and controllable diffusion models, from classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance to latent diffusion and region-based conditioning for interactive editing, allow flexible control over attributes of the generated content, but they do not directly address bandwidth constraints. How to make a diffusion model generate images that respect a specified bandwidth budget while preserving perceptual quality and avoiding wasted computation therefore remains an open problem.

Predicting the intermediate trajectories between an initial and a target distribution is a central problem in generative modeling. Tasks such as crowd navigation or modeling cell-state transitions under perturbation involve learning a transport map between two empirically observed endpoint distributions, rather than from the noisy prior required by denoising diffusion and flow matching. The Schrödinger bridge problem seeks an optimal stochastic map between a pair of endpoint distributions that minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence to an underlying reference process. Schrödinger bridge matching solves this problem by learning a drift field that matches a mixture of conditional stochastic bridges between endpoint pairs, and generalized Schrödinger bridge formulations add a non-linear state cost, interpretable as the potential energy of the system, to describe systems whose optimal dynamics are not captured by the standard squared-Euclidean cost of entropic optimal transport.

These approaches have important limitations. They typically assume conservation of mass from the initial to the target distribution, which fails to capture dynamical population behaviors such as the growth and destruction of mass that are common in single-cell population data. They also model a single stochastic path: samples are transported from the initial distribution to the target through independent stochastic trajectories, without accounting for branching dynamics, so these methods are inherently limited to unimodal transitions and cannot capture branched or divergent evolution from a common origin to multiple distinct modes. When a system follows a branched trajectory that diverges toward several target modes, approximating the multi-modal target by simulating many independent particles is susceptible to mode collapse, with particles concentrating on dominant high-density modes or traversing only low-energy intermediate paths. Even when particles do reach several modes, counting where they end up gives only an indirect estimate of how mass splits across trajectories: it neither describes how mass is distributed over time nor reveals when the population begins to diverge toward different targets.

Yet branching is central to many real-world systems. When a homogeneous cell population undergoes a perturbation such as a gene knockout or a drug treatment, it frequently undergoes fate bifurcation, splitting into multiple phenotypically distinct outcomes or committing to divergent cell fates. Such trajectories are observable in single-cell RNA sequencing data, where each subpopulation evolves independently and grows or contracts along its trajectory toward a distinct terminal state. Predicting how cell states change after a perturbation is a crucial problem for therapeutic design, but the intermediate states between the unperturbed and perturbed populations are usually unknown, and intermediate snapshots are often sparse or unavailable. Related work leaves this gap open. Branched dynamics have been explored for optimal transport and Brownian motion, but matching one initial distribution to multiple terminal distributions through stochastic bridges has not been explicitly formulated; branching Brownian motion, for instance, describes particles that proliferate in number rather than a fixed population whose mass divides among distinct trajectories with their own terminal states. Some unbalanced transport methods that model growth rely on reconstruction losses on observed intermediate snapshots and fail to learn meaningful trajectories when these snapshots are unavailable, and existing models of perturbation responses either predict only the terminal perturbed state or model a single unimodal trajectory between one pair of boundary distributions.

This raises the following questions. Given samples from an initial population and from a terminal population that has split into several distinct modes, each holding a known share of the total mass, how can one learn a set of energy-minimizing stochastic bridges that represent the divergence of the population from a common origin into multiple distinct terminal states? How can such a model determine when and where branching occurs, and how mass is redistributed among branches over time, so that each terminal mode receives its observed share while trajectories follow low-energy paths under a task-specific state cost? And can such branched dynamics be recovered from initial and terminal snapshots alone, without intermediate-time supervision and without the mode collapse that affects single-path bridge matching?

Understanding how a scene has changed and forecasting how it will look next from Satellite Image Time Series (SITS) is fundamental to many critical applications, yet it poses a profound challenge: predicting the future requires a deep understanding of past change. Two tasks are central. In temporal change description, given a sequence of temporally ordered satellite images of the same area, the goal is to generate a natural-language description that accurately summarizes the key dynamic changes that occurred over the observation period, such as urban expansion or agricultural cycles; this requires comprehending the temporal evolution and, ideally, the underlying causal narrative of the changes. In future satellite image forecasting, given the same historical sequence, the goal is to generate a plausible image for the next time point. A critical and often overlooked requirement is that the forecast be temporally consistent: the generated changes should be a logical continuation of the trends and dynamics observed in the historical data, not merely a plausible standalone picture.

Although foundation models such as Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and diffusion-based image generators have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their application to this domain remains fragmented and fundamentally limited. On the understanding side, static image captioning ignores temporal context, while existing temporal change description methods lack the semantic depth of MLLMs: they fuse information across images through simple interactions, their long-range temporal reasoning is limited, and they struggle to capture why changes occur. General-purpose MLLMs, even video-capable ones, are not optimized for this setting either: video-centric models are typically tuned for densely sampled frames with fixed, short intervals, whereas consecutive satellite acquisitions are sparse and irregular, with gaps that can span several years. On the generation side, single-image synthesis cannot model evolution, and temporal forecasting approaches struggle with long-term consistency because they do not grasp the semantic drivers of change: their conditioning is typically low-level (e.g., edge maps), based on simple metadata, or limited to text guidance, and it lacks fine-grained temporal semantic interaction, so they can generate what a scene looks like but cannot reason about why it should look that way given its history. As a result, change understanding and future forecasting have been treated as disjointed tasks, even though both are limited by a common bottleneck: modeling long-range temporal dynamics.

This raises several questions. How can a model reason about why changes occurred across a long, irregularly sampled sequence of satellite images, and describe them accurately? How can such an understanding of past change be used to generate what will happen next, so that the forecast is a temporally consistent continuation of the observed trajectory rather than only a realistic-looking image? Can enhancing long-range temporal understanding improve performance on both tasks simultaneously, with the understanding of past change directly informing the forecast? Finally, how can the temporal consistency of a forecast be rigorously evaluated, given that standard image-quality metrics cannot penalize a prediction that is perceptually realistic but inconsistent with historical trends?

Reinforcement learning has been highly effective in many domains, ranging from robotics to gaming and recommender systems. Value-based algorithms such as Deep Q-Networks are a cornerstone of off-policy reinforcement learning and are widely used in discrete action spaces because of their simplicity, training stability, and sample-efficiency. However, they rely on estimating Q-values for individual state-action pairs and require a maximization over the action space, both to derive the greedy policy and to evaluate the best next-state value in the Bellman target. This maximization is straightforward when the actions can be enumerated, but in continuous action spaces evaluating the Q-value over the entire action space becomes computationally infeasible, which has traditionally restricted value-based methods to discrete actions.

In continuous control, actor-critic methods such as DDPG, TD3, and SAC are typically used instead: a critic is trained on off-policy data to estimate Q-values, and an actor (policy) is trained to output actions that maximize the critic. While powerful, these methods often suffer from instability caused by the coupled training of actor and critic, from sensitivity to hyperparameters, and from the difficulty of predicting in high-dimensional action spaces. The additional actor network brings its own hyperparameters, which makes reproducibility a challenge, and adds computational and memory overhead. Moreover, an actor trained by gradient ascent on the Q-function landscape can only find locally optimal actions, which becomes a serious limitation when the Q-function is complex or non-convex, for instance when the action space is constrained so that actions must remain within specific safety bounds. Training several actors to explore different modes of the Q-function alleviates this, but adds computational overhead and inference-time latency, and the actor's parameterization may still be too limited to capture complex optimal actions.

Actor-free, value-based alternatives must instead carry out the maximization over continuous actions themselves, and finding the maximizing action has been their primary bottleneck. Methods that perform this maximization numerically, through mixed-integer programming, the cross-entropy method and other sampling-based or evolutionary search, or gradient ascent on the action, tend either to return suboptimal local maxima or to be computationally impractical, and sampling becomes progressively less efficient as the action dimension grows. Discretizing the action space is effective in low dimensions but does not scale to high-dimensional tasks. Another line of work restricts the functional form of the Q-function so that its maximizer can be obtained directly, for example by assuming that the advantage is quadratic in the action or that the Q-function is convex in the action; such assumptions limit expressivity and practical applicability. Representing the Q-function with a radial basis function output layer makes the best action easier to identify, but introduces an implicit trade-off between how expressive the Q-function can be in modeling multiple local optima and how accurately its maximizing action is recovered.

This raises the question of whether an actor-free, value-based algorithm can efficiently and accurately select optimal actions in continuous action spaces without imposing restrictive assumptions on the shape of the Q-function, while remaining stable to train, robust across diverse tasks, and scalable to high-dimensional action spaces. Such an algorithm would retain the simplicity of Q-learning and avoid the cost and instability of learning a separate actor; it could also avoid the local optima that trap gradient-based actors when the Q-function is highly non-convex, as in constrained action spaces. Can such an approach be made competitive with established actor-critic methods for continuous control, and can it outperform them where gradient-based action maximization struggles?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: maximization-free q-learning with importance sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate an actor-free, value-based algorithm where the Q-function is represented by a neural network, and the maximization over the action space is approximated using importance sampling. For a given state, sample multiple actions from a learned proposal distribution, compute the Q-values for each sampled action, and then use importance weights to correct for the probability of sampling. The proposal distribution is learned using the Q-function's gradients and can be reused across states.
CONTROLS: Compare to Deep Q-Networks with both discrete action spaces (e.g., Atari games) and discretized action spaces (e.g., continuous control with low-dimensional action spaces like Pendulum or Cartpole).
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method can significantly outperform traditional value-based algorithms when the action space is continuous and diverse, as it can explore the action space more efficiently. However, it might struggle with high-dimensional or complex action spaces, where the proposal distribution becomes too coarse.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:invertible rescaling for gradient-based action search
PROPOSAL: Design an invertible transformation for the Q-function's input space, allowing the use of gradient-based methods to search for the maximum. This transformation is learned jointly with the Q-function and needs to satisfy certain properties (e.g., monotonicity, differentiability) that ensure the computation of the maximum remains tractable. A suitable candidate for such transformation could be a normalizing flow model, composed of invertible transformations like affine transformations, permutations, and spline connections.
CONTROLS: Compare to the standard gradient ascent on the Q-function when using discretized action spaces.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: With a well-designed invertible rescaling, this approach can outperform importance sampling in high-dimensional action spaces, as it directly targets the Q-function's extreme points. However, the additional optimization variables and training time required for learning the invertible transformation might make it harder to train and scale.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: invertible rescaling for gradient-based action search
PROPOSAL: In the invertible rescaling model for gradient-based action search, modify the normalizing flow model to incorporate a learnable distribution over the action space, conditioned on the state. This allows the algorithm to adaptively focus on the most promising region of the action space for each state. The condition of the distribution on the state can be learned jointly with the Q-function, using gradient-based methods.
CONTROLS: Compare to the previous version of the invertible rescaling model and contrast with a learned proposal distribution in maximization-free Q-learning.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By conditionally adaptively focusing on the most promising region of the action space, this approach can achieve significant speed-ups and improve accuracy in searching for the maximum, especially in high-dimensional or complex action spaces. However, training the conditional distribution might require more care to avoid mode collapse or vanishing gradients.

Video anomaly analysis is a key application of computer vision for public security. Most early work formulates it as temporal video anomaly detection: marking the segments of a video whose behavior deviates from learned normal patterns, whether with one-class models trained only on normal clips, unsupervised reconstruction or future-frame prediction objectives, or weakly supervised learning from video-level labels. Such detectors have reached high performance on benchmarks, yet they output only frame-wise anomaly scores, without spatial or semantic context, and give no insight into why a segment is abnormal. These limits of interpretability have motivated a shift from temporal detection toward downstream tasks with user-friendly, explainable outputs: spatial video anomaly localization, which predicts bounding boxes around the regions that contain the abnormal activity, and textual video anomaly understanding, which decides whether a video contains an anomaly and produces a human-readable description explaining it, typically with fine-tuned multimodal large language models. Each line of work, however, provides either spatial or textual cues on its own and focuses on a single type of task, so that existing methods offer only an incomplete analysis of video anomalies. A holistic analysis would answer when an anomaly happens, where it is, what it is and why it is abnormal, each of the existing benchmark tasks addressing one of these sub-problems.

A second challenge is the heavy reliance on dataset-specific supervision. Detection and localization models require temporal masks or spatial bounding boxes, yet anomaly definitions vary widely across datasets, so a model tuned on one domain often fails on another and must be retrained for unseen domains or anomaly types. In real-world applications, privacy and security concerns may also make training data unavailable for some sensitive scenes. Open-set detectors that fuse language semantics in order to detect and classify novel anomalies still require task-specific training and give very limited insight into why frames are abnormal. As partial remedies, recent work has explored zero- and few-shot approaches built on frozen vision-language backbones or multimodal large language models, but most of these approaches have a limited task scope and still rely on annotated datasets. The only strictly zero-shot, training-free method addresses temporal detection alone: a frozen vision-language model captions the frames and a prompted large language model converts the captions into frame-wise anomaly scores. It is effective when anomalies are clearly distinguishable from normality but occasionally fails on more complex anomaly types, and it offers neither spatial grounding nor any direct semantic explanation beyond generic captions. Prompt-tuning methods, which optimize textual prompts to guide frozen models, require induction on an annotated training set and pay for it in generality, since the learned prompts tend to be task- or domain-specific. The generality problem is worse still for instruction-tuned multimodal models: they produce rich narrative explanations, but they require extensive annotation and computational resources, lack temporal or spatial coverage, and are optimized to return answers from seen question-answer pairs that describe a closed set of anomaly types.

Multimodal large language models already encode rich visual-semantic priors for commonsense reasoning, which suggests that fine-tuning may not be necessary for every task. This raises the questions addressed here: can temporal detection, spatial localization and textual explanation of video anomalies be delivered together, as one holistic and interpretable analysis, in a strictly zero-shot manner, with frozen pretrained models and without any additional training data, annotations or gradient updates? And can such an analysis remain at least as accurate as existing zero-shot detectors while staying robust across domains whose definitions of anomaly differ?

Modern problem-solving increasingly relies on neural networks, which encode vast amounts of information in their trainable parameters during learning, with applications ranging from computer vision and natural language processing to the natural sciences. While these parameters capture rich knowledge, accessing and interpreting it remains a challenge.

Metanetworks were introduced to analyze and process other neural networks by treating their weights, gradients and sparsity patterns as structured inputs. Early work focused on evaluating the generalization of trained networks and revealing properties of their behavior, commonly by flattening the parameters or extracting statistics from them before feeding them into multi-layer perceptrons. Metanetworks have since been applied to extracting structure from implicit neural representations, learning optimizers, editing models, evaluating policies and enabling Bayesian inference. Designing them nevertheless remains challenging because of the complexity and high dimensionality of the structures they operate on.

A major difficulty is functional equivalence: many distinct parameter configurations realize the same input-output function. Swapping two hidden units of a multi-layer perceptron leaves its input-output mapping unchanged, provided their outgoing connections are permuted accordingly, and for networks with tanh activations the input-output mapping is known to determine the architecture and the weights up to permutations and sign flips. Such identifiability results have been extended to broader classes of multi-layer perceptrons and to convolutional networks, and recent work has characterized the symmetry groups of multihead attention and mixture-of-experts layers, establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for functional equivalence. The parameter space is thus only a proxy for the underlying function class, and the map from parameters to functions is not injective. A metanetwork that relies solely on raw parameters therefore risks overlooking the symmetries of the architecture it processes, and may produce incompatible outputs for two networks that compute exactly the same function.

Building on the permutation symmetry of hidden neurons, permutation-equivariant metanetworks have been developed that account for neuron reordering within hidden layers, and more recent architectures extend beyond permutations by incorporating additional symmetries such as scaling and sign changes. Equivariance (for metanetworks that output weights) or invariance (for metanetworks that output predictions) with respect to a symmetry group of the processed architecture guarantees that different parameterizations of the same function are treated consistently. However, these approaches enforce strict equivariance at the level of individual weights, which imposes rigid constraints on the layers and often leads to sparse, less expressive models. Yet the true goal is not to preserve the weights themselves but the functions they implement, that is, to respect the functional equivalence classes of the parameters. Strict equivariance is a sufficient way to achieve this, but it is not clear that it is necessary.

Relaxed or approximate equivariance has emerged elsewhere in deep learning to handle imperfect symmetries in real-world data, for instance through relaxed convolution weights, soft constraints added to the training objective or relaxed group convolutions, and its bias-variance trade-offs have been analyzed theoretically. These relaxations were, however, developed for symmetries that only approximately hold, and often treat equivariance as something to be approximated. In weight space, by contrast, the symmetries are exact and are precisely what defines functional equivalence, so it is unclear how weight-level equivariance could be loosened without breaking the guarantee that functionally equivalent inputs are processed consistently.

This raises several questions. Is strict equivariance necessary for metanetworks? What is the right requirement for a map acting on weights to preserve functional identity, so that functionally equivalent inputs always yield functionally equivalent outputs, and can a requirement weaker than strict equivariance meet it? Can metanetwork layers satisfying such a requirement be built in a principled, practical and trainable way for the architectures whose weights metanetworks commonly process, such as feedforward, convolutional and multihead attention networks? And would moving beyond strict equivariance in this way give metanetworks a better trade-off between symmetry preservation and representational expressivity in practice?

Conditional image generative models have, in recent years, demonstrated extraordinary capabilities, producing highly realistic images from both textual descriptions and class labels, and they have rapidly evolved from experimental research tools into widely accessible applications. Because they hold considerable promise to produce virtually unlimited amounts of data, researchers have started exploring their use as a source of synthetic training data for downstream machine learning models. However, recent research has revealed that as these models grow in size and capability, they tend to produce images of higher quality, better aligned with human preference, but with diminished diversity, which hinders their utility as synthetic training data generators.

Two families of techniques have been introduced to mitigate the shortcomings of such vanilla synthetic data. Learning-based approaches aim to improve the overall utility of synthetic data by reducing the distribution shift between generated and real samples; they use real data to train or fine-tune parts of existing conditional generative models. Guidance-based sampling methods instead define reward functions that steer the generation process and characterize the utility of generated samples in terms of generation quality or diversity. Yet the implicit or explicit utility functions behind these methods often disregard the potential distribution shift between synthetic and real data, and many guidance methods treat quality, diversity or safety as ends in themselves rather than as means to increase the utility of a synthetic image corpus for training downstream models. Moreover, in-depth analyses of conditional image generative models have highlighted a tension between quality and diversity. This tension becomes more apparent when diversity is defined as the variation among generated samples without reference to any target distribution. Contextualizing the desired diversity through real exemplar data holds the promise of limiting potentially disadvantageous variations in synthetic data.

Using exemplar data at inference time to guide generation is reminiscent of few-shot in-context learning in large language models, where a small number of examples suffices to adapt to new tasks without fine-tuning, and where providing more examples tends to help. In conditional image generation, however, most few-shot approaches require partial model training or fine-tuning, and the use of exemplar data at inference time remains underexplored. One prior inference-time method, Contextualized Vendi Score Guidance (c-VSG), leverages a handful of contextualizing real images to ground the diversity of generations to that of the real data; but, contrary to in-context learning, increasing the number of exemplars did not improve its performance. Meanwhile, fine-tuning with reward feedback has proven successful for improving generation quality, but it has not been tested whether it would also increase diversity given a proper reward.

The problem is therefore how to exploit a small set of real exemplar images to characterize, and jointly improve, both the quality and the diversity of the images produced by off-the-shelf conditional generators with respect to a target real distribution, ideally without fine-tuning the generator. Can strong quality and diversity be achieved this way, and can the benefit grow gracefully as more exemplars become available, unlike existing exemplar-based guidance? How does such an approach compare with training-based ways of using the same few real images? And does improving quality and diversity grounded in real data actually translate into greater utility of the synthetic images as training data for downstream models?

Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a pivotal technique for advancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models on complex tasks. In reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR), the language model is treated as a policy whose chain of thought is modeled as a sequence of actions, and it is optimized with rewards from an automatic verifier that compares the final answer extracted from each sampled solution with a reference answer. Most RLVR algorithms are on-policy; a widely used example is Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which estimates the advantage of each trajectory by normalizing its reward against a group of trajectories sampled for the same question. On-policy optimization is stable but computationally expensive, because the experience generated during the costly rollout phase is typically discarded after a single gradient update. This not only squanders substantial compute but also forfeits the opportunity for the model to learn from its own earlier successful explorations, which makes training inefficient, can make it unstable, and imposes a bottleneck on scaling RL for reasoning.

Experience replay is a classical RL technique to address this issue: previously collected interactions are stored and reused, which improves sample efficiency, helps stabilize training and accelerates convergence, and prioritized variants emphasize the most informative transitions. It has been argued that AI is entering a period in which experience will become the dominant medium of improvement. A non-trivial challenge, however, lies in how to exploit past experiences according to their differing value and how to manage the replay process over the course of learning, and efficient experience replay mechanisms remain largely underexplored in RLVR for large reasoning models. Recent off-policy approaches incorporate historical or external data, for example by mixing expert demonstrations with on-policy updates or by deriving direct off-policy update rules, and recent replay methods for reasoning models reuse successful trajectories collected early in training or produced by a well-trained policy. However, the impact of the quality of the data within the replay buffer remains underexplored, and several replay methods do not correct for the distribution mismatch between the past policy that generated a stored trajectory and the current policy.

Several features make the problem challenging. An experience in RLVR consists of a question together with the trajectories sampled for it, and it is unclear whether all questions are equally useful for training, or whether all successful trajectories for a question are equally worth reusing. Because the verifiable reward only checks the final answer, a successful trajectory may still rest on invalid reasoning. The usefulness of a stored experience may also change as the model's capabilities evolve during training. Finally, reusing past successes pushes the policy toward exploitation, while prior work shows that aggressively minimizing policy entropy can cause collapse, so the reuse of experience has to be balanced against continued exploration.

This raises the following research questions. What makes a reasoning experience valuable for RLVR optimization, and which measurable properties of a question and of its trajectories, available during training, indicate that value? Given the vast quantity of experience collected during rollouts, how can a reasoning model effectively exploit its own stream of experience, deciding which past experiences to keep, prioritize and replay, how to combine them with fresh on-policy exploration, and how to account for the policy mismatch of replayed trajectories, so as to maximize learning toward scaling RL compute for large reasoning models and to improve reasoning performance, sample efficiency and training stability relative to standard on-policy RLVR?

enonce:
Visual localization of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) is essential for applications such as digital-twin modeling, mapping, surveillance, large-area and infrastructure inspection, and search-and-rescue operations, yet it faces challenges that ground-level localization systems do not address. Ground-level approaches benefit from similar viewpoints between query and reference images, whereas aerial applications encounter dramatic perspective differences and must scale to large areas. In many scenarios, these systems require high-precision localization while operating with limited resources, for example without an internet connection or without GNSS/GPS support, which makes large image databases or heavy 3D models impractical.

Current UAV localization algorithms either retrieve the closest match from a database of posed images, which is inaccurate, or rely on 3D models of the scene, which are expensive in memory and computation; in resource-limited settings, such as connectivity-limited environments, this can degrade accuracy. Image retrieval methods based on global descriptors struggle with the large viewpoint and illumination changes of UAV imagery, and even with view synthesis or self-supervised learning their performance drops under extreme perspective shifts, so retrieval alone remains insufficient for accurate 6-DoF localization. Structure-based methods build a 3D model with structure-from-motion, establish 2D-3D correspondences against meshes or dense depth maps, and estimate the pose with PnP solvers inside RANSAC, but such complete 3D models require extensive manual effort to create for each operational area. Most UAV-specific positioning methods estimate only 2-DoF or 3-DoF poses rather than the full 6-DoF pose required by advanced applications. Recent approaches based on level-of-detail (LoD) city models improve storage efficiency, but they still assume unchanged environments, perform poorly in building-sparse areas such as highways, and depend on positioning sensors for initialization.

A compelling alternative is geodata, such as orthographic aerial views (digital orthophotos) and elevation maps (digital surface models). Such data are lightweight, scalable and better suited to low-resource settings, and they are increasingly accessible through free releases from government geoportals, for instance in the European Union; where public access is limited, they can be synthesized with photogrammetric tools. For example, covering an area of approximately 0.265 km² can require a 3D model of around 8 GB, whereas geodata require about 30 times less memory. Surprisingly, no existing UAV localization approach seems to fully leverage these data sources: previous work has not used the combination of orthophotos and elevation models for UAV pose estimation, so no existing method is directly applicable to this scenario. Modern feature matchers (dense, semi-dense, sparse, and geometry-aware) perform robustly in many scenarios, but their effectiveness with orthographic geodata remains unexplored. A major reason for this gap is the absence of aligned cross-domain datasets and of full-pose, paired, large-scale benchmarks designed for localization with these types of geodata. Existing UAV localization datasets provide only partial pose information (2-DoF or 3-DoF), feature predominantly nadir views with limited viewpoint diversity, rely on entirely synthetic environments or synthetically rendered views that introduce domain gaps, or lack integrated geodata; the one concurrent collection that includes orthographic geodata focuses its pose evaluation on 3-DoF and suffers from a misalignment between its low-resolution satellite imagery and its aerial photogrammetry data. Furthermore, visual localization methods often need to solve image retrieval before estimating the pose; because these two steps are coupled, it is difficult to disentangle the contribution of each component to the final error.

The problem is therefore the following: given an orthophoto raster, an elevation raster, and a query UAV image taken from an arbitrary viewpoint, determine the georeferenced 6-DoF pose of the camera (localization) and, optionally, its intrinsic parameters (calibration). The key challenge is bridging two fundamentally different projection models: perspective projection for UAV imagery and orthographic projection for geodata. This difference creates a domain gap that is particularly pronounced in oblique views, where perspective distortion is significant. A second domain gap arises from visual and structural discrepancies between query and reference data caused by differences in acquisition time: reference geodata may have been collected months or years before a flight, so orthophotos differ in appearance (color shifts, illumination variations, seasonal differences) and elevation models differ in geometry (construction changes, vegetation growth, infrastructure evolution). These changes vary unpredictably across locations and seasons, cannot easily be addressed through simple data augmentation or domain adaptation, and cannot be faithfully replicated by synthetic alternatives.

This raises several open questions. Can lightweight 2.5D orthographic geodata serve as the only reference for accurate full 6-DoF UAV pose estimation and camera calibration? Can state-of-the-art feature matchers, designed largely for perspective imagery, bridge the perspective-orthographic gap, especially for oblique viewpoints, and how can the perspective disparity between query and reference be reduced? How difficult is it to recover camera intrinsics from aerial imagery in this setting? And how do characteristics of the reference data, namely temporal visual and structural domain shifts, data resolution, and the covisibility between the query image and the reference area (which depends on imperfect upstream retrieval), affect localization accuracy?

This experiment will help us understand how to leverage uncertainty information to improve the robustness and reliability of UAV localization systems.

enonce:
Transporting mass between probability distributions is a ubiquitous problem in machine learning and beyond. Optimal transport (OT) provides a principled approach to such problems by seeking to minimise the total cost of transportation under a chosen cost function, and computational OT, from Sinkhorn's algorithm to more recent neural approaches, has been applied successfully in domains such as biology and extensively within machine learning. More recently, ideas from the flow-based approaches that have revolutionised generative modelling have been leveraged to solve the entropy-regularised dynamic OT problem known as the Schrödinger bridge (SB): finding the most likely evolution of a population between two prescribed distributions, relative to a reference stochastic process. With a Brownian reference process, the static form of this problem is exactly entropy-regularised OT for the quadratic cost. Flow-based SB solvers offer significant scalability advantages, enabling the approximation of OT maps between high-dimensional continuous datasets such as images. Early flow-based solvers were built on the classical Iterative Proportional Fitting (IPF) scheme, which preserves both marginals only at convergence, requires expensive caching of simulated trajectories and tends to 'forget' the reference measure; such methods have since been superseded by solvers based on the Iterative Markovian Fitting (IMF) scheme, which avoids these issues.

Beyond the standard two-marginal problem, multi-marginal OT seeks a joint coupling over several marginals that minimises a total cost. Tree-structured costs are often considered, as they frequently arise in applications while allowing improved scalability by exploiting the tree structure. In the corresponding tree-structured SB problem, stochastic processes run along the edges of a tree and marginals are prescribed only at a subset of the vertices; with Brownian motion along each edge as the reference, it is an entropy-regularised multi-marginal OT problem with a tree-structured quadratic cost. Star-shaped trees, with marginals fixed on the leaves and an unknown centre, are of particular significance because they correspond to an entropy-regularised form of the Wasserstein barycentre problem. The Wasserstein barycentre provides a natural notion of 'average' for probability distributions and is widely studied because of its importance in applications such as Bayesian learning, clustering and representation learning. Computing barycentres is notoriously challenging. Many successful approaches approximate the solution with a finite set of points, but such in-sample methods struggle to scale as dimensionality increases and cannot generate new samples; alternative methods provide continuous approximations through neural parameterisations, but often require multi-level or adversarial optimisation procedures. To date, the only neural ODE/SDE approach to barycentre computation extends the IPF-based diffusion Schrödinger bridge to the tree-structured SB setting, and therefore inherits the drawbacks of IPF; it has been reported to suffer training instability at low entropic regularisation, struggling to match the prescribed marginals at the vertices.

In parallel, one of the most successful approaches to Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation is the iterative fixed-point method, which repeatedly updates a candidate barycentre by solving for the OT map from it to each marginal and pushing it forward through the weighted average of these maps. It performs strongly and has been observed to converge in only a few iterations, but every iteration requires solving a complete OT problem to each marginal, which is expensive because solving even a single OT problem can be challenging.

This raises several questions. Can a scalable, flow-based solver be built for the tree-structured SB problem, and hence for entropic Wasserstein barycentres, that avoids the shortcomings of IPF-based schemes while being guaranteed to converge to the tree-structured SB solution? In the barycentre case, can the fast convergence of fixed-point schemes be retained without paying for a complete OT solve to every marginal at every iteration? And can flow-based barycentre solvers of this kind offer a viable alternative to existing algorithms for continuous Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation?

enonce:
Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a powerful and principled approach for generative modeling, and in particular for high-quality visual generation. By learning a time-dependent velocity field that continuously transforms samples from a base distribution into a target distribution, FM models generate data by integrating an ordinary differential equation (ODE). This framework offers advantages over diffusion-based methods, including faster convergence, stable training, and direct control over sample trajectories.

Despite these strengths, inference in FM models is costly and has become a bottleneck. ODE integration is inherently sequential: each step depends on the output of the previous one, which makes the process slow and difficult to parallelize. High-fidelity generation requires a large number of fine-grained steps, which pushes latency up and makes real-time or interactive use difficult. As data dimensionality and model complexity increase, so does the inference burden. The issue is even more pronounced in video generation, where models operate on high-dimensional spatio-temporal data and the cost of sequential integration compounds across frames, making efficient inference essential for long videos.

Static reduction strategies such as distillation, trajectory truncation and consistency training have been proposed to reduce inference latency. However, they often degrade output quality, producing blurry textures, semantic drift or broken spatial coherence; in video, they often cause temporal flickering and motion inconsistency, which severely degrade realism even when individual frames look plausible. Many of them also require retraining the model with auxiliary objectives or handcrafted losses, which increases the engineering burden and restricts transferability across model families. As a result, these approaches are less modular, harder to scale, and often infeasible to deploy in time-sensitive or interactive pipelines.

In language models, a promising line of work for accelerating inference is speculative decoding, in which multiple drafts are proposed in parallel and selectively verified by the full model, reducing latency without retraining it. This idea, however, does not directly extend to image and video generative models such as FM, and two challenges stand out. First, unlike in language models, no readily available draft model exists: how can drafts be produced whose trajectories closely couple with those of the full model? Second, the performance of FM is highly sensitive to the velocity output: even a small perturbation in velocity can accumulate along the integration path and lead to severe generation errors. How, then, can drafted velocities be evaluated, and how can the drift of the resulting trajectory away from the full-model trajectory be controlled?

The open problem is therefore how to substantially reduce the inference latency of existing FM models, for both image and video generation, without retraining, without degrading output quality relative to standard full-step generation, and in a way that transfers across model families.

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: draft model acceleration via random path pruning
PROPOSAL: We propose to evaluate the feasibility of accelerating inference in FM models by selectively pruning short, random paths through the velocity field during the integration process. By doing so, we can reduce the overall number of integration steps required for achieving the same quality of output. We will experiment with various pruning strategies, including pruning based on velocity magnitude, Euclidean distance, and maximum gradient.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no pruning. (2) Ablation study: Different pruning strategies and their combinations. (3) Control: Randomly subsampling the paths.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a latency reduction of up to 30% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and a significant decrease in video generation latency. However, this approach may lead to variations in generation quality depending on the pruning strategy used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: learning draft models for fm using Curriculum Learning
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of generating high-quality drafts in FM models, we propose using Curriculum Learning to learn a draft model that closely couples with the full model. We will define a gradual curriculum of temporally corrected velocities that guide the learning process of the draft model. As the curriculum progresses, the draft model will learn to produce velocities that are increasingly similar to those produced by the full model. This will enable the draft model to not only accelerate inference but also maintain high quality output.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different curriculum learning schedules. (3) Control: Learning draft models using random sampling of the velocity field.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 40% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. The quality of the drafts will be strongly dependent on the quality of the curriculum learning schedule.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: draft model acceleration via random path pruning
PROPOSAL: We revise our initial proposal to include an incentive mechanism that rewards the draft model for producing velocities that result in generated samples that are closer to the ground truth. This can be achieved by incorporating a reconstruction loss into the draft model's training objective, which encourages the draft model to produce high-quality samples that are close to the target distribution. By doing so, we can improve the accuracy and quality of the draft model's outputs.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no pruning and no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different loss functions and weights for the reconstruction loss. (3) Control: Learning draft models using random sampling of the velocity field without reconstruction loss.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 50% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. However, the introduction of the reconstruction loss may lead to increased training time and potential mode collapse issues.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: learning draft models for fm using curriculum learning
PROPOSAL: We revise our proposal to use a more efficient curriculum learning schedule that utilizes progressive meta-learning. Instead of learning a fixed curriculum, we will use a dynamic curriculum that adapts to the performance of the draft model and the full model. This will enable the draft model to learn more effectively and efficiently, and potentially lead to better performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different progressive meta-learning schedules. (3) Control: Using a fixed curriculum learning schedule.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 45% with minimal quality degradation in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. The progressive meta-learning schedule may lead to improved performance, but it may also increase computational costs due to the need to adapt the curriculum during training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: draft refinement via multi-step prediction
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-step prediction mechanism to refine the outputs of the draft model. This mechanism will utilize a secondary model trained to predict the corrections needed to refine the draft's output, rather than relying on a single pass through the full model. By predicting these corrections step-by-step, we can iteratively refine the draft's output, potentially leading to significant quality improvements.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different numbers of refinement steps and secondary model architectures.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve high-quality outputs comparable to the full model, with a latency reduction of up to 40% in text-to-image generation, and significant latency reduction in video generation. However, the multiple steps of refinement may lead to increased training time and potential issues with convergence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: lazy evaluation of fm velocity fields
PROPOSAL: We propose a lazy evaluation approach for the velocity fields used in FM models. By storing the velocity fields in a compressed and hierarchical manner, we can significantly reduce the computational cost of evaluating the velocity field for a given sample. This approach can be particularly effective when combined with the draft model and refinement mechanisms, as it can help to reduce the latency of the overall system.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no lazy evaluation. (2) Ablation study: Different compression techniques and hierarchical representations, on a single random seed.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a significant reduction in computational cost, with a latency reduction of up to 25% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the compressed representation may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or discontinuities in the velocity field.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: model-parallelizable fm through decomposition
PROPOSAL: We propose a decomposition-based approach to make FM models parallelizable. By decomposing the velocity field into smaller, independent components, we can parallelize the evaluation of the velocity field across multiple GPUs or machines, significantly reducing the latency of the overall system. This approach can be particularly effective for large-scale FM models and video generation tasks.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no decomposition. (2) Ablation study: Different decomposition techniques and parallelization strategies.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a significant reduction in latency, with a speedup of up to 4x in text-to-image generation, and an even larger speedup in video generation. However, the decomposition may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or discontinuities in the velocity field, and complex decomposition strategies may increase engineering burden.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: uncertainty-based draft model deployment
PROPOSAL: We propose an uncertainty-based approach for deploying draft models, where the draft model is only used to generate samples when the uncertainty in the velocity field is high, and the full model is used otherwise. This approach can help to mitigate potential quality degradation issues and reduce the overall latency of the system.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning. (2) Ablation study: Different uncertainty measures and threshold values for draft model deployment.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 30% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the deployment strategy may lead to potential issues with quality degradation or inconsistent behavior at high uncertainty values.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adaptive draft model switching
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive approach for switching between the draft model and the full model based on the performance of the system. By continuously monitoring the quality and latency of the generated samples, we can dynamically switch between the two models to achieve the optimal trade-off between quality and latency. This approach can help to adapt to changing system conditions and optimize performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model with no draft model learning, with a much shorter training budget for the baseline. (2) Ablation study: Different switching policies and performance metrics.
COST: 110 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 35% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation. However, the adaptive switching strategy may lead to potential issues with instability or mode collapse.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: hybrid fm architectures
PROPOSAL: We propose a hybrid approach that combines the strengths of multiple architectures to achieve improved performance in FM models. By combining the draft model, full model, and lazy evaluation, we can create a flexible and adaptable architecture that can dynamically adjust to changing system conditions and optimize performance. This approach can help to achieve the optimal trade-off between quality, latency, and computational cost.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Full-step FM model. (2) Ablation study: Different combinations of draft model, full model, and lazy evaluation, judged qualitatively from a few examples rather than with the main metric.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a latency reduction of up to 50% in text-to-image generation, and smaller but still noticeable reductions in video generation, while maintaining high quality and performance. However, the hybrid architecture may lead to potential issues with complexity, overhead, and stability.

enonce:
Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly expanded in capability and are now widely used in domains such as conversational agents, healthcare and finance, where they often process sensitive personal information. Early privacy concerns focused mainly on memorization and leakage of training data, but recent studies show that LLMs can also infer private attributes of an author, such as location, identity or demographics, from subtle semantic cues in seemingly innocuous text. With sufficiently capable models, such inferences can be surprisingly accurate and often go undetected by users, who continue to share content unaware of the risk. Moreover, text sent to external services may be intercepted in transit or retained by providers, for example for model training, increasing the risk of misuse or data breaches.

Traditional anonymization methods rely on rule-based de-identification, such as named entity recognition or pattern matching, to remove surface-level identifiers like names, social security numbers or explicit locations. They frequently overlook the context-dependent semantics that LLMs can exploit, so private information that is embedded in context rather than stated explicitly remains inferable. This gap calls for anonymization techniques that account for semantic context and defend against inference-based privacy threats, while preserving the meaning and readability of the text, that is, techniques that achieve a good privacy-utility trade-off.

A growing body of work pursues LLM-based anonymization to protect semantic-level private information from model inference. In feedback-guided adversarial anonymization, an LLM anonymizer rewrites the input text while a second LLM, acting as an adversary, attempts to infer private attributes from the rewritten output; based on this adversarial feedback, the anonymizer iteratively refines its output to prevent the inferences that remain possible. With GPT-4 as both anonymizer and adversary, this approach achieves a substantially better privacy-utility trade-off than traditional industry-grade anonymizers. However, reliance on large proprietary models is costly and requires sending the very text that should be protected to potentially untrusted external systems. Attempts to transfer these anonymization capabilities into smaller models have been explored only to a limited extent, and existing approaches still depend on a proprietary model to provide the adversarial feedback, incurring similar costs and privacy concerns.

The open problem is therefore whether, and how, small language models that can run locally under modest compute budgets can become effective anonymizers that protect semantic-level private information against inference by strong LLM adversaries, without relying on any external model at inference time. Can such models reach a privacy-utility trade-off comparable to, or better than, that of anonymizers built on frontier proprietary LLMs, including on texts where personal information is conveyed by the overall context rather than by explicit mentions, while remaining cheap enough to deploy in settings with strict data-confidentiality requirements?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: evaluating the impact of feedback granularity on adversarial anonymization
PROPOSAL: Investigate how different levels of feedback granularity from the adversary affect the convergence rate and final performance of feedback-guided adversarial anonymization, using a small language model (e.g. BART) as the anonymizer and a strong LLM adversarial model (e.g. LaMDA) on a synthetic dataset of online comments.
CONTROLS: Compare the anonymizer's performance with and without feedback from the adversary, and evaluate the effects of refining feedback granularity on test accuracy, precision, recall and F1 score against a baseline LLM's ability to infer personal attributes from the anonymized text.
COST: 100 GPU-hours to train and test.
PREDICTION: Expected result is that higher feedback granularity will improve anonymizer performance, particularly against stronger adversaries, but with diminishing returns, until diagnosis via a grid search to determine the optimal feedback granularity value, where further experimentation may show it’ll be result in a failing dependency if granularity is reduced any lower than we arrive at.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: analyzing the trade-offs between anonymizer capacity and adversary strength
PROPOSAL: Explore whether small language models of varying capacities (e.g. RoBERTa, ALBERT) can become effective anonymizers by evaluating their performance on a diverse set of synthetic online comment datasets against strong, moderate, and weak LLM adversaries (e.g. using LaMDA, BART, and T5, respectively).
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of anonymizers with different capacities on a range of metrics, including test accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and the amount of information they require to maintain a good privacy-utility trade-off, in the same setting as the proposal.
COST: 200 GPU-hours to train and test, plus synthetic data generation.
PREDICTION: Expected result is that an anonymizer capacity of at least 300M parameters is necessary to match the performance of GPT-4 on the task, but we should find a more modest capacity model, e.g., T5 with 220M parameters, reaches a trade-off that’s competitive for lower data governance costs.

ACTION: REVISE 2

Time series data arise ubiquitously across a broad range of domains, including healthcare, finance, industrial manufacturing, weather forecasting and urban computing, and their characteristics can differ vastly from one domain to another. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have unleashed new potential for exploiting these data in time series tasks such as forecasting, imputation and classification. There are roughly two families of approaches: one fine-tunes or prompts off-the-shelf LLMs with time series converted into a suitable format, while the other trains time series foundation models from scratch on vast time series corpora by adapting LLM-inspired architectures and training strategies. In both cases, the quality of the time series data is critical to model performance: low-quality data can negate the benefits of bespoke technical advances and may even degrade performance. In practice, time series datasets are frequently marred by pervasive quality issues, including missing values, corruption induced by sensor failures, and irregular sampling. Consequently, there is a pressing need to assess, accurately and efficiently, the quality of time series data crawled from diverse domains.

General-purpose data attribution methods, such as influence functions and Shapley-value approaches (together with cheaper approximations such as KNN-based or gradient-based Shapley values), estimate the contribution of individual training samples in a model-agnostic way, but they overlook properties specific to time series such as continuity, temporal dependencies and non-stationarity. Existing attempts at time series data quality estimation therefore stress the need for methods tailored to temporal characteristics. For instance, TimeInf adapts the influence function to time series, drawing on earlier work on infinitesimal robustness for autoregressive processes and on influence functionals for time series, and TimeShap extends the Shapley value, a cooperative game-theoretic attribution method, to time series. However, these methods have largely neglected the fact that real-world time series originate from diverse domains with distinct properties and substantial distribution shifts, which limits their effectiveness to a single domain. Furthermore, both influence-function and Shapley-value techniques struggle to strike a balance between estimation fidelity and computational efficiency: influence functions require computationally intensive Hessian and gradient calculations, while Shapley values incur exponential computational costs.

Recently, estimating data quality through LLM judgments has emerged as a promising approach for text, where carefully designed prompts guide LLMs to produce accurate quality assessments. The underlying rationale is that LLMs are proficient in understanding quality criteria for natural language, such as writing style, required expertise, factual accuracy and educational value. Such efforts point to the potential of LLMs for cross-domain and interpretable data quality estimation, but they remain restricted to text and code, and the time series setting is largely unexplored.

It is therefore tempting to ask whether LLMs can be exploited to determine the quality of diverse time series data. Such an approach could leverage the knowledge of time series from many domains that LLMs acquire during large-scale pretraining, thereby circumventing the prohibitive computational cost of calculating influence functions or Shapley values in a domain-by-domain manner. However, it remains under-explored whether LLMs can truly comprehend the key characteristics that underpin the quality of diverse time series data, and how to effectively steer them to distinguish between high- and low-quality time series according to desired quality criteria. The open problem is thus how to rate the quality of time series data drawn from heterogeneous domains in a way that is accurate, computationally efficient and adaptable across domains.
