Facial rigging aims to make a static neutral facial mesh animatable by defining a set of controllable deformations, typically represented either as blendshape rigs driven by activated action units in systems based on the Facial Action Coding System (FACS), or as skeletal rigs driven by joint positions. Whereas full-body auto-rigging usually follows a two-step pipeline of skeleton construction and skinning, facial rigs are often anatomically inspired and implemented with FACS blendshapes. In a linear FACS blendshape rig, each blendshape is a vertex offset from the neutral mesh corresponding to one action unit, i.e. a specific muscle movement such as "Right Eye Close", and a complex expression is obtained by adding the weighted offsets of the activated blendshapes to the neutral mesh. Rigging is an essential step for creative AI, bringing digital avatars to life by enabling expressive and realistic facial movements across a wide range of applications. However, creating a facial rig is laborious and expensive, often requiring skilled artists tens of hours to complete a single asset. Methods that transfer expressions from 2D images or videos to 3D avatars do not remove this bottleneck, since they assume that the avatar already has a rig.

Existing facial auto-rigging methods typically transfer a complete set of blendshapes from a predefined template mesh to a neutral target mesh, which often requires dense correspondences or a mesh topology shared by the template and the target. More recent approaches build transferable latent spaces between faces or use triangulation-agnostic networks to bypass these limitations, but they still require a template blendshape rig, which can compromise accuracy when the template and target shapes differ substantially. Only one prior approach, NFR, can directly rig facial meshes from explicitly controllable FACS parameters without relying on a template, and it has so far been demonstrated primarily on humanoid heads. Furthermore, existing approaches, NFR included, have yet to accommodate meshes with multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs or teeth, which limits their ability to animate highly expressive avatars: an "eye look-down" pose, for example, is difficult to reproduce if the mesh lacks eyeballs.

Learning such a rigging model also raises a data problem. Accurate 3D supervision requires neutral meshes paired with complete rigs made by artists, and because manual rigging is so costly such rigged examples are scarce; a model trained solely on them is likely to generalize poorly to the wide variety of facial shapes, styles and topologies met in practice.

The problem is therefore to automatically turn a single static neutral facial mesh into an expressive rig controllable by FACS parameters (i) without relying on predefined template blendshapes, so that target meshes need not closely resemble a template; (ii) for in-the-wild meshes with varying topologies and shapes, including both humanoid and non-humanoid heads; and (iii) for meshes made of multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs and teeth, which must move coherently with the rest of the face. How can such a rigging system be built, and how can it be trained to generalize across this diversity when only a limited number of rigged meshes is available as 3D ground truth?

Geometry reconstruction is a fundamental problem that enables a wide range of applications in fields such as virtual reality and robotics. In recent years, neural reconstruction methods have gained significant attention; a key advantage of these methods is their ability to represent the geometry of a scene continuously, which can help in many downstream tasks. However, vision-based sensors often struggle in adverse weather conditions, or even become completely unusable when objects are obscured by occlusions.

Radio frequency (RF) sensing, specifically wireless millimeter-wave (mmWave) sensing, can see through occlusions, remains robust under challenging visibility conditions and, unlike X-rays, is not dangerous to humans, making it a compelling alternative for 3D reconstruction. This could open up many applications, for example checking whether the items inside a box are the correct items, are damaged, or pose a threat, without ever opening the box. On the other hand, mmWave resolution is extremely low compared to vision: a single radar image provides far less visual context than a camera image, which makes it hard to extract a 3D reconstruction from one radar image alone. Some prior RF systems have performed 3D point cloud reconstruction or human body tracking by leveraging movement or by emulating larger antenna apertures, but the recovered point clouds are still too sparse and noisy to reliably recover detailed geometry; through-wall human sensing relies on human motion to combat specularity, and deep learning on mmWave radar data has mostly targeted self-driving scenarios, where image resolution matters little. Other works have proposed neural implicit representations for RF sensing, aiming to concentrate scene information out of heavy noise through neural optimization, but these systems are designed for large-scale environments such as streets or satellite imagery and are far from achieving millimeter-level precision. When objects are close to the radar, the propagation characteristics of RF signals change dramatically: incoming waves can no longer be approximated as planar, so processing methods designed for large-scale scenes, such as beamforming, introduce a considerable amount of distortion and noise, often exceeding the noise acceptable for gradient descent and leading to unstable optimization. Existing neural RF reconstruction work is thus either limited to far-range scenes or, for individual objects, evaluated only on simulated data, which for wireless signals cannot come close to representing the complexity of real-world measurements. Meanwhile, the multi-view reconstruction and inverse rendering methods of computer vision (multi-view stereo, neural radiance fields, Gaussian splatting, neural implicit surfaces, physically based inverse rendering) are all derived from RGB images and are not easily transferable to mmWave data: even lensless RGB images can be mapped back to a lens-based imaging model without altering the underlying ray physics, whereas for RF signals such a transformation is fundamentally invalid.

The open problem is therefore to overcome the fundamental dilemma between massive RF noise in the input and the reconstruction of complete, high-resolution, millimeter-level 3D surface geometry of near-range objects, including objects hidden behind occlusions. This is not straightforward, because inferring surface geometry from RF signals differs fundamentally from image-based reconstruction in three main ways. First, wireless systems lack a lens-based imaging model: whereas lenses filter and focus the relevant light rays, radar antenna arrays perform lensless imaging and capture all incoming RF signals without directional filtering, which leads to low signal-to-noise ratios because irrelevant signals cannot be excluded. Second, RF signals and visible light propagate differently: visible light is predominantly scattered diffusely by surfaces, whereas RF signals, whose wavelengths are on the order of millimeters, are dominated by specular reflections, so volumetric rendering techniques designed for scattering-based vision sensors are unsuitable for RF imaging. Third, physically modeling lensless RF measurements is computationally expensive: whereas lens-based rendering samples along 1D rays, modeling what each antenna receives requires accounting for contributions from the full 3D space, leading to cubic complexity that makes naive implementations intractable at millimeter resolution.

How can accurate, millimeter-level 3D geometry of near-range objects be reconstructed from noisy real-world RF measurements, in line of sight and through occlusions, despite lensless imaging, specular reflections and the cost of modeling signal contributions from the full 3D space?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: spectral clustering for rf feature extraction
PROPOSAL: This experiment uses spectral clustering to automatically extract salient RF features relevant for 3D reconstruction in the presence of occlusions. We will train a spectral clustering model on a dataset of mmWave radar images and evaluate its performance in extracting features that are useful for 3D reconstruction. We will compare the performance of spectral clustering to other approaches like PCA and t-SNE.
CONTROLS: We will use mmWave radar images from the existing DriveWave dataset as controls and compare the performance of the spectral clustering model to other approaches.
COST: Estimated to require 10 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the spectral clustering model.
PREDICTION: We expect spectral clustering to improve feature extraction in occluded scenes, but we worry that the model may struggle to generalize across different occlusion patterns and radar sensor settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: neural indoor/outdoor discriminators for robustness
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes adding a neural indoor/outdoor discriminator module to the RF 3D reconstruction network to improve robustness in indoor and outdoor domains with varying levels of occlusions. We will train a neural network to distinguish between indoor and outdoor environments and use this module to adapt the reconstruction network for improved performance.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the proposed model to the state-of-the-art RF 3D reconstruction model without the discriminator module, using the same mmWave radar image dataset. We will also evaluate the performance of the model in both indoor and outdoor scenarios.
COST: Estimated to require an additional 20 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the model with the discriminator module.
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the addition of the indoor/outdoor discriminator module will improve the robustness and accuracy of the RF 3D reconstruction network in both indoor and outdoor scenarios, but may require careful tuning of the discriminator network to achieve good performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: volumetric processing for through-occlusion imaging
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes adapting the volumetric processing approach used in computer vision for 3D shape reconstruction to the RF domain, using a combination of simulated RF data and real-world mmWave radar images to train and evaluate the performance of this approach in through-occlusion imaging.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of volumetric processing to state-of-the-art RF 3D reconstruction methods, using datasets of mmWave radar images with and without occlusions.
COST: Estimated to require 15 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the volumetric processing model.
PREDICTION: We expect that volumetric processing will help improve the accuracy and robustness of through-occlusion imaging, but may require careful tuning of the model architecture and training parameters to achieve good performance.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: volumetric processing for through-occlusion imaging
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes adapting the volumetric processing approach used in computer vision for 3D shape reconstruction to the RF domain, using a combination of simulated RF data and real-world mmWave radar images to train and evaluate the performance of this approach in through-occlusion imaging of objects in boxes. Specifically, we will use a neural implicit surface model to represent the volumetric data and evaluate its performance in reconstructing detailed 3D surface geometry of objects behind occlusions.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of volumetric processing to state-of-the-art RF 3D reconstruction methods, using datasets of mmWave radar images of objects in boxes with and without occlusions. We will also evaluate the performance of the model in different box sizes and occlusion patterns.
COST: Estimated to require 18 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the volumetric processing model.
PREDICTION: We expect that volumetric processing will help improve the accuracy and robustness of through-occlusion imaging, but may require careful tuning of the model architecture and training parameters to achieve good performance, particularly when dealing with complex occlusion patterns and small box sizes.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: volumetric processing for through-occlusion imaging
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes adapting the volumetric processing approach used in computer vision for 3D shape reconstruction to the RF domain, using a combination of simulated RF data and real-world mmWave radar images to train and evaluate the performance of this approach in through-occlusion imaging of objects in boxes. Specifically, we will use a neural implicit surface model to represent the volumetric data and evaluate its performance in reconstructing detailed 3D surface geometry of objects behind occlusions.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of volumetric processing to state-of-the-art RF 3D reconstruction methods (previous revision was 18 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the volumetric processing model), using datasets of mmWave radar images of objects in boxes with and without occlusions. We will also evaluate the performance of the model in different box sizes and occlusion patterns.
COST: Estimated to require 18 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the volumetric processing model.
PREDICTION: We expect that volumetric processing will help improve the accuracy and robustness of through-occlusion imaging, but may require careful tuning of the model architecture and training parameters to achieve good performance, particularly when dealing with complex occlusion patterns and small box sizes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: dictionary learning for radar feature extraction
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes using dictionary learning to extract and represent features from mmWave radar data in a more robust and efficient manner. We will train a dictionary learning model on a large dataset of mmWave radar images and evaluate its performance in extracting features that are useful for 3D reconstruction.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of dictionary learning to other feature extraction methods, such as PCA and spectral clustering, using the same mmWave radar image dataset.
COST: Estimated to require 25 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the dictionary learning model.
PREDICTION: We expect dictionary learning to improve the accuracy and efficiency of feature extraction, but may require careful tuning of the dictionary learning parameters and the choice of dictionary size to achieve good performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: hierarchical neural network for 3d reconstruction
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes using a hierarchical neural network architecture to improve the accuracy and robustness of 3D reconstruction from mmWave radar data. We will train a hierarchical neural network model on a large dataset of mmWave radar images and evaluate its performance in reconstructing detailed 3D surface geometry.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the hierarchical neural network to other 3D reconstruction methods, such as volumetric processing and dictionary learning, using the same mmWave radar image dataset. We will also evaluate the performance of the model in different occlusion patterns and box sizes.
COST: Estimated to require 40 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the hierarchical neural network model.
PREDICTION: We expect the hierarchical neural network to improve the accuracy and robustness of 3D reconstruction, but may require careful tuning of the model architecture and training parameters to achieve good performance, particularly when dealing with complex occlusion patterns and small box sizes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: debiasing radar data for 3d reconstruction
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes using debiasing techniques to mitigate the effects of system-induced bias in mmWave radar data and improve the accuracy of 3D reconstruction. We will apply debiasing techniques to a large dataset of mmWave radar images and evaluate the impact on 3D reconstruction performance.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of debiasing techniques to other methods, such as dictionary learning and hierarchical neural networks, using the same mmWave radar image dataset.
COST: Estimated to require 30 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the debiasing techniques.
PREDICTION: We expect debiasing to improve the accuracy and robustness of 3D reconstruction, but may require careful tuning of the debiasing parameters and the choice of debiasing method to achieve good performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: physics-informed neural networks for rf modeling
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes using physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to model the underlying physics of mmWave radar data and improve the accuracy of 3D reconstruction. We will train a PINN model on a large dataset of mmWave radar images and evaluate its performance in reconstructing detailed 3D surface geometry.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of PINN to other methods, such as dictionary learning and hierarchical neural networks, using the same mmWave radar image dataset. We will also evaluate the performance of the model in different occlusion patterns and box sizes.
COST: Estimated to require 50 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the PINN model.
PREDICTION: We expect PINN to improve the accuracy and robustness of 3D reconstruction, but may require careful tuning of the PINN architecture and training parameters to achieve good performance, particularly when dealing with complex occlusion patterns and small box sizes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: multi-task learning for comprehensive 3d understanding
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes using multi-task learning to integrate multiple 3D reconstruction tasks, including obstacle detection, shape estimation, and labeling, into a single unified framework. We will train a multi-task learning model on a large dataset of mmWave radar images and evaluate its performance in achieving comprehensive 3D understanding.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of multi-task learning to other methods, such as dictionary learning and hierarchical neural networks, using the same mmWave radar image dataset. We will also evaluate the performance of the model in different occlusion patterns and box sizes.
COST: Estimated to require 60 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the multi-task learning model.
PREDICTION: We expect multi-task learning to significantly improve the accuracy and robustness of 3D reconstruction, especially in complex scenarios with multiple tasks and occlusions.

enonce:
Dictionary learning, in its most general form, assumes that observations X are generated by latent variables Z through an unknown function, X = g(Z). The goal is to recover the latent generative process from observational data alone, a fundamental task in both science and machine learning. This nonparametric formulation unifies a wide range of latent variable models, including independent component analysis, factor analysis and causal representation learning.

Identifiability, the ability to recover the true generative model from data, is crucial for understanding the hidden world. Yet in general dictionary learning, where both the latent variables and the generating process are unknown, the problem is fundamentally ill-posed without additional assumptions, akin to finding a needle in a haystack. To reduce this ambiguity, most prior work imposes strong parametric constraints that limit the space of possible solutions. The practice is so widespread that, although dictionary learning is fundamentally nonparametric, it is almost always instantiated as a linear model, in which observations are sparse linear combinations of latent variables. Such linearity can be overly restrictive and fails to capture the complexity of many real-world generative processes. Sparse autoencoders, commonly used in mechanistic interpretability, especially for foundation models, are a relevant example: although effective in some settings, they are rooted in sparse linear dictionary learning, which raises concerns about their ability to represent the inherently nonlinear structure of large-scale neural representations.

Many efforts have been made to relax the linearity assumption. In nonlinear independent component analysis, one line of work leverages auxiliary variables as weak supervision to achieve identifiability under statistical independence, while another constrains the mixing function itself. In causal representation learning, identifiability often depends on access to interventional data or counterfactual views, which presuppose some control over the data-generating process. Some basic conditions cannot be avoided: just as linear dictionary learning needs conditions such as the restricted isometry property so that distinct latent codes map to distinguishable observations, the nonlinear generating function must be smooth and injective so that no information is lost. But avoiding information loss is not sufficient for full recovery of the latent variables in the nonlinear regime, which is why existing guarantees rely on restricted function classes or on auxiliary information such as domain or time indices, interventions or counterfactual data.

A gap therefore remains between theoretical guarantees and practical utility. Theoretically, while additional assumptions can yield recovery guarantees, it is rarely possible to verify whether they hold in practice; understanding which guarantees remain valid when assumptions are violated is therefore essential for reliably uncovering the truth in general settings. Practically, what matters is less identifiability under ideal conditions than which inductive biases promote recovery, especially when the ground truth is unknown. Yet most existing approaches offer no guarantees under even mild violations of their assumptions, which makes their associated biases, such as contrastive objectives or weak supervision, difficult to generalize across settings.

The challenge is to make identifiability actionable in general settings: only observational data are available, the generating function is nonlinear and unknown, no parametric constraint or auxiliary supervision can be relied upon, and only basic conditions such as invertibility and differentiability are assumed, accepting that recovering every latent variable may then be infeasible. In such settings, two questions remain open:
- What aspects of the latent process can still be recovered with guarantees?
- What inductive biases should be introduced to guide recovery, ideally ones that could be adopted universally across models and settings?
A related question is whether, and under which additional conditions that require no auxiliary information, all latent variables could still be recovered.

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: natural assumption bounds for the hanin norm
PROPOSAL: Prove a bound for the Hanin norm of the Jacobian of a smooth, but unknown, generating function g(Z). Specifically, we will derive an upper bound in terms of the differentiability order and a Lipschitz constant of g. We will assume that g may acordo with any sequence of k times continuously differentiable functions.
CONTROLS: Compare to known bounds in related literature, e.g. Elazar-Pinhas (2020) on Hanin norm bounds for contexts of deep learning.
COST: 0.5 GPU-hours (analytical computation)
PREDICTION: The bound we derive should be slightly looser than existing bounds but will be scalable to higher-dimensional data; the bound may not hold for rough generative functions.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: from hanin norm bounds to invertibility conditions
PROPOSAL: Prove a sufficient condition for a diffeomorphism (smooth and bijective) between the latent space Z and the image space X (i.e., 1 : 1), in terms of the Hanin norm bound derived in proposal 1. The condition will require a lower bound on the determinant of the Jacobian of g(Z) that grows polynomially with the dimensionality of the data.
CONTROLS: Compare to known results on diffeomorphism bounds, e.g. Guillou (2018) on diffeomorphism conditions using inverse function theorem.
COST: 1.0 GPU-hours (matrix computations and diagonalization).
PREDICTION: The condition should be useful for implying invertibility, but it may not hold in cases where the generative function has vanishing eigenvalues or extremely high-dimensionality, which can cause numerical instability.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: alternating minimization for non-linear dictionary learning
PROPOSAL: Implement an alternating minimization approach for optimizing a non-linear dictionary, using a simplified version of the Hidden Neural Tangent Kernel (HNTK) to facilitate computation. We will alternate between updating the non-linear dictionary and the latent representations in the data. The goal is to demonstrate empirical success in recovering the nonlinear structure of simple generative processes.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing baselines, such as deep clustered sparse coding or non-linear dictionary learning with cyclic optimization. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (empirical evaluation using synthetic data).
PREDICTION: The approach may recover some structure of the generative process but is likely to fail for complex, high-dimensional data; further optimization or initialization strategies may help alleviate the non-convexity of this problem.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: natural assumption bounds for the hanin norm
PROPOSAL: Refine the bound in proposal 1 by incorporating a regularization term that encourages a certain degree of sparsity in the Jacobian of the generating function. This term will enhance the stability of the bound and allow it to hold for a broader class of functions.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original bound in proposal 1 and study the trade-off between sparsity and conservativeness. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 0.5 GPU-hours (computations and marginalization).
PREDICTION: The refined bound should improve the usability of the previous results, but it may become less tight or lose some generality, trading off the relationships between these two requirements.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: comparison to partial information theory
PROPOSAL: Compare the identifiability guarantees derived from the Hanin norm bounds and diffeomorphism conditions to those that can be obtained from partial information theory, specifically the concept of sufficient statistics for the generative process. We will study how the strength of these guarantees compares for different classes of generative functions.
CONTROLS: Specifically, analyze the comparisons in terms of the dimensionality of the sufficient statistics, the complexity of the generative process, and the information available in the data.
COST: 0.5 GPU-hours (information-theoretic calculations and comparisons).
PREDICTION: The comparison may highlight situations in which one of these approaches is more suited to the generative process at hand, but it may also reveal that the best results come from using these approaches in combination.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: recovering compression parameters through surrogate optimal transport
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to recover the parameters of a generative process that is compressing the latent variables, by formulating the optimization problem as a surrogate optimal transport problem. This involves solving a Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality formulation, where the goal is to find a transport plan between the distributions of the latent and observed variables.
CONTROLS: Use the same alternating minimization approach as in proposal 3 to optimize the transport plan, and study its convergence properties.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (combining gradient descent and OT optimization).
PREDICTION: The method may help recover the compression parameters even when the generative process is highly non-linear, but it may suffer from high computational cost and can be heavily dependent on the choice of the optimizer for the OT problem.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: a surrogate noise model for simulation and inference
PROPOSAL: Develop a method for simulating and inferring generative processes by treating the noise as a surrogate for a probabilistic unknown. Specifically, this involve using a fixed-point iteration to calculate an approximation of the noise distribution, and a related algorithm for inferring the generative process parameters from the conditional expectation of this distribution.
CONTROLS: Compare the robustness of the surrogate noise model to different perturbation schemes for simulating real-world data, and study its capacity to recover the generative process.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (fixed-point iteration and Monte Carlo inference).
PREDICTION: The surrogate noise model may help improve the robustness of the inference procedure, but it may be computationally expensive and could suffer from either over-smoothing or over-fitting, depending on the choice of the probabilistic unknown.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: alternating minimization for non-linear dictionary learning
PROPOSAL: Modify the alternating minimization approach in proposal 3 to incorporate an initial warm-up phase using a linear approximation of the generating function. This allows the algorithm to adapt to the non-linearities in the data more effectively, potentially improving convergence towards the optimal dictionary.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of this revised approach to the original alternating minimization, and assess the trade-off between warm-up duration and overall convergence time.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (combining empirical evaluation and optimized warm-up schedule).
PREDICTION: The warm-up phase may improve the algorithm's ability to adapt to non-linear data generating processes but could also increase the overall computational cost and risk of over-optimization.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: type-based inference with transformer language models
PROPOSAL: Devise a type-based inference framework for recovering the latent structure of language models, leveraging their internal types and transformer architecture to constrain the generative process. This will involve analyzing the Transformer layers' behavior and designing inference algorithms that exploit the structure of the language model's hidden states.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the type-based inference approach on a variety of language models and assess its performance on tasks such as text generation and semantic parsing. Evaluate all methods on the same held-out test set and report the mean and standard deviation over five seeds.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (large-scale language model simulations).
PREDICTION: The type-based inference framework may uncover novel insights into the latent structure of language models, but it may require substantial computational resources and may be challenging to generalize across different model architectures.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: universality of alternating minimization for non-linear dictionary learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the universality of the alternating minimization approach derived in proposal 3, specifically whether it can be applied to recover the generative process in a wide range of settings, including those with complex and high-dimensional data, sparse or noisy observations, and varying degrees of non-linearity. We will perform extensive numerical experiments and analytical investigations to evaluate the robustness of the approach.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the alternating minimization to other state-of-the-art approaches for non-linear dictionary learning and assess its robustness under various perturbations of the data-generating process.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (numerical experiments and sensitivity analysis).
PREDICTION: The universality analysis may indicate that alternating minimization has broad applicability, but it may also reveal limitations, such as vulnerability to certain types of outliers or difficulties in handling data with shifted or removed features.

enonce:
Large language models (LLMs) excel at generating fluent text yet remain prone to both intrinsic aleatoric ambiguity and epistemic gaps in their learned knowledge. The latter can lead to hallucinations—confident outputs that are factually incorrect. Quantifying these uncertainties is critical for building safe AI systems deployable in high-stakes applications. In free-form natural language generation tasks such as question answering, this is especially challenging, as lexically distinct responses can still be semantically equivalent: uncertainty has to be measured over meanings rather than over token sequences.

A standard way to do so defines a distribution over semantic clusters of responses, obtained by marginalizing over output sequences and approximated by Monte Carlo sampling. The total predictive uncertainty over these clusters decomposes into an aleatoric part, the entropy over clusters (semantic entropy), which captures the irreducible ambiguity among valid answers, and an epistemic part, which reflects the model's lack of knowledge or data coverage. For a question such as "Name a way to measure the Hubble constant", several distinct but correct answers (for instance, the distance ladder or gravitational lensing time delays) reflect aleatoric uncertainty, whereas answers that contradict scientific facts or admit ignorance reveal gaps in the model's knowledge and signal that it should abstain.

Estimating these quantities often relies on drawing large IID sample sets, which often contain semantically redundant outputs and waste compute. Semantic entropy quantifies aleatoric uncertainty by clustering generated outputs into semantic equivalence classes, and mutual information computed via iterative prompting has been used to lower-bound certain forms of epistemic uncertainty; despite their conceptual appeal, both require extensive sampling to produce stable estimates, limiting their use in low-resource settings. Diversity-oriented heuristics such as temperature scaling or nucleus sampling, on the other hand, do not account for semantics. A more recent method steers generation toward semantic diversity, but it relies on token substitutions and remains restricted to autoregressive models (ARMs). Moreover, diversity heuristics are commonly applied during sampling without correcting for the bias they introduce, even though the uncertainties of interest are defined under the model's own distribution.

Meanwhile, uncertainty estimation methods have focused on ARMs, whereas masked diffusion models (MDMs), which extend masked language modeling by learning iterative denoising schedules that progressively resolve masked spans, have recently emerged as strong alternatives. Despite achieving text quality on par with state-of-the-art ARMs, MDMs remain largely overlooked in the context of uncertainty quantification.

This leaves several questions open. How can stable estimates of semantic aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty be obtained for free-form answers from a small, fixed budget of generations, so that the samples cover distinct meanings instead of repeating the same ones? How can this be done while keeping the estimates faithful to the model's own predictive distribution? And can a single approach serve both autoregressive and masked diffusion language models?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: uncertainty quantification for masked diffusion models
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the feasibility of using a modified version of the recent method for steering generation toward semantic diversity to MDMs, and adapt it for use with a small, fixed budget of generations. This involves replacing the token substitutions with masked diffusion-based sampling methods and investigating the effect on semantic aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty estimates.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original token substitution approach in the context of ARMs, to see if the MDM adaptation maintains performance; ablate the effect of varying the number of mask schedules used during sampling.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The modified approach may achieve comparable or even better results for MDMs compared to the original token substitution method, especially with a small budget of generations. However, it might struggle with estimating epistemic uncertainty due to the complexity of the masked diffusion process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating aleatoric uncertainty estimates with i.i.d. sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of varying the batch size and sampling method (e.g., uniform, top-k, temperature scaling) on the stability and accuracy of semantic aleatoric uncertainty estimates using a fixed number of IID samples, focusing on maintaining semantic diversity while minimizing wasteful redundancy.
CONTROLS: Compare with the baseline I.I.D. sampling using a standard batch size and sampling method (e.g., greedy or argmax), to see the effects of batch size and sampling strategy on uncertainty estimates; explore the effect of using nested or stratified sampling to better capture semantic diversity. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that large batch sizes hinder semantic diversity, while better sampling strategies can largely mitigate this issue. However, the approach may still be computationally expensive, limiting its scalability to various applications.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 2
TITLE: exploiting semantic clusters for aleatoric uncertainty estimation
revise: Replace the proposal with a new approach that explicitly incorporates semantic clustering into the I.I.D. sampling process, leveraging a pre-trained clustering model to identify and prioritize distinct semantic clusters from a given prompt. This would enable the generation of a smaller, more diverse set of samples that better capture semantic aleatoric uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline I.I.D. sampling approach without explicit clustering, to see the effect of incorporating clustering on the accuracy and stability of aleatoric uncertainty estimates; ablate the impact of using different clustering models or thresholding strategies to select relevant clusters.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show significant improvements in the quality and accuracy of aleatoric uncertainty estimates, particularly when the sentence-level clustering model is fine-tuned on the specific question-answering task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: leveraging mutual information for epistemic uncertainty estimation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of mutual information as a lower bound for epistemic uncertainty, specifically leveraging the iterative prompting approach from previous work to estimate the mutual information between the input prompt and the generated responses, while controlling for the introduction of bias through diversity heuristics.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline approach that uses a simple variances-based estimator; ablate the effect of using different model architectures, batch sizes, and sampling methods on the resulting epistemic uncertainty estimates; compare with a known lower bound estimator using embeddings for a validation of the estimates.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that mutual information can provide a strong lower bound for epistemic uncertainty, outperforming the variance-based estimator, but the complexity and sensitivity of the method might limit its applicability in certain contexts.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 3
TITLE: better lower bounds for conditional epistemic uncertainty estimation
REVISION: Introduce a corrected and improved version of mutual information estimation that specifically targets conditional epistemic uncertainty, accounting for the input prompt and the generated responses. This involves refining the iterative prompting approach and leveraging a learned embedding space to better capture the conditional structure of the uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original proposal and validate the estimates by comparing with known and established results from other works that operate under similar contexts.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The improved approach may significantly enhance the quality of the epistemic uncertainty estimates, closing the gap with the gold standard methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: constrained sampling for aleatoric uncertainty estimation
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel sampling approach that incorporates constraints on the generated responses, specifically designed to promote semantic diversity while controlling for ambiguity. This will be achieved through a combination of pre-trained semantic embeddings and a customized sampling algorithm, which iteratively refines the response space to better capture aleatoric uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline I.I.D. sampling approach and the clustering-based approach from proposal 2; ablate the impact of using different embedding spaces or constraint functions on the resulting uncertainty estimates.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that the proposed constrained sampling approach can effectively balance the trade-off between semantic diversity and ambiguity, resulting in highly accurate and stable aleatoric uncertainty estimates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: analyzing the effect of sampling temperature on uncertainty estimation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of sampling temperature on semantic diversity and accuracy of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty estimates for both autoregressive and masked diffusion language models. This will be achieved through a comprehensive analysis of generated responses under various temperature settings, and the resulting uncertainty estimates compared against baseline approaches.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original sampling temperature settings used in the baseline approaches; ablate the effect of using different initial temperatures or other sampling strategies.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that a specific temperature range is optimal for both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty estimation, with deviating from this range negatively impacting the quality of the estimates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: estimating epistemic uncertainty via proxy tasks
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of proxy tasks and side objectives to estimate epistemic uncertainty in language models. This involves training a meta-model that learns to predict epistemic uncertainty by ranking the confidence of different models on proxy tasks, and evaluating its performance on real-world uncertainty estimation tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare with the mutual information-based approach from proposal 3; ablate the impact of using different proxy tasks or side objectives on the resulting uncertainty estimates.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that proxy tasks and side objectives can provide a novel and effective way to estimate epistemic uncertainty, potentially outperforming the mutual information-based approach in certain contexts, but the method's effectiveness may depend on the choice of proxy task and quality of the meta-model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: comparison across language model architectures
PROPOSAL: Compare and contrast the performance of the uncertainty estimation methods developed in this work across different language model architectures, including autoregressive and masked diffusion models. This will involve adapting the proposed approaches to each model type and evaluating their effectiveness on a range of uncertainty estimation tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare with oracles, or established methods for uncertainty esimation on each model type; ablate the impact of using different model architectures or training procedures on the resulting uncertainty estimates.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that different types of language models have distinct strengths and weaknesses in terms of uncertainty estimation, and that the proposed approaches can effectively adapt to these differences, leading to improved overall performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: guidelines for uncertainty-aware model selection
PROPOSAL: Derive practical guidelines for selecting language models based on their uncertainty estimation capabilities, by investigating the relationships between uncertainty estimation performance, model architecture, and task requirements.
CONTROLS: Compare with established methods for model selection and calibration; evaluate the impact of incorporating uncertainty-aware selection on downstream task performance.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results may show that incorporating uncertainty-aware model selection can significantly improve the robustness and reliability of language models in various applications, leading to better decision-making in real-world scenarios.

Large language models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress across a wide range of natural language understanding and generation tasks, but their massive parameter counts demand prohibitively large computational and memory resources for both training and deployment. Even in settings with a reasonable amount of compute, training or fine-tuning such models remains challenging.

One promising way to reduce the computational burden of fine-tuning is low-precision floating-point (FP) arithmetic such as FP8. Modern accelerators (e.g., NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, AMD CDNA 3, Google TPUs) increasingly support low-precision FP arithmetic natively, and FP8 can theoretically double the throughput of FP16 matrix multiplication. Because FP8 formats (such as E4M3 or E5M2) have a narrow representable range, a higher-precision tensor must first be scaled by a per-tensor factor obtained from a max-reduction over its absolute values, and then scaled element-wise and rounded, before the low-precision multiplication can run. This quantization overhead is memory-bound and grows quadratically with matrix size, whereas the cost of matrix multiplication grows cubically. As a consequence, FP8 is known to accelerate mainly large-dimensional matrix multiplications (empirically, when each matrix dimension exceeds roughly 4K elements), while small-dimensional computations can even suffer an unexpected slowdown.

These overheads are especially critical for low-rank adaptation (LoRA), a widely used approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning. LoRA keeps the pretrained weights frozen and inserts small trainable low-rank matrices (adapters) that capture task-specific knowledge, greatly reducing memory cost by training few parameters. For such small-dimensional matrices, the overhead of FP8 quantization can outweigh the gains of FP8 multiplication, and the separate forward and backward paths of the adapters add further quantization operations at every iteration. Yet fast LoRA fine-tuning matters in practice: many applications require training numerous adapters, for example one adapter per user for personalized recommendation or personalized alignment from human feedback, task-specific adapters for multi-task learning and mixtures of LoRA experts, adapters for different domains, multilingual summarization, and rapid updates in dynamic, user-specific environments. Efficiently accelerating LoRA fine-tuning is therefore essential for timely, scalable and cost-effective adaptation of LLMs under practical computational constraints.

Existing lines of work leave this gap open. Quantized LoRA methods (such as QLoRA with 4-bit NormalFloat weights, QA-LoRA with group-wise INT4 weights, and follow-ups that refine the quantization with integer linear programming, SVD-based adapter initialization, dynamic rank allocation or information recovery) compress the frozen backbone through weight-only quantization. They focus on memory efficiency rather than fine-tuning speed: the added quantization and dequantization often make them slower than standard LoRA, and weight-only quantization cannot exploit hardware acceleration of low-precision matrix multiplication. Conversely, FP8 training methods (hybrid E4M3/E5M2 formats, mixed-precision FP8 training with high-precision master weights, studies of large-scale FP8 stability and outliers, unit scaling) are designed for the large-dimensional matrices of full LLM training, not for the small matrices that characterize LoRA.

This raises the following questions. How large is the quantization overhead when FP8 arithmetic is applied to LoRA fine-tuning, which parts of the computation does it come from, and does it persist across typical adapter ranks? Can LoRA fine-tuning be organized so that it genuinely benefits from native FP8 arithmetic, delivering real end-to-end speedups over existing quantized LoRA methods, while retaining the memory savings that make LoRA attractive and reaching accuracy comparable to existing quantized LoRA fine-tuning?

The ability to model complex, real-world phenomena is one of the central challenges in machine learning. Domains such as geospatial modeling, where terrain varies drastically across regions, or speech analysis, where signals exhibit bursts of volatility, are often characterized by pronounced non-stationarity: their statistical properties change across the input space, so that sharp, localized events can coexist with smooth, slowly varying regions. Gaussian processes (GPs) offer a principled framework for such problems, providing robust uncertainty estimates and flexible, non-parametric modeling. Despite these advantages, exact GPs suffer from two major limitations: their expressivity is constrained by the choice of kernel, and exact inference costs O(N^3) time and O(N^2) memory in the number N of training points, rendering it impractical for modern large-scale applications.

Most current approaches force a trade-off between expressivity and efficiency. On one hand, random Fourier features achieve impressive scalability: the kernel is approximated by an explicit, finite-dimensional feature map obtained by Monte Carlo sampling from its spectral density, so that the GP reduces to a Bayesian linear regression whose cost is linear in the number of data points, and the approximation error is backed by theoretical guarantees. Yet this construction depends on Bochner's theorem, which fundamentally restricts it to stationary kernels that assume uniform behavior across the entire domain; its globally supported sinusoidal features are inherently spatially invariant. Applying such models to non-stationary data leads to systematic mis-specification, resulting in compromised predictive accuracy and uncalibrated uncertainty estimates. Sparse variational GPs reduce the cost of exact inference through a set of inducing points, but they rely on iterative optimization whose cost grows cubically with the number of inducing points. On the other hand, expressive models such as deep GPs, spectral mixture kernels, and input-dependent kernels can capture non-stationarity, but they often reintroduce prohibitive computational costs, complex inference schemes, and challenges in optimization and hyperparameter tuning, and they typically retain a high complexity in the number of training points. Hybrid approaches that combine scalable approximations with expressive models, such as kernel interpolation, deep kernel learning, deep random features, and adaptive or compositional Fourier-feature representations, still tend to trade off scalability, expressivity, and interpretability.

The gap between scalable stationary models and complex non-stationary ones therefore remains. This raises the central question of whether the random-feature paradigm can be generalized beyond Bochner's theorem to the non-stationary setting: can one construct an explicit, randomly sampled feature map whose induced kernel adapts to local, input-dependent structure, while preserving the linear-in-data training and prediction cost that makes random features attractive? Such a construction should also be principled, with guarantees, comparable to those available for random Fourier features, that the induced kernel is valid and that the random approximation converges to it as the number of features grows. Finally, it remains open whether such an approach can offer a better trade-off between predictive accuracy, uncertainty quality, and computational cost than both stationary random features and more complex non-stationary GP models.

Recent frontier models such as OpenAI o1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1 and Kimi k1.5 provide compelling proof of concept for leveraging long chains of thought to enhance the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). Following these advances, Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) techniques such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization (DAPO) have emerged as the de facto standard for strengthening LLM reasoning. In RLVR, the policy model is trained by sampling multiple responses (rollouts) to a prompt, checking each final answer against a ground-truth answer, and then reinforcing correct answers while penalizing incorrect ones. GRPO, a variant of Proximal Policy Optimization that dispenses with a costly value model, computes the advantage of each response by normalizing its reward with the mean and standard deviation of the rewards in its group.

This works well when the responses to a prompt contain both right and wrong answers, but it does not account for the case where a group of rollouts is entirely correct or entirely incorrect and therefore receives identical rewards. Such prompts are referred to as zero-variance prompts. For them, the normalized rewards (the advantage values) collapse to zero, so there is no training signal and all rollouts for those prompts are rendered uninformative. Put differently, the policy is rewarded for a correct response only when at least one incorrect response exists in the same group, and penalized for an incorrect response only when at least one correct response is present. Zero-variance prompts typically arise when a problem is too difficult or too easy for the current model: early in training, when the model often fails to solve a problem even once across multiple attempts, and near convergence, when it has become strong enough to solve many problems in every attempt.

Ignoring these prompts may seem conceptually reasonable, but it remains problematic because rollout generation is itself a major bottleneck in RL training, so the compute spent sampling responses to zero-variance prompts is simply wasted. Recent methods acknowledge this inefficiency and try to filter zero-variance prompts out, either before rollout, by predicting from the training history which prompts are likely to yield identical rewards and skipping them, or after rollout, by repeatedly sampling and discarding them until a batch contains only prompts with mixed outcomes. These methods view zero-variance prompts merely as a cost to be avoided and implicitly assume that they offer no value for policy optimization. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has investigated whether zero-variance prompts themselves can serve as a valuable source of learning signal.

This raises several open questions. Can the responses to a prompt whose rollouts are all correct, or all incorrect, provide meaningful feedback for policy optimization, even though the group contains no contrasting response? If so, how should such feedback be formulated so that it remains informative and does not destabilize training? And would exploiting these prompts, instead of discarding them, lead to better reasoning performance and more stable learning than both standard group-relative training and the prevailing practice of filtering them out?

PROPOSAL: Develop a technique to extract patterns or insights from sequences of rollouts where the correct answer is consistently provided or consistently absent. This can be done through sequential pattern mining or sequential Bayesian inference. The extracted patterns can then be fed back into the policy training process to help improve its performance.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline where no pattern mining is performed, and a variant where the mine extracted patterns are used to augment the policy loss. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might reveal meaningful relationships between rollouts and the underlying task, but might also require significant resources and may be affected by the curse of dimensionality.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: using hierarchical auxiliary tasks to overcome zero-variance prompts
PROPOSAL: Instead of using a single auxiliary task, use a hierarchical structure of tasks where each task builds upon the previous one. For example, the first task might be to predict the output space for a given prompt, the second task might be to estimate the confidence in the answer based on the output space, and the third task might be to predict the correct answer based on the output space and confidence estimates. These hierarchical tasks are then added to the policy loss, encouraging the policy to learn from the zero-variance prompts.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline where only the primary task is used, and a variant where multiple auxiliary tasks are combined without hierarchical structure. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might enable the policy to learn more robustly from zero-variance prompts by providing a more comprehensive understanding of the task, but may also require careful design of the hierarchical tasks and risk overfitting to these specific tasks.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: tracking task difficulty in a dynamic skills graph
PROPOSAL: Develop a graph-based framework to track the difficulty of different tasks as the policy learns. The graph represents the policy's skills and how they relate to each other, with edges indicating the difficulty of transitioning between skills. The policy can then use this graph to dynamically adjust its learning strategy based on its current strengths and weaknesses, including when to focus on difficult tasks that are currently zero-variance.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline where no dynamic skills graph is maintained, and a variant where the graph is used only for visualization purposes. Evaluate all methods on the same held-out test set and report the mean and standard deviation over five seeds.
COST: 280 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might enable the policy to learn more efficiently by adaptively focusing on difficult tasks, but may also require significant resources to maintain and update the graph, and may be affected by the complexity of the graph structure.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: exploiting zero-variance prompts through transition-state reinforcement learning
PROPOSAL: Reformulate the policy optimization problem as a transition-state reinforcement learning problem, where the goal is to learn the optimal transition between states (rollouts) that are currently zero-variance. This is done by computing the value function for each state and using this to guide the policy in transitioning between states.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline where no transition-state reinforcement learning is used, and a variant where the policy is trained on a fixed set of states. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might enable the policy to learn more robustly from zero-variance prompts by explicitly modeling the transitions between states, but may also require significant resources to compute the value function and may be affected by the curse of dimensionality.

PROPOSAL: Develop a benchmarking framework to evaluate the efficacy of the various methods proposed to exploit zero-variance prompts. This includes designing a set of tasks that exhibit zero-variance behavior and testing the proposed methods on these tasks. The results are then compared against a set of baselines to provide a holistic understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of each approach.

PREDICTION: This evaluation framework will provide a comprehensive understanding of the efficacy of zero-variance prompt exploitation methods, but may require additional resources to establish and maintain the benchmarking framework.

Diffusion models have catalyzed an enormous research wave in generative modeling. Conceptually, they couple a stochastic forward noising process with a reverse-time ordinary or stochastic differential equation whose density evolution is governed by the Fokker–Planck equation, a linear second-order parabolic partial differential equation. Learning consists of estimating time-indexed scores or velocities and integrating them for sampling. A growing body of work also explores probability-flow backbones: deterministic flows trained via flow matching and its optimal-transport variants, rectified flows, and stochastic interpolants that bridge flows and diffusion.

Yet the partial-differential-equation lens on generative modeling need not be limited to Fokker–Planck. Other classical linear second-order equations, elliptic and hyperbolic, offer different structural advantages but remain comparatively underexplored; Poisson flow models, for instance, recast generation through electrostatics-inspired fields. On the hyperbolic side, recent work has replaced the Fokker–Planck equation with the telegrapher equation (the one-dimensional damped wave equation) and its stochastic Kac representation, in which a particle moves at constant speed and reverses direction at the jump times of a Poisson process. A network is fit by regression to a closed-form conditional velocity of this process and integrated backward in time from noise to data, with each image coordinate following an independent one-dimensional Kac process. The resulting probability flows have a finite propagation speed: starting from localized mass, the distribution remains inside a causal cone, the flow is Lipschitz in Wasserstein distance, and velocity norms, hence kinetic energy, stay globally bounded. Diffusion, by contrast, spreads mass instantaneously with effectively infinite propagation speed, which manifests as stiff, rapidly growing reverse-time velocities and as ill-conditioned fields with Lipschitz blow-ups near the end of denoising; indeed, diffusion arises as a limit of the damped wave equation as the damping and the propagation speed tend to infinity. A finite speed cap thus acts like a built-in stability constraint: trajectories cannot accelerate without bound, and late-time integration is less stiff.

So far, however, these finite-speed flows have been developed only for unconditional image generation, and they lack two ingredients that make diffusion-style generators practical. The first is guided conditional generation. Classifier-free guidance, which mixes conditional and unconditional predictions to steer samples toward a condition, is a standard tool for diffusion models, but it is unclear whether guidance can be carried over to finite-speed dynamics without losing the bounded-energy property that distinguishes them from diffusion, whose kinetic energy can diverge near data time. The second is fast sampling. Practical generators are expected to deliver high-quality samples with very few network evaluations, yet it is unknown whether finite-speed flows can be brought down to a handful of sampling steps, or even a single one, without a severe loss of sample quality, and whether their finite-speed, bounded-energy structure can explain, and ideally guarantee, that a coarse few-step sampler stays close to the full sampling trajectory.

This leads to three questions. How can guided conditional generation be built on finite-speed Kac flows while provably keeping the guided velocity field at finite kinetic energy? How can such flows be turned into few-step, ideally one-step, image generators that preserve both sample quality and the numerical stability benefits of finite-speed probability flows? And can the finite-speed structure provide theoretical guarantees that a few-step sampler remains close to the full flow along the entire generation path, not only in its final samples? Answering them would show whether hyperbolic, finite-speed dynamics can be a credible alternative to diffusion for fast image generation.

Graphs are powerful abstractions for representing complex relationships between entities, from social networks to molecular structures, and learning effective graph representations is crucial for node classification, graph classification and link prediction. Over the past decade, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become the dominant paradigm for graph representation learning, building representations through a message-passing mechanism that iteratively aggregates local neighborhood information. Despite its success, message passing faces several key limitations, such as limited expressiveness and difficulty in capturing long-range dependencies. Numerous efforts address different aspects of these limitations: graph transformer architectures incorporate long-range interactions across broader graph contexts, positional encodings inject structural priors to improve global topological awareness, and graph rewiring techniques modify the topology to mitigate structural bottlenecks and enhance information diffusion.

However, these advances remain constrained by a cognitive discrepancy. Humans perceive global structure intuitively, following visual Gestalt principles: they understand the whole before analyzing the individual parts. GNNs and their variants, by contrast, operate through bottom-up processing. People instantly recognize ring structures, symmetric structures and critical bridges in a drawing of a graph, yet even advanced architectures struggle with such basic topological understanding: standard message-passing networks provably cannot identify bridges, and graphs that people tell apart at a glance can fool message passing unless sophisticated topological computations are added. Although architectural innovations have made significant theoretical and practical progress, their essence is still to identify and repair different aspects of the inherent defects of message passing. Approaches that perceive graphs visually remain largely unexplored for graph learning, despite their natural alignment with how humans perceive network structures, and despite a flourishing computer vision ecosystem whose models excel at holistic pattern recognition and global structure understanding. Recent work has begun to bring graph drawings into existing architectures, for instance into vision-language models for graph reasoning or into GNNs to enhance expressivity, but it treats graph layouts and vision models as black boxes, without examining how visual and message-passing models fundamentally differ in the way they understand graphs.

A second obstacle is measurement. Established benchmarks built from molecules, citation networks or protein interaction graphs tightly couple domain-specific node features with topology, which makes their separate contributions hard to quantify and can let models succeed through feature-based shortcuts rather than genuine structural understanding. Models that replace the true molecular topology with fixed-structure expander graphs have been shown to match or exceed performance on several molecular benchmarks, suggesting that node features often dominate structural information in standard datasets, potentially masking differences in how models perceive graph topology. The theoretical evaluation of GNNs has centered on the Weisfeiler-Lehman test, which measures the ability to distinguish pairs of non-isomorphic graphs of the same size; valuable for theory, it is limited to binary discrimination between fixed-size graph pairs. Recent graph benchmarks oriented toward large language models focus on structural analysis tasks such as node counting, cycle detection and path finding, and typically rely on a limited set of random graph generators (such as Erdős–Rényi or Watts–Strogatz) that inadequately capture topological diversity. What remains missing is a way to assess human-like graph cognition: the intuitive ability to perceive, abstract and reason about fundamental global graph properties, and to recognize the same connectivity patterns across varying scales and contexts.

This leads to the questions addressed here. Could models designed for visual perception, which carry no graph-specific inductive bias, offer a viable pathway to graph structural understanding, and do they process graph information in the same way as message-passing GNNs or through fundamentally different strategies? How can a model's ability to perceive and abstract global graph properties be evaluated rigorously, in isolation from domain-specific features, including whether it recognizes the same structural pattern regardless of graph size? And what does it take for a graph learning model to acquire the holistic, scale-robust understanding of topology that humans display effortlessly?

Diffusion models, and text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models in particular, have made astonishing progress in the quality of generated images. At the same time, emerging work on generative depth estimation has revealed that advanced T2I models hold a latent potential for depth estimation: the rich visual priors stored in a pre-trained T2I model can be leveraged to obtain strong zero-shot monocular depth estimation. Exploring a framework that bridges image generation and depth estimation is an essential step toward building unified models for both generation and visual perception.

Existing routes toward such unification each carry a substantial cost. The pioneering generative depth estimation paradigm repurposes a pre-trained T2I diffusion model by fine-tuning its denoising network with full parameters on depth data. It achieves powerful zero-shot depth estimation, but the parameter updates made during training irreversibly and catastrophically degrade the model's original image generation capability; later generative depth estimators that refine this recipe (for example with flow matching, geometry switchers or detail-preserving tuning strategies) inherit the same full-parameter fine-tuning and therefore the same loss. A second route unifies generation and depth estimation with a parallel dual-model architecture, in which two diffusion models run side by side and interact through feature-exchange operations; this requires running two diffusion models in parallel, and the interaction registers new knowledge into the pre-trained generator, which can affect its original image generation behaviour. A third, data-driven route trains a unified generation-and-perception model from scratch on massive multitask data (on the order of a hundred million samples). Despite remarkable progress, these solutions may be considered inefficient or resource-intensive, and potentially suboptimal.

Since a rich visual prior is already stored in advanced T2I models, a natural question arises: can a T2I model effortlessly acquire depth estimation capability without degrading its image generation capability? More concretely, starting from a fixed pre-trained T2I model, with a focus on modern transformer-based diffusion models, how can its latent depth estimation ability be unleashed so that a single model serves both image generation and depth estimation, keeping the original generation ability fully intact, adding only a small fraction of extra learnable parameters, and without resorting to massive multitask training data, while still reaching depth accuracy competitive with full-parameter fine-tuning and with existing unified models?

The problem is challenging. Among the effectively infinite pixel-level combinations that a T2I model learns to generate, there may exist underlying information highly correlated with scene depth; however, because text prompts provide only weak guidance and depth information is sparsely represented within the overall data distribution, extracting depth-relevant features from a fixed pre-trained T2I model is difficult. Any additional capacity must also make efficient use of the visual knowledge already present in the pre-trained model, so that depth estimation is obtained at a small parameter and data cost rather than by building and training a second large model.

Understanding how a scene has changed and forecasting how it will look next from Satellite Image Time Series (SITS) is fundamental to many critical applications, yet it poses a profound challenge: predicting the future requires a deep understanding of past change. Two tasks are central. In temporal change description, given a sequence of temporally ordered satellite images of the same area, the goal is to generate a natural-language description that accurately summarizes the key dynamic changes that occurred over the observation period, such as urban expansion or agricultural cycles; this requires comprehending the temporal evolution and, ideally, the underlying causal narrative of the changes. In future satellite image forecasting, given the same historical sequence, the goal is to generate a plausible image for the next time point. A critical and often overlooked requirement is that the forecast be temporally consistent: the generated changes should be a logical continuation of the trends and dynamics observed in the historical data, not merely a plausible standalone picture.

Although foundation models such as Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and diffusion-based image generators have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their application to this domain remains fragmented and fundamentally limited. On the understanding side, static image captioning ignores temporal context, while existing temporal change description methods lack the semantic depth of MLLMs: they fuse information across images through simple interactions, their long-range temporal reasoning is limited, and they struggle to capture why changes occur. General-purpose MLLMs, even video-capable ones, are not optimized for this setting either: video-centric models are typically tuned for densely sampled frames with fixed, short intervals, whereas consecutive satellite acquisitions are sparse and irregular, with gaps that can span several years. On the generation side, single-image synthesis cannot model evolution, and temporal forecasting approaches struggle with long-term consistency because they do not grasp the semantic drivers of change: their conditioning is typically low-level (e.g., edge maps), based on simple metadata, or limited to text guidance, and it lacks fine-grained temporal semantic interaction, so they can generate what a scene looks like but cannot reason about why it should look that way given its history. As a result, change understanding and future forecasting have been treated as disjointed tasks, even though both are limited by a common bottleneck: modeling long-range temporal dynamics.

This raises several questions. How can a model reason about why changes occurred across a long, irregularly sampled sequence of satellite images, and describe them accurately? How can such an understanding of past change be used to generate what will happen next, so that the forecast is a temporally consistent continuation of the observed trajectory rather than only a realistic-looking image? Can enhancing long-range temporal understanding improve performance on both tasks simultaneously, with the understanding of past change directly informing the forecast? Finally, how can the temporal consistency of a forecast be rigorously evaluated, given that standard image-quality metrics cannot penalize a prediction that is perceptually realistic but inconsistent with historical trends?
