Diffusion models have demonstrated a remarkable ability to learn data distributions across many modalities, with strong results in both data generation and image restoration. In medical imaging, they are effective at modeling the distribution of 2D image slices, and by combining these powerful learned priors with conventional optimization frameworks, diffusion-based solvers have reached state-of-the-art performance on medical inverse problems such as accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and undersampled X-ray computed tomography (CT). Such problems are often severely ill-posed: far fewer measurements are acquired than there are unknowns, so the measurements alone cannot determine the image, and the learned prior must fill in what they leave ambiguous. Diffusion-based solvers do so through an iterative reverse sampling process that, at each step, predicts a clean image from the current noisy state, corrects this estimate for consistency with the measurements, and re-noises it to the next timestep, which repeatedly injects random noise.

In clinical practice, however, medical data are fundamentally large 3D volumes. Individual 2D slices matter for review, but a complete and accurate volumetric reconstruction is often essential for downstream tasks such as precise tumor volume assessment, surgical planning, and tracking disease progression over time. Translating the success of 2D diffusion-based solvers to 3D is difficult: because of the curse of dimensionality, the memory, computational, and data requirements of training a diffusion prior directly on volumetric data are prohibitive for most academic and even industrial labs. A common and practical workaround is to train a diffusion model on 2D slices and apply this 2D prior slice by slice to reconstruct the volume.

This workaround eases the training burden but creates a critical new problem: the reconstructed volumes lack consistency along the third dimension (the z-axis). Because each slice is processed independently during the reverse diffusion process, the intrinsic randomness of the sampling procedure leads to severe inter-slice discontinuities and artifacts, degrading the diagnostic and analytical quality of the stacked volume. Existing remedies have important drawbacks. The most direct one augments the 2D prior with a hand-crafted regularizer such as total variation, applied in an additional optimization step to enforce smoothness between adjacent slices. This is effective, but it introduces sensitive hyperparameters that require careful tuning, can over-smooth the volume or produce cartoon-like textures that erase fine diagnostic details, and acts as an external correction that masks the symptoms rather than addressing the intrinsic cause. More principled approaches try to learn a more complete 3D prior, for instance by training on 3D patches or by combining priors from two perpendicular 2D planes, but they increase the complexity of the training or inference pipeline and may impose constraints on the data, such as requiring cubic volumes.

A similar discontinuity arises in video restoration, where applying a pre-trained 2D image diffusion model to video inverse problems often produces temporal flickering across frames. Prior work attributed this flickering to the uncoordinated stochasticity inherent in diffusion sampling and alleviated it by synchronizing the stochastic noise components across frames. Whether the same mechanism is the fundamental cause of inter-slice inconsistency in 3D medical reconstruction, and how such a remedy would transfer from video to volumetric medical data, remains open.

This raises the following questions. How does the stochasticity of independent slice-wise sampling give rise to inter-slice inconsistency when 2D diffusion priors are used for 3D medical reconstruction? Is it possible to enhance inter-slice consistency directly within the diffusion sampling process itself, obviating the need for external, artifact-inducing optimization, ideally without new loss terms, additional sensitive hyperparameters, model retraining, or extra computational cost, so that the remedy could be dropped into existing 2D diffusion-based 3D reconstruction pipelines? And can inter-slice consistency be improved while preserving the natural anatomical variation between slices and fine diagnostic details, rather than trading them away for smoothness?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: slice synchronization via shared noise projection
PROPOSAL: We will apply a 2D diffusion-based solver to 3D volumetric MRI data, but instead of processing each slice independently, we will sample each slice from a shared noise distribution that is projected onto the current state of the solver, thus ensuring consistency between the slices. We will test two variants: one where the shared noise is static across all slices, and one where it is dynamic and updated at each step.
CONTROLS: We compare our proposed slice synchronization method to (1) a naive baseline where each slice is processed independently, and (2) an augmented baseline where a total variation regularizer is applied to enforce smoothness between adjacent slices.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The slice synchronization method should improve upon the naive baseline in terms of inter-slice consistency, with the dynamic noise variant performing better than the static one. However, it may also trade off some of the fine diagnostic details due to the constraint imposed by the shared noise distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: analyzing stochastic consistency using advanced diffusion diagnostics
PROPOSAL: We will embed advanced diffusion diagnostics into the 2D diffusion-based solver to directly measure the temporal consistency of the sampling process, quantifying the correlation between adjacent slices and identifying potential sources of inter-slice discrepancies. By comparing these diagnostics across different variants of the solver, including and without the slice synchronization method proposed in our previous experiment, we will analyze the mechanism behind inter-slice inconsistency and provide a deeper understanding of its origin.
CONTROLS: The baseline for our diagnostics will be the existing implementation of the 2D diffusion-based solver without any additional modifications.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The advanced diffusion diagnostics are expected to uncover the inherent stochasticity and its effects on slice consistency, supporting evidence for the potential benefits of our proposed slice synchronization method. However, inconsistent results might challenge our current assumptions and necessitate a reevaluation of the underlying problem.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating 3d patch-based diffusion priors in a 2d+1 framework
PROPOSAL: We will adapt the 2D diffusion-based solver to operate within a 2D+1 framework, where each 2D slice is augmented with a per-pixel description of the slice's spatial relationship to adjacent slices in the 3D volume. This framework will be used to train a set of 2D diffusion priors, each conditioned on 3D patches of volume data. During inference, the 2D diffusion model will use the spatial relationship descriptions to predict a clean image slice that is consistent with adjacent slices.
CONTROLS: We compare our 2D+1 framework with the naive baseline of applying a unconditioned 2D diffusion model to each slice independently, and with a 3D diffusion-based solver that has been trained directly on volume data.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method is expected to improve upon the naive baseline by leveraging the spatial relationships between slices, but may inherently require large amounts of memory and computational resources due to the need to compute and store the per-pixel spatial relationships. If we're lucky, it might challenge the effectiveness of our proposed slice synchronization method.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: analyzing stochastic consistency using advanced diffusion diagnostics
PROPOSAL: We will extend our experimental setup in this proposal to also include 3D diffusion-based solvers with and without slice-wise stochastic synchronization, and compare the consistency metrics across these setups. Furthermore, we will use the advanced diffusion diagnostics to analyze the origin and propagation of inter-slice discrepancies in both 2D and 3D diffusion-based solvers, providing further insights into the mechanism behind inter-slice inconsistency.
CONTROLS: The baseline for our diagnostics will be the existing implementation of 2D and 3D diffusion-based solvers without any additional modifications or synchronization.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By combining our previous experiments, we will gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between stochastic consistency and inter-slice inconsistency in diffusion-based solvers, and validate our observations on a more comprehensive set of solvers, ultimately strengthening our proposal for slice synchronization.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: analyzing stochastic consistency using advanced diffusion diagnostics
PROPOSAL: We will extend our experimental setup in this proposal to also include 3D diffusion-based solvers with and without slice-wise stochastic synchronization, and compare the consistency metrics across these setups. Furthermore, we will use the advanced diffusion diagnostics to analyze the origin and propagation of inter-slice discrepancies in both 2D and 3D diffusion-based solvers, providing further insights into the mechanism behind inter-slice inconsistency.
CONTROLS: The baseline for our diagnostics will be the existing implementation of 2D and 3D diffusion-based solvers without any additional modifications or synchronization. We will also compare our results to a phase of the experiment where the synchronization is delayed, illustrating the dynamic nature of the synchronization improvement.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By combining our previous experiments, we will gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between stochastic consistency and inter-slice inconsistency in diffusion-based solvers, and validate our observations on a more comprehensive set of solvers, ultimately strengthening our proposal for slice synchronization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adaptive temporal filtering for stabilized diffusion reconstruction
PROPOSAL: We will explore the integration of adaptive temporal filtering techniques into the diffusion-based reconstruction framework to stabilize and smooth out the variations caused by stochastic sampling, aiming to reduce inter-slice inconsistency. This approach will involve incorporating a learnable filter capable of adaptively attenuating or amplifying temporal frequencies in the diffused signal, based on image characteristics such as multi-scale texture and gradient fields.

Proteins realize their biological functions through intricate three-dimensional conformations, and predicting such structures has long been a central challenge in computational biology. AlphaFold2 marked a breakthrough by combining multiple sequence alignments with geometric constraints in an end-to-end framework, achieving near-experimental accuracy. Building on this foundation, AlphaFold3 reformulates the architecture into an all-atom framework and introduces a diffusion-based structure module, thereby enabling the generative modeling of not only proteins but also a wide spectrum of biomolecular complexes. Consequently, this series of models is widely adopted as a family of foundation models for downstream applications such as virtual screening and protein design. However, AlphaFold3's architecture, which relies on iterative Pairformer recycling and multi-step diffusion, requires substantially greater computational overhead than AlphaFold2, restricting its accessibility in downstream workflows.

More specifically, on long sequences the execution time of AlphaFold3 is measured in minutes, which severely limits its usability in downstream tasks that demand high throughput. For instance, small-scale laboratory screening often requires predictions for thousands of candidates, and when extended to large public databases this number grows to an infeasible scale; protein design tasks typically involve comparable computational demand. Previous work has attempted to mitigate this by manually reducing the number of recycling iterations on simpler structures, thus trading accuracy for efficiency. However, such compromises inevitably degrade predictive performance. Moreover, in hallucination-based design approaches, the multistep iterative refinement process hinders feasible gradient backpropagation, ultimately preventing the broader community from adopting AlphaFold3 as a foundation model for diverse applications.

To accelerate the diffusion process, recent advances in generative modeling have explored high-order solvers and consistency models. While high-order solvers improve efficiency, they rarely reduce the number of sampling steps below ten. Consistency models, on the other hand, have achieved remarkable success in image generation and have benefited from refined training schedules. However, transferring them to an AlphaFold3-style architecture raises two difficulties. First, standard consistency schedules assume fixed-dimensional data and pair timesteps at a constant Euclidean interval, which does not accommodate variable protein sequence lengths: on long sequences even a small step can trigger a drastic distribution shift that demands an unrealistic predictive leap, while on short sequences the same interval provides only a weak learning signal, so training dynamics can become unstable or collapse. Second, the iterative diffusion sampler is not the only source of iteration: the architecture also refines its internal pair and single representations through repeated recycling of the Pairformer trunk, whose cost grows with sequence length and which conventional diffusion-acceleration methods do not address at all.

The open problem is therefore whether an AlphaFold3-class all-atom biomolecular structure generator can be compressed into a predictor that runs in essentially a single forward pass -- removing both the multi-step denoising and the recycling overhead -- while retaining the accuracy of the full iterative model on protein, protein-ligand and nucleic-acid complexes. This matters because accuracy alone is not what blocks adoption: throughput and differentiability do. A useful accelerated model must remain reliable in the tail, not merely on average, since high-throughput screening and design pipelines discard most candidates and are harmed more by occasional implausible structures than by small average losses; it must stay cheap enough to be called thousands of times; and it must be light enough that gradients can be propagated through it, so that design methods which optimize sequences against a folding model become feasible with an all-atom model rather than only with earlier, cheaper architectures. Given this problem, how should one design experiments to establish whether such an acceleration is achievable without a loss of predictive fidelity?

Transformers, powered by attention mechanisms, have become the default backbone for sequence modeling across language, vision, speech, and decision making. Their success is often linked to selective access to an ever-growing key-value cache while retaining parallel training and inference. In large language models, this selective ability, composed across multiple attention layers and residual pathways, supports long-range memory retrieval and the algorithmic behaviors associated with in-context learning (for example induction heads and pattern completion), as shown by empirical and mechanistic studies.

Causal softmax attention combines strong selectivity with parallel efficiency: at each step it forms a distribution over past indices and mixes their values, while all steps can be computed in parallel. Given queries, keys and values $Q,K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}$ with rows $q_t$, $k_i$, $v_i$, define masked scores $s_{t,i}=q_t^\top k_i/\sqrt{d}$ for $i\le t$ and $-\infty$ otherwise, and set $\alpha_{t,\cdot}=\mathrm{softmax}(s_{t,\cdot})$, a probability distribution over $\{1,\dots,t\}$. The step-$t$ read is $o_t=\sum_{i\le t}\alpha_{t,i}v_i$, which lies in the convex hull of $\{v_1,\dots,v_t\}$; stacking all steps yields $O=AV$ with $A_{t,i}=\alpha_{t,i}$, so a single matrix multiply produces all outputs.

This convex-mixture view explains the efficiency of attention, but it also reveals a dilemma between lossless storage and lossy processing. The key-value cache stores the full context, but the read is lossy: each head applies the same weights to all coordinates of $v_i$, so the output lies in the convex hull of the stored values and all channels are synchronized. As a result, even simple per-channel indexing, such as returning $(v_{i_1,1},\dots,v_{i_D,D})$ where each coordinate $j$ is taken from its own past index $i_j$ (for example, a coordinate-wise argmax), cannot be represented unless all chosen indices coincide. This limitation hinders Transformers in long-range modeling with non-sequential or irregular timestep indexing, and in tasks where channel-wise structure is critical, such as multivariate time series modeling.

Most recent advances in attention aim to improve expressivity and efficiency, typically by designing richer selection distributions while still reading values through a token-separable linear combination. These include sparse attention patterns, low-rank projections, and kernelizable variants with normalization or gating. Efficiency-oriented work accelerates attention through factorized implementations, or replaces the cache with streaming state space models and recurrent networks that keep a fixed-size state. Across these lines, computation becomes faster or the distribution richer, but the read remains a linear mix: channels share weights, and even simple per-channel indexing cannot be realized in one step. Some recent works explore more complex combinations, such as nonlinear mixing or hard/top-k selection, yet these mainly target training stability or accuracy in specific cases and do not address the lossy-processing limitation.

This leaves an open problem: how can the read of an attention-style sequence mixer be redesigned to remove this linear read bottleneck and support per-channel, context-dependent selection from memory, so that different channels can retrieve different past indices in the same step, while keeping causal parallelism and the asymptotic time complexity of the underlying selection mechanism (for example, quadratic in sequence length for softmax attention and linear for linear-time variants)? And does closing this gap between lossless storage and lossy processing translate into better sequence modeling in practice?

Traditional multimodal models are typically divided into two categories: multimodal understanding (e.g., answering questions about images) and multimodal generation (e.g., generating images from text prompts). Unified Multimodal Generative Models (UMGMs) aim to integrate these two capabilities within a single framework. Recent UMGMs have demonstrated strong performance on a wide range of tasks, such as visual question answering, image captioning, visual reasoning, classification, reading comprehension, and image generation. They typically embed multiple input types into a shared representation space and use one single autoregressive transformer backbone to model cross-modal interactions, so that the same model produces both textual and visual outputs. Training generally follows a two-stage paradigm: pretraining focused on text-image alignment, followed by fine-tuning for specific downstream tasks, where instruction tuning (fine-tuning on diverse, task-specific instructions paired with expected outputs) has become a widely adopted strategy for aligning model behavior with human intent.

Although UMGMs show impressive zero-shot performance on many unseen instructions, their effectiveness is inconsistent across tasks, particularly when the relevant task data is absent from the pretraining corpus. Adding new task data to the training set can substantially improve performance on those tasks, but because novel multimodal tasks keep emerging, repeatedly merging new data and retraining the model is computationally expensive and impractical. This calls for ways to let UMGMs adapt flexibly and efficiently over time, in line with the principles of continual learning, where models acquire new capabilities incrementally.

Studies in continual learning have shown that sequentially fine-tuned models suffer from catastrophic forgetting: a model fine-tuned on new tasks tends to forget or overwrite previously acquired knowledge. Several works have explored continual instruction tuning for multimodal large language models, with methods that are typically regularization-based, architecture-based, replay-based, or prompt-based, and mixture-of-experts adapters have also attracted growing attention in continual learning for their scalability and modularity. However, these multimodal models produce language-only outputs, so prior research has focused exclusively on multimodal understanding tasks such as visual question answering, and existing methods address only intra-modal catastrophic forgetting, where old tasks, new tasks, and pre-trained capabilities all belong to the same output modality, typically text. This assumption holds for multimodal models with unimodal outputs, but it is insufficient for UMGMs, which generate both text and images from a single backbone. For UMGMs, forgetting may occur not only within a modality (intra-modal) but also across modalities (inter-modal): for example, continually tuning the model on a sequence of multimodal understanding tasks might erode its pre-trained image generation ability. This inter-modal forgetting remains largely unexplored, and it is unclear whether methods designed for the intra-modal setting can handle both forms of forgetting at once.

The central question is therefore: can UMGMs continually acquire new capabilities through instruction tuning without suffering catastrophic forgetting, both within a modality (e.g., multimodal understanding) and across modalities (e.g., improving multimodal understanding while preserving visual generation)? Answering it requires establishing whether inter-modal forgetting actually occurs in UMGMs, explaining what causes it, and finding an efficient way to adapt these models to new tasks that retains performance on earlier tasks as well as the pre-trained capabilities of the other modality.

The multi-objective multi-armed bandit problem generalizes the classical, single-objective multi-armed bandit to settings with multiple, potentially conflicting objectives. Pulling an arm yields a vector of objective-specific rewards, so a single "best" arm is often ill-defined and optimality must account for trade-offs across objectives. The setting of interest here is the multi-objective linear contextual bandit: at each round, every arm of a finite set is described by a d-dimensional context vector, which may be chosen adversarially; each of the L objectives has its own fixed but unknown parameter vector; and the agent, after choosing an arm, observes an L-dimensional reward vector whose entry for each objective is the inner product of the arm's context with that objective's parameter, plus zero-mean sub-Gaussian noise.

One simple way to handle trade-offs is scalarization, which maps reward vectors to a scalar via, for example, weighted sums, minimax, or other nonlinear transforms, thereby reducing the problem to a single-objective bandit. However, selecting a suitable scalarization is itself nontrivial, and an arm that is optimal under one scalarization can be markedly suboptimal under another. An alternative is to reason directly in the vector space via Pareto optimality: the Pareto front comprises the arms whose mean reward vectors are not dominated component-wise by that of any other arm. Because it compares reward vectors objective-wise, Pareto optimality is more general than committing to a fixed scalarization. Performance is then usually measured by the Pareto regret, which sums over rounds the smallest uniform increase that would make the mean reward vector of the chosen arm non-dominated.

Prior work on Pareto regret in multi-objective bandits proposes and studies upper-confidence-bound (UCB) algorithms, which typically compute an empirical Pareto front at every round and are therefore complex. Approaches that identify the Pareto front by eliminating arms do not carry over to the contextual setting, where the Pareto front changes with the contexts and an arm discarded early may later be Pareto optimal. By contrast, the Pareto regret of Thompson Sampling has not been studied for multi-objective bandits: the only Thompson Sampling algorithm proposed for this problem comes without theoretical analysis, and the analyses of randomized scalarization in multi-objective Bayesian optimization concern the Bayesian regret under a known Gaussian prior, with bounds that increase with the number of objectives. This gap is noteworthy: in many single-objective contextual and non-contextual bandits, Thompson Sampling and its variants are empirically competitive with or superior to UCB methods, yet their worst-case (frequentist) analyses are typically more delicate. Extending Thompson Sampling to several objectives introduces additional challenges, including coordinating randomized samples across multiple objectives, ensuring optimism of the randomized estimates across all objectives simultaneously, and handling the possibility of multiple Pareto-optimal arms.

A second issue concerns the performance measure itself. The standard Pareto regret compares per-round mean reward vectors; consequently, a policy that plays only Pareto-optimal arms incurs zero Pareto regret, even when an alternative selection of arms over the same number of rounds would yield strictly larger cumulative rewards in every objective. Pareto regret therefore does not distinguish between policies that obtain different cumulative rewards while selecting only Pareto-optimal arms, and the resulting shortfall can grow with the number of rounds.

This raises two questions. First, can a computationally efficient, Thompson Sampling-type randomized algorithm for the multi-objective linear contextual bandit be designed with worst-case Pareto regret guarantees, how close can these guarantees come to those known for randomized algorithms in the single-objective linear setting, and how must they depend on the number of objectives? Second, how should optimality and regret be defined in this setting so that they also account for cumulative rewards under repeated selections, penalizing policies that are Pareto optimal round by round but inefficient in aggregate?

Reinforcement learning has been highly effective in many domains, ranging from robotics to gaming and recommender systems. Value-based algorithms such as Deep Q-Networks are a cornerstone of off-policy reinforcement learning and are widely used in discrete action spaces because of their simplicity, training stability, and sample-efficiency. However, they rely on estimating Q-values for individual state-action pairs and require a maximization over the action space, both to derive the greedy policy and to evaluate the best next-state value in the Bellman target. This maximization is straightforward when the actions can be enumerated, but in continuous action spaces evaluating the Q-value over the entire action space becomes computationally infeasible, which has traditionally restricted value-based methods to discrete actions.

In continuous control, actor-critic methods such as DDPG, TD3, and SAC are typically used instead: a critic is trained on off-policy data to estimate Q-values, and an actor (policy) is trained to output actions that maximize the critic. While powerful, these methods often suffer from instability caused by the coupled training of actor and critic, from sensitivity to hyperparameters, and from the difficulty of predicting in high-dimensional action spaces. The additional actor network brings its own hyperparameters, which makes reproducibility a challenge, and adds computational and memory overhead. Moreover, an actor trained by gradient ascent on the Q-function landscape can only find locally optimal actions, which becomes a serious limitation when the Q-function is complex or non-convex, for instance when the action space is constrained so that actions must remain within specific safety bounds. Training several actors to explore different modes of the Q-function alleviates this, but adds computational overhead and inference-time latency, and the actor's parameterization may still be too limited to capture complex optimal actions.

Actor-free, value-based alternatives must instead carry out the maximization over continuous actions themselves, and finding the maximizing action has been their primary bottleneck. Methods that perform this maximization numerically, through mixed-integer programming, the cross-entropy method and other sampling-based or evolutionary search, or gradient ascent on the action, tend either to return suboptimal local maxima or to be computationally impractical, and sampling becomes progressively less efficient as the action dimension grows. Discretizing the action space is effective in low dimensions but does not scale to high-dimensional tasks. Another line of work restricts the functional form of the Q-function so that its maximizer can be obtained directly, for example by assuming that the advantage is quadratic in the action or that the Q-function is convex in the action; such assumptions limit expressivity and practical applicability. Representing the Q-function with a radial basis function output layer makes the best action easier to identify, but introduces an implicit trade-off between how expressive the Q-function can be in modeling multiple local optima and how accurately its maximizing action is recovered.

This raises the question of whether an actor-free, value-based algorithm can efficiently and accurately select optimal actions in continuous action spaces without imposing restrictive assumptions on the shape of the Q-function, while remaining stable to train, robust across diverse tasks, and scalable to high-dimensional action spaces. Such an algorithm would retain the simplicity of Q-learning and avoid the cost and instability of learning a separate actor; it could also avoid the local optima that trap gradient-based actors when the Q-function is highly non-convex, as in constrained action spaces. Can such an approach be made competitive with established actor-critic methods for continuous control, and can it outperform them where gradient-based action maximization struggles?

Deep neural networks trained with first-order optimization methods have achieved remarkable empirical success across diverse domains. Despite their widespread adoption, a rigorous theoretical understanding of their optimization dynamics and generalization behavior remains incomplete, particularly for networks with ReLU activations. The difficulty stems from the non-smoothness and non-convexity of the loss landscape induced by ReLU activations and network architectures, which complicate classical analyses. Intriguingly, over-parameterized models often reach zero training error and still generalize well in the absence of explicit regularization, a phenomenon that has spurred substantial theoretical research into its underlying mechanisms.

A prominent line of research analyzes neural network training through the neural tangent kernel (NTK). In the infinite-width limit, the dynamics of gradient descent (GD) can be characterized by functions in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of the NTK, and convergence guarantees have been established for both shallow and deep networks: provided the width is sufficiently large, GD converges to a global minimum within a neighborhood of its initialization. In this regime, generalization errors of order $L\sqrt{\mathbf{y}^\top(\mathbf{H}^\infty)^{-1}\mathbf{y}/n}$ have been obtained for networks of depth $L$ trained on $n$ examples, where $\mathbf{H}^\infty$ denotes the NTK Gram matrix over the training data, but only for widths polynomial in $n$, $L$ and $1/\lambda_0$, with $\lambda_0$ the smallest eigenvalue of $\mathbf{H}^\infty$. Requiring $\lambda_0>0$ is a strong assumption, because this eigenvalue tends to zero as the size of the training set grows. A weaker assumption is that the data are separable by the NTK features at initialization with a margin $\gamma$. Under this assumption, a logarithmic width suffices for two-layer ReLU networks, with a risk bound of order $1/(\gamma^2\sqrt{n})$ derived from Rademacher complexity; this width result relies on the 1-homogeneity of two-layer ReLU networks, a property that does not hold for deep networks. Extensions to deep ReLU networks yield bounds that still decay only as $1/\sqrt{n}$ and contain either factors exponential in depth, such as $4^L$, or additional width-dependent terms. A rate of order $1/(\gamma^2 n)$ has so far been derived only for two-layer ReLU networks. More generally, uniform-convergence analyses based on Rademacher complexity or covering numbers can lead to vacuous bounds, typically depend exponentially on the depth, and usually yield rates of order $1/\sqrt{n}$.

A complementary line of research relies on algorithmic stability. Building on the observation that the spectral norm of the Hessian of wide networks scales with the width $m$ as $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{m})$, stability analyses have obtained bounds of order $\widetilde{O}(1/(n\gamma^2))$ for shallow networks, which is almost optimal in view of known lower bounds, and have been extended to deep networks with bounds of order $\widetilde{O}(e^{O(L)}/(n\gamma^2))$. These analyses, however, assume smooth activation functions and cannot be applied to non-smooth ReLU networks; for deep networks, they also incur an exponential dependence on depth, both in the bound and in the required width.

In summary, existing results either exhibit the suboptimal $1/\sqrt{n}$ dependence on the sample size, are restricted to shallow networks, require smooth activations, or depend exponentially on the depth $L$. A natural and fundamental question is therefore whether GD on deep ReLU networks can achieve generalization rates comparable to the minimax optimal rates established in the kernel setting, namely the SVM-type rate of order $1/(n\gamma^2)$. Specifically, for fully connected deep ReLU networks trained by gradient descent with the logistic loss on binary classification data that are NTK-separable with margin $\gamma$: Can risk bounds of the optimal order $1/(\gamma^2 n)$ be established? Can the exponential dependence on the depth $L$ be replaced by a polynomial dependence $\mathrm{poly}(L)$? And how much over-parameterization (network width) do such guarantees require?

Neurons operate in ways that reflect their cell type, connectivity, and the brain region in which they are embedded. Understanding how these structural and physiological factors shape neural activity is an important open question and is central to modern theories of neural function. Cell type- and circuit-specific effects are also increasingly implicated in neurological disorders: particular neuronal subtypes can be selectively affected in neurodegenerative disease, and neuron subtypes can be targeted to improve efficacy in real time in closed-loop brain stimulation. Together, these directions highlight a broader need to understand how features such as cell type and brain region contribute to a neuron's role in the brain, motivating the development of methods that can extract aspects of neuron identity.

Much of what is known about neuronal cell types and their connectivity comes from molecular, anatomical, and morphological labeling techniques that tag neurons based on gene expression profiles or structural features. These approaches have revealed a rich taxonomy of neuronal classes, but they are resource intensive and typically provide only a sparse labeling of one or a few classes at a time, so identity labels are costly and difficult to obtain at scale. There is currently no molecular access to different cell types or projection classes in nonhuman primates and humans, which has created major roadblocks in studying neuron diversity in humans. For these reasons, there is growing interest in methods that can infer aspects of neuronal identity directly from large-scale neural population activity.

Deep learning approaches to this question have only recently begun to be explored. Early methods relied on intrinsic single-neuron features such as waveform shape or interspike interval profiles, but these signals capture only part of what distinguishes one neuron from another. More recent approaches incorporate some information about the ongoing population activity, but reduce the surrounding activity to fixed low-dimensional summaries, which obscures the fine-grained coordination patterns that are often key to neuronal identity. Furthermore, these models usually require retraining or finetuning on each new set of neurons, limiting their ability to generalize in a zero-shot manner across animals.

Making use of population context is itself challenging. The number of recorded neurons varies widely across experiments, individuals, and sessions, making it non-trivial to define a consistent input structure or population-level operation, and recordings span multiple experimental conditions, including different stimuli and behaviors, which makes it hard for a model to generalize across recording sessions. These limitations point to the need for methods that leverage rich population context while producing neuron-level representations that transfer robustly across recordings.

This raises several questions. Can a representation of each individual neuron be learned from population activity, when identity labels are scarce, such that it captures aspects of the neuron's identity such as its cell type and brain region? Can such representations transfer to entirely new sessions and animals without retraining or additional metadata? And how does the identity information they capture depend on the amount and diversity of recordings available for learning, compared with the number of labeled neurons?

Inverse problems arise in many domains, including computer vision, protein science, medical imaging and scientific computing. The goal is to reconstruct an unknown signal x ∈ R^n from noisy measurements y ∈ R^m, with y = A(x) + η, where A is a known forward operator and η is additive measurement noise. Diffusion models have recently shown powerful capabilities in modeling complex data distributions, and they provide a powerful class of priors for high-dimensional data, such as natural images, when solving inverse problems.

Methods for solving inverse problems fall broadly into two families. Maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference seeks the single most probable x: it delivers fast optimization, but struggles with high noise and multimodal posteriors and easily converges to local minima. The Bayesian alternative samples from the posterior p(x|y) ∝ p(x) p(y|x) to generate plausible reconstructions, quantify uncertainty and handle multimodality. Both critically depend on a powerful prior, such as a pretrained diffusion model, that encodes the complex statistical structure of the data.

Although diffusion-based solvers have shown remarkable success across diverse inverse problems, current methods suffer from three complementary limitations. (1) Iterative guidance methods, such as DPS, DDRM, DDNM, ΠGDM and TMPD, try to sample the intermediate posteriors p(x_t|y) along the reverse diffusion, which requires the intractable likelihood p(y|x_t) at every intermediate timestep. They approximate it, for example through Tweedie's formula, and apply likelihood-gradient corrections directly to the intermediate states. Because such gradients generally contain components orthogonal to the data manifold, these corrections systematically push the intermediate states off the learned manifold and violate the training-time noise conditioning of the denoiser, leading to failed reconstructions such as accumulated artifacts; even second-order corrections of the guidance trajectory still modify intermediate states and risk drifting off the manifold. (2) Stochastic MAP methods that optimize in image space, such as ReSample, DiffPIR, DAPS, SITCOM and DIIP, can match the measurements well with very sharp details, but they require carefully tuned hyperparameters to avoid overfitting to noise, which limits their effectiveness when the noise is high or unknown. Some of them are formulated as posterior samplers yet use a heuristic measurement-noise level much smaller than the true one to strengthen measurement consistency, which makes them effectively MAP-like and equally sensitive to noise. (3) Deterministic MAP methods that optimize over the diffusion model's input noise, such as DMPlug, remove randomness but are sensitive to measurement noise and, lacking posterior exploration, often get stuck in a single mode, especially in severely ill-posed problems such as phase retrieval. Early stopping can limit noise overfitting, but its criterion is task- and noise-dependent, and at high noise levels the optimizer often becomes trapped in a local mode anyway. In short, enforcing data consistency in the middle of the diffusion process can break adherence to the prior, while optimizing only for fidelity leads to overfitting or mode collapse.

These failure modes point to two requirements. A solver should maintain manifold feasibility: the states it feeds to the pretrained denoiser should remain close to the high-probability manifold of the corresponding noise level, so that the final reconstruction lies on the learned data manifold. At the same time, it should explore the posterior well enough to escape spurious local modes, rather than collapsing onto the mode nearest to its initialization.

A further practical difficulty is that the level, and even the type, of measurement noise is often unknown and may not be Gaussian, which makes the likelihood term itself intractable. Existing methods handle this with tunable hyperparameters that control the strength of the likelihood term, or with task-specific early-stopping criteria, typically tuned for one particular type and level of noise; they must therefore be re-tuned for each task, dataset and noise level, which is impractical when the noise is unknown.

This raises the following questions. How can a pretrained diffusion prior be used to sample from the posterior of an inverse problem without approximating intractable intermediate likelihoods and without ever feeding off-manifold states to the denoiser? How can such a sampler explore the solution space well enough to avoid spurious local modes in severely ill-posed, multimodal problems, so that its reconstructions do not depend on the initialization? Can it be robust to measurement noise, in the sense that its reconstructions do not overfit the noise, without hand-tuned regularization weights or early stopping? And can it handle measurement noise of unknown level and type with a single fixed set of hyperparameters across tasks, datasets and noise levels, at a computational cost that remains practical?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: dynamic consistency and manifold preservation
PROPOSAL: Develop a method called Dynamic Consistency and Manifold Preservation (DCMP), which iteratively updates the diffusion guidance process by matching the intermediate states to the manifold — instead of directly feeding them back to the denoiser. First, we use the learned denoiser to define a manifold — where data likelihood is high — by calculating the mean of the denoiser output for a range of noise inputs. Then, at each timestep, we check if the guidance signal differs significantly from the manifold. If it does, we re-align the guidance trajectory to be closer to the manifold. This should maintain the learned data distribution, avoiding drift off the manifold and guaranteeing manifold feasibility.
CONTROLS: Compare against DPS and DDRM.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: DCMP should significantly reduce the off-manifold drift seen in current methods and maintain reliable reconstructions, even at high noise levels. A minor issue could be that manual tuning of parameters for DCMP would be needed for different noise distributions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: uncertainty-aware reconstruction guidance
PROPOSAL: Introduce an uncertainty-aware variant of the guidance process, Uncertainty-Aware Reconstruction Guidance (UARG), by modelling and learning the compact uncertainty via an ensemble of diffusion models, each with a distinct noise schedule. During the guidance process, we draw samples from the distributions output by the ensemble, and combine them to inform the reconstruction guidance signal. This approach can estimate and incorporate the uncertainty, adapting the guidance process to the inherent uncertainty in the posterior and, consequently, escape spurious modes more effectively.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard guidance methods, and assess the impact of ensemble size on performance.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: UARG would have improved performance over standard guidance methods for challenging inverse problems, but careful ensemble size and model selection could be required, while estimating uncertainty could increase computational cost.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: probabilistic forward mappings
PROPOSAL: To address the intractable likelihoods, develop Probabilistic Forward Mappings (PFM), a probabilistic, invertible, and differentiable approximation of the forward operator A. We achieve this by training a probabilistic neural network that maps the true forward operator to a Gaussian process, allowing us to treat the forward operator as a probabilistic function and comptuted the likelihoods, p(y|x), in closed-form. PFM can be efficiently inverted to produce samples from the intractable forward process.
CONTROLS: Compare against approximate likelihood methods (e.g. Tweedie's formula) and assess the impact of model capacity on performance.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: PFM should provide accurate approximations of the likelihoods without adding additional hyperparameters or prior knowledge, but the performance would heavily depend on the choice of model and capacities.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: uncertainty-aware reconstruction guidance
PROPOSAL: Revising the previous proposal, introduce Uncertainty-Aware Reconstruction Guidance (UARG), but with an additional regularization term that encourages the ensemble of diffusion models to be consistent with the probabilistic forward mappings (PFM) - leading to a framework that simultaneously model the uncertainty of the inverse posterior, and approximates the intractable likelihoods in a probabilistic manner. This synergy can help the guidance process to dichotomize from potential spurious modes more effectively and estimate the noise level adaptively.
CONTROLS: Compare against UARG without the regularization term, standard guidance methods, and assess the impact of model capacity on performance.
COST: 450 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised UARG should improve upon both UARG and PFM individually, offering a more comprehensive approach to uncertainty modelling and probabilistic likelihoods estimation, with the potential downside of increased computational cost.

ACTION: REVISE
 NUMBER: 2
 TITLE: uncertainty-aware reconstruction guidance
PROPOSAL: Revising the previous proposal, introduce Uncertainty-Aware Reconstruction Guidance (UARG), but with an additional emphasis on robustness to noise levels - by learning a noise-adaptive versioning of the guidance process, which monitors the current noise level and weighs its contribution accordingly. To achieve this, we use a neural network that takes both the guidance state and the estimated noise level as inputs and outputs a noise-adaptive guidance signal. This approach can help the guidance process to adapt to the uncertainty in the noise, leveraging this learned noise robustness to supervise spurious modes and produce more accurate reconstructions.
CONTROLS: Compare against UARG without the noise-adaptive term, standard guidance methods, and assess the impact of noise level estimation accuracy on performance.
COST: 375 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised UARG should reduce the need for hand-tuning regularization weights and early stopping, and improve noise robustness, but may increase computational cost due to the additional neural network component.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adaptive diffusion guidance sampling
PROPOSAL: Develop an adaptive sampling method, Adaptive Diffusion Guidance Sampling (ADGS), which dynamically selects the most informative samples from the guided diffusion process, allowing for an efficient exploration of the solution space while maintaining a constrained number of samples. By iteratively Assessing the Information Content (AIC) of the samples and dynamically sampling from the intermediate posteriors, we can estimate which samples contribute most significantly to the reconstruction, and reserve computation resources accordingly.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard sampling methods (e.g. Independent Sampling, Sequential Sampling) and assess the impact of hyperparameters on performance.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ADGS should improve the efficiency of the sampling process while maintaining accurate reconstructions, but its effectiveness might depend heavily on the choice of AIC metric and the specific inverse problem at hand.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: inference-time model distillation
PROPOSAL: Introduce Inference-Time Model Distillation (ITMD), a technique to reduce the computational resources needed for inference by distilling a large diffusion model into a smaller, more efficient version while preserving the accuracy of the original model. Specifically, we use a knowledge distillation framework with the goal of matching the output probabilities of the original model, while minimizing a metric of similarity between the two models' weights.
CONTROLS: Compare against pruning and quantization methods for model size reduction, and assess the impact of hyperparameters on performance.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ITMD should lead to a significant reduction in computational resources required for inference, without a substantial loss in accuracy, making it feasible to deploy the proposed methods on edge devices and for large-scale real-world applications. However, finding the optimal distillation parameter might be challenging.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: manifold-aware reconstruction uncertainties
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to quantify the reconstruction uncertainty in a probabilistic and mathematically grounded manner, by modeling the output variability of a diffusion-based sampler conditioned on the true forward operator and noise, leading to a lognormal distribution over reconstructions. This estimate can be directly mapped back to the original reconstruction problem, unbiasedly estimating the subtle noise artifacts, ill-posedness of images, providing informative information on reconstruction reliability.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing uncertainty estimation methods (e.g. MC dropout, variational inference) and assess the impact of model capacity on performance.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed method should provide a robust and accurate measure of reconstruction uncertainty, capable of distinguishing between low-confidence regions and more reliable areas, but it may be computationally expensive due to the need to condition on the true forward operator.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 6
TITLE: manifold-aware reconstruction uncertainties
PROPOSAL: Revising the previous proposal, refine the method to estimate manifold-aware reconstruction uncertainties by incorporating the probabilistic forward mappings (PFM) estimates directly within the uncertainty estimation process. This allows us to capture the inductive bias and prior knowledge of the diffusion model to directly inject uncertainty information into the reconstruction uncertainty calculations, leading to a more principled and accurate estimate of uncertainties. Additionally, introduce a novel strategy to actively leverage this uncertainty information to actively correct for errors and spurious modes.
CONTROLS: Compare against the previous manifold-aware uncertainty estimation method and assess the impact of incorporating PFM on performance and computational cost.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The refined method should lead to more accurate uncertainty estimates, and the active correction mechanism should help correct for spurious modes, but it remains to be seen whether the increased complexity and computational costs would be justified.

TITLE: experimentally validating the approach on challenging inverse problems
PROPOSAL: Develop a comprehensive suite of experiments on a diverse set of real-world inverse problems, including image super-resolution, image inpainting, image deblurring, phase retrieval, and high dynamic range (HDR) image reconstruction. Evaluate the proposed methods' performance on these experiments, assessing both quantitative metrics and qualitative visual inspections, and systematically comparing against state-of-the-art methods. Collectively, these experiments should provide a broad validation of the proposed approach's efficacy across various real-world inverse problems.
CONTROLS: Compare against DPS, DDRM, and other state-of-the-art inverse problem solvers on a diverse range of benchmarks.
COST: 5,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The comprehensive experiments should convincingly demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of the proposed methods on challenging real-world inverse problems, showing that the improvements outweigh the increased complexity.

Modern generative paradigms, including diffusion, flow matching and consistency models, have achieved state-of-the-art performance and form the backbone of leading image and video generation systems, including large multi-modal generative models. Despite their success, they share a critical drawback: both training and sampling demand substantial computational resources. Multi-step frameworks such as diffusion and flow matching produce a sample by iteratively integrating a probability-flow ordinary differential equation, typically requiring 40 to 100 network function evaluations (NFEs). The problem is magnified for large-scale models, for which efficient sampling is paramount: the continuous, long-term cost of inference often surpasses the one-time training cost, directly affecting economic viability and practical deployment. For example, the largest open multi-modal image generators (about 20B parameters) typically need about 100 NFEs, i.e. roughly 40 seconds on a single A100 GPU for one 1024×1024 image.

Numerous efforts aim to accelerate generative inference by reducing the number of sampling steps. Early single-step generators such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) often suffered from unstable training dynamics. To accelerate multi-step diffusion models, various distillation techniques have been introduced. They range from student-teacher methods, in which a student learns to reproduce a frozen teacher's sampling trajectory in fewer steps (e.g., progressive distillation, which requires an iterative distillation procedure), to distribution matching distillation (e.g., DMD and DMD2), which uses adversarial-style training with auxiliary networks to align the generator's output distribution directly with the data distribution. In parallel, consistency models and their variants (e.g., LCM and PCM), as well as related shortcut and MeanFlow objectives, have been designed explicitly for high-quality generation in very few steps, and recent work shows that multi-step and few-step models can be cast as instances of a single unified any-step training objective.

Despite this progress, existing few-step methods face a difficult trade-off between simplicity, efficiency and quality. (a) Complexity and instability: adversarial approaches, such as GANs, DMD-style distribution matching and hybrid frameworks that combine teacher guidance with adversarial signals (e.g., SANA-Sprint), require auxiliary trained networks (discriminators or fake-sample score networks) and/or frozen teacher models; distribution matching methods typically keep separate copies of a generator, a real-score model and a fake-score model. This introduces training instability and sensitivity to hyperparameters, and it increases architectural complexity and GPU memory overhead. For ultra-large models, the added complexity often translates into out-of-memory failures or brittle training dynamics, so few-step approaches have rarely been applied to models beyond about 3B parameters, and the only open-source few-step model released for a large model was obtained by distribution matching distillation with its GAN loss removed, an indirect sign of the high cost of adversarial losses at scale. (b) Performance degradation: methods trained without adversarial guidance, such as consistency models, often show a sharp decline in quality at very low NFEs (fewer than 4), and within the unified any-step view, current few-step methods struggle to reach high-quality one-step generation without resorting to a GAN-style loss.

The open problem is therefore how to train a generator that produces high-quality images in a single function evaluation, or very few, without discriminators, auxiliary score networks or frozen teacher models, so that training remains simple, stable and memory-efficient enough to scale to full-parameter training of the largest (10B to 20B parameters) text-to-image and multi-modal generators, without sacrificing the quality obtained by multi-step sampling.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: low-nfe consistency for large multi-modal models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the feasibility of consistency-based models for single-function or very low-NFE generation, by adapting the any-step training objective of [1] to constrain the output of the generator to a function of the input, plus a small, learnable residual. Evaluate the performance of this "residual-constrained" consistency model on a range of large text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard unconditional flow-based model variant, and with a separately-trained student teacher model with 5 iterations of progressive distillation.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The residual-constrained consistency model should provide a quality drop of less than 1.5 points on the MSMFT metric, compared to the unconditional flow-based model, while achieving a reduction in NFEs. However, very large models may still face training instability due to the use of large learnable residuals.

References:
[1] any-step training objective (not specified reference)
[2] DALL-E 2 dataset
[3] MSMFT metric (not specified reference)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adversarial-free distilled sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate a method for distilled sampling without adversarial losses, by computing the output of a given step through a combination of its own knowledge up to that point and the cached output from the preceding steps. Implement this method using a non-adversarial student-teacher approach, where the teacher is a frozen version of the model and the student takes fewer steps to sample an image. Evaluate this "distilled samplifier" on a set of large text-to-image models, using the COCO dataset [4] and the Inception score [5].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard progressive distillation approach and a baseline of the full model taking 5-10 steps.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The distilled samplifier should achieve a quality improvement of more than 1 point in Inception score, even when the teacher model is frozen, while reducing the number of NFEs significantly. However, evaluation metrics may become less reliable at very low NFEs, making quality assessment challenging.

References:
[4] COCO dataset
[5] Inception score

TITLE: adversarial-free distilled sampling (not changed)
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 2 to include an evaluation of the training time of the distilled samplifier, and investigate its impact on model capacity. Add an experiment where the student model and teacher model have the same capacity, but the student is trained with a reduced number of iterations, and another where the student model has a significantly reduced capacity compared to the teacher model, to analyze its effects on training time and inference quality.

PROPOSAL: Modify the architecture of the distilled sampler to use a denoising autoencoder instead of a simple student model, which will allow it to learn the structure of the data distribution directly from the teacher model. This will reduce the need for pre-training the student model and improve its ability to generalize to new input distributions. Evaluate the performance of this "autoencoder-based distilled sampler" on the same COCO dataset [4] and Inception score [5] as before.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: momentum-guided consistency
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new variant of the consistency model, where the generator is trained to produce output that not only matches the input, but also a momentum-buffered version of the input. This momentum buffer is initialized with a value close to zero and updated on each iteration of the training process. Evaluate the performance of this "momentum-guided consistency model" on a range of large text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].

COST: 1100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The momentum-guided consistency model should stabilize the training dynamics and improve the quality of generated images, especially when the input sequence has a strong temporal structure. However, it may increase the number of NFEs required for convergence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: conditional pre-training for low-nfe models
PROPOSAL: Investigate a method to improve the performance of low-NFE models by pre-training them on a large dataset with conditional inputs and then fine-tuning them on a smaller dataset with the target format of images or text. This will allow the model to learn a richer representation of the data distribution and improve its ability to generate high-quality output in a single function evaluation. Evaluate the performance of this "conditionally pre-trained low-NFE model" on a range of text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with unconditional pre-training and the residual-constrained consistency model from proposal 1.
COST: 1600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The conditionally pre-trained low-NFE model should achieve significant improvements in MSMFT score and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, but the fine-tuning stage may require careful hyperparameter tuning to maintain performance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: low-nfe consistency for large multi-modal models
PROPOSAL: Refine the residual-constrained consistency model by splitting the residual into two parts: a shared residual that is conditioned on the input sequence, and a private residual that is specific to each instance of the input sequence. This will allow the model to learn more robust and transferable representations of the data distribution. Evaluate the performance of this "split-residual consistency model" on a range of large text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard unconditional flow-based model variant and the momentum-guided consistency model.
COST: 1300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The split-residual consistency model should achieve improved MSMFT scores and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, especially when evaluated on diverse and out-of-distribution test sets. However, it may be more challenging to train due to the increased complexity of the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: constructive diffusion initialization
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of constructive diffusion initialization to improve the performance of low-NFE models. This involves pre-training a large model using reversible denoising diffusion [6] and then initializing the lower-capacity model with the final stage of the diffusion process. Evaluate the performance of this "constructively initialized low-NFE model" on a range of text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with standard random initialization and the split-residual consistency model from proposal 1.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The constructively initialized low-NFE model should achieve improved MSMFT scores and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, due to the more effective initialization of the model weights. However, it may require careful tuning of the diffusion process and initialization hyperparameters.

Reference:
[6] reversible denoising diffusion

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: attention-augmented low-nfe models
PROPOSAL: Modify the architecture of the low-NFE models by adding self-attention layers to allow for more flexible and adaptive interactions between different parts of the input sequence. This will enable the model to better capture long-range dependencies and generate more coherent and detailed output in a single function evaluation. Evaluate the performance of this "attention-augmented low-NFE model" on a range of text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard model architecture and the split-residual consistency model from proposal 1.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The attention-augmented low-NFE model should achieve improved MSMFT scores and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, especially when the input sequence has complex and long-range dependencies. However, it may be more challenging to train due to the increased complexity of the model and the potential for catastrophic forgetting of important features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: early-stopped multi-sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of early-stopped multi-sampling as a final stage of the inference process for low-NFE models. This involves sampling multiple times from the model, but stopping each sequence at an early stage and using the generated output as the final result. This will allow the model to explore different possible output paths and avoid getting trapped in local minima. Evaluate the performance of this "early-stopped multi-sampling" on a range of text-to-image models, using the DALL-E 2 dataset [2] and the MSMFT metric [3].
CONTROLS: Compare with standard single-sampling and the attention-augmented low-NFE model from proposal 6.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The early-stopped multi-sampling approach should achieve improved MSMFT scores and generate higher-quality images in a single function evaluation, especially when evaluated on sequences with multiple modes or complex structure. However, it may require careful tuning of the early-stopping threshold and sampling schedule to achieve optimal performance.
