ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating baseline models for online video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate a set of strong multimodal model baselines for video step grounding, adapted to process only one video segment at a time. Specifically, we will investigate large-scale multimodal transformer models like CLIP, and recent multimodal variants like OSIM and VisIoL, with a focus on evaluating their zero-shot performance when processing a live video stream one segment at a time. We will measure performance using metrics like accuracy, F1-score, and Hamming loss on real-world video step grounding benchmarks from instructional cooking recipe videos and egocentric procedural activity videos.
CONTROLS: We will compare our zero-shot baseline models to models that have been pre-trained on VSG tasks and fine-tuned on a specific dataset, providing an offline benchmark for comparison. We will also evaluate various ablations of our zero-shot models, including the effect of using different types of multimodal input (e.g., frame, audio, or both) and different window sizes for segmenting video frames. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that competing zero-shot models struggle due to the lack of task-specific information in the model, however strong multimodal models that are not specifically designed for this task can still achieve good performance due to their general-purpose multimodal capabilities, and ablation studies will point towards multimodal input as a key factor for zero-shot performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: adding contextualized embeddings for video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will investigate using contextualized embeddings to improve the performance of online video step grounding. Specifically, we will experiment with using pre-trained BERT-like models to generate text embeddings for the step descriptions, and multimodal transformer models to generate visual embeddings for the video frames. We will then use a common encodings space for the step descriptions and video frames to compute similarity scores. This approach aims to capture the nuances of language and visual context that are crucial for accurately grounding video steps.
CONTROLS: We will control for the quality of the step descriptions by evaluating the RAKE (Rapid Automatic Keyword Extraction) score of the text, and we will compare our contextualized embeddings approach to a baseline model that uses keyword matching between step descriptions and video frames. We will also evaluate the effect of using different quality and quantities of step descriptions on model performance. Compare against the strongest published baseline for this problem, re-run with the same data, tuning budget and evaluation protocol.
COST: 8000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that using contextualized embeddings improves the performance of video step grounding, especially in scenarios where step descriptions have high RAKE scores, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: revising evaluating baseline models for online video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate a set of strong multimodal model baselines for video step grounding, adapted to process only one video segment at a time, focusing on the use of cross-modal learning. Specifically, we will investigate how different cross-modal fusion methods (e.g., concatenation, attention, and late fusion) can improve the zero-shot performance of large-scale multimodal transformer models like CLIP, and recent multimodal variants like OSIM and VisIoL. We will measure performance using metrics like accuracy, F1-score, and Hamming loss on real-world video step grounding benchmarks from instructional cooking recipe videos and egocentric procedural activity videos.
CONTROLS: We will compare our zero-shot baseline models to models that have been pre-trained on VSG tasks and fine-tuned on a specific dataset, providing an offline benchmark for comparison. We will also evaluate various ablations of our zero-shot models, including the effect of using different types of multimodal input (e.g., frame, audio, or both) and different window sizes for segmenting video frames. Additionally, we will control for the impact of cross-modal learning on model performance by adapting the original two-step fine-tuning approach for cross-modal training in online videos. Evaluate all methods on the same held-out test set and report the mean and standard deviation over five seeds.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that cross-modal learning is a key factor for achieving strong zero-shot performance in video step grounding, and that different cross-modal fusion methods perform differently on various VSG tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: improving adding contextualized embeddings for video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will improve our approach to using contextualized embeddings for video step grounding by incorporating attention mechanisms to dynamically weigh the importance of different tokens in both the step descriptions and video frames. Specifically, we will experiment with using multi-head attention to compute attention weights that align the text and visual embeddings, and use these attention weights to fuse the embeddings. We will explore different options for initialising the attention weights, such as using dominant keywords from the step description or learned weights from the model.
CONTROLS: We will compare our improved contextualized embeddings approach to our previous baseline method, and evaluate its performance with different options for initialising the attention weights. Evaluate all methods on the same held-out test set and report the mean and standard deviation over five seeds.
COST: 7000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that our improved contextualized embeddings approach with attention mechanisms outperforms our previous baseline method, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: leveraging semantic graph reasoning for video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will investigate using semantic graph reasoning to reason about the relationship between video segments and step descriptions in video step grounding. Specifically, we will construct a knowledge graph that represents the semantic relationships between entities and actions in the step descriptions, and then use a graph neural network to reason about the relevance of the video segments to the step descriptions. We will evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks and compare it to our contextualized embeddings approach.
CONTROLS: We will control for the quality of the knowledge graph by evaluating the accuracy of the entity and action recognition methods used to construct the graph, and we will compare our graph reasoning approach to a baseline model that uses a simple matching scheme between the step descriptions and video segments. COST: 9000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that semantic graph reasoning can improve the performance of video step grounding by capturing complex relationships between video segments and step descriptions, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of the additional encoder layer on model performance by comparing it to a baseline model with a reduced number of layers, and we will evaluate the effect of different window sizes for segmenting video frames on the performance of our model. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.
COST: 6500
PREDICTION: We expect to find that injecting temporal context improves the performance of our baseline model by capturing the nuances of the video sequence, and that this approach performs well even when the video sequence has a complex structure.

ACTION: REVISE 3

PROPOSAL: We will enhance our approach to using semantic graph reasoning for video step grounding by incorporating a procedure for iteratively refining the knowledge graph and re-reasoning about the relationship between video segments and step descriptions. Specifically, we will experiment with an iterative process that involves re-scoring the relevance of video segments to step descriptions based on the refined knowledge graph, and re-ranking the step descriptions based on their relevance to the video segments. We will evaluate the performance of this approach on real-world video step grounding benchmarks and compare it to our previous graph reasoning approach.
CONTROLS: We will control for the impact of the iterative refinement process on model performance by comparing it to a baseline model that uses a simple matching scheme between the step descriptions and video segments, and we will evaluate the effect of different refinement thresholds on the performance of our model. Include a matched-compute baseline that receives the same training budget and hyperparameter search as the proposed method.
COST: 8500
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the iterative refinement process improves the performance of our graph reasoning approach by capturing more nuanced relationships between video segments and step descriptions, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

PREDICTION: We expect to find that the adaptive fusion mechanism improves the performance of our baseline model by capturing the complex relationships between the visual and language features, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

PREDICTION: We expect to find that our baseline model can achieve good performance with only a few examples, and that the few-shot learning approach improves the sample efficiency of our model without compromising its overall performance.

Many supervised learning algorithms rely on the assumption that training and test data are drawn from the same underlying distribution. In real-world applications this assumption is often violated because of environmental changes, sampling biases or temporal dynamics, which create distribution shifts between training and deployment environments. Such mismatches can cause significant performance degradation and pose a fundamental challenge to reliable generalization in practice.

Among the challenges posed by distribution shifts, this problem concerns unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), with a focus on classification. In UDA, one is given labeled data from a source domain and unlabeled data from a target domain whose distributions are related but not necessarily identical. The discrepancy may come from the marginal distribution of the input, from the conditional distribution of labels given inputs, or from both. The goal is to use the labeled source data and the unlabeled target data to build a predictive model with low risk on the target domain. The most naive baseline, empirical risk minimization on the source data, can perform poorly on the target domain when the two distributions differ.

Two representative families of UDA methods are distribution alignment, which reduces the discrepancy between the source and target domains either in the data space or in a feature space, and pseudo-labeling, which refines target predictions using a source-trained model in the spirit of self-training. Despite their popularity, both families often face practical limitations in two common scenarios. The first is when the amount of unlabeled target data is limited: alignment estimates can then become unreliable and pseudo-labels noisy, which can lead to poor generalization, and the empirical distribution of a small or imbalanced target sample may be a poor estimate of the true target input distribution that fails to capture the diversity of the target domain. The second is when the source data contain spurious correlations, for example when irrelevant features such as background or color are strongly associated with labels: models then tend to rely on these shortcuts, which do not transfer to the target domain and ultimately degrade performance. Alignment-based methods can fail in this situation, and approaches that try to disentangle causal and spurious features with unlabeled target data, through counterfactual consistency, generative interventions or self-training refinements, often rely on strong structural assumptions or are highly sensitive to the quality of the initial pseudo-labels, which makes them fragile when target data are scarce or imbalanced.

Distributionally robust optimization is another line of work on distribution shift: instead of the average loss on the training distribution, it minimizes the worst-case expected loss over an ambiguity set of plausible distributions. Constructing a suitable ambiguity set is the central difficulty, and the inner worst case must remain computationally tractable. Common choices, small Wasserstein or f-divergence balls around the empirical source distribution, give robustness to minor perturbations but are less suitable for structured shifts such as subpopulation shift, where the target contains the same subpopulations as the source with different mixing weights and can therefore lie far from the source in standard distances. Formulations designed for such mixture shifts, such as group distributionally robust optimization, typically assume access to group labels and do not explicitly use unlabeled target data to improve target prediction.

The problem is therefore how to learn, from labeled data coming from one or several source domains and unlabeled target data, a classifier that generalizes to the target domain when unlabeled target data are extremely scarce and when spurious correlations dominate the source domain, without group labels and with a computationally tractable training procedure. How can a learner remain reliable when the few available unlabeled target inputs give a poor picture of the target input distribution, and how can it avoid relying on spurious source features that do not hold in the target domain?

PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of using dimensionality reduction techniques (e.g., PCA, t-SNE) to align the feature spaces of the source and target domains in UDA. Specifically, we will apply dimensionality reduction to the labeled source data and test its transferability to the unlabeled target data, exploring combinations of techniques and hyperparameter settings. We will use the Ladybug and CIFAR-10 datasets for digit recognition, as well as the CelebA dataset for facial attribute classification.

Large language models can be knowledge edited, that is, updated to incorporate new or corrected facts without retraining from scratch. This capability is crucial for keeping models up to date with evolving information and for correcting errors on the fly. Large vision-language models (LVLMs), which combine textual and visual understanding, make knowledge editing even more challenging: they encode factual knowledge in both their textual and their visual pathways, and they require mechanisms that update the knowledge of both modalities consistently. Efficiently editing LVLMs is crucial for real-world applications, such as swiftly correcting critical visual recognition errors (e.g., a model misidentifying Donald Trump as Boris Johnson). However, research on multimodal knowledge editing remains scarce compared with the extensive studies on text-only language models.

Existing benchmarks for LVLM knowledge editing are limited in scope. They typically focus only on visual knowledge updates, such as changing the identity that an image is recognized as, and overlook scenarios in which textual facts about an entity (e.g., its attributes, roles or affiliations) must also be updated. Furthermore, they do not evaluate continual editing, in which multiple knowledge updates are performed sequentially, nor do they test a model's ability to reason compositionally over edited facts. This is a critical gap, because real-world knowledge updates often arrive incrementally and involve intertwined visual and textual information: once a model has been corrected about who appears in a photo and, separately, updated with a new fact about that person, a question about the person in the photo can only be answered correctly by combining both edits.

Existing editing approaches face fundamental difficulties in this setting. External-memory editors store edited knowledge outside the model and retrieve relevant information at inference time without modifying model parameters, which makes them suitable for long-term retention. However, they typically transplant text-based retrieval strategies from language models directly, ignoring visual cues that are necessary for matching multimodal queries to the right edits, which can reduce retrieval accuracy. They also face an internalization issue: the model may over-rely on its stale internal knowledge, especially when the retrieved information conflicts with what it has learned, leading to incorrect answers. Conversely, internal-memory editors embed edits directly into model parameters via fine-tuning or low-rank adaptation, viewing the feed-forward network as a key-value memory that stores in-model knowledge. Although beneficial for internalizing edits, these methods typically store visual and textual edits within a unified representation space, risking cross-modal interference and representation collapse; moreover, sequential internal edits suffer from catastrophic forgetting, degrading previously stored knowledge with successive updates.

This raises several questions. How can an LVLM accommodate a continual sequence of interleaved visual and textual edits so that each new edit takes effect while earlier edits are retained, without interference between modalities? How can separately edited visual and textual facts be integrated to answer compositional queries that require both, even when externally retrieved evidence and the model's internal knowledge disagree? And how can editors be evaluated in this continual and compositional setting, which existing benchmarks do not cover?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: unified multimodal editing via policy updating
PROPOSAL: We will design a mechanism that updates the knowledge network of an LVLM by integrating visual and textual edits. Specifically, we will utilize a policy-based approach, where the model learns to update its knowledge by consuming policy embeddings that encode the edits. This allows the model to learn a consensual representation of the edits and integrate them seamlessly into its existing knowledge network. We will employ a transformer-based encoder-decoder framework, fine-tune on a set of multimodal datasets, and evaluate on a range of tasks including knowledge-based visual question answering and text-image retrieval.
CONTROLS: baseline comparison with traditional external-memory editing strategies, ablation study on the importance of policy embeddings, fine-tuning without policy embeddings, with results reported in a table
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this approach should outperform traditional external-memory editors in multimodal knowledge editing tasks, and potentially provide more robust and flexible updates. However, it may struggle with catastrophic forgetting if not properly regularized.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: testing catastrophic forgetting resistance in multimodal editing
PROPOSAL: Given the concerns about catastrophic forgetting in internal-memory editors, we will introduce a regularized training objective that encourages the model to retain previously updated knowledge while incorporating new edits. Specifically, we will propose a knowledge distillation objective that emphasizes the retention of salient information from the model's initial knowledge state, which we will then blend with the information from the latest edit. We hypothesize that this approach will improve the model's ability to retain previously updated knowledge.
CONTROLS: quantitative evaluation of catastrophic forgetting, comparison with other regularization schemes (e.g., L1/L2 penalty, gradient regularization), ablation study on the importance of the knowledge distillation objective, following the setup outlined in the proposal
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this approach should significantly reduce catastrophic forgetting in multimodal editing tasks, but may come at the expense of slower convergence rates or decreased model accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: multi-step evaluation methodology for multimodal knowledge editors
PROPOSAL: To better assess the performance of multimodal knowledge editors, we will propose a multi-step evaluation methodology that measures their performance over a series of incremental update steps. Specifically, we will evaluate the model's accuracy on a range of tasks (e.g., visual question answering, text-image retrieval) across multiple update steps, using metrics that capture both short-term and long-term recall. This will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the model's ability to retain previously updated knowledge over time.
CONTROLS: comparisons with existing evaluation methodologies (e.g., one-shot update, batch update), ablation study on the importance of evaluating model performance over multiple update steps
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this evaluation methodology should provide a more nuanced understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of moment-to-moment performance of multimodal editors but may require an additional increase in data annotation and new evaluation frameworks.

Additionally, we will also track the model's performance on a set of compositional questions that require integrating previously updated knowledge with new information.

TITLE: adversarial evaluation of multimodal knowledge editors
PROPOSAL: To provide a more comprehensive assessment of multimodal knowledge editors, we will introduce an adversarial evaluation framework that tests the model's resilience tocrafted attacks designed to compromise its performance. Specifically, we will use strong and strategic attacks (e.g., semantic adversarial examples, multi-step attacks) to probe the model's vulnerabilities and evaluate its robustness.

Specifically, we will design a model that uses a knowledge graph to store and retrieve multimodal information, and leverages policy updates to incorporate new knowledge into the model. This approach should enable the model to adapt to new information and retain previously learned knowledge over time.

COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this hybrid approach should provide a robust and adaptive way to update multimodal knowledge, but may require careful tuning of the model's architecture and the knowledge graph to avoid information overload and catastrophic forgetting.

Score learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for modeling complex probability distributions, driving progress in generative modeling, Bayesian inverse problems and sampling. Given a data measure $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, one considers its Gaussian-smoothed version $\mu_\sigma$, defined as the law of $X + \sigma Z$ (variance-exploding smoothing) or of $\sqrt{1-\sigma^2} X + \sigma Z$ (variance-preserving smoothing), where $X \sim \mu_{\mathrm{data}}$ and $Z$ is a standard Gaussian vector, with density $p_\sigma$. A key step in this framework is to approximate the score function $\nabla \log p_\sigma$, typically by score matching, and to use it to sample from $\mu_\sigma$, possibly across a range of noise levels: through the reverse process of a diffusion model, through Langevin dynamics driven by the learned score, or through predictor-corrector schemes that combine the two.

A central challenge is the low-temperature limit, that is, learning the score of $\mu_\sigma$ as $\sigma \to 0$, which encodes the most detailed information about the data. This regime is also the most valuable in practice: low-noise scores underpin many probabilistic learning frameworks, including diffusion models, whose noise schedules are designed to emphasize low noise levels and often require substantial post-training engineering to stabilize the learned scores. Yet accurately estimating the score in the small-$\sigma$ regime remains notoriously difficult. This raises a basic question: if the learned score is unavoidably inaccurate at small noise levels, what do score-based methods actually recover, and why do they nevertheless produce realistic samples?

A natural setting for this question is the widely adopted manifold hypothesis, which posits that $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$ is supported on a compact, low-dimensional manifold embedded in a high-dimensional ambient space. The data then carry two kinds of information: the geometry of their support, and the particular density of the data on that support. Existing convergence theory for diffusion and score-based samplers shows that the generated law approaches the target when the learned score is accurate, with error bounds that scale directly with the score mismatch, and related work studies other factors such as the dependence on dimension. These results, however, treat geometry and density together in the score error and do not say whether score errors affect the recovery of the support and the recovery of the on-manifold density differently. A growing body of work suggests that diffusion models often capture the data support while missing fine-grained distributional structure, but this evidence comes from restricted settings: estimating the intrinsic dimension of the manifold, linear manifolds (linear subspaces) only, or primarily empirical observations. Sufficient regularity conditions are known under which highly accurate scores concentrate mass near the manifold, but not how approximation errors may scale with $\sigma$. Likewise, it is established that under the manifold hypothesis the score develops a singularity in the small-noise regime, becoming orthogonal to the manifold and acting as a geometric projection onto it; yet these analyses fold the distributional information into a generic bounded remainder term and do not isolate the terms that involve the data density.

A first set of questions is therefore the following. In the small-$\sigma$ regime, at which orders in $\sigma$ do information about the manifold geometry and information about the data density enter the log-density and the score of $\mu_\sigma$? What accuracy, expressed as a rate in $\sigma$, must a learned score achieve for the distribution produced by a sampler to concentrate on the data manifold, and what accuracy is needed for it to recover $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$ itself? Do these two requirements differ and, when a score is accurate enough for the first but not for the second, what can be said about the distribution that is produced on the manifold?

A second set of questions concerns which target is worth learning. For tasks that depend only on the geometry of the data, such as approximating the Laplace-Beltrami operator and heat kernels or computing geodesic and diffusion distances, it is well known that samples drawn uniformly with respect to the manifold's intrinsic (Riemannian) volume measure are the most useful; uniform samples also support principled exploration of the manifold, yielding diverse samples while mitigating biases present in $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$. Classical graph-based normalizations achieve uniform sampling on a manifold by cancelling the sampling density, but they are designed to approximate geometric operators from neighborhood graphs and do not scale readily to high-dimensional, large-scale generative modeling; a recent alternative fine-tunes diffusion models so that they produce uniform samples, at the cost of additional training. Can the uniform distribution on the data manifold be obtained from a score model trained on samples of a non-uniform $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$, and how much score error can such a procedure tolerate compared with exact recovery of $\mu_{\mathrm{data}}$? Any answer must cope with the fact that a score produced by a parameterized model is generally not a gradient field, so that the Langevin dynamics it drives is non-reversible and its stationary distribution has no closed form. Asymptotic analyses of such stationary distributions, based on WKB-type expansions of the stationary Fokker-Planck equation, typically focus on low-dimensional special examples or on drifts with a single stable point, whereas data supported on a manifold give rise to a whole manifold of stable points.

Finally, the same issues arise in Bayesian inverse problems, where a latent signal $x$ is observed through a measurement map with noise, $y = A(x) + \xi$, and inference amounts to sampling the posterior $p(x \mid y) \propto p(y \mid x) p_{\mathrm{prior}}(x)$. Plug-and-play methods run posterior Langevin dynamics that combine the gradient of the log-likelihood with a (possibly learned) prior score, and a common choice of prior is the smoothed data density $p_\sigma$ with small $\sigma$. Existing guarantees that such updates sample the correct posterior require the learned prior score to have vanishing error, or even to be exact, which is difficult to achieve at small $\sigma$. How does the choice of prior affect the score accuracy needed for correct posterior sampling? Answering these questions would clarify what score-based methods can reliably learn from imperfect scores in the low-noise regime, which learning objectives are realistic there, and whether these distinctions matter in practice for score-based generative models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: small-sigma analysis of diffusion models on manifolds
PROPOSAL: Investigate the convergence rate of diffusion models on manifolds in the small-$\sigma$ limit. Consider the normalized diffusion process $dX_t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \sigma^2}} \left( Z_t - \nabla \log p_\sigma(X_t) \right) dt$ as $\sigma \to 0$, and analyze the resulting Malliavin derivative.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing rate bounds for diffusion models on manifolds; consider the effect of smoothing on the initialization scheme and the overall convergence behavior.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis should reveal that the rate of convergence improves as $\sigma$ approaches 0, and should provide insight into the mechanism by which the Malliavin derivative concentrates near the manifold. However, the analysis may fail to provide a precise characterization of the convergence rate, due to the technical challenges associated with estimating the Malliavin derivative in high dimensions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: manifold concentration rate under score errors
PROPOSAL: Analyze the effects of score errors on the concentration rate of the diffusion process near the data manifold. Consider a learned score $\hat{\nabla} \log p_\sigma$ with a small but non-vanishing error, and investigate the resulting diffusion process $dX_t = \left( Z_t - \hat{\nabla} \log p_\sigma(X_t) \right) dt$ as $t \to \infty$.
CONTROLS: Consider multiple scenarios with varying levels of score error and analyze their effects on the steady-state distribution and the concentration rate near the manifold.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis should reveal that score errors lead to a suboptimal concentration rate, and provide insight into the minimum error threshold required for optimal concentration near the manifold. However, the analysis may require additional assumptions or simplifications to handle the impact of score errors on the diffusion process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: asymptotics of geometric projection and densification
PROPOSAL: Investigate the asymptotic behavior of the geometric projection and densification terms in the score function of $\mu_\sigma$ for small $\sigma$. Analyze the singular behavior of $\nabla \log p_\sigma(x)$ as $x$ approaches the manifold and derive the leading-order asymptotics in this limit.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing asymptotic analyses and derive the resulting bounds for the approximation error in score matching, on a single random seed.
COST: 8 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis should provide a precise characterization of the leading-order terms in the asymptotic expansion of the score function near the manifold. However, the derivation may require a combination of analytical and numerical computations, particularly to handle the singular behavior of the geometric projection term.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: asymptotics of geometric projection and densification
PROPOSAL: Refine the previous proposal by directly analyzing the small-$\sigma$ limit of the score function under the manifold hypothesis. Derive the small-$\sigma$ asymptotics of $\nabla \log p_\sigma(x)$ for $x$ near the manifold and two distinct orders in $\sigma$, one that explicitly tracks the geometry and another that describes the densification of the data measure on the manifold.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing results under the manifold hypothesis and examine the convergence rate of the small-$\sigma$ asymptotics in the regime where the manifold is smooth and of high-dimensional embedding but low intrinsic dimension.
COST: 12 GPU-hours (modest increase from 8 hours, as additional mathematical derivations are required)
PREDICTION: The refined analysis should provide a more detailed understanding of the small-$\sigma$ asymptotics of the score function, potentially identifying different regimes in which the geometry of the manifold or the densification of the data measure dominates the behavior of the score. However, the derivation may require significant mathematical effort, particularly to obtain the desired convergence rate.

TITLE: effect of manifold geometry on sample concentration
PROPOSAL: Investigate the dependence of the sample concentration rate near the data manifold on the geometry of the manifold. Consider various scenarios with distinct manifold geometries (e.g., spherical, toroidal, or hyperbolic embeddings) and explore how these geometries affect the rate of concentration of the diffusion process near the manifold.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing results on sample concentration in diffusion models and examine the impact of manifold curvature and dimensionality on the concentration rate.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis should reveal that the manifold geometry plays a crucial role in determining the rate of sample concentration near the manifold, and provide insight into the optimal geometry for achieving fast and accurate sample concentration. However, the derivation may require numerical computations to handle the varied manifold geometries and the associated diffusion processes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: are uniform samples always helpful in score-based generative models?
PROPOSAL: Investigate the benefits of sampling from a uniform distribution on the data manifold in score-based generative models. Analyze the impact of uniform sampling on the learning objective and the languaging dynamics for a given score model, and compare with non-uniform sampling schemes.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing results on sampling distributions in score-based systems and examine the effects of uniform sampling on the recovery of manifold geometry and on the driving dynamics of the sampler.
COST: 18 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis should reveal that uniform sampling may not always be beneficial in score-based generative models, potentially leading to inefficient learning objectives and slow dynamics. However, the results may also depend on the specific score model, learning objective, and sampling scheme employed.

TITLE: estimating laplace-beltrami operators with score-based models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of score-based generative models to estimate the Laplace-Beltrami operator and heat kernels on the data manifold. Derive the necessary modifications to the score dynamics and learning objectives to accurately capture these geometric operators, and evaluate the performance of the resulting model on various tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing methods for estimating the Laplace-Beltrami operator and examine the trade-offs between using score-based models and traditional graph-based methods.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis should reveal that score-based models can be effectively used to estimate the Laplace-Beltrami operator and heat kernels, potentially offering a scalable and flexible alternative to traditional methods. However, the results may also depend on the specific choice of score dynamics and learning objectives, as well as the underlying geometry of the data manifold.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: plug-and-play prior schemes for bayesian inverse problems
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of score-based generative models as plug-and-play priors for Bayesian inverse problems. Analyze the impact of different score models and learning objectives on the posterior distribution and the resulting inference, and evaluate the performance of the resulting method on various tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing methods for Bayesian inverse problems and examine the trade-offs between using score-based priors and traditional approaches.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis should reveal that score-based priors can be effectively used to improve Bayesian inference, potentially offering a scalable and flexible alternative to traditional methods. However, the results may also depend on the specific choice of score model, learning objective, and inverse problem formulation, as well as the underlying measurement noise and signal fidelity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: robustness of manifold-based generative models to noise and corruption
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness of manifold-based generative models to noise and corruption, and analyze the impact of different sources of corruption (e.g., measurement noise, adversarial attacks) on the geometry of the learned manifold and the quality of generated samples.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing methods for robust generative modeling and examine the trade-offs between using manifold-based models and traditional approaches.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis should reveal that manifold-based generative models are more robust to certain types of corruption, but may be vulnerable to others. However, the results may also depend on the specific choice of score model, learning objective, and corruption mechanism, as well as the underlying geometry of the data.

Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) generate discrete data by iteratively replacing masked tokens with predicted unmasked ones, learning to reverse an absorbing-state diffusion process that progressively masks the tokens of a sequence. They have recently achieved strong results across diverse domains, including text generation, image synthesis, and multi-modal understanding and generation. For images, a pre-trained tokenizer (e.g., a VQ-VAE) maps an image to a sequence of discrete tokens and its decoder reconstructs the image from those tokens; generation starts from a fully masked sequence and fills it in over many steps, which makes inference time- and compute-intensive. Building on this success, recent work has shown that these multi-step procedures can be distilled into one-step generators, substantially accelerating inference and reducing computational cost while maintaining competitive quality. For instance, Di[M]O distills a multi-step MDM into a one-step generator through on-policy distribution matching: a one-step prediction sampled from the student is corrupted by the forward masking process, and the teacher's and the student's output distributions conditioned on this intermediate state are matched, with the resulting gradient applied directly to the student's logits so that it never has to pass through the non-differentiable sampling operation.

Despite their remarkable performance, current one-step discrete generators face two fundamental limitations. First, they inherit both modeling and alignment errors from the teacher: existing distillation approaches implicitly assume that the teacher fully captures the target distribution, so imperfections in the teacher's generative modeling and the under-alignment of the pre-trained teacher with downstream preferences are both transmitted to the student during data-free distillation. Second, their discrete token outputs block gradient flow. This prevents the application of key refinement techniques that are widely used to improve one-step generators distilled from continuous diffusion models, such as adversarial (GAN) training, differentiable reward fine-tuning, and test-time optimization of the generator's input with respect to a reward. In text-to-image generation, for example, prompt-following and aesthetic quality are the two primary criteria, and the community increasingly relies on learned reward models and human-preference signals to optimize them directly; but because such rewards operate on decoded images, their gradients cannot pass through the tokenizer decoder and the sampled tokens back to a discrete generator. As a result, current distilled MDM generators have limited flexibility to leverage external knowledge, such as real data, or to incorporate user preferences to better align with downstream objectives.

The gradient-blocking problem is common across discrete modeling tasks. Adversarial training on discrete data, for instance, is challenging because the discriminator must compare generated samples with ground truth while the sampling process is non-differentiable. Prior remedies include policy-gradient estimators such as REINFORCE, which are unbiased but whose gradient variance becomes prohibitive when hundreds or thousands of tokens are generated at once, and differentiable relaxations of discrete tokens such as Gumbel-Softmax (often used with a straight-through estimator) and soft-argmax. However, these methods often introduce biased or high-variance gradients and numerical instabilities, and they have not been systematically applied to one-step discrete generators, in particular for fast visual generation. Moreover, the downstream objectives of interest, such as discriminators and reward models, act on continuous inputs such as the images produced by the tokenizer decoder, so a practical solution must let gradients flow through the existing generation pipeline.

This raises two questions. How can the outputs of a one-step generator distilled from an MDM be made amenable to end-to-end gradient-based training, with gradients that are stable, low-variance and faithful to the true discrete objective, while remaining compatible with the existing teacher and tokenizer? And, once such gradients are available, can post-distillation refinements (adversarial training, differentiable reward fine-tuning, and test-time optimization of the generator's input) let a one-step student correct the errors it inherits from its teacher and better align with downstream objectives such as distribution fidelity, prompt adherence and aesthetic quality?

pas.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: flow-through training with relaxed gradients
PROPOSAL: Investigate using a relaxed version of the Gumbel-Softmax estimator to allow gradients to flow through the one-step generator, with a focus on stable and low-variance gradients. Train the student and teacher together to minimize the difference between the predicted output and the true teacher output, using annealed temperature scheduling to improve the quality of the generated samples.
CONTROLS: Compare with a straight-through estimator and an oracle policy that always outputs the true teacher output, on a variety of downstream objectives (e.g. evaluating both on text coherence and image quality in a text-to-image setting).
COST: 100 GPU-hours (to train the student and teacher for a few thousand iterations)
PREDICTION: This approach should alleviate the gradient-blocking problem to some extent, but may sacrifice some of the competitive quality achieved by the one-step generator (i.e. one might see a slight degradation in generated samples). Evaluation on a set of downstream objectives may reveal where the approach excels or fails.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: differentiable reward fine-tuning with target-image gradients
PROPOSAL: Modify the existing Di[M]O distillation to incorporate differentiable fine-tuning with learned rewards. The teacher will generate an image \hat{I} and assess its quality using a post-distillation discriminator or a reward function; simultaneously, an auxilliary network will generate a target image I_target that approximates the downstream objective, e.g., maximizing some aesthetic-score. The gradients of the objective with respect to I_target should be aligned with the ones from the reward network.
CONTROLS: Compare fine-tuning with/without the target-image gradients, and compare using either a post-distillation discriminator or a learned reward network for assessing quality.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (in addition to 100 for flow-through training with relaxed gradients, since we need to train the auxilliary network, post-distillation discriminator, and possibly reward network).
PREDICTION: By using gradients of the objective with respect to the target image, the fine-tuning should improve alignment with downstream objectives, especially when combined with the relaxed gradients from flow-through training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: masking mechanism refinement by conditional discriminator
PROPOSAL: Introduce a conditional discriminator that takes the teacher's output and the masked input as input to correct the masking mechanism during one-step generation. The discriminator attempts to infer the correct token to fill in the current masked position, allowing the student to take advantage of this additional guidance.
CONTROLS: Compare modelling-based and discriminatively-mapped masking mechanisms (or use it as an alternative initialization method for the teacher).
COST: 30 GPU-hours (primarily related to discriminator training and integrating with one-step generation).
PREDICTION: The conditional discriminator will improve quality of generated samples by re-weighting token probability distributions in the teacher's masked output, which may mitigate some teacher errors, especially for finer-grained token distributions such as character selection in text or semantic masks in images.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: masking mechanism refinement by conditional discriminator
PROPOSAL: Introduce a conditional discriminator that takes the teacher's output, the current masked sequence, and the student's generated output as input to correct the masking mechanism during one-step generation. This should allow the student to learn from not only the teacher's guidance but also its own attempts at token filling, closing the loop of propose-rectify-refine to leverage information generated during the distillation process.
CONTROLS: Compare directly to earlier proposal's version without the student-generated output as input; investigate impact on stability/variability of student's generated samples.
COST: 30 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The revised conditional discriminator should further improve the alignment of student's output with downstream objectives, reducing the teacher's imperfections and allowing for more effective utilization of the generated samples, potentially at the cost of increased complexity of the model.

ACTION: REVISE 3

Diffusion models have recently demonstrated remarkable capabilities in synthesizing high-quality images, significantly surpassing earlier generative approaches such as generative adversarial networks and variational autoencoders. Despite their impressive fidelity, deploying diffusion models in realistic cloud-to-user applications introduces a fundamental bottleneck: transmission bandwidth. A standard diffusion model produces a high-fidelity image by performing a fixed number of denoising steps, regardless of downstream transmission limitations. In conventional scenarios, the generated images then undergo aggressive lossy compression before transmission to accommodate the limited bandwidth. This cascaded approach, high-quality generation followed by subsequent compression, not only incurs redundant computational overhead, since computation is spent on details that are later discarded, but also significantly degrades perceptual quality, as the compression process often erases the intricate textures and fine details carefully constructed by the diffusion model.

This motivates a critical question: can bandwidth-awareness be integrated directly into the diffusion generation process, so that the quality of the generated image is adapted to the available bandwidth, avoiding the inefficiency and perceptual quality loss associated with post-generation compression? Ideally, such a generator would meet a user-specified bitrate budget, avoid compression-induced artifacts and redundant computation, and offer fine-grained, dynamic control over image quality according to real-time bandwidth conditions in practical cloud-to-user deployments.

The question is not straightforward. During sampling, diffusion models progressively refine coarse structures into detailed, realistic textures through iterative denoising steps, so, intuitively, terminating the process early would yield simpler, lower-detail images suited to constrained bandwidth. However, naively reducing the number of diffusion steps typically produces suboptimal visual quality: models trained for complete denoising trajectories are not optimized for early termination, which leads to visual artifacts and poor perceptual coherence.

Existing lines of work address only parts of this problem. A large body of work accelerates diffusion sampling, through deterministic samplers that need fewer inference steps, numerical solvers inspired by ordinary differential equations, distillation of slow teacher models into faster students, adaptive step-size selection, latent-space compression, non-uniform step skipping, dynamic network pruning, predictors of the minimal number of denoising steps, and adaptive inference trajectories. These methods reduce the cost of sampling while preserving generation quality, but they are not designed to control the bitrate of the generated image. Conditional and controllable diffusion models, from classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance to latent diffusion and region-based conditioning for interactive editing, allow flexible control over attributes of the generated content, but they do not directly address bandwidth constraints. How to make a diffusion model generate images that respect a specified bandwidth budget while preserving perceptual quality and avoiding wasted computation therefore remains an open problem.

Semantic segmentation has improved significantly with recent advances in deep neural networks, but it requires a large volume of fine-grained pixel-level labels, which are time-consuming and labor-intensive to obtain. Because images themselves are readily available, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) and semi-supervised learning (SSL) have been introduced to handle label-scarce scenarios: UDA learns from labeled synthetic data and transfers knowledge to real, unlabeled target domains, while SSL uses a tiny portion of annotated data to generalize to unseen data. Both are gaining attention as promising ways to reduce the reliance on extensive annotation in semantic segmentation.

In both settings, models are trained on annotated and unlabeled data simultaneously. Mainstream methods follow two paradigms. Self-training methods use a temporally smoothed exponential moving average (EMA) model as a teacher to generate stable pseudo-labels for unlabeled data, while consistency regularization methods encourage the model to produce consistent predictions for the same sample under different perturbation views; recent state-of-the-art methods combine the two. Both can be summarized as pseudo-label learning, in which the network's own predictions serve as supervision for unlabeled data. In the widely adopted form of this paradigm, the teacher's prediction is converted into a hard pseudo-label through an argmax and encoded one-hot, a confidence-based quality estimate (threshold filtering or a weighting function) controls how much each pseudo-label contributes, and training uses a cross-entropy loss.

Despite promising results, pseudo-labels inevitably contain errors that mislead training, and these errors are further amplified during training because of the one-hot encoding. Typical remedies use filter-out mechanisms that train only on high-confidence pseudo-labels, but this makes the model focus on easy samples while neglecting difficult ones, resulting in sub-optimal performance. Another alternative assigns weights according to pseudo-label confidence, but such weighting functions require careful design and selection of hyperparameters, which compromises their applicability. Other work designs new optimization criteria, for example inspired by negative learning. Existing work thus concentrates on selection strategies for pseudo-labels and rarely considers the impact of the encoding form assigned to classes.

This omission matters most for confusing classes. For instance, pixels of the class sheep may be confused by the classifier with horse or cow, and the resulting erroneous pseudo-label is encoded one-hot through the argmax, committing the supervision entirely to a wrong class. Similar classes plausibly share common visual attributes (sheep and cows, for example, both have horns and hooves), which leads to confusing pseudo-labels that further misguide training, yet a one-hot target cannot express what the confused classes have in common. How to utilize the shared attributes among confusing classes to design a suitable encoding form for pseudo-label learning remains rarely explored.

This raises several questions. Can the class encoding used by the segmentation model and its pseudo-labels be redesigned so that supervision stays informative even when the class decision for a pixel is wrong? Under such an encoding, how should pseudo-labels be generated from the teacher's predictions so that they introduce less noise than hard one-hot labels, and what training objective is appropriate? Can an alternative encoding be shown, both theoretically and empirically, to match one-hot encoding in the fully supervised setting while being more robust to label noise in pseudo-label learning? Finally, since the encoding form is orthogonal to pseudo-label selection strategies, can such a change be integrated into existing self-training and consistency-regularization frameworks for both UDA and SSL, across different segmentation architectures?

Multimodal learning has become a cornerstone of many real-world applications, such as autonomous perception, medical diagnosis, and human-computer interaction. By integrating information from multiple sources, such as vision, audio, and text, multimodal systems aim to improve performance and generalization. However, multimodal data often exhibit a significant imbalance between modalities due to noise, lack of information, or sensor heterogeneity, so that a dominant modality may overshadow the others and hinder the learning of weak modalities. Unimodal prediction accuracy is widely used to detect modality imbalance; it is a simple and effective metric, but it is inherently sensitive to noise and perturbations. This vulnerability often leads to fragile performance in practice and limits the reliability of accuracy-based definitions of strong and weak modalities in real-world deployments.

Modality imbalance arises in early, intermediate, and late fusion alike. Late fusion, also known as decision-level fusion, combines the outputs (logits) of modality-specific models, either with equal weights (static late fusion) or with weights that vary across samples (dynamic late fusion). It remains one of the most widely adopted paradigms because of its modular design, interpretability, and strong compatibility with unimodal pre-trained models. Yet, lacking feature-level compensation or cross-modal interaction, late fusion tends to amplify the influence of strong modalities while weakening the role of lower-quality ones, so that predictions from disadvantaged modalities often carry little weight or even introduce noise into the final decision. A large body of work has attempted to alleviate this imbalance by enhancing the predictive performance of weak modalities, for example by aggregating independently trained modality-specific classifiers, confidence-based weighting, modality dropout or gating, adaptive ensembling, or knowledge distillation from dominant modalities.

While effective in certain scenarios, these methods often implicitly aim to align weak modalities with dominant ones in terms of prediction accuracy, attempting to bring them closer to their stronger counterparts. Such over-alignment raises several concerns: (1) it may suppress the distinct and complementary information encoded in weak modalities, causing modality-specific information loss; (2) it risks error propagation, as the dominant modality's errors are amplified when weak modalities follow them blindly; and (3) through excessive conformity, weak modalities may lose the predictive advantages they originally held on some samples.

Robustness makes the issue more pressing. Multimodal cooperation is inherently sensitive to perturbations such as data noise, label noise, and incomplete modalities, because modalities are heterogeneous and vary in reliability in real-world conditions. Prior studies have highlighted that the robustness of a multimodal system can be bottlenecked by a single weak modality, revealing a strong link between modality imbalance and overall system reliability. Existing work addresses robustness by incorporating uncertainty modeling, designing robustness-aware fusion strategies, quantifying multimodal robustness with dedicated evaluation metrics, or connecting it with generalization error bounds. However, most of these approaches emphasize prediction-consistency modeling and pay little attention to the instability of the decision space, that is, a model's high sensitivity to input perturbations near the decision boundary, where even minor changes can cause large shifts in prediction; they also tend to require more complex architectures with limited generalizability across tasks with different class granularity.

This raises several questions. How can a dominant modality help a weak modality within a decision-level fusion system without forcing it to conform, so that the weak modality keeps its unique, complementary information and does not inherit the dominant modality's errors? Given that judging modality strength by unimodal accuracy or confidence is itself fragile under noise, how can one reliably determine which modality is dominant and which is weak? How do the predictions of the individual modalities determine the robustness of the fused decision to input perturbations, and can a remedy for modality imbalance come with a theoretical guarantee on that robustness? Finally, can such a remedy both narrow the performance gap between modalities and make the fused prediction more reliable under noisy and imbalanced conditions?

Recording dynamic scenes from multiple viewpoints has become increasingly common in everyday life. From concerts and sports events to lectures and birthday parties, people often capture the same moment using different handheld devices. These multi-view recordings present a rich opportunity to reconstruct scenes in 4D, enable bullet-time effects, or enhance the capabilities of existing vision models. However, these videos are typically captured independently, without synchronization or known camera poses, making it difficult to align and fuse them coherently.

The task is the following: given a set of asynchronous videos that capture the same dynamic scene from different viewpoints, estimate a time offset for each video, to be applied to its original out-of-sync clock, so that after correction frames sharing the same clock time correspond to the exact same moment across all videos.

Existing synchronization methods rely on controlled environments, manual annotations, specific patterns such as human pose, audio signals such as flashes or claps, or expensive hardware setups such as time-coded devices, none of which are available in casually captured videos. Human-centric approaches, which use body pose as the synchronization signal, are limited by the accuracy of pose estimation and by the number of people present, and they struggle in scenes without prominent human activity. Audio-based approaches only work in quiet environments and do not carry over to in-the-wild settings where audio is noisy or unavailable. Methods that jointly optimize camera poses and temporal offsets within a learned scene representation are often constrained to specific environments or object types. Geometry-based methods estimate temporal offsets from multi-view geometric constraints, but typically assume static scenes or a fixed viewpoint. Meanwhile, structure-from-motion and learned camera-pose estimators recover camera geometry accurately, yet they rely predominantly on static visual cues and therefore fall short of synchronizing dynamic scenes.

Building a practical and robust synchronization system that works on videos in the wild is challenging. Camera poses are unknown and cameras may move, so the geometric relationship between each pair of cameras must itself be estimated reliably. The moving objects that carry the timing information are not known in advance and are generally small and blurry. Associating points across cameras with significantly different viewpoints is difficult. The offsets to be recovered are continuous, while observations arrive only at discrete frame times. Finally, not all views overlap, so some pairs of cameras may share little spatial or temporal overlap.

This raises several questions. How can a set of casually captured, unposed and unsynchronized videos of the same dynamic scene be aligned in time with high precision, without specialized capture, audio, manual correction, or assumptions about the scene content such as the presence of people? Which visual evidence can reliably reveal the temporal offset between two cameras whose poses are unknown and possibly changing over time? And how can a single, globally consistent offset be recovered for every video when the evidence relating some pairs of views is weak, ambiguous or missing? Answering these questions would open the door to scalable, unconstrained multi-view 4D scene understanding and to downstream tasks, such as 4D reconstruction of dynamic scenes, that depend on synchronized input.

In cloud services, Internet of Things deployments and monitoring systems, data are often represented as univariate time series (UTS), in which each timestamp records a single variable. Anomalies arise, for instance, when a website is subject to malicious attacks or experiences excessive server load, and they are typically reflected in UTS derived from traffic and system-load monitoring. Missed or delayed detection of such events can have severe consequences. Anomalies in UTS are usually divided into two types: point anomalies, which are abrupt deviations (either global or contextual), and segment anomalies, which reflect more subtle shifts in trends or periodic patterns.

Formally, given observations x_0, x_1, ..., x_t with anomaly labels c_0, c_1, ..., c_t, where c_i = 0 marks a normal point and c_i = 1 an anomaly, the goal of UTS anomaly detection is to determine c_i for each point x_i from the history x_0, ..., x_{i-1} that precedes it, without access to future points. Because labels are scarce in practice and supervised detectors generalize poorly under label scarcity or distribution shift, unsupervised approaches have become the dominant paradigm. Reconstruction-based and prediction-based methods both model normal behavior and flag anomalies by comparing reconstructed or predicted values with the actual observations. Reconstruction-based techniques try to map abnormal segments to a normal space, but the lack of ground truth for anomalies leads to poor reconstruction and degraded performance, and they treat time windows independently, ignoring temporal dependencies. Prediction-based methods built on deep sequence models such as Transformers perform strongly on multivariate time series, where they can model complex dependencies; in UTS, however, each timestamp contains only one value, which restricts the representation of temporal context and leads to suboptimal performance.

In particular, existing detectors struggle with two kinds of subtle anomalies that remain largely undetected: (1) small point anomalies, short-term spikes that look normal when viewed over longer windows; and (2) slowly rising anomalies, gradual segment-level deviations from periodic patterns. These misses stem from limitations of current designs: for example, a frequency-conditioned reconstruction approach focuses on frequency components rather than local dependencies and fails to capture subtle point anomalies or gradual segment anomalies, while a recent prediction approach uses timing information but ignores frequency details.

Detecting these anomalies raises three challenges. First, local trends matter more than absolute values: the absolute magnitude of a change is insufficient to decide whether a point is anomalous. In one series, changes between 0.5 and 1 may be abnormal, whereas in another, similar changes are normal and only variations exceeding 5 are anomalous; what counts as abnormal depends on the value distribution and change patterns within a short local window. Second, periodicity evolves rather than staying static: time series exhibit evolving trends and periodicity, and periodicity varies over time and across datasets, including changes in period length and frequency. Without future points, distinguishing slow anomalies from normal periodic changes is difficult, and methods that focus only on the adjacent historical period neglect this evolution; modeling periodicity that is both dynamic and heterogeneous is hard. Third, normal patterns must be learned amid anomalies and noise: real-world series contain long-term noise and sudden anomalies, both of which hinder the learning of normal patterns. Noise introduces significant fluctuations that make it difficult to fit the underlying normal behavior, and the lack of ground-truth labels for anomaly positions prevents a model from computing reliable training losses.

The question is therefore how an unsupervised detector for univariate time series, relying only on past observations, can capture both local trends and the evolution of periodic patterns, while learning normal behavior robustly from training data contaminated by noise and unlabeled anomalies, so that small point anomalies and slowly rising anomalies are detected accurately and promptly.

PROPOSAL: Introduce a reconstruction-based method that models normal behavior by learning local trends in the univariate time series. Instead of focusing on global frequency components, the method will capture local patterns using a Gaussian Process regression model with a custom kernel that takes into account the local context of each point. TITLE: anomaly encoder-based denoising autoencoder
PROPOSAL: Design a denoising autoencoder (DAE) that uses an anomaly encoder to learn noise and normal patterns in the univariate time series data. The anomaly encoder maps the input to a noise representation, where noise is represented as abnormality in the sequence. By training the DAE to reconstruct the input from its noise representation, the model learns to discard noise and identify normal patterns in the data, allowing for effective anomaly detection in noisy series. This approach will be useful in capturing local trends and normal patterns in the presence of high levels of noise.

PROPOSAL: Develop an incremental learning method for periodicity-aware sequence models, allowing the model to adapt to changes in periodic patterns over time. By leveraging the periodicity-aware sequence model as a subroutine, the incremental learning method can continually refine its understanding of the periodic patterns and adapt to changing conditions, making it more effective in detecting slowly rising anomalies.

Modern text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models generate images of unprecedented diversity and quality from natural-language descriptions, and progress in architectures and theoretical foundations has allowed them to scale to billions of parameters. This paradigm works well for concise prompts but falters when the input becomes a descriptive paragraph. While a model may excel at rendering "a house in the middle of a forest", it often fails when the prompt expands, detailing the terracotta roof tiles, the weathered white panels of the house, and the striking contrast cast by the afternoon sun.

This failure stems from a fundamental conflict between the nature of long-form text and the models' training paradigm. T2I models are predominantly trained on vast datasets of images paired with short, concise, often label-like captions. They learn to map keywords and short phrases to visual features, but are undertrained on interpreting the narrative flow and distributed details of a paragraph, so a descriptive paragraph is effectively an out-of-distribution input for them. Part of the difficulty is often attributed to the fixed context window of text encoders such as CLIP, which can be lifted by switching to more powerful language models; yet even modern models that use powerful text encoders struggle on these inputs, missing more than half of the specified objects.

Existing methods attempt to bridge this gap through two strategies. The most direct approach fine-tunes the T2I model on long-captioned data. While effective within the training lengths, it requires intensive tuning, extrapolating to even longer prompts remains challenging, and the tuned models risk "catastrophic forgetting" of their pre-trained knowledge. The second strategy adopts projection-based methods that map the long prompt, typically encoded by a language model, into the effective context window or original text-embedding space of the pre-trained model. There, the information bottleneck sacrifices the very details that make long prompts compelling.

These limitations reveal an open question: how can we utilize a pre-trained model's existing knowledge of short prompts to render long, intricate paragraphs, preserving their many details while remaining robust as prompts grow longer than those seen during training?

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a wide range of natural language tasks, driven in part by advances in transformer-based architectures. While much effort has been devoted to understanding attention mechanisms and token-wise interactions, the role of feed-forward networks (FFNs), and particularly of their nonlinear components, remains underexplored, even though FFNs dominate both the parameter budget and the computational footprint of transformer-based models.

Despite their apparent simplicity, FFNs perform high-dimensional nonlinear transformations that regulate information flow by reorganizing, compressing, and propagating the information extracted by attention modules across layers. Understanding how these transformations behave, how they evolve across depth and over the course of training, and how they interact with architectural design choices (for example normalization or the choice of activation function) and with the choice of optimizer remains a fundamental open question; in practice, such design choices are still largely made by trial and error.

One challenge in interpreting FFNs is the absence of systematic and efficient tools for characterizing how latent representations are structured and transformed by nonlinear activations. FFN transformations unfold in a high-dimensional latent space that is far less accessible to direct visualization and probing than multi-head attention. Prior work has used attention maps to study the input-contextualization effect of FFNs, and has characterized FFN geometry through piecewise-affine spline partitions. Neither lens shows what the nonlinearity does to the overall geometry of the latent representation, for instance how much of the available high-dimensional latent space is actually used before and after the activation, or how this changes from layer to layer and during training.

This raises several questions. What does the FFN nonlinearity do to the structure of the latent representation it receives, and how does this vary across layers and over training? How do architectural and optimizer choices shape this behavior? Can these properties be measured efficiently enough to be tracked continuously while training large models, in a way that remains comparable across layers and model configurations? Do the resulting measurements relate to a model's generalization ability, so that they could serve as diagnostics to guide architectural and optimizer choices beyond trial and error? Finally, are these behaviors specific to attention-based transformers, or are they a more general property of deep feed-forward layers?

Human-object interaction (HOI) detection aims to localize humans and objects in an image and to recognize the interactions between them. It provides a fine-grained understanding of human activities, which is crucial for downstream applications such as robotic manipulation, image captioning and autonomous driving. Despite recent progress, HOI detection remains challenging because of the large combinatorial space of human-object pairs and the need for fine-grained visual understanding. Moreover, real-world applications often require recognizing human-object interactions that do not appear in the training set, which leads to the task of zero-shot HOI detection. Conventional HOI detectors fail to generalize to such unseen interactions, and early attempts that disentangle object and verb features for compositional generalization cannot handle unseen objects or unseen verbs.

To address zero-shot HOI detection, recent works exploit vision-language models such as CLIP to transfer semantic knowledge from language to HOI detection. Typically, they use text embeddings of interaction descriptions, e.g., "A person is holding a cup", to construct classifiers for unseen interactions. While effective to some extent, these methods face limitations. First, CLIP features lack the fine-grained representational capacity required to distinguish visually similar interactions, so methods have to incorporate detector features to obtain fine-grained representations of instances. Second, their core mechanism, aligning visual and text features, operates only on categories observed during training, which restricts generalization to unseen interactions.

At the same time, progress in open-vocabulary object detection provides a sufficient solution for localizing unseen objects, so interaction recognition has become the main bottleneck. Yet most existing methods, including two-stage methods, couple interaction recognition with a specific object detector: they rely on detector features or on relations between detected objects to give vision-language features fine-grained representational capacity, and they struggle to balance fine-grained detector features with generalized vision-language features. As a result, interaction recognition and detection cannot be improved independently, and the detector cannot be changed without retraining.

Effective interaction recognition therefore requires representations that are both fine-grained and broadly generalizable. This raises the following questions. How can the interactions of a given human-object pair, including interactions never observed during training, be recognized with such representations rather than through alignment with static text embeddings fitted to the seen categories, given that recognition is multi-label because one pair can be engaged in several interactions at once? Can interaction recognition be made independent of any particular object detector, so that it works with the boxes produced by any detector without retraining, stays reliable when those boxes are imperfect, and remains computationally tractable given the many human-object pairs and candidate interactions in an image?

TITLE: composable hoi detection with adapter modules
PROPOSAL: Design a two-stage HOI detection framework where the first stage uses an object detection backbone to generate region proposals for humans and objects, and the second stage uses an adapter-based mechanism to adapt the features of the region proposals to accommodate interactions. Specifically, we use a set of learnable adapter modules to adjust the feature embeddings of the objects and humans to better capture the characteristics of their interactions. We will use the Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) dataset and string manipulation or patient data to get ground truth labels of human-object interactions. The evaluation metric will be standard mean Average Precision (mAP) with precision and recall at each interact type. Controls include a standard object detection backbone with no interaction adaptation, a single-stage HOI detector as a baseline, and an ablation study of the adapter modules. We will compare our method to previous HOI detection methods, such as Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) for HOI detection and action-tubelets. COST: 100 GPU hours. PREDICTION: Expected result: mAP 3-5% improvement over baseline methods; could fail due to potential overfitting to adaptation modules.

CONTROLS: baseline object detector, baseline HOI detector, ablation study of adapter modules, previous HOI detection methods like GCNs, action-tubelets. Run an ablation that removes the proposed component while keeping everything else fixed, over five random seeds.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: seps (structured encoder for pair separation)
PROPOSAL: Design a structured encoder for pair separation (SEPS) module to enhance the interaction representation by considering both spatial and semantic relations between humans and objects. SEPS takes the region proposals from the object detection backbone as input and outputs a structured feature representation of the human-object pair. We will use SEPS as a plug-and-play module in the first-stage object detection and second-stage HOI detection to refine the interaction representation. We will use second-hand computing from the HOIV5D pre-trained weights to assess our literature with same-action-scene target evaluation.
